papers.abstract: Camera-controlled video generation re-renders a video along a target camera trajectory, yet moving the camera around an object, the most natural way to change the viewpoint of an object-centric scene, remains difficult. Existing methods condition either on camera parameters, which are scale-ambiguous in monocular video, or on explicit geometry such as warped point clouds or depth, which breaks down under large viewpoint changes. We present AnyCam, a method that represents the camera with an anchor object in the scene: we reconstruct it in 3D and render it along the target trajectory, a camera signal that is scale-aware, view-complete and easy to specify relative to the object. A video diffusion model transfers the content and dynamics of the source video to the new viewpoint. Its H-Concat layout aligns source and target frames in time, so the model can be distilled into AnyCam-AR, a streaming few-step generator for on-the-fly camera control. Both models are trained on paired videos with pixel-aligned anchor renderings from multi-camera videos and static-scene captures. Experiments on diverse datasets and trajectories show that AnyCam performs favorably against camera-controlled video generation and 3D reconstruction methods in camera control and visual quality.
authors: Weijie Lyu, Zhixin Shu, Yuntian Ke, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of changing viewpoints around objects, where camera parameters are scale-ambiguous and explicit geometry can fail under large viewpoint changes.
Reconstructs an anchor object in 3D and renders it along a target trajectory to represent the camera relative to the scene.
Uses a video diffusion model with H-Concat temporal alignment to transfer source-video content and dynamics to the new viewpoint.
Introduces AnyCam-AR, a streaming few-step generator for on-the-fly camera control.
Experiments across diverse datasets and trajectories show favorable camera control and visual quality compared with existing camera-controlled generation and 3D reconstruction methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of AnyCam. (a) The user selects an anchor object in the source video. SAM 2 [37] tracks it to give the source camera representation (the anchor cut-out), and SAM 3D [8] reconstructs it; the reconstruction is aligned to the source cameras and rendered along the target trajectory to give the target camera representation. The noisy target latent and the source latent are concatenated along the height (H-Concat), each half receives its camera representation through channel concatenation, and the diffusion transformer denoises the target half, which the VAE decodes into the target video. (b) The numbers under the tokens are their RoPE positions (t, h), with the role ID as a third entry in the fourth layout. The grids mark which source frames each target frame attends to. Frame concatenation [1, 7, 28] places the whole source after the target, so the first target frame needs the complete source video and therefore the generation cannot stream. Channel concatenation [15] merges the two frames into one token, which loses information and lowers fidelity to the source video [1]. Frame interleaving [52] doubles the length of the temporal axis. A shared position with a role phase [49] needs an additional positional encoding to tell the two streams apart. Our H-Concat keeps the source and target as separate tokens at the same temporal index and offsets the source in height, so the base model is used without new parameters or a custom attention mask.

Figure 10. Video-to-video comparison on CO3D. Each case takes two rows with the source frame (Input), the ground-truth frame and the frame of every method at the same time. 3DGS [20] is optimized per scene on the 81 source frames. AnyCam-AR, HY-WorldPlay [41] and InSpatio-World [40] are autoregressive models. On the sides of the objects that the source video does not show, AnyCam and AnyCam-AR match the ground truth, while 3DGS and DepthDirector [7] break down and most other baselines show the object from a wrong angle or lose it. For the television (bottom), ReDirector [30] and DepthDirector show only the floor and HY-WorldPlay shows its back.

Figure 6. Visual comparison on DAVIS. AnyCam follows every trajectory and keeps the scene intact, since the anchor rendering fixes the scale of the motion relative to the anchor and covers it from every side. Methods that warp estimated geometry show holes and stretched content at new viewpoints: TrajectoryCrafter [56] tears the airplane apart during rotation (rows 1 and 2), GEN3C [39] leaves stripes (row 2), and DepthDirector [7] breaks down under zoom-in and rise (rows 3 to 6). Methods conditioned on camera parameters guess the scale of the motion: ReCamMaster [1] loses the airplane after the orbit (row 2), Wan-Fun-Cam [44] zooms far past the train into the tree (row 4), ReDirector [30] and Wan-Fun-Cam collapse into noise under large orbit and rise (rows 2 and 6).

Figure 11. Single-image comparison on CO3D. Each block shows one case with the input image (Input), the ground-truth frame and the frame generated by each method of Tab. 3 from the same target camera. The 3D reconstruction methods render only the object and often distort its shape, e.g., LGM [42] for three of the four objects and TRELLIS [48] for the handbag and the bench. Most video generation baselines move to an incorrect viewpoint. GEN3C [39], TrajectoryCrafter [56], ReDirector [30] and Wan-Fun-Cam [44] lose the banana (top right). GEN3C, TrajectoryCrafter, DepthDirector [7], ReCamMaster [1] and ReDirector shift the sandwich (bottom right) to the right. AnyCam and AnyCam-AR match the viewpoint and the appearance of the ground truth.
Figure 21. Anchor selection prompt. System prompt given to Qwen3-VL-32B together with 8 frames of the video.

Figure 8. Long-video comparison on CO3D (left) and RealEstate10K (right). The anchor rendering gives every chunk a reference to the object, so AnyCam-AR stays registered to the scene over hundreds of frames. The baselines drift as their errors accumulate over the chunks: both lose the cellphone (left, rows 5, 6), and both turn away from the house (right, rows 1, 2) and the deck (right, rows 5, 6).

Figure 7. Single-image to video comparison on Mip-NeRF 360. Since the anchor rendering is object-relative and view-complete, AnyCam always reaches the target viewpoints. Wan-Fun-Cam [44] and ReCamMaster [1] are conditioned on camera parameters, whose scale a single photo cannot determine, and barely move away from the input view (rows 1 to 3). GEN3C [39], TrajectoryCrafter [56] and DepthDirector [7] warp a depth map that covers only the visible surface, which leaves distorted or missing content (rows 1 to 3).

Figure 4. Anchor rendering as a camera signal only. The anchor (center console) is poorly reconstructed with no texture (column 3), compared with its cut-out in the source video (column 2). AnyCam still recovers the appearance of the console and the cabin from the source video and controls the camera movement correctly, showing that the rendering only provides a camera signal and the model is robust to poor reconstructions.

Figure 12. Additional visual comparison on DAVIS (same layout as Fig. 6). The camera zooms out from the swing (rows 1 and 2) and rises by 60◦ over the display shelf, the skate bowl and the railway crossing (rows 3 to 8). AnyCam shows the whole swing frame after the zoom-out and looks down on the other three scenes. DepthDirector [7] breaks apart on the swing (rows 1 and 2) and the crossing (rows 7 and 8) and turns toward the sky above the skate bowl (rows 5 and 6). Wan-Fun-Cam [44] moves closer to the swing instead of away from it (rows 1 and 2), stays at the height of the input at the shelf (rows 3 and 4) and turns into noise on the skate bowl and the crossing (rows 6 and 8).

Figure 13. Comparison with the Plücker-ray models. Wan-Fun-Cam† and Wan-Fun-Cam-AR† are trained on our data with our recipe and receive the camera as Plücker rays instead of the anchor rendering. Top: DAVIS [32, 34] with a 60◦ rise, AnyCam and Wan-Fun-Cam†; the numbers on the input frames give the frame index. Middle: a 333-frame CO3D [38] video (166 frames out and back) generated from an 81-frame source video; bottom: a 165-frame RealEstate10K [63] video generated from a single image; AnyCam-AR and Wan-Fun-CamAR†; the labels on the ground-truth frames give the frame index and the video length. Wan-Fun-Cam† distorts the street in the last frames of the rise. Wan-Fun-Cam-AR† drifts off the bench, which the frame border cuts off from frame 94 on. On RealEstate10K, it moves into the armchair instead of toward the coffee table. AnyCam and AnyCam-AR follow the target views.

Figure 15. Failure case: small anchors. When the anchor covers only about 1% of the frame, its rendering gives little information about the rotation of the camera. For the agave plant (row 1, 0.7% of the frame), the output camera barely moves, and for the garden stool (row 2, 1.2%) it turns much less than the target orbit. Both rows show AnyCam.

Figure 2. Camera representations. Yellow represents the input camera. (a) Camera parameters are scale-ambiguous: a small object near the input camera and a large object farther away give the same input image, but the same target camera parameters (blue and red camera) see them at a different size, position and angle (blue and red boxes), so the target view is not determined. (b) A point cloud or depth warp of the input image only covers the surface seen from the input camera. Under a large viewpoint change, views are often heavily distorted (red box). The points in the target view sometimes come from the inside of the object or from the back of the image (blue box). The renderings are wrong and mislead the subsequent video generation. (c) Our anchor rendering uses the complete reconstructed object, so target cameras at any angle (green) see the whole anchor with the correct size and pose.
Figure 5. Training samples. Top: MultiCamVideo [1], a dynamic scene captured by two synchronized cameras. Bottom: DL3DV [24], two clips of a static capture.

Figure 9. CO3D target trajectories of the three difficulty levels for one sequence (hydrant), seen from above. Positions are normalized by the median radius of the source cameras. The target camera moves from source frame 0 to the first real target camera (dotted) and then follows real CO3D cameras, with ground truth at the dots.

Figure 14. Moving and deforming anchors. The anchor need not be static or rigid: a swimming swan (DAVIS [32, 34], row 1), a walking dinosaur (row 2), and a person from the DyCheck dataset [9] (bottom left: holding a teddy bear; bottom right: sitting in a chair). The condition renders the anchor reconstructed from one frame, while the generated video keeps the motion of the source, e.g., the swimming swan, the walking legs, and the moving hands and arms. Row 2 shows AnyCam-AR; all other examples show AnyCam.

Figure 16. Different anchors in the same video. For each source video, the user picks two or three objects as anchors and a target trajectory around each of them. The tags above each example name the anchors and their trajectories. Each anchor has its own trajectory, so the rows show camera control through different objects of one video, not one camera applied to several anchors. Each condition renders only its anchor. The numbers on the source frames give the frame index. All outputs are from AnyCam. In the first video, the camera pushes in toward the mirrorless camera or the instant camera on the table, or pulls back and rises over the armchair. In the second video, it orbits around the food truck toward its front or pushes in to the sandwich board.

Figure 17. Different anchors in the same video (continued). Same setting as Fig. 16. All outputs are from AnyCam. In the gaming room, the output orbits around the gaming chair or moves toward the PC tower. In the second video, it orbits around the carved armchair or rises over the side table.

Figure 18. Different anchors in the same video (continued). Same setting as Fig. 16. All outputs are from AnyCam. The output moves toward the telephone or the perfume bottle while the person keeps moving as in the source. In the studio, it rises over the writing desk or turns toward the stool.

Figure 19. The anchor leaves the frame. The camera moves past anchor A until A leaves the view; starting at the switch frame, the condition renders anchor B, a second object reconstructed from the first source frame, and the camera continues toward it. The numbers on the source frames give the frame index; tags A and B mark the anchor in the condition. All rows show AnyCam. The output keeps moving after A has left and approaches anchor B (the sports car, the red car, the white SUV and the PC tower in rows 1 to 4).

Figure 20. Switching the anchor during a video. The target camera follows one continuous trajectory. The condition renders anchor A up to frame 32 and anchor B from frame 33 (tags A and B), and both anchors are reconstructed from the first source frame. The numbers on the source frames give the frame index. Rows 1 to 3 show AnyCam, row 4 shows AnyCam-AR. After the switch, the output moves toward the side table, the perfume bottle, the bentwood chair and the PC tower.

Table 3. Single-image comparison on CO3D. oPSNR, oSSIM and oLPIPS are computed inside the object mask. AnyCam achieves better reconstruction quality than 3D reconstruction methods (top) and video generation methods (bottom).

Table 6. Video-to-video comparison on CO3D by target difficulty. Easy targets have an arc center within 45◦ of the nearest source camera; medium targets have an arc center at least 90◦ away; and hard targets sweep 150◦ to 200◦ across the unobserved side of the object (34 cases each). IoU compares the anchor tracked in the generated video with the CO3D object mask.
Table 5. Long-video comparison on RealEstate10K. AnyCamAR’s rotation error is less than half that of InSpatio-World [40].

Table 1. Video-to-video comparison on CO3D. IoU compares the anchor tracked in the generated video with the CO3D object mask. AnyCam and AnyCam-AR generate videos more similar to the ground truth and with better visual quality and object consistency. FPS is measured on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU.

Table 2. Video-to-video comparison on DAVIS. AnyCam has the lowest translation error and the best visual quality and consistency; although GEN3C [39] and ReDirector [30] achieve better rotation accuracy, their visual quality suffers.
Table 4. Single-image comparison on Mip-NeRF 360. AnyCam is best on all ground-truth metrics and FID.

Table 8. Long videos on CO3D, all metrics. 30 sequences; the source is an 81-frame clip played forward and backward to the target length, and the target follows the real CO3D cameras around the object for 165 or 249 frames, or for 166 frames and back (333 frames). PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS compare each generated frame with the ground-truth frame of the same camera, and oPSNR, oSSIM and oLPIPS do so inside the object mask. Unseen views are the ground-truth frames whose camera is at least 45◦ in azimuth away from the arc covered by the source clip, i.e. sides of the object the input never shows; the way back is the second half of the 333-frame videos. Anchor IoU compares the anchor tracked in the generated video with the object mask, and Lost is the fraction of frames where the track is lost. Best in bold, second underlined, ranked within each group.

Table 7. Attention fine-tuning versus LoRA. LoRA [16] of rank 32 on the attention and feed-forward layers, trained with a learning rate of 10−4, versus fine-tuning the self-attention layers and the patch embedding with a learning rate of 5 × 10−5. Both are trained on the same data for 10K steps with a batch size of 32. The attention fine-tuning row is AnyCam; the cases and metrics are those of its DAVIS and CO3D comparisons (Tabs. 1 and 2). Better in bold.
Table 9. Streaming cost of AnyCam-AR on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q GPUs, median of 4 DAVIS [32, 34] videos at 832× 480.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for camera-controlled video generation using 3D reconstruction of an anchor object, fitting Video Diffusion and 3D Foundation Models.
papers.title: AnyCam: Anything Can Represent Camera for Video Generation
papers.tldr: AnyCam enables camera-controlled video generation by using a reconstructed 3D anchor object to specify scale-aware, view-complete camera motion.

papers.abstract: We present LuxAvatar, a feed-forward framework for real-time head avatar animation and relighting from a single portrait. To achieve both 3D controllability and complex facial light transport, we factorize avatar synthesis into an animatable 3D intrinsic Gaussian proxy and a causal autoregressive neural shader. This proxy disentangles canonical geometry and reflectance attributes, rapidly rasterizing deformed Gaussians into view- and motion-consistent PBR buffers. Conditioned on these buffers, our neural shader formulates forward rendering as a conditional video diffusion process, bypassing explicit PBR computation to synthesize realistic shading effects under target illumination. We achieve real-time streaming through heterogeneous distillation from a pretrained multi-step bidirectional relighting teacher to a two-step causal autoregressive neural shader, inheriting broad synthetic lighting priors while minimizing conditioning and decoding latency. To further specialize these priors to human heads, we construct a hybrid relighting dataset for domain-specific fine-tuning, capturing authentic facial dynamics and physically grounded light transport. Extensive experiments show that our framework enables 3D-controllable, real-time portrait animation and relighting, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity, motion control, and lighting accuracy.
authors: Yipengjing Sun, Chenyang Wang, Boyao Zhou, Jiapeng Zhu, Ka Leong Cheng, Shengping Zhang
bullets: Factorizes synthesis into an animatable 3D proxy for geometry and reflectance and a neural shader for complex facial light transport.
Renders view- and motion-consistent physically based buffers from deformed Gaussians to condition relighting.
Uses a two-step causal autoregressive shader distilled from a multi-step bidirectional video-diffusion teacher for low-latency streaming.
Fine-tunes on a hybrid relighting dataset designed to capture realistic facial dynamics and physically grounded lighting.
Experiments report improved visual fidelity, motion control, and lighting accuracy over prior methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LuxAvatar. (a) Intrinsic Gaussian Head Proxy: Given a single reference image I , our feed-forward network predicts decoupled geometry and material attributes on a canonical UV manifold. Driven by target FLAME and camera parameters, the canonical Gaussians are deformed and rasterized into 4D-consistent PBR buffers {Ct}. (b) Causal Neural Shader: Conditioned on {Ct}, the reference image, and target scene illumination, our distilled causal neural shader autoregressively streams photorealistic relit video chunks in just two denoising steps, while reusing KV caches across chunks to maintain temporal coherence.

Figure 4. Environment-map relighting comparison. Rows 1–2 show self- and cross-reenactment on VFHQ, while Rows 3–4 show self-reenactment on FaceOLAT and novel-view cross-reenactment on NeRSemble, respectively. The last column displays the relit ground truth for Row 3 and driving frames for other rows. Target illumination is visualized via diffuse (top) and mirror (bottom) spheres.

Figure 3. Hybrid relighting data curation. Three complementary data sources provide (a) intrinsic and relit appearance supervision, (b) real video targets preserving facial details and natural motion, and (c) physically grounded supervision under continuously varying illumination.

Figure 5. Background harmonization comparison. We show cross-reenactment results on (a) VFHQ and (b) NeRSemble, with reference images and target backgrounds shown at the top. The last column displays the driving frames.
Figure 6. Effect of the causal neural shader. On the unseen NeRSemble dataset, our shader synthesizes expression-dependent wrinkles and reduces eyeglass distortion.
Figure 7. Effect of hybrid training data. Top: relighting comparison under the same target lighting. Bottom: head animation under dynamic lighting.
Table 4. Runtime ablation on RTX 5090 D GPUs. (a) SingleGPU causal neural shader ablation. (b) Optimized dual-GPU fullpipeline breakdown.

Table 1. Quantitative comparison on the VFHQ and FaceOLAT test sets. Best results are in bold. FPS is based on each method’s total inference time for a 57-frame clip. †UIKA + Relit-LiVE uses DiffusionRenderer inverse rendering to obtain PBR inputs before relighting. ∗With inference optimization on a single GPU.
Table 2. Training strategy and intrinsic proxy ablations.
Table 3. Long-sequence stability. Evaluated on five sequences of 982–984 frames. FG/BG denote foreground/background.

papers.title: LuxAvatar: Real-Time Relightable Head Avatars via Causal Neural Shading of 3D Intrinsic Proxies
papers.tldr: LuxAvatar enables real-time, controllable head animation and relighting from a single portrait by combining an intrinsic 3D Gaussian proxy with a distilled causal neural shader.

papers.abstract: We present MEMO (a Mesh for Every MOment), a method that reconstructs the geometry of complete dynamic scenes, captured by multiple synchronized cameras, and extracts a mesh at every frame. Existing dynamic Gaussian splatting methods either model appearance alone or target isolated objects segmented by foreground masks, and all of them recover meshes by TSDF fusion or Poisson reconstruction, whose fixed grids limit the detail they can capture. At the core of MEMO is a per-Gaussian motion model inspired by Gaussian processes, which represents each Gaussian's position and rotation over time as a combination of temporal Gaussian kernels. The model keeps every Gaussian a valid surface element throughout the sequence and carries an implicit representation of the dynamic geometry, so a mesh can be derived at any time from a field defined by the Gaussians. Although common in real captures, large and fast motion poses a challenge that dynamic Gaussian splatting methods usually overlook. To account for it, we design a track-based initialization scheme that fits each Gaussian's initial trajectory to point tracks in closed form. We evaluate MEMO on Blender-Moments, a new benchmark of nine animated scenes with ground-truth meshes at every frame, and on two real-world datasets. MEMO reconstructs the most accurate geometry among state-of-the-art methods, and remains competitive in novel-view synthesis and training time. Project page: https://memo-4d.github.io
authors: Roy Or-El, Jeong Joon Park, Ira Kemelmacher-Shlizerman
bullets: Addresses limitations of dynamic Gaussian splatting methods that focus on appearance or isolated objects and derive meshes through detail-limited TSDF/Poisson fusion.
Models each Gaussian’s position and rotation over time using temporal Gaussian kernels inspired by Gaussian processes.
Maintains Gaussians as valid surface elements throughout the sequence, enabling mesh extraction at any frame from an implicit geometry field.
Uses track-based initialization to fit Gaussian trajectories in closed form for large and fast motion.
On Blender-Moments and two real-world datasets, achieves the most accurate geometry among compared methods while remaining competitive in novel-view synthesis and training time.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MEMO. The motion model translates and rotates each Gaussian and its oriented normal (arrows) from the canonical state to time t. Training backpropagates (red) LRGB, LD between the geometric and depth normals Ng and Nd, and LN between Nd and the oriented normals No. Mesh extraction follows Gaussian Wrapping [21]: tetrahedralizing the pivots, evaluating the vacancy field at each pivot (red occupied, blue vacant), and recovering its 0.5 level set with marching tetrahedra.

Figure 5. Meshes of MEMO and the baselines, rendered from novel viewpoints. The top rows show three Blender-Moments scenes beside the ground truth, and the bottom rows show the real scenes Flame salmon and Yoga, with each method’s color render inset and the crop outlined in red. Deformable-3DGS represents the appearance-only methods, as its meshes look the best among them, and the gray dots are Gaussian floaters. MEMO produces clean surfaces and preserves fine details such as facial features and Lego studs, where D-2DGS leaves noise and holes and DG-Mesh oversmooths. D-2DGS fails on Yoga, as its render shows.

Figure 6. Novel views of fast motion on Blender-Moments, Neural 3D Video, and SelfCap. On real scenes, panels crop the moving part, with the full frame inset and the crop outlined in red. MEMO keeps the limbs, hands, and face sharp, where the baselines blur or break them.

Figure 3. Motion model for one coordinate of the position displacement ∆µi(t) of a Gaussian Gi. At a query time t, the prediction is the sum of the Mpos + 2B weighted interior (blue) and boundary (red) kernels.

Figure 4. 200 sampled tracks of Lego from our initialization with a single first-frame anchor, over the first-frame mesh. The fitted trajectories follow the bucket through its full sweep before training begins. Dots are track positions every tenth frame, and curves of the same color are the fitted trajectories.

papers.abstract: A single casual video leaves a moving scene under-determined: a point seen once from each place can slide toward or away from the camera and still match every frame. We constrain the reconstruction with the structure of the motion itself. Building on DynMF, we model a scene's motion as a handful of SE(3) trajectories, each rigid, and let every point follow one of them alone, never a blend. DynMF2 computes this factorization directly from 3D point trajectories, with no rendering, by Expectation-Maximization (EM). Its M-step fits, in closed form, every rigid motion to the points assigned to it, and its E-step reassigns every point to the motion that explains it with the least error. The background is simply one more motion, the camera's, so no masks are needed. Three tools then revise the factorization: requery adds trajectories where the rendering shows parts the tracker missed, merge joins motions that move together, and split separates those that do not. Thus the number of motions follows the scene. Without masks, DynMF2 clearly outperforms the mask-based baselines in view synthesis on iPhone and NVIDIA and in 3D tracking on iPhone. It recovers what masks leave out, from thin parts and details to small movers far in the background. Its motions segment the moving parts of MOVi-F and iTACO scenes competitively, although DynMF2 is never trained to segment. What moves in a scene is not decided in advance: it emerges from the rigid motions themselves.
authors: Agelos Kratimenos, Yile Hua, Kostas Daniilidis
bullets: Addresses the under-determined nature of reconstructing moving scenes from a single casual video.
Models each point as following exactly one SE(3) motion, including the camera motion for the background.
Alternates closed-form rigid-motion fitting with point reassignment based on reconstruction error.
Requery, merge, and split operations adapt the number of motions to missed, shared, or distinct movements.
Outperforms mask-based baselines in view synthesis and 3D tracking, while producing competitive unsupervised motion segmentation.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DynMF2 on Truck. Left: 3D trajectories from a tracker, depth and the cameras, without masks and with no motion yet. Middle: EM minimises the energy of Eq. (3), giving each whole trajectory one rigid motion. Left to right are its iterations, each over all frames. From k-means, which splits the background, the M-step fits every motion at every frame with Eq. (4) and the E-step moves each trajectory to its lowest-error motion with Eq. (5), until no ki changes. Right: the trajectories with their motions over the trained model’s rendered segmentation. The background is the camera’s motion.

Figure 6. Motion segmentation on two MOVi-F scenes (top) and two iTACO clips (bottom): input frame, ground truth (the moving objects in MOVi-F, the moving part in iTACO), Segment Any Motion, Trace Anything, 4RC, Track4World, MoSE3 and the motions of DynMF2, coloured to match the ground truth, with the static scene left uncoloured and unmatched groups in light grey. MoSE3 is concurrent work.

Figure 4. Views of five scenes, held out except for backpack, whose single camera leaves only training views. Columns: ground truth, SoM, MoSca, DynMF2, and the motions of DynMF2, one colour per motion drawn over its rendering.

Figure 3. The three tools on real scenes, shown as rendered motion segmentations with one colour per motion. (a) Requery on Jumping, from left to right: the raised arms belong to the background at first, the rendering error marks them and the new tracks (cyan) land on them, and after the revision the arms get motions of their own. (b) Merge on Truck, before and after: seven pieces of the background become one motion, and the vehicles keep theirs. (c) Split on teddy, before and after: the right leg leaves the motion of the body.

Figure 5. Ablations. Each row changes one part of DynMF2 and shows the change in score. (a) NVIDIA, test mPSNR over seven scenes. (b) MOVi-F, mIoU of the motions, 147 validation scenes. Tools are removed from the last one back. One run per scene.

papers.title: DynMF2: Rigid Motion Factorization by Expectation-Maximization for Monocular 4D Reconstruction and Motion Segmentation
papers.tldr: DynMF2 uses EM to factor monocular 4D point trajectories into independently moving rigid parts, enabling mask-free reconstruction, tracking, and motion segmentation.

papers.abstract: Constructing complete 3D worlds from a single panorama is challenging because large portions of the scene remain unobserved. Existing panoramic-video methods expand spatial coverage through dense sequential generation, but neighboring frames contain substantial redundancy, long trajectories accumulate errors, and independently generated directions may be inconsistent. We present WorldExpand, which formulates single-panorama world expansion as the generation of sparse, complementary, and high-resolution panoramic observations. This representation concentrates the generation budget on informative scene regions and preserves the fine-grained details required for 3D construction. WorldExpand addresses two key challenges: where to observe and how to synthesize. Our Coverage-Guided View Selection identifies informative target locations using scene-adaptive quadrants and warp-based coverage scores, while our Joint Panoramic Diffusion uses Gaussian-splatting-based geometric warps to jointly synthesize four pose-grounded and cross-view-consistent panoramas. A diagnostic-guided global--local attention schedule retains global attention only in sensitive layers, reducing the training and inference costs of high-resolution joint generation. The resulting posed panoramas can be directly fed into an existing reconstruction pipeline to build an explicit 3D representation. Experiments show that WorldExpand recovers content behind occluders and around distant corners, improves both novel-view synthesis and downstream 3D reconstruction metrics across various datasets, and generalizes robustly to diverse in-the-wild scenes. WorldExpand runs significantly faster than the state-of-the-art panoramic-video method while producing higher-resolution observations with stronger cross-view consistency.
authors: Yuyang Yin, Chenjie Cao, Xuhui Zuo, Yuning Gong, Pengfei Wang, Junta Wu, Zhenwei Wang, Yao Zhao, Tengfei Wang, Yunchao Wei, Chunchao Guo
bullets: Targets the challenge of unobserved regions, redundant dense video generation, error accumulation, and inconsistent independently generated views.
Selects informative target locations with scene-adaptive quadrants and warp-based coverage scores.
Jointly synthesizes four pose-grounded panoramas using Gaussian-splatting-based geometric warps and panoramic diffusion.
Uses a diagnostic-guided global–local attention schedule to reduce high-resolution generation costs.
Recovers occluded and distant-corner content, improves novel-view synthesis and 3D reconstruction, and runs faster than a state-of-the-art panoramic-video method.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of WorldExpand. Given one panorama, we select four viewpoints that expose complementary unseen regions, jointly synthesize their panoramic observations with selective crossview communication, and align multi-view depths to reconstruct an expanded Gaussian scene.

papers.abstract: Scene rearrangement is an essential task for 3D content creation applications, requiring generation of diverse, aesthetic and functional scene rearrangements. We present SceneDesigner3D, an agentic evolutionary search method for 3D indoor scene rearrangement that systematically explores the design space of 3D scenes and generates multiple solutions according to common interior design principles. Given an input scene and a text prompt, SceneDesigner3D represents the rearrangement as an editable program and evolves a population of candidate layouts. Starting from distinct design ideas, a VLM agent mutates the programs by refining promising candidates, exploring new rearrangement strategies or redesigning from scratch, while verifying the layouts for physical validity. Proposals are scored by a VLM judge for adherence to the input prompt and satisfaction of design principles such as balance, zoning and emphasis, as well as numerically computed principles such as circulation and clutter. An archive of top-performing, structurally varied candidates further increases diversity of rearrangements. Experiments on the SAGE-10k and SceneSmith datasets show that SceneDesigner3D improves prompt adherence and computed design principle scores over baselines by up to 5.1% and 15.2%, respectively. Code will be made publicly available.
bullets: Represents scene rearrangements as editable programs and evolves populations of candidate layouts.
A VLM agent mutates candidates through refinement, exploration, or redesign from scratch, with physical-validity checks.
A VLM judge scores prompt adherence and qualitative principles, while numerical metrics assess circulation and clutter.
An archive preserves high-performing, structurally diverse solutions.
Experiments on SAGE-10k and SceneSmith report up to 5.1% better prompt adherence and 15.2% better computed design-principle scores than baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. Given an input 3D scene and a text prompt, SceneDesigner3D evolves a population of programs that rearrange its objects. The prompt is decomposed into requirements, design seeds are initialized and objects are described by a VLM. An agentic evolutionary search explores the design space through various strategies (colored paths: object movement relative to parent). Each candidate is judged by a VLM against its parent on the prompt requirements and design principles, and combined with numerically computed principles into its fitness. An archive keeps diverse candidates as inspiration for future iterations, giving diverse layouts that follow the prompt and design principles.

Figure 4. Mean prompt adherence (PA, top) and design principles (DP, bottom) scores of each method under the two VLM judges, Qwen3VL and Gemma 4, on SAGE, SAGE-Opus and SceneSmith. Both VLMs follow the same trend across methods; τ is the Kendall rank correlation between their method rankings.

papers.abstract: Collaborative reconstruction with consumer phones promises faster and more complete indoor maps. However, heterogeneous devices introduce degraded observations and unreliable cross-device associations, so a single poor contributor or incorrect match can corrupt the shared Gaussian map. To address this, we propose \textbf{CADENCE}, a collaborative Gaussian simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) system that separates finding cross-device matches from deciding whether and how peer observations update the map. To find matches, a sensor-grounded regional memory summarizes committed observations and ranks candidate peer regions using appearance, relative pose, gravity, barometric altitude, and observation quality. Deterministic geometric verification and optional physical checks then decide which of the proposed matches are accepted. Once a match is accepted, separate cue-based confidences control how its observations contribute to pose constraints, geometry, appearance, and memory. As a result, useful depth can still contribute even when color is unreliable. Throughout this process, local tracking remains isolated from mapping, verification, and networking. We evaluate CADENCE on eight Matterport3D houses that were not used to train the memory. On these houses, regional memory achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of $0.95$ to $0.97$ and thus outperforms appearance retrieval, while verification keeps false-link rates below $0.5\,\%$. Furthermore, soft confidence weighting reduces the mean receiver peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) loss from $2.66$ to $1.05$\,dB across eight degradations while retaining useful peer depth. Finally, using inertial and platform motion, CADENCE tracks all twelve held-out iPhone scans with a mean absolute trajectory error of $6.98$\,cm, and its refined maps achieve better average rendering quality than the baselines.
authors: Reshad Ul Karim, Abrar Samin, Md Rashad Al Hasan Rony
bullets: Targets indoor collaborative reconstruction failures caused by heterogeneous sensors, poor observations, and incorrect cross-device associations.
Uses regional memory with appearance, relative pose, gravity, barometric altitude, and observation quality to rank peer-region matches.
Applies deterministic geometric verification and optional physical checks before accepting matches, while isolating local tracking from mapping and networking.
Cue-specific soft confidence weights let reliable depth contribute even when color is degraded.

On eight held-out Matterport3D houses, memory reached 0.95–0.97 AUROC, verification kept false-link rates below 0.5%, and confidence weighting reduced mean PSNR loss from 2.66 to 1.05 dB; all twelve held-out iPhone scans were tracked with 6.98 cm mean absolute trajectory error.

papers.abstract: A first-person (ego) image reveals what a camera sees, but not who or what carries it. Given a synchronized third-person (exo) image, camera wearer identification asks who is ego: which candidate carries the ego camera? We extend this task beyond humans to robots, vehicles, animals, and drones, and broaden its spatial scope (where is ego) from selecting a provided candidate mask to wearer segmentation with absence prediction and mutual camera localization across ego-exo views. We introduce FindEgo-1M, comprising 1.16M real and simulated ego-exo pairs across 12 wearer types, 17 domains, and 111 test settings. Our approach exploits a geometric relation: the ego camera's projection into the exo image, i.e., the epipole, lies on or near its wearer. We introduce EgoRay-ZS, the first method to turn a frozen feed-forward 3D reconstruction model, VGGT-$\Omega$, into a training-free solution for wearer identification and segmentation. Its geometric readout ranks candidate masks or segmentation proposals by angular offset and distance to the ego camera, while the relative pose provides mutual camera directions. We then develop the full EgoRay model through pose-supervised training on FindEgo-1M and label-free test-time adaptation constrained by candidate masks. Without task-specific training, EgoRay-ZS achieves 78.0% identification accuracy on TF2023's original labels, versus 52.9% reported for the dataset-trained PEN. On FindEgo-1M, EgoRay achieves state-of-the-art chance-corrected accuracy of 87.1 and 77.7 on seen and unseen settings. On matched queries, EgoRay also outperforms GPT-6 Astra by 31.6 and 21.3 points on seen and unseen settings, respectively, while running $18\times$ faster. Data, code, and models will be released.
authors: Yifan Jin, Zheng Zhang, Tianwen Qian, Dong Wang, Bo Zhao, Yanwei Fu, Yuqian Fu
bullets: Extends camera-wearer identification from humans to robots, vehicles, animals, and drones, while adding wearer segmentation, absence prediction, and mutual camera localization.
Introduces FindEgo-1M, with 1.16M real and simulated ego–exo image pairs spanning 12 wearer types, 17 domains, and 111 test settings.
EgoRay-ZS uses the ego camera’s projected epipole and a frozen 3D reconstruction model for training-free candidate ranking and segmentation.
The fully developed EgoRay adds pose-supervised training and label-free test-time adaptation constrained by candidate masks.
EgoRay reaches 87.1% and 77.7% chance-corrected accuracy on seen and unseen settings, respectively, and is faster and more accurate than the reported baselines in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Upgrading feed-forward geometry to metric scale with visual-inertial odometry (VIO) raises the question of which correction should align dense feed-forward prediction with sparse metric VIO anchors. Existing methods use either a similarity transformation, which cannot represent depth-dependent distortion, or a projective transformation, which alters pre-calibrated intrinsics. We prove that the transformations compatible with pre-calibrated intrinsics form a ten-dimensional manifold. Beyond Sim(3), this manifold contains three degrees of freedom (DoF) that locate the plane at infinity and leave residuals growing quadratically with depth range after any similarity alignment. These DoF are invisible in the image and can be resolved only by metric depth along viewing rays or by multi-view constraints. To estimate them, we propose ProManO, a probabilistic manifold optimization framework in which every anchor is weighted by its along-ray uncertainty and inlier probability within a single expectation-maximization (EM) procedure. ProManO certifies the similarity synchronization and refines the plane at infinity only where it is observable, which guarantees an objective value no worse than that of the optimal similarity alignment. Experiments on EuRoC, CID-SIMS, Oxford Spires, and KITTI-360 demonstrate that ProManO achieves the highest mean F1 and outperforms Sim(3) alignment on all four datasets. The project page is available at https://h0xg.github.io/ProManO/.
authors: Lingxiang Hu, Zhenjun Zhao, Qi Shao, Naima Ait Oufroukh, Fabien Bonardi, Raymond Ghandour, Shenghai Yuan, Javier Civera, Baoru Huang
bullets: Existing Sim(3) alignment cannot model depth-dependent distortion, while unrestricted projective alignment changes pre-calibrated intrinsics.
The valid intrinsic-preserving transformations form a ten-dimensional manifold with three additional degrees of freedom beyond Sim(3).
ProManO estimates these degrees of freedom using probabilistic manifold optimization and EM, weighting anchors by along-ray uncertainty and inlier probability.
The method refines the plane at infinity only when observable and guarantees an objective no worse than optimal similarity alignment.
Experiments on EuRoC, CID-SIMS, Oxford Spires, and KITTI-360 report the highest mean F1 and improvement over Sim(3) on all four datasets.

papers.abstract: Path-traced rendering shows CT and MR volumes with realistic lighting, but it restarts after every change of view, clipping plane or transfer function (TF), the map from voxel intensity to colour and opacity, which limits the frame rate. Feed-forward Gaussian splatting models such as RenderFM predict the Gaussians directly from the volume instead of fitting them to each scan, and are fast. RenderFM, however, handles only CT, runs its network again after every TF edit, has no clipping operator, and places its Gaussians on a uniform 3-mm grid that blurs organ boundaries and cut faces. We present RenderFM-Next, a feed-forward model that addresses these limits. One network handles both CT and MR. Its Gaussians are predicted once per volume: a new TF needs no pass of this network, and a clipping plane cuts them exactly, using operators from prior work. The model predicts coarse 3-mm Gaussians for the whole volume and refines them to 1.5 mm only where refinement improves the image. A small score head ranks the coarse Gaussians by how much refining them would reduce the rendering error; at render time the user chooses how many are refined, and those next to a clipping plane are always refined, which sharpens cut faces. We build a benchmark of about 2,000 CT and MR scans with path-traced references under clinical presets, TF edits and clipping. Our RenderFM-Next improves over RenderFM retrained on this benchmark by 2.8 dB on CT and 2.4 dB on MR and renders a 1600x1600 view in 4-6 ms. Refinement adds 0.30 / 0.69 dB over the same model trained without it (0.51 / 1.17 dB on cut faces), and refining a learned 10% of the coarse Gaussians matches a random 50% with 2.4x fewer Gaussians. Project page: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/renderfmnext/
authors: Zhongpai Gao, Benjamin Planche, Meng Zheng, Anwesa Choudhuri, Chaoyi Zhou, Terrence Chen, Ziyan Wu
bullets: Addresses RenderFM’s single-modality support, repeated inference after transfer-function edits, lack of clipping, and blurred boundaries from a uniform 3-mm grid.
Predicts coarse Gaussians once per volume, supports both CT and MR, applies new transfer functions without network reruns, and clips splats exactly.
Uses a score head to selectively refine Gaussians from 3 mm to 1.5 mm, prioritizing regions where refinement improves quality and areas near clipping planes.
On a benchmark of about 2,000 CT and MR scans, it improves over retrained RenderFM by 2.8 dB on CT and 2.4 dB on MR, rendering 1600×1600 views in 4–6 ms.
Refining 10% of learned coarse Gaussians matches random refinement of 50% using 2.4× fewer Gaussians; gains are especially strong on cut faces.

papers.abstract: Recent feed-forward approaches mark a paradigm shift in novel view synthesis by eliminating the reliance on per-scene optimization, directly inferring 3D representations from input views. However, their reliance on global scene-token context incurs substantial memory and latency overhead, constraining their ability to handle increasingly dense source-view contexts. Compressing source representations offers an intuitive way to limit this token budget. Prior general-purpose compression methods are not tailored for novel view synthesis, as their fixed, target-agnostic nature fails to adapt evidence allocation to individual target views. To overcome this, we introduce TACC, a target-aware compression module tailored for feed-forward latent NVS. Specifically, TACC organizes each source view into a progressive carrier hierarchy. Driven by source-target geometric relevance, it adaptively retrieves tokens to dynamically allocate exact computational quotas. This selective retrieval directly yields a compact, target-conditioned representation. Extensive experiments on the RE10K demonstrate that under dense input settings, TACC achieves $9.23\times$ and $64\times$ higher Effective FPS than Full Context on LagerNVS and LVSM, respectively. Effective FPS excludes one-time source encoding and Carrier construction.
authors: Yiming Fan, Yijia Guo, Zewen Guo, Liwen Hu, Yuheng Yuan, Yang Li, Zhiwei Li, Xitong Ling, Caihong Yuan, Shengbo Chen, Tiejun Huang, Lei Ma
bullets: Feed-forward NVS methods face memory and latency bottlenecks as source-view context grows.
TACC builds a progressive carrier hierarchy for each source view.
Source-target geometric relevance guides selective token retrieval and target-conditioned compression.

Effective FPS excludes one-time source encoding and carrier construction.

papers.abstract: Artistic mesh generators turn a dense 3D object into an artist mesh: a compact, quad-dominant mesh that is easy to edit. Most of current models are auto-regressive methods which decode a mesh token by token, take tens to hundreds of seconds per mesh. Diffusion- and flow-based generators are much faster, but their meshes still fall short of artist quality. To our knowledge, PostMesh is the first post-training method for a diffusion- or flow-based artist mesh generator, and it needs no expensive artist-made ground truth: the generator is trained on its own samples, scored by a reward computed from the dense input and the output. We propose an artistic mesh reward that keeps the output consistent with the dense input while making the mesh structure into artistic. We also propose a multi-negative flow preference optimisation that transfers the reward to the generator. After a short LoRA post-training, PostMesh is comparable to or better than slow autoregressive generators on most artist-mesh quality metrics and in a blind VLM preference test, at a fraction of their time.
bullets: Targets fast diffusion- and flow-based generators whose meshes lag in artist quality.
Uses self-generated meshes scored by a reward based on the dense input and output, avoiding expensive artist-made ground truth.
Introduces an artistic mesh reward balancing input consistency with artist-friendly mesh structure.
Applies multi-negative flow preference optimisation through short LoRA post-training.
Reports comparable or better quality than slow autoregressive generators on most metrics and in a blind VLM preference test, with much lower generation time.

papers.abstract: Physically based rendering (PBR) material estimation facilitates relighting, material editing, and 3D content creation. As the reflectance of a surface heavily depends on whether it is a metal or a dielectric, producing any map that determines albedo involves a decision on metalness, which we call the "intended metalness" of the map. Rendering maps with mismatched intended metalness yields physically implausible or misinterpreted materials. The metallic--roughness workflow makes metalness explicit and thus encourages base color to match it, but does not enforce this match, especially for automated methods directly predicting each map. Therefore, we propose ReMeDi, which enforces the match through two components. First, we reparameterize base color as a metalness-weighted blend of its two variants, estimated under the all-metal and all-dielectric hypothesis, respectively. Second, as available supervision cannot teach a single network both hypotheses at every pixel, we restrict each of two separate networks to one hypothesis, so that each variant is ensured to follow its hypothesis. Besides enforcing the match, this also improves each estimated material map. Experiments show that ReMeDi outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both material accuracy and relighting fidelity.
authors: Fan Fei, Xin Huang, Yixin Zhu, Jiawei Lu, Xin Yang, Jinglin Liang, Ruining Tang, Yifei Feng, Boxin Shi, Chunchao Guo
bullets: Addresses physically implausible or misinterpreted materials caused by mismatched intended metalness in automated map prediction.
Reparameterizes base color as a metalness-weighted blend of all-metal and all-dielectric variants.
Uses two separate networks, each dedicated to one material hypothesis, because supervision cannot cover both hypotheses in one network.
Experiments report better material accuracy and relighting fidelity than state-of-the-art methods.
Scope: performance depends on estimating and combining the two metalness-specific material variants.

papers.abstract: Relighting reconstructed 3D scenes remains challenging due to the complex nature of light transport: slow or approximate visual feedback restricts the editor's ability to fine-tune the results to satisfaction. We present a hybrid relighting approach that enables interactive, high-fidelity updates of direct and indirect indoor illumination without per-edit optimization. Our approach permits the editor to make a wide range of relighting edits at room-scale, with near-instant feedback. Our key insight is to precompute geometric light exchange rather than illumination responses, retaining an inexpensive transport solve that accommodates changes in emission and surface reflectance. We evaluate direct illumination on reconstructed 2D Gaussians using visibility-aware sampling of one-sided emitters, while propagating diffuse interreflection through sparse radiosity on a triangle proxy. A sparse projection fitted through Gaussian alpha compositing transfers the proxy solution to the reconstruction. Our formulation further supports fast fixture transformations and emitter insertion by recomputing light source injection. Across eight relighting conditions of our synthetic test suite, our sub-second edits improve relighting fidelity over prior path-traced editing by an average of 5\,dB PSNR, while reducing editing latency by up to three orders of magnitude. Qualitative results further demonstrate realistic, interactive relighting of real-world captures.
authors: Noah Rothenberger, Dor Verbin, Serge Belongie, Bernhard Kerbl
bullets: Supports room-scale edits to direct and indirect indoor illumination with near-instant feedback.
Precomputes geometric light exchange while retaining an inexpensive transport solve for changing emission and reflectance.
Combines visibility-aware direct lighting on 2D Gaussians with sparse radiosity on a triangle proxy, then projects results back to the reconstruction.
Handles fast fixture transformations and emitter insertion through recomputed light-source injection.

Across eight synthetic conditions, improves fidelity by 5 dB PSNR on average and reduces latency by up to three orders of magnitude versus prior path-traced editing; real-world captures show qualitative realism.

papers.abstract: Real cameras are not pinholes, yet most dynamic Gaussian splatting assumes they are. Footage is therefore undistorted first, losing field of view or detail, especially with wide-angle and fisheye cameras. Static Gaussian splatting has largely solved this with ray-based rendering, which suits any camera. Native 4D Gaussians, which model motion in space-time, cannot use it directly: each Gaussian's orientation and size cannot be recovered reliably from its covariance. We present AnyCam4D, which trains native 4D Gaussians on original footage by ray-based rasterization, preserving field of view and resolution at about the per-step cost of standard projection. Our key contribution is a numerically stable way to obtain orientation and size: we condition a square root of the 4D covariance. Trained models render through other cameras, with rolling shutter, depth of field or chromatic aberration. With a synthetic 170-degree fisheye camera, training on original images improves peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) by 3.0-8.1 dB. On real footage, AnyCam4D has lower perceptual error than the standard projection adapted to each camera, at comparable PSNR and without camera-specific derivations. With the synthetic camera rotated 60-80 degrees away from the capture rig's view, it leads by 6.2 dB against ground truth.
authors: Sascha Kirch, Rafael Pag\'es, Jan Ond\v{r}ej, Clara P\'erez-Molina, Sergio Martin
bullets: Addresses distortion from undistorting wide-angle and fisheye footage, which can reduce field of view and detail.
Uses ray-based rasterization for native 4D Gaussians at roughly the per-step cost of standard projection.
Stabilizes Gaussian orientation and size estimation by conditioning a square root of the 4D covariance.
Supports rendering through cameras with rolling shutter, depth of field, and chromatic aberration.
Improves synthetic 170° fisheye PSNR by 3.0–8.1 dB and achieves lower perceptual error on real footage; gains reach 6.2 dB for substantially shifted viewpoints.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal self-supervised learning for paired side-scan sonar and underwater optical imagery is a promising direction for benthic habitat understanding, but it remains underexplored because existing methods do not fully exploit the one-to-many correspondences and geographic metadata available in real opti-acoustic surveys. This limits the ability to learn representations that are both semantically meaningful and geometrically consistent from abundant unlabeled marine data. To address this problem, we present GeoCAM, a geography-guided framework that learns a shared embedding space for sonar tiles and their associated optical views without semantic annotations. GeoCAM achieves its goal by combining three components: (i) a Set Attention Aggregator that adaptively summarizes multiple optical observations into a single tile-level representation; (ii) a geometry-weighted InfoNCE objective that converts GPS-derived footprint overlap into soft positive supervision; and (iii) an optional cross-modal masked reconstruction branch that encourages physically grounded cross-modal alignment. Experiments on the BenthiCat SSS-CAM dataset show that GeoCAM can be effectively exploited to learn which sonar and camera samples describe the same seabed patch, improving cross-modal retrieval and alignment over strong contrastive baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/FadiZidiDz/GeoCAM.
authors: Fadi Abdeladhim Zidi, Andrea De Salve, Giuseppe Celeste, Abdellah Zakaria Sellam, Paolo Spagnolo, Cosimo Distante

Aggregates multiple optical views with a Set Attention Aggregator.
Uses GPS footprint overlap as soft positive supervision in a geometry-weighted InfoNCE loss.
Optionally adds cross-modal masked reconstruction for physically grounded alignment.
On BenthiCat SSS-CAM, improves cross-modal retrieval and alignment over contrastive baselines.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting have enabled efficient underwater reconstruction, but sparse observations, light attenuation, and backscatter still leave scene regions underconstrained and cause novel-view artifacts. We present OceanFix, a reference-guided framework for sparse-view underwater 3D reconstruction that combines diffusion-based view repair with Gaussian scene refinement. Our repair model follows a two-stage training strategy that separates underwater appearance adaptation from geometric refinement. The first stage learns underwater appearance from reference observations and estimated medium features. The second uses camera poses and reference depth to align reference features, with relative-depth supervision guiding structural repair without requiring target-view depth at inference. We further propose medium-aware distillation that transfers repaired views into the 3D scene according to geometric repair demand and channel-specific optical observability. Through iterative rendering, repair, and distillation, OceanFix refines underconstrained regions while retaining supervision from the observed views. Experiments on underwater datasets demonstrate that OceanFix improves rendering quality in sparse-view 3D reconstruction, reducing visible artifacts and recovering finer scene details.
authors: Gen Li, Maoxin Chen, Yao Xiao, Xinyang Li, Yu Pan
bullets: Addresses underconstrained regions and artifacts caused by sparse observations, light attenuation, and backscatter.
Combines diffusion-based view repair with Gaussian scene refinement in an iterative render–repair–distill pipeline.
Uses two-stage training to adapt underwater appearance and then enforce geometric structure from camera poses and reference depth.
Applies medium-aware distillation based on geometric repair needs and channel-specific optical observability.
Experiments on underwater datasets show improved rendering quality, fewer visible artifacts, and finer recovered details.

papers.abstract: Recent 3D generative models can produce high-quality meshes with complex structures and fine geometric details, with broad applications in games, film, and digital design. However, high-quality generation typically relies on long multi-step sampling processes that repeatedly evaluate large networks, leading to long inference times. At the same time, reference-driven tasks such as game-asset reconstruction and product digitization demand close correspondence to the input image: generated geometry must faithfully reconstruct the specific reference object. Acceleration must therefore reduce sampling computation while preserving the model's ability to reconstruct that object. To enable fast and faithful 3D generation, we introduce Spe3DUp, a coarse-to-fine framework based on Faithful Trajectory Distillation (FTD). FTD directly supervises few-step students with the teacher's input-conditioned denoising trajectories to preserve its generation behavior. We apply FTD separately to coarse geometry generation and geometric refinement, compressing both sampling processes while maintaining correspondence to the reference input. We further accelerate the complete mesh-generation pipeline with efficient geometry decoding and parallel remeshing. Experiments show that Spe3DUp maintains geometric quality and input correspondence close to those of the teacher, accelerates the coarse and refinement DiTs by 10.0x and 19.9x, respectively, and achieves a 7.7x end-to-end speedup over the original teacher pipeline.
authors: Liangchao Xu, Jiaye Fu, Youtian Lin, Feihu Zhang, Yao Yao
bullets: Targets the slow, multi-step sampling required by high-quality 3D generation.
Introduces Faithful Trajectory Distillation (FTD), which trains few-step students using input-conditioned teacher denoising trajectories.
Applies FTD separately to coarse geometry generation and geometric refinement in a coarse-to-fine framework.
Further accelerates mesh decoding and remeshing through efficient decoding and parallel processing.
Reports 10.0× and 19.9× speedups for coarse and refinement DiTs, and 7.7× end-to-end acceleration while maintaining quality and input correspondence.

papers.abstract: In 2D-3D localization, a camera estimates its pose by matching an image to a 3D map. A camera held in a hand or mounted on a robot can often choose its viewpoint before it takes the image. In this work, we ask whether an image detectability field is a useful viewpoint utility when the planner reads only the geometry of the map. The field can be queried at any 3D point near a surface. From the local geometry around the point, it predicts how likely a 2D image detector is to fire at the projection of the point. We use the trained field as it is, without fine-tuning it for view selection. A fixed SuperPoint and EPnP-RANSAC localizer then estimates the pose from the chosen view. We answer in two settings, each with a test registered before the runs. On synthetic ShapeNet objects with sparse point maps, summing the field over the visible landmarks beats counting them by +2.0 points of localization success rate (object-clustered 95% interval [+0.7, +3.2]). It also beats summing Harris-3D ranks by +2.2 [+0.8, +3.5]. On real indoor scenes from SceneFun3D, our adaptation of the learned view scorer LWL falls below counting on the test rooms. We therefore add the field to a learned per-landmark planner. On the test rooms with sparse maps whose landmarks the field also selects, the planner with the field beats the same planner without it by +1.8 points. It beats the planner with Harris-3D or curvature in its place by +1.0 and +0.8 points. All three room-clustered intervals lie above zero. In both settings, the field helps in sparse maps and is on par with Harris-3D in dense maps.
authors: Han Sun, Jun Li, Christy Jie Liang
bullets: The goal is to choose camera viewpoints using only map geometry before capturing an image.
A learned field predicts how likely local 3D geometry is to produce detectable 2D features, and is queried over visible landmarks.
With fixed SuperPoint and EPnP-RANSAC localization, field-based scoring improves localization success over landmark counting and Harris-3D on synthetic sparse maps.
In real indoor scenes, the field performs poorly as a standalone scorer but improves a learned per-landmark planner over versions without the field, Harris-3D, or curvature.
Benefits are observed in sparse maps; performance is on par with Harris-3D in dense maps.

papers.abstract: Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.
authors: Shenxing Wei, Jinxi Li, Zihui Zhang, Ajay Kumar, Wei Wang, Bo Yang
bullets: Uses a pretrained pointmap model to extract explicit geometric priors without requiring camera poses.
Selects relevant reference views with query-centric surfel voting.
Predicts coarse continuous surfaces through cross-attention between query rays and reference features.
Refines high-frequency details and analytical normals using local raylet-based 3D feature aggregation.
Trained on 9 diverse datasets and reports strong zero-shot generalization across 6 unseen datasets, outperforming prior methods in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.

papers.abstract: The 3D points kept in a map decide whether a camera can be localized against it, and this choice matters more as the map becomes sparser. Existing 3D keypoint detectors usually define saliency by semantics, repeatability, reconstruction or descriptor matchability. None of these definitions asks whether a point will actually be detected in an image, and as a result most of the points they select are not detected again in images. In this paper, we define 3D saliency as image detectability: the response of a 2D interest-point detector at a surface point, aggregated over all views in which the point is visible. We propose DetField, a continuous field over 3D space that takes a point cloud as input and predicts detectability at any location around it. The supervision is the response of a 2D detector, back-projected from images onto the point cloud. Multi-scale curvature invariants are passed to the decoder at every query point, bypassing the voxel pooling of the encoder. In a localization benchmark that isolates the choice of 3D points, DetField outperforms Harris-3D and five learned 3D keypoint methods on objects and on real indoor scenes. On unseen rooms, it improves localization success by 7.4 points over Harris-3D, the strongest baseline. On objects, it also leads under a 2D detector not used in training. On sparse maps, it stays ahead of Harris-3D on both objects and real scenes.
authors: Han Sun, Jun Li, Christy Jie Liang
bullets: Motivation: Existing 3D keypoint criteria do not directly measure whether points will be detected again in images, especially in sparse maps.
Method: Define 3D saliency as a surface point’s 2D interest-detector response aggregated across visible views, and supervise predictions by back-projecting these responses onto the point cloud.
Architecture: A continuous 3D field predicts detectability at arbitrary locations, using multi-scale curvature invariants at query points to avoid voxel-pooling information loss.
Results: DetField outperforms Harris-3D and five learned 3D keypoint methods on objects and real indoor scenes; on unseen rooms, it improves localization success by 7.4 points over Harris-3D.
Scope: The method also leads with an unseen 2D detector on objects and remains ahead of Harris-3D on sparse maps.

papers.abstract: Generating coherent and explorable 3D worlds from scattered images with little or no visual overlap is a fundamental and long-standing challenge in computer vision, which existing geometry-aware methods fail to address. Meanwhile, existing image- and video-based methods may generate unseen regions but produce inconsistent geometry across views. To bridge this gap, we present WorldBridge, a framework for coherent and controllable 3D world generation under scattered images with little or no visual overlap. WorldBridge encodes scattered references into a global scene context to guide geometry and appearance generation across views. Our temporal and spatial reference attention mechanism further enhances the fidelity of temporal references along the target trajectory and supports flexible spatial references outside it. A plug-and-play latent-reference consistency strategy improves reference fidelity through reprojection-guided test-time optimization. We also introduce the WorldBridge benchmark suite to evaluate 3D world generation from scattered, low-overlap references, which is rarely explored by current benchmarks. Both qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate that our method enables controllable and coherent 3D world generation, surpassing the existing state-of-the-art solutions. Our project page is available at https://davidyan2001.github.io/WorldBridge/.
authors: Weilong Yan, Jingyu Hu, Hongli Xu, Yifan Zhan, Beibei Lin, Anbang Wang, Qinqian Lei, Jingwei Huang, Robby T. Tan
bullets: Addresses the inconsistency and limited coverage of existing geometry-, image-, and video-based methods for scattered-view 3D generation.
Encodes references into a global scene context to guide geometry and appearance across views.
Uses temporal and spatial reference attention to preserve trajectory fidelity while supporting references outside the target path.
Applies plug-and-play latent-reference consistency with reprojection-guided test-time optimization.
Introduces a benchmark suite for scattered, low-overlap 3D world generation and reports qualitative and quantitative gains over prior state-of-the-art methods.

papers.abstract: Consistent and controllable 3D stylization is critical for visual computing applications such as immersive visualization, augmented and virtual reality content creation, and artistic scene rendering. While 2D image stylization has advanced significantly, extending these methods to 3D remains challenging due to the need for cross-view consistency, where stylized renderings must align across all viewpoints. Applying 2D stylization independently to each rendered view often results in inconsistencies across perspectives. Existing methods attempt to improve consistency by leveraging implicit radiance field representations, which model scene appearance as a function of spatial locations. However, these methods struggle with ambiguity in updating colors, as the indirect dependence between pixel appearance and learnable scene parameters makes it difficult to enforce consistent stylization during optimization. This work presents Surface-based Scene Stylization (Surf-Style), which reconstructs object surfaces in a 3D scene and uses these surfaces to achieve geometric consistency and localized stylization. Surf-Style defines a learnable appearance model over 3D space, which is modified to replicate the visual style of a reference image. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our method achieves superior consistency and offers greater flexibility in controllable stylization, including the ability to target specific surface regions and combine different styles.
authors: Wanrong Hong, Ancheng Lin, Mukesh Prasad, Jun Li
bullets: Addresses cross-view inconsistencies caused by independently stylizing rendered 2D views.
Reconstructs scene surfaces to provide geometric consistency and localized style control.
Learns a 3D appearance model optimized to reproduce the style of a reference image.
Supports targeting specific surface regions and combining multiple styles.
The abstract reports better consistency and greater controllability than existing methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Difference between naive image-based stylization, NeRF-based methods, and our surface-based approach in 3D scene stylization. (a) Crossview Consistency: Naively stylizing rendered images without enforcing 3D geometry constraints lead to cross-view inconsistencies. NeRF-based methods [6], [8], [32], [41] offer limited consistency, as they use shared parameters (e.g., neural networks, voxel grids) to model appearance within a volume, causing appearance changes to spill over into unrelated regions. In contrast, our surface-based method recovers a surface model from the trained NeRF and stores appearance information independently at face vertices, reducing conflicts and inconsistencies. (a.1) and (a.2) Cross-view consistency illustration. (b) Controllable stylization: The naive method does not support geometryaware selection. NeRF-based approaches struggle to target specific regions, as they do not explicitly represent object structures. Our surface-based method enables selection over individual faces through explicit geometric modeling, allowing for localized stylization.

Fig. 3. Volume-based rendering vs. Surface-based shading. In volume rendering, pixel col rs are computed by interpolating features from surrounding grid points in 3D space, which often leads to imprecise and diffuse stylization. In contrast, our Surface-based approach stores appearance parameters directly on mesh vertices. A custom shader then interpolates these features along the mesh surface, enabling more spatially localized stylization effects.

papers.abstract: Unsupervised cross-modal homography estimation is challenging because appearance differences obscure shared geometric structures. Separating modality transfer from homography estimation helps reduce these differences, but accurate alignment still requires effective geometric representations and consistency constraints on the two subtasks. We propose GeoCo (Geometry-Aware and Consistency-Constrained Homography Estimation), a framework that addresses these two requirements without cross-modal transformation labels. Its homography estimator, RVHomo, adapts hierarchical features from a frozen vision foundation model (VFM) and fuses them with local CNN features to capture structural context and spatial detail. Two geometric consistency constraints encourage modality transfer to preserve geometry and homography predictions to remain consistent under synthetic geometric transformations. Through two-stage progressive distillation, we further obtain GeoCo-D, which uses the lightweight RVHomo-D estimator. An intermediate model first learns to perform cross-modal matching without modality transfer, then transfers prediction and feature knowledge to the student, eliminating online VFM extraction. Experiments on GoogleMap, OPT-SAR, FSD, and VIS-IR show that GeoCo reduces mean average corner error by 17.4-46.7% relative to the best-performing baseline on each dataset. GeoCo-D also outperforms all compared baselines while using 98.5% fewer parameters and 70.4% fewer FLOPs than the complete GeoCo teacher.
authors: Zhuoran Yang, Junchen Yu, Runmin Zhang, Linshan Li, Chenghao Zhang, Hui-liang Shen, Si-Yuan Cao
bullets: Addresses appearance gaps between modalities that obscure shared geometric structure during homography estimation.

Geometric consistency constraints enforce geometry preservation during modality transfer and prediction consistency under synthetic transformations.
Progressive distillation produces GeoCo-D, which avoids online foundation-model feature extraction through a lightweight estimator.

Across four datasets, GeoCo reduces mean average corner error by 17.4–46.7% versus the strongest baseline per dataset; GeoCo-D uses 98.5% fewer parameters and 70.4% fewer FLOPs than the teacher while outperforming compared baselines.

papers.abstract: World-space human mesh recovery can lose spatial consistency even when camera-space body estimates are accurate. A single sequence-wide scale resolves global scale ambiguity but cannot correct local scale distortion along a reconstructed camera path. We present ScaleCurve, a framework that estimates time-varying metric corrections from human-ground geometry. We construct scale observations by comparing predicted foot geometry with locally fitted ground planes. Joint temporal optimization downweights inconsistent observations and couples neighboring scale estimates, allowing calibration to adapt along the camera path without freely following measurement noise. We scale camera translation increments and integrate them into a calibrated trajectory. With this camera fixed, we refine the lifted body motion using 2D image evidence and pretrained 3D dynamics, while restricting global trajectory rescaling. ScaleCurve achieves state-of-the-art performance on most evaluated metrics on both EMDB-2 and SLOPER4D. Consistent gains across three HMR backbones demonstrate its compatibility with diverse body estimates without retraining. Code will be made publicly available.
bullets: Addresses local scale distortion that remains after applying a single sequence-wide scale.
Derives scale observations from predicted foot geometry and locally fitted ground planes.
Jointly optimizes temporally consistent scale estimates while downweighting unreliable observations.
Calibrates camera translation increments, then refines lifted body motion with 2D evidence and pretrained 3D dynamics.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on most metrics across EMDB-2 and SLOPER4D, with gains across three HMR backbones without retraining.
