papers.abstract: Long sequence reconstruction must correct accumulated drift while preserving locally consistent geometry. In robotics and autonomous driving, embodied acquisition provides recurring platform- environment geometry and repeated observations of scene structure and platform motion. We present Embodied-VGGT, which exploits these cues to establish reliable local relationships and selectively preserve them during global refinement. Memory-Augmented Grounded Chunks (MAGC) builds on Scal3R's global context memory and uses relative scale references derived from predicted ground geometry to regularize test-time memory updates, encouraging cross-chunk consistency while limiting changes to reliable local geometry. Superpoint Alignment (SA) and Cross-Loop Optimization (CL) jointly address the robust establishment and preservation of geometric relationships. SA balances ground and non-ground evidence across spatial regions to estimate inter-chunk translation. CL uses geometric and motion consistency across interleaved windows to select coherent chunk groups, each receiving a shared Sim(3) correction that preserves its internal relative transformations during global optimization. Experiments on five public driving benchmarks demonstrate consistent and substantial improvements in long sequence reconstruction. On KITTI Odometry, Embodied-VGGT achieves a mean absolute trajectory error of 7.30 m and a Chamfer distance of 2.67 m, reducing these errors by 46.8% and 23.3% compared with the state-of-the-art baseline under same evaluation protocol. To facilitate reproducibility, we released our code: https://github.com/Ang-Sheep/Embodied-VGGT.
authors: Yiheng Han, Ziang Chen, Zhuyong Fu, Yiqing Yin, Nan Ma
bullets: Targets drift accumulation and local-geometry degradation in robotics and autonomous-driving reconstruction.
Uses Memory-Augmented Grounded Chunks (MAGC) to regularize test-time memory updates with predicted ground-geometry scale references.
Combines Superpoint Alignment for inter-chunk translation with Cross-Loop Optimization, which applies shared Sim(3) corrections to coherent chunk groups.
Improves reconstruction consistently across five public driving benchmarks; on KITTI Odometry, it reports 7.30 m trajectory error and 2.67 m Chamfer distance.
Code is publicly available for reproducibility.

papers.abstract: Accurate novel-view synthesis of B-mode ultrasound images requires modeling acoustic propagation through tissue and the resulting appearance variations across probe poses. We propose Ultrasound Propagation Physics-informed Gaussian Splatting (UPP-Gauss), which integrates these acoustic interactions into an explicit Gaussian representation. UPP-Gauss constructs acoustic maps by sampling three 3D Gaussian fields using the probe pose and acoustic beam propagation direction, then combines these maps according to ultrasound propagation to synthesize B-mode images. Across three acoustically diverse datasets, UPP-Gauss achieves the best reconstruction quality with efficient rendering, improving PSNR over the best baseline on each dataset by 1.43 dB on average. These results demonstrate accurate and efficient B-mode novel-view synthesis through explicit Gaussian modeling of ultrasound propagation.
authors: Guil Jung, Seok-Hwan Oh, Myeong-Gee Kim, Young-Min Kim, Hyeon-Jik Lee, Sang-Yun Kim, Hyeok-Jun Kwon, Hyuk-Sool Kwon, Hyeon-Min Bae
bullets: Models appearance changes caused by tissue acoustics and varying probe poses.

Achieves the best reconstruction quality across three acoustically diverse datasets, improving PSNR over the strongest baseline by 1.43 dB on average.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has demonstrated remarkable performance in aerial scene reconstruction, motivating its recent extension to true digital orthophoto maps (TDOMs) generation. We propose Tortho-Gaussian++, a novel 3DGS training framework that suppresses geometric drift and floaters and automatically prunes unreliable peripheral regions, coupled with a robust gravity-aligned TDOM rendering solution. First, we explore geometric support via viewing-ray-based geometric observability analysis, quantitatively characterizing the reliability for each Gaussian and subsequently pruning peripheral regions with particularly weak geometric support. Second, the optimizer state initialization is refined for newly created Gaussians during densification, intrinsically suppressing drift and floaters without external priors. Lastly, a robust gravity direction estimation solution is designed, combining image-derived gravity cues, camera-distribution priors and nadir views, to achieve a gravity-aligned orthogonal projection reference for TDOM rendering. Extensive experiments on multiple large-scale UAV (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle) datasets demonstrate that our Tortho-Gaussian++ outperforms vanilla 3DGS by 0.5-3.5 dB in average PSNR and yields comparable or superior performance to prior-guided 3DGS methods. Notably, it reduces the training time, VRAM and Gaussian number by 45.5%, 47.2%, and 58.6%, respectively. Qualitative evaluations confirm that our method effectively suppresses drift and floaters, while robust gravity direction estimation reduces tilt-induced facade artifacts in TDOMs.
authors: Xiang Wang, Xin Wang, Zongqian Zhan
bullets: Addresses unreliable geometry and gravity misalignment in 3DGS-based aerial TDOM reconstruction.
Uses viewing-ray geometric observability to assess Gaussian reliability and prune weakly supported peripheral regions.
Refines optimizer-state initialization for densified Gaussians to suppress drift and floaters without external priors.
Estimates gravity robustly from image cues, camera-distribution priors, and nadir views for aligned orthogonal rendering.
On multiple large-scale UAV datasets, it improves average PSNR over vanilla 3DGS by 0.5–3.5 dB and reduces training time, VRAM, and Gaussian count.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed Tortho-Gaussian++. (A) Viewing-ray-based geometric observability analysis quantifies the geometric support of each Gaussian during training, enabling automatic pruning of weakly supported Gaussians after training. (B) Optimizer-state inheritance transfers the parent’s accumulated moment estimates to newly created Gaussians while retaining the shared optimizer step count, suppressing geometric drift and floaters caused by amplified parameter updates. (C) Robust gravity direction estimation combines imagederived gravity cues, camera-distribution priors, and nadir views through confidence-based selection and fusion. The resulting down-vector establishes a gravity-aligned orthogonal projection reference for rendering the pruned Gaussian scene into a TDOM.

papers.abstract: Understanding large-scale 3D urban scenes requires representations that capture both multi-scale geometric structures and complex spatial relationships. However, existing 3D vision-language methods primarily emphasize global semantic alignment or object-level representations, leaving structured relational modeling underexplored within unified contrastive and generative frameworks. In this paper, we present 3D CoCa v3, a scene-graph-enhanced contrastive and generative framework for urban 3D scene understanding. Our framework features a Pyramid Vision Encoder for multi-scale geometric representation learning and a language-model-based decoder with question-guided caption retrieval and visual cross-attention. We further introduce MSG-based relational descriptions to enrich contrastive 3D-language alignment with structured spatial relationships. To support semantic and relational supervision, we construct City3D-9.6K, a multi-view urban vision-language dataset with aligned visual-geometric observations, scene captions, and scene graphs. Extensive experiments on City-3DQA demonstrate that 3D CoCa v3 achieves 88.35% and 64.79% overall top-1 accuracy on the sentence-wise and city-wise splits, surpassing 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points, respectively. Furthermore, 3D CoCa v3 achieves the best performance on GeoEval3D, demonstrating its effectiveness in urban spatial reasoning and geometric understanding. Code is available at https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/3DCoCav3.
authors: Nannan Zhang, Ting Huang, Zeyu Zhang, Haoyu Chen, Yanjie Zhu, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses limited structured relational modeling in existing 3D vision-language methods.
Uses a Pyramid Vision Encoder, a language-model decoder with question-guided caption retrieval and visual cross-attention, and MSG-based relational descriptions.

On City-3DQA, reaches 88.35% sentence-wise and 64.79% city-wise top-1 accuracy, improving over 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points.
Achieves the best performance on GeoEval3D, indicating strong urban spatial reasoning and geometric understanding.

A multimodal decoder subsequently integrates question-relevant scene captions and projected visual features into a LoRA-adapted Qwen backbone for urban 3D question answering.

papers.abstract: In-Hand Object Scanning (IHOS) from monocular video captured by a commodity smartphone holds immense potential to democratize 3D digitization for non-expert users, facilitating applications in digital archiving, augmented reality, and custom fabrication. Yet, IHOS remains largely understudied due to a lack of realistic datasets and systematic benchmarks. To bridge this gap, we introduce ToysRUs, a high-quality dataset featuring diverse figurines captured by 4K Ultra High-Definition (UHD) monocular videos. Studying IHOS from first principles, we examine structure-from-motion (SfM) for camera pose estimation, which is key to IHOS. We identify two key challenges: small baselines between consecutive frames, and sparse feature matches across large-view, long-range frames, further exacerbated by dynamic hand occlusions. Guided by these insights, we propose performing SfM on video sub-sequences sampled at sufficient angular intervals, and iteratively stitches the corresponding sub-trajectories into a unified global trajectory. Furthermore, for high-fidelity surface reconstruction, we introduce occlusion-aware 2D Gaussian Splatting, which incorporates opacity rendering and omits the opacity loss on hand regions. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms existing approaches, including neural implicit representations and 3D foundation models, in both geometric accuracy and photometric fidelity.
authors: Di Wu, Jeeeun Kim, Shu Kong
bullets: Introduces ToysRUs, a high-quality 4K UHD monocular-video dataset of diverse figurines for in-hand object scanning.
Identifies small inter-frame baselines, sparse long-range matches, and dynamic hand occlusions as key challenges for structure-from-motion.
Estimates camera poses by running SfM on angularly spaced video subsequences and iteratively stitching their trajectories.
Uses occlusion-aware 2D Gaussian Splatting that models opacity while excluding hand regions from the opacity loss.
Reports better geometric accuracy and photometric fidelity than existing neural implicit and 3D foundation-model approaches.

figures.caption: Figure 9: Qualitative comparisons. We visualize the reconstruction results using splat mode, Gaussian centers, RGB rendering, and the final reconstructed surface mesh. Our full OA-2DGS pipeline (w/ A, W) effectively integrates opacity supervision with the hand occlusion mask, proving essential for extracting clean, high-fidelity object geometry under severe hand occlusions.

Figure 6: Visual results on Toys RUs. Among all the compared methods, Castoags produces the most visually high-fidelity surface reconstructions. Refer to Table 2 for quantitative comparisons, and Suppl. Fig. 12 for more qualitative comparisons.

Figure 16: We change filament and 3D print the same object at a large and a small scale, respectively. At a small scale, we see a failure on the pigtail because of minimal overhang that require a little to no supporting structure underneath, which is automatically generated by the slicer. Nevertheless, this demonstrates that the reconstructed colored surfaces by our method serve as a base model for custom fabrication and 3D printing.

Figure 4: Flowchart of the proposed method. Given an RGB video, it segments and tracks the foreground object, background, and hand. Then, it performs SfM over subsequences of frames on the foreground object, resulting in multiple sub-trajectories of camera poses and point clouds (§4.2). Next, it stitches them into a global camera trajectory and a dense point cloud (§4.3, Fig. 5). Lastly, it applies occlusion-aware 2DGS to reconstruct a colored surface (§4.4).

Figure 7: Benchmarking on IHO w.r.t Chamfer Distance (CD) and time cost. Red boxes highlight unsatisfactory reconstructions by Color-NeuS or imperfect ground truth. Castoags outperforms Color-NeuS, which is the most competitive method (Table 2). However, Color-NeuS takes 12 hours to reconstruct one figurine, whereas Castoags takes 20 minutes. Refer to Suppl. §D for more metrics. Zoom-in for better visualization.

Figure 15: Illustration of 3D printing. To further examine the quality of reconstructed surfaces, we turn to 3D printing to physically print the object based on its reconstructed surface. In brief, we use a Bambu Lab multi-color printer equipped with the Automated Material System (AMS). An internal camera in the printer helps monitor printing progress, which can be view in mobile app.

Figure 2: The left panel displays all the 40 figurines in the Toys RUs dataset. The right panel illustrates the acquisition of ground-truth colored surface by using a professional scanner, and a video of toying this figurine captured by a hand-held smartphone (Fig. 1).
Figure 11: Failure modes of Dynhor [26]. As the foundation models cannot reliably handle uncommon figurines, Dynhor performs poorly on Toys RUs.

Figure 10: Sampling interval of CamStitch. We vary the sampling interval to produce subsequences for SfM execution, the first step in CamStitch. Too small intervals such as 1 risk CamStitch with the notorious small baseline issue (Fig. 3); too large intervals (>8) yield too few feature matches to reliably run SfM, degrading the final performance. Nevertheless, CamStitch is resilient to a large range of sampling intervals.

Figure 8: Visual results with progressive modifications on SfM (Table 3). Naive SfM, operating on raw video frames, fails to recover camera poses. When focusing only on target objects, SfM improves but produces incomplete camera trajectories. CamStitch (a crucial component in Castoags) recovers the full camera trajectory and helps reconstruct high-quality mesh.

Figure 5: Stitching sub-trajectories and point clouds. Although a pair of inter-subsequence frames may have too few 2D feature matches, 2D feature matches from more inter-subsequence frames and intra-subsequence 2D-to-3D correspondences (derived from SfM) collectively produce sufficient amounts of 3D correspondences. With such, we compute a Sim3 transformation matrix between the two point sets, allowing to stitch sub-trajectories and point sets into a global trajectory and a dense cloud, respectively.

Figure 13: Qualitative results on OmniObject3D. We evaluate camera pose estimation (left) and surface reconstruction (right). CamStitch yields camera trajectories aligned with the ground truth (GT pose), resolving track drift in naive SfM (SfM w/ fg). Castoags produces high-fidelity surfaces compared to Color-NeuS [72], preserving finer geometric details consistent with the ground truth (GT mesh). We also provide quantitative results on camera pose estimation (see Table 7) and surface reconstruction (see Table 8).
Figure 14: Failure cases. Castoags reconstructs incomplete mesh surfaces under specific conditions: single-color textures, transparent materials, and smooth surfaces.

Figure 12: Extensive visualizations on the Toys RUs dataset. We visually present 10 additional reconstructed results corresponding to the quantitative metrics in Table 2. While Color-NeuS [72] achieves comparable visual quality, it requires ∼12 hours per object, which severely hinders its practical application in IHOS. In contrast, our approach delivers highly competitive visual fidelity in merely ∼20 minutes, demonstrating a massive leap in efficiency.

Figure 3: A dilemma in pose estimation on an IHOS video. (A): Leveraging dense frames suffers from the notorious small baseline issue [40, 58, 8, 5], yielding erroneous depth estimates and camera trajectory drift. (B): Sampling sparse frames ensures wide baseline but produces insufficient feature matches, causing unreliable pose estimation, early termination, and incomplete reconstruction.

papers.tldr: A monocular in-hand scanning framework combines a new smartphone-video dataset, improved camera pose estimation, and occlusion-aware Gaussian Splatting for more accurate 3D object reconstruction.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders photorealistic novel views in real time, but its per-scene training (optimization) remains slow. Recent fast training methods such as FastGS shorten training to a few minutes by reducing the number of Gaussians. Profiling FastGS, we find two costs that remain even in its compact model. First, rasterization is still the largest cost, and redundant work remains in it. Second, the loss computation does not shrink with the number of Gaussians, so its share of the training time grows as the model becomes compact. We present SprintGS, a training framework built on FastGS that keeps the model compact and reduces both costs. For rasterization, scheduled tile culling limits each Gaussian to the tiles where it matters, using a coarse footprint that is annealed to the exact one before training ends; convergence-aware pruning removes converged, nearly transparent Gaussians; and a shuffle-efficient backward pass reduces the data exchanged between GPU threads. For the loss, a fused loss computes the loss and its image gradient in the forward pass without a loss map, removing most of its cost. SprintGS trains 2.15x faster than FastGS at comparable quality, and 1.81x faster in its high-quality setting. It also accelerates other fast training methods and dynamic, sparse-view, and surface reconstruction.
bullets: Targets remaining bottlenecks in fast 3DGS training: rasterization and loss computation.
Uses scheduled tile culling, convergence-aware pruning, and a shuffle-efficient backward pass to reduce rasterization overhead.
Introduces a fused loss that computes the loss and image gradient during the forward pass without constructing a loss map.
Trains 2.15× faster than FastGS at comparable quality and 1.81× faster in its high-quality setting.
Also accelerates dynamic, sparse-view, surface-reconstruction, and other fast-training settings.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces SprintGS, an efficient training framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces redundancy in rasterization and loss computation.
papers.title: SprintGS: Eliminating Redundancy for Fast 3D Gaussian Splatting Training
papers.tldr: SprintGS speeds up compact 3D Gaussian Splatting training by eliminating redundant rasterization and loss-computation work while preserving comparable quality.

papers.abstract: A cart can follow its reference trajectory while its cargo floats above the deck. Asset4D-Bench tests whether coding agents recover objects, motion and interactions from visual references as editable Blender scenes. Its 114 conditions span image editing, video reconstruction with matched full or partial starter assets, and independently selected from-scratch tasks. We independently reopen projects and measure them against native reference states. The 228 archived scores include original delivery outcomes and versioned measures of scene quality. On 24 from-scratch tasks, each model earns full dynamics credit on 14. Of these, three GPT-6.1-Sol and eight GPT-6-Astra reconstructions earn zero relation points. Under the fixed scoring weights, relations contribute 5.15 points to the 6.50-point Sol-minus-Astra difference in mean recovered fidelity. Differences in execution and recovery policy across archived runs preclude a causal estimate of starter-asset effects.
authors: Chengyi Sun, Deyuan Liu, Lei Zhao, Jungang Li, Qi Jia
bullets: Covers 114 conditions across image editing, video reconstruction with full or partial starter assets, and from-scratch tasks.
Uses independently reopened projects and 228 archived scores to assess scene quality against native reference states.
On 24 from-scratch tasks, all models received full dynamics credit on 14 tasks, but some reconstructions still had zero relation points.
Relation errors accounted for most of the reported mean-fidelity gap between GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra under the fixed scoring weights.
Archived execution and recovery differences prevent causal conclusions about the effect of starter assets.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) optimization updates the Gaussian parameters one training view at a time, tens of thousands of times. Unlike such single-view updates, multi-view batches reduce dependence on individual training views, and second-order optimization reduces the number of updates with larger, structured parameter changes. Because fewer updates leave fewer chances to correct a change that fits only the views used in one update, scene coverage becomes more important for each second-order update. Multi-view second-order updates, however, are expensive. Pixel sampling reduces this cost, but two issues remain. First, selecting views without considering overlap leaves some views redundant. To address this, we propose a view selection strategy that reduces this redundancy. Second, existing work processes the sampled pixels of each view in a separate pass and recomputes alpha compositing for these pixels from scratch. We introduce two implementation strategies that reduce both overheads by processing the sampled pixels of multiple views in joint passes and reusing the transmittance and accumulated color cached during rendering. On three datasets, our method reaches higher PSNR than the sampled second-order baseline in less than half its optimization time, with competitive SSIM and LPIPS.
authors: Hyunseung Son, Young Sun Choi, Youngsik Yun, Kibeom Hong, Youngjung Uh
bullets: Motivation: Multi-view second-order updates can improve optimization but are costly and sensitive to scene coverage.
Method: Select less-redundant views to increase coverage within each update.
Implementation: Jointly process sampled pixels across views and reuse cached transmittance and accumulated color.
Results: Across three datasets, achieves higher PSNR in less than half the optimization time, with competitive SSIM and LPIPS.
Scope: Evaluated on three datasets against a sampled second-order baseline.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of one update of our method. From Gaussians initialized by a sparse SfM point cloud or a dense pretrained 3DGS model, Scene-Distributional View Sampling selects training views with low redundancy, forming the multi-view batch Bt. The views are rendered, and pixels are sampled per tile so that their rays provide residuals. Tile-Grouped Multi-View Accumulation packs the sampled rays from view-local tiles into a single grouped layout and derives Ĵ for all views jointly. BucketPrefix Jacobi Preconditioning caches the transmittance and accumulated color at a few Gaussians per ray during rendering, so the preconditioner computation starts from them in parallel. Nview, Ntile, and Ngroup denote the numbers of selected views, tiles per view, and grouped tiles.

papers.selection_reason: Efficient second-order optimization for 3D Gaussian splatting scene reconstruction.
papers.title: Efficient Scene-Distribution-Aware Second-Order Optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: An efficient scene-aware second-order optimizer for 3D Gaussian Splatting improves view coverage and rendering reuse to achieve higher PSNR in under half the time of a sampled second-order baseline.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 4D trackers recover camera motion, depth, and point trajectories from short video clips, but chaining windows over long videos degrades their accuracy. We find that replacing inter-window alignment with ground-truth transforms leaves tracking error essentially unchanged. Static-point error instead grows with time since last observation: repeatedly predicting a static point from windows that no longer observe it corrupts previously recovered geometry. We call this failure forgetting. Merely retaining the last observed positions of unseen points reduces error by 26% on PointOdyssey without modifying the tracker. We introduce Recall4D, a training-free framework that augments a frozen tracker with a persistent world state and sparse motion anchors. Static points retain their world-space positions outside the camera view and are refined by averaging observations decoded at sparse keyframes while in view. For dynamic objects, the tracker decodes sparse representative anchors, while geometric skinning propagates their displacements to dense queries. Across two long-horizon benchmarks, Recall4D improves the accuracy of its backbone while running 7.6-9.0$\times$ faster, and its accuracy gains carry over to five further backbones and three other long-sequence tasks, demonstrating its generality.
bullets: Inter-window misalignment is not the main cause of long-video tracking degradation; static-point error increases after points leave view.
Retaining last observed positions reduces PointOdyssey error by 26% without changing the tracker.
The training-free method augments frozen trackers with persistent world state, sparse keyframes, and geometric skinning for dynamic objects.
It improves backbone accuracy across two long-horizon benchmarks while running 7.6–9.0× faster.
Gains transfer across five additional backbones and three other long-sequence tasks, indicating broad applicability.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free persistent world state to mitigate forgetting in long-horizon 4D reconstruction.
papers.title: Recall4D: Forgetting, Not Misalignment, Limits Long-Horizon Feed-Forward 4D Reconstruction
papers.tldr: Recall4D shows that long-horizon 4D reconstruction fails mainly because trackers forget previously observed geometry, and fixes this with persistent state and sparse motion anchors.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based 3D reconstruction models such as VGGT and $\pi^3$ predict cameras, depth and point maps directly from many input views. Causal attention models such as StreamVGGT extend them to online video but cache all past tokens, so their total compute grows quadratically with the stream length. Recurrent models such as CUT3R and TTT3R keep a fixed-size state at constant cost, but they progressively forget early geometry. We present LinearVGGT, a hybrid model distilled from StreamVGGT, which uses Mamba2 layers for efficient sequence modeling in three of every four global layers. The remaining layers use register-guided sparse attention to retrieve a few relevant past frames, compensating for the limited exact long-range recall of Mamba2. Our distillation needs only 9\% of the GPU hours and 31\% of the training frames that StreamVGGT uses to learn from VGGT. LinearVGGT keeps an almost constant latency of 27 ms per frame over 1,024 frames and is on average $12 \times$ faster than StreamVGGT. It outperforms its teacher and is competitive with the state-of-the-art streaming model LingBot-Map, while running $2.5\times$ faster and using $2.7\times$ less memory.
authors: Haoyu Kang, Pingzhi Li, Ruichen Zhang, Tianlong Chen
bullets: Addresses the quadratic compute of token-caching streaming transformers and the long-term forgetting of fixed-state recurrent models.
Uses Mamba2 in three of every four global layers, with register-guided sparse attention to retrieve relevant past frames.
Distillation from StreamVGGT requires 9% of its GPU hours and 31% of its training frames.
Maintains approximately 27 ms per frame over 1,024 frames and is 12× faster than StreamVGGT.
Outperforms its teacher and matches state-of-the-art streaming performance while running 2.5× faster and using 2.7× less memory than LingBot-Map.

papers.abstract: Scenes inside a scattering medium contain solid surfaces, such as the seabed or rocks, and a semi-transparent medium, such as water, fog, or smoke. Recent Gaussian-based methods produce realistic images of scenes in scattering media, but traces of the medium can remain visible in surface-only renders. Neural fields separate surfaces and medium more accurately, but they are slow to train and difficult to edit. Both approaches evaluate the medium only along camera rays, so its effects along reflected and refracted rays are not modeled. These limitations prevent reliable surface recovery, independent editing of surfaces and the medium, and consistent rendering of inserted objects. We present FoamSurf, a hybrid representation that models surfaces with planar Gaussian surfels and the medium with space-filling Voronoi cells. A single differentiable ray tracer composites both along arbitrary rays, while training priors keep them separate without segmentation masks. Across real underwater scenes, synthetic scenes, and dense fog, FoamSurf achieves image quality on par with the state of the art and the most accurate surface-medium separation among the compared methods. The recovered components can be removed, edited, or stylized independently, and the same reconstruction supports inserted mesh objects with attenuation and scattering along both direct and reflected or refracted rays. Together, these capabilities enable scene restoration, editing, and composition within a single reconstructed model. Project page: https://grzegorzwilczynski.com/foamsurf/
authors: Grzegorz Wilczy\'nski, Julia Farganus, Krzysztof Byrski, Rafa{\l} Tobiasz, Miko{\l}aj Zieli\'nski, Dominik Belter, Przemys{\l}aw Spurek
bullets: Addresses residual medium artifacts, slow training, difficult editing, and ray-limited medium modeling in existing methods.
Represents surfaces as planar Gaussian surfels and the medium as space-filling Voronoi cells.
Uses one differentiable ray tracer to composite both components along arbitrary rays, with training priors instead of segmentation masks.
Across underwater, synthetic, and foggy scenes, matches state-of-the-art image quality and provides the most accurate surface–medium separation among compared methods.
Supports independent removal, editing, and stylization, plus inserted objects with attenuation and scattering along direct and indirect rays.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of FoamSurf. Surfels (left, bottom) hold the surfaces and Voronoi cells (left, top) hold the water. One differentiable ray tracer visits surfel hits and cell boundaries in their order along the ray. It tracks one transmittance for the direct signal and one for the backscatter (bottom plot). Each medium segment lowers them at its own rates, and each surfel hit lowers both. The tracer also renders the surface alone, the medium alone, and the surfel opacity. The loss compares the rendered view with the photo. Its gradients update both representations, and densification and pruning adapt the surfels.

Figure 7. Lego with three surrounding clouds. Rows show the full scene, object, and medium, with PSNR against separate ground truth. All methods share initial surface points. (c) Inserted lights scatter in the water and reach the seabed. (d) Surfaces and water are stylized separately, and the close-ups show each component alone, because the reconstruction keeps them apart.

M.

papers.abstract: An RGB-D camera that films an object being moved, often from one viewpoint, sees one side of it and how its parts move. We present ArtKit, which takes such a video as input to create an articulated model with complete parts, a kinematic tree, and typed joints. Our central idea is generating the hidden geometry and verifying it against what the camera sees. A generative part prior proposes complete, part-decomposed geometry based on the first frame. Point tracks, grouped into rigid trajectories, split and merge the generated parts into links. We then fit revolute and prismatic joints, with a visibility-aware energy ensuring that the articulated model explains the depth observed across the video. A rule checks against the video to choose between synchronous group fits and per-frame chain fits, so that one pipeline serves a diverse range of articulated objects, such as household items and robotic hands. Finally, we regenerate each link of the chosen fit as one part and keep it wherever it agrees better with the observations. We evaluate on Articulate-100 and on HArt, a new benchmark of 60 PartNet-Mobility objects and 8 robotic hands and grippers rendered as RGB-D videos with ground-truth parts and joints. ArtKit reduces the axis and part motion errors of the strongest baseline by more than half on the objects, as well as the axis error on the hands. ArtKit also runs on real recordings and generated videos.
authors: Sylvia Yuan, Dan Wang, Vivian Yu, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Xinrui Cui
bullets: Addresses incomplete visibility when objects are moved and filmed from one viewpoint.
Uses a generative part prior, rigid point trajectories, and motion-based splitting/merging to form links.
Fits revolute and prismatic joints with visibility-aware depth consistency.
Chooses between synchronous-group and per-frame chain fitting, then regenerates links to better match observations.

Evaluated on Articulate-100, the HArt benchmark, and real recordings; it substantially reduces reported axis and part-motion errors versus the strongest baseline on benchmark objects, and reduces axis error on hands.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview. [G] Generative part prior (Sec. 3.1). Hunyuan3D and X-Part propose complete parts from the first frame, and a visibility-aware Chamfer fit places them into O0. [S] Motion-driven re-segmentation (Sec. 3.2). Point tracks are grouped into robust rigid trajectories, with tracks that no rigid body explains left out, the generated parts are split and merged into links, and the links give the articulation graph. [O] Observation-driven articulation (Sec. 3.3). Typed joints are fitted to the depth of every frame with track and smoothness terms by a pool of synchronous group fits and per-frame chain fits, each giving per-frame joint amounts qk,f . The video alone is used to select one fit. Each selected link then re-prompts X-Part with its own box, and the regenerated part is kept where it fits the link’s points better.

Each method is shown at the start and end state of the input video, rendered in the same frame as the ground truth, with parts colored by their matched ground-truth part and the predicted joint axes drawn as red arrows; [Failed] marks a method that returned no model. papers.abstract: Four-dimensional cone-beam computed tomography (4D-CBCT) images the anatomy of a breathing patient, but sees each breathing phase from only a few angles. Breathing, however, is a smooth motion that repeats; it has a phase. Existing methods exploit this either by reconstructing the anatomy as a function of the breathing phase, often through bins, or by estimating smooth dynamic motions in time. Yet none of these grounds one smooth motion in the phase. We thus propose to share projections across breathing phases with splines. Specifically, we represent the 4D volume with dynamic Gaussians whose motion uses B-splines in space and time. We ground the motion state in the respiratory phase, which we read from well-studied conventional surrogates. Projections at the same phase in different breathing cycles then constrain the same anatomy and motion. On simulated lung scans, our method, BreathSplat, outperforms recent dynamic methods in reconstruction and motion accuracy, including those given the ground-truth phase. We further show qualitatively, on two real patient scans, that our method provides clearer reconstructions than the state of the art.
authors: Sujong Shin, Sang-Il Choi, Kwang Moo Yi
bullets: Addresses sparse-angle imaging of anatomy undergoing repeated breathing motion.
Represents the 4D volume with dynamic Gaussians whose spatial and temporal motion follows B-splines.
Uses conventional respiratory surrogates to ground motion states in breathing phase.
On simulated lung scans, it improves reconstruction and motion accuracy over recent dynamic methods, even those given ground-truth phase.
Qualitative results on two real patient scans show clearer reconstructions than the state of the art.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview. Before optimization we use a conventional surrogate to retrieve the respiratory phase of every projection. We deform one set of canonical Gaussians with the low-rank B-spline motion of DIGS [18], whose temporal B-splines we define on this phase, making the motion periodic and aligned to breathing cycles by construction. We then fit both the motion and the Gaussians with the projections, with a TV prior considering the edges.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on a real patient scan. We show the reconstruction outcome for SPARE (Varian patient 1, phase bin 06). The first and third rows show axial and coronal slices, and the others are the zoom-ins. All columns use the same slice locations and display windows. Fu et al. and STNF4D are provided with the SPARE phase bins. Our method clearly reconstructs the pulmonary vessels and the bone edges, while other methods show lower quality.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison. The first and third rows show axial and coronal slices of DIR Case 3 with irregular breathing, and the second and fourth rows show the zoom-ins. All methods use the same time point, slice locations, and display windows. Our method provides the best reconstruction with fine pulmonary structures.

Figure 5. Qualitative comparison on 4D-Lung and SPARE. The first and third rows of each panel show axial and coronal slices of (a) 4D-Lung Case 4 and (b) SPARE Case 3, both simulated with irregular breathing, and the second and fourth rows show the zoom-ins. All methods within each case use the same time point, slice locations, and display windows. Our method provides the best reconstruction with fine pulmonary structures.

Figure 1. Teaser. Our method reconstructs a real patient scan more sharply than the state of the art. Pulmonary vessels and bone edges that the dynamic baselines blur stay sharp in our reconstruction. Each panel shows the same axial slice of SPARE [43] (Varian patient 3, phase bin 01) with the same display window, and the inset enlarges the marked region.
Figure 6. Evaluation-only body masks. We show the masks for DIR Case 1, 4D-Lung Case 1, and SPARE Case 3. These masks are separate from the body region that we take from V0.

Figure 7. Edges of V0 and of the reference volumes. Comparison of the edge map from the static FDK reconstruction V0 with those from the reference volumes (Sec. 4.1) at three time points in one breathing cycle of simulated SPARE Case 3. Most edges of V0 lie on edges of the reference volumes at all three time points.

Table 1. Comparison with the state of the art. We average the values over the 10 DIR and 4D-Lung cases and all evaluated time points. We mark methods that use ground-truth phase bins with ∗. We also provide the baseline motion error assuming static reconstruction. We mark the best values of each column in bold, excluding our method with the ground-truth phase, which we provide as reference. Our method provides the best performance on every metric.

Table 3. Ablation study. We compare with various modifications of our method on the synthetic data. Accurate grounding is critical to the best performance. Using one value per phase bin to represent motion provides slight degradation, but results in abrupt motion as bins are discontinuous. Implementation choices also provide minor gains. Edge PSNR is the PSNR of voxels within two voxels of edges.

Table 4. Hyperparameter sensitivity. We report the changes in body metrics on the 10 DIR and 4D-Lung cases relative to the selected values. We select the values on the three SPARE cases. All values of K use the same number of projection renderings. On DIR and 4D-Lung, the selected values are within 0.05 dB in body PSNR of the best value in each sweep.

Table 2. Landmark and volume accuracy on real anatomy. We also report the tracking performance (TRE) of expert-annotated landmarks of the five DIR cases, simulated from their real phase volumes. We also report the body PSNR averaged over the 10 phases of the first cycle. We mark methods that use ground-truth phase bins with ∗. We also report the error which a static model would make as reference. Our method tracks the landmarks the best, which also leads to better body PSNR.

papers.abstract: We present ArtTet, a method that reconstructs an articulated object from multi-view observations of two articulation states and outputs one watertight mesh per rigid part together with the joints that move them. Mesh splatting gives explicit triangles, but it treats the object as one scene. It extracts a single global surface and cannot keep the triangles of different parts apart; the mesh it exports is layered, self-intersecting, and full of holes. ArtTet follows a divide-and-conquer strategy instead. We first divide the object into rigid parts with dynamic- and geometric-constrained articulation and ownership inference. A multibody registration of the two states recovers the parts and their screw joints. Rigid-body rules on attachment, contact, and swept motion then correct joint types and part labels without any part annotation. We then divide space into part cells with an articulated tetrahedral partition, and conquer each cell with its own differentiable signed distance field on a shared tetrahedral grid. In these partitioned marching tetrahedra the fields are mutually exclusive by construction, so the extracted part meshes are closed and never overlap. All part meshes are optimized jointly from the images of both states through the recovered joints. On Articulate-100, ArtTet gives the most accurate axis directions, part motions, and part geometry over all objects among methods that use no part masks, and its part meshes have virtually no open boundary edges. We also show reconstructions of real captures from the SplArt dataset.
authors: Sylvia Yuan, Dan Wang, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Xinrui Cui
bullets: Addresses layered, self-intersecting, and hole-filled meshes produced when articulated objects are reconstructed as a single scene.
Uses two articulation states to infer rigid parts, screw joints, motion, and part ownership without part annotations.
Applies rigid-body rules for attachment, contact, and swept motion to refine joint types and labels.
Uses an articulated tetrahedral partition and mutually exclusive signed distance fields to extract non-overlapping closed part meshes.
On Articulate-100, achieves the best reported axis, motion, and geometry accuracy among methods without part masks, with virtually no open boundary edges; also works on real SplArt captures.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ArtTet. (A) Dynamic- and geometric-constrained articulation and ownership inference. A multibody initialization splits the fused depth of both states into a static body and K rigid parts with joints Tk. A refinement alternates a symmetric energy on the motions with ownership repair on the labels, under dynamic and geometric joint constraints. A triangle model is then fitted to the images through the fixed joints. (B) Divide. A Delaunay tetrahedralization of the observed points is labeled as empty or as one of the parts by a visibility minimum cut over both states and a swept-motion exclusion, giving one cell per part. (C) Conquer. Each part owns a signed distance field ϕk on a shared tetrahedral grid. The exclusive fields ψk cannot overlap, differentiable marching tetrahedra extracts one closed mesh per part, and all meshes are optimized from the images of both states through the joints.

Figure 7. Qualitative comparison on Articulate-100. Part meshes in state 1, colored by part; both states are in Fig. S4. Gaussian methods are shown after TSDF fusion, which merges neighboring parts and leaves holes and blobs on thin panels. ArtTet keeps doors and drawers as separate closed meshes that move about the recovered joints.

Figure 8. Ablations. Top, part labels and joint axes (red) in state 1, with the ground-truth axes in transparent blue for each row of Table 2 and the ground truth, colored by part. Bottom, a second object in state 0 meshed by TSDF fusion, restricted Delaunay, the partition alone, and partitioned marching tetrahedra, each with a close-up of the boxed region to its right.

Figure 5. Optimizing the part fields. (a) Raw fields of the frame and the door overlap (left). The exclusive fields give each point to the part that is most inside, so the parts meet at a seam (right). (b) The target is outside in free space, follows the observed depth at the surface, is inside only within a shell ∆ behind it, and is outside where nothing was seen. (c) Every sign change on a grid edge costs, so a lone flip without image support is removed. (d) A door swept along a wrong joint enters the static divider, which the swept loss penalizes.

Figure 4. Articulated tetrahedral partition. (a) The segment from a camera to its observed depth crosses only empty space, so every tetrahedron on it gains a free-space vote. (b) A ray of state 1 that sees the door is moved into the canonical frame by T −1 k of the door. (c) Posed at η, the door sweeps the shaded region and passes through two tetrahedra labeled static (red outline). The one that touches the door goes to the door (blue), and the other goes to the outside (white).

Figure 3. Joint typing. (a) rk adds the coverage of the target (red) to the forward fit (green). (b) A drawer fit picks up a small rotation about a nearly orthogonal axis, but a pure translation explains it almost as well. (c) A real hinge lies on its part, a spurious axis does not.
Figure 6. Real captures from SplArt [19]. Input photo and textured part meshes in the second state. Both states are in Fig. S2.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has recently gained popularity as a faster alternative to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) in 3D reconstruction and view synthesis methods. Leveraging the spatial information encoded in 3DGS, this work proposes FOCI (Field Overlap Collision Integral), an algorithm that is able to optimize trajectories directly on the Gaussians themselves. FOCI leverages a novel and interpretable collision formulation for 3DGS using the notion of the overlap integral between Gaussians. The formulation presented applies to different robot morphologies (e.g., fixed and mobile base manipulators, legged robots, UAVs) and handles both static and dynamic Gaussian-Splat environments. Contrary to other approaches, which represent the robot with conservative bounding boxes that underestimate the traversability of the environment, we propose to represent the environment and the robot as Gaussian Splats. This not only has desirable computational properties, but also allows for orientation-aware planning, allowing the robot to pass through very tight and narrow spaces. We extensively test our algorithm in both synthetic and real Gaussian Splats, showcasing that collision-free trajectories for legged, aerial and manipulator robots can be computed in seconds, even with hundreds of thousands of Gaussians making up the environment. The code is available at https://github.com/leggedrobotics/foci
authors: Mario Gomez Andreu, Carlos Martinez Cuenca, Maximum Wilder-Smith, Victor Klemm, Vaishakh Patil, Marco Hutter, Jesus Tordesillas
bullets: Represents both robots and environments as Gaussian Splats instead of conservative bounding boxes.
Uses the Field Overlap Collision Integral to optimize trajectories across fixed-base, mobile, legged, and aerial robots.
Supports static and dynamic Gaussian-Splat environments and orientation-aware planning through narrow spaces.
Experiments on synthetic and real scenes show trajectories can be computed in seconds, including environments with hundreds of thousands of Gaussians.
Scope: evaluated for legged, aerial, and manipulator robots in Gaussian-Splat environments.

papers.abstract: Recent dynamic Gaussian splatting methods encode temporal change, either as smooth functions of time or as constrained updates between frames. We observe that their reconstruction quality degrades significantly under fast motion. In challenging dance sequences, their PSNR drops by 1.1-4.0 dB on high-motion frames compared to low-motion frames. To overcome this limitation, we propose VersionGS, a method that directly encodes per-frame Gaussian states and uses motion estimation only to guide reconstruction. Within each group of frames, unchanged Gaussians keep their current versions in a shared dictionary, while modified Gaussians are appended as new versions. To maximize version reuse, we introduce selective sequential construction, which refines the Gaussians selected by optical flow, photograph differences or rendering errors and leaves the others unchanged. The dictionary is then pruned, fine-tuned with simulated quantization and encoded as images. Adjusting the pruning ratio trades off storage and quality without rebuilding the dictionary. On the fast dance sequences of DanceNet3D, VersionGS improves foreground PSNR by 2.7 dB over the best baseline, and its PSNR decreases by less than 0.3 dB on the highest-motion frames. On N3DV and Technicolor, it requires 6.0x and 5.7x less storage than TAD-GS, the strongest baseline overall, while achieving even higher PSNR. Finally, playback is fast and requires no motion model or neural network, only a 3DGS rasterizer.

papers.abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) and wave-based imaging systems play a critical role in sensing under adverse conditions, but are fundamentally constrained by a trade-off between collection speed and spatial resolution. Reducing measurements to enable rapid collection of fragment geometric information across sensing dimensions, leading to highly non-injective inverse problems that destabilize conventional image-domain reconstruction and super-resolution methods. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) exemplifies this challenge in sparse-aperture sampling. We introduce SPIRIT, a physics-informed inverse rendering framework for sparse-aperture SAR. Rather than enhancing formed images, SPIRIT reconstructs an explicit three-dimensional surface. By adopting an optimization strategy and explicitly modeling visibility, phase coherence, and wave propagation, SPIRIT aggregates distributed geometric features across sparse aperture views into a coherent reconstruction. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that SPIRIT recovers accurate geometry and signal under extreme sparsity, reducing data collection by over 90% while achieving low geometric and signal error and consistently outperforming baselines.
bullets: Targets the speed–resolution trade-off and ill-posed reconstruction caused by sparse-aperture SAR sampling.
Optimizes a 3D surface representation rather than enhancing a preformed image.
Models visibility, phase coherence, and wave propagation to combine geometric evidence across aperture views.
Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show accurate geometry and signal recovery with over 90% less data and lower errors than baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SPIRIT. Sparse coherent measurements are encoded into an explicit surface representation and evaluated through a differentiable RF forward model. The renderer produces predicted measurements at observed and unobserved aperture locations; consistency with the observed sparse measurements constrains the recovered geometry, while the learned structural prior regularizes unobserved components of the scene.

Full-aperture integration produces the most complete formed image, whereas restricted aperture subsets emphasize different portions of the target. papers.abstract: Generating 3D-consistent novel views from 2D diffusion models remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. In this work, we introduce a framework that enhances geometric alignment for monocular view synthesis under drastic camera changes by jointly generating a target view and its corresponding depth map. By conditioning the diffusion pipeline on the single source image, source depth, and target camera rays, our approach forces the model to inherently reason in 3D space even under extreme viewpoint shifts. To guarantee spatial fidelity, we propose a novel per-pixel depth consistency constraint, which verifies and enforces 3D consistency across generated views. Our framework establishes a robust pipeline for geometrically consistent view synthesis, yielding superior visual accuracy and spatial alignment compared to current state-of-the-art methods. With this work, we pave the road towards robust 3D world models capable of understanding complex environments from a single view image.
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in 2D diffusion models under large camera viewpoint changes.
Conditions diffusion on a source image, source depth, and target camera rays to encourage 3D reasoning.
Introduces a per-pixel depth consistency constraint to preserve spatial fidelity across views.
Reports superior visual accuracy and spatial alignment compared with existing state-of-the-art methods.
Targets robust single-image understanding for future 3D world models.

figures.caption: Figure 3 ESC Framework. The framework extends Qwen MM-DiT with depth information and Plücker rays conditioning by leveraging LoRA adapters and a Ray ControlNet. At inference time, we leverage PCC-based sampling to enforce improved generated scene geometry.

These inconsistent pixels are highlighted in red (e), with nf = 13703 pixels exceeding the error threshold δ. papers.abstract: The appearance of a scene is determined by the albedo, roughness, metallicity and normal of every point on its surface, and by the light that reaches it, its irradiance. Recovering these intrinsics from images is ambiguous, and methods that predict them per pixel give the same surface point a different decomposition in every view. We introduce PointX, a simple feed-forward model that predicts intrinsics per 3D surface point instead. A multi-view transformer encodes a set of unposed images, and for any queried surface point, PointX pools the point's tokens across the views in which it appears and decodes the point's intrinsics once. Each point of a 3D reconstruction of the scene, such as a point cloud or a mesh, thus receives a single prediction, which is exactly consistent across views by construction and enables view-consistent relighting and editing. The same model also predicts per-view maps, from one image or many, by querying the point seen at every pixel. These maps agree across views up to the precision of the estimated geometry and correspondences. PointX is significantly more consistent than existing methods, while remaining competitive in accuracy from a single image and improving as views are added. Project page: https://pointx-paper.github.io/
authors: Miguel Farinha, Sam Sartor, Iliyan Georgiev, Giuseppe Vecchio, Ronald Clark, Michael Fischer
bullets: Per-pixel intrinsic prediction can assign inconsistent decompositions to the same surface point across views.
A multi-view transformer encodes unposed images and aggregates tokens from views observing each queried 3D point.
The model predicts one intrinsic decomposition per point, making results exactly view-consistent by construction.
It can also produce per-view maps by querying the 3D point at each pixel, with consistency limited by geometry and correspondence accuracy.
PointX is more consistent than existing methods, competitive from a single image, and improves as more views are added.

figures.caption: Figure 2. PointX overview. A multi-view transformer, conditioned on the geometry estimated by frozen VGGT-Ω [90], turns each view v into a token map tv . papers.abstract: Bathymetry measurement and estimation is critical for understanding the structure of underwater environments. While multibeam echosounders (MBES) provide accurate depth measurements, their deployment on surface vessels limits spatial resolution in deep water. Sidescan sonar (SSS), in contrast, can be deployed on autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) to operate closer to the seafloor, enabling high-resolution acoustic imaging. However, the inherent ambiguity in measurements and the limited observation coverage of sonar datasets degrade the performance of state-of-the-art methods for underwater bathymetry estimation from SSS. In this paper, we propose a differentiable neural rendering framework for SSS that enables effective estimation of bathymetry from SSS measurements. Our approach incorporates a measurement model based on SSS geometry, explicitly accounting for its wide elevation aperture and associated ambiguities. We evaluate our method on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating improved robustness and accuracy compared to alternative approaches.
authors: Tianxiang Lin, Sacchin Sundar, Fenghao Liu, Onur Bagoren, Katherine A. Skinner
bullets: Addresses limited-resolution MBES deployment in deep water and ambiguity in SSS-based bathymetry estimation.
Models SSS measurements with geometry-aware rendering, including the wide elevation aperture and related ambiguities.
Evaluated on synthetic and real-world datasets.
Reports improved robustness and accuracy compared with alternative approaches.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Pipeline overview. Our proposed method optimizes the sonar neural implicit bathymetry networks and renderer by the total rendering loss. The neural renderer then estimates the acoustic radiance, which is used for the final SSS image formation model. The networks are supervised by the reference SSS images and other constraints included in the reconstruction loss.

papers.abstract: Recent neural implicit and Gaussian splatting approaches have achieved impressive results in multi-view surface reconstruction. However, jointly optimizing geometry and appearance introduces ambiguities. A parametric appearance model can compensate for geometric errors, reproducing the input images accurately without an accurate surface. We demonstrate accurate neural implicit surface reconstruction using only multi-view patch photoconsistency with geometry-based visibility, without volumetric rendering or parametric appearance models. For each reference ray, sphere tracing computes the first surface intersection. Its position and normal define a local patch whose photoconsistency is evaluated across visible neighboring views using colors sampled directly from the input images. For efficient sphere tracing, we use a 1-Lipschitz multi-layer perceptron. We use a single photoconsistency loss, without foreground masks or auxiliary geometric regularization. Experiments show that our method achieves the lowest mean Chamfer distance on BlendedMVS (BMVS) among compared methods and matches the geometric accuracy of leading reconstruction methods on DTU.
authors: Gabriel Lenain, Edmond Boyer, Jean Ponce
bullets: Addresses geometry–appearance ambiguity in neural implicit and Gaussian-splatting reconstruction.
Uses sphere-traced first surface intersections to define local patches and compare colors across visible neighboring views.
Employs a 1-Lipschitz MLP for efficient sphere tracing and trains with a single photoconsistency loss.
Achieves the lowest mean Chamfer distance among compared methods on BlendedMVS and matches leading geometric accuracy on DTU.

papers.abstract: Existing depth-from-focus methods can struggle with weak focus cues, new cameras, or fewer focal slices. We present FocusAnchor, a recurrent model that uses focus-volume lookups to refine metric depth and repeatedly aligns a relative depth prior from a frozen foundation model to the current depth estimate. The aligned prior guides subsequent refinement in a feedback loop, carrying metric scale recovered from textured regions into regions where focus cues are weak while preserving scene structure. To support transfer across cameras, we synthesize training stacks with randomized camera parameters and focus distances. However, stack synthesis blurs existing image noise differently across slices, creating artificial depth cues even on textureless surfaces. We add independent per-slice noise to suppress these cues. We also introduce variable-stack training to improve robustness with fewer focal slices and support more practical mobile capture. Compared with FOSSA ViT-B, FocusAnchor reduces AbsRel by 36% on NYU Depth V2 and by 9% on DDFF-12 after fine-tuning. In zero-shot evaluation, FocusAnchor and its variable-stack variant, FocusAnchor-flex, achieve the two lowest AbsRel values on all five benchmarks. On ZEDD test, FocusAnchor achieves 9% lower AbsRel than the best competing method, FOSSA ViT-B, while FocusAnchor-flex achieves lower AbsRel with 40% fewer focal slices on ZEDD validation.
authors: Ashkan Ganj, Hang Su, Tian Guo
bullets: Addresses weak focus cues, camera changes, and limited numbers of focal slices in depth-from-focus.
Uses a recurrent refinement loop combining focus-volume lookups with an aligned relative depth prior.
Synthesizes varied camera and focus settings, adds independent per-slice noise to suppress artificial cues, and trains with variable-length stacks.
Reduces AbsRel by 36% on NYU Depth V2 and 9% on DDFF-12 versus FOSSA ViT-B after fine-tuning.
Achieves the lowest AbsRel across five zero-shot benchmarks; FocusAnchor-flex maintains lower AbsRel on ZEDD validation with 40% fewer slices.

papers.abstract: Early identification of cerebral palsy (CP) relies on observational assessments of spontaneous infant movement, such as the General Movement Assessment (GMA) and the Baby Observational Selective Control AppRaisal (BabyOSCAR), which require trained raters and substantial scoring time. Existing automated approaches derive hand-engineered features from two-dimensional keypoints, which describe image-plane motion rather than the three-dimensional behavior of individual joints. We present Baby Biomechanical 3D Body (BB3D), an infant-adapted, biomechanical pipeline that estimates joint-angle trajectories from single-camera video. Against a multi-view markerless motion capture reference in 17 infants, BB3D's median Procrustes-aligned error was 17.5~mm for joint centers and 20.4~mm for marker sites. A spatio-temporal transformer, pretrained on BB3D joint-angle trajectories from 1k+ single-camera recordings, and fine-tuned on 550 videos from 350 infants, predicted each individual BabyOSCAR item with a mean within-site AUC of 0.79 and the BabyOSCAR total with a Spearman correlation of 0.86 on held-out recordings. Without being trained on diagnosis, the predicted total separated infants with CP from those without CP with an AUC of 0.86, exceeding a replicated two-dimensional feature classifier (0.67) but below the expert clinician rater's total (0.97). Predicted scores also carried information about functional ability and body distribution, though less than expert clinician scores. These results show that biomechanically grounded representations of monocular video can support scalable, joint-level assessment of selective motor control in infancy
authors: Divya Joshi, Ruize Yang, Colleen Peyton, R. James Cotton
bullets: Addresses the time and expertise required for observational assessments such as GMA and BabyOSCAR.
BB3D estimates 3D joint-angle trajectories from single-camera infant video rather than relying on 2D keypoint motion.
A transformer trained on BB3D trajectories predicted BabyOSCAR items and totals on held-out recordings.
The predicted BabyOSCAR total separated infants with and without cerebral palsy better than a replicated 2D-feature classifier, but worse than expert ratings.
Predictions also reflected functional ability and body distribution, though less strongly than clinician scores.

papers.abstract: Tracking a fast-moving point in 3D is prohibitive when RGB frames are blurred or too far apart to reveal its motion. Event cameras record brightness changes between frames, providing measurements inside these temporal gaps. We introduce TrackAnyMotion, which combines monocular RGB frames and events to track arbitrary points in 2D and 3D, including at times when no RGB frame is available. The motion expected for a static point, given scene geometry and camera motion, provides a reference for identifying independently moving objects. An independent-motion decoder combines geometric motion cues with event guidance and 2D tracks, feeding its predictions back into iterative 2D and 3D refinement. We also introduce HyperEvent, a synthetic RGB--Event dataset with high-frequency 3D trajectories, geometry, and independent-motion labels. At RGB frame timestamps on this benchmark, TrackAnyMotion reduces 3D and 2D endpoint errors by 70\% and 32\%, respectively.
authors: Roberto Pellerito, Zijia Dai, Laurent Kneip, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses fast-motion tracking when RGB frames cannot resolve motion between timestamps.
Uses scene geometry and camera motion to estimate static-point motion and identify independently moving objects.
Combines geometric cues, event guidance, and 2D tracks in an iterative 2D/3D refinement process.
Introduces HyperEvent, a synthetic dataset with high-frequency 3D trajectories, geometry, and independent-motion labels.
On HyperEvent at RGB timestamps, reduces 3D and 2D endpoint errors by 70% and 32%, respectively.

papers.abstract: Recovering the continuous world-space motion of both hands from egocentric video is essential for applications such as human-to-robot policy transfer and augmented reality. Achieving this goes beyond reconstructing the hands from each individual frame, as the context that a frame needs is often spread over time, especially around occlusions or when a hand moves out of sight. Recent works have explored how to exploit temporal context, yet they mostly draw it from fixed-length windows. Such windows cannot guarantee that every frame has the context required to reconstruct the hands in world space with accurate poses and metric scale. To address this limitation, we introduce MemHand, a memory-enhanced framework for world-space hand motion reconstruction. MemHand maintains two complementary forms of memory. The Short-Term Event Memory keeps the context of the well-observed hand around each occlusion or out-of-sight event and supplies it to frames with weak or missing visual evidence. In addition, since the metric scale holds over the whole recording, the Long-Term Scale Memory retains the most reliable observations across the video as scale anchors within a bounded state. Across benchmarks featuring severe occlusions and frequent out-of-sight intervals, MemHand achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and generalizes well to unseen domains. Benefiting from the synergy of both memories, it cuts W-MPJPE by 57\% on ARCTIC and 70\% on HOT3D relative to StableHand, delivering continuous and metrically accurate world-space hand poses and trajectories. We will release our code and models at the project page: https://irmvlab.github.io/memhand.github.io
authors: Junyi Ma, Zhangshuo Qi, Erhang Zhang, Mingjie Li, Hesheng Wang
bullets: Targets failures caused by occlusions and hands moving out of view, where fixed temporal windows may lack sufficient context.
Uses Short-Term Event Memory to transfer well-observed hand context to frames with weak or missing visual evidence.
Uses Long-Term Scale Memory to preserve reliable metric-scale anchors throughout an entire recording.
Reports 57% and 70% W-MPJPE reductions versus StableHand on ARCTIC and HOT3D, respectively, with strong cross-domain generalization.
Code and models are planned for public release.

papers.abstract: Satellite-based 3D reconstruction is limited by sparse observations and changes across acquisition dates. Existing methods use generative priors to recover missing visual detail, but ghosting, streaking, and blur persist in their Gaussian scenes. These artifacts become particularly apparent in low-elevation renderings. We introduce CityRecast to suppress these artifacts through Gaussian scene repair and supervision calibration. To correct the Gaussian distributions that produce these artifacts, we first use multi-angle warm-up to constrain their spatial extent. This reduces the initial ghosting carried into progressive refinement. Surface-guided replacement then continues to repair the Gaussian distribution while preserving existing appearance. To provide more reliable supervision for this process, observation calibration mitigates interference from multi-temporal observations. Joint refinement further reduces conflicts among generated views. Experiments on DFC2019 and IARPA demonstrate reduced artifacts in low-elevation renderings while maintaining satellite-view fidelity. Compared with Skyfall-GS, CityRecast reduces FID-CLIP by 25.3% on DFC2019 and 51.8% on IARPA. MUSIQ increases by 14.54 and 24.95 points, respectively.
authors: Shuo Cui, Yingyan Hou, Wanxuan Lu, Hongfeng Yu, Daobing Zhang, Xian Sun
bullets: Addresses artifacts caused by sparse observations and changes across acquisition dates.
Uses multi-angle warm-up to constrain problematic Gaussian spatial extents before refinement.
Applies surface-guided replacement and joint refinement to repair Gaussians while preserving appearance and reducing view conflicts.
Observation calibration mitigates interference from multi-temporal observations during supervision.
On DFC2019 and IARPA, it improves low-elevation rendering quality while maintaining satellite-view fidelity, outperforming Skyfall-GS on reported FID-CLIP and MUSIQ metrics.

papers.abstract: We present DOPER, an RGB pose estimation framework that shares a visual backbone across object detection, segmentation, and keypoint prediction to recover the 6D pose of known objects through Perspective-n-Point. Starting from synthetic training, DOPER adapts to real observations using partial supervision while retaining synthetic keypoint labels. Calibrated multi-view observations provide geometric constraints for keypoint supervision. During inference, optional heatmap refinement fits a rigid pose directly to the predicted keypoint distributions, resolving ambiguous correspondences without depth input or a learned pose refiner. Starting from underspecified CAD models, DOPER progressively refines the object representation and pose estimator. Results on SPEED+ and SHIRT further demonstrate effective adaptation to illumination changes and accurate temporal pose estimation. Across the evaluated single-view and multi-view configurations, DOPER achieves state-of-the-art detection AP results on HANDAL, HOPEv2, HOT3D, and T-LESS while using only RGB and running in real time (35 Hz per object model on one GB300). These results demonstrate the effectiveness of jointly learning detection and pose keypoints, with real observations and geometric constraints.
authors: Hugo Hadfield, Alperen Degirmenci, Jonathan Tremblay
bullets: Addresses 6D pose estimation for known objects using only RGB, without depth or a learned pose refiner.
Shares a visual backbone across detection, segmentation, and keypoint prediction, recovering pose through Perspective-n-Point.

Reports real-time operation and state-of-the-art detection AP across several benchmarks, plus adaptation to illumination changes and temporal pose estimation.

papers.abstract: Recovering editable computer-aided design (CAD) models from underwater stereo images requires accurate and complete geometry, yet stereo reconstruction produces displaced points and missing regions. The original views retain cross-view disagreement and ray evidence lost during point-cloud fusion. Aqua2CAD exploits this evidence in two stages: view-conditioned correction and quality filtering establish reliable geometric support, while multi-view observations condition a learned shape prior to infer missing surfaces in the original metric frame. The recovered points support surface fitting and solid assembly with manually revised face groups. On an OceanSim-based synthetic benchmark, Aqua2CAD reduces point-cloud Chamfer distance by 60% relative to the stereo reconstruction. Compared with a matched point-only completion backbone, it improves missing-region recovery at 5,mm from 16.27% to 24.16%. With a shared CAD backend, exterior acceptance increases from 6/19 to 14/19. Qualitative results on selected real underwater captures demonstrate recovery of the main structures of six 3D-printed objects.

papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems for computed tomography (CT) remain largely restricted to specific anatomical regions, examination types or predefined abnormalities, limiting their ability to provide comprehensive and spatially grounded interpretations. Here we present FORA, a general-purpose CT model that recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts and generates reports across the 28 CT protocols represented in our cohort. Trained on 304,962 routine CT examinations supervised by their accompanying reports, FORA learns to localize abnormalities without manually annotated lesions. Its architecture combines multiple-instance learning with an interpretable concept bottleneck that connects spatial evidence, radiological findings and report generation. We first developed and benchmarked the architecture on chest radiographs, achieving state-of-the-art performance, before training a separate model on three-dimensional CT examinations. On 36,619 held-out CT examinations, FORA achieved a macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.918 for radiological concept recognition, exceeding the strongest of 18 existing CT models by 0.21. FORA also ranked first on three public benchmarks, outperforming Merlin on its own test set without training on that institution's data (AUROC 0.907 versus 0.826). On independent localization benchmarks for pulmonary emboli, renal masses and rib fractures, FORA's strongest spatial evidence fell within annotated lesions at rates up to 348 times greater than chance. FORA achieved more than threefold higher macro-averaged finding recall than the strongest existing report generator. These results show that a single model can combine broad abnormality recognition, spatial localization and report generation across 12 CT examination types, using routine reports without lesion-level supervision.
authors: Sezgin Er, Utku Turkbey, Alperen Gur, Omer Faruk Durugol, Suprosanna Shit, Murong Xu, Julia Wolleb, Jiayi Wang, Xiaoliang Wang, Hadrien Reynaud, Teodora Spasojevic, Dong Yang, Andriy Myronenko, Pengfei Guo, Yufan He, Can Zhao, Marc Edgar, Andreas Maier, Michael Moor, Mehmet Kemal Ozdemir, Daguang Xu, Bernhard Kainz, Bjoern Menze, Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci
bullets: Addresses the limited anatomical and abnormality coverage of existing CT AI systems.
Recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts across 28 CT protocols.
Uses multiple-instance learning and an interpretable concept bottleneck linking spatial evidence, findings, and report generation.
Trained on 304,962 routine CT examinations without manually annotated lesions.
Achieved strong concept recognition, localization, benchmark, and report-generation performance on held-out and independent evaluations.

papers.abstract: 3D perception is shifting from task-specific pipelines to geometric foundation models: monocular depth networks, feed-forward 3D/4D reconstruction models, and vision--language models that predict geometry. However, their progress cannot be measured reliably. Published numbers are not comparable, because every paper samples frames, sets resolutions, and selects test splits differently. They are not robust because the alignment required for every up-to-scale prediction can outweigh the gap between models: fitting depth in the wrong space nearly triples its error, and standard trajectory alignment understates the error of failing methods by up to $2.6\times$. And they rarely cover long recordings, dynamic scenes, or aerial views. We present SpatialArena, an open arena that scores geometric models with the same metrics and rules, with robust and deterministic alignment. SpatialArena spans five tasks, from monocular depth to SLAM. It covers 23 public datasets with 418,929 images across indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes, together with Spatial Arena, our own captures with accurate poses and depth. Evaluating 52 models, we find that single-image depth is close to saturation on public benchmarks but not on large, uncontrolled scenes, and that progress now comes from consistency across frames and views, where feed-forward 3D/4D models match or surpass monocular specialists and overtake video depth models. The benchmark, toolbox, and leaderboard will be publicly released.
authors: Yu Chen, Haosen Yang, Su Ee Tan, Zhensong Zhang, Jifei Song, Jiankang Deng
bullets: Existing results are difficult to compare because papers use different sampling, resolutions, test splits, and alignment procedures.
The arena evaluates five tasks—including monocular depth, 3D/4D reconstruction, and SLAM—on 23 public datasets plus new captures spanning indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes.
Its deterministic alignment and common metrics address evaluation failures that can substantially distort reported errors.
Across 52 models, single-image depth is near saturation on public benchmarks but remains challenging in large, uncontrolled scenes.
Progress increasingly depends on cross-frame and cross-view consistency: feed-forward 3D/4D models match or exceed monocular specialists and outperform video depth models.
