papers.abstract: Reconstructing a scene for physics simulation requires recovering its spatial layout and the support relationships that govern its behavior. We present Support2Sim, a Real2Sim system that reconstructs simulation-ready scenes from a single RGB image. Our design objective is to maximize source fidelity, support realization, and stability within a practical time budget for scene generation. Support2Sim infers a support graph, which a contact-guided pose initializer uses to propose poses for objects with multiple supports. The initializer generates and ranks candidates by geometric fit and source-image agreement. A coarse-to-fine refiner allocates a fixed search budget across supported objects and evaluates pose updates with physics rollouts. After an accepted update, it searches from the new pose at a finer translation and rotation scale. We benchmark our method on 50 scenes spanning four datasets. Compared with the strongest baseline, Support2Sim improves source-mask IoU after 10 seconds by 21.4 pp, realizes 87.1% versus 73.2% of intended supports, and reduces mean object drift from 79.6 to 45.3 mm. See our project page at https://support2sim.github.io for more details.
authors: Samarth Chopra, Ankit Prabhu, Akshayan Nagarajah, Sumer Murthy, Pratik Chaudhari, Vijay Kumar
bullets: Targets visually faithful Real2Sim reconstruction with reliable object supports and practical generation time.
Infers a support graph and uses contact-guided pose initialization for objects with multiple supports.
Refines object poses through coarse-to-fine search, geometric/image agreement, and physics rollouts.
Across 50 scenes from four datasets, it improves 10-second source-mask IoU by 21.4 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
It realizes 87.1% of intended supports and reduces mean object drift from 79.6 to 45.3 mm.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods rely on 2D foundation models applied to registered images captured alongside the 3D point clouds. However, such images may not be available in many cases, while direct 3D point cloud segmentation methods require semantic class supervision and are challenging to deploy in a zero-shot manner. To address these issues, we present SplatSeg3D, which segments a bare colored point cloud in an open-vocabulary manner without requiring the accompanying images, camera poses, class supervision, or instance mask proposals. To achieve this, we first surfelize the input point cloud and obtain oriented 2D Gaussians. We then render views of the scene by splatting, with a view selection strategy that maximizes scene coverage with as few views as possible. Next, we apply text-prompted segmentation on the rendered views, giving each 3D point a set of multi-view semantic cues, fused to produce a 3D segmentation of the scene. We evaluate SplatSeg3D on semantic segmentation and novel-class instance segmentation on 4 standard benchmarks: Scannet, Scannet++, Replica, and S3DIS. Our pipeline not only performs better or on-par with the state-of-the-art, but we also achieve these results efficiently across runtime and compute requirements. Code will be published.
authors: Sandeep Inuganti, Mahdi Chamseddine, Marcel Rogge, Martin R. Oswald, Didier Stricker, Jason Rambach
bullets: Addresses settings where registered images, camera poses, class supervision, or instance proposals are unavailable.
Surfelizes point clouds into oriented 2D Gaussians and selects a small set of coverage-maximizing splatted views.
Applies text-prompted segmentation to rendered views, then fuses multi-view semantic cues onto 3D points.
Evaluated on semantic and novel-class instance segmentation across ScanNet, ScanNet++, Replica, and S3DIS.
Reports performance on par with or better than state of the art while reducing runtime and compute requirements.

papers.abstract: Surgical resection planning centers on generating executable resection surfaces from anatomical evidence and operative constraints. Medical multimodal foundation models enable anatomical understanding, and segmentation models predict resection regions, but neither translates these capabilities into explicitly constrained, executable resection surfaces. We present GeoSurge, an anatomy-grounded framework that combines mask-derived metrics with structure-aware point-cloud tokens to generate executable, editable resection surfaces. To make resection geometry learnable and editable, GeoSurge maps actions to parametric geometry through a surface-action grammar. Using this grammar, anatomy-oriented and tumor-centered templates generate candidates, which are filtered by hard constraints and semantic deduplication. Training supervision is then derived from candidate-expert geometric agreement and independently recomputed feasibility metrics. At inference, the reasoner uses patient evidence and surgical requirements to select or revise an action, which an independent geometry engine subsequently materializes and verifies. GeoSurge achieves the best overall scores on DeepTumour Liver and CRLM-QA, improving the constraint satisfaction rate from 73% to 100% on CRLM and from 56% to 99% on GeoSurge-Bench.
authors: Wenjie Deng, Zijian Tu, Xueyin Zhou, Huayi Wang, Zhuoyun Du, Mingyu Chen, Haochao Ying, Jian Wu
bullets: Addresses the gap between anatomical understanding or segmentation and explicitly constrained resection-surface generation.

Uses geometric agreement and independently recomputed feasibility metrics for supervision; a separate geometry engine materializes and verifies plans.
Reports constraint satisfaction improvements from 73% to 100% on CRLM and from 56% to 99% on GeoSurge-Bench, with best overall scores on both named benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Segmenting a 3D object into semantically meaningful parts requires joint reasoning about geometric structure and semantic context. Pretrained 3D experts provide spatially grounded region proposals, while 2D experts provide semantic cues for identifying object parts. The challenge is to integrate these complementary capabilities into a framework that can both produce meaningful part segmentations and progressively refine them. We present PartAgent, a training-free agentic framework for 3D part segmentation built upon two complementary modules: (i) Structural-Semantic Expert Integration combines regions predicted by the 3D expert with multiview semantic evidence from the 2D expert through image-to-surface correspondences, constructing compositional part partitions at multiple granularities. (ii) Observation-Driven Closed-Loop Partition Refinement observes the current partition and its supporting evidence to select targeted inspection, evidence repair, composition, or reselection actions. It verifies proposed changes and uses the updated state and action outcomes to guide subsequent decisions. On PartObjaverse-Tiny-WT, PartAgent achieves 68.41 mIoU, outperforming the strongest competing method by 8.53 points. Across 3DCoMPaT200, PartNeXt, PartNetE, and PartObjaverse-Tiny, PartAgent achieves the highest mIoU on each dataset, averaging 69.36 across the four datasets, 7.28 points above the highest mean among competing methods.
authors: Yang Cao, Zhe Zhu, Yiheng Zhang, Zhengqiang Zhang, Haoyuan Li, Le Wan, Dan Xu
bullets: Combines spatially grounded 3D region proposals with semantic cues from 2D experts via image-to-surface correspondences.

Achieves 68.41 mIoU on PartObjaverse-Tiny-WT and the highest mIoU across four evaluated datasets, averaging 69.36.

papers.abstract: Accurate and efficient monocular 3D hand pose estimation is an important perception capability for embodied human interaction and dexterous manipulation. Recent diffusion-based methods model pose uncertainty by iteratively denoising 3D joint coordinates. However, directly diffusing the final joints requires the generative process to simultaneously explore plausible poses and recover precise coordinates, often relying on additional denoising steps or multiple hypotheses and consequently increasing inference cost. In this work, we propose DiffAnchor, a few-step anchor-space diffusion framework that diffuses anchors rather than joints. Our key insight is that stochastic exploration does not need to operate directly on the final output. Instead, diffusion searches for informative intermediate anchors that serve as local 3D regressors, while anchor-to-joint offset prediction and weighted aggregation complete precise joint localization. Specifically, fixed context anchors provide stable global references, whereas noisy dynamic anchors are iteratively refined toward informative joint regions. An importance-guided anchor selection and replenishment mechanism further retains useful anchors, removes ineffective ones, and explores insufficiently covered regions. This design reduces the precision burden of the diffusion process and enables accurate prediction using only a few denoising steps and a single hypothesis. Extensive experiments on HO-3D V2, NYU, ICVL, and InterHand2.6M demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on the first three benchmarks and competitive performance on challenging interacting-hand estimation, while maintaining inference efficiency comparable to deterministic regression baselines.
authors: Changlong Jiang, Youci Tang, Haohong Kuang, Hang Xu, Jinghong Zheng, Ran Wang, Zhenghong Yu, Chen Feng, Xiaofeng Yue, Yang Xiao
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of joint-space diffusion, which must jointly explore pose uncertainty and recover precise coordinates.
Uses fixed context anchors and iteratively refined noisy dynamic anchors to locate informative 3D regions.
Predicts anchor-to-joint offsets and aggregates them with weights for precise joint localization.
Importance-guided selection and replenishment retain useful anchors and improve coverage.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on HO-3D V2, NYU, and ICVL, competitive interacting-hand performance, and efficiency comparable to deterministic regression baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of DiffAnchor. Given an input image, the image encoder extracts multi-scale visual features. Joint-specific informative anchors are selected for weighted anchor-to-joint aggregation, whereas highconfidence denoised anchors are retained and the remaining anchors are replenished with newly sampled candidates. After a few iterations, the final 3D hand pose is obtained from the anchor-to-joint ensemble.

Fig. 4. Architecture of the diffusion decoder. Anchor embeddings serve as spatial queries, while image features and diffusion-timestep embeddings condition anchor interaction and image-to-anchor feature aggregation.
Fig. 3. Architecture of the image encoder. Extracted pyramid image features are flattened, concatenated, and enhanced using deformable self-attention.

papers.abstract: Composing an editable 3D scene from images requires an asset for each object and a layout that places the assets. 3D generation and CAD retrieval now supply the assets, but layout still lacks a general solution: scene generation methods couple it with generation, and pose estimators handle one object at a time and need true-size CAD models, depth, or iterative refinement. We present X-3DComposer, a feed-forward model that predicts the layout separately from asset generation. Given one or more images of a scene, the object masks, and an asset for each object from any source, it jointly predicts the rotation, translation, and per-axis scale of all objects in a single forward pass of about one second. The key idea is to treat objects as views: renders of the assets are processed together with the scene images by a multi-view geometry model adapted from VGGT-$\Omega$, and each object pose follows in closed form from the cameras predicted for its renders. Camera intrinsics, camera poses, and depth are optional inputs. When the meshes produced by five scene generation methods are kept fixed and only their layout is replaced, the layouts of X-3DComposer are more accurate than the native layouts of these methods. Compared with the stand-alone layout model SceneMaker, it reduces the scene-level Chamfer distance by 52% on IndoorMix, our test set from six indoor datasets, and by 28% on 3D-FUTURE.
bullets: Separates scene layout prediction from asset generation, addressing a key limitation of existing 3D scene composition methods.
Takes one or more scene images, object masks, and one asset per object from any source.
Jointly predicts every object’s rotation, translation, and per-axis scale in a single forward pass of about one second.
Processes asset renders and scene images together with a multi-view geometry model, deriving poses in closed form from predicted cameras.
Improves fixed-asset scene layouts over native layouts from five scene-generation methods; reduces scene-level Chamfer distance versus SceneMaker by 52% on IndoorMix and 28% on 3D-FUTURE.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview. Scene views, object crops, and asset renders are processed as one set of views by a model adapted from VGGT-Ω. (a) The optional conditions and their encoders. (b) Object identity: the embeddings ei, added where the masks Mi lie, link the masks, crops, and renders of each object. The layout (Ri, ti, si) is read out in closed form from the predicted render cameras P̂i,m and log-scales ℓi,m.

Figure 10. Comparison with FoundationPose and PoseGAM on real HOPE photos. All methods use the same photo, intrinsics, groundtruth masks, and true-size object models; FoundationPose and our final model also use the sensor depth. papers.abstract: A faithful 4D reconstruction should capture both the shape and motion of objects, even when they disappear from view. Existing methods preserve previously observed geometry and extend motion through occlusion using local spatial and motion associations. However, treating short-term contact or shared motion as sufficient evidence of persistent rigidity can introduce incorrect motion constraints and distort overall reconstruction. To address this limitation, we present PRC4D, a physical relation-constrained framework that identifies reliable rigid relations and uses them to maintain spatial consistency through occlusion. PRC4D combines 3D contact and relative motion consistency with sequence-level verification to distinguish persistent couplings from transient interactions. The resulting graph guides observed-pose refinement and motion propagation from visible to occluded components without altering reconstructed geometry. Experiments on diverse real-world multi-object sequences and controlled occlusion simulations demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy, reduced relative pose errors, and more consistent object configurations under changing visibility.
authors: Junho Kim, Hyunyoung Choi, Jiseok Kim, Seongwon Lee
bullets: Addresses incorrect rigidity assumptions caused by transient contact or shared motion.
Combines 3D contact, relative-motion consistency, and sequence-level verification to identify persistent rigid relations.
Uses a relation graph to refine observed poses and propagate motion to occluded components without changing reconstructed geometry.
Experiments on real-world multi-object sequences and controlled occlusion simulations show improved accuracy, lower relative pose errors, and more consistent configurations under changing visibility.

papers.abstract: Neural architecture search and LLM-driven evolution often reduce evaluation to a scalar fitness score, discarding failures that could explain why designs succeed or fail. We present a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves, the loop identifies two principles for 3D medical image segmentation. First, reallocating computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin-anatomy boundaries while reducing cost. Second, support-confined region contrast addresses errors between nested anatomical compartments, with anatomy-dependent triggers selecting when the rule applies. These principles produce LeanNeXt (0.78 MACs and 0.92 training-step time relative to nnU-Net; +1.63 Dice points on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation) and trigger-routed LeanNeXt+. The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop shows how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.
authors: Songtao Jiang, Yuan Wang, Fucheng Niu, Hualiang Wang, Jian Wu, Zuozhu Liu
bullets: Scalar fitness-only search discards diagnostic failure information; the proposed loop analyzes structured errors and tests falsifiable architectural hypotheses.
Under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, agents use counterfactual controls to convert validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules.

The loop finds that shifting computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin boundaries while reducing cost, while support-confined region contrast helps separate nested compartments.
LeanNeXt reaches 0.78× nnU-Net MACs and 0.92× training-step time, with a +1.63 Dice-point gain on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation.
Trigger-routed LeanNeXt+ improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and surpasses the larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30× its parameter count.

papers.abstract: Many frameworks dealing with 3D (oriented) point clouds define locality in the ambient Euclidean space: $k$-nearest-neighbor graphs and radius balls in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are critical to define which points are "close to one another" and should exchange information. This can unintentionally merge sampled surfaces that are close in space but geometrically distinct such as the two faces of a thin leaf. Then, features are more prone to leak across boundaries which hinder performance. To address this, we propose to define a sub-Riemannian contact metric on position-orientation space $\mathbb{M}=\mathbb{R}^3\times \mathbb{S}^2$: points are lifted to $(x,n)$ with $n$ a surface normal, and "motion" is constrained to a non-holonomic horizontal distribution in which spatial velocity must stay in the plane orthogonal to the normal which can reorient at a cost. From this, we derive an explicit score, which locally approximate the distance, to compare oriented points for downstream tasks. We report improved segmentation and correspondence accuracy near contact when using the score as a drop-in change inside PointNet++ aggregation mechanism as well as reduced leakage when using it to simulate heat diffusion on oriented points.
bullets: Ambient-space neighborhoods can incorrectly connect geometrically distinct surfaces, such as opposite sides of a thin leaf.
The method lifts each point to position–orientation space, �mathbb{R}^3\times\mathbb{S}^2�, and constrains motion relative to surface normals.
An explicit local distance score compares oriented points for use in downstream processing.
Used within PointNet++ aggregation, the score improves segmentation and correspondence accuracy near contacts.
The score also reduces leakage in simulated heat diffusion on oriented points.

papers.abstract: Multi-view feed-forward models show strong scalability, but their reliance on costly geometric annotations limits data scaling. Existing 3D self-supervised approaches reduce this reliance through cross-view completion (e.g., CroCo, MuM, Muskie) or novel-view synthesis (e.g., RayZer, E-RayZer), typically learning image representations and cross-view interactions jointly. We argue that learning single image representations from scratch is unnecessary for 3D pretraining methods, as doing so fails to benefit from the continuing advances in 2D foundation models (e.g., DINO, CLIP, frontier VLMs). We introduce MaskedVGGT, which freezes a strong pretrained 2D encoder and pretrains only an added, randomly initialized multi-view transformer, focusing on learning interactions across views. MaskedVGGT pretrains the multi-view transformer through masked self-distillation without annotations: a student predicts targets at masked locations based on complete anchor views and heavily masked remaining views, while an exponential-moving-average teacher provides prediction targets based on unmasked inputs. In experiments across model sizes up to 1B parameters, MaskedVGGT pretraining followed by fine-tuning outperforms single-stage supervised VGGT-$\Omega$ training with the same training data, model architecture, and total number of optimization updates. MaskedVGGT also outperforms E-RayZer, CroCo, MuM, and Muskie, providing evidence for the effectiveness of building multi-view pretraining on strong 2D representations. Finally, extending pretraining with additional unlabeled videos further improves generalization, and the learned representations transfer to diverse downstream tasks. These results demonstrate an effective division of learning: reuse strong image representations from 2D pretraining and learn cross-view interactions from unlabeled multi-view data without relying on geometric annotations.
authors: Zichen Zou, Xiaosong Jia, Wen-Ming Chen, Zuxuan Wu, Yu-Gang Jiang
bullets: Addresses the annotation cost that limits scaling of supervised multi-view 3D learning.
Adds a randomly initialized multi-view transformer while reusing pretrained 2D image representations.
Trains with masked self-distillation: a student predicts masked views using complete anchor views, guided by an EMA teacher.
Outperforms supervised VGGT-Ω training and several prior self-supervised methods across model sizes up to 1B parameters.
Additional unlabeled videos improve generalization, with representations transferring to diverse downstream tasks.

papers.abstract: Dynamic Gaussian splatting is usually initialised either with random points or with a structure-from-motion (SfM) cloud of the first frame. Neither says anything about what moves, where and when. We introduce ST-SfM, a sparse spatio-temporal SfM for synchronised, calibrated multi-camera video that splits the scene into two branches. Static structure is detected once per camera on a temporal-median image, gated for temporal stability and matched along epi-polar lines. Motion is detected as space-time interest points (STIPs) in the video volume, described with HOG3D and matched only between candidates that agree both epipolarly and in time. Union-find tracks that refuse inconsistent merges are triangulated with RANSAC over all view pairs, giving static 3D points and dynamic 4D points (x, y, z, t) with sub-frame times. We use ST-SfM derived sparse 4D cloud to initialise 4D Gaussian splatting. In comparison with random initialisation on N3DV scenes we get improvements in PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS.
bullets: Addresses the lack of motion-aware initialization in existing dynamic Gaussian splatting pipelines.
Separates static and dynamic scene structure using temporally stable features and space-time interest points.
Matches features using epipolar and temporal consistency, then triangulates tracks with RANSAC.
Produces static 3D points and dynamic 4D points with sub-frame timestamps.
Improves PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS over random initialization on N3DV scenes.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian splats enable real-time rendering but require substantial storage. Existing compression methods either encode the primitives of a given splat or optimize a compact representation independently for each scene. Yet a Gaussian splat is only one realization of a scene: different arrangements of primitives can produce nearly identical rendered views. We exploit this freedom on the decoding side with SplatTok, a learned scene-resynthesis codec. Trained across thousands of real-world scenes, a transformer encodes an existing splat into compact, spatially anchored latent tokens, and a shared decoder synthesizes a new set of standard Gaussian primitives without preserving correspondence to the input. The representation is learned through rendering supervision rather than primitive reconstruction. At compression time, a quantization-aware latent search refines only the scene code, keeping the networks frozen, and closes most of the encoder's remaining error. On standard benchmarks, using only renders of the input splat for the latent search, without the original training images, SplatTok matches the PSNR of the feed-forward codec FCGS with 4 to 6.5 times smaller files, compressing input splats about 75 to 110 times. With the training images, it exceeds the PSNR of the per-scene method HAC++ with 13 to 41% smaller files. A single model trained on DL3DV generalizes to unseen scenes with millions of Gaussians and supports multiple target rates without retraining.
authors: Sai Karthikey Pentapati, Shashank Nelamangala Sridhara, Birendra Kathariya, Peng Yin, Guandao Yang, Alan C. Bovik
bullets: Addresses the high storage cost of 3D Gaussian splats and the unnecessary need to preserve primitive correspondence.
Uses a transformer encoder and shared decoder trained across real-world scenes with rendering-based supervision.
Performs quantization-aware latent search at compression time while keeping the networks frozen.
Matches FCGS quality with 4–6.5× smaller files using only input-splat renders, and surpasses HAC++ quality with 13–41% smaller files when training images are available.
A single model generalizes to unseen large scenes and supports multiple target rates without retraining.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic scenes from RGB video requires reasoning about both 3D geometry and motion across viewpoints, yet existing methods either split reconstruction and tracking into fragmented pipelines or face prohibitive dense spatiotemporal decoding costs. We introduce MoGe-4D, a feed-forward framework that unifies geometry and motion prediction via ordered queries of paired allocentric and egocentric dynamic point maps. Each query maps source pixels to a target time simultaneously in both camera frames, resolving relative camera pose in closed form while flexibly serving depth, dynamic registration, and dense 3D tracking. For efficient dense querying, MoGe-4D decouples scene modeling from query decoding: a high-capacity context encoder caches coarse global spatiotemporal features once, while a lightweight query encoder rapidly decodes dense point maps at flexible resolutions. Furthermore, as supervising dense 4D queries demands continuous 3D correspondences whose raw trajectory storage is prohibitive, we introduce RigIDTrack, a synthetic data pipeline and dataset that compresses surface dynamics into rigidity-regularized affine bodies, recovering exact arbitrary-frame 3D trajectories with $\sim15\%$ storage overhead over RGB-D video. Across diverse benchmarks, MoGe-4D achieves state-of-the-art dense 3D tracking, matches dedicated 3D foundation models in reconstruction, and runs substantially faster than prior 4D baselines.
authors: Ruicheng Wang, Linlin Xin, Sicheng Xu, Jianfeng Xiang, Zelong Lv, Yu Deng, Yue Dong, Guangzhong Sun, Tong Zhang, Jiaolong Yang
bullets: Predicts paired allocentric and egocentric dynamic point maps to jointly model geometry, motion, camera pose, depth, registration, and tracking.
Uses cached global spatiotemporal features plus a lightweight query encoder for efficient dense decoding at flexible resolutions.
Introduces RigIDTrack, a synthetic pipeline and dataset that represents surface dynamics with rigidity-regularized affine bodies and compact trajectory storage.
Reports state-of-the-art dense 3D tracking, reconstruction performance matching dedicated 3D foundation models, and substantially faster inference than prior 4D baselines.

papers.abstract: Geometric rotary position encodings (RoPE) incorporate 3D camera geometry into multi-view attention by rotating token features according to viewing rays, depths, and reprojected image coordinates. Each coordinate is rotated across a progression of frequencies--its frequency band--yet existing implementations leave this band to inherited defaults, either retaining standard 2D RoPE's top frequency or letting the frequency span grow exponentially with the attention head dimension. We show that this unstandardized setting can reverse benchmark rankings. In novel view synthesis on RealEstate10K, RayRoPE matches the strongest baseline in the 47M model (144-channel heads), yet trails by 1.2 dB in the 25M model (48-channel heads), and exhibits the same reversal when varying head size alone at fixed model width. Populating a 243x range with four frequencies instead of the 3x default at 48 channels recovers 0.9 dB of that gap. Across view synthesis and two-view depth estimation, overly narrow bands consistently blur correspondence, whereas all three projection-based encodings perform reliably when their top frequency lies within 0.3--3 rotations per 8-pixel patch (10--90 rotations across 256x256 RealEstate10K). At the opposite extreme, overly wide bands degrade RayRoPE through a forward-backward asymmetry: averaging rotations over a predicted depth interval damps high frequencies in the forward pass, yet leaves their gradients with respect to predicted depth undamped. Blocking only those high-frequency depth gradients recovers 90--93% of the lost PSNR, showing that forward smoothing does not guarantee backward stability. Guided by this analysis, we distill practical guidelines--setting bands in image coordinates, populating spans in small heads, and avoiding unconditional same-view damping--and advocate reporting and matching frequency bands in future multi-view benchmarks.
authors: Seonghyun Jin, Youngmin Kim, Jong Chul Ye
bullets: Unstandardized frequency bands can reverse benchmark rankings across model head sizes.
Narrow bands blur correspondences; reliable performance occurs when top frequencies span roughly 0.3–3 rotations per 8-pixel patch.
Very wide bands destabilize RayRoPE because high-frequency depth gradients remain undamped despite forward-pass smoothing.
Expanding a 48-channel band from a 3× to 243× span recovers 0.9 dB of a reported performance gap.
The study recommends image-coordinate band selection, denser frequency population in small heads, and avoiding unconditional same-view damping.

papers.abstract: Text-to-scene methods turn a short instruction into a furnished 3D room, but the room that a particular person wants rarely comes across fully in words: many preferences surface only when the person sees a concrete room and can point to what they like and dislike in it. We therefore study personalized indoor scene synthesis under hidden user preferences: over several turns, a system shows a 3D scene, and the user, who sees only rendered images of the scene, replies with brief free-form feedback and a satisfaction score. The system must therefore bring the whole room toward the user's preferences from feedback that comments on only part of it at a time. It must also be able to change every part of the room, because a preference concerns not only single objects but the look and atmosphere that surfaces, lighting, textiles, furniture and their arrangement create together. We present PreferenceScene, in which a large language model keeps an explicit estimate of the user's preferences for every design attribute of the room and, after each turn, infers the taste behind the feedback and revises the whole estimate, including the parts that the feedback does not mention. A scene instantiation module builds every estimated value as its own part of the room, so that each of these parts can follow the user's preferences. We evaluate on the test set of a benchmark with 320 instances in ten room types, with a simulated user and a render-based evaluator. PreferenceScene matches the hidden preferences better than five published text-to-scene baselines adapted to the same interaction, and its match rises with every turn. It even surpasses them when they are given the preferences directly, and a vision-language model rates its scenes as the most realistic and functional.
authors: Seongrae Noh, RyunHa Lee, HyeongYeop Kang
bullets: Addresses the gap between text instructions and preferences that emerge only after users view concrete rooms.
An LLM maintains and updates explicit preferences for every room design attribute, including unmentioned aspects.
A scene instantiation module applies these preferences across objects, lighting, textiles, surfaces, furniture, and layout.
On a 320-instance, 10-room-type benchmark with simulated users, preference matching improves over interaction turns.
It outperforms five adapted text-to-scene baselines and receives the highest realism and functionality ratings from a vision-language model.

papers.abstract: LiDAR reconstruction supports closed-loop autonomous driving simulation, but hours of per-scene optimization make large asset libraries costly to build and maintain. We present Instant LiDAR, a feed-forward pipeline that reconstructs multiple LiDAR scans as reusable Gaussian assets in minutes without per-scene optimization. LiDAR measurements provide strong geometric priors, but directly initializing Gaussians from them yields poor reconstruction due to nonuniform sampling and a limited field of view. Sparse returns leave surface gaps, while combining scans expands coverage but introduces redundant primitives. To address these challenges, Instant LiDAR combines measurement-anchored Gaussian prediction, sampling-aware Gaussian scales, and multi-frame consolidation. The predictor refines attributes anchored to recorded returns, while the scales adapt spatial support to LiDAR sampling. Multi-frame consolidation merges overlapping predictions into a compact asset spanning the driving log. Compared with NuRec, Instant LiDAR reconstructs scenes approximately 46 times faster on Physical AI (PAI) and 70 times faster on Waymo. It also achieves comparable downstream 3D detection accuracy on Waymo.
authors: Xin Kang, Jiahui Huang, Jiawei Ren, Sipeng Zhang, Yu Chen, Weihua Zhang, Junjie Lai
bullets: Eliminates costly per-scene optimization, reducing reconstruction to minutes.

Maintains comparable downstream 3D detection accuracy on Waymo.

papers.abstract: Generating 3D garments for digital characters requires preserving a reference design while adapting the garment to the target body's shape and pose. Sewing-pattern methods can struggle to reproduce unfamiliar designs and fine details, while image-to-3D generators offer rich shape priors but typically lack explicit 3D body context. We present \textbf{BodyWeave}, a framework that unifies garment generation and fitting through native 3D body conditioning. Building on 3D generative priors, BodyWeave uses the body as a spatial reference throughout geometry generation: a \textbf{Global Body Adapter} guides garment placement and extent in the shared coordinate frame, while \textbf{Local Body Attention} guides surface refinement using nearby body geometry. A \textbf{Surface Penetration Loss} supervises decoded surfaces to reduce body intersections, and the resulting geometry conditions material synthesis to produce garments with physically based rendering attributes. To support learning across designs and wearers, we construct \textbf{GarmentWeave3D} with 293K aligned garment--body observations, including 114K same-design cross-body pairs. Evaluations on out-of-domain \textbf{Artist-Created Garments} demonstrate high geometric fidelity and low body penetration. Cross-body evaluations demonstrate accurate adaptation to new wearers with consistent garment--body spacing, while appearance comparisons show faithful fabric reproduction. Additional results and resources are available at https://gavin-jy.github.io/bodyweave-page/
authors: Junyi Zhang, Yuanchuan Wang, Qichao Wang, Wenzhe Qian, Shizhuo Cheng, Min Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of preserving unfamiliar garment designs while adapting them to different body shapes and poses.
Uses a Global Body Adapter for garment placement and extent, plus Local Body Attention for nearby surface refinement.
Introduces a Surface Penetration Loss to reduce intersections between garments and bodies.

Reports high geometric fidelity, low penetration, accurate cross-body adaptation, and faithful fabric appearance on artist-created garments.

papers.abstract: The realistic rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has drawn interest from real-time applications that require maps to be built online. This led to coupling 3DGS with SLAM, providing camera poses and initial Gaussians for the map. However, the map is still optimized with designs inherited from conventional SLAM, which train only on keyframes selected for localization and regularize geometry with uncertain frontend depth. These designs overlook the model complexity of a 3DGS map: with millions of parameters but few views of each region, the map overfits to sparse inputs. Resolving this is challenging, as every view and Gaussian added to the map competes for the same real-time budget. We close this gap from both sides. To add views while keyframes preserve the structure of the map, we progressively admit non-keyframe images as mapping updates complete and allocate the limited updates across different groups of frames according to the supervision each group provides. To control the model complexity of the map, edge-guided initialization places new Gaussians where image detail requires them. To complement the uncertain frontend depth, Self-Referenced Opacity Regularization (SOR) uses accumulated rendering evidence, at no extra rendering cost, to suppress the opacity of Gaussians that persistently contribute in front of a map-derived surface reference. Together, these designs improve both the appearance and the geometry of online maps within the real-time budget.
authors: Dong Hwi Kim, Park Sangwon, Chaehyeon Song, Ayoung Kim
bullets: Online 3DGS maps can overfit because millions of parameters are optimized from sparse views under a real-time budget.
Non-keyframe images are progressively admitted after mapping updates, with updates allocated according to each frame group’s supervision value.
Edge-guided initialization adds new Gaussians where image detail requires greater representation capacity.
Self-Referenced Opacity Regularization suppresses Gaussians that persistently appear in front of a map-derived surface reference, complementing uncertain frontend depth.
The combined approach improves online-map appearance and geometry while preserving real-time constraints.

papers.abstract: Hands grasp objects with soft skin. A fingertip flattens against a mug, and a palm curves around a bottle. Yet hand-object datasets and estimators represent the hand as a rigid articulated mesh, which hovers above or penetrates the object where skin would press against it. Existing refiners keep the mesh rigid and adjust only the pose, trading pose accuracy for physical plausibility. We ask whether a rigid hand can instead touch the object as skin does while staying close to its original pose. We lift annotated or estimated rigid hands to contact-consistent meshes through an optimization that (i) slightly adjusts the joints and wrist to bring the fingers onto the object, (ii) deforms the skin so that penetrating regions settle onto the surface, and (iii) keeps this deformation consistent over time. Since deformation reaches only skin already near the object, we further train a lightweight head on the lifted annotations to predict where an estimated hand should touch and steer the deformation there. Unlike existing refiners, the lift more than doubles the skin lying on the object surface for three published estimators while barely changing the pose. Guidance from the learned head further improves grasp stability by closing contact gaps that the estimate leaves open. Existing hand-object datasets and estimators can thus adopt contact-consistent hands without changing the hand model or retraining the estimators.
bullets: Rigid hand meshes often hover above or penetrate objects instead of modeling soft-skin contact.
The method jointly makes small joint/wrist adjustments, settles penetrating skin onto object surfaces, and enforces temporal consistency.
A lightweight learned head predicts likely contact regions to guide deformation of estimated hands.
The lifted meshes more than double skin coverage on object surfaces across three published estimators with minimal pose change.
The approach improves grasp stability and works with existing hand models and estimators without retraining them.

papers.selection_reason: Contact-consistent hand mesh deformation is directly relevant to manipulation and 3D hand-object modeling.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing the 3D poses of hands and objects from a single image, together with the contact between them, is fundamental to understanding manipulation. To be practical, the reconstruction must generalize to unseen objects, and the contact must be localized precisely. Yet joint feed-forward estimators often rely on predefined object sets, while contact is typically predicted from image features alone, without the explicit geometry needed to localize it. To address both limitations, we present HORCRUX, a unified feed-forward transformer with coarse-to-fine contact estimation. For unseen objects, a frozen foundation model encodes the object from a given or image-reconstructed mesh rather than from object-specific knowledge. A shared transformer then reasons jointly over the object and one or two hands to keep them aligned. For precise contact, coarse per-joint predictions from latent features are resolved over finer hand regions using the reconstructed geometry. Across seven benchmarks, HORCRUX achieves state-of-the-art object and hand pose accuracy among joint estimators and outperforms a dedicated contact estimator in fine-grained contact. These results suggest that contact is best estimated jointly with reconstruction, whose geometry directly localizes it.
authors: Seonghwan Park, Yong-Hoon Kwon, Min-Gyu Park
bullets: Addresses two limitations: dependence on predefined object sets and imprecise contact prediction from image features alone.
Uses a frozen foundation model to encode given or image-reconstructed object meshes for unseen-object generalization.
A shared transformer jointly reasons over the object and one or two hands to maintain alignment.
Refines coarse per-joint contact predictions over fine hand regions using reconstructed geometry.
On seven benchmarks, achieves state-of-the-art joint hand/object pose accuracy and outperforms a dedicated contact estimator in fine-grained contact.

papers.title: Generalizable Feed-Forward 3D Hand-Object Reconstruction with Coarse-to-Fine Contact Estimation

papers.abstract: 3D foundation models (3DFMs) enable dense reconstruction in a feed-forward pass, yet their effective span is limited by cross-view attention. Local consistency has been expanded through geometric alignment of video chunks and recursive updates of an implicit memory, and large-scale scenes with pose graphs. However, both strategies are prone to drift, largely due to the lack of metric-scale observability from monocular geometry. We present Xtream,a hybrid streaming pipeline that maintains an explicit metric state through a factor graph over keyframes, while using a 3DFM as a geometric front end. Xtream incorporates metric information in two ways: through metric scale predictions from 3DFMs; or through inertial measurements if available. Across the large-scale benchmarks of VBR, Oxford Spires and KITTI, Xtream achieves state-of-the-art performance in 3DFM-based online reconstruction, reducing average absolute trajectory errors compared with published baselines and concurrent work. https://ernestolozano.github.io/xtream
authors: Ernesto Lozano, Alberto Jaenal, Javier Civera
bullets: Addresses drift in long-range reconstruction caused by limited cross-view attention and unobservable monocular metric scale.
Uses a 3D foundation model as a geometric front end within a streaming pipeline.
Maintains an explicit metric state over keyframes using a factor graph.
Incorporates metric scale from 3D foundation models or inertial measurements when available.
Evaluated on VBR, Oxford Spires, and KITTI, with lower average absolute trajectory errors than published baselines and concurrent work.

papers.title: Xtream: An Explicit Metric State for Large-Scale Streaming Reconstruction
papers.tldr: Xtream enables drift-resistant large-scale streaming 3D reconstruction by combining a 3D foundation model with an explicit metric factor-graph state.

papers.abstract: Pretrained latent diffusion models are effective priors for transfer learning, from geometry estimation to physics simulation. Existing approaches fine-tune the diffusion backbone but freeze the encoder of the VAE to preserve the latent distribution. However, a frozen encoder may miss salient details in non-RGB inputs and is limited to three channels. We introduce Diffusion Prior Anchoring (DPA), a regularizer applied during VAE fine-tuning that uses a score-distillation update to steer latents toward the high-density manifold on which the pretrained diffusion model denoises accurately. We validate DPA across three image and video models (FLUX 3, LTX-Video, Wan2.2) and four tasks: monocular depth estimation, MRI reconstruction, wind-flow simulation, and surface normal estimation, where DPA lowers the prediction error by 7.5% relative to the frozen VAE, 4.9% to decoder-only fine-tuning, and 4.0% to unanchored VAE fine-tuning. Its gain grows the further the target data lies from the RGB training distribution, from 3.3% on monocular depth estimation to 7.2% on complex-valued MRI. DPA also applies to modified VAEs, including pruned and multi-channel variants. With a four-channel VAE that encodes depth and surface normals, it lowers depth estimation error by 9.3%.

bullets: Frozen VAE encoders preserve the latent distribution but can miss task-specific details and are restricted to three channels.
DPA regularizes VAE fine-tuning with score-distillation updates that steer latents toward the diffusion model’s high-density denoising manifold.
Across three image/video models and four tasks, DPA reduces prediction error by 7.5% versus a frozen VAE.
Benefits increase as data departs from RGB, reaching 7.2% on complex-valued MRI; DPA also supports pruned and multi-channel VAEs.
A four-channel VAE for depth and surface normals achieves a 9.3% reduction in depth-estimation error.

papers.abstract: Learning spatial representations often relies on explicitly predicting geometric quantities, but how physical geometry is organized within learned representations remains less understood. We ask whether 3D structure can emerge from learning relations across 2D observations, without 3D prediction targets. We introduce RePT, which learns compact relations between distinct physical points through cross-view 2D point prediction. The learned relation space develops a geometric organization in which magnitudes, angles, and neighborhoods reflect physical 3D displacement. A single linear readout fitted on 16 scenes recovers displacement length and angle on 39 held-out scenes without refitting (Pearson r = 0.72 and 0.78). The ARKitScenes-trained checkpoint also retains strong geometric organization on ScanNet++, showcasing generalizability. In controlled comparisons, distinct-point relational prediction consistently yields stronger geometric organization than matched same-point correspondence learning. This organization depends on additive relations and adaptive scene context, and higher point-transfer accuracy does not by itself produce stronger organization. More broadly, our results suggest that 3D geometry need not be an explicit prediction target and can instead emerge as a structural property of representations trained to relate 2D observations, pointing to relational prediction as a complementary route to learning the representations that spatial intelligence builds on.
authors: Xize Duan, Binke Hou, Xingqiao Huang, Xinyuan Guan, Jiaxin Huang, Kaiyuan Hu, Zipeng Sun, Hong Kang, Meng Bi, Xue Liu, Yili Jin
bullets: Learns compact relations between distinct physical points using cross-view 2D point prediction.

A linear readout trained on 16 scenes generalizes to 39 held-out scenes, recovering displacement length and angle (Pearson r = 0.72 and 0.78).
Geometry remains organized across ARKitScenes and ScanNet++, and distinct-point relational prediction outperforms matched same-point correspondence learning in controlled comparisons.
Organization depends on additive relations and adaptive scene context; point-transfer accuracy alone is insufficient.

papers.abstract: Initialization-free bundle adjustment (InitFree BA) aims to jointly recover camera poses and scene structure without requiring an initial global estimate. It is a very challenging problem, especially compared to traditional BA where a good estimation is assumed. While recent methods optimize surrogate Object Space Error (OSE) objectives from random initialization, a low objective value does not necessarily yield an accurate reconstruction, revealing a gap between optimization and reconstruction. We show that existing InitFree BA pipelines struggle to produce accurate 3D reconstructions on modern SfM benchmarks, and demonstrate that incorporating learned metric depth substantially improves their practical feasibility. We introduce InitFree-SfM, a complete initialization-free SfM pipeline combining learned correspondences, metric depth, depth-consistent track construction, and joint metric refinement. Within this framework, we propose a simple depth-augmented OSE (dOSE), which complements the directional constraints of OSE by constraining landmark positions along their viewing rays. Our approach substantially outperforms existing InitFree BA methods and achieves competitive accuracy with established SfM pipelines, including on challenging low-overlap image collections. Importantly, our analysis challenges the prevailing emphasis on surrogate objectives in previous InitFree BA research, revealing that geometric constraints play a central role in accurate reconstruction, while OSE-based optimization provides further improvements.
authors: Simon Weber, Mateo de Mayo, Je Hyeong Hong, Carl Olsson, Daniel Cremers, Ronald Clark
bullets: Addresses the gap between low surrogate-objective values and accurate 3D reconstruction in initialization-free bundle adjustment.
Combines learned correspondences, metric depth, depth-consistent tracks, and joint metric refinement.
Introduces depth-augmented OSE (dOSE) to constrain landmark positions both directionally and along viewing rays.
Substantially outperforms prior initialization-free BA methods and reaches competitive accuracy with established SfM pipelines, including on low-overlap image collections.
Finds that geometric constraints are central to reconstruction accuracy, while OSE optimization provides additional gains.

Overall, our simple yet effective pipeline offers a new perspective on initialization-free BA, highlighting the central role of geometric constraints beyond surrogate objective optimization.

papers.abstract: Multi-view 3D foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D points from a set of photos in one forward pass. Many cameras store a portrait shot sideways, with an orientation tag telling viewers how to turn it, and this tag can be ignored, lost or wrong. We measure how rotated photos affect five such models on three datasets. A few rotated photos lower camera pose accuracy for every model, and the sideways photos already in a standard benchmark do the same. Even the most robust model still loses accuracy. The failure is also silent: the models' confidence does not reliably flag it, and most official image loaders ignore the tag. The fixes we test each correct only part of the problem. These findings call for orientation checks in reconstruction pipelines and benchmarks.
bullets: Evaluates five multi-view 3D foundation models across three datasets under photo-rotation errors.
Even a few rotated images reduce camera-pose accuracy for every tested model.
Sideways photos already present in a standard benchmark also harm performance.
Model confidence does not reliably reveal the failure, while common image loaders may ignore orientation tags.
Tested corrections address only part of the issue, motivating orientation checks in pipelines and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Characterizing how tornadoes evolve over space and time is critically important for understanding and preparing for these highly destructive weather events. Towards this end, we develop algorithms capable of forming time-resolved 3D reconstructions of laboratory smoke tornadoes from sparse one-sided videos. Even in a controlled environment, reconstruction is severely underconstrained: appearance is view dependent, motion is non-rigid, and the unobserved volume admits many geometries. We present Tornado4D, a physics-guided 4D Gaussian framework capable of reconstructing laboratory tornadoes from sparse, one-sided videos. Tornado4D uses knowledge of the enclosure geometry to introduce rotational airflow field priors that constrain how the 3D structure evolves over time. These rotational priors allow us to reconstruct otherwise unobserved structure. We evaluate reconstruction accuracy by computing novel-view synthesis accuracy on a held out camera view: Tornado4D outperforms frame-by-frame 3DGS and video-based 4DGS by a considerable margin.
authors: Yucheng Zhu, Maria J. Molina, Christopher Metzler
bullets: Addresses the underconstrained reconstruction of non-rigid, view-dependent tornado smoke from limited observations.
Uses enclosure geometry to impose rotational airflow constraints on evolving 3D Gaussian structure.
Recovers otherwise unobserved tornado structure over space and time.
Evaluated using novel-view synthesis on a held-out camera view.
Outperforms frame-by-frame 3DGS and video-based 4DGS by a considerable margin.

Advection-guided multi-frame supervision refines the canonical state, causal dynamic reconstruction combines CFD advection with learned residuals, and post-training calibration adjusts the opacity of the reconstructed tornado.

Figure 7. Novel-view comparison across methods. All methods are trained with all cameras and rendered at t = 20. Columns rotate from the enclosure-facing front view to 180◦. Ours maintains a coherent volumetric funnel across viewpoints, whereas 3DGS and 4DGS exhibit substantial artifacts away from the front.

Figure 8. Temporal novel-view comparison. From the fixed enclosure-facing front view, we render Ours, independently trained per-frame 3DGS, and 4DGS at five time points. Ours preserves a coherent funnel throughout the sequence with fewer floating and dark artifacts.

The field captures the dominant rotation and upward transport used by both reconstruction stages, while learned residual velocities correct local mismatch to the observed smoke.

papers.abstract: Gaussian splatting from sparse training views renders high-quality images near training views, but reconstruction quality degrades at distant regions, which are undersampled by the training set. Feed-forward novel view synthesis (NVS) models use strong learned priors to resample the scene from substantially different viewpoints, but they take more than ten times as long to render and produce high-frequency artifacts on out-of-domain scenes. We propose a plug-and-play method that enhances an existing sparse-view Gaussian model with a pretrained feed-forward NVS model. We observe that the two are complementary in the frequency domain: the prior is more accurate at low frequencies, and the Gaussians at high frequencies. The reliability of the prior relative to the Gaussians is inversely proportional to the image frequency, so the optimal fusion weight is a first-order low-pass filter with one parameter that can be fitted. Our key idea is then to intelligently fuse the reliable part of each of the two methods. To remove the slow feed-forward model at render time, we use these fused images as teachers and distill them back into Gaussians, balanced with supervision from input views. Our method improves the quality of various sparse-view Gaussian methods without sacrificing rendering speed, and our analysis works on different prior models. Project page: https://linwk20.github.io/spectral-fusion-gs/
authors: Weikai Lin, Jun Dai, Sheng Zhao, Junjie Zhao, Yuhao Zhu
bullets: Sparse-view Gaussian splatting degrades in undersampled, distant regions, while feed-forward NVS models are slower and can produce high-frequency artifacts.
The method exploits complementary frequency behavior: feed-forward priors provide more reliable low frequencies, whereas Gaussians preserve high-frequency details.
A fitted first-order low-pass filter determines frequency-dependent fusion weights between the two representations.
Fused outputs serve as teachers for distilling the improvement back into Gaussians, with input-view supervision retained.
The plug-and-play approach improves multiple sparse-view Gaussian methods without sacrificing rendering speed and generalizes across prior models.

papers.abstract: Incompressible diffeomorphic registration requires continuous spatial mappings that preserve local tissue volume (det(D\Phi) = 1) without topological folding (det(D\Phi) > 0). Standard velocity-field methods (SVF, LDDMM) approximate incompressibility via numerical ODE integration or soft penalties, exhibiting numerical volume drift (~10^-4 to 10^-1), iterative grid inversions, and linear backpropagation memory O(L * N_vox). We formulate an exact structure-preserving framework for 3D registration based on cascaded coordinate shears. By decomposing the divergence-free Lie algebra sdiff(\Omega) into six coordinate-shear generators whose convective non-linearities vanish identically, each elementary stage integrates analytically to a closed-form triangular shear with det(DS_k) = 1 and exact machine-precision inverse requiring zero iterations and zero spatial interpolations. Multi-stage compositions generate the connected volume-preserving group SDiff_0(\Omega). We establish: (i) an unconditional global diffeomorphism proof closing the Hadamard-Caccioppoli injectivity gap; (ii) a Dirichlet boundary confinement lemma; (iii) an anisotropic Riemannian similarity invariance; (iv) a Sobolev H^2 spectral budget preventing chaotic mixing; and (v) an exact reversible backpropagation engine eliminating O(L) trajectory storage (0.00 MB intermediate activations). We prove second-order O(h^2) sub-voxel convergence across 16^3 to 64^3 lattices and second-order trajectory accuracy for palindromic Strang splitting (468.1x error reduction vs. Lie-Trotter; drift |det(D\Phi)-1| <= 2.22e-16). Execution is 2.1x-4.0x faster than SVF with 78.4% GPU memory reduction. On cardiac cine-MRI (ACDC, N=100) and brain MRI (OASIS-1, N=414), our model achieves competitive Dice (0.884 and 0.841) while strictly maintaining 0.0000% folding and zero volume drift.
bullets: Addresses numerical volume drift, folding risk, iterative inversion, and trajectory-memory costs in incompressible diffeomorphic registration.
Uses six divergence-free coordinate-shear generators composed into analytically invertible triangular transformations with unit Jacobian.
Provides theoretical guarantees including global diffeomorphism, boundary confinement, similarity invariance, and limits on chaotic mixing.
Palindromic Strang splitting achieves second-order trajectory accuracy; the abstract reports zero folding and machine-precision volume preservation.
On ACDC and OASIS-1, it reports competitive Dice scores of 0.884 and 0.841, with faster execution and reduced GPU memory versus SVF.

papers.abstract: Event cameras register brightness changes pixel by pixel with microsecond precision, whereas the dense depth that could supervise them is costly to acquire and exists only at isolated instants. Condensing the stream into frames eases learning, but at the expense of the very timing that sets event sensing apart. We propose a self-supervised approach in which each event is assigned its own depth in continuous time, and the camera motion is recovered from the same observations. Supervision arises from geometry: lifted into 3D by its predicted depth and displaced by the camera motion at the instant it fired, an event should coincide with others produced by the same edge, so any misalignment exposes an error in depth or motion. Differentiable rendering then turns these per-event estimates into dense depth maps at target times within each window, faithful to the events behind them. On MVSEC, the approach outperforms prior event-only self-supervised methods in most sequences and depth ranges, with the widest margins at night, and recovers camera rotation more accurately than an earlier unsupervised event-based method. Ablations isolate the roles of local spatiotemporal context, the temporal backbone, and the alignment objective. These results position motion-compensated event alignment as a principled source of supervision for continuous-time depth and ego-motion estimation.
bullets: Addresses costly, temporally sparse depth supervision while preserving the microsecond timing of event cameras.
Predicts each event’s depth and the camera pose at its firing time, then uses geometric alignment of shared edges as supervision.
Uses differentiable rendering to convert per-event estimates into dense depth maps at chosen times.
On MVSEC, outperforms prior event-only self-supervised methods across most sequences and depth ranges, especially at night.
Also improves camera-rotation accuracy over an earlier unsupervised event-based method; ablations examine context, temporal modeling, and alignment.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Continuous-Time Depth Learning and Ego-Motion Estimation from Asynchronous Events
papers.tldr: A self-supervised method jointly estimates continuous-time per-event depth and camera motion by aligning motion-compensated events, producing dense depth maps without synchronized depth labels.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward geometry models such as VGGT recover camera parameters, depth maps, and point maps from one to hundreds of views in a single forward pass, making them powerful backbones for multi-view 3D perception. However, VGGT's global attention is quadratic in the number of frames and dominates end-to-end runtime on long sequences, which has motivated a range of training-free efficiency methods such as token merging. These methods, however, come with a drop in accuracy that makes them hard to use in place of VGGT. We propose GPA-VGGT, a training-free acceleration method that replaces global attention in early blocks with frame attention augmented by a shared cross-frame K/V set. In the remaining blocks, we merge only keys and values while preserving all queries, restore the attention mass of the tokens each merged key represents, and randomly project the matching metric to 128 dimensions to reduce matching cost. Across diverse multi-view geometry tasks, GPA-VGGT provides training-free acceleration at speedups comparable to prior work while preserving the information required for precise geometric estimation, retaining over 99% of VGGT's pose accuracy under AUC@3.
bullets: Targets VGGT’s quadratic global-attention runtime on long multi-view sequences.
Uses frame attention with shared cross-frame keys/values in early blocks.
Later merges only keys and values, preserves all queries, and restores represented-token attention mass.
Randomly projects the matching metric to 128 dimensions to reduce matching overhead.
Achieves speedups comparable to prior training-free methods across multi-view geometry tasks while preserving precise estimation.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of GPA-VGGT. Early blocks 0–8 replace global attention with frame attention augmented by a shared cross-frame K/V set containing special tokens and content-adaptive pooled image-token summaries. Later blocks 9–23 preserve all queries and merge only K/V tokens, using a weaker merge ratio in the core blocks 13–16. (a) Pooled summaries are constructed by assigning patch tokens to stride-8 seeds according to cosine similarity and averaging the K/V tokens within each content-adaptive cluster; the summary size determines the + log s correction. (b) K/V matching is computed after a 128-dimensional Gaussian projection, while all queries are retained for global attention.

Figure 5. Qualitative reconstruction under estimated camera poses. Each column shows the point cloud produced by the corresponding method, and red boxes indicate the enlarged regions below. GPA-VGGT most closely matches the geometry reconstructed by vanilla VGGT.

Figure 2. Two sources of accuracy degradation in existing token-merging methods. Top: Query merging collapses the block-12 outputs of 83 tokens into 12 shared outputs, whereas retaining all queries while merging only K/V preserves the output diversity of the unmerged model. Bottom: Omitting the + log s correction disproportionately allocates attention to the first frame. Restoring the correction recovers an attention distribution close to that of the unmerged model.

Figure 1. Accuracy and runtime scaling with the number of input frames. Although existing acceleration methods substantially reduce end-to-end runtime, they incur pronounced camera-pose degradation under the strict AUC@3 metric. GPA-VGGT achieves comparable runtime while maintaining camera-pose accuracy close to that of vanilla VGGT.

Figure 3. Effect of cross-frame context in the early blocks. Top: Replacing global attention with frame attention substantially displaces the block-8 output field from the full-global-attention reference, whereas the shared cross-frame K/V set largely preserves it. Bottom: Pairwise alignment of per-frame drift directions. Cross-frame special tokens partially align the drift, and image-token summaries further reduce its variation, preserving a coherent geometric reference across views.

papers.abstract: Radiology reports describe findings in text only, without visually marking them on the scan, so readers cannot directly see which abnormality each reported finding refers to. We introduce CTLink, a text-prompted 3D segmentation model that segments findings described in a chest CT report. CTLink was trained on 4123 noncontrast chest CT scans with 9547 segmented report findings, including ReXGroundingCTv2, a newly annotated dataset of 1134 scans and 1895 findings with every instance of each finding segmented. On the 200 ReXGroundingCT validation scans, CTLink achieved a hit rate of 0.816, an instance F1 score of 0.456, and a mean Dice score of 0.400, compared with 0.533, 0.175, and 0.234 for VoxTell, a publicly available text-prompted segmentation model (P < .001 for all). On the test set of the MICCAI 2026 ReXGrounding challenge, an ensemble of seven CTLink models achieved the highest hit rate (0.782) and instance F1 score (0.386) of all 48 participating teams. On 50 test scans segmented twice by independent radiologists, CTLink matched or exceeded inter-rater agreement. Diffuse non-focal findings remained the main limitation, partly because their extent is outlined inconsistently even between radiologists. The CTLink model weights are available at https://huggingface.co/rajpurkarlab/CTLink, and the dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGroundingCT.

Introduces a 3D text-prompted segmentation model trained on 4,123 noncontrast chest CT scans and 9,547 segmented findings.

papers.abstract: Generative Pre-Training (GPT) represents a profound milestone in natural language processing, serving as the foundation for most of today's state-of-the-art large language models. By casting diverse understanding and generation problems into a shared token representation, GPT enables a single architecture and unified optimization loop to master heterogeneous tasks across massive corpora, giving rise to powerful foundation models for natural language. In contrast, 4D spatiotemporal vision lacks a common representational protocol: perception (such as depth and camera estimation) and generation are either handled by separate one-way pipelines or bolted together from unaligned single-modality spaces. In this work, we introduce WorldLatent, a framework that formulates a unified 4D latent space as a common protocol for both world perception and generation. Rather than relying on fragmented, task-specific models or stacked single-modality representations, our framework proposes a multimodal VAE architecture that compresses and fuses complex 4D visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into a single structured latent representation. Within this formulation, perception and generation operate as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space, enabling one generative model to learn both capabilities simultaneously within a single training loop. Experiments across representative 4D benchmarks verify that our fused latent protocol achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent 4D generation, and controllable editing from a single model. By demonstrating that diverse 4D tasks can be seamlessly unified under a shared representational protocol, our work provides a scalable foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.
authors: Jingxi Chen, Yujia Chen, Cornelia Fermuller, Yiannis Aloimonos, Wen-Sheng Chu, Du Tran
bullets: Addresses the lack of a common representation for 4D spatiotemporal vision.
Uses a multimodal VAE to fuse visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into one structured latent representation.
Frames perception and generation as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space.
A single model achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent generation, and controllable editing across representative benchmarks.
Positions the shared latent protocol as a foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.

figures.caption: Figure 2. WorldLatent training pipeline. (a) WorldVAE training: Multiple 4D spatiotemporal modalities, including monocular RGB video, depth maps, and camera Plücker coordinates (ray direction d and moment m), are compressed via modality-specific encoders (E1– E4) and fused by a Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT) into a unified latent bottleneck, z4d (WorldLatent). Modality-specific decoders (D1–D4) then reconstruct the original modalities from this shared latent space. (b) Any-to-4D generative modeling: With the WorldVAE frozen, a unified diffusion model is trained within the learned latent space. It takes Gaussian noise, text prompts (Ctext), and partial or empty 4D latents c4d(S) (e.g., S = ∅ for text-to-4D generation, RGB-only for perception, or depth-only for editing) to synthesize the full 4D latent z4d. Finally, the frozen decoders (D1–D4) map z4d back into temporally coherent video, 3D geometry, and camera trajectories.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of zero-shot video depth estimation. Results are shown across the MPI Sintel, Bonn, and ScanNet datasets. For each clip, we display the input RGB frames, ground-truth depth, predictions from the teacher model (DA3-Giant) and WorldLatent-14B (Ours).

Figure 5. Any-to-4D: text-to-4D world generation with WorldLatent. Given only a text prompt, our model jointly denoises appearance, depth, and camera rays from noise, producing an RGB video together with aligned depth maps and a 3D scene with camera trajectory.

Figure 4. Any-to-4D: world editing and depth-conditioned re-rendering with WorldLatent. (1) Given an input RGB video, our model first performs 4D perception to estimate dense depth maps. (2) Conditioned on these predicted depth maps and new text prompts, the same model then performs 4D re-rendering to synthesize appearance-edited RGB videos. For each example, we show the input video, the predicted depth and camera outputs from our 4D perception stage, and the re-rendered videos across diverse text prompts.

Figure 6. Linear subspace decomposition of WorldLatent. Visualization across videos re-rendered from an identical depth sequence under different text prompts (Row 1). The 16-D appearance projection Π∥z4d (Row 2) varies markedly with visual style, whereas the orthogonal 16-D geometry-and-camera projection Π⊥z4d (Row 3) remains nearly invariant.

Figure 7. Additional 4D perception visual results. Qualitative video depth comparison on KITTI [14] (Top) and Sintel (Bottom). Panels (from left to right, top to bottom) show: input RGB, ground-truth depth, WorldLatent-14B (Ours), DA3-Giant (Teacher), VGGT-1B, CUT3R-512, MonST3R, DUSt3R, MASt3R, Video-Depth-Anything-L, DepthCrafter, Marigold-v1.1, and Metric-VDA-Large.
Figure 8. Additional 4D perception visual results. Qualitative video depth comparison on Bonn (Top) and ScanNet (Bottom), panel layout follows Fig. 7.

Figure 9. Additional depth-conditioned re-rendering results. For each input RGB video (kitchen inspection, cloth folding, and multihuman tracking), we show our estimated depth maps and 3D geometry with camera poses (top row). The estimated depth is then combined with two new text prompts to re-render the scene (bottom row), changing its appearance while keeping its geometry and motion.
Figure 10. Additional text-based 4D generation results. For each text prompt, we show the generated RGB video (top), depth maps (middle), and 3D geometry with camera poses (bottom).

Table 2. Comparison with state-of-the-art methods on 4D perception. Zero-shot evaluation across dynamic and static multi-domain datasets under scale-and-shift alignment. Evaluated capabilities include (1) Depth estimation, (2) camera Pose estimation, (3) 4D Generation, and (4) controllable Re-rendering/editing from depth maps. +GA denotes the test-time global alignment optimization used by baseline methods. Bold and underlined values indicate the best and second-best results, respectively. WorldLatent performs comparably to dedicated 3D/4D perception specialists, while providing additional capabilities for generation and re-rendering.

Table 1. 4D WorldVAE reconstruction quality and efficiency. WorldVAE jointly compresses RGB, depth, and camera rays into the exact the numbers of DiT tokens as an RGB-only VAE while enabling high-fidelity 4D reconstruction.

papers.tldr: WorldLatent unifies 4D perception and generation in a shared latent space, allowing one model to perform both tasks and support controllable 4D editing.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based view synthesis models render each target viewpoint from the source images, without an explicit 3D representation, which lets them reproduce fine detail and view-dependent effects. However, their decoder attends to every source token for every frame, so rendering slows with each source image. Rasterization avoids this by culling primitives that the viewpoint does not see, but source tokens cannot be culled this way, as they have no explicit position or extent. Our key insight is that source tokens are nonetheless spatial anchors: each encodes a local region of the scene, so the decoder's attention for any viewpoint concentrates on a few of them. A lightweight router predicts these tokens from the source tokens and the viewpoint, and the decoder attends only to a fixed budget of top-ranked tokens, so its cost no longer depends on the number of source tokens. We supervise the router with the decoder's attention, using non-maximum suppression to demote redundant tokens. With 24 source images and two views' worth of tokens, our model renders 6.4 times faster than LagerNVS, at a PSNR only 0.68 dB lower. One ranking serves every budget, so the budget can change at render time.
bullets: Source tokens act as local spatial anchors, enabling viewpoint-dependent token culling without explicit 3D geometry.
A lightweight router ranks tokens using source features and the target viewpoint; the decoder attends only to a fixed top-token budget.
Router training uses decoder attention supervision and non-maximum suppression to reduce redundant selections.
With 24 source images, rendering is 6.4× faster than LagerNVS while achieving PSNR only 0.68 dB lower.
A single token ranking supports changing the compute budget at render time.

papers.abstract: Large image-to-3D generators recover detailed heads from a single photograph but treat every image as a new object. For several images of one person, they hallucinate unseen regions independently without using information from the other images. We present Head Anything, which generates detailed head meshes from a few images with changing expressions and viewpoints. Instead of training a multi-image prior, we turn a pretrained single-image generator with a native 3D latent space into a joint generator that denoises all images together. Since global attention between images is hard to learn from scarce 3D head data, lightweight correspondence-attention adapters let every 3D token attend only to its corresponding points in the other images. We obtain correspondences by fitting a neural parametric head model to the generator's own single-image outputs, requiring no ground truth at test time. Training on both ground-truth and fitted correspondences makes the adapters robust to fitting errors. Each mesh stays pixel-aligned with its own image and borrows the unseen regions from all others. On head scans, Head Anything lowers the head Chamfer distance of the best image-to-3D generator by 32% and its cross-frame inconsistency by 47%, and its meshes improve face tracking. Code and models will be released.
authors: Umut Kocasari, Bart{\l}omiej Baranowski, Richard Shaw, Eduardo P\'erez-Pellitero, Matthias Nie{\ss}ner
bullets: Addresses the problem of single-image 3D generators hallucinating unseen head regions independently across images of the same person.
Converts a pretrained single-image 3D generator into a joint multi-image denoiser using lightweight correspondence-attention adapters.
Derives correspondences by fitting a neural parametric head model to the generator’s own outputs, without test-time ground truth.
Maintains pixel alignment for each image while borrowing unseen regions from the others.
On head scans, reduces Chamfer distance by 32% and cross-frame inconsistency by 47%, while improving face tracking.

The details of correspondence attention and how it is applied in each stage are shown in Fig. 3.

Figure 4. Mesh generation comparison on NeRSemble, AVA-256, VFHQ and CelebV-HQ. Our meshes, rendered with surface normals in the input camera, have a better surface quality than those of the baselines.

Figure 3. Correspondence attention. (a) Φf→g maps a token position p of frame f to its corresponding point in frame g. (b) Keys are sampled trilinearly in S1 and taken from the K nearest occupied tokens in S2.
