papers.abstract: Live free-viewpoint video streaming of humans enables immersive telepresence and interactive XR applications. However, this requires reconstructing each frame in real time, transmitting the data within strict bandwidth budgets, and decoding it on lightweight client GPUs. Existing approaches, whether relying on per-frame optimization or feed-forward inference, generate massive 3D Gaussian payloads that exceed practical streaming limits, while aggressive compression severely degrades rendering quality. In this work, we present HoloSplat, a real-time streaming framework for human-centric volumetric video. HoloSplat splits a feed-forward reconstructor before its Gaussian head, introducing a multi-rate streaming codec driven by server-side token compression and client-side token restoration. On the server side, we apply opacity-guided token pruning, PCA-based dimensionality reduction, and lossless geometry coding for token anchors. On the client side, a feature reconstruction hypernetwork is fused into the Gaussian head to recover compression-induced quality loss. Furthermore, we introduce Neural Session Calibration (NSC), which rapidly fine-tunes the Gaussian head online using incoming camera views during a warm-up phase. This resolves quality degradation from novel camera parameters and varying capture conditions with zero per-frame overhead. In our evaluations, HoloSplat averages 32.2 FPS on four RTX 5090 GPUs at 50 Mbit/s. It decodes each frame into 3D Gaussians in 22.1 ms on an RTX 3050 Ti laptop GPU, transmitting 22.8$\times$ less data than uncompressed float32 Gaussians, while calibrated decoding improves PSNR by 1.050 dB.
authors: Chaofan Li, Qihan Ding, Shihan Wang, Zhehao Shen, Boyu Shen, Quanyu Chen, Haoyu Wu, Lan Xu, Xin Lou
bullets: Targets the challenge of streaming feed-forward 3D Gaussian human reconstructions under strict bandwidth and lightweight-client constraints.
Splits the reconstructor before its Gaussian head and uses multi-rate token streaming with server-side compression and client-side restoration.
Combines opacity-guided pruning, PCA reduction, lossless anchor geometry coding, and a feature-reconstruction hypernetwork.
Neural Session Calibration fine-tunes the Gaussian head during warm-up to handle novel cameras and changing capture conditions without per-frame overhead.
Achieves 32.2 FPS at 50 Mbit/s, 22.1 ms decoding on an RTX 3050 Ti, 22.8× less data than float32 Gaussians, and a 1.050 dB PSNR gain after calibration.

figures.caption: Figure 7. One frame takes 172 ms on one GPU, yet frame-parallel workers overlap and throughput scales nearly linearly with GPUs. (a) Mean server stage times and median client times; (b) a one-second window on four GPUs (one row per worker), where frames 61–72 (red) execute concurrently and packets leave in capture order; (c) throughput over all 16 sequences.

Figure 2. Every alternative misses one of the three per-frame budgets of live free-viewpoint video; HoloSplat meets all three. Red marks the failing stage; thumbnails show what each route sends. Rates are DNA-Rendering payloads at 30 FPS, with HoloSplat at Pro (Tabs. 2 and 3); times are on RTX 5090 GPUs, except avatar training (Tab. S30) and our client on an RTX 3050 Ti laptop GPU. Camera videos are eight 1024×1024 HEVC [64] streams with lossless mattes.

Figure 3. HoloSplat splits a frozen feed-forward reconstructor before its Gaussian head and streams tokens with a multi-rate codec combining server-side token compression and client-side token restoration. On the server (blue), each frame undergoes eight-view matting, PointSplat up to its head, opacity-guided token pruning, PCA to rank r with b-bit quantisation, and lossless anchor coding. On the client (orange), the fused decoder integrates inverse PCA, a lightweight feature reconstruction hypernetwork, and the NSC update into the Gaussian head, then prunes the lowest-opacity 20% of Gaussians. During warm-up (purple), NSC fine-tunes the Gaussian head on the incoming views of frames 0–29; its update, the hypernetwork update, and the frame-zero PCA basis are sent once. A Pro packet drawn to scale (frame 90 of 0678 02) totals 323.0 kB (270.2 kB coefficients, 51.4 kB anchors, and 1.4 kB header; frozen, \ learned).

Figure 6. From eight views, HoloSplat preserves facial detail and garment lacing where offline 4C4D smears the face, 3DGStream splinters the lace into needles, and HiCoM blurs both, while NSC corrects PointSplat’s appearance errors on unseen rigs. Held-out views with per-view PSNR; insets zoom 2× on the face and lacing. Baselines fit our eight input views; Ours Pro uses the fused hypernetwork decoder and NSC.

Figure 4. Neural session calibration improves quality across datasets while token coding costs little. Decoded by inverse PCA alone, the Pro stream loses up to 0.60 dB to our uncompressed reconstruction with the same pruning; the hypernetwork keeps it within 0.12 dB, and NSC adds +1.154, +1.419, and +1.436 dB on top. Evaluated on the 16 DNA-Rendering test scenes and on held-out cameras over all frames after the one-second warm-up on HiFi4G and ActorsHQ. NSC is fitted on the input views, without the codec for Uncompressed + NSC.

Figure 5. Coding tokens before the Gaussian head beats posthead attribute coding by 2.8–10.3 dB across rates. The same session PCA, quantisation, and Zstd encoder at three split points of the frozen reconstructor, with opacity-guided token pruning and no hypernetwork, on the 16 DNA-Rendering test scenes. Curves join each split point’s best settings; stars mark the Lite, Pro, and Ultra settings.

Table 3. From the same eight views, every tier of HoloSplat beats every per-frame optimisation method, and Pro beats offline 4C4D, in PSNR, LPIPS, and bytes on all 16 test sequences. Official settings on DNA-Rendering frames 30–89 (Sec. S5).

Table 2. With the same calibration, the smallest Gaussian format needs at least 2.24× the bytes of Ultra and 3.47× those of Pro. Decode: per-frame decoding to Gaussians on an RTX 3050 Ti laptop (ours), an RTX 5090 (CodecSplat), or CPU reference decoders (formats; FCGS on GPU); Tab. S12 drops NSC.

Table 1. HoloSplat sends a fraction of PointSplat’s Gaussian bytes and exceeds its PSNR and SSIM at every tier across four camera rigs. Quality on a black background within the ground-truth mask bounding box and mean per-frame kB; held-out cameras on HiFi4G, ActorsHQ, and synthetic X-Humans. All tiers use the fused hypernetwork decoder and NSC; the second row (uncompressed tokens with NSC) is a reference, and bold marks the best non-reference result.

papers.abstract: We introduce CrownFusion, a latent diffusion model to generate 3D dental crown designs from geometry images, a 2D-grid encoding of surface coordinates. Departing from traditional approaches that use point clouds, our "CrownImage" representation not only unlocks the full power of image-based generative architectures, but also preserves fine geometric detail by operating at far higher spatial resolutions than point clouds to alleviate smoothing artifacts in the 3D generation. Conditioned on jointly learned embeddings of the surrounding dentition, our probabilistic diffusion model produces anatomically plausible crowns with morphological variations tailored to individual patient cases. To accommodate multiple valid designs, we propose an occlusal fit metric based on proximity to the antagonist teeth. We evaluate our method through quantitative experiments and qualitative studies involving expert testimonials. We also release the FDI 16 Crown Dataset, comprising 11,513 annotated intra-oral scans, to support future research in dental CAD.
authors: Johan Ziruo Ye, Xingguang Yan, S{\o}ren Hauberg, Angel X. Chang, Hao Zhang, Peter Lempel S{\o}ndergaard
bullets: Encodes 3D surface coordinates as high-resolution 2D geometry images to preserve fine detail and reduce smoothing artifacts.
Conditions generation on jointly learned embeddings of the surrounding dentition.
Supports multiple valid crown designs and evaluates occlusal fit using proximity to antagonist teeth.
Assessed through quantitative experiments, qualitative studies, and expert testimonials.
Releases the FDI 16 Crown Dataset with 11,513 annotated intra-oral scans for dental CAD research.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview. From left to right: (1) Input: prepared tooth (bronze) and surrounding dentition (gray) from an intraoral scan. (2) Baseline: point cloud-based methods with Poisson reconstruction yield overly smooth geometry eroding occlusal detail. (3) Ours: a diffusion transformer generates a geometry image encoding of the crown surface, which is then meshed to recover the 3D crown, preserving fine occlusal features.
Fig. 3. Overview of CrownFusion. Left: VAE reconstruction from geometry images. Right: conditional generation via SiT diffusion in the learned latent space.

Fig. 2. CrownImage construction pipeline. M : crown mesh. Muv: parametrized mesh on the unit disk via boundary-fixed harmonic mapping. Muv∗: fisheye-transformed UV mesh (inner disk expanded, outer annulus compressed). O: rasterized geometry image encoding (x, y, z) and α. M∗: remeshed crown recovered by triangulating O.

Fig. 5. Generation comparison. Left: dental arch with prepared abutment (top) and the reference crown in context (bottom). Right: occlusal views of crowns generated by DMC, VBCD, and CrownFusion, colored by signed distance to the antagonist (blue: gap; red: intersection). VBCD shows a large uniform gap, indicating poor occlusal contact. DMC exhibits a localized intersection (red). CrownFusion achieves the closest antagonist proximity with no intersections, and preserves well-defined occlusal anatomy.

Fig. 6. Generated crown samples for the same input. CrownFusion captures expected axes of variation: fissure depth, secondary fossae detail, and distolingual cusp morphology vary, while marginal ridge height and overall crown outline remain largely stable.
Fig. 4. Surface distance heatmaps to GT show VF-Net’s errors concentrated at cusps and fissures, while our geometry image VAE is close to GT across the crown surface.

Table 2. Comparison of CrownFusion against previous methods for dental crown design. Crown similarity is measured by Chamfer Distance (CD-L2, mm) to a dental technician selected crown. Occlusal fit is evaluated against the three nearest antagonist teeth (by mean distance of 10th-percentile closest points) and surface intersections (count out of 1,000 sampled points, and area in mm2). CrownFusion achieves the best occlusal fit with fewer intersections and competitive antagonist proximity.
Table 1. We report reconstruction errors, in CD and EMD, for the FLUX-based VAE in our CrownFusion and several prior point cloud-based baselines.

papers.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) ultrasound provides valuable volumetric context for anatomical assessment, motivating reconstruction from widely available two-dimensional (2D) slices. Sparse slices leave much of the volume unobserved, even when their acquisition poses are known. Existing methods interpolate observed intensities or incorporate learned 2D image features into 3D reconstruction, but their complementary roles in predicting smooth structure and residual details remain less explored. We introduce XFreq, a geometry-aligned framework for sparse 3D ultrasound reconstruction. It uses known slice poses and finite footprints to query 2D image features at 3D locations, complementing splatted intensities and sampling geometry. A low-frequency decoder predicts a smooth 3D field from the splat representation, while a high-frequency decoder additionally incorporates the queried 2D features to predict residual details. A learned gating module regulates the residual contribution based on geometry and cross-slice feature variation. We evaluate XFreq on an in-house fetal brain dataset and the public CETUS cardiac dataset, using slices resampled from 3D ultrasound volumes and fivefold cross-validation. Among the compared methods, XFreq achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM in most settings across both datasets, reaching 26.82 dB PSNR on CETUS with 32 input slices. Ablation studies further show the contributions of local feature querying, geometric cues, and residual prediction, with gains generally increasing as more input slices are used. Our findings highlight the value of geometry-aligned cross-view feature integration for reconstructing 3D ultrasound volumes from sparse 2D slices.
authors: Yuhuan Lu, P. Ellen Grant, Davood Karimi
bullets: Addresses missing volumetric information when reconstructing 3D ultrasound from sparse, pose-known 2D slices.
Queries 2D image features at 3D locations using slice poses and finite footprints, alongside splatted intensities and geometry.
Uses separate low- and high-frequency decoders, with a learned gate controlling residual detail contributions.
Evaluated on in-house fetal brain and public CETUS cardiac data with fivefold cross-validation; achieved the highest PSNR and SSIM among compared methods in most settings.
Ablations support the value of local feature querying, geometric cues, and residual prediction; performance gains generally grow with more input slices.

figures.caption: Figure 2. XFreq architecture. Splatted intensities and pose geometry supply shared 3D features to both decoders. Geometry aligned queries aggregate 2D features for the high frequency residual and feature variance for the gate. Data consistency is applied after prediction.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of 3D ultrasound reconstruction. (a) Reconstruction results on FetalBrain and CETUS with 8 and 32 input slices. (b) Enlarged regions comparing reconstruction details and absolute errors.

Figure 4. Spatial distribution of PSNR gains from queried image features. Curves show the mean ∆PSNR (dB) of XFreq over the w/o Queried Features variant, while colored labels indicate the corresponding standard deviations across five patient folds.
Figure 1. Sparse observations and cross-view feature querying.

Table 1. Comparison of reconstruction methods on FetalBrain and CETUS. Unobserved foreground PSNR (dB) and 3D SSIM are reported as mean ± standard deviation across five patient folds. N denotes the number of input slices. For supervised methods, indented rows labeled “w/o DC” report predictions without the shared data consistency correction.

Table 2. Ablation studies. We consider three aspects of XFreq: reconstruction branches and fusion, queried image features, and geometry design. ∆ denotes XFreq minus the corresponding ablation variant.

papers.abstract: Active 3D reconstruction aims to allocate a sparse view budget to recover complete geometry and high-fidelity renderings. However, existing methods degrade sharply in multi-room homes: myopic next-best-view scoring gives transit no credit for distant rooms and over-polishes irreducible nearby residuals, whereas dense mappers reach far rooms only by streaming thousands of frames. We propose ROAM-GS, a training-free active multi-room reconstruction framework that couples persistent goals with selective views: each decision selects a goal and a variable-horizon prefix toward it, capturing only at its endpoint. A Surface Reconstruction Memory scores poses by projecting post-update defects and viewing directions. Persistent goals credit transit with their remaining value and are released once arrivals stop measurably improving them. Without per-scene tuning, ROAM-GS achieves state-of-the-art multi-room reconstruction while preserving single-room Replica fidelity, raising mean coverage from 74% to 93% on HSSD and from 47% to 96% (+11.7 dB PSNR) on HM3D, and matching 90-minute dense mapping using $173\times$ fewer views.
authors: Jiawei Jiang, Haonan Zhou, Wendi Hu, Jiabei Hu, Yina Xiang, Kaiyue Zhou, Gaoang Wang
bullets: Addresses myopic view selection, which neglects distant rooms and over-focuses on nearby irreducible errors.
Uses a training-free planner that selects a goal and a variable-length transit path, capturing only at the endpoint.
A Surface Reconstruction Memory scores candidate poses using projected post-update defects and viewing directions.
Persistent goals assign value to transit and are released when further arrivals stop improving reconstruction.
Raises coverage from 74% to 93% on HSSD and 47% to 96% on HM3D, while matching dense mapping with 173× fewer views.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ROAM-GS. Each posed RGB-D capture updates the Gaussian map Gt, the occupancy grid Vt, and the Surface Reconstruction Memory Mt, whose cells store observed directions Ds and score query views by new-angle and defect gains without rendering. Persistent goals (top) keep a target region rg through search, travel, and observe until an arrival capture measurably improves it. Selective views (bottom) truncate the path to the goal view at variable horizons: only the prefix endpoint (orange) is captured, while query poses (hollow) are credited from memory. The joint score S = B + V selects the goal and prefix, and the agent captures once at qπ .

Figure 5. Novel view synthesis on HSSD and HM3D after 500 views. Test viewpoints are excluded from the trajectories of all methods. PSNR (dB) is shown in the top-left corner of each view, and red boxes highlight challenging regions.
Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on HSSD and HM3D after 500 views. ROAM-GS avoids local trapping and achieves substantially higher multi-room coverage.

Figure 3. PSNR and Cov10 versus captured views on HSSD (top) and HM3D (bottom) for the runs in Table 1. Within each Small, Medium, and Large group, PSNR is shown on the left and Cov10 on the right. Curves show means over three seeds, and shaded bands show the standard deviation at 50, 100, 300, and 500 views.

papers.abstract: Multi-View Stereo (MVS) and Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) provide complementary cues for dense 3D reconstruction. While MVS leverages explicit geometry for metric depth, it struggles in challenging regions where feature matching is unreliable. Conversely, MDE provides robust structural priors but typically yields scale-ambiguous results. Existing hybrid methods mainly exploit monocular cues in a unidirectional manner, leaving the mutual enhancement between MDE and MVS insufficiently explored. To address this limitation, we propose BridgeMVS, a unified cascaded multi-stage MVS framework that bridges monocular depth features and multi-view cost volume representations through Bidirectional Dynamic Fusion (BDF). At each stage, BDF performs dynamic mono-to-cost and cost-to-mono updates, where monocular structural features guide cost volume refinement for more robust MVS depth estimation, while multi-view geometric evidence recalibrates monocular representations to improve their metric-scale consistency. Furthermore, the fused monocular and multi-view representations are progressively propagated from coarse to fine stages and constrained by stage-wise relative-scale MDE supervision and metric-scale MVS supervision, enabling cross-branch interactions to benefit subsequent high-resolution depth estimation. In addition, BDF is designed as a plug-and-play module that can be conveniently integrated into existing cascaded MVS frameworks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BridgeMVS achieves state-of-the-art performance on the DTU, Tanks-and-Temples, and ETH3D benchmarks, while simultaneously boosting the accuracy of monocular depth estimation. Notably, BridgeMVS ranks first on both the Tanks-and-Temples Intermediate and Advanced benchmarks. The source code is available at \href{https://github.com/JianfeiJ/BridgeMVS}{https://github.com/JianfeiJ/BridgeMVS}.
authors: Jianfei Jiang, Haochen Yu, Qiankun Liu, Rui Yang, Hongyuan Liu, Xianglong Meng, Jiansheng Chen, Huimin Ma
bullets: Addresses MVS failures in poorly matched regions and MDE’s scale ambiguity by combining their complementary cues.
Introduces Bidirectional Dynamic Fusion, enabling monocular features to refine MVS cost volumes and geometric evidence to recalibrate monocular features.
Progressively propagates fused representations from coarse to fine stages with relative-scale MDE and metric-scale MVS supervision.
Works as a plug-and-play module for existing cascaded MVS frameworks.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on DTU, Tanks-and-Tamples, and ETH3D, ranking first on Tanks-and-Temples Intermediate and Advanced; it also improves monocular depth accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of BridgeMVS. The framework contains a cost volume-based MVS branch, a DPT-based MDE branch, and a Bidirectional Dynamic Fusion (BDF) module at each cascade stage. BDF bidirectionally fuses regularized cost volumes and monocular features, producing enhanced multi-view and monocular representations that are progressively propagated from coarse to fine stages under metric-scale MVS supervision and relative-scale MDE supervision.

Figure 3: Overview of the proposed bidirectional dynamic fusion module. It first aligns and fuses monocular features and multi-view cost volumes, then performs bidirectional dynamic aggregation, followed by depth-guided feature fusion and residual update to produce refined multi-view cost volumes and monocular features.

Figure 1: (a) Benchmark performance. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods [33, 34, 32, 20, 35] on three standard MVS benchmarks [36, 37, 38]. (b) Visualization comparison on Scan 48 from DTU [36]. Benefiting from bidirectional dynamic fusion, BridgeMVS improves MVS depth estimation [35] in challenging regions and enhances the accuracy of monocular depth estimation [39] under multi-view geometric constraints. Absolute relative error maps are visualized after aligning the relative depth with GT using the ROE solver [40].

Figure 7: Qualitative comparison of depth maps and absolute relative error maps on the RobustMVD [65] benchmark. For each method, the first row shows the predicted depth maps and the second row shows the corresponding error maps.
Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of depth maps in most challenging scan48 and scan 77 on DTU. Our method predicted more accurate depth maps in weakly textured and reflection areas.

papers.abstract: We introduce AvatarAnyone, a method for reconstructing avatars from casual YouTube videos as layered meshes, with each garment and footwear as a separate mesh layered on top of the body mesh. In such videos, people differ in garment classes, clothing types, and layers, and each combination needs a different reconstruction. A single fixed layered reconstruction pipeline therefore fails. AvatarAnyone solves this problem with AI agents that plan a custom optimization for each person's reconstruction. The agents predict the garment classes, the clothing type, and the layering. They use these predictions to choose an initialization and stage the optimization. Because the avatars are layered meshes, they support applications such as virtual try-on and cloth simulation. We change the clothing layers of an avatar and render it in different garments and poses. We can also simulate a clothing layer as cloth over the animated body with a standard cloth simulator. Most existing avatars are one fused surface or a set of Gaussians and cannot do this. We load the avatars directly into Blender, Unreal Engine, and robotics simulators such as MuJoCo. As the avatars are meshes, they support contact modeling with other objects. We show results from around 150 YouTube videos. On four datasets, AvatarAnyone outperforms existing mesh-based methods for animatable monocular reconstruction. Our project page is available at https://miraymen.github.io/avataranyone.
authors: Aymen Mir, Peter Wonka, Stefanos Zafeiriou, R{\i}za Alp G\"uler
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reconstructing people with varying garment classes, clothing types, and layer combinations.
Agents predict clothing structure and plan a person-specific initialization and staged optimization.
Represents the body, garments, and footwear as separate meshes rather than a fused surface or Gaussian representation.
Supports virtual try-on, pose changes, cloth simulation, contact modeling, and import into Blender, Unreal Engine, and MuJoCo.
Evaluated on around 150 YouTube videos and four datasets, where it outperforms existing mesh-based methods for animatable monocular reconstruction.

The answers form the layer plan P , which builds the optimization for that person. Top: the agent finds a tucked shirt, trousers, and short hair. Bottom: the agent finds one garment, a dress, and long hair. The plan selects the layers, the initialization of each layer, and the order of the layers. The agent gate rejects a generated initialization that carries a head (red) and retries until an initialization is clean. The joint optimization fits all layers. The bars C(P) show the order of the layers at the waist and at the shoulders, from the body outwards. Each layer gets its own texture. papers.title: AvatarAnyone: Agentic Reconstruction of Mesh-Based Layered Avatars from YouTube Video
papers.tldr: AvatarAnyone uses AI agents to reconstruct customizable, layered mesh avatars from casual YouTube videos, enabling garment editing, animation, and cloth simulation.

papers.abstract: Language often refers to an object by its parts, as in asking to point to a part or to turn an arbitrarily posed object so that two named parts lie in given directions. Both tasks need the direction from the object's center to the part's center, not the part's own orientation. A natural approach segments the part and takes the centroid of its mask. However, high mask overlap predicts the pointing direction poorly when a part is spread out relative to its distance from the object center. Language-guided part segmentation is trained and evaluated by mask overlap, which leaves a gap between the masks it produces and the part geometry that these tasks use. We close this gap by learning point evidence, weights over the observed points whose weighted centroid gives the part's location. Geometric Readout Supervision (GRS) trains these weights through the centroid's position and adds direction supervision on the parts used in reorientation commands. GRS improves both tasks even with a single frozen encoder and a single input pose. We implement this supervision in GeoRead3D, a system for pointing and reorientation from part descriptions. A language model maps each description to a known part name. Dual-Route Part Evidence combines refined segmentation evidence with directly predicted point evidence to locate each part. On PartNeXt and Artiverse, GeoRead3D points within $22.5^\circ$ for 74.1% and 60.0% of queries, 5.8 and 7.3 percentage points above the strongest baselines. Its reorientation success exceeds the strongest baselines by 10.4 and 7.8 points.
authors: Zhangcheng Hou, Kevin Tonkich, Tomoaki Ohtsuki
bullets: Part-mask overlap can poorly reflect the direction from an object’s center to a spatially extended part.
Geometric Readout Supervision trains point evidence through centroid position and adds direction supervision for reorientation.
Dual-Route Part Evidence combines refined segmentation with directly predicted point evidence.
On PartNeXt and Artiverse, it reaches 74.1% and 60.0% pointing accuracy within 22.5°, outperforming the strongest baselines by 5.8 and 7.3 points.
Reorientation success exceeds the strongest baselines by 10.4 and 7.8 points, using a frozen encoder and a single input pose.

(d) During training, GRS supervises position on every queried part and direction on both parts of each anchor pair. Heatmaps show evidence for the lens of a held out 3DCoMPaT microscope.

papers.selection_reason: Language-grounded 3D part localization and reorientation, directly relevant to spatial intelligence and 3D vision.
papers.title: GeoRead3D: Grounding Part Descriptions for 3D Pointing and Reorientation
papers.tldr: GeoRead3D improves 3D pointing and object reorientation from part descriptions by learning part locations as weighted point centroids rather than relying on mask overlap.

papers.abstract: 3D indoor scene synthesis requires generating objects to form a complete and coherent scene. Existing approaches rely heavily on manually annotated datasets, leading to high costs and limited generalization. We present SceneCast, an annotation-free framework that trains on large-scale, unlabeled videos, addressing two key challenges: (1) Videos provide only partial views of a scene, requiring the model to extrapolate unseen 3D regions, which is inherently error-prone; (2) Raw videos available online are uncurated, suffering from uncontrolled conditions and variable data quality. First, we design a Transformer-based model that predicts objects sequentially and is fine-tuned with reinforcement learning (RL), where an LLM acts as a spatial common-sense evaluator. The LLM provides reward signals through chain-of-thought reasoning and code-executable geometric checks to refine object configurations. Second, we introduce \trim, a data curation approach that generates training videos with controllable video generation models. Crucially, it retains only high-quality prefix clips via multi-criteria quality assessment with an entropy-based weighting strategy. Evaluated on curated synthetic video sets, our annotation-free approach outperforms state-of-the-art supervised methods in scene quality.
authors: Ziyang Zong, Canming Xia, Haoran Xu, Guang Tan
bullets: Addresses costly annotations and limited generalization in existing indoor scene synthesis methods.
Uses a Transformer to sequentially predict objects and extrapolate unseen 3D regions from partial video views.
Fine-tunes scene configurations with RL using LLM rewards based on spatial reasoning and executable geometric checks.
Curates synthetic training videos by retaining high-quality prefix clips selected with multi-criteria, entropy-weighted assessment.
Outperforms state-of-the-art supervised methods in scene quality on curated synthetic video sets.

figures.caption: Figure 1. SceneCast overview. (a) Our generation model predicts 3D objects sequentially, starting from an initial set of objects. The model is fine-tuned with a reinforcement learning phase with LLM feedback. (b) Our ViTrim strategy removes low-quality tail segments from generated video using multiple quality assessment criteria, ensuring only valid clips are used for training.

Figure 2. SceneCast pipelines. (a) Transformer-based autoregressive 3D indoor scene completion backbone network. (b) LLM-driven reinforcement learning fine-tuning loop incorporating CoT spatial reasoning, automatic geometric code execution, and multi-dimensional reward fusion. (c) ViTrim pipeline for high-quality video segment selection.

Figure 3. Generation samples from an empty scene. SceneCast performs well in producing reasonable and complete object layouts, with correct collision avoidance. ATISS and DiffuScene generate misaligned objects and unnatural layouts. Perhaps restricted by the video generation model, VIPScene generates a small number of objects with narrow coverage of the scene, missing objects that are commonly found in realistic scenes (e.g., wardrobe for bedroom, sofa for livingdiningroom). SAGE [52] lacks the understanding of the actual physical space, resulting in the generation of duplicate or poorly arranged objects (e.g., bedroom without bed, impassable passageway).

Figure 5. LLM reasoning process. (a) Position refinement for minor spatial overlap; (b) Size correction for severe object interpenetration; (c) Layout saturation detection and generation stopping. The LLM Agent applies CoT reasoning and self-programmed geometric computation. In each case, Size[x,y,z] denotes the corrected 3D dimension of an object, Position[x,y,z] its refined 3D centroid. CONTINUE indicates proceeding with object generation, while STOP terminates the process when layout is complete or spatially invalid.
Figure 4. Scene completion results from partial scenes. Starting from a few objects, SceneCast completes the scenes more thoroughly and plausibly.

Table 2. Ablations on the bedroom set. (a) Unified reward ablation. Each row augments the previous one with a single component, isolating its effect. The LLM reward outperforms handcrafted rules, and code execution provides a further gain over language-only reasoning. (b) ViTrim ablation. All models share identical architecture and training hyperparameters, while only the data curation strategy differs. Rows 1–2 isolate the effect of trimming, row 3 isolates the spatial IoU signal and rows 4–5 compare entropy-based vs uniform weighting.(c) SceneCast completion quality across condition coverage on held-out 3D-FRONT scenes.

Table 1. Quantitative results. ATISS [38], DiffuScene [48], and VIPScene [21] are compared. SceneCast performs best across all metrics. PIoU (↓) is newly introduced to measure physical plausibility; baseline PIoU values are computed on their released scenes.

papers.selection_reason: Presents SceneCast, a framework for 3D indoor scene synthesis using synthetic videos and LLM-based rewards. This fits the 3D Vision topic as a foundation model for scene generation.
papers.title: SceneCast: Learning Indoor Scene Synthesis from Curated Synthetic Videos with LLM Reward
papers.tldr: SceneCast learns coherent 3D indoor scene synthesis without manual annotations by combining curated synthetic videos with LLM-guided reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Interactive segmentation models turn a few clicks into a segmentation prediction across domains, so annotators only decide where the prediction still needs correction. Annotation thus becomes a loop of inspecting the prediction and clicking again. Each step of this loop is a visual judgment, which suits general-purpose multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents. In this work, we focus on letting these agents run this loop on 3D volumes. However, the MLLM in such an agent takes only 2D images as input, so the agent must observe the 3D volume in 2D. Since the loop calls the MLLM many times, this observation must be token-compact enough to keep every call cheap, yet informative enough to show error regions in the 3D prediction. We meet both needs with tri-planes, the three orthogonal planes that cross at one point in the volume. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that tri-planes are context-efficient yet keep sufficient detail to show error regions in the 3D prediction. Building on tri-planes, we introduce TriSegAgent, an MLLM agent that refines the 3D prediction iteratively. Within the agent, the MLLM only judges the prediction on tri-planes, while a visual harness turns each judgment into a 3D action in code. To make the loop reliable, the harness places each click at an exact voxel in the volume and checks whether to accept the 3D prediction. To evaluate the agent, we build a diverse benchmark of 690 regions of interest (ROIs) from 35 public medical datasets across three imaging modalities. With frontier MLLMs, TriSegAgent reaches an overall Dice about 10 points above the strongest baseline, and its lead is even larger on targets below 3 cm. With flash-level MLLMs, it outperforms a recent 3D segmentation agent built on a frontier MLLM.
authors: Qingqiao Hu, Jialin Li, Meilong Xu, Kehan Qi, Yipeng Zhang, Lin Tian, Hongwei Bran Li, Klaus Mueller, Xiaoling Hu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of giving 2D-input MLLMs informative, token-efficient views of 3D prediction errors.
Represents each volume with three orthogonal planes intersecting at a point, preserving detail around error regions.
An MLLM judges tri-plane predictions while a visual harness converts judgments into precise voxel-level 3D clicks and validates predictions.
Evaluated on 690 ROIs from 35 public medical datasets across three imaging modalities.
Achieves about 10 Dice points over the strongest baseline with frontier MLLMs, with larger gains for targets smaller than 3 cm; also outperforms a recent 3D agent using flash-level MLLMs.

(a) The localization model floc locates the target, and preprocessing turns its prior into the initial prediction M0 in view v0. (b) The MLLM judges the tri-planes ot of view vt with Mt as an overlay: if it reports an error, the interactive segmentation model fseg turns a click at into Mt+1; otherwise, verification starts. (c) The MLLM judges up to K verification views in turn; the first view with an

The three targets measure 13, 21, and 22 mm from top to bottom; gray is the ground truth and orange the 3D prediction, and a panel without orange has no prediction in view. nnI-Agent: nnInteractive Agent [48] with GPT-6.1-Sol [85]. papers.selection_reason: Introduces TriSegAgent, an MLLM agent for 3D annotation using tri-planes. This combines Multimodal Foundation Models (MLLMs) with 3D Vision (3D Foundation Models) for spatial reasoning and context efficiency.
papers.title: TriSegAgent: Context-Efficient 3D Annotation with MLLMs via Tri-Planes
papers.tldr: TriSegAgent uses compact tri-plane views to let MLLM agents iteratively correct 3D segmentations efficiently and accurately.

papers.abstract: Generating 3D indoor scenes requires a representation that captures object semantics, instance identity, height structure, and orientation while respecting room geometry. Methods that model scenes as sequences of object vectors learn spatial constraints implicitly, leaving collisions and boundary violations to losses or post-processing; semantic-map methods make occupancy explicit, but collapse instance and directional structure. We introduce RoomTokens, a sliced structured-token representation in which each token stores semantic class, instance-color identity, and facing field. This representation allows a scene to be generated as a discrete grid while preserving cues for instance grouping, orientation estimation, and 3D extent prediction. To learn the RoomToken distribution, we propose MDIRT (Masked Diffusion over RoomTokens), a masked discrete diffusion model that denoises semantic/instance-color/facing channels jointly with a shared cross-slice backbone. Architectural tokens are clamped as explicit floor- plan constraints, so the model samples furniture layouts that respect room geometry while retaining instance and object-attribute structure. Experiments on 3D-FRONT show that RoomTokens with MDIRT improve layout fidelity and physical consistency over sequence/vector- and map-based methods, suggesting structured spatial tokens as a practical choice for discrete 3D scene synthesis.
bullets: Represents scenes with tokens encoding semantic class, instance identity, and facing direction across spatial slices.
Uses masked discrete diffusion to jointly denoise these channels with a shared cross-slice backbone.
Clamps floor-plan tokens as explicit constraints, helping generated layouts respect room boundaries and geometry.
On 3D-FRONT, the approach improves layout fidelity and physical consistency over sequence/vector- and map-based methods.
Scope: targets discrete 3D indoor scene synthesis and relies on floor-plan constraints for geometry control.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of MDIRT. Given selected height slices and an architectural mask, we clamp the fixed room structure and denoise masked interior RoomTokens with a shared UNet with cross-slice attention. The denoiser predicts semantic, instance-color, and facing slices under semantic-gated validity constraints: architecture/background tokens carry no instance-color or facing cues, while furniture tokens do. The valid RoomToken grid is then grouped into object records, whose category, size, and pose are used to retrieve and place matched 3D assets.

Figure 1: Top. Comparison of scene representations for indoor scene generation. Object sequences (a) encode object attributes but lack explicit spatial relationship information. Semantic maps (b) make spatial structure explicit, but lack vertical, instance, and orientation information. We propose RoomTokens (c) to address these missing factors by encoding semantic occupancy, instance identity, and facing cues in a sliced spatial grid. Bottom. We introduce MDIRT (d), a masked discrete diffusion model over RoomTokens, which denoises missing token fields while keeping architectural tokens fixed so generated scenes respect room boundaries.

Figure 4: Arch-mask-conditioned qualitative comparison on 3D-FRONT. We use semantic orthographic views to focus the comparison on layout evaluation. Baselines show boundary violations, collisions, or blocked door/window openings, while MDIRT preserves clear openings, room geometry, and structured object cues.

Figure 2: RoomToken data representation. (a) A 3D scene is represented as horizontal slices taken at selected vertical heights. (b) Each slice encodes three aligned 2D channels: semantic class, instance-color identity, and the facing field. Stacking these channels over all heights forms a sliced token volume. (c) The resulting 3D representation of stacked slices (RoomTokens) stores semantic, instance, and orientation information, with height derived from the slice index.

This collision raises COL while the walkable floor remains connected.

Figure 7: Arch-mask-conditioned qualitative comparison on 3D-FRONT in isometric view.
Figure 8: More arch-mask-conditioned generated results by MDIRT in isometric view.

papers.selection_reason: Structured-token masked diffusion for 3D indoor scene synthesis; fits 3D vision generation and scene representation.
papers.title: RoomTokens: Masked Diffusion over Structured Tokens for Indoor Scene Synthesis
papers.tldr: RoomTokens and MDIRT generate indoor furniture layouts as structured discrete grids that preserve semantics, instances, orientation, and room geometry.

papers.abstract: Dense visual SLAM built on learned two-view geometry is evaluated in good light; in low light it fails silently. Two frames of 9-level quantized noise, no scene at all, give MASt3R-SLAM's network a cross-view geometric self-consistency of 0.936; a real dark frame pair gives 0.935. Starved of structure, the network invents the same geometry for both views and the system trusts the agreement: on a dark sequence it consumes 1,605 frames, emits 7 keyframes, rejects no factor-graph edges and reports full frame rate, while over 95% of the correspondences it accepts violate the ground-truth epipolar geometry. One inflated statistic is read by two subsystems against thresholds in opposite directions, so keyframing starves while relocalization accepts almost every candidate. The same statistic, read at keyframe-pair baselines, separates the confident collapse from working runs on the ETH3D dark sequences without ground truth or extra computation (in-sample). Low-light-adapted weights take tracked trajectories from 1/6 to 5/6, as does retuning two thresholds; neither yields accurate ones, because the adaptation withdraws confidence from wrong geometry rather than finding right geometry. Replayed on a Jetson AGX Orin carried by a legged robot, the mechanism's signature reproduces on the two darkest of four routes, and which of its faces appears varies with route geometry and sensor encoding. The network does not lose confidence in the dark; it manufactures it.
authors: Shrikrishna Bhagirath Rajule, Srinath Neelamagam, Aniket Bera
bullets: Noise-only and real dark frame pairs produce nearly identical, high self-consistency, masking the absence of reliable scene structure.
On a dark sequence, the system processed 1,605 frames and produced 7 keyframes while rejecting no factor-graph edges; over 95% of accepted correspondences violated ground-truth epipolar geometry.
A single inflated statistic is interpreted in opposite ways by keyframing and relocalization, starving keyframes while accepting almost every relocalization candidate.
Reading the statistic at keyframe-pair baselines separates confident collapse from working runs on ETH3D dark sequences without ground truth or extra computation, in-sample.
Low-light weights and threshold retuning increased tracking but did not recover accurate geometry; the failure signature also reproduced on the two darkest of four Jetson robot routes.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. The mechanism. Two frames enter the pointmap network; a correspondence is accepted when the two views’ geometry predictions agree within 10 cm; the confident fraction is the one statistic both rules read. The keyframe rule fires when it falls below 0.333 and the relocalization rule accepts an anchor when it rises above 0.30. In good light it sits near 0.4 and both rules behave. Starved of structure, the network invents geometry that agrees with itself, the statistic rises to about 0.7, keyframing starves (7 keyframes in 1 605 frames) and relocalization accepts wrong anchors (497 of 543 on plant_dark). Frames: the robot’s gripper camera, lights on and at 1/100 s.

Fig. 6. The robot’s ladder, first room. Top: four of the five levels as captured by the gripper camera (lights on 1/100 s gain 0.05; L2 1/40 s, L3 1/100 s, L4 1/200 s at gain 0.40). Mobile-LIO is a depth-inertial odometry pipeline that uses the phone's depth and inertial data and no ARKit poses. papers.abstract: Reliable 3D object detection for autonomous trucks requires both the semantic detail provided by cameras and the geometric and motion cues measured by 4D radar. Existing radar-camera detectors commonly construct global radar bird's-eye-view (BEV) representations, whose computational and memory costs grow with the perception range. Sparse query-based detectors offer greater efficiency, but global feature construction can obscure point-level radar geometry and motion information. We present QSRadar, a query-conditioned sparse radar fusion framework for efficient long-range 3D detection. Built on a Sparse4Dv3-style visual-temporal detector, QSRadar retrieves a compact set of raw radar points around each evolving object hypothesis. The selected points are represented in an anchor-aligned coordinate frame, augmented with motion residuals, radar cross section, and sweep timing, and aggregated by a query-conditioned set encoder. Radar neighborhoods are retrieved again after each anchor refinement, coupling evidence selection with object estimation. Under the official MAN TruckScenes validation protocol, QSRadar achieves 38.09 mAP and 52.20 NDS, compared with 37.08 mAP and 50.78 NDS for our reproduced Sparse4D-Radar global Radar-BEV baseline. In matched tests on an RTX 4090 D, QSRadar reduces latency by 45%, peak memory usage by 49%, and GFLOPs by 43%.
authors: Chenhao Yan, Hongyu Liu, Xiang Cai, Yifei Sun, Zhe Zhang
bullets: Avoids costly global radar BEV construction by retrieving sparse radar neighborhoods around each object hypothesis.
Encodes radar points in anchor-aligned coordinates with motion residuals, radar cross section, and sweep timing.
Re-retrieves radar evidence after each anchor refinement, linking point selection to object estimation.
On MAN TruckScenes validation, achieves 38.09 mAP and 52.20 NDS versus 37.08 mAP and 50.78 NDS for the reproduced global Radar-BEV baseline.
On an RTX 4090 D, reduces latency by 45%, peak memory by 49%, and GFLOPs by 43% in matched tests.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of QSRadar. Current anchors guide visual sampling and local radar retrieval, while query features modulate radar point encoding. Visual and radar features are concatenated and fused to update queries and anchors. Updated anchors trigger new radar retrieval at the next layer, forming an iterative loop. Six decoder layers produce box, class, and velocity predictions.

papers.abstract: Recent geometric foundation models can successfully convert a video sequence into frames of registered point clouds, but cannot predict moments beyond the observed temporal resolution. We propose a continuous-time 4D reconstruction method that extracts 3D structure and camera poses at any time instant, with additional guidance from event-camera measurements. While event cameras provide evidence at microsecond resolution to continuously fill the temporal gap, integrating them into existing RGB-based foundation models remains challenging. We formulate the problem as interpolation in the latent feature space and augment event-based losses in the image space as an auxiliary task to boost accuracy. Operating in the latent space leverages the powerful geometric priors of foundation models, while the event loss provides physically grounded guidance. To effectively address the lack of paired training data, we further propose a self-supervised training framework that uses pseudo-ground-truth labels of estimated geometry and simulated events generated from high-frame-rate RGB videos. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed pipeline outperforms baselines that temporally interpolate either the input RGB videos or the estimated geometry, and that it generalizes to unseen real-world scenarios. Controlled experiments with synthetic corruptions show that it remains robust under motion-blur and low-light conditions.
authors: Gwangtak Bae, Seunggu Kang, Junho Kim, Eun Sun Lee, Changwoon Choi, Young Min Kim
bullets: Addresses the limited temporal resolution of RGB-based geometric foundation models.
Interpolates in latent feature space while using image-space event losses for physically grounded guidance.
Uses self-supervision with pseudo-ground-truth geometry and simulated events from high-frame-rate RGB videos.
Experiments report better performance than RGB- or geometry-interpolation baselines and generalization to unseen real-world scenes.
Synthetic corruption tests indicate robustness to motion blur and low-light conditions.

papers.selection_reason: Continuous-time 4D reconstruction using event cameras and latent interpolation, fitting 3D vision research.
papers.title: Continuous-time 4D Reconstruction via Event-guided Latent Feature Interpolation
papers.tldr: A continuous-time 4D reconstruction method interpolates foundation-model features using event-camera guidance to recover geometry and camera poses between video frames, including under challenging visual conditions.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving systems must not only interpret the current scene but also anticipate perceptual challenges such as occlusions, sparse observations, and recurring failure patterns. However, most existing LiDAR semantic segmentation methods operate in a frame-centric manner, processing each scan independently and discarding past contextual experience, which limits robustness under dynamic scene changes. We propose DREAM, a Dual-memory REAsoning framework for continual LiDAR seMantic segmentation that reframes perception as an experience-driven and anticipatory process. DREAM maintains two complementary memory banks in a strictly online setting: a latent memory that stores compact semantic abstractions of previously observed scenes, and an error memory that records representations associated with uncertain predictions. At each timestep, relevant memory entries are retrieved via cosine similarity and integrated into the feature space through a lightweight modulation mechanism, enabling the model to reinforce consistent semantic patterns while suppressing recurring failure modes. The backbone remains frozen and no past scans are replayed, ensuring computational efficiency and bounded memory growth. Extensive experiments on multiple large-scale LiDAR benchmarks demonstrate that DREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance, with consistent improvements on dynamic and small-scale objects, highlighting the effectiveness of persistent and error-aware memory for robust long-horizon perception.
bullets: Targets frame-by-frame LiDAR segmentation methods that discard contextual experience and struggle with dynamic changes, occlusions, and sparse observations.
Maintains a latent memory of compact semantic scene abstractions and an error memory of uncertain-prediction representations.
Retrieves relevant memories via cosine similarity and applies lightweight feature modulation to reinforce consistent patterns and reduce recurring failures.
Operates online with a frozen backbone, no past-scan replay, and bounded memory growth.
Experiments on multiple large-scale LiDAR benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance, especially for dynamic and small-scale objects.

papers.abstract: High-resolution images contain rich visual details that require fine geometric structures for faithful 3D reconstruction. However, generating extremely detailed 3D geometry from images requires substantial computational resources and training data, making high-resolution geometry generation challenging for existing state-of-the-art models. In this paper, we present SuperFine3D, an efficient framework for generating extremely detailed 3D geometry through global-local recursive refinement. SuperFine3D learns a shared refinement operator from paired coarse-to-fine representations and recursively reuses it to progressively synthesize finer geometry beyond the training resolutions, without requiring additional paired supervision at target resolutions. To make recursive refinement computationally efficient, we introduce spatial-cell attention, which restricts high-resolution interactions to local spatial neighborhoods while maintaining bounded communication across neighboring cells. We further propose spatially anchored cross-scale guidance, which leverages globally contextualized coarse geometry to guide local detail synthesis and preserve structural consistency. In addition, geometry-aware training objectives encourage the refinement process to preserve stable geometric structures while introducing fine-grained surface details. Experiments demonstrate that SuperFine3D generates geometry at a $4096^3$ decoder-grid resolution, corresponding to a sparse $256^3$ latent lattice, using a shared refinement operator trained only on $512^3$--$1024^3$ representations. Compared with a full-attention recursive baseline, SuperFine3D achieves a $9.4\times$ speedup in end-to-end inference and reduces peak GPU memory usage by $23.0\%$, while improving cross-scale structural consistency and producing cleaner surfaces with finer geometric details.
authors: Lihan Li, Junwei Zhou, Yu-wing Tai
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and data demands of high-resolution 3D geometry generation.
Learns a shared coarse-to-fine refinement operator and reuses it recursively beyond the training resolutions.
Uses spatial-cell attention for efficient local interactions and spatially anchored cross-scale guidance for global structural consistency.
Trained on 512³–1024³ representations, it generates geometry at 4096³ decoder-grid resolution with a sparse 256³ latent lattice.
Compared with full-attention recursive refinement, it achieves 9.4× faster inference, 23.0% lower peak GPU memory, and cleaner, finer surfaces.

papers.abstract: Recovering globally consistent 3D human motion from monocular videos remains challenging under dynamic camera motion. Although SLAM and human mesh recovery (HMR) provide complementary camera and body estimates, directly combining them often leads to inconsistent orientations and accumulated trajectory drift. We present GravHMR, a training-free, plug-and-play framework that couples SLAM and HMR through a shared gravity-aligned reference. By allowing gravity to be estimated independently of the HMR backbone, GravHMR accommodates world-grounded HMR models with or without explicit gravity-view representations. Specifically, Yaw-Aware Orientation Optimization (YAOO) resolves heading inconsistencies by correcting body and velocity orientations about the shared gravity axis. Conditioned on these corrected orientations, Gravity-Aware Trajectory Optimization (GATO) anchors root trajectories in the metric SLAM world by jointly leveraging 2D reprojection, the metric scale implicit in the human body, and the body's own motion. On EMDB-2, GravHMR achieves state-of-the-art performance with 154.0 mm W-MPJPE100 using ViPE and 189.8 mm using masked DROID-SLAM, outperforming TRAM (222.4 mm) under the same masked DROID-SLAM camera estimates. It further reduces W-MPJPE100 by 44.3% over GVHMR (276.5 mm) and by 20.0% over GVHMR + HTD-Refine (192.4 mm) with the same HMR backbone.
authors: Hanglei Jin, Chenglu Sun, Junchen Ge, Yuchao Wang, Siqi Chen, Yuzhi Huang, Jingyan Jiang, Zhi Wang
bullets: Addresses orientation inconsistency and trajectory drift when combining SLAM with human mesh recovery under dynamic camera motion.
Uses independently estimated gravity to support world-grounded HMR models with or without explicit gravity-view representations.
YAOO corrects body and velocity heading around the shared gravity axis.
GATO optimizes root trajectories using 2D reprojection, metric body scale, and body motion in the SLAM world.
On EMDB-2, reports 154.0 mm W-MPJPE100 with ViPE and 189.8 mm with masked DROID-SLAM, outperforming listed baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of GravHMR. Given a monocular video, off-the-shelf HMR and SLAM backbones provide initial human motion and camera geometry, respectively. GravHMR couples these estimates through a shared gravity-aligned reference. Yaw-Aware Orientation Optimization (YAOO) corrects the headings of the body and of its motion about gravity while keeping the gravity-relative body tilt predicted by HMR. Gravity-Aware Trajectory Optimization (GATO) then recovers the global root trajectory from 2D pose observations under the corrected orientations and the SLAM camera geometry, and Flow-Aware Temporal Consistency (FATC) finally regularizes its temporal derivatives.

Figure 5. GravHMR corrects global motion beyond locally plausible poses. We compare reconstructions without (orange) and with (blue) GravHMR on two EMDB-2 sequences. Gray meshes and dashed curves indicate ground-truth bodies and root trajectories, respectively.

GravHMR uses ViPE cameras; TRAM uses its masked DROID-SLAM cameras with ground-truth intrinsics. Each rendered 15 s window is aligned to the ground truth on its first 60 frames. Figure 1. Motivating observation: orientation inconsistency in world-grounded human reconstruction. Directly lifting camera-space body estimates into the world using independently estimated SLAM camera poses can propagate orientation errors, as illustrated by TRAM (red). In contrast, GravHMR reconciles body and camera orientations through a shared gravity reference, yielding an upright reconstruction more consistent with the ground truth (gray).

papers.abstract: Understanding a scene requires both geometry and semantics: geometry recovers its spatial structure, and semantics separates it into objects. Current models obtain the two from separate networks or separate passes. We present PINE, a one-step Omni Diffusion Transformer that predicts the point map, the surface normals, and the instance map of an image in one forward pass. PINE treats each map as a token stream, and a stream mask decides which streams interact. A camera-aware ray encoding positions every token by its camera ray rather than its pixel. Grounding attention adds the affinity of pretrained DINOv3 features to the attention logits. Trained on only 139K synthetic images for geometry, PINE achieves state-of-the-art point maps whether or not intrinsics are given and the best average rank on surface normals. It also exceeds SAM on large objects with less than 1 percent of its training images, and it predicts all three maps 5.7x faster than MoGe-3 with SAM.
authors: Zeyu Ren, Jie Ni, Rui Qian, Jiahao Wei, Hao Tang, Yongtai Liu, Zeyu Zhang
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of estimating geometry and semantics with separate networks or passes.
Uses an Omni Diffusion Transformer with separate token streams for point maps, surface normals, and instance maps.
Employs stream-masked interactions, camera-ray token encoding, and DINOv3-based grounding attention.
Trained on 139K synthetic geometry images, it achieves state-of-the-art point maps and the best average rank for surface normals.
Outperforms SAM on large objects and predicts all three maps 5.7× faster than MoGe-3 with SAM.

papers.abstract: Modifying 3D assets requires enacting targeted structural transformations while strictly preserving the geometric identity of unedited regions. While recent probability flow models enable training-free editing, bounding these modifications within a high-dimensional latent space presents severe mathematical challenges. Current inversion-free trajectories rely on global velocity updates, which often cause spatial bleed into preserved structures and induce trajectory under-commitment, causing edits to stall mid-path. To resolve these dual failures, we introduce FocusFlow, a segmentation-free framework that structures the integration trajectory into two disjoint phases. During early coarse structure formation, FocusFlow applies Feature-Divergence Localization (FDL) to spatially gate the velocity field using intrinsic cross-attention. Once coarse structure has formed, FocusFlow applies Reference Generation Guidance (RGG), a trajectory-correction term that drives convergence to the target shape by pulling the trajectory toward an explicit clean-latent target. Evaluated on the joint Google Scanned Objects and PartObjaverse-Tiny benchmarks, FocusFlow obtains the best preservation scores and the largest edit magnitude among compared methods, suggesting that it can reduce the traditional preservation-modification trade-off. By providing stable, localized geometric control without manual spatial annotations, this phase-scheduled approach lowers technical barriers to the modification of synthetic 3D media.
authors: Tri Ton, Siwoo Lim, Joshua Tian Jin Tee, Chang D. Yoo
bullets: Addresses spatial bleed and stalled edits in inversion-free probability-flow editing.
Uses Feature-Divergence Localization to gate velocity updates during early coarse structure formation.
Applies Reference Generation Guidance later to pull the trajectory toward a clean latent representing the target shape.
On Google Scanned Objects and PartObjaverse-Tiny, reports the best preservation scores and largest edit magnitude among compared methods.
Requires no segmentation or manual spatial annotations, though its scope is evaluated on these benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Judgments about the beauty of buildings and streets inform architectural design, urban planning, and heritage conservation, yet increasingly rely on scanned 3D models over material fabric. Automatic aesthetic assessment remains largely confined to 2D photographs. We ask what survives when image aesthetic assessment crosses this dimensional gap to produce dense, per-point aesthetic descriptions of heritage and urban point clouds. We examine three routes that sidestep costly, and sometimes ethically dubious, human labeling at scale: (1) lifting scalar scores from image aesthetic models (NIMA, SAAN) onto geometry; (2) training Aesthetic Visual Analysis (AVA) regression heads on frozen vision backbones (DINOv3, TIPS, SigLIP2, PE, RADSeg) or, in a 3D-native variant, a generalist point encoder on feed-forward AVA reconstructions; and (3) querying lifted vision-language features with a natural-language aesthetic label, taking similarity as a score. The two supervised routes transfer poorly: heads fitting AVA in-domain produce architectural class profiles that neither reproduce one another nor track other signals, while the 3D-native probe stays near chance due to reconstruction geometry quality. Text querying is markedly more coherent. Projecting out the class-text direction from point features raises mean cross-model agreement on architectural part profiles from +0.035 to +0.352, and from +0.113 to +0.293 per point; the four backbones passing a semantic sanity check correlate at 0.31-0.73, while the failing one remains an outlier. Since model agreement is not agreement with human aesthetic perception, we detail a part-aware rating protocol to clarify where human and automatic ratings disagree. We provide a reproducible transfer protocol, an account of which pseudo-labeling routes carry signal, and dense aesthetic pseudo-labels meant as hypotheses rather than ground truth.
authors: Sophia Kovalenko, Alexander M. Rusnak, Vittoria Meroni, Yasmine Kroknes-Gomez, Fr\'ed\'eric Kaplan
bullets: The work addresses automatic aesthetic assessment for scanned 3D buildings and streets, extending methods beyond 2D photographs.
It compares image-score lifting, supervised AVA regression heads on frozen vision backbones, a 3D-native probe, and natural-language querying of lifted vision-language features.
Supervised transfer routes perform poorly: their architectural profiles are inconsistent, and the 3D-native probe remains near chance because of reconstruction quality.
Text querying improves cross-model agreement after projecting out the class-text direction, with agreement rising from +0.035 to +0.352 for architectural profiles and from +0.113 to +0.293 per point.
The authors provide a reproducible transfer protocol and a part-aware human-rating protocol to identify disagreements between automatic scores and human perception.

papers.abstract: Avatars created from a single photo are fixed once made: regions the photo never showed, such as the back of a garment, are hallucinated and remain that way. We present Refreshable Animatable Gaussian Avatars (RAGA), a full-body Gaussian avatar that is created from a single image in about one second and can be refreshed whenever new images of the same person become available, without retraining or gradient-based optimization. RAGA maps each new observation into canonical UV space, accumulates it as visibility- and angle-weighted running sums, and re-decodes the fused map with the same decoder used for the photo. Although this decoder is trained only on single images, it makes use of the fused evidence. On 163 clips from five datasets, RAGA created from one photo outperforms LHM, LHM++ and IDOL, including on three datasets never used in training. Refreshing from later frames adds 0.49 dB PSNR overall and 0.68 dB on views turned at least 135{\deg} from the photo, where SSIM and LPIPS also improve. Given the same 16 images on all clips, LHM++ gains 0.15 dB, against 0.48 dB for RAGA. Creating an avatar takes 1.08 s and animating it 48.1 ms per frame on a laptop RTX 3080 GPU, with body fitting and matting included in creation and pose estimation included in animation. Code will be released on GitHub.
authors: Sadia Mubashshira, John Quarles, Kevin Desai
bullets: Addresses fixed, hallucinated unseen regions in single-photo avatars, such as the back of clothing.
Maps new observations into canonical UV space, fuses them using visibility- and viewing-angle weighting, and re-decodes the result with the original decoder.
Evaluated on 163 clips across five datasets, including three unseen during training; it outperforms LHM, LHM++, and IDOL from a single photo.
Refreshing with later frames improves reconstruction quality, especially for views turned far from the original photo.
Runs in 1.08 seconds for creation and 48.1 ms per animation frame on an RTX 3080 laptop GPU.

papers.abstract: Modern monocular hand estimators recover detailed 3D meshes from individual images, yet effectively leveraging their predictions across multiple views remains challenging. Independently predicted meshes can disagree in scale, placement, and articulation, limiting the integration of complementary multi-view information. Hence, we present AlignHand, a calibrated multi-view framework that builds on a frozen monocular hand reconstruction prior to align and enhance its predictions. Specifically, AlignHand refines cross-view joint observations and estimates their reliability to establish a shared metric reference for alignment. Once the meshes are brought into a common frame, their complementary surface evidence is selectively fused across anatomical regions, followed by pixel-aligned refinement that predicts bounded residual displacements from local image features. This global-to-local integration enables AlignHand to exploit complementary observations while preserving the strong monocular prior. Extensive experiments on DexYCB-MV, HanCo, and HO3D-Eval-MV demonstrate that AlignHand achieves the lowest MPVPE and MPJPE among the compared methods under the respective evaluation protocols, reducing MPVPE by 30.1%, 29.1%, and 8.0%, respectively, compared with a matched geometry baseline.
authors: Zhilu Yang, Kun Yang, Shiyan Wang, Anqi Xu, Xinran Huang, Yizheng Jiao, Huan Yang, Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
bullets: Addresses inconsistencies in independently predicted meshes across scale, placement, and articulation.
Refines cross-view joints and estimates their reliability to establish a shared metric reference.
Fuses aligned surface evidence by anatomical region, then applies pixel-aligned bounded residual refinement.
Evaluated on DexYCB-MV, HanCo, and HO3D-Eval-MV, achieving the lowest reported MPVPE and MPJPE among compared methods.
Reduces MPVPE by 30.1%, 29.1%, and 8.0% versus a matched geometry baseline under the respective protocols.

papers.abstract: Unified 3D understanding and generation require compact sequences preserving spatial structure. Dense grids yield long sequences, while serialization can separate spatial neighbors. We propose Sparse Proximity Aware Compression (SPAC), a shared sparse SDF vocabulary combining sparse encoding with reversible spatial merging. A Sparse SDF VQ-VAE quantizes near-surface features while retaining explicit coordinates, using reconstruction supervision for surface fidelity and detail. 3D Byte-Pair Encoding (3D-BPE) merges recurring face-adjacent patterns using relative offsets before serialization. Macro tokens expand exactly into leaf tokens and coordinates. After Morton serialization, a shared LLM reads geometry for captioning and predicts tokens that decode into meshes for text-conditioned generation. With fixed geometry, architecture, and band width in voxels, sparse encoder cost grows approximately quadratically with resolution. 3D-BPE reduces mean complete LLM sequence length by 45.4 percent, including coordinates, text, and control tokens. SPAC achieves strong results in both 3D captioning and text-conditioned mesh generation. Ablations show gains over leaf tokens and Morton 1D-BPE in both tasks. The project page at https://yangjj007.github.io/spac/ .
authors: Junjie Yang, Rui Qian, Yijiang Li, Jinyi Xu, Yuhao Yan, Xinjian Yi, Yanfeng Li, Mingxuan Li, Xiang Wan, Jicong Fan, Siqi Liu, Ahmed Elazab, Changmiao Wang
bullets: Targets long sequences from dense 3D grids and spatially disconnected serialization.
Uses a sparse SDF VQ-VAE with explicit coordinates and reconstruction supervision to preserve surface detail.

papers.abstract: Streaming 3D reconstruction must preserve geometry under limited memory, yet STAC's fixed-resolution spatial key-value (KV) cache grows as scenes expand. We propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework that compresses and reuses spatial memory for long-term reconstruction in unbounded scenes. Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC) organizes KV states into an octree with adaptive resolutions across regions and layers. Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC) guides KV merging by measuring attention-output changes, balancing storage savings with geometric preservation. Temporal Context Refinement (TCR) reuses cached intermediate features and recomputes only a short backbone suffix to refine historical predictions with later observations. Integrated into four pretrained streaming backbones, STAC++ reduces spatial memory consumption while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality on long sequences and large scenes, with further quality gains from refinement at limited computational overhead. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
authors: Boyi Zhu, Youcheng Cai, Dong Wang
bullets: Addresses the memory growth of STAC’s fixed-resolution spatial KV cache as scenes expand.
Uses an adaptive-resolution octree cache, with resolutions varying across regions and network layers.
Merges KV states based on attention-output changes to balance memory savings and geometric preservation.
Refines historical predictions by reusing cached features and recomputing only a short backbone suffix.
Integrated with four pretrained backbones, it reduces memory while maintaining competitive quality and adds refinement gains at limited computational overhead.

papers.tldr: STAC++ is a training-free, plug-and-play framework that compresses and refines spatial memory to enable long-term streaming 3D reconstruction in large, unbounded scenes.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive diffusion world models deliver strong video generation performance, yet they typically output only RGB frames rather than explicit 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene representations, creating a gap between learned visual world dynamics and usable 3D assets for downstream robotics, simulation and rendering. To bridge this gap, we introduce ArgsWorld, an autoregressive diffusion model that also produces an explicit 3DGS scene. For each generation chunk, the diffusion transformer jointly processes clean historical image latents and noisy latents for new views. It keeps the historical image latents fixed and refreshes the scene features so that the Gaussian representation can be revised as new regions come into view. Our 3D Self-Forcing Distillation trains the model on its own generated histories using a mixture of single-view and multi-view data. Distribution matching supervises direct image latents and latents of Gaussian renderings at both generation and additional cameras. ArgsWorld unifies 3D scene reconstruction from posed images, scene generation from image or text prompts, and scene extrapolation across camera segments with disconnected endpoints. Experimental results demonstrate that ArgsWorld achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple 3D scene modeling tasks. Project page: https://m4a1tastegood.github.io/ArgsWorld/
authors: Weiming Chen, Shuaiyan Liu, Xinyu Shao, Zhewen Chen, Tian Guan, Yonghong He, Xitong Ling
bullets: Addresses the gap between RGB-only video world models and usable 3D scene representations.
Jointly processes fixed historical image latents and noisy new-view latents while refreshing Gaussian scene features as regions are revealed.
Uses 3D Self-Forcing Distillation with single- and multi-view data, plus distribution matching for direct and Gaussian-rendered image latents.
Supports 3D reconstruction, image- or text-prompted scene generation, and camera-segment extrapolation with disconnected endpoints.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across multiple 3D scene modeling tasks.

papers.abstract: As code agents evolve, their scope is expanding from generating simple static 3D meshes to constructing structurally complete, complex, interactive 3D scenes. However, existing datasets mainly rely on converting or captioning pre-existing 3D assets, consisting mostly of single-turn code data for static single objects and struggling to scale task diversity and scene complexity, leaving such training data scarce. We present 3DCodeFactory, an automated framework that directly constructs diverse, complex 3D training data from abundant raw text (e.g., diffusion prompts and product descriptions). The framework first leverages an image generator to synthesize 3D reference images from raw text as visual anchors, guiding the generation of concrete modeling specifications and interactive functional requirements; meanwhile, it jointly constructs visual, specification, and functional rubrics from the reference images and requirements to automatically score and filter multi-turn agent rollouts. Based on this framework, we release 3DCodeFactory-Data, comprising 5,045 high-quality task instances and multi-turn interaction trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B on 3DCodeFactory-Data significantly improves performance on BlenderWorld, P3D-Bench, and 3DCodeBench, consistently outperforming models trained on existing open-source 3D code datasets, with our 27B model further surpassing the same-series 2.4T flagship Qwen3.8-Max in overall performance.
authors: Zhaoyu Wang, Xueru Wen, XingYu Li, Jie Lou
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of training data beyond static, single-object 3D code generation.
Uses image-generated 3D references to guide modeling specifications and interactive requirements.
Automatically creates visual, specification, and functional rubrics to score and filter agent rollouts.
Releases 3DCodeFactory-Data with 5,045 high-quality task instances and interaction trajectories.
Fine-tuned Qwen3.5 models improve performance across BlenderWorld, P3D-Bench, and 3DCodeBench; the 27B model surpasses Qwen3.8-Max overall.

papers.abstract: Freehand orthographic drawings capture early design intent, yet recovering executable sketch--extrude CAD programs from raster front, right, and top views remains challenging: noisy, dimension-free 2D layouts must be reconciled into an ordered construction history. We introduce Hand2CAD, a benchmark of 215K ABC-derived synthetic orthographic-drawing--CAD program pairs and 1,000 real three-view sets drawn by CAD-trained participants. Recovering CAD programs from orthographic drawings requires both cross-view geometric reasoning and alignment between visual features and program representations. We propose OrthoLatentCAD to address these two challenges. It fuses local geometry with global context on canonical planes, exchanges evidence between paired plane lines indexed by the same shared-axis coordinate, and maps the spatial representation to ordered program latents through queries inherited from a frozen CAD autoencoder. Across the evaluated one- to three-view configurations, OrthoLatentCAD outperforms protocol-matched baselines in procedural accuracy, compiled geometry, and CAD-kernel validity while benefiting from additional views. Without real-data fine-tuning, it also outperforms the baselines on held-out real drawings. We will release the dataset, code, and evaluation scripts.
authors: Xiaolei Zhou, Xinjie Zhu, Chuangjie Fang, Chenyu Wang, Jianwei Zheng
bullets: Introduces Hand2CAD, comprising 215K synthetic orthographic-drawing–CAD program pairs and 1,000 real three-view sets.

Uses canonical-plane spatial features that combine local geometry and global context, exchange evidence across shared-axis-aligned plane lines, and map to ordered program latents via a frozen CAD autoencoder.
Outperforms protocol-matched baselines in procedural accuracy, compiled geometry, and CAD-kernel validity across evaluated view configurations.
Benefits from additional views and outperforms baselines on held-out real drawings without real-data fine-tuning.
Dataset, code, and evaluation scripts are planned for release.
