papers.abstract: Vision-based 3D occupancy prediction infers voxel-wise geometry and semantics from multi-view images, where 2D-to-3D view transformation is a crucial step. Many existing methods adopt a backward-projection paradigm, projecting uniformly distributed 3D reference points onto image planes to aggregate multi-view features. However, their scene-agnostic sampling patterns overlook the non-uniform distribution of scene geometry, allocating many references to empty space and reducing sampling efficiency under a fixed sampling budget. To address this challenge, we propose SAP, a scene-adaptive projection framework that leverages depth-based geometric priors to guide view transformation. Specifically, we back-project metric depth maps predicted by a frozen depth model into 3D space to obtain geometric priors. To leverage these priors, we design a Scene-Adaptive Projection Encoder comprising two complementary components. First, Prior-Guided Reference Generation constructs a hybrid reference set for feature sampling, allocating references within prior-supported height regions and retaining full-range sampling where valid support is unavailable. Furthermore, to account for potential spatial misalignment caused by depth estimation errors, Radial-Structured Feature Aggregation explores multiple candidate locations through learned radial offsets to aggregate potentially displaced feature evidence. Extensive experiments on Occ3D demonstrate that SAP achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently improves results across diverse occupancy frameworks.
authors: Yuan Wu, Zhiqiang Yan, Zhengxue Wang, Guangfa Wang, Jun Li, Jian Yang
bullets: Uniform reference sampling wastes a fixed sampling budget on empty regions because scene geometry is non-uniform.
A frozen depth model provides metric depth priors that guide 2D-to-3D feature transformation.
Prior-Guided Reference Generation combines prior-supported height sampling with full-range sampling when support is unavailable.
Radial-Structured Feature Aggregation uses learned radial offsets to handle depth-induced spatial misalignment.
Experiments on Occ3D report state-of-the-art performance and consistent gains across diverse occupancy frameworks.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are widely used as 3D priors for novel view synthesis and 3D scene generation. Fine-tuned for perception, generation models also excel at dense prediction such as depth estimation. However, methods that apply video generation models to 3D reconstruction either predict depth without cameras or generate geometry and estimate cameras through many iterative denoising steps, which makes them slower. In this paper, we present $\textbf{VG3R}$, which turns a pretrained video generation model into a feed-forward 3D reconstruction model. Our key observation is that such a model already captures the depth and camera motion of a video, but not in the form required for reconstruction. We introduce two components: $\textit{clip-level shift prediction}$, which corrects depth distortion caused by the unknown shift in decoded inverse depth, and a $\textit{multi-layer camera head}$, which predicts per-frame cameras parameters by combining features across transformer blocks. Using Wan2.1 as its video backbone, VG3R reconstructs a scene and estimate the camera of every frame without iterative denoising. It achieves the lowest ATE and reconstruction errors among methods built on video generation models, runs about 4 and 14 times faster than Aether and Geo4D. VG3R also demonstrates competitive depth estimation and 3D reconstruction performance compared with geometry foundation models. Project page: https://github.com/KTH-RPL/VG3R
authors: Jingong Chen, Qingwen Zhang, Lin Lian, Xinxin Zuo, Yang Wang, Chulwoo Pack, Kyle Gao, Patric Jensfelt, Kwanghee Won
bullets: Addresses the slowness and incomplete camera modeling of prior video-generation-based 3D reconstruction methods.
Corrects decoded inverse-depth distortion using clip-level shift prediction.
Predicts per-frame camera parameters with a multi-layer camera head that fuses features across transformer blocks.
Using Wan2.1, reconstructs scenes without iterative denoising and reports the lowest ATE and reconstruction errors among comparable video-generation methods.
Runs about 4× faster than Aether and 14× faster than Geo4D, while remaining competitive with geometry foundation models.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview. VG3R encodes the input video with the frozen VAE of Wan2.1 and processes its latents with a LoRA-adapted transformer at a fixed timestep, with blocks ordered from bottom to top. The final-block features are decoded into inverse depth x̂ through the output layer and VAE decoder D. ClipShift uses these features to predict a single shift ĉ for a video clip, recovering depth up to a global scale. LayerTap combines features from multiple transformer blocks and pairs each latent frame with the first to predict per-frame cameras. Depth and cameras yield the reconstructed point maps. Gray losses are used only during training.

papers.selection_reason: Turns a pretrained video generation model into a feed-forward 3D reconstruction model with camera estimation; relevant to generalist 3D perception from video priors.

papers.abstract: Vision Banana showed that a closed image generator, instruction-tuned to paint perception outputs as RGB images, becomes a generalist vision model. Does this carry over to \emph{open} generators, and if not, what fails? We answer with \textbf{Open Vision Banana (OVB)}, an open framework that adapts the 7B diffusion generator of Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic, instance, and referring segmentation, using a single shared low-rank adapter and public data. Each task is a \emph{task contract} whose RGB encoder, instruction, and decoder share one specification and are checked before training. Studying 42 externally evaluated checkpoints from two 100k-update runs, six exact weight-space merges, and eight controlled shorter runs, we find that the gap to the closed system is specific and measurable. Geometry is learned early while absolute scale is not: median-aligned NYUv2 $\delta_1$ stays at 0.89--0.93 throughout training as unaligned $\delta_1$ wanders between 0.11 and 0.50. The scale is not committed by a single sample: a ten-seed ensemble lifts unaligned $\delta_1$ from 0.348 to 0.516 without retraining. Depth and 2D segmentation compete for the shared adapter, and weight merging moves along this trade-off without escaping it. Finally, lower validation flow loss comes with lower Cityscapes accuracy (Spearman $\rho\approx-0.9$ between loss reduction and mIoU), so the loss cannot select checkpoints. We release code, contracts, training data, and all evaluation outputs.
authors: Xu Lin, Ruilin Yao, Haoran Xu, Zixiang Wang, Ming Ma, Yu Zhao, Pu Miao, Chonghan Liu
bullets: Adapts Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and referring segmentation.
Uses a shared low-rank adapter, public data, and task contracts that align each task’s encoder, instruction, and decoder before training.
Geometry is learned early, but absolute depth scale remains unstable; ensembling predictions improves unaligned depth accuracy without retraining.
Depth and 2D segmentation compete for adapter capacity, and weight merging does not remove this trade-off.
Lower validation flow loss correlates with worse Cityscapes mIoU, making the loss unreliable for checkpoint selection; code, data, contracts, and evaluations are released.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Open Vision Banana overview. A source image x and a task instruction pq condition a frozen generative backbone (Qwen-Image-2.1 in all experiments; the backbone is a configuration choice) that carries one newly initialized rank-64 LoRA adapter δ shared by all tasks. The source enters as visual tokens and reference latents, the instruction as the text condition, and the target latent is generated from noise in 50 flow steps. The generated RGB image r̂q is converted by a parameter-free decoder Dq into a structured prediction ŷq: metric depth, a class-ID map, instance masks, or a binary mask. Bottom: a task contract Cq = (Eq, pq, Dq; Sq) ties encoder, instruction, and decoder to one specification and is validated before training. The scene is a rendered illustration; its RGB tiles are produced by the contract encoders from exact annotations and are not model predictions.

Fig. 3. Training data and task mixture of the main runs. (a) The 1,098,435 training records by task and source; one record is an image–instruction–target triple, so an image can appear in several records. Small sources are listed to the right of their bar; “Indoor observed” combines ARKitScenes, DIODE, and SUN RGB-D frames with at least 98% observed depth, and “Earlier pool” is the segmentation data of the earlier OVB stages. (b) Each task’s share of the pool (light) against its per-update sampling probability (dark), and the expected number of times each record is drawn over the 3.2M draws of a 100k-update run. Sampling reweights the pool: semantic segmentation and editing replay are drawn more often than their size implies, referring segmentation less often.

(a) Median-aligned NYUv2 δ1 is flat at 0.89–0.93 from the first evaluated checkpoint, while unaligned δ1 moves between 0.11 and 0.49: training changes the scale, not the geometry. (b) Cityscapes mIoU declines in both runs while depth improves; ReasonSeg peaks early in B and recovers late in A.

Fig. 5. Qualitative results: metric depth and semantic segmentation of Qwen-Image-2.1 with run B at 20k updates (EMA adapter, merged) on benchmark validation images. Depth is the RGB code before decoding.

(a) Each task is an explicit, decodable RGB code given by a specification Sq, an encoder Eq, an instruction pq, and a decoder Dq; the depth card shows the colormap path along the edges of the RGB cube, each vertex labeled with the metric depth it encodes under Eq. (2). (b) Checks that run on the training manifest and configuration before the first update. Run A uses peak lr 3 × 10−5 (shown) and run B uses 1 × 10−5; editing replay is included with the intent of preserving generation, which we have not measured (Sec. 6).

papers.selection_reason: Unified perception through generation in RGB space, including metric depth and segmentation, directly relevant to 3D foundation models and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Open Vision Banana: An Open Framework for Unified Visual Perception through Generation in RGB Space
papers.tldr: Open Vision Banana shows that an open 7B diffusion generator can unify depth and segmentation perception tasks, but shared-adapter interference, unresolved depth scale, and misleading validation loss limit performance selection.

papers.abstract: Online surface reconstruction from LiDAR scans requires observation models that respect the sensor's physical measurement geometry. Unlike unordered point sets, LiDAR returns carry anisotropic range noise along known rays, which also implicitly identify free space. We introduce the Occupancy Planar Patch (OPP), an incremental bounded planar patch representation that evaluates surface likelihoods and free space directly in range-space, allowing sensor noise, plane uncertainty, and ray clearance to be explicitly modelled during reconstruction. A single ray-to-patch association weight jointly updates plane geometry, refines surface boundaries, and blends camera imagery. The method is evaluated using six sequences from the Oxford Spires and Multi-Campus datasets. OPP achieves the highest precision and lowest reconstruction error among evaluated methods, while producing stored maps among the most compact. By conservatively admitting surfaces only where geometric evidence is certain, OPP prioritises structural precision over unconstrained completeness, which is well suited for architectural modelling. Geometric reconstruction operates in real time, requiring 81 ms per frame on a representative sequence, with texture projection adding 134 ms.
authors: Jiahao Wang, Chaehyeon Song, Dongjiao He, Jan Quenzel, Lintong Zhang, Ayoung Kim, Maurice Fallon
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between unordered point-set models and LiDAR’s anisotropic, ray-based measurements.
Represents surfaces as bounded planar patches evaluated in range-space, incorporating sensor noise, plane uncertainty, and ray clearance.
Uses a single ray-to-patch association weight to jointly update geometry, refine boundaries, and blend camera imagery.
Across six Oxford Spires and Multi-Campus sequences, it achieved the highest precision and lowest reconstruction error among evaluated methods, with compact maps.
Prioritises conservative structural precision over complete surface coverage; reconstruction ran in real time at 81 ms per frame, with texture projection adding 134 ms.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: One integration step of the OPP reconstruction framework. Given sensor poses Tt, LiDAR point clouds Pt, and RGB images It, each motionundistorted LiDAR ray (ot,dt, rt) is traced to query intersecting candidate patches via spatial acceleration (Sec. III-B), evaluated in range-space to compute soft assignment responsibilities γk (Sec. III-C), and used to concurrently update the supporting plane via an extended Kalman filter (Sec. III-D) and its continuous 2D occupancy boundary via GGAP-RBF [34] (Sec. III-E). Finally, visual appearance from camera images is projected onto texture atlases Ak to update the textured OPP model (Sec. III-F).

Fig. 5: Qualitative reconstruction comparison across OSD (Keble03, Bodleian02) and MCD (kth day 10). Each row shows: (a) ground-truth tripod reference scan (not used during reconstruction); (b) accumulated raw LiDAR scan coloured by beam ring index; (c) volumetric mesh baseline (VDBFusion [2]); (d) OPP planar patches (ours); and (e) textured OPP model (ours). Insets in row 3 (b–d) highlight walking pedestrians: dense motion trails visible in raw LiDAR scan (b) and integrated into the volumetric mesh (c) are cleanly carved away in OPP (d) via range-space transmission clearance (Sec. III-E). In textured OPP (e), patch areas left unobserved by MCD’s narrower camera coverage remain white.

Fig. 3: Continuous boundary and texture layers are defined on a patch’s supporting plane: (a) allocated CSRBF kernels with their centres and radii; (b) the resulting 2D occupancy field (red is occupied, blue is free space); and (c) the associated texture atlas.

Fig. 6: Memory and map growth over time on Keble03 (2.1 s rolling mean). Top: map size and patch count M , whole map (solid) vs. resident (dashed). Bottom: process memory with (solid) and without (dashed) texturing.

Fig. 7: Per-frame processing time distributions across the six benchmark sequences without (top) and with (bottom) texture projection. Histograms are normalised by frame count; dashed lines mark sequence medians.

Fig. 4: Ray clearance mechanisms of Eq. (8) across two geometric scenarios: (a, c) The beam passes through an opening in patch k to land on a farther surface j. The separated range Gaussians yield high transmission, carving free space on k; (b, d) Patches k and j are coplanar patches at the same depth. The overlapping range Gaussians yield high exclusion, suppressing duplicate planes.

TABLE I: Quantitative performance across benchmark sequences, evaluated using the metrics defined in Sec. IV-B. Accuracy and completeness report mean and mode distance errors against ground truth; precision, recall, and F1 are evaluated at 1 cm (strict surface localisation) and 5 cm. Bold indicates the best and underline indicates the second best. We reiterate that our approach is optimised for accuracy rather than unconstrained completeness.

TABLE III: Ablation of system components, evaluated using the same metrics as in Table I (at 5 cm). Completeness, recall, and F1 are greyed out as our design prioritises reconstruction accuracy and precision alongside map compactness. Bold indicates the best performance.
TABLE II: Parameters used during benchmarking: (a) DP-GMM (Sec. IIIC), (b) EKF (Sec. III-D), and (c) GGAP-RBF (Sec. III-E).

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel planar patch representation for LiDAR reconstruction that explicitly models sensor noise and geometry, relevant to 3D perception.
papers.title: Occupancy Planar Patch: Incremental Probabilistic Bounded-Plane Reconstruction from LiDAR Data
papers.tldr: OPP incrementally reconstructs precise bounded planar surfaces from LiDAR by modelling measurement uncertainty and free space directly along sensor rays.

papers.abstract: Coding agents can translate 3D measurements into CAD geometry, but reconstructing engineering models for the built environment demands semantic interpretation and consistent construction constraints beyond surface fitting. We formulate scene-level Scan-to-BIM (Building Information Modeling) as an agentic 3D coding task and introduce S2Bench, comprising public and proprietary scans of 128 real-world scenes across five domains, paired with expert-curated reference models spanning diverse spatial scales. A shared framework lets agents measure scans in Python, build class-labeled components in a live CAD/BIM kernel, and iteratively refine their code. We also propose parallel asynchronous collaboration, where a lead delegates versioned tasks, continues modeling while workers execute, and integrates revision-bound proposals. Evaluating five agents and a collaborative team across 1,028 reconstructions shows that scan-to-model residuals directly guide geometric repair, whereas inferring semantic classes and construction relations requires joint geometric, visual, and engineering reasoning that agents struggle to ground and verify. Consequently, the leading agent fits scan geometry closely ($96\%$ coverage within $5\,\text{cm}$) yet reaches only $63\%$ mIoU, and no agent passes all engineering checks on more than $38\%$ of scenes. Coverage and engineering conformance drop with scene scale, whereas running a smaller model as a team improves all three axes with greater coverage gains on larger scenes. The project page is available at https://tumcms.github.io/S2Bench.github.io/
authors: Changyu Du, Stavros Nousias, Syed Salman Ahmed, Kai Dietmair, Mohammad Alrabab'h, Andr\'e Borrmann
bullets: Introduces 1,028 reconstructions across 128 real-world scenes, five domains, and varied spatial scales, using expert-curated BIM references.
Agents measure scans with Python, create labeled components in a live CAD/BIM kernel, and iteratively refine reconstruction code.
Parallel asynchronous collaboration enables a lead agent to delegate, model concurrently, and integrate versioned worker proposals.
The leading agent achieves 96% scan coverage within 5 cm but only 63% semantic mIoU; no agent passes all engineering checks on over 38% of scenes.
Larger scenes reduce coverage and engineering conformance, while smaller-model teams improve performance, especially on larger scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of S2Bench. S2Bench pairs scans of 128 scenes across five built-environment domains and spatial scales with expert-curated reference models (top). A coding agent builds a component model by writing and inspecting code in a live CAD/BIM kernel (middle). Despite high geometric fidelity, agentbuilt models can fail semantic accuracy (1: door as wall) or engineering consistency (2: open wall joint).

Figure 2. Reconstruction framework. (a) Within an isolated workspace, a harness runs one agent or a team to measure scans in Python and iterate code in Rhino 8, receiving structured feedback (execution errors, validity checks, and agent-written validation) and rendered views before exporting the program, model, and IFC. (b) Single-agent timeline and revisions. (c) Team run on the same scan: the lead (solid icon) delegates regions to three workers, keeps modeling, and merges their parts under a shared 45-minute deadline.

Figure 3. Reconstructed models compared with the input scan and reference. Colors denote component semantic classes, and tunnel and interior views are cut open for visibility. * and ** mark two Qwen outputs whose raw-coordinate 5 cm scan coverage (R5) is 0% due to frame/unit errors and are transformed for display only: (*) rotated 180◦ to undo a flipped local frame, and (**) scaled by 1,000 from metres to millimetres. Additional comparisons across 48 scenes appear in Supp. Figs. 11 to 14.

Figure 6. What agents do, and where errors enter. (a) An interior region in the scan and five reconstructed models, with rings marking scan door locations. (b) Sample outputs by Sol and Opus alongside each agent’s mean share of meshes and kernel solids across 128 scenes. (c) Share of runs (%) with scan checks or declared interference, contact, and support checks, and median program executions.

Figure 9. Kimi K3.1 Pro on Japan RC Bridges Bridge_3 (bridge). The run takes 43 minutes and executes the model program 8 times. The delivery has 9 components, lies within 5 cm of 63.3% of the scan points, and reaches 32.4% mIoU. The agent first reads the span as one slab (step 3), then finds vertical faces below both deck edges and models them as edge girders (step 4). It builds the components as hexahedra between fitted planes and declares contact and interference checks (step 6). When a thickness check fails, it sets the expected value to the value of the model (steps 7–8). The comparison with the scan shows misfits at the abutment tops, and the agent finds that its earlier sections were clipped and revises the end blocks (steps 9–12).

Figure 10. GPT-6.1 Sol on STSD horse-1-6_2 (tunnel). The run takes 27 minutes and executes the model program 9 times. The delivery has 276 components, lies within 5 cm of 99.7% of the scan points, and reaches 47.3% mIoU. The agent fits the tunnel axis (step 3) and a lining profile. It enters the stations of the ring joints as a list of constants (step 5) and models the joints as bands 8 mm wide (step 6). It assigns the invert to the tunnel wall (step 6). Two declared checks fail and are repaired in the geometry: an interference between rail and invert (steps 6–7) and the contact of the walkway brackets (steps 9–10). papers.selection_reason: Introduces S2Bench, a benchmark for agentic 3D reconstruction in the built environment, evaluating coding agents on scan-to-BIM tasks.
papers.title: From Point Clouds to Engineering Models: Benchmarking Agentic 3D Reconstruction in the Built Environment
papers.tldr: S2Bench benchmarks agentic Scan-to-BIM reconstruction and shows that agents can fit 3D geometry well but still struggle with semantic interpretation and engineering-valid modeling.

papers.abstract: Accurate road surface reconstruction is essential for autonomous-driving mapping and simulation, but existing methods trade reconstruction quality for cross-scene inference. Optimization-based methods recover detailed surfaces through costly per-scene optimization, while feed-forward methods lack road-specific constraints and often produce large elevation errors. We propose \textbf{BReD}, a feed-forward framework for reconstructing road elevation, appearance, and semantics from calibrated six-camera sequences. BReD first estimates coarse elevation through LiDAR-supervised depth learning and BEV lifting, using only cameras at inference. A lightweight BEV residual diffusion model then conditions elevation refinement on a camera-derived depth--elevation discrepancy and elevation-aware image features. Diffusion-indexed perturbations expose the model to different discrepancy corruption levels during training, while inference performs one deterministic refinement from the clean discrepancy. The refined elevations are temporally aggregated to anchor road-aligned Gaussians, whose attributes are predicted by a geometry-prior-guided decoder without test-time optimization. On four held-out nuScenes scenes, BReD achieves 7.34 cm elevation RMSE and 90.92\% semantic mIoU, compared with 14.43 cm for RoGS without test-time LiDAR and 8.88 cm for its test-time-LiDAR-assisted variant; both RoGS variants require per-scene optimization.
bullets: Targets the trade-off between high-quality optimization-based reconstruction and weak cross-scene generalization in feed-forward methods.
Estimates coarse road elevation via LiDAR-supervised depth learning and BEV lifting, using only calibrated six-camera sequences at inference.
Refines elevation with a lightweight BEV residual diffusion model conditioned on depth–elevation discrepancies and elevation-aware image features.
Aggregates refined elevations into road-aligned Gaussians and predicts their attributes with a geometry-prior-guided decoder.
On four held-out nuScenes scenes, achieves 7.34 cm elevation RMSE and 90.92% semantic mIoU, without test-time optimization or LiDAR.

figures.caption: Figure 1. BReD overview. (a) BEVDepth* predicts frame-wise coarse elevation using LiDAR depth supervision during training and camera-predicted depth at inference. (b) ReD* combines depth–elevation discrepancy, BEV context, and elevation-aware image features for single-step residual denoising. (c) Refined elevations are temporally aggregated, and FFGS predicts road-Gaussian attributes without test-time optimization. (d) Reconstructed RGB, semantics, and elevation.

Figure 4. Surround-view elevation errors. Results for (a) BReD, (b) RoMe, (c) RoGS w/o LiDAR, and (d) RoGS w/ LiDAR. Colors show signed vertical errors; statistics report RMSE and valid counts in 5m distance bins.
Figure 6. Progressive elevation evolution. Top: Holistic elevation maps. Bottom: Zoomed-in 12m × 12m ROI. Visually, the surface transitions from zcoarse to zrefined, and ultimately to zfinal.

Figure 2. BEV Residual Diffusion. During training, the cameraderived discrepancy x0 is retained at t = 0 or perturbed at t > 0. A timestep-conditioned ConvGRU predicts a bounded elevation update. Inference uses the clean t = 0 state in one denoising step.
Figure 7. Elevation RMSE versus camera-to-observation XY distance. (a) Stage-wise progression showing error reduction from zcoarse to refined stages. (b) Comparison against state-of-theart baselines.

Centered around zcoarse, vertical elevation candidates with offsets [−10,−6,−2,+2,+6,+10] cm are projected onto multi-view image planes via World2Cam. Multi-scale features {P2, P3, P4} are bilinearly sampled (BiLinear) and aggregated through an FPN block to produce fms.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a feed-forward 3D road surface reconstruction framework using BEV residual diffusion, fitting the 3D vision parent topic.
papers.title: BReD: BEV Residual Diffusion for Feed-Forward Road Gaussian Reconstruction
papers.tldr: BReD uses camera-only BEV residual diffusion to efficiently reconstruct detailed road geometry, appearance, and semantics without per-scene optimization.

papers.abstract: 3D vision-language models (3D VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning. However, their reliance on multi-view inputs produces long visual token sequences, imposing substantial computational overhead during inference. Existing pruning methods often rely on token salience or feature diversity as proxies for representativeness, without explicitly modeling the representation gap between the original token set and the retained subset, thereby leading to suboptimal representation of the original scene. In this paper, we propose ReMiC, a training-free, representation-driven token pruning framework based on minimax hierarchical clustering. ReMiC treats retained tokens as prototypes for the original observations, formulating pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget. Local prototype initialization allocates tokens according to regional representation needs, while global prototype refinement updates the selected prototypes using cross-region information to further reduce the maximum representation error. Extensive experiments conducted on three representative 3D VLMs across five 3D scene understanding benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of our method. Notably, by retaining only 10% of visual tokens, ReMiC preserves 93.2% of the performance of Video-3D LLM and achieves a $2.04\times$ faster inference speed.
authors: Bangfeng Yan, Chaoning Zhang, Yuanhao Liu, Pengcheng Zheng, Mengyuan Li, Wei Dong, Sheng Zheng, Yang Yang
bullets: Targets the long visual token sequences created by multi-view 3D inputs.
Formulates pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget.
Uses local prototype initialization followed by global cross-region refinement via minimax hierarchical clustering.
Evaluated across three 3D VLMs and five 3D scene-understanding benchmarks.
With 10% of visual tokens retained, preserves 93.2% of Video-3D LLM performance and delivers 2.04× faster inference.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the ReMiC framework. ReMiC serves as a training-free, plug-and-play module inserted between the visualgeometric encoder and the LLM. In Stage 1, local prototype initialization builds a minimax tree within each spatial region and jointly cuts the trees under a shared token budget to select initial prototypes. In Stage 2, global prototype refinement reassigns all original tokens to their nearest prototypes across regions and reselects a prototype for each cluster.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison. (a) Frame-wise maximum representation errors of different pruning methods. (b) Visualization of retained tokens in the 3D scene. Red boxes highlight the piano and both toolboxes.

Figure 1. Illustration of the relationship between original tokens and retained prototypes. Retained prototypes are shown as solid squares with white borders. Translucent patches of the same color indicate the original tokens they represent across views.
Table 2. Performance comparison with other baselines on Ross3D and GS-Reasoner. Avg. reports the average percentage of original performance retained across the three benchmarks and ten metrics.
Table 6. Efficiency analysis of our ReMiC. Times are reported in seconds and Memory in GB.
Table 3. Ablation study on region count L.
Table 4. Ablation Study on Tree Cutting Strategies.
Table 5. Ablation study on prototype refinement strategies.

papers.selection_reason: Representation-driven token pruning for 3D VLMs via minimax clustering; directly fits token pruning, spatial intelligence, and 3D foundation models.
papers.title: ReMiC: Representation-Driven Token Pruning for 3D VLMs via Minimax Hierarchical Clustering
papers.tldr: ReMiC is a training-free token-pruning method that preserves 3D VLM performance while reducing inference cost by selecting representative visual tokens.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is commonly optimized with multiple reconstruction losses, which naturally forms a multi-objective optimization problem. This issue becomes more pronounced when perceptual losses are introduced to improve visual quality, as different objectives may impose competing update directions on Gaussian primitives and make it difficult to simultaneously improve fidelity, perceptual quality, and representation efficiency. Based on this view, we reformulate 3DGS training as a multi-objective optimization problem and derive selective conflict-aware position updates that reduce interference between competing objectives while preserving the contribution of each loss. We further observe that gradient conflicts persist throughout training and are most severe in Gaussian position parameters, indicating that objective conflict is closely tied to geometry optimization. We therefore treat position-gradient conflict as a geometry-aware signal to guide densification and pruning. Experiments show that our method achieves better rendering performance while improving representation compactness and rendering efficiency over existing 3DGS variants.

papers.abstract: Knowing the layout of the physical world matters for many applications, yet the sensors we rely on for it (e.g., cameras and LiDAR) can fail in darkness, in adverse weather, or behind walls. Wireless signals do not face these limitations: every link between a base station and a user is shaped by the buildings it passes, reflects from, or is blocked by, leaving information about the surrounding scene embedded in the wireless channel measured at the endpoints. However, mapping channel measurements to the environment is a severely ill-posed problem: a measurement records only the structures that interact with the transmitted electromagnetic waves along its propagation paths, and even these observations can often be explained by multiple plausible scenes. We therefore formulate wireless scene reconstruction as posterior inference and develop a hierarchical framework with two complementary stages to approach this problem. A wireless foundation model, pretrained to respect propagation physics, transforms each channel measurement into a representation of the scene structure that shaped the observation. A diffusion model then jointly integrates representations from multiple measurements to model and sample the posterior over building occupancy, with consensus over samples producing the final reconstruction. We demonstrate that the framework can accurately recover building footprints from wireless channel measurements alone and show that its performance depends critically on both design components: physics-grounded representations expose scene-relevant information, while joint posterior inference coherently integrates complementary observations.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($\delta_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

papers.abstract: Streaming visual geometry transformers retain historical key-value (KV) states as cross-view geometric memory, but growing caches constrain long-sequence inference. We systematically characterize KV quantization in streaming geometry and uncover two linked challenges: Nonuniform Geometric Sensitivity and Cache-Geometry Mismatch. Quantization sensitivity varies across precision choices and cache locations, while perturbed retrieval changes geometry-head inputs and propagates through subsequent predictions and KV writes. Guided by these findings, we propose QuantStream3D, to our knowledge the first dedicated KV quantization framework for streaming visual geometry transformers. Geometry-Guided Mixed-Precision KV Quantization protects sensitive cross-view evidence, while Geometry-Aligned Quantization-Aware Distillation jointly adapts transformer blocks and geometry heads on student-generated quantized history. Across five benchmarks and two backbones, QuantStream3D achieves near-lossless geometric accuracy in most settings with predominantly 2-bit KV caches, and many configurations surpass unquantized inference. Compared with LLM-oriented KV quantizers, it reduces TUM absolute trajectory error and NeuralRGBD completeness error by up to 57.4% and 69.7%, respectively. Integration with existing native cache-pruning methods further pushes compression while improving reconstruction quality on NeuralRGBD. Our optimized StreamVGGT backend achieves $5.05\times$ physical KV compression and 23.1% lower latency at batch size one. Under a fixed memory budget on the same GPU, it supports $5.4\times$ the maximum batch size and up to $1.67\times$ the peak throughput of unquantized inference. Code and pretrained checkpoints will be made publicly available.

papers.abstract: We introduce PAWS, a parametric model of canine shape and pose, learned from 3D scans of real dogs. Capturing the full diversity of dogs is challenging, as different breeds vary in size, proportion, and body shape. To capture this range, we scanned 31 dogs across multiple breeds and sizes performing a range of natural movements. From this dataset, we build a parametric model that combines an anatomically faithful skeleton with a linear shape space learned from the 3D scans. Unlike previous models, our model is learned from real dogs in varying poses, allowing for realistic modelling of canine pose and shape. We demonstrate that building on PAWS provides a robust framework for downstream tasks, such as surface reconstruction and image regression. In particular, we show that a limited number of anatomically valid degrees of freedom is sufficient to accurately estimate dog pose and shape.

papers.abstract: In a dark capture, the darkness is not uniform. How much light reaches a surface depends on where it lies relative to the few light sources, and the camera compresses what remains with a tone curve. Most low-light 3D reconstruction methods either apply one curve to every pixel of a view, so a dark object beside a lamp and a bright one in an unlit corner receive the same correction, or store the darkness in the 3D representation, where it can absorb scene detail. We present VeilGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting method for low-light novel view synthesis that treats the degradation as a veil drawn over a clear scene. Each Gaussian carries an albedo and a shading latent instead of spherical harmonics, separating surface colour from illumination. Each view is darkened by a spatially varying gain followed by a global tone curve, and rendering without this veil gives the restored scene. A small network predicts a coarse basis for the gain from the observation, and its coefficients are solved for each view rather than learned. Training through this solve discourages the Gaussians from absorbing what the veil can explain. VeilGS needs no paired normal-light supervision and stores no per-view parameters. On Gaussian-DK, its restored renders score best on no-reference NIQE and CLIP-IQA and are rated highest in a blind user study with 55 participants. On LOM, it achieves results competitive with the state of the art.

papers.abstract: Growers and traders rely on root morphology to assess wild ginseng, yet breakage can obscure important structural traits. We study point cloud completion to provide geometric references for morphological analysis. Does providing more observed points always improve 3D completion? We test whether selected subsets improve recovery of the original missing region while keeping the pretrained completer fixed. We introduce BioCL-POS, an external selector that predicts how the completer responds to candidate inputs. For each candidate, we predict the displacement and distance from shared spatial locations to the nearest points in its completion. We use these spatial responses to estimate recovery quality and supervise them with measurements from actual completions. At inference, we select an input from the observed geometry and run the completer once. We evaluate four frozen completers on controlled gaps in ginseng and tree data at 5%,10%, and 20% omission, and examine 30% omission on ginseng. At 5--20% omission, we outperform full-input completion and all five alternative selectors on both datasets with all four completers. We achieve lower mean reconstruction error and higher mean F-score and coverage. We thus show that selecting observations can improve geometric recovery without retraining the completer, providing more accurate geometric references for subsequent morphological analysis.
authors: Yulu Wang, Tingting Yao, Taolue Liu
bullets: Addresses whether using all observed points is always best when reconstructing missing root geometry.
Uses an external selector to predict a completer’s spatial response to candidate observation subsets.
Selects one input based on predicted recovery quality, then runs the pretrained completer once.
Outperforms full-input completion and five alternative selectors across four frozen completers on ginseng and tree data with 5–20% omissions.
Improves reconstruction error, F-score, and coverage; performance is also examined at 30% omission on ginseng.

papers.abstract: Point cloud denoising and upsampling require samples that accurately recover the underlying surface from noisy or sparse observations. A central challenge in both tasks is preserving surface coverage while refining point locations. We introduce GAAFormer (Geometry-Anchored Attention Transformer), a unified generative octree transformer that performs both tasks with a shared network. Its decoder anchors attention neighborhoods to geometry, providing spatial context for occupancy prediction and point generation. Fixed voxel windows and alternating shifts preserve the grouping of surviving nodes as the output tree changes. The design retains the encoder, positional encoding, prediction heads, and parameter count of a serialized-attention backbone. We establish a deletion-consistency property of the neighborhood rule and evaluate both tasks using the same model. On PUNet, GAAFormer achieves a mean Chamfer distance (CD) of $6.0643\times10^{-5}$, reducing CD and Hausdorff distance by 3.35% and 19.34%, respectively, relative to the serialized backbone. For upsampling, it achieves CD values of $0.8475$, $1.7057$, and $1.0147$ ($\times10^{-5}$) on PU-GAN, PU1K, and Sketchfab, respectively, with improvements in CD, Hausdorff distance, and point-to-surface distance over the same backbone on PU-GAN and Sketchfab. These results establish a single architecture for point cloud denoising and upsampling. Within the shared encoder-decoder, the same geometry-anchored attention module improves both noise removal and dense point generation without task-specific redesign or additional parameters.
authors: Haoxi Tian (School of Civil Engineering,Geomatics, Southwest Petroleum University)
bullets: Addresses the challenge of recovering accurate surface geometry while preserving coverage in noisy or sparse point clouds.
Uses a generative octree Transformer whose decoder anchors attention neighborhoods to geometry for occupancy prediction and point generation.
Fixed voxel windows, alternating shifts, and a deletion-consistent neighborhood rule preserve grouping as the output tree changes.
Retains the serialized-attention backbone’s encoder, positional encoding, prediction heads, and parameter count.
Improves denoising and upsampling metrics over the serialized backbone, with gains reported in Chamfer, Hausdorff, and point-to-surface distances on several benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Moving objects introduce cross-frame inconsistencies that complicate camera estimation and static geometry recovery in driving scenes. Recent feed-forward Gaussian methods explicitly separate static and dynamic primitives, but often estimate camera parameters and geometry from shared features that jointly encode both components, leaving static reconstruction susceptible to dynamic interference. To address this challenge, we propose S2D-Splat, a feed-forward framework for static-first Gaussian reconstruction with layer-wise feature guidance. Our framework separates static and dynamic features before camera and geometry estimation, enabling the static branch to recover camera parameters and static 3D Gaussians with reduced dynamic interference. Intermediate static features are cached at each layer and reused as fixed conditioning at corresponding layers of the dynamic branch. This asymmetric information flow preserves the established static representations while providing stable geometric context for reconstructing dynamic 3D Gaussians. An instance-level motion decoder further queries the fused static and dynamic representations to estimate object trajectories, supporting motion-aligned Gaussian fusion and temporal interpolation. Experiments on Waymo and zero-shot evaluations on nuScenes and the MM-AU accident dataset demonstrate that S2D-Splat outperforms existing approaches on most evaluated metrics and generalizes to highly dynamic, pre-collision driving scenarios.
authors: Jinheng Li, Tianchen Deng, Bufan Zhang, Qu Chen, Jianwu Fang
bullets: Addresses camera and geometry errors caused by moving objects interfering with static-scene estimation.
Separates static and dynamic features before estimating camera parameters and 3D Gaussians.
Caches intermediate static features to condition the dynamic branch while preserving stable static representations.
Uses an instance-level motion decoder for object trajectories, motion-aligned Gaussian fusion, and temporal interpolation.
Outperforms existing methods on most evaluated metrics on Waymo and transfers zero-shot to nuScenes and MM-AU accident scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of S2D-Splat. Given unposed images, we encode each frame into patchified features and use SAM2 to classify tokens as static or dynamic, which a Motion-Static Separator then refines into clean static and dynamic tokens (camera in , static in , dynamic in , suppressed dynamic in ). The static tokens pass through alternating attention and are decoded by heads into camera parameters and a static Gaussian field, with each layer’s camera and static tokens cached in a Tokens Bank. The dynamic reconstruction mirrors this but takes the fused static and dynamic tokens as input, re-fusing the extracted dynamic tokens with the Tokens Bank after each layer to yield global tokens and a dynamic Gaussian field. From the global tokens, instance-specific queries retrieve each instance’s motion, and all components merge to form the full scene reconstruction.

Figure 1: We propose S2D-Splat, a feedforward Gaussian reconstruction framework that achieves precise dynamic-static decoupling and instance-level motion prediction for complex driving scenes. It disentangles multi-frame input into static and dynamic representations, reconstructs each representation independently, and fuses them into a global representation that guides a motion decoder to recover accurate and temporally consistent per-instance 3D trajectories (e.g., Query 1, Query 2).

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D object detection remains a significant challenge for outdoor scenes, with existing methods often struggling to effectively transfer the rich semantic knowledge from powerful 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into a 3D context. We propose a novel, two-part framework for this task. First, we introduce a direct, object-level distillation method. We generate class-agnostic 3D proposals to source regions from the entire scene, without relying on any manual labels. We leverage a spatially-aware VLM to extract a semantic embedding from each proposal's projected 2D bounding box and supervise our 3D model to predict this embedding on a per-instance basis. Second, to enhance zero-shot capability and inject domain-specific information, we employ a powerful Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as an image captioner to generate rich textual captions for each of these proposals. These captions are integrated into the training objective to directly align the 3D features with these rich semantics, creating a composite loss that combines direct feature distillation with caption-based semantic enrichment. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach, establishing a new state of the art in 3D open-vocabulary detection on the Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes.
authors: Thomas E. Huang, Alex Zihao Zhu, Hao Xiang, Tianyi Cai, Jingwei Ji, Yuliang Zou, Jiafan Yu, Xin Huang, Mingxing Tan
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of transferring rich 2D VLM knowledge to outdoor 3D object detection.
Uses class-agnostic 3D proposals and spatially aware VLM embeddings from projected 2D regions for object-level distillation.
Generates proposal-level captions with an MLLM to add domain-specific semantic information and improve zero-shot capability.
Trains with a composite objective combining direct feature distillation and caption-based semantic alignment.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Data Generation Pipeline. (a) Generic Objects Extraction: We use RANSAC and DBSCAN on the raw point cloud to generate class-agnostic 3D proposals across the entire scene, which are then projected to all 2D camera views. (b) Visual Feature Extraction: The proposals are used to RoI pool features from the VLM vision encoder, creating the visual distillation targets f vis. (c) Language Feature Extraction: The proposals are used to crop and mask the images and then sent to a MLLM for captioning, which are then encoded by the VLM text encoder to create the language distillation targets etext.

Fig. 2. Overall Pipeline. During (a) training, our detector is supervised with three losses: class-agnostic bounding box loss Ldet along with two distillation losses, Visual Alignment loss Lvis and Language Alignment loss Llang, for feature alignment. During (b) inference, we directly use the trained detector to predict boxes and open-vocabulary embeddings. Text-based queries are encoded by the VLM text encoder, and cosine similarity between the embeddings and queries are used to assign the final class label.

papers.abstract: Recent foundation models have drastically improved the generalization of monocular relative depth estimation, yet recovering accurate metric depth from their estimates for depth perception tasks remains challenging due to scale ambiguity and local metric-scale inconsistency. Existing approaches recover metric depth from sparse observations using either explicit global affine transformation algorithms or implicit data-driven depth completion networks. The former cannot accommodate spatially varying relative-to-metric relationships, while the latter are sensitive to the distribution of sparse observations and may not fully exploit generalizable relative depth priors. To simultaneously address these issues, this study extends our previous work MTD and proposes MTDv2, a hybrid metric depth perception framework that combines explicit depth metricization with data-driven metric depth refinement. The explicit depth metricization process performs segment-wise affine transformations to recover spatially varying metric scales while preserving the geometric structure of relative depth, followed by pixel-wise depth refinement that propagates metric observations along paths with minimal accumulated geometric variation. The data-driven depth refinement process subsequently extends the explicit single-path depth propagation to a learnable multi-path formulation while preserving its interpretability. Extensive experiments conducted on 16 public datasets demonstrate the robust and generalizable depth scale recovery capability of MTDv2 across diverse sources of sparse observations and different depth estimation paradigms, as well as its broad applicability to downstream 3D perception tasks. Code will be publicly available at https://mias.group/MTD upon publication.
bullets: Addresses scale ambiguity and spatially varying relative-to-metric relationships in monocular depth estimation.
Uses segment-wise affine transformations to recover local metric scales while preserving relative-depth geometry.

Supports downstream 3D perception tasks; the abstract does not specify quantitative gains or limitations beyond its stated scope.

papers.abstract: We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming prior work in all of these dimensions. We release a family of models that define a new Pareto frontier in terms of metric accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime. We release code and weights at https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-depth-pro-2/
authors: Peiyun Hu, Marko Mihajlovic, Lyndon Duong, Lahav Lipson, Wei Dong, Ama\"el Delaunoy, Stephan R. Richter, Vladlen Koltun
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between sharp boundaries in single-frame methods and temporal consistency in multi-frame methods.
Uses one network to process both still images and video and predict dense metric depth at full resolution.
Reports improvements over prior work in metric accuracy, sharpness, and temporal consistency.
Releases multiple models spanning a Pareto frontier across accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime.
Code and model weights are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Native 3D generation has largely been built around latent diffusion, with recent advances concentrating on stronger variational autoencoders (VAE) and increasingly elaborate latent representations, from vecset and triplanes to structured sparse voxels. Despite their architectural differences, these methods all share the same premise: geometry is first compressed into a latent space and only then modeled by the generator. We take a different route and propose Direct3D-V3, a latent-free diffusion transformer (DiT) framework that discards the VAE altogether and operates in the native voxel domain, directly modeling raw SDF voxel grids during both training and sampling. To make this direct voxel formulation geometrically reliable, we introduce an implicit manifold regularization over neighboring voxels to suppress non-watertight surfaces, and convert predicted SDF grids into meshes via Marching Cubes so that rendered normal losses can supervise the model directly from its predicted SDF. To improve alignment between the conditioning image and generated geometry, Direct3D-V3 also predicts the camera parameters of the conditioning image as an auxiliary task, encouraging the DiT to learn the mapping from image observations to 3D shape. This latent-free design removes the reconstruction bottleneck, brings training under an objective in the native voxel domain, and yields meshes with substantially richer local detail. The predicted camera and native SDF voxel output further make Direct3D-V3 extensible to generative reconstruction, where diffusion is interleaved with normal-guided refinement to improve alignment with the observed view while the generative prior completes unseen regions. Project page: https://dreamtechai.github.io/Direct3D-V3.
authors: Shuang Wu, Jiachen Qian, Youtian Lin, Feihu Zhang, Philip Torr, Yao Yao, Xun Cao
bullets: Addresses the reconstruction bottleneck and representational complexity of VAE-based latent 3D diffusion.
Uses a latent-free diffusion transformer that models raw SDF voxel grids during training and sampling.
Applies neighboring-voxel manifold regularization and rendered normal supervision through Marching Cubes.
Predicts conditioning-image camera parameters as an auxiliary task to improve image-to-geometry alignment.
Supports generative reconstruction by combining diffusion with normal-guided refinement for observed and unseen regions.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Framework of Direct3D-V3. Rather than compressing geometry into a learned latent representation, Direct3D-V3 trains and samples directly on raw SDF voxel grids. During training, we extract the SDF voxel grid and surface patch SDF values from the ground-truth mesh, and add Gaussian noise to the surface patch SDF values to form the DiT input x𝑡 . During inference, the first-stage model is used only to provide the surface patch indices; sampling then starts from Gaussian noise on these sparse patches, and the latent-free DiT predicts the clean SDF values directly in the native voxel domain. The patch-level DiT uses the noisy SDF signal, DINOv2 image tokens, and timestep embedding to reason efficiently over global shape semantics, while a lightweight voxel-level DiT refines voxel-level SDF values within each selected patch. In parallel, a camera prediction branch combines patch-level features with image tokens to regress normalized intrinsic and extrinsic parameters, encouraging the generated shape to remain spatially aligned with the conditioning image.

Fig. 5. Generative reconstruction pipeline. Given the input images, we use pre-trained predictors to estimate the corresponding foreground mask and normal map as auxiliary observations. The key reconstruction mechanism lies in how these cues are coupled with the latent-free DiT output: the mask calibrates the predicted camera, while the normal map drives direct refinement of the predicted SDF voxel grid. At each guided sampling step, the DiT proposes a clean SDF grid together with an image-view camera. We first align the rendered mask with the estimated one to correct the camera, and then compare rendered surface normals with the estimated normal map to update the SDF values. The refined SDF is re-noised and passed back to the sampler, coupling observation-driven correction with the learned generative prior for the final reconstruction.
Fig. 3. The architecture of the dual-granularity DiT.

Fig. 4. Illustration of the Implicit Manifold Regularization (IMR). Without the decoder-induced geometric prior used in latent-based pipelines, a latentfree DiT can predict locally inconsistent TSDF fields, leading to abrupt zerolevel crossings and non-watertight meshes after Marching Cubes. Since the surface manifold is implicitly defined by the zero level set of the TSDF, we regularize this manifold by penalizing neighboring voxels whose predicted SDF values differ by more than one voxel length 𝜂. This local constraint encourages coherent TSDF transitions around the surface, reducing holes and producing a more watertight extracted mesh while preserving the generated shape.

Fig. 14. Additional visual results generated by Direct3D-V3.
Fig. 9. Qualitative comparison for multi-view generative reconstruction on scenes from the Tanks and Temples dataset.

Fig. 11. Qualitative ablation of the camera prediction branch. Adding the branch improves alignment between the generated mesh and the conditioning image, especially for structures visible from the conditioning view.

Fig. 10. Qualitative ablation of the core components. The patch-level DiT alone produces coarse and incomplete geometry. Fig. 13. Failure case of single-view generative reconstruction. When the first-stage surface indices are poorly aligned with the conditioning image, normal-guided SDF refinement operates on inaccurate sparse support and can distort the mesh.

papers.title: Direct3D-V3: Latent-Free Diffusion Transformers in the Native Voxel Domain
papers.tldr: Direct3D-V3 generates 3D shapes directly as native SDF voxel grids, avoiding latent representations to improve geometric detail and enable view-aligned reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward models have been very successful in 3D reconstruction with ad hoc attention designs that relate all view patches densely. However, the cost of this dense global attention grows quadratically with the number of views, preventing the model from applying to larger-scale reconstruction settings. In this paper, we argue that most dense attention computations are unnecessary from a classical structure-from-motion perspective: 3D structures stem from geometrically matching regions in 2D. We bring this principle to learning-based feed-forward reconstruction with our Sparse Geometric Attention Reconstruction (SGAR) method. In SGAR, each patch token attends to only a small set of patch tokens from other views, chosen by a lightweight learned key selection module trained to predict cross-view 3D proximity of tokens. Thus, dense global attention is replaced by much more efficient geometric-similarity-guided sparse attention. SGAR is a general method that can be applied to different feed-forward models by fine-tuning. In our experiments, we show that SGAR is the fastest among both state-of-the-art dense and sparse methods and the most accurate sparse one. It runs up to 12-times faster than dense attention at 1,000 views with stable pose accuracy where existing sparse methods fail, and shows the best performance in reconstructing more complete geometries on the same time budget.
authors: Aoxiang Fan, Maria Pilligua, Corentin Dumery, Oliver Heinimann, Pascal Fua
bullets: Dense global attention scales quadratically with the number of views, limiting large-scale reconstruction.
A lightweight key-selection module predicts cross-view 3D proximity and selects only relevant patch tokens.
The approach can be integrated into different feed-forward reconstruction models through fine-tuning.
Experiments report the fastest runtime among compared dense and sparse methods, with the strongest accuracy among sparse methods.
At 1,000 views, SGAR runs up to 12× faster than dense attention while maintaining stable pose accuracy and producing more complete geometry under equal time budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative comparison. Point clouds predicted by FastVGGT, ZipMap and SGAR (DejaView), with the ground truth, on one scene of each of 7-Scenes (chess/seq-03), ETH3D (courtyard, laser scan), LaMAR (HGE) and Mip-NeRF 360 (bonsai, SfM points). Left: four of the input views. Below each reconstruction: the AUC@30 of its cameras. SGAR (DejaView) keeps the structure of the scene where the other efficient models fragment it, most visibly on the long LaMAR trajectory.

Figure 3. Overview of SGAR. We replace the global dense attention of DejaView [8] with our sparse geometric attention as an example. The images are encoded by DINOv2 and augmented with camera and register tokens. A single shared block, unrolled over its L steps, runs frame attention, key selection and sparse attention. In sparse attention, each patch attends to the special tokens of all views, the patches of the reference view, a summary of each cluster, and all the patches of the nearest clusters, so that its cost grows near-linearly with the number of views. Key Selection projects the patch tokens by Wadj into a geometric embedding and clusters the embeddings by spherical k-means into √ N clusters, re-clustered at every step. Each cluster probes its m = 4 nearest clusters, itself first. With the patches sorted by cluster, the selected keys form a block-sparse mask over tiles of 128 tokens. A contrastive loss pulls together the embeddings of patches that observe the same surface in the ground-truth geometry and pushes the others apart.

papers.abstract: Understanding how objects move in dynamic scenes requires recovering their 3D motion from visual observations and predicting their positions at unobserved times. Existing methods either optimize scene-specific velocity fields or impose predefined physical and kinematic assumptions. We instead study learning a continuous-time dynamics operator across scenes, mapping multi-view visual observations to 3D object kinematics. We introduce Adaptive Pixel Flows (\ours{}), which learns this operator from multi-view RGB-D observations without per-scene optimization or predefined motion models. The method fuses observations from all cameras into a shared voxel grid in world coordinates, from which the network predicts a continuous-time velocity field. Because the operator is trained across scenes, it learns motion priors that carry over to unseen scenes. The field can then be integrated from observed states to predict object positions between observations and beyond the observed sequence. On held-out PhysInOne scenes, \ours{} improves F1 over the strongest competing method by 2.5\% for in-between prediction and 15\% for future prediction. Compared with per-scene velocity-field methods, the improvements are 30\% and 85\%, respectively. Applied zero-shot to Spring-Gaus, it improves future-prediction F1 by 12\%.
bullets: Addresses 3D motion recovery and temporal prediction without per-scene optimization or predefined physical assumptions.
Fuses all camera observations into a shared world-coordinate voxel grid and predicts a continuous-time velocity field.
Integrates the learned field from observed states to estimate intermediate and future object positions.
Improves F1 on held-out PhysInOne scenes by 2.5% for in-between and 15% for future prediction over the strongest competitor.
Transfers zero-shot to Spring-Gaus, achieving a 12% future-prediction F1 improvement.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces FFGaussType, a feed-forward method to convert 2D geometry into 3D Gaussian assets. This advances 3D scene generation and geometry-aware representation, relevant to 3D vision and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: AdaPixFlow: Learning Continuous-Time 3D Dynamics Across Scenes from Sparse Multi-view Observations
papers.tldr: AdaPixFlow learns a cross-scene continuous-time 3D motion operator from sparse multi-view RGB-D observations to predict object positions between and beyond observed frames.

papers.abstract: Immersive 3D content allows text and graphical elements, such as subtitles, annotations, and icons, to be placed inside a scene rather than displayed as flat overlays. Placed this way, they respect occlusion and perspective and take on user-assigned materials and lighting while preserving their original shapes. In Gaussian scenes, however, each new glyph or icon requires its own iterative optimization, which limits scalable content creation. We present FFGaussType, which converts extruded glyph and SVG outlines into Gaussian assets in a single forward pass. A point encoder maps anchors sampled on the known surface to a single feature plane, from which a decoder shared by all assets predicts neural Gaussians carrying surface normals. This separates geometric conversion from material and lighting choices, and the feature plane supports image and video coding for compact delivery. We construct a paired dataset of 27,221 glyph and SVG icon assets with anchors and calibrated normal and silhouette renderings, holding out font families for evaluation. Conversion from prepared anchors takes 9.1 ms per asset, at a fraction of the compute and memory of prior baselines. On unseen font families and test icons, FFGaussType achieves $1.62^\circ$ normal error and $0.985$ silhouette IoU, the best among the compared feed-forward converters, matching the fidelity that per-asset fitting needs thousands of steps to reach. The code and dataset will be released after publication.
authors: Haoan Feng, Tianfu Wang, Peimeng Guan, Dae Yeol Lee, Guan-ming Su
bullets: Addresses the scalability problem of iteratively optimizing every glyph or icon for Gaussian scenes.
Encodes sampled surface anchors into a shared feature plane, then decodes neural Gaussians with surface normals.
Separates geometry conversion from material and lighting, while supporting compact image and video delivery.
Uses a paired dataset of 27,221 glyph and SVG icon assets, with font-family holdouts for evaluation.
Achieves 1.62° normal error and 0.985 silhouette IoU on unseen assets; conversion takes 9.1 ms per prepared asset.

papers.title: FFGaussType: Feed-Forward Conversion of Glyph and SVG Geometry into Compact Gaussian Assets
papers.tldr: FFGaussType converts glyph and SVG geometry into compact, renderable Gaussian assets in one fast forward pass instead of per-asset optimization.

papers.abstract: Three-dimensional point clouds are a fundamental data modality, and a large family of machine learning architectures has been developed to respect their natural symmetries to rigid motions and permutations. A principled way to compare these architectures, which vary widely in complexity and cost, is through their expressive power. That is, an architecture is complete if it can distinguish any two inputs not related by the symmetries it respects. Simple distance-based message-passing networks are known to be incomplete, and while there exist complete alternatives, they typically rely on computationally intensive mechanisms like high-order representations of the rotation group or higher-order Weisfeiler-Leman-type tests. In this work, we devise a novel, simple, equivariant message-passing architecture for point clouds, and prove that it is complete. We complement our theoretical result with experiments showing that our architecture separates challenging point clouds that distance-based message passing provably cannot distinguish. Our results suggest that high-order equivariant features may not be necessary to enhance the expressivity of point cloud architectures, and can help settle completeness for other equivariant architectures for which such results are currently unknown. We give initial evidence for this by proving completeness of a slightly modified version of SEGNN.
authors: Nadav Dym, Tal Amir, Gia Chi Dang, Christopher Morris
bullets: Targets the limited expressive power of distance-based message-passing networks under rigid-motion and permutation symmetries.
Develops a novel geometric, equivariant message-passing architecture and proves that it can distinguish any non-equivalent point clouds.
Experiments show it separates challenging point-cloud pairs that distance-based methods cannot distinguish.
Results suggest high-order equivariant features may not be necessary for achieving completeness.
Also proves completeness for a slightly modified version of SEGNN, providing evidence for broader applicability.

papers.abstract: Single-photon lidar records the arrival time of each returning photon, enabling 3D reconstruction from few views and scarce photons. However, leading neural methods such as Transientangelo require over an hour of non-convex per-scene optimization, and their accuracy degrades as photon flux decreases. We propose FirstCross, a network-free approach that instead solves a short sequence of convex problems on a voxel grid. For a solid object, the Poisson likelihood of a ray with given signal and background rates depends on the scene solely through its first crossing, the point where the ray first enters the object. Decomposing this likelihood yields two tractable terms. The first penalizes surfaces in front of detected photons and admits a tight convex closure, namely volume rendering with a running-maximum transmittance in place of NeRF's product transmittance. The second accounts for photons that no surface explains and admits a convex upper bound once the object is assumed to be thick behind each detected surface point. Compared with Transientangelo under its own real-data protocol, FirstCross achieves lower depth error across every test scene, view count, and flux level. With three views and 100 times fewer photons than at the protocol's lowest flux, our mean object depth error stays under half of Transientangelo's with all photons. Given our detected surface points, the best classical fusion has 1.3 to 1.8 times our three-view error across flux levels. On real room-scale captures with 1% of their photons, TransientNeRF has 2.8 to 7.7 times our error. FirstCross lets few-view single-photon scanners cut exposure to 1% and reconstruct an object in about a minute on one GPU.
authors: Chi-Wei Lee, Cheng-Han Chiang, Yi-Chun Chang, An-Kai Chen, Po-Chih Kuo
bullets: Addresses the high cost and low-flux sensitivity of neural single-photon reconstruction methods.
Uses a network-free sequence of convex voxel-grid problems based on each ray’s first surface crossing.
Models detected-photon and unexplained-photon likelihood terms with convex relaxations.
Outperforms Transientangelo across tested scenes, view counts, and flux levels under its evaluation protocol.
Reconstructs room-scale objects from 1% of the photons in about a minute on one GPU.

papers.abstract: Compared to single-robot deployments, multi-robot teams can significantly improve search-and-rescue (SAR) mission success by covering large areas in parallel. To collaborate effectively, these robots must be registered in a common reference frame. Standard registration methods typically rely on external infrastructure or significant map overlap, but real deployments require infrastructure-free, stationary initial alignment for immediate operation. While global LiDAR point cloud registration addresses this, existing single-scan methods often fail silently in aliased or degenerate environments. Approaches scaling beyond two agents also remain rarely evaluated in real-world scenarios. We propose a centralized, deployment-ready framework for pre-mission multi-robot registration. Our system performs pairwise coarse-to-fine alignment and actively rejects impossible pose hypotheses via deterministic plausibility checks. We validate the framework on a real-world custom dataset of four synchronized robots in various environments with ground truth. The checks reject more than a third of the incorrect pairwise registrations while falsely rejecting less than 1% of the correct ones, and reduce the number of team registrations with a wrong robot pose by 38%. Dataset and code are publicly available.
bullets: Addresses infrastructure-free, stationary initial registration for multi-robot search-and-rescue teams.
Uses centralized pairwise coarse-to-fine alignment with deterministic mutual-observation plausibility checks.
Evaluated on a real-world dataset with four synchronized robots across varied environments and ground truth.
Rejects over one-third of incorrect pairwise registrations while falsely rejecting fewer than 1% of correct ones.
Reduces team registrations containing a wrong robot pose by 38%; code and dataset are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Recovering metric-scale geometry from observations at a single viewpoint remains fundamentally ill-posed, limiting the reliability of novel view synthesis. Recent methods rely on learned monocular depth priors, which provide strong structural estimates but can suffer from scale ambiguity and dataset-dependent biases. We propose DfD-GS, a feed-forward framework that predicts a metric-scale 3D Gaussian scene representation from a single-view all-in-focus--defocused image pair. The key idea is to exploit defocus blur as a physical metric depth cue. DfD-GS first estimates a defocus-based metric disparity map from the all-in-focus--defocused image pair and the corresponding defocus strength. This estimate is used to align and refine a monocular depth prior to metric scale. Visible and hidden 3D Gaussians are then predicted for occlusion-aware novel view synthesis. Experiments on synthetic-defocus datasets constructed from Booster and Middlebury show that DfD-GS outperforms single-image baselines in metric depth estimation and novel view synthesis. On WildRGB-D, DfD-GS achieves lower AbsRel and LPIPS but higher depth RMSE than the single-image baselines. Additional analyses show that DfD-GS maintains a more stable metric scale under field-of-view changes. Qualitative results on a real dataset show recovery of the main scene structure under optical defocus.
authors: Shiori Ueda, Rinto Yagawa, Hideo Saito, Shohei Mori
bullets: Addresses scale ambiguity and dataset bias in monocular single-view depth estimation.
Estimates metric disparity from defocus blur and uses it to align and refine a monocular depth prior.

Shows more stable metric scale under field-of-view changes; on WildRGB-D, it improves AbsRel and LPIPS but has higher depth RMSE.

papers.abstract: Autonomous rendezvous and proximity operations require not only an accurate estimate of the pose of the target spacecraft, but also a reliable indication of when this estimate can be trusted. Conformal prediction provides such an indication with a formal guarantee, by producing pose uncertainty sets that contain the true pose with a specified probability. Such a guarantee, however, assumes that calibration and test data follow the same distribution, an assumption that is violated in orbital perception, where labelled calibration images are available only from synthetic renderings while operational images are real. In this work, we show on the SPEED+ dataset that conformal pose estimation calibrated on synthetic images loses its coverage guarantee on real images, and that many of the resulting failures are silent: the predicted pose set appears valid but excludes the true pose. To address this, we calibrate on synthetic images translated to the appearance of real images. Since translation alters appearance while preserving geometry, the synthetic pose labels remain valid and no labelled real images are required. Experiments with two translation models show that this calibration restores coverage above the specified level for miscoverage levels of 0.1 and above, and reduces silent failures from up to 43.5% to at most 3.3% of the test images, bringing conformal pose estimation a step closer to trustworthy deployment in space.
authors: Nidhal Eddine Chenni, Arunkumar Rathinam, Djamila Aouada
bullets: Synthetic-only calibration loses its formal coverage guarantee on real spacecraft images, causing silent failures where uncertainty sets exclude the true pose.
The method translates labeled synthetic images to real-image appearance while preserving geometry and pose labels.
Evaluated on the SPEED+ dataset with two translation models, it restores coverage above the target for miscoverage levels of 0.1 and higher.
Silent failures decrease from as much as 43.5% to at most 3.3% of test images.
The approach targets trustworthy spacecraft rendezvous and proximity-operation deployment without requiring labeled operational imagery.
