papers.abstract: A corridor, its mirror reflection, and its image on a display can look identical, yet their physical surfaces lie at different depths. We test whether bounded camera motions distinguish these explanations. Intervene3D takes an image and an initial geometry estimate, predicts the view under each hypothesis and candidate motion, and selects a motion by maximin separability. It reports the mechanism and first physical surface only if the available motions separate the hypotheses still in contention. Otherwise it abstains. An adequacy test also rejects observations that no hypothesis explains. On a matched synthetic benchmark with exact landmarks, disabling abstention gives confident answers on 76.4% of unresolvable scenes. With abstention, none receives a confident answer under exact or noisy landmarks. At 100% accuracy on answered scenes, maximin selection answers 61.0% of scenes and summed selection 43.1%. The adequacy test lowers wrong answers on strongly curved mirror scenes from 56.8% to 12.4%. Real display experiments compare two hypotheses using one frozen depth-network estimate. The second image supplies photometric evidence and is never passed through the depth network. One executed motion reduces the pooled median surface error of twelve networks by 31.5%. These networks have larger error inside the annotated panel than outside on 33.4% of illusion-benchmark images. They place the first physical surface behind the glass on 36.9% of Mirror3D frames.
authors: Reshad Ul Karim, Abrar Samin, Sammam Mahdi, Syeda Maliha Tabassum, Md Rashad Al Hasan Rony
bullets: Visual observations can be identical for real corridors, mirror reflections, and displays despite different physical surface depths.
The system predicts views under competing hypotheses and candidate motions, choosing the motion that maximizes worst-case separability.

On synthetic scenes, maximin selection answered 61.0% with 100% accuracy, while disabling abstention produced confident answers for 76.4% of unresolvable scenes.
In real display experiments, one motion reduced pooled median surface error by 31.5% across twelve depth networks; substantial errors remained on illusion images.

papers.abstract: We present PaveSplat, a feed-forward Gaussian splatting method that adds a learned residual to the analytic surface-aligned covariance, keeping surfels paving the visible surface across rendering resolutions. Pixel-aligned feed-forward Gaussian splatting predicts one primitive per pixel from a few images in a single pass, and its rendering quality depends on how well these primitives cover the surface. Recent surfel-based methods compute the surface-aligned covariance analytically from predicted depth. However, this covariance has no way to correct the surfel orientation where the depth-derived frame is ill-posed. The surfels then cover the surface loosely; at the training resolution each surfel's one-pixel minimum footprint covers the gaps, but they show up as holes when the same prediction is re-rendered at a higher resolution. To address this, we keep the analytic covariance as an initialization, with its axes aligned to the surface tangents, and add an identity-initialized unit-quaternion residual that reorients a surfel only where this improves rendering, turning surfels that the analytic frame mis-aims back onto the surface. On RealEstate10K, PaveSplat achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among single-Gaussian-per-pixel methods at every scale (1x-8x). The native-resolution gain is small; the benefit appears when the same prediction is rendered at higher display resolutions without re-running the network. On zero-shot DL3DV, it leads PSNR within this group at every scale and ranks first or second on SSIM/LPIPS. A coverage-hole analysis shows fewer uncovered pixels than both baselines under high-resolution re-rendering.
authors: Janghun Kim, Hyun-Cheol Kim, Eunbin An, Myeonghun Oh, Hyon-Gon Choo
bullets: Targets holes that appear when pixel-aligned Gaussian predictions are re-rendered above their training resolution.
Initializes each surfel with a depth-derived, surface-aligned covariance.
Adds an identity-initialized unit-quaternion residual to reorient surfels when the analytic frame is ill-posed.
Outperforms single-Gaussian-per-pixel baselines across scales on RealEstate10K and leads or ranks highly on zero-shot DL3DV.
Produces fewer uncovered pixels during high-resolution re-rendering; native-resolution gains are small.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of PaveSplat covariance construction. From the predicted depth, (a) the surface-aligned prior sets the analytic frame Ra=[ê1 ê2 n̂], supplying tangent-aligned shape and the initial orientation. (b) Two per-primitive refinements act on this prior: in-plane scale multipliers (orange) set the anisotropic radii si=s̄i mi, and a residual reorientation (blue) — the only added learned covariance parameter — adapts orientation via q=qa⊗∆q. (c) The two recombine as R=RaR∆ into the final covariance Σ, rendered to the novel view.

Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison on RealEstate10K. Per scene: inputs, ground truth, DepthSplat [18], SurfSplat [7], and PaveSplat; top row = full-frame native render (crop boxed), bottom row = 8× crop. In these high-margin cases, PaveSplat keeps more support along thin structures.

Fig. 1: Three ways to cover a surface with surfels. Per regime: the per-pixel Gaussians for one scene as covariance ellipsoids from a novel view (top) and a schematic of how surfels lie on the surface (bottom). (a) Fully-learned covariances (DepthSplat [18]) leave scale uncontrolled, so oversized ellipsoids over-spread while small ones fail to tile. (b) The analytic prior (SurfSplat [7]) sets the frame from depth with no pathway to correct it, leaving anisotropic surfels mis-oriented to the tangents. (c) PaveSplat makes the analytic frame per-pixel correctable (q=qa ⊗ ∆q), so surfels reorient to pave the surface. This isolates surfel shape and coverage.

Fig. 4: PaveSplat leaves fewer coverage holes under high-resolution rerendering (RealEstate10K). The coverage-hole rate (black-hole fraction) = share of pixels rendering near-black (max RGB channel <0.02) where the GT has content (max channel >0.02). (a) vs. re-render scale (per-scene median line, IQR band, log-y): holes open under upsampling, fewest for PaveSplat at every re-rendered scale. (b) perscene distribution at 8× (box = median/IQR, whiskers to the 10th/90th percentile): PaveSplat < SurfSplat < DepthSplat (per-scene Wilcoxon, both p<10−10).

papers.abstract: Roadside LiDAR detectors are expensive to train on real labels, and digital twins promise to replace these labels, but a detector trained on a twin meets a different sensor, different objects and different annotation conventions on the real site. We describe the pipeline that placed first in the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge (IEEE BigData 2026 Cup, 0.5541 combined score) and fifth on its V2X-Real track (0.8102). Every detector is a CenterPoint model trained only on synthetic data, on a single 8 GB laptop GPU. Most of the gain came from correcting differences between the twin and the real site rather than from the detector. We align the twin's coordinates, point density and box convention with the test sensor, generate the pedestrians and riders that the twins lack, plus street clutter as unlabeled negatives, and rebuild twin objects at real size and real point density. A non-learned resampling to the per-cell point density of unlabeled real frames lifts LUMPI realism from 0.589 to 0.947, against 0.949 between real frames. Label-free post-processing then exploits what a fixed roadside sensor guarantees: static structures recur in every frame, and real objects have characteristic point statistics. Reporting the validation and test gain of each component side by side, we find that corrections of systematic sim-to-real differences transfer to the test set, typically keeping a quarter to three quarters of their validation gain, while choices that fit the few objects of a validation set do not.
bullets: Problem: Digital-twin-trained detectors face real-site differences in sensing, object coverage, and labeling, making real annotation costly but sim-to-real transfer difficult.
Method: Train CenterPoint only on synthetic data, while aligning coordinates, point density, box conventions, object sizes, and clutter with the real roadside sensor.
Method: Add missing pedestrians and riders, use unlabeled real frames for non-learned density resampling, and apply label-free post-processing based on static-scene and point-statistic cues.
Results: The pipeline ranked first on LUMPI (0.5541) and fifth on V2X-Real (0.8102); density resampling improved twin realism from 0.589 to 0.947, near the real-frame value of 0.949.
Contribution: Component-wise validation and test analysis shows systematic sim-to-real corrections transfer better than validation-set-specific object-fitting choices.

papers.title: Fixing the Twin, Not the Detector: Sim-to-Real Roadside LiDAR Detection from Digital-Twin Data

papers.abstract: Editing a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) capture of a person so that they wear a new garment requires every rendered view to agree on the same garment details. Existing 3D virtual try-on (VTON) pipelines, however, edit training views largely independently and fuse them with hand-designed heuristics such as manually chosen reference views and fixed attention-blending weights. The resulting inconsistencies are baked into the 3D representation and surface as texture drift, blurred prints, and implausible geometry in novel views. We present GS-VTON-MVT, a three-stage framework that combines implicit and explicit 3D reasoning for consistent 3DGS try-on. (i) A multi-view inpainting transformer jointly edits a set of training views with full cross-view self-attention, so that cross-view correspondence is learned rather than imposed. (ii) A geometry-guided multi-modal ControlNet conditions the diffusion editor on the garment image together with depth and surface normals rendered from the current 3DGS state, supplying explicit structure where visual evidence is weakest. (iii) A pose-adaptive persona-aware attention replaces the fixed blending weight between current-view and reference-view features with weights derived from camera-pose proximity. On the 3D-VTONBench benchmark, GS-VTON-MVT improves FID, KID, LPIPS-based cross-view consistency, and user preference over general-purpose 3D editors and prior 3D try-on methods.
authors: Sarthak Batra, Armin Mustafa, Adrian Hilton
bullets: Addresses texture drift, blurred garment prints, and implausible geometry caused by independently editing views and heuristic fusion.
Uses a multi-view inpainting transformer with full cross-view self-attention to learn view correspondence.
Conditions diffusion editing on the garment image plus 3DGS-rendered depth and surface normals.
Adapts attention blending to camera-pose proximity instead of using fixed weights.
Improves image quality, cross-view consistency, and user preference on 3D-VTONBench versus general-purpose 3D editors and prior 3D try-on methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of GS-VTON-MVT. (1) A subject-specific 3DGS scene Gsrc is reconstructed from posed multi-view images. (2) The Multi-View Inpainting Transformer (MVT) jointly edits a subset of training views with cross-view attention, producing a consistent edited set Xtrain that is used to personalize a Stable Diffusion inpainting model with LoRA. (3) During 3DGS editing, RGB, depth, and normal maps are rendered from the current scene; the garment region is masked, and the personalized inpainting model, guided by depth, normal, and garment ControlNet branches fused by cross-attention, produces a geometry-aligned target Iedit that supervises the update of the Gaussians, yielding the edited scene Gtgt.

Fig. 2: Qualitative comparison on in-the-wild subjects. Each subject is captured from multiple views and processed with the full pipeline; we show two of the input views, the target garment, and the same two views produced by GS-VTON-MVT and by the baseline. Baseline outputs are resized to the aspect ratio of the input. Faces are blurred for privacy.
Table 1: Comparison with prior methods on 3D-VTONBench. Lower is better for all metrics.
Table 3: User study: preference rate (%) per method for each criterion. Higher is better.
Table 2: Ablation of GS-VTON-MVT components on 3D-VTONBench.

papers.title: Multi-View Transformer with Geometry-Guided Multi-Modal ControlNet for 3D Virtual Try-On
papers.tldr: GS-VTON-MVT enables more consistent 3D virtual try-on by jointly editing views with learned cross-view attention and geometry-aware garment conditioning.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing interactive physical twins from video requires accurately capturing how objects deform while maintaining efficient simulation. We observe that reproducing motion in a video does not guarantee correct responses to new forces when the physical representation restricts how an object can deform. In spring-based twins, coupling between volume and shape responses creates such a limitation. We present MorphTwin, which enriches local deformation modes to capture and independently control these responses while retaining standard spring forces and explicit simulation. To support interpretable material editing and transfer, we use offline calibration to map shared relative response changes to stiffness updates on each reconstructed graph. Under identical inverse settings on synthetic scenes, MorphTwin reduces the mean absolute error of Poisson's ratio by 75.8% and the mean relative error of Young's modulus by 22.1% compared to PhysTwin. We introduce an egocentric stereo and RGB-D benchmark covering interactions with objects of varying stiffness. Real-world experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and up to 14.4% lower future tracking error than PhysTwin at interactive speeds.
authors: Haoqin Hong, Ding Fan, Fubin Dou, Tianyu Huang, Yuzhuo Chen, Zhemeng Zhang, Hanxiao Jiang, Congcong Zhu, Gerhard Petrus Hancke, Jingrun Chen, Rynson WH Lau
bullets: Addresses the limitation that matching observed video motion may not yield correct responses to new forces, especially in spring-based models coupling volume and shape changes.
Enriches local deformation modes while retaining standard spring forces and explicit simulation.
Uses offline calibration to translate shared relative response edits into stiffness updates for interpretable material editing and transfer.
On synthetic scenes, reduces Poisson’s-ratio error by 75.8% and Young’s-modulus relative error by 22.1% versus PhysTwin.
A new egocentric stereo and RGB-D benchmark and real-world tests show improved reconstruction accuracy and up to 14.4% lower future tracking error at interactive speeds.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MorphTwin. Part A: Sparse video observations provide geometry and motion cues. Part B: We fit the physical model to observed motion, followed by Gaussian appearance optimization with physics fixed. Part C: Relaxable response carriers enable separate volumetric and shear control. Offline calibration maps shared relative response changes to spring stiffnesses for each graph, enabling material editing and reuse. Online interaction retains explicit spring dynamics.

Figure 8. Visual overview of our 15 self-captured, spatiotemporally aligned egocentric RGB-D sequences listed in Table 8. For each sequence, we show a representative temporally aligned sample from the main RGB view and the left and right egocentric views. The morphology and manipulation labels shown in each panel follow the terminology used in Table 8.

Figure 5. Material editing on our egocentric interaction benchmark. Four representative sequences from our 15-sequence benchmark show reconstruction, future prediction, and material editing under the same hand interactions. At the same observation time within each row, stiffening the pillow and hat reduces deformation, while softening the mousepad and book enables bending.

Figure 4. Reconstruction and prediction on PhysTwin scenes. PGND can exhibit unstable future predictions, while PhysTwin’s explicit mass-spring model may not fully reproduce material responses. Semi-transparent GT overlays highlight discrepancies.

Figure 9. Reconstruction and future prediction on all 15 sequences of our benchmark under the All Views setting. Figure 3. Response carriers and calibration. Part (A): Candidate carriers on local four-node cells are jointly selected to meet bulk and shear response targets while minimizing auxiliary mass, then realized using auxiliary nodes and spokes. Under standardized volumetric and deviatoric strains, internal relaxation yields the corresponding responses. Part (B): Each graph is calibrated at its reference state to relate carrier controls to changes in material response. A shared response space then maps the same material edit to graph-specific spring updates.

Figure 7. Response coordinates and graph calibration. (a) Response coordinates improve fitting accuracy and generalization to unseen loads under matched two-parameter budgets. (b) Targetgraph calibration reduces response and unseen-strain energy errors compared with copied spring multipliers.

Figure 6. Elastic parameterization and observability. (a) Volumetric and shear response fitting with one or two elastic controls. (b) Mass identification under known-force excitation. (c) Friction loss without contact and during sliding contact.

Figure 10. Material editing and reuse across objects. Initial object renderings and their particle representations are shown on the left. (a) Material editing. Soft (0.25×), original (1×), and stiff (4×) settings produce progressively smaller deformations under identical interaction forces, alongside a rigid-projection control. The camera, scale, and observation time are shared across settings. (b) Material reuse. Calibration for each graph realizes exchanged material response targets on Apple and Torus, making Torus softer and Apple stiffer. Particle colors indicate the source material settings. Gray particles show the unloaded configuration. Displacements in (b) are magnified 20× for visualization.

Figure 12. Progressive crack formation in the cloth twin under two opposing grasps. Columns show successive interaction stages. Top: Gaussian renderings show the evolving cloth appearance. Middle: deformed particles, with failed-connection endpoints highlighted in orange. Bottom: failed connections in reference coordinates reveal the spatial progression of damage independently of deformation. The main component remains connected as the crack opens, motivating appearance bindings that follow surviving local connections before complete separation.

Figure 13. MorphTwin’s interactive interface for composing and manipulating reconstructed physical twins. Part (a): Shared workspace; numbered markers link controls to the operating workflow. Part (b): Grasp controls for selecting positions, adjusting radii and force limits, and grasping or releasing objects. Part (c): Elastic editing and interaction-preset reuse.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces MorphTwin, a method for reconstructing interactive physical twins from video by enriching local deformation modes, which is relevant to simulation-based manipulation and 3D reconstruction.
papers.title: MorphTwin: Enriching Deformable Material Responses from Videos for Morphable and Interactive Physical Twins
papers.tldr: MorphTwin reconstructs deformable physical twins from video with independently controllable deformation responses, improving material accuracy and future-motion prediction over PhysTwin.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis, but Gaussian rasterization attenuates fine-scale scene structure through the projected covariance of each primitive. We show that contracting these projected covariances at inference time can mitigate the effective bandwidth limitation induced by finite Gaussian footprints, motivating a multi-aperture rendering framework for super-resolution. Based on this insight, we propose AGSR (Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution), a lightweight inference-time framework that progressively fuses multi-aperture renderings using uncertainty-guided feature aggregation and geometric conditioning from transmittance and depth cues. AGSR operates as a plug-in enhancement for pre-trained 3DGS models. Experiments on the Mip-NeRF 360 benchmark show that AGSR outperforms lightweight image-space super-resolution baselines, with gains increasing as the underlying Gaussian representation deteriorates. The results provide evidence that covariance contraction exposes bandwidth-sensitive structural cues attenuated by native Gaussian rasterization. AGSR achieves these improvements while maintaining real-time performance with up to 139k parameters.
authors: Ayman Alkhateeb, Hadi Amirpour, Christian Timmerer
bullets: Addresses fine-scale detail loss caused by the finite projected footprints of 3DGS Gaussians.
Uses progressive multi-aperture rendering with covariance contraction, uncertainty-guided feature aggregation, and transmittance/depth conditioning.
Acts as a lightweight plug-in for pre-trained 3DGS models without retraining.
Outperforms lightweight image-space super-resolution baselines on Mip-NeRF 360, with larger gains for lower-quality Gaussian representations.
Maintains real-time performance with up to 139k parameters.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of AGSR. Covariance contraction produces multi-aperture RGB, transmittance, and depth renderings with progressively smaller projected footprints and correspondingly higher effective bandwidth. Cross-aperture variations form a structural uncertainty field that guides a three-stage geometry-aware fusion network. Higher-bandwidth observations are fused sequentially and refined through residual PixelShuffle reconstruction to produce the final super-resolved output.

Fig. 1: Projected Gaussian covariances influence the effective bandwidth of individual rasterization kernels. By systematically contracting the covariance, AGSR generates multiaperture observations that reveal structural cues attenuated by native rasterization. The resulting uncertainty field guides geometry-aware super-resolution for enhanced detail reconstruction.

Fig. 3: Visual comparison of 2× and 4× super-resolution on 3DGS representations trained on highly subsampled images (tf = 8). AGSR exploits structural cues revealed by multi-aperture rendering to recover fine-scale detail that is poorly reproduced by degraded Gaussian representations. Quantitative metrics (PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS) are reported below each crop.

Fig. 4: Quantitative performance (PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS) of AGSR compared with native 3DGS and bicubic baselines across varying training degradation factors (tf ). As the training factor increases, the quality of the underlying Gaussian representation deteriorates substantially. AGSR becomes increasingly advantageous as the underlying representation degrades, with the strongest gains observed under moderate and severe degradation, outperforming the baselines across most settings and metrics.

TABLE I: Complexity analysis of the progressive aperture fusion network. We report the parameter count, computational complexity (GMACs), and full-pipeline inference speed (FPS) in both FP32 and FP16 precisions. Parameter counts and GMACs correspond to the cumulative deployed inference model required to produce each stage’s output. FPS is evaluated targeting Full HD (1920×1080) and includes both 3DGS rasterization and network inference overhead.
TABLE II: Quantitative comparison across multiple training degradation factors (tf ). Best performance highlighted in bold.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes AGSR, a plug-in framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses multi-aperture rendering and uncertainty-guided feature aggregation to improve super-resolution and structural fidelity.
papers.title: AGSR: Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution for Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: AGSR improves 3D Gaussian Splatting super-resolution at inference time by fusing renderings with contracted Gaussian covariances and geometric uncertainty cues.

papers.abstract: Accurately extracting and mapping road surface elements is crucial for applications such as high-definition maps, road asset management, and intelligent transportation systems. This study first provides a comprehensive review of the benchmark datasets for extracting and mapping road elements, encompassing overhead-to-perspective data, large-to-local scales, and coarse-to-fine details. Subsequently, we thoroughly review the relevant approaches for extracting road surface elements. However, we argue that existing datasets still require enhancements in semantic richness, data modality diversity, and scenario complexity. To bridge these gaps, this paper presents WHU-Road3D, a large-scale multimodal dataset for fine-grained road surface mapping to address these shortcomings. WHU-Road3D provides approximately 100 km of diverse Chinese highways and urban streets. It features a rich combination of MLS point clouds, associated panoramic images, vehicle trajectories, detailed vectorized annotations, and pointwise instance annotations for road surface elements. The dataset carefully annotates 15 distinct categories of road elements, including common markings like road boundaries, zebra crossings, lane dividers, stop lines, as well as 10 types of direction symbols. To our knowledge, WHU-Road3D stands as the first multimodal dataset for mapping such a comprehensive range of road surface elements, designed to facilitate cutting-edge research in instance segmentation, full-element extraction and mapping on road surfaces. Beyond these immediate applications, WHU-Road3D also provides a valuable source for hierarchical road topology reasoning, map updating, and street scene generation. The dataset, along with the code for our benchmark methods, will be made publicly available at \href{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}.
authors: Xiaoxin Mi, Zhen Cao, Chong Liu, Yuhao Li, Zhen Dong, Bisheng Yang, Yang Jia, Shengwu Xiong
bullets: Addresses gaps in existing datasets, including limited semantic richness, modality diversity, and scenario complexity.
Covers approximately 100 km of Chinese highways and urban streets.
Combines MLS point clouds, panoramic images, vehicle trajectories, vectorized annotations, and pointwise instance labels.
Annotates 15 road-element categories, including boundaries, crossings, lane dividers, stop lines, and 10 direction-symbol types.
Supports research in instance segmentation, full-element extraction, road mapping, topology reasoning, map updating, and street-scene generation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal image fusion traditionally generates a single fused image from paired observations at a specific viewpoint, limiting comprehensive scene perception and adaptability to diverse perceptual objectives. To overcome these limitations, we present LIFT, a novel framework for our proposed language-controlled 3D image fusion (L3D-IF) paradigm that extends multimodal image fusion from 2D images to free-viewpoint 3D scenes, enabling language-guided fusion tailored to diverse perceptual objectives. First, LIFT formulates Semantic Modality Binding (SMB), which interprets language instructions to identify semantic targets and their associated modality preferences and grounds these targets in corresponding regions of a shared Gaussian scene, establishing persistent semantic-to-spatial correspondences for consistent fusion control across viewpoints. Second, Language-Conditioned Gaussian Appearance (LCGA) is developed to achieve scene-wide multimodal appearance modeling by combining adaptive multimodal blending with language- and viewpoint-conditioned appearance refinement, enabling spatially adaptive realization of diverse fusion appearances while preserving source fidelity at pure-modality endpoints. Finally, we construct a Multi-View Language-Supervision (MVLS) dataset that associates language instructions and calibrated viewpoints with modulated fused images, providing effective supervision for learning instruction-dependent fusion from finite multi-view observations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LIFT achieves coherent multimodal fusion across continuous viewpoints, accurate semantic target localization, and consistent regional fusion control under diverse language instructions.

papers.abstract: We propose MergeableRF, a method for radiance field relighting through model parameter merging. Given multi-view images of a scene under known basis lights, our goal is to relight the scene by directly combining the parameters of radiance fields trained under these lights. This is motivated by the linearity of light transport: the image under a mixture of lights is the same weighted combination of the images under each light. However, combining the parameters of independently trained radiance fields does not produce the corresponding combination of images. To address this, we represent a scene with shared geometry and a separate appearance network for each basis light. We start these networks from the same initialization and introduce merge-aware training, which teaches their parameter combinations to reproduce the corresponding combinations of images. Given a target HDR environment map, we compute its basis-light coefficients and use them to merge the appearance networks into a single relit model. Our method supports both Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), without material estimation, additional relighting networks, or target-specific optimization. Unlike image-space blending, it requires only one rendering pass per viewpoint. Experiments on synthetic Neural Gaffer objects and real OLATverse captures demonstrate relighting quality competitive with methods trained on the same multi-light observations.
authors: Yinan Wang, Rohan Kadkol, Hyunjin Yoo, Jean-Fran\c{c}ois Lalonde, James J. Clark
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between combining independently trained radiance-field parameters and combining their rendered images.
Uses shared scene geometry and separate, identically initialized appearance networks with merge-aware training.
Relights a target HDR environment by computing basis-light coefficients and merging the corresponding appearance networks.
Supports both NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting, requiring one rendering pass per viewpoint.
Demonstrates competitive relighting quality on synthetic and real multi-light captures.

Every method uses the setting reported in Tab. 1. Our results come from a single render of the merged network, with no optimization for the new lighting. All methods handle the backpack well. The shiny helmet and iron are harder. Our models get the overall color and shading right but miss the sharp reflections, because our basis lights are smooth.

Figure 1. Mergeable radiance fields. (a) One radiance field, a NeRF or a set of 3D Gaussians, is shared by K basis illuminations Li. For every element j that contributes to a pixel (a sample along its ray for NeRF, a Gaussian that overlaps it for 3DGS), the field provides a feature zj and the viewing direction dj . Each basis light has its own small appearance MLP with parameters ϕi, trained on the images Ii of the scene under Li. All MLPs start from the same initialization. To make them mergeable, some of the training samples are rendered with a random convex combination ϕmix of the MLPs and supervised by the same combination of the basis images, which is the true image under the mixed light (bottom row). (b) To relight, we approximate a new environment map LA by a non-negative combination of the basis lights with weights βi, and take the same weighted sum of the MLP parameters, ϕM = ∑ i βiϕi. The merged MLP ϕM then renders the relit image in a single pass with the unchanged radiance field. (c) Three scenes relit under four unseen environment maps at a held-out view, one render each.

papers.abstract: We present a stereo visual odometry (SVO) framework that integrates geometric feed-forward models (GFMs) for dense depth prediction with factor-graph-based visual odometry to achieve accurate localisation and dense metric mapping. Our key idea is to exploit sparse but reliable metric geometry estimated from stereo and temporal multi-view observations to calibrate dense GFM predictions, while retaining the robustness and efficiency of model-based SVO. Rather than directly conditioning the GFM on potentially noisy stereo depth, optimised 3D landmarks are used to jointly estimate a scale-shift transformation over all keyframes within each local submap, yielding metrically consistent dense depth predictions. To balance accuracy and computational efficiency, we introduce a hierarchical factor-graph architecture. At the local level, sliding-window optimisation estimates high-frequency camera poses and multi-view-refined 3D landmarks. Dense predictions are generated only for selected keyframes and registered within each submap using SE(3) Generalised ICP. Consecutive submaps are further aligned in Sim(3) using their shared geometry, allowing residual scale inconsistencies to be corrected. These intra- and inter-submap constraints are incorporated into a global factor graph to produce a consistent trajectory and dense metric reconstruction. Extensive experiments on public and in-house datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive odometry accuracy against geometric and learning-based baselines while providing accurate dense metric reconstruction and improved robustness to failures in learned depth prediction.
authors: Fahira Afzal Maken, Sagun Man Singh Shrestha, Edward Vanderfeen, Lucas Carvalho de Lima, Rongxin Li, Changming Sun, Milad Ramezani
bullets: Uses reliable stereo and temporal 3D landmarks to calibrate dense geometric feed-forward depth predictions.
Jointly estimates scale-shift corrections across keyframes in local submaps instead of relying directly on noisy stereo depth.
Employs hierarchical factor graphs for local pose/landmark optimisation, submap registration, and global trajectory consistency.
Aligns dense keyframes with SE(3) Generalised ICP and consecutive submaps with Sim(3) geometry alignment.
Experiments report competitive odometry, accurate dense metric reconstruction, and improved robustness to learned-depth failures.

papers.abstract: Recovering accurate visible-surface depth from a single RGB-D image and an object mask is essential for robotic grasping and manipulation of transparent objects. Specular reflections cause missing depth, while refraction corrupts nonzero returns with background depth, making raw measurements unreliable as surface anchors. Under a fixed sampling budget, refining an initial single-view prediction within a single search interval either misses large refraction offsets or sacrifices fine local resolution. To resolve this single-view trade-off, MIR-Depth constructs Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses: a 3D-aggregated global inverse-depth volume and depth-axis-filtered pixel-wise local volumes around a prior-guided initial depth. Selective Recurrent Refinement then introduces out-of-bounds lookup masking and validity-masked softmax fusion to iteratively update inverse depth from these volumes using a multi-scale ConvGRU. Finally, Spatially Gated Correction applies a learned per-pixel spatial gate to the full-resolution residual, preserving accurate initial geometry without imposing raw sensor readings as hard constraints. Experiments on TransCG, TODD, TRansPose, ClearPose, and HouseCat6D show that MIR-Depth achieves lower error than ReMake, DFNet, BP-Net, and PSD. Real-robot evaluations confirm accurate surface geometry for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction. Code and pretrained models will be publicly available.
authors: Xinzhe Fu, Qi Shao, Yuanfei Xie, Taoyu Wu, Zhihao Cao, Long Hu, Hong Liang, Xianzhi Li, Anh Nguyen, Baoru Huang, Rongsheng Li
bullets: Addresses missing and corrupted depth caused by specular reflection and refraction in transparent-object RGB-D images.
Builds coordinate-aware global and local multi-range inverse-depth hypotheses around a prior-guided prediction.
Uses recurrent refinement with out-of-bounds masking and validity-aware fusion, followed by spatially gated residual correction.
Reportedly achieves lower error than several prior methods across five datasets.
Real-robot evaluations show improved surface geometry for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of MIR-Depth. A frozen Depth Anything V2 model provides the relative-depth prior. Transformer and CNN encoders extract RGB-mask, relative-depth, and raw-depth features, which are summed at each scale. The summed features provide multi-scale context, while a decoder and depth head predict initial depth D0. Coordinate-Aware Multi-Range Hypotheses construct one shared global inverse-depth volume aggregated by a 3D hourglass alongside medium and fine pixel-wise local volumes filtered by depth-axis convolutions. Selective Recurrent Refinement queries these volumes, encodes lookup features together with per-offset validity indicators, and fuses active ranges to update inverse depth through a multi-scale ConvGRU. Spatially Gated Correction weights the full-resolution residual relative to D0 to produce completed depth for 6-DoF grasp pose prediction.

papers.abstract: When reconstructing high-quality 3D assets from images, existing approaches often excel at one objective while compromising another, and frequently overlook the intrinsic quality of the reconstructed surfaces. We present MODL, a framework that jointly optimizes geometry and view-dependent appearance directly on a watertight triangle mesh. Our approach combines Laplacian-preconditioned optimization for smooth vertex updates with curvature-adaptive remeshing to preserve fine details and well-shaped triangles. The triangle mesh is optimized subject to multi-view normalized cross-correlation constraints, but without segmentation, geometric supervision or alpha-blending. Evaluations on object reconstruction datasets demonstrate that MODL achieves competitive novel-view synthesis while producing geometrically accurate models with superior intrinsic mesh quality. Our results highlight the potential of direct mesh optimization to unify photorealistic rendering, geometric reconstruction, and practical 3D asset creation.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between novel-view appearance and intrinsic mesh quality in image-based 3D reconstruction.
Optimizes a watertight triangle mesh using Laplacian-preconditioned vertex updates and curvature-adaptive remeshing.
Uses multi-view normalized cross-correlation constraints without segmentation, geometric supervision, or alpha-blending.
Evaluations show competitive novel-view synthesis alongside geometrically accurate models and superior mesh quality.
Scope: focused on reconstructing textured objects from images.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative comparison of the output mesh geometry and appearance between several GS methods and MODL.
Figure 5. Output 3D assets for MODL on the Aria DTC [9] dataset.

Figure 2. Radar chart of the metrics assessing 3D asset quality. BER, SIR, and AR focus on mesh quality, CD measure geometric accuracy, and PSNR portrays image synthesis capability (see Section 5.3). Methods using TSDF Fusion for post-processing provide competitive geometric accuracy and intrinsic mesh quality, but are lacking in well-formed triangles and rendering capabilities. Triangle Splatting [20] without TSDF Fusion is the antithesis, providing the best rendering capabilities and well-formed triangle shapes, but lacks in mesh quality (since the output is a triangle soup) and geometric accuracy. MeshSplatting [19] provides a nice balance between rendering and geometric quality, but the meshes are nonmanifold and have poor connectivity overall. MODL yields the most balanced 3D assets in terms of the combined mesh, geometric, and photometric quality.

Figure 3. The remeshing operations of Botsch and Kobbelt [2]. To maintain a desired target triangle edge length, edges are: (a) split if the actual edge length exceeds the target length; (b) collapsed if the current edge length is smaller than the target length. In practice, we use a buffer size around the target edge length such that triangle edges that are close to this length are not split or collapsed. Following the Botsch and Kobbelt [2] algorithm: (c) edges are flipped when doing so improves the vertex valence distribution of the mesh; and (d) vertices are moved towards their one-ring neighborhood centroid in a local tangent plane and are then projected back onto the surface.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing an editable 3D scene from video requires matching visible structure while plausibly completing unseen surfaces. Agents can write scene-construction programs, but direct reconstruction attempts often produce errors in layout, scale, and lighting. We introduce SceneAnything, an automated system for reconstructing mesh scenes from real and generated videos, enabling text-to-scene construction when paired with video generation. A software harness coordinates agents, pretrained vision models, and graphics tools through an explicit reconstruction protocol. Shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates ground component construction: a scene-owner agent plans the environment and briefs authors, who write parameterized Blender programs. A visibility- and fit-based level-of-detail rule selects the construction level, while unseen regions are completed and marked as inferred. Assembled scenes use fitted lighting and supported motion, and revisions undergo programmatic checks and independent visual comparisons. Accepted programs and lessons are reused across scenes. We evaluate on 100 scenes; subset comparisons show improved original-view fidelity over direct-agent reconstruction and higher novel-view content similarity than the compared video-to-3D methods. We will release the harness, agent instructions, reusable libraries, and scenes.
authors: Bowen Xue, Saeed Hadadan, Fabrice Rousselle, Zahra Montazeri, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Milos Hasan
bullets: Targets reconstruction errors in scene layout, scale, lighting, and unseen-surface completion.
Uses shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates to coordinate scene planning and component construction.
Agents generate parameterized Blender programs, with visibility- and fit-based level-of-detail selection.
Adds inferred unseen regions, fitted lighting, motion support, programmatic checks, and visual comparison-based revision.
Evaluated on 100 scenes, showing better original-view fidelity than direct-agent reconstruction and stronger novel-view content similarity than compared video-to-3D methods.

papers.abstract: Generating realistic 3D assets remains constrained by classical representations: surface meshes and compact physically based materials struggle to express objects whose appearance arises from fine geometry or complex light transport, while existing Gaussian-splatting generators typically bake fixed illumination into appearance. We introduce VideoRNG, a two-stage method that generates complete, relightable 3D assets from a text prompt or a single image without prescribing a mesh or analytic material model. A video generator fine-tuned from a pretrained video diffusion backbone first produces a structured RGBA turntable sequence under a known pose, camera, and illumination. A feed-forward large reconstruction model initialized from a pretrained video diffusion backbone then maps the video-VAE latent frames of selected turntable frames directly to millions of anisotropic Gaussians with learned neural appearance features. A shared directional decoder and stochastic Gaussian ray tracer turn this representation, which we call ray-traced Relightable Neural Gaussians (rtRNG), into radiance under novel viewpoints and illumination. To preserve high-frequency appearance while learning geometry, we introduce depth-anchored appearance training, and we make million-Gaussian reconstruction practical through foreground token selection and cost-aware distributed sampling. VideoRNG generates complex assets such as fur, feathers, and spider webs that can be interactively rendered, relit, and integrated into scenes.
authors: Bowen Xue, Saeed Hadadan, Fabrice Rousselle, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Zahra Montazeri, Milo\v{s} Ha\v{s}an
bullets: Addresses the limitations of meshes, analytic materials, and illumination-baked Gaussian representations for complex appearance and light transport.
Uses a fine-tuned video diffusion model to generate structured RGBA turntable sequences with known pose, camera, and lighting.
Reconstructs selected video-VAE latent frames as millions of anisotropic Gaussians with learned neural appearance features.
A shared directional decoder and stochastic Gaussian ray tracer support novel-view rendering and relighting.
Demonstrates interactive scene integration for assets such as fur, feathers, and spider webs.

The MLP labeled “4L × 64” is the per-asset decoder distilled from the nine-layer, width-512 shared decoder described in Section 3.4 for final rendering. (d) The resulting asset supports novel views and lights through stochastic Gaussian ray tracing.

papers.abstract: A unified 3D medical foundation model promises reusable, frozen features that serve a wide variety of tasks such as segmentation, classification and registration on MRI, CT and PET as well as specialist models do. Generalist models still need separate backbones for localized and global tasks, specialist models are confined to a single modality, with the concern that spanning modalities under-emphasizes fine anatomy, and both typically rely on end-to-end fine-tuning to be competitive. We present VoxForge, a single encoder that integrates recent advances in 3D architecture, self-distillation and cross-modal curricula to learn transferable features from permissively licensed MRI and CT volumes. We evaluate it strictly frozen, the test a reusable foundation model must pass, against state-of-the-art generalist and specialist models on segmentation, classification and registration across MRI and CT, and on PET, which it never sees. VoxForge has the best or tied-best average rank in every task group, serves localized and global tasks across modalities at the level of state-of-the-art specialists, and is extremely label-efficient, matching top-performing models on TotalSegmentator CT with a tenth of the labels.
bullets: Addresses the need for one reusable model across localized and global tasks and multiple imaging modalities.
Combines 3D architectural advances, self-distillation, and cross-modal curricula, trained on permissively licensed MRI and CT volumes.
Evaluated strictly frozen across segmentation, classification, and registration on MRI and CT, with zero-shot evaluation on PET.
Achieves the best or tied-best average rank in every task group and performs at specialist-model levels across modalities.
Shows strong label efficiency, matching top-performing TotalSegmentator CT models with one-tenth of the labels.

papers.title: VoxForge: A Unified Foundation Model for Dense 3D Features Across MRI, CT and PET
papers.tldr: VoxForge is a single frozen 3D encoder that provides transferable dense features across MRI, CT, and unseen PET for segmentation, classification, and registration.

papers.abstract: Point-image alignment learns useful object representations, but different local feature patterns can produce the same pooled descriptor and receive the same alignment signal. We introduce MS-Point, a cross-modal pretraining framework that directly supervises intermediate point features and their neighborhood responses. At selected encoder stages, we compute neighborhood averages and residuals before pooling and align their branch descriptors with image features. Branch-level objectives align each representation with its visual target, while cross-level consistency and adaptive fusion coordinate information across branches. A common interface of intermediate features and spatial neighborhoods supports both graph encoders and point Transformers. Evaluations across object classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning demonstrate the transfer value of this design. Same-backbone comparisons and capacity-matched and computation-matched controls connect these improvements to the structure of supervision. Together, our findings support directly supervising intermediate features and neighborhood variation to learn transferable, geometry-aware representations across modalities.
bullets: Addresses ambiguous supervision from aligning only pooled point-cloud descriptors.
Computes neighborhood averages and residuals at multiple encoder stages before pooling.
Uses branch-level cross-modal alignment, cross-level consistency, and adaptive fusion.
Supports both graph encoders and point Transformers through a shared intermediate-feature interface.
Evaluations show transfer value across classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning.

papers.abstract: Dense metric mapping from a single camera and IMU remains challenging: visual-inertial odometry (VIO) provides metric motion but sparse geometry, whereas feed-forward depth models predict dense structure without ensuring metric scale. We present Accord, which constructs an accurate online dense metric map from any camera with an IMU. A VIO filter publishes metric poses, a depth foundation model conditioned on them predicts depth for short keyframe windows, and a factor graph fuses the resulting submaps. Recent work has explored several approaches to this problem. What is essential is the multi-view agreement (Accord), which is considered in SLAM as a source of geometric self-consistency. Accord anchors each keyframe window to metric 3D points triangulated from the filter poses, then exploits bidirectional dense depth agreement between co-visible images to estimate and correct per-image scale errors while preserving the metric scale established by the anchors. Context keyframes further improve depth prediction, and the resulting submaps are fused in a factor graph. We evaluate a single mapping configuration across five public camera-IMU setups and a new Phone-rig/GoPro dataset. With nothing tuned per dataset/setup and every map aligned only by Accord's own trajectory, Accord achieves consistently best/second-best mean F-score at 5 cm on every platform. Accord is open-source along with the phone-rig dataset for the benefit of the research community
authors: Jaafar Mahmoud, Arthur Movsesyan, Cuong Huynh, Mikhail Iumanov, Sergey Zagoruyko, Sergey Kolyubin
bullets: Addresses the gap between metric-but-sparse VIO geometry and dense-but-scale-ambiguous monocular depth.

Adds context keyframes and fuses submaps in a factor graph for online dense mapping.
A single untuned configuration performs consistently among the best across five public camera-IMU setups and a new Phone-rig/GoPro dataset; code and data are released.

papers.abstract: We propose the radiometric camera, a model that lifts any central geometric camera model to a radiometric one. The lifted model keeps the projection of the geometric model and adds a finite aperture, a free-form focus surface and a generic vignetting function. We calibrate it by inverse rendering directly on the relative irradiance of the sensor, from the same images of standard calibration targets used in geometric calibration. Geometric calibration absorbs the bias of its feature detections. The proposed radiometric calibration uses no features, and our radiometric cameras have lower reprojection errors on held-out test sets. The focus surface extends defocus modeling from the thin lens to any central camera, and we use it in a first multi-view radiometric reconstruction, which recovers the in-focus reflectance of a texture from defocused images. The vignetting is estimated jointly and accurately reproduces a flat field measured through a diffuser. Because every standard camera model lifts to a radiometric one, the radiometric camera naturally and directly extends generative scene models beyond multi-view geometry to multi-view radiometric ones, where phenomena such as lighting and attenuation can be accurately estimated.
authors: Ties Harder, Felix Seegr\"aber, David Nakath, Hendrik Sauer, Kevin K\"oser, James Pritts
bullets: Models finite aperture, free-form focus surfaces, and generic vignetting while preserving the original camera projection.
Calibrates directly from sensor irradiance using standard calibration-target images, without feature detections.
Achieves lower reprojection errors on held-out tests than geometric calibration, according to the abstract.
Supports multi-view reconstruction of in-focus texture reflectance from defocused images and jointly estimates vignetting.
Provides a foundation for extending multi-view geometry to radiometric scene models involving lighting and attenuation.

Our radiometric refinement does not rely on a detector and removes most of the bias in both evaluations.

Figure 7. The focus model. Left: the learned focus surfaces, a hemisphere for the fisheye at f/4 and a plane for the Tamron 20 mm at f/8. Right: a texture estimated from defocused images. The lift adds the aperture: the rays through all aperture points a meet in the point of focus xf (p) on the focus surface F , which is close to a plane for the perspective model and surrounds the camera for the fisheye. Where the scene is off F , the cone of these rays meets it in a region (thick blue), from which p collects its light.
Figure 1. Our radiometric camera model can be applied in down stream tasks like vignetting correction in panorama stichting or texture learning in inverse rendering.

papers.abstract: Localizing object boundaries is important for embodied visual systems, since small boundary errors can change the inferred geometry of physical surfaces. We study whether deep stereo models produce boundaries consistent with simple shape priors when local image and disparity cues are weak. We create a synthetic stereo dataset consisting of objects drawn from a highly constrained family of shapes, with randomized depth, slant, color and texture. Despite the simplicity of this shape space, we find that several state-of-the-art stereo models retain systematic boundary errors, even when finetuned or trained from scratch on the dataset. We then introduce a simple generative stereo model that jointly predicts disparity and a distance field representing object boundaries. The model improves boundary localization and produces contours that adhere more closely to the underlying shape space. These results expose limitations in the boundary predictions of current stereo architectures when local evidence is weak, and motivate further study of whether generative models can better combine regional grouping evidence with global geometric structure.
authors: Linbo Tang, Aneel Damaraju, Todd Zickler
bullets: The study tests whether stereo models learn simple global shape priors for boundary localization.
A synthetic dataset varies depth, slant, color, and texture across objects from a constrained shape family.
Several state-of-the-art models retain boundary errors even after training or fine-tuning on this dataset.
A generative stereo model jointly predicts disparity and an object-boundary distance field.
The findings highlight limitations of current architectures and motivate combining regional evidence with global geometry.

papers.abstract: Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. Cognitive science suggests this generalization stems from a top-down generative inference strategy. In contrast, state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction neural networks typically rely on amortized, feedforward inference. While fast, this pattern-matching approach degrades when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training. Inspired by the generative nature of human vision, we propose Infer3D, an inverse generative modeling framework that recovers the latent variables of a generative model to best match the monocular input. To prevent degenerate flat outputs, we couple the generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network that constrains the optimization space to a valid, multi-view-consistent 3D manifold. Across a variety of controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D demonstrates superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process confusing stimuli, we introduce an adaptive inference strategy that expends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD examples while efficiently routing in-distribution inputs. Project website: https://amanikiruga.github.io/infer3d-site/
authors: Amani Kiruga, Mark Hamilton, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, William T. Freeman, Vincent Sitzmann, Yilun Du, Ayush Tewari
bullets: Targets the poor out-of-distribution generalization of fast, feedforward 3D reconstruction networks.
Uses inverse generative modeling to recover latent variables that best explain a monocular image.
Combines a generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network to avoid degenerate flat reconstructions.
Reports stronger OOD reconstruction accuracy than feedforward networks across controlled synthetic and real-world tasks.
Introduces adaptive test-time inference that allocates more computation to ambiguous inputs.

papers.abstract: Generative design of formed sheet panels must preserve geometric manufacturing conditions while exploring layouts and improving performance. STAMP embeds these conditions directly in the shape representation. Each panel is described by its material layout and a reference surface with one height at each occupied position in a plane perpendicular to the drawing direction. Nominal thickness is prescribed along the normal. The representation allows curved surfaces, ribs, and openings. It excludes reference-surface undercuts and keeps nominal thickness fixed without manufacturing penalty terms. Because these conditions belong to the representation, every generated and optimized panel satisfies them regardless of training-set size. Boundary-conditioned diffusion generates alternative layouts, and predictor gradients guide a surface optimization that retains outlines, openings, and designated fixed regions. We demonstrate STAMP on automotive hood inner panels using CarHoods10k. With a comparable number of stored values, depth maps reconstruct surfaces more accurately than point-cloud and voxel baselines. From only five training designs, one of three training runs yields novel and varied layouts. A generator trained on 500 designs, 6.5% of the training set, already reaches the layout variety of the full-data model. Across 11 held-out design families, predictor-based selection among existing dataset designs yields an average gap of 0.18 mm to the best available FEA deformation, versus an expected 1.59 mm for random selection. It does better than random selection in all 11 families. At a 10% depth-change bound, a network not used in the search predicts an average deformation reduction of 24.8% for six generated and existing panels, with a 3.2% average mass increase computed from geometry. Engineers can thus explore and optimize panels within this manufacturing-informed design space.
bullets: Represents panels with material layouts, height-based reference surfaces, fixed nominal thickness, ribs, openings, and curved surfaces while excluding undercuts.
Uses boundary-conditioned diffusion to generate layouts and predictor gradients to optimize surfaces while preserving specified outlines, openings, and fixed regions.
On automotive hood inner panels, depth maps reconstruct surfaces more accurately than point-cloud and voxel baselines at comparable storage.
With limited training data, STAMP generates varied layouts; predictor-based selection outperforms random selection across all 11 held-out design families.
A 10% depth-change bound produced a predicted average deformation reduction of 24.8% with a 3.2% average mass increase for six panels.

papers.abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.
authors: Mingliang Zhai, Chuanhao Li, Jiaming Tan, Zhen Li, Yuwei Wu, Yunde Jia, Zian Meng, Yuanyang Yin, Kaipeng Zhang

papers.abstract: Zero-Shot Multimodal Anomaly Detection (ZSMAD) aims to identify both appearance and geometric defects in novel categories without relying on target-specific training data, making it especially valuable in real-world scenarios constrained by data scarcity, privacy concerns, or high annotation costs. While recent approaches successfully adapt vision-language models like CLIP to achieve this open-vocabulary generalization, they still face significant challenges: (i) severe geometric information loss during 3D-to-2D point cloud rendering; (ii) spatially noisy 2D feature maps produced by raw CLIP patch embeddings, compounded by shallow late-stage modality fusion; and (iii) severe cross-modal semantic misalignment due to decoupled processing streams. To address these limitations, we propose AggCLIP, a novel framework that adapts frozen CLIP representations for ZSMAD by explicitly incorporating local geometric structure and visual spatial context. Specifically, to accurately localize fine-grained defects, we design a Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation (GSA) module that refines back-projected 3D point features via density-adaptive neighborhood weighting, alongside a Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation (CSA) module that smooths multi-scale 2D patch embeddings using a lightweight trainable adapter. Furthermore, to prevent semantic drift between modalities, we introduce a Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive (DSPC) loss, which aligns the abstract concepts of normality and abnormality across the point cloud and RGB streams. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed AggCLIP framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies benchmarks under both one-vs-rest and cross-dataset zero-shot settings, notably surpassing the strongest competitive methods by up to 2.9% in pixel-level AUPRO.
authors: Zhi Li, Hanyu Wang, Fei Shen, Zhengtao Zhang
bullets: Targets appearance and geometric defects in unseen categories without target-specific training data.
Uses Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation to refine 3D point features with density-adaptive neighborhoods.
Uses Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation to smooth multi-scale CLIP patch embeddings with a trainable adapter.
Introduces Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive loss to align normality and abnormality concepts across modalities.
Reports state-of-the-art results on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies, with up to 2.9% higher pixel-level AUPRO than competing methods.

(b) The proposed AggCLIP framework effectively addresses these gaps. It refines noisy back-projected point features via the Geometry-Aware Spatial Aggregation (GSA) module, suppresses 2D spatial noise using Context-Aware Spatial Aggregation (CSA) paired with a learnable Adapter, and directly enforces deep cross-modal semantic interaction via the Dual-Stream Prompt Contrastive (DSPC) loss.

papers.abstract: Multimodal language models for materials science rely on effective mechanisms for incorporating three-dimensional structural representations. MatterChat addresses this challenge using a large bridge module between a pretrained structural encoder and the LLM, together with a separate contrastive alignment stage. We instead ask whether this bridge can adaptively select and combine representations from multiple structural encoders according to the target property. We find that supervised and generative material encoders provide complementary information for property prediction. We found that, for Zatom-1, this information is not concentrated in the final layer. Instead, the most informative representations occur at different depths depending on the target property. This motivates Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF), a lightweight attention-based bridge that uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations. The bridge is trained directly on downstream prediction tasks, allowing representation selection and material-language alignment to be learned jointly without separate contrastive pretraining. Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, with up to 47.8% lower RMSE, while using substantially fewer trainable parameters and halving the overall training time. Further experiments incorporating UMA-S demonstrate TCAF's flexibility across encoder combinations, with the three-encoder configuration achieving the highest macro-average classification accuracy of 89.61%.
authors: Huu Binh Ta, Alex Morehead, N. Benjamin Erichson, Ferdinando Fioretto, Sandeep Madireddy
bullets: MatterChat uses a large bridge and separate contrastive alignment; this work instead learns representation selection jointly on downstream tasks.
Different target properties benefit from representations at different depths of Zatom-1, while CHGNet and Zatom-1 provide complementary information.
Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations.
Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, including up to 47.8% lower RMSE, with fewer trainable parameters and half the training time.
Adding UMA-S shows flexibility across encoder combinations; the three-encoder setup reaches 89.61% macro-average classification accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our proposed Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF) methodology. (a) Frozen domain encoders (Zatom-1 and CHGNet) extract complementary atom-level representations from a crystal structure. Here, features from all 16 Zatom-1 layers are retained, and CHGNet features are projected from 64 to 512 dimensions. (b) The property requested by the prompt selects a learned task residual, which is added to 32 latent queries. Two Perceiver blocks apply cross-attention to the structural features, followed by latent self-attention and a feed-forward network. These taskconditioned queries allow the bridge to weight encoder sources and layer depths differently for each property. (c) The fused latents are projected into the language-model embedding space and combined with prompt embeddings. A frozen language model then generates the response. The trainable components are optimized jointly using a downstream language-modeling objective.

papers.abstract: Image-to-code methods for 3D scene reconstruction produce executable code that generates editable digital content and supports visual simulation. However, existing methods primarily rely on appearance similarity, which provides limited guidance for distinguishing errors in geometry, materials, and illumination. Light shapes scene appearance through its interactions with geometry and materials, influencing shading, cast shadows, and reflections. We therefore present LightHarness, a VLM-based agentic framework that incorporates explicit lighting reasoning into iterative scene reconstruction. To be specific, we leverage complementary geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues to jointly refine scene structure and appearance, and propose Lighting Reasoning Memory to maintain light-source hypotheses, which supports evidence, and revision history throughout iterations. Together, they support reasoning about partially visible and unseen sources, with evidence-guided verification directing subsequent revisions. Our framework reconstructs explicit scenes through coherent reasoning about geometry, materials, and illumination without additional training or differentiable rendering. Extensive experiments demonstrate superior image-to-code reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, further supporting downstream scene editing, object insertion, and versatile relighting.
authors: Zeting Luo, Yifan Li, Shuai Yang
bullets: Addresses the limits of appearance-only guidance for diagnosing geometry, material, and illumination errors.
Combines geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues during iterative scene refinement.
Uses Lighting Reasoning Memory to track light-source hypotheses, evidence, and revision history, including partially visible or unseen sources.
Requires no additional training or differentiable rendering.
Reports improved reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, with benefits for editing, object insertion, and relighting.

figures.caption: Figure 10. Application of harmonious object insertion. Our method (b, d) enables physically realistic lighting, reflection, occlusion and geometric projection, while (c) generative model-only method struggles with these real-world principles.

Figure 7. Application of texture editing. Our method supports texture replacement with multiple reference images with precise and executable code reconstruction, while directly applying even front-tier generative models leads to inaccurate structure.

Figure 6. Qualitative ablation of key designs. Our full framework reproduces scene layout and illumination more precisely, while removing individual components introduces errors in basic scene layout (c), light placement (c-f), and light source shape (e).
Figure 11. Limitation on complex invisible lighting reasoning. Although effective, our framework still struggles with inferring complex invisible objects from scarce light and shadow cues.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison between other SoTA image-to-code baselines. Across diverse indoor and outdoor scenes, our LightHarness better preserves object arrangement and characteristic lighting effects, including strong back-lighting, localized illumination, and structured cast shadows, achieving more faithful reconstructions of scene structure and appearance.
Figure 5. Hard case verification. Our method more faithfully reconstructs the diagonal shadow and surrounding building structure relative to other methods.
Figure 9. Application of relighting with realistic shadow.

Figure 2. Conceptual comparison of image-to-code paradigms. (a) Appearance feedback emphasizes rendered–reference similarity. (b) Tool-grounded refinement uses perception and spatial analysis to improve layout. (c) LightHarness combines enriched evidence and persistent memory for explicit lighting reasoning throughout reconstruction.
Figure 8. Application of relighting with realistic reflection.
Table 2. Quantitative ablation experiment. We evaluate on a 16-image subset for efficiency. Our full model achieves the best. BT scores are re-normalized here.

Table 1. Quantitative comparison of image-to-code reconstruction. We report four appearance consistency metrics covering PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS and DreamSim, and measure novel-view consistency by a mean-centered Bradley-Terry (BT) score which is estimated from pairwise judgments using an additional ±15◦ view following SceneRig [19]. papers.title: Beyond Appearance: Evidence-Guided Programmatic 3D Scene Reconstruction with Agentic Lighting Reasoning
