papers.abstract: Single-image intrinsic decomposition is an inherently ill-posed problem, requiring the disentanglement of strongly coupled appearance factors from a single RGB observation. Recent methods address this ambiguity with diffusion priors, at the cost of large, iterative, and often stochastic models. We show that accurate decomposition does not require a large generative model. Our key idea is to decouple reconstruction from decomposition on top of a strong pretrained representation. First, an $X \rightarrow X$ teacher learns to reconstruct each intrinsic map from DINOv3 features using a shared decoder, without paired RGB-to-intrinsic supervision. Then, a DINOv3-based student predicts the corresponding teacher representations from RGB through lightweight, modality-specific projections, enabling training on partially annotated datasets and predicting all intrinsics in a single forward pass. \textbf{RAID}, predicts intrinsic properties in the structured latent space, enabling a compact 165M-parameter model, 100x faster than diffusion-based methods. Despite its compact size, it achieves competitive or superior decomposition quality, with improved robustness to input resolution. Additionally, our learned projections yield interpretable, modality-specific feature spaces.
authors: Claudia Cuttano, Tamy Boubekeur, Elena Garces, Giuseppe Vecchio
bullets: Addresses the ill-posed disentanglement of appearance factors from a single RGB image.
Trains a shared decoder to reconstruct intrinsic maps from DINOv3 features, separating reconstruction from decomposition without paired RGB-to-intrinsic supervision.
Uses lightweight, modality-specific projections to predict teacher representations from RGB and support partially annotated data.
Predicts all intrinsic properties in one forward pass with a compact 165M-parameter model, reported as 100× faster than diffusion-based methods.
Achieves competitive or superior decomposition quality, improved resolution robustness, and interpretable modality-specific feature spaces.

figures.caption: Figure 2. RAID overview. (a) We first learn an X → X reconstruction autoencoder across RGB and intrinsic signals, i.e. albedo, irradiance, normals, roughness, and metallicity. A frozen DINOv3 backbone with trainable AdaptFormer modules encodes each modality into a shared, decodable feature space; one DC-AE decoder reconstructs the input modality from that space. (b) We then freeze the reconstruction model and learn to infer its features from RGB. A student encoder and modality-specific projections predict the features that the teacher extracts from the corresponding GT maps. Feature alignment guides these predictions, while supervision on the decoded maps enforces pixel alignment. At inference, the teacher is removed: the student, projections, and same shared decoder produce all five maps.

Figure 6. Qualitative robustness to input resolution. We compare RGB↔X, MVInverse, and RAID with and without multi-resolution training at input resolutions from 256×256 to 2048×2048. At each resolution, we show the predicted albedo and surface normal maps. RGB↔X exhibits artifacts at both extremes, whereas MVInverse degrades at high resolution. The single-resolution variant of RAID produces more consistent predictions than either baseline, suggesting that our adaptation to intrinsic decomposition preserves the resolution robustness of the pretrained DINOv3 representation. Multi-resolution training further improves prediction consistency.

Figure 5. Feature-space selection. Given an image and a query patch +, we compute cosine similarity between the query and patch features in each modality-projected feature space (red: high, blue: low). The resulting maps show that albedo, normal, irradiance, and metallicity projections induce different selection axes, grouping regions according to the corresponding physical property.

Figure 4. Resolution robustness and memory scaling. Albedo PSNR (↑) and LPIPS (↓) on Hypersim and InteriorVerse for input resolutions from 512 to 2048 pixels. Marker area encodes peak inference GPU memory. We compare our models trained with and without multi-resolution supervision against MVInverse and RGB↔X (InteriorVerse only). Our model is more stable across resolutions; multi-resolution supervision further improves highresolution accuracy while keeping peak memory below 3GB.

Figure 3. X → X autoencoder reconstructions. The reconstruction stage receives a map X as input and reconstructs the same signal at the output. The autoencoder preserves the spatial structure and modality-specific details of the input maps. These reconstructions indicate that heterogeneous intrinsic signals can be represented in a shared DINOv3 feature-to-map space, which is later used to supervise the RGB-to-intrinsics student.
Figure 7. Additional qualitative results. Intrinsic maps predicted by RAID for additional input images.

Table 1. Comparison on InteriorVerse and Hypersim. RAID offers the best overall accuracy–efficiency trade-off, maintaining competitive albedo and normal estimation while achieving the best material estimates (roughness and metallicity) on InteriorVerse and irradiance estimates on Hypersim. With only 165M parameters, it is the smallest and fastest model in this comparison, delivering over 100× the throughput of the fastest diffusion baseline [41] on InteriorVerse. Compared with the feed-forward baseline [36], it uses about one-sixth as many parameters and achieves 2× FPS at 1024×768. For albedo and irradiance, we report PSNR, RMSE, and LPIPS; for metallicity and roughness, PSNR, RMSE, and MAE; and for normals, mean angular error and pixel accuracy at 11.25◦ and 30◦. FPS is measured on an NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU at 640×480 on InteriorVerse and 1024×768 on Hypersim. Best results bold, 2nd best underlined.

Table 2. Choice of pretrained representation. We compare DINOv3 with leading Vision Foundation Models spanning selfsupervised and image–text pretraining. With each VFM, we train a reconstruction autoencoder and then an RGB student to predict the teacher features. DINOv3 consistently achieves the best performance across all modalities on Hypersim. Best result in bold.

Table 3. Ablation of the reconstruction teacher and output loss. No teacher regresses maps directly in pixel space, while No pixel loss uses teacher feature alignment alone. Combining feature alignment with supervision on the decoded maps (RAID) gives the strongest overall performance, leading across all four modalities on InteriorVerse and on irradiance on Hypersim. Direct regression achieves higher albedo PSNR and slightly lower mean normal error on Hypersim at the cost of a separate decoder per modality.
Table 4. Data statistics. Number of training and test images, together with the available intrinsic-map annotations for each dataset.
Table 5. Training configuration. Both stages use the same six training datasets and keep the DINOv3 backbone frozen.
Table 6. Reconstruction upper bound. X → X reconstruction of ground-truth maps by the teacher, compared with RGB → X prediction by RAID. Both use the same decoder.

papers.title: RAID: Representation Autoencoder for Intrinsic Decomposition
papers.tldr: RAID performs fast single-image intrinsic decomposition by predicting intrinsic representations from RGB with a compact DINOv3-based model instead of using iterative diffusion.

papers.abstract: Efficient and accurate 3D surface reconstruction from multi-view images remains a fundamental challenge in Gaussian splatting. Many existing methods rely on sparse geometric initialization and iterative densification, resulting in substantial optimization overhead and difficulties in balancing rendering quality and geometric accuracy, particularly in reflective and weakly textured regions. To address these limitations, we propose RAPID, a geometry-first framework that uses multiview polarization cues to recover dense surface priors. We integrate surface normals into depth maps using sparse geometric anchors. These depth maps are then fused across views. Curvature-adaptive sampling and oriented Gaussian initialization then support efficient optimization. Experiments on the PISR dataset demonstrate an approximately \(5\times\) speedup over PhyGaP, which is a state-of-the-art Gaussian-based reconstruction method. RAPID reduces the average optimization time from approximately 21 minutes (PhyGaP) to 4 minutes while maintaining competitive novel-view synthesis quality and mesh reconstruction accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of RAPID in accelerating Gaussian optimization from polarimetric multi-view inputs.
authors: Daisong Ouyang, Linlin Xia, Liangkun Yan, Song Gu, Shedong Zhao, Xin Dai, Yi Zheng
bullets: Addresses optimization overhead and geometric inaccuracies in reflective and weakly textured regions.
Recovers dense surface priors by integrating polarization-derived normals with sparse geometric anchors, then fuses depth across views.
Uses curvature-adaptive sampling and oriented Gaussian initialization for efficient optimization.
On the PISR dataset, achieves approximately 5× faster optimization than PhyGaP while maintaining competitive novel-view synthesis and mesh reconstruction quality.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview. Our method recovers surface normals from multi-view polarization observations, integrates them into dense depth maps using sparse depth anchors, and initializes oriented 2D Gaussians through TSDF surface fusion and curvature-adaptive sampling. Surface-constrained optimization and unified Insert, Split, Merge, and Prune updates then refine the representation for novel-view synthesis and mesh reconstruction.
Figure 4. Mesh reconstruction results of different methods. Meshes extracted from three real-world scenes in the PANDORA [9] dataset.

Figure 5. Qualitative results of different methods on novel view synthesis. We zoom in on BlackLoong’s forelimb and RedLoong’s body to assess geometric reconstruction accuracy in regions with complex details.
Figure 3. Four possible azimuth angles. The figure illustrates the π/2 and π ambiguities.

Table 2. Quantitative results of different methods on novel view synthesis.

papers.abstract: Inferring the unseen side of a 3D assembly requires reasoning about part placement and occlusion. Different assemblies can match the observed views while producing different hidden views, leaving the target ambiguous. We introduce SixthView, a benchmark in which models predict a sixth orthographic view from five observed views and information about the component shapes. The benchmark contains 602 synthetic polycube assemblies with 2--10 parts and requires a dense grid of part labels for the missing view, allowing both exact-view and cell-level evaluation. For each item, we exhaustively verify that all legal assemblies consistent with the exact component geometry and observed label grids yield the same target view. With these inputs, the task tests symbolic assembly and coordinate reasoning. The image-only variants additionally require shape recovery from rendered views, where occlusion can make different 3D shapes look identical. We evaluate three vision-language models under four input conditions. Across 552 items with complete evaluations, exact-grid accuracy with images plus exact text ranges from 33.2% to 85.4%. Adding exact text to separate images improves accuracy by 19.7--63.0 percentage points, whereas adding images to exact text changes it by only $-0.5$ to $+2.1$ points. Separate image panels outperform a merged sheet by 6.7--11.1 points. The results show that performance depends strongly on access to exact symbolic information, with little further improvement from images once the geometry is specified. GitHub: https://github.com/facebookresearch/sixthview_benchmark
authors: Pooya Khosravi, Jen-Feng Chang, Fnu Pramono
bullets: The task predicts a sixth view from five observed views plus component-shape information, requiring part-placement, occlusion, and coordinate reasoning.
It includes 602 synthetic polycube assemblies with 2–10 parts and evaluates dense part-label grids using exact-view and cell-level metrics.
The benchmark verifies that every legal assembly consistent with the inputs has the same hidden target view, removing inherent ambiguity.
Across three vision-language models, exact-grid accuracy ranges from 33.2% to 85.4% across evaluated conditions.
Adding exact text geometry substantially improves image-based performance, while adding images to exact text provides little benefit; separate image panels also outperform merged sheets.

Figure 2. Paired experimental contrasts. RQ1 compares exact text with rendered evidence. RQ2 adds exact symbolic evidence to the images. RQ3 jointly changes image count and effective panel resolution by composing the same panels into one sheet.

Table 3. Primary exact-grid / cell accuracy (%) on the common complete-case panel (N = 552), with three repetitions per item. papers.abstract: Segmenting each reported finding in a radiology scan would allow findings to be measured and tracked over time and let AI systems generate reports that are verifiable, but so far AI models have performed poorly at this task. To advance this task, we organized the ReXGrounding Challenge at MICCAI 2026, the first challenge dedicated to it. Given a non-contrast chest CT scan and the set of findings from its report, participants trained models to produce the corresponding set of 3D segmentations. The challenge used 2,992 training and 200 validation scans from the ReXGroundingCT dataset, and evaluated methods on a held-out test set of 300 scans with 582 findings, exhaustively annotated by board-certified radiologists. In total, 48 teams from 15 countries made 760 submissions, and the best method reached a Dice of 0.375 and a hit rate of 0.77, matching agreement between two independent radiologist groups (Dice 0.32, hit rate 0.76, on a 50-scan subset). On the 100 scans of the pre-challenge benchmark, the winner reached a Dice of 0.390, against 0.285 for VoxTell, the best model before the challenge, which five of the six best teams fine-tuned. Non-focal findings remained far harder to segment than focal ones, instance F1 stayed below inter-reader agreement (0.34 vs. 0.47), and models sometimes segmented the right abnormality in the wrong location. Top methods thus match radiologist agreement in Dice, but non-focal findings, findings with multiple instances, and adherence to the anatomical location described in the text remain open problems.

papers.abstract: Text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation requires layouts satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints. However, existing diffusion methods rely primarily on static textual conditions, limiting their ability to assess evolving scenes and translate semantic discrepancies into executable object-level corrections. MLLM-based post-hoc refinement provides semantic feedback but remains decoupled from denoising, potentially disrupting scene coherence.We propose ReflectScene, an MLLM-guided closed-loop diffusion framework. First, we introduce Hierarchical Prior-Grounded Scene Understanding that aligns structured layouts with multi-view visual evidence, to interpret object-specific context and scene global semantics via a frozen multi-modal large language model (MLLM). Second, we propose MLLM-Guided Semantic Reward Evaluation to distill MLLM's diagnoses and assessments on possible candidate corrections into a lightweight Reward Predictor, enabling correction decision making with reduced computation burden. Finally, Decision-Conditioned Trajectory-Consistent Diffusion is proposed to integrate selected corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection, correcting object layout in the generated scene while preserving non-target arrangements throughout denoising.Experiments on 3D-FRONT demonstrate improved functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive generation quality and diversity.
authors: Jiawei Shen, Jie Feng, Junpeng Zhang, Guanbin Li, Wanyi Chen, Weisheng Dong, Guangming Shi
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints with static text-conditioned diffusion.
Uses hierarchical scene understanding to align structured layouts with multi-view visual evidence and interpret both object context and global semantics.
Distills MLLM feedback about candidate corrections into a lightweight reward predictor for efficient correction decisions.
Integrates selected object-level corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection during denoising.
On 3D-FRONT, improves functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive quality and diversity.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ReflectScene. ReflectScene integrates hierarchical scene understanding and MLLM-guided decisions into objectcentric diffusion. At each denoising step, intermediate clean estimates are assessed to select object-level actions, providing transient conditioning, while buffered non-STOP actions are executed every 50 steps to update a persistent correction state. This state is projected onto subsequent clean estimates before DDPM posterior sampling, with decision-effect consistency learning promoting target recovery and non-target preservation.

papers.abstract: Accurately matching human intentions in 3D space is an important goal of artificial intelligence. Recently, 3D Intention Grounding (3D-IG) has emerged, aiming to localize target 3D objects given a natural-language intent. Unlike conventional visual grounding with descriptive referring expressions, 3D-IG intents are abstract and non-descriptive, making object localization substantially more challenging. This requires inferring latent functional requirements from non-descriptive intents and aligning them with object-level 3D representations. However, existing methods largely rely on implicit intent-object matching, leading to logical gaps and limited interpretability, robustness, and generalization. To address these challenges, we propose Chain-of-Causal Reasoning (CoCR), a causality-inspired functional dependency reasoning framework that explicitly bridges abstract intentions and candidate objects through intermediate functional requirements. Specifically, CoCR progressively decomposes complex intents into ordered functional requirements, thereby forming an explicit intent-function-object reasoning chain that links abstract intentions to object suitability. Building on this chain, we construct a causality-inspired functional dependency graph to model requirement-attribute relationships and introduce a causal-visual alignment module that aligns function-aware representations with the geometric-semantic features of 3D point clouds, enabling bidirectional verification between structured functional reasoning and visual evidence. Extensive experiments on 3D Intention Grounding and 3D Visual Grounding demonstrate that our method enhances intent-aware object localization. Our code is available at https://2490o.github.io/CoCR.
authors: Zihao Zhang, Aming Wu, Yang Li, Yahong Han
bullets: 3D intent grounding must localize objects from abstract, non-descriptive language, which is harder than conventional visual grounding.
CoCR decomposes complex intents into ordered functional requirements, forming an intent–function–object reasoning chain.
A functional dependency graph models requirement–attribute relationships, while causal-visual alignment connects functional reasoning with 3D geometric and semantic features.
Bidirectional verification links structured functional reasoning with visual evidence for more interpretable and robust localization.
Experiments on 3D intention and visual grounding show improved intent-aware object localization; the abstract gives no specific numerical results.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The overall architecture. First, point cloud data and intent text are encoded by the model. The intent text is processed by the Intent Causal Parsing module for step-wise decomposition, transforming the natural language intent into functional requirements. Subsequently, Intent Causal Grounding is performed through the construction of a causal graph, defining the causal relationships between functional requirements and object attributes. The graph is iteratively updated via causal–visual feature alignment and causal pruning. Finally, causal reasoning is conducted based on the updated graph to achieve object selection and localization.

papers.abstract: Continual learning of 3D Gaussian fields aims to maintain faithful reconstructions of the evolving world. However, directly fine-tuning an existing Gaussian field on new observations can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously reconstructed content. To address this challenge, existing methods employ selective local optimization, replay, or parameter regularization, yet still struggle to balance adaptation to scene changes with preservation of still-valid content. Our key insight is to view 3D Gaussian primitives themselves as self-regulating continual learners. Based on this insight, we introduce GaussLearner, which equips each Gaussian with a closed continual-learning loop connecting observation, self-regulation, and adaptation at the primitive level. At each novel state, GaussLearner first attributes pixel-wise inconsistencies in current observations to their contributing Gaussians. Each Gaussian then self-regulates through a learning weight that balances current observations against cross-state reliability. This weight governs both Gaussian parameter adaptation and optimizer memory refresh. As current inconsistencies are resolved, the adaptation outcome renews each Gaussian's reliability for future states. The resulting field is a globally coupled population of locally self-regulating learners. Across scenes from CL-Splats, WAT, and our CL-3D dataset, GaussLearner improves average PSNR by 3.41 dB over the strongest baseline. On CL-3D, it achieves the best reconstruction quality on both changed and unchanged views.
authors: Gaoxiang Linghu, Haonan Zhou, Xuanhe Liu, Weili Xu, Kaiyue Zhou, Jun Xiao, Gaoang Wang
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting when updating 3D Gaussian fields with new observations.
Attributes pixel-wise inconsistencies to contributing Gaussians for primitive-level adaptation.
Uses per-Gaussian learning weights to balance current evidence with cross-state reliability.
The weights control both parameter updates and optimizer-memory refresh, renewing reliability over time.
Improves average PSNR by 3.41 dB over the strongest baseline across CL-Splats, WAT, and CL-3D; performs best on changed and unchanged views in CL-3D.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Framework of GAUSSLEARNER. Each Gaussian acts as a stateful continual learner with scene parameters and cross-state reliability. At each scene state, pixel-wise inconsistencies in current observations are attributed to their contributing Gaussians. Each Gaussian then self-regulates through a per-Gaussian learning weight that balances current observations against cross-state reliability. This weight governs both parameter adaptation and optimizer-memory refresh. Cross-state reliability is updated at state boundaries using resolved pressure and final support. The resulting field is a globally coupled population of locally self-regulating continual learners.

Figure 2. Comparison of 3D Gaussian continual learning paradigms. (a) Existing methods treat Gaussians as update targets. Replay and regularization may retain obsolete content or hinder adaptation, while selective local optimization can propagate 2D detection errors into 3D updates. (b) GAUSSLEARNER instead views each Gaussian primitive as a continual learner equipped with a closed learning loop.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparisons on CL-3D. From top to bottom are ClubRoom, Fridge, OfficeHub, and StudyNook. GAUSSLEARNER adapts to revised content while preserving still-valid regions, with less forgetting and fewer reconstruction artifacts.

papers.abstract: Semantic labels say what a building element is, not what it does: two identical-looking windows on one facade may be operable or fixed, a column may carry load or only decorate. We ask whether 3D point representations encode such architectural function. On 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings with 15 functional attributes per element, we hold out entire buildings and compare hand-crafted descriptors, networks trained from scratch and frozen self-supervised point transformers. Descriptors and frozen features are read by the same linear layer. No network trained from scratch, from PointNet to a 108M-parameter PTv3, clearly exceeds the descriptors (0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements), whereas frozen Utonia reaches 0.732. Random-weight controls of the same architectures (0.649 and 0.652) attribute the gain to pretraining (Utonia: +0.080, 95% building interval [+0.035, +0.124]). Pretrained features improve at every tested number of labelled buildings while descriptors and random features plateau, and, in the configurations we tested, fine-tuning erodes the benefit: at today's data scale, function is better read from pretrained representations than learned from scratch.
bullets: The study probes 15 functional attributes across elements in 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings, holding out entire buildings for evaluation.
Models are compared using a shared linear readout, including hand-crafted descriptors, supervised point networks, frozen pretrained transformers, and random-weight controls.
From-scratch networks do not clearly beat descriptors, which reach 0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements.
Frozen Utonia reaches 0.732 mAP, with its gain over matched random-weight controls attributed to pretraining.
Pretrained features improve as labeled buildings increase; in tested settings, fine-tuning reduces their advantage.

papers.tldr: Frozen self-supervised 3D point features encode architectural function better than hand-crafted descriptors or models trained from scratch, especially with limited labeled buildings.

papers.abstract: Localizing a query from a few posed reference images avoids building a 3D point map. We ask what the camera predictions of learned 3D models add to geometric estimation from the same references, and where failures arise. Across eight learned models and variants and five test sets, we compare reference budgets, swap pose components, and intervene on the references a model sees. At fine pose-error thresholds, geometric estimation with one additional reference is significantly more accurate than every model on two references on Cambridge and NAVER B1 and never significantly worse, alone or as a fallback behind a shared acceptance gate; with the same three references, the more accurate approach depends on the scene. The gain from the learned translation magnitude depends on reference selection: it improves seven of the eight models on 12-Scenes with the spread-out pairs we select, but none of the five we test with the two top-ranked retrieved references. Where retrieval also returns references from other locations, at NAVER Gangnam Station, models fail at different stages. A robust alignment brings Pi3X and MapAnything within 3.3 pp of adding references as needed. In controlled tests, aligning on the nearby references largely restores VGGT, Pi3X and MapAnything but not Depth Anything 3, and pose-conditioned Pi3X recovers only if the far poses are masked and left out of its input-pose normalization.
authors: Jaehyun Kim, Wonseok Kang, Jeongmin Lee, Tae-Wan Kim
bullets: Compares eight learned 3D models with geometric estimation across five test sets, varying reference counts, pose components, and reference inputs.

With two references, geometric estimation plus one additional reference is more accurate at fine pose thresholds than every tested model on Cambridge and NAVER B1, and is never significantly worse as a fallback.
With three references, the better approach depends on the scene; translation magnitude helps most when references are spread out rather than top-ranked retrieved images.
At NAVER Gangnam Station, retrieval from multiple locations causes models to fail at different stages; robust alignment narrows Pi3X and MapAnything’s gap to adding references.
Controlled tests show alignment restores several models’ performance, but not Depth Anything 3; pose-conditioned Pi3X additionally requires masking distant poses during input-pose normalization.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates learned 3D models for camera localization from posed references, relevant to 3D perception and pretrained 3D foundation models.
papers.title: What Do Learned 3D Models Add to Localization from Posed References?
papers.tldr: Geometric localization can outperform learned 3D models with fewer references, while learned pose cues help mainly when references are selected appropriately and model inputs are well aligned.

papers.abstract: Abstracting structured buildings from limited observations is essential for 3D urban modeling and digital twins. Partial point clouds and overhead images of the same building provide incomplete 3D surface measurements and visual cues to its footprint, roof geometry, and rooftop structures, respectively. This motivates a unified framework that aligns geometric and visual cues in 3D and reconstructs buildings from either or both modalities. Building on this connection, we present Any2Building, a unified model for Level of Detail 2 (LoD2) building reconstruction from partial point clouds, overhead images, or both, with optional coarse geometric priors. At its core is an occupancy-grounded shared spatial queries representation that organizes available observations within a common 3D grid. Supervised by complete building surface voxels, these queries connect observational evidence to target geometry, enabling a shared generator to learn structural priors across tasks and providing spatial guidance for recovering missing structure. A trained voxel conditional surface-generation and low-poly remeshing pipeline then converts the predicted structure into compact LoD2 building models. To support this framework, we introduce BuildingWorld-Image, comprising approximately one million paired samples of partial point clouds, overhead images, and LoD2 building models across 18 cities. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that Any2Building outperforms existing methods in geometric reconstruction accuracy across unimodal and multimodal point-cloud completion, single-image building generation, and prior-assisted generation, while maintaining detailed and robust recovery when point cloud input modality is degraded.
authors: Hongye Hou, Zhuoxiao Li, Liu Xiangyu, Tengxi Wang, Jing Ou, Dongli Wu, Shuai Zhang, Tongyan Hua, Wufan Zhao
bullets: Addresses incomplete building reconstruction for 3D urban modeling and digital twins.
Uses occupancy-grounded shared spatial queries on a common 3D grid to align geometric and visual cues.
Generates building surfaces with a voxel-conditional pipeline, followed by low-poly remeshing.
Introduces BuildingWorld-Image with about one million paired samples across 18 cities.
Reports improved geometric reconstruction across unimodal, multimodal, and prior-assisted settings, including degraded point-cloud inputs.

papers.abstract: $\pi^4$ is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, $\pi^4$ achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters---less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at https://github.com/yyfz/Pi4.
authors: Yifan Wang, Weiguang Zhao, Ni Yang, Haoyu Guo, Junting Dong, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
bullets: Recovers dense geometry, camera poses, metric scale, point tracks, and moving-object masks from single- or multi-image inputs.
Uses a geometry branch plus a geometry-conditioned motion branch that lifts image correspondences into 3D.
Achieves the best overall average rank on geometry benchmarks and competitive 2D/3D tracking and segmentation performance.
The full system has about 0.5B parameters and can process scenes with thousands of images despite training on at most 64 views.
The paper also describes its data and training recipe, design studies, and releases code and models.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models predict dense point maps from multiple images in a single pass. Without explicit geometric constraints, however, their predictions are often inconsistent across views and lack fine-grained precision. Recent methods incorporate geometric priors such as camera pose or depth, but use them merely as auxiliary inputs, process each view independently, or refine the geometry only where the priors are available. We present Refin3R, which refines feed-forward point maps with Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, propagating SfM geometry over the image grid. In its dual-branch architecture, a 2D branch extends SfM geometry beyond its coverage using geometry-aware backbone features, while a 3D branch reasons over the SfM points of all views, capturing multi-view structure that the image grid alone cannot represent. The two branches exchange information bidirectionally to jointly refine each view, yielding dense and accurate point maps. Across ScanNet++, ETH3D, Tanks\&Temples, and out-of-domain human and surgical scenes, Refin3R consistently outperforms feed-forward and geometry-guided methods in point map accuracy while running faster than the strongest geometry-guided baseline.
authors: Jongmin Lee, Jaeyeong Kim, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses cross-view inconsistency and limited fine-grained precision in dense point maps.
Uses SfM points as geometric guidance, extending them across image grids rather than treating them only as auxiliary inputs.
Combines a geometry-aware 2D branch with a multi-view 3D branch that reasons over SfM points.
Bidirectional information exchange jointly refines point maps for each view.
Reports higher point-map accuracy than feed-forward and geometry-guided methods across multiple in- and out-of-domain scenes, while running faster than the strongest geometry-guided baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Refin3R. A feed-forward model provides dense depth Dff and geometry-aware features F, and SfM provides partial but accurate depth Dsfm (Sec. 3.2). For each view, a 2D U-Net refines the dense depth on the image grid, while a sparse 3D U-Net refines the SfM points of all views that project into its image, with both branches exchanging information (Secs. 3.3 and 3.4). A spatial propagation network (SPN) fuses their estimates into the refined depth (Sec. 3.5), which is back-projected into the final point map.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison. Each row shows one example from ScanNet++, ETH3D, Tanks&Temples, 4D-DRESS, and MVdVRK, with only one input view visualized. papers.abstract: Routine X-ray modalities like cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) are optimized for high-contrast mineralized tissues, leaving soft-tissue abnormalities buried beneath photon noise and below human visual perception. Thus, detecting non-calcified pathologies requires secondary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We demonstrate that sub-visual radiographic signatures of soft-tissue pathology are physically preserved within routine CBCT scans and can be extracted for opportunistic screening using a targeted, physics-guided deep learning pipeline, even under extreme paired-data scarcity. Using the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) as a model system (N = 212 paired CBCT-MRI joints), we address the severe overfitting of high-capacity 3D networks through a two-stage framework. First, we employ a frozen full-grid 3D masked autoencoder (BertsWin) pre-trained on 6,550 unlabeled CBCT volumes via the GradientConductor (GCond) optimizer and an anatomy-aware objective (PhysLoss) redirecting gradient flow into the [-300, 300] HU soft-tissue window. Second, automated localization of the condylar zenith drives a deterministic 3D cropping that eliminates 81% of background osseous variance. Evaluated via a patient-isolated 3x10-fold stratified cross-validation protocol, a statistically robust sub-visual signal for MRI-verified synovial effusion (ROC AUC = 0.793) emerges exclusively from representations pre-trained with the PhysLoss and GCond regime. Crucially, only this setup captures true 3D anatomical chirality (p < 0.001) and high intra-patient structural consistency (0.791) over inter-patient noise; conversely, identical architectures pre-trained with standard L2 loss or unmasked variance decomposition (MVC) collapse to random guessing. These findings establish a generalizable paradigm for repurposing routine, low-contrast radiographic scans into opportunistic screening tools for occult soft-tissue disease.
bullets: CBCT typically obscures non-calcified abnormalities, which are usually assessed with MRI.
A two-stage pipeline combines anatomy-focused 3D masked-autoencoder pretraining with automated, targeted cropping of the temporomandibular joint.
In 212 paired CBCT–MRI joints, the approach detected synovial effusion with ROC AUC 0.793 using patient-isolated cross-validation.
The signal emerged only with the proposed physics-guided pretraining and captured 3D anatomical chirality and intra-patient consistency.
The study supports opportunistic screening of occult soft-tissue disease from routine radiographic scans, demonstrated in the TMJ.

papers.abstract: Detecting multiple reflection symmetries in 3D shapes requires aggregating geometric evidence over a large space of candidate planes, making traditional voting approaches computationally expensive. We introduce the Fourier Accelerated Symmetry Transform (FAST), a training-free framework that combines geometric pair voting with efficient spectral computation. Exploiting the fact that global reflection planes pass through the shape centroid, we reduce the search to plane orientations, while geometric consistency filtering and independent witnesses suppress unreliable pair hypotheses. Our key insight is to represent these votes as a signal over plane orientations and efficiently compute a continuous, smoothed symmetry field in the spherical-harmonic domain. Specifically, we exploit the Funk-Hecke theorem, the spherical counterpart of the Fourier convolution theorem for rotationally symmetric kernels, to transform Gaussian smoothing into multiplication of harmonic coefficients. This enables efficient field evaluation, from which symmetry candidates are extracted, refined, and geometrically verified. Across two benchmarks, including a new benchmark of highly symmetric shapes, FAST achieves the highest clean multi-plane detection $F_1$ scores among evaluated methods (0.861 and 0.947), with GPU inference below 4 ms per shape: over $100\times$ faster than the next-fastest evaluated multi-plane GPU baseline. FAST also demonstrates strong robustness to geometric noise and competitive single-plane detection, achieving 94.9% success on clean single-plane shapes.
bullets: Reduces the search from plane positions and orientations to orientations by assuming global reflection planes pass through the shape centroid.
Combines geometric pair voting, consistency filtering, and independent witnesses to suppress unreliable symmetry hypotheses.
Uses the Funk–Hecke theorem to perform Gaussian smoothing efficiently in the spherical-harmonic domain.
Extracts, refines, and geometrically verifies symmetry candidates from the continuous symmetry field.
Achieves clean multi-plane detection F1 scores of 0.861 and 0.947, with GPU inference below 4 ms per shape and strong noise robustness.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of FAST. (a) Each pair of surface points induces a candidate reflection plane. papers.abstract: An agent or robot in a scanned building must locate its camera in rooms that no model saw during training. Point cloud registration methods can align each RGB-D frame with the building's colored point cloud, accurately but at a high cost. We observe that geometric refinement brings nearby initial poses to the same final pose, so the learned component only needs to find the place. Kolibri does this with a graph network of 55,712 parameters that describes 10 cm cubes of points, called cells, by their color, local shape and neighbors. With the same refinement, it matches GeDi on 96 unseen ScanNet rooms (81.4% against 80.3% within 5 cm and 5{\deg}) and on a held-out test of 10 further rooms, in 82 ms per frame on an RTX 2080 Ti. The saved time allows for search without a room label. In one point cloud of 100 rooms, Kolibri loses 1.3 points against knowing the room, while retrieving the room first loses 56.0. In a hospital emergency department scene from a real scan, it localizes 86.5% of the frames rendered from the scan in 384 ms each, where GeDi needs 91 minutes per frame on cubes of the scan for a similar recall. The method needs colors that agree between the frame and the point cloud. On gray frames and across cameras with different color responses, point cloud registration methods keep the lead.
authors: Leonel Aguilar, Bartu Tuncay, Christoph Hoelscher
bullets: Addresses fast localization in previously unseen rooms from colored point clouds.
A 55,712-parameter graph network represents 10 cm point-cloud cells using color, local shape, and neighboring cells.
Matches GeDi on unseen ScanNet rooms: 81.4% vs. 80.3% within 5 cm and 5°; runs in 82 ms per frame on an RTX 2080 Ti.
Efficient search largely removes the need for a known room label, losing only 1.3 points versus room-aware retrieval in a 100-room cloud.
Performance depends on consistent colors between the RGB-D frame and point cloud; gray frames and cross-camera color differences favor registration methods.

papers.abstract: 3D semantic occupancy prediction requires representing complex spatial structures and modeling contextual relationships across a scene. 3D Gaussian primitives provide a sparse and adaptive representation of scene geometry and semantics, while Mamba offers efficient sequence modeling for capturing dependencies among primitives. However, Gaussian primitives are irregular and unordered, making sequence construction challenging, as conventional spatial ordering may overlook their anisotropic geometry and feature-semantic relationships. In this paper, we present GaussianMamba, a dual-branch Mamba framework that explicitly incorporates Gaussian-specific geometric and feature-semantic relationships into complementary scanning strategies. The first branch refines a locality-preserving traversal using anisotropic Gaussian support derived from primitive scale and orientation. The second branch reorders spatially organized groups according to feature-semantic affinity and adjusts local features using geometry-weighted semantic differences. The resulting sequences are processed by separate Mamba modules, and their features are fused through a support-aware mechanism that incorporates local feature discrepancies arising from the distinct scanning paths. Experiments on nuScenes-SurroundOcc and SSCBench-KITTI-360 demonstrate consistent improvements over GaussianFormer and GaussianFormer-2 in both IoU and mIoU.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of ordering irregular, unordered Gaussian primitives without losing anisotropic geometry or semantic relationships.
Uses a dual-branch design with geometry-aware locality traversal and feature-semantic reordering of spatial groups.
Processes both sequences with separate Mamba modules and fuses them using support-aware local feature discrepancies.
Demonstrates consistent IoU and mIoU improvements over GaussianFormer and GaussianFormer-2 on nuScenes-SurroundOcc and SSCBench-KITTI-360.

papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for predictive visual representation learning. However, our analysis of I-JEPA reveals a growing discrepancy between semantic and geometric learning: improved semantic recognition during pretraining is accompanied by degraded 3D geometric representations. We hypothesize that this partly stems from predicting highly abstract latent representations with incomplete spatial context, favoring semantic regularities over fine-grained geometric information. To address this issue, we introduce CascadeJEPA, a spatially coupled cascaded prediction framework that promotes richer patch-level interactions through full-grid context encoding and cross-attention between prediction stages, while largely preserving the original I-JEPA architecture. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial improvements over I-JEPA across multiple 3D geometric tasks while maintaining strong semantic recognition performance. Furthermore, its advantages extend to future feature forecasting and world model planning, highlighting the potential of enhanced geometric representations to support predictive world modeling.
authors: Kailai Zhou, Ziqi Chen, Xiaoning Xu, Yuefeng Wu, Zixuan Fu, Zijun Lin, Zhihao Li, Youwei Pang, Xiaoqi Zhao, Xun Cao, Bihan Wen
bullets: I-JEPA can improve semantic recognition while degrading 3D geometric representations.
CascadeJEPA addresses this by encoding full-grid spatial context and using cross-attention between cascaded prediction stages.
The approach largely preserves the original I-JEPA architecture while enabling richer patch-level interactions.
Experiments show substantial gains across multiple 3D geometric tasks without sacrificing strong semantic recognition.
Benefits also extend to future feature forecasting and world-model planning.

This unidirectional coupling promotes richer patch-level interactions while largely preserving the original I-JEPA architecture.

papers.abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon
authors: Oleg Pavlov, Nikita Gavrilov, Soslan Kabisov, Gennadii Savrasov, Andrey Kuznetsov, Anton Konushin, Dmitrii Zhemchuzhnikov
bullets: Targets privacy and affordability challenges for practitioners handling proprietary CAD parts.
Decomposes reconstruction into sequential visual decisions about what to build and correct.
Uses geometric tools for precise construction while focusing the agent on visual reasoning.
Runs on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops and integrates with FreeCAD.
The authors report higher reconstruction quality than prior approaches across the main benchmarks, including frontier-model-based systems.

papers.abstract: Triangle Splatting represents scenes using semi-transparent triangles, but it evaluates each triangle at the pixel center and culls any triangle with an inradius smaller than one pixel. The former causes severe aliasing, while the latter culls most of the scene at lower resolutions. We show that the integral of the Triangle Splatting window over a pixel admits an exact closed-form solution. The angle bisectors split the triangle into three sub-triangles, in each of which the window is a power of the distance to one edge. Each piece therefore has a closed-form antiderivative, and Green's theorem reduces the integral and its gradients to one term per side of the sub-triangle clipped against the pixel. The integral over the whole triangle, which we show has a closed form, then allows conservative culling, removing only triangles that cannot meet the renderer's alpha cutoff at any pixel. This exact formulation anti-aliases existing models without retraining, exhibits less temporal aliasing than 2x2 supersampling, and enables multi-scale training, matching or outperforming supersampled training at reduced resolutions.
authors: Brent Zoomers, Joni Vanherck, Leander Winters, Jeroen Put, Lode Jorissen, Nick Michiels
bullets: Addresses severe aliasing and excessive low-resolution culling in Triangle Splatting.
Derives a closed-form pixel integral by decomposing each triangle into edge-distance-based sub-triangles and applying Green’s theorem.
Uses the exact whole-triangle integral for conservative alpha-based culling.
Anti-aliases existing models without retraining and shows less temporal aliasing than 2×2 supersampling.
Supports multi-scale training, matching or outperforming supersampled training at reduced resolutions.

papers.abstract: Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only USD 0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available at https://github.com/yfChang-cv/MAVE.

Reports 27.5–41.1-point overall gains over corresponding vanilla baselines; one configuration reaches 73.2 while reducing reconstruction time by 53%.

papers.abstract: Underwater imaging is a challenging task due to factors such as scattering, absorption, and turbulence, which degrade image quality and limit visibility. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for enhancing underwater images that leverages the benefits of joint learning for simultaneous image enhancement and depth estimation. We introduce Joint-ID, a transformer-based neural network that can obtain high-perceptual image quality and depth information from raw underwater images. Our approach formulates a multi-modal objective function that addresses invalid depth, lack of sharpness, and image degradation based on color and local texture. We design an end-to-end training pipeline that enables joint restoration and depth estimation in a shared hierarchical feature space. Additionally, we propose a synthetic dataset with various distortions and scene depths for multi-task learning. We evaluate Joint-ID on synthetic and standard datasets, as well as real underwater images with diverse spectra and harsh turbidity, demonstrating its effectiveness for underwater image enhancement and depth estimation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability of Joint-ID to perform feature matching and saliency detection for visually guided underwater robots. Our proposed method has the potential to improve the visual perception of underwater environments and benefit applications such as oceanography and underwater robotics. Supplements are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/joint-id/home
authors: Geonmo Yang, Gilhwan Kang, Juhui Lee, Younggun Cho
bullets: Targets underwater degradation from scattering, absorption, turbulence, poor sharpness, and invalid depth.
Uses an end-to-end transformer with a multi-modal objective for simultaneous restoration and depth estimation.
Introduces a synthetic dataset containing varied image distortions and scene depths for multi-task learning.
Evaluated on synthetic, standard, and real underwater imagery with diverse spectra and turbidity.
Also supports feature matching and saliency detection for visually guided underwater robots.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing animatable 3D human avatars from images is important for applications such as gaming and augmented reality. Feedforward methods make avatar reconstruction accessible by reducing inference time to a few seconds, but recent approaches rely heavily on scaling model capacity, training data, and computation. We ask whether such scaling is necessary. To this end, we introduce ARG-Avatar, an efficient feedforward framework with only 68M trainable parameters that achieves SOTA reconstruction quality. Our key insight is that 3D animation and rendering already provide strong geometric correspondences that existing methods largely attempt to learn from data. In light of this, we design the Foreground Avatar Coordinate RoPE attention (FACRoPE) and Intermediate Token Rendering (ITR) pipeline to guide avatar tokens to attend to their corresponding patches. Experiments across multiple datasets show that ARG-Avatar consistently outperforms prior methods when using two or more input images. Compared with LHM++, ARG-Avatar uses approximately 9$\times$ fewer trainable parameters, 4.8$\times$ fewer training sequences, and 14$\times$ less training compute, while running 6$\times$ faster and achieving a 2.7 dB PSNR improvement on the out-of-distribution NeuMan benchmark.
authors: Jianjin Xu, Soham Dasgupta, Fernando De la Torre
bullets: Targets the cost of feedforward avatar reconstruction, which often depends on scaling model capacity, data, and computation.
Introduces FACRoPE attention and an Intermediate Token Rendering pipeline to exploit geometric correspondences from 3D animation and rendering.
Uses 68M trainable parameters while achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction quality.
Outperforms prior methods across multiple datasets with two or more input images.
Compared with LHM++, uses about 9× fewer parameters, 4.8× fewer training sequences, and 14× less compute; it runs 6× faster and improves NeuMan PSNR by 2.7 dB.

papers.abstract: Segmenting small parts on high-resolution 3D scans, such as nails on hand scans and teeth on intraoral scans, poses three challenges: 1) each part covers a tiny fraction of the scan, 2) its boundary is only a subtle change of height and curvature, and 3) it faces its own direction. Existing methods fall into two groups, and both fall short. The first group processes the whole scan at once and sees each part too coarsely. Point and mesh networks must shrink the scan to fit in memory, so a small part keeps only a few of its points. Multi-view methods render images of the whole object, so each part fills only a few pixels and a tilted part is seen from the side. The second group first finds each part and then segments it up close. But these methods find the parts with knowledge about one kind of part, for example the shape of the dental arch for teeth. Such knowledge does not carry over to other kinds of parts. We find that accuracy is limited by how a part is seen, from which direction and at what scale, not by how many points land on it. We therefore present FrameSeg3D. It first predicts a local frame for every part, its center and the direction it faces, from a low-resolution view of the whole scan. It then segments the part in views around its frame normal at the scanner's resolution, so covering the whole scan no longer costs resolution. Because every part arrives centered, facing the camera, and at a fixed scale, one segmentation network can serve different kinds of parts and learn from few labeled masks. We test FrameSeg3D on two kinds of parts, nails and teeth. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods on hand scans (mean Dice 0.970 on nails) and on the Teeth3DS+ test fold (per-tooth IoU 96.5), with the most accurate tooth boundaries (boundary IoU 70.5).
authors: Xinwen Zhang, Tongyan Wang, Huawei Lin
bullets: Small parts are difficult to segment because they occupy few points or pixels, have subtle boundaries, and face different directions.
The method predicts a center and facing direction for each part from a low-resolution whole-scan view.
It then creates normalized, high-resolution views around each local frame for segmentation, avoiding whole-scan resolution loss.
A shared segmentation network can handle different part types and learn from few labeled masks.
On nails and teeth, it reports mean Dice 0.970, per-tooth IoU 96.5, and boundary IoU 70.5.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of FrameSeg3D. (a) Frame prediction. A frame network sees a low-resolution, top-down overview of the whole scan. It predicts a heatmap peaking at each part’s center c𝑘, a normal map that gives the part’s direction z𝑘 there (color), and a name map (not shown). Together they give each part’s local frame (arrows). The circled thumb’s nail is tilted 49◦ from the mat. (b) In-frame segmentation. Twelve cameras within 60◦ of z𝑘 render each part at 0.08mm per pixel, so it is seen centered, facing the camera, and at a fixed scale. A segmentation network segments every view, the masks are lifted back to the vertices, and the frame is re-centered once. Each task trains its own frame network; one segmentation network serves both. All panels but the camera insets are real outputs of FrameSeg3D on test scans.

papers.title: FrameSeg3D: Learned Local Frames for Segmenting Small Parts on High-Resolution 3D Scans
papers.tldr: FrameSeg3D segments tiny parts in high-resolution 3D scans by predicting each part’s local orientation and analyzing it at full scanner resolution.

papers.abstract: Deformation-based 4D Gaussian splatting (4DGS) enables dynamic scene rendering. However, evaluating deformation networks for all Gaussians at every frame is compute-intensive on edge devices. We find that Gaussian trajectories are often locally predictable, yet prediction reliability varies across Gaussians and time. Thus, we propose CueSplat, a post-training framework that exploits local temporal regularity while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen and retaining its Gaussian set. Specifically, CueSplat predicts Gaussian attributes from recent history and uses a lightweight learned router to select exact deformation updates within a scene-specific budget calibrated offline. Selection accounts for prediction reliability and rendering contribution. Selected indices are reused across nearby frames to reduce routing overhead, while selected Gaussians still receive exact updates each frame. To control accumulated prediction error, we use drift signals to schedule three consecutive full-deformation frames that rebuild the prediction history. Evaluated across four mainstream 4DGS algorithms, CueSplat achieves up to $6.74\times$ and $8.15\times$ speedups on Jetson AGX Orin and Orin NX, respectively, with a negligible quality drop (at most $0.16$ dB in dataset-average PSNR).
authors: Qingyuan Tang (Shanghai Jiaotong University), He Zhu (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Shixuan Sun (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Anbang Wu (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Jingwen Leng (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Minyi Guo (Shanghai Jiaotong University), Yu Feng (Shanghai Jiaotong University)
bullets: Addresses the high cost of evaluating deformation networks for every Gaussian at every frame in 4DGS.
Uses a frozen pretrained backbone, local temporal prediction, and a lightweight router to select exact updates within an offline-calibrated scene budget.
Selection considers prediction reliability and rendering contribution; selected Gaussians are reused across nearby frames to reduce routing overhead.
Drift-triggered full-deformation frames periodically rebuild prediction history and limit accumulated error.
Across four 4DGS algorithms, achieves up to 6.74× speedup on Jetson AGX Orin and 8.15× on Orin NX, with at most a 0.16 dB average PSNR drop.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of CUESPLAT. (1) Calibration and training determine the scene budget Ks and router Rθ through oracle and router quality gates. (2) Selective inference predicts all attributes from accepted history, selects and reuses indices, and replaces selected predictions with exact outputs from frozen Dϕ. The merged state is rendered and stored in history. (3) Adaptive refresh uses drift signals to schedule three consecutive full-deformation frames that rebuild history, with partial precomputation after target timestamps are fixed.

Figure 5. Dataset-average throughput on (a) A6000 and (b) Orin NX. Gray bars show the frozen-backbone baselines, and green bars show CUESPLAT. All twelve backbone–dataset pairs benefit, with peak speedups of 5.04× on A6000 and 8.15× on Orin NX.

papers.selection_reason: Sparse deformation scheduling for dynamic Gaussian splatting is relevant to efficient 3D scene generation on edge devices.
papers.title: CueSplat: Learning to Schedule Sparse Deformation for Dynamic Gaussian Splatting on Edge Devices
papers.tldr: CueSplat accelerates dynamic Gaussian splatting on edge devices by selectively applying exact deformations while predicting the rest from temporal history, with minimal rendering-quality loss.

papers.abstract: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) is an important step in accelerating the generation and discovery of new materials. In recent years, diffusion-based CSP methods have made significant progress. However, existing models still suffer from generation bias when facing diverse materials spaces, while systematic approaches for tracing the sources of such performance variations remain limited. To address this issue, we propose LAS (Layered Analysis Strategy), a mechanism analysis framework that identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as two key factors affecting generation difficulty and further reveals their relationships with model generation performance. Building on these findings, we further propose DSADiff (Data Structure-Aware Diffusion), a data structure-aware diffusion model that transforms the key factors identified by LAS into a unified generation difficulty representation and uses it to jointly drive feature modeling and training strategy optimization. This enables the model to adapt its representation and generation capability to samples with different data structures and difficulty levels, thereby mitigating learning bias across samples. Experiments on three CSP benchmark datasets, including Carbon-24, demonstrate that DSADiff consistently improves both Match Rate and RMSE, with a maximum Match Rate improvement of 9%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods and achieving new state-of-the-art performance. This work deepens the understanding of diffusion-based CSP models from the perspective of generation bias and provides a new direction for designing less biased generative models for complex materials spaces.
bullets: LAS identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as key sources of generation difficulty and performance variation.
DSADiff combines these factors into a unified generation-difficulty representation.
The representation guides both feature modeling and training-strategy optimization across samples with different structures and difficulty levels.
Across three CSP benchmarks, including Carbon-24, DSADiff improves Match Rate and RMSE, with up to a 9% Match Rate gain.
The method reports new state-of-the-art performance and offers a framework for analyzing and reducing bias in complex materials spaces.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting enables object-level operations on Gaussian primitives, yet existing segmentation methods are largely trained and evaluated through rendered views. This mismatch can produce accurate rendered masks from incomplete 3D selections since alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates learning on dominant contributors while leaving occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised. We propose VODA, a plug-and-play supervision objective that exploits local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervises all Gaussians in selected depth clusters, bypassing contribution-weighted gradient delivery. To evaluate volumetric completeness, we introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and the Removal Depth Error (RDE), a metric comparing predicted and ground-truth depth changes. Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA consistently improves volumetric segmentation on Removal-3D while maintaining or improving performance on LERF and ScanNet. Further analysis shows that VODA recovers lower-contribution Gaussians, while simple gradient reweighting and spatial propagation fail to reproduce comparable gains.
bullets: Rendered mask supervision can leave occluded or low-contribution Gaussians poorly learned despite accurate 2D masks.
VODA uses local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervise every Gaussian in selected depth clusters.
The authors introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and Removal Depth Error (RDE) to measure volumetric completeness.
Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA improves Removal-3D segmentation while maintaining or improving LERF and ScanNet performance.
Analysis indicates that VODA recovers low-contribution Gaussians more effectively than gradient reweighting or spatial propagation.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of VODA. The depth-aware rasterizer groups per-pixel contributors using adjacent depth gaps and selects the cluster with the largest total rendering contribution. Alphaweighted pixel features are aggregated into detached Gaussian-level targets. A direct feature loss supervises every Gaussian in the selected cluster, including low-contribution Gaussians, without contribution-weighted gradient delivery. The baseline feature-rendering loss remains active.
Figure 6: Qualitative removal on Removal-3D. Each scene is rendered after removing the queried Gaussians. VODA leaves less residual target content and better reveals the surface behind the object.

Figure 2: Comparison of supervision and association strategies for per-pixel Gaussian contributors. (a) Rendering-based feature learning delivers contribution-weighted gradients, giving weak supervision to low-contribution Gaussians. (b) Direct association links each pixel to a sparse subset of contributors selected by contribution-based rules. (c) VODA directly supervises every Gaussian in the selected depth cluster, including low-contribution Gaussians associated with the same object.

Figure 1: A plausible rendered mask does not imply complete 3D selection. For the query “sheep,” (a) the selected Gaussians render a plausible object mask, but (b) the depth change after removing the same Gaussian set indicates incomplete object removal in the reconstructed scene. papers.abstract: Event cameras keep capturing structure where conventional cameras blur or saturate, which makes them attractive for 3D perception in fast or poorly lit scenes. Event datasets with dense 3D ground truth, however, are far smaller and less diverse than the image collections behind feed-forward 3D reconstruction models. We present Déjà-Events, an event-only model that predicts depth, camera pose and pointmaps from multiple views in a single forward pass. Rather than relying on scarce 3D labels, we distil it from Déjà View, a feed-forward RGB model that refines its tokens by repeatedly applying one shared transformer block. On paired RGB and event recordings, the event student learns to reproduce the frozen teacher's final tokens, which requires no depth or pose ground truth and trains only about 1% of its parameters. Because events are dense at edges and moving texture but nearly absent in textureless regions, we further introduce sparsity-aware adaptive gating, which adapts the shared block's gates to events and adjusts them per patch by event density, so that accuracy holds as refinement steps are added. Trained only on simulated data, Déjà-Events achieves the lowest pointmap error among the event-based methods we evaluate, on EventScape and zero-shot on the real MVSEC and DSEC datasets. On DSEC it halves the error of the strongest baseline (0.15 vs. 0.30 AbsRel) with about a tenth of its parameters. It also has the lowest depth error on EventScape and DSEC and the lowest trajectory error on EventScape.
bullets: Uses paired RGB–event recordings to match a frozen RGB teacher’s final tokens, avoiding depth and pose ground truth while training only about 1% of parameters.
Introduces sparsity-aware adaptive gating to adjust shared transformer refinement per patch according to event density.
Trained only on simulated data, it generalizes zero-shot to real MVSEC and DSEC data.
Reports the lowest pointmap error among evaluated event-based methods; on DSEC, it achieves 0.15 AbsRel versus 0.30 for the strongest baseline with about one-tenth the parameters.
Also obtains the lowest depth error on EventScape and DSEC, and the lowest trajectory error on EventScape.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview. A frozen RGB DVLT teacher (top) and an event student with the same architecture (bottom) process aligned RGB frames and events. In each training iteration both run the shared block for the same sampled number of steps K, and the loss matches their final tokens (Sec. III-B). The student trains low-rank adapters in DINOv2 and in the shared block, and its gates are unfrozen and corrected per patch in both attention blocks (Sec. III-C).

Fig. 3. Sparsity-aware adaptive gating in one attention block, applied in both frame and global attention. The step gate (centre) scales the attention update, the MLP update and the output token, and is fine-tuned for events. A patchwise correction (dashed), a small MLP over the event density σ and the interval embedding, rescales the attention and MLP gates of each patch.

papers.abstract: Inverse rendering decomposes an image into intrinsic properties such as appearance, illumination, geometry, and material, yet these properties are inherently interdependent. A reliable decomposition should produce intrinsic maps that are not only individually plausible, but also mutually compatible in explaining the image. However, existing methods either model intrinsic channels in isolation or treat inverse and forward rendering as separate processes, leaving the interdependence underexploited. In this paper, we introduce IntrinSync, a unified framework that captures this interdependence through joint-channel modeling and reciprocal inverse-forward rendering. At the channel level, we jointly decompose an input RGB into albedo, shading, surface normal, roughness, and metallic maps through a 1-to-N mapping, enabling information exchange across channels throughout generation. At the process level, we establish inverse-forward reciprocity through a dual cycle-consistent objective that aligns corresponding predictions across a closed loop. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate that our method achieves competitive intrinsic estimation and forward rendering performance, improving coherence and physical consistency. Beyond decomposition, IntrinSync provides a physically grounded interface for image editing, allowing intrinsic properties to be explicitly manipulated and rendered back into RGB images.
bullets: Addresses the incompatibility that can arise when intrinsic properties are estimated independently.
Jointly maps RGB images to albedo, shading, surface normals, roughness, and metallic maps, enabling cross-channel information exchange.
Uses a dual cycle-consistent objective to align inverse decomposition with forward rendering.
Experiments on three datasets show competitive intrinsic estimation and rendering performance with improved coherence and physical consistency.
Supports image editing by allowing intrinsic properties to be manipulated and rendered back into RGB.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of joint-channel intrinsic decomposition with reciprocal rendering. For inverse rendering, the input RGB image conditions a joint 1-to-N denoising process that predicts multiple intrinsic channels simultaneously. For forward rendering, the predicted intrinsic channels jointly condition an N-to-1 process to synthesize the corresponding RGB image.

Figure 5: Qualitative Comparison of inverse rendering. We visualize qualitative comparison with baseline methods on Hypersim (Roberts et al., 2021), InteriorVerse (Zhu et al., 2022), and MatrixCity (Li et al., 2023). Each row shows an input image and decomposed intrinsic channels from different methods. More results are shown in the appendix.
Figure 8: Intrinsic-guided image editing. Our framework enables controllable image editing by either directly manipulating intrinsic channels or using text prompts to modify selected properties.

Figure 10: Qualitative comparison of albedo estimation on synthetic images. We show additional results across diverse synthetic scenes, comparing the predicted albedo maps of our method with existing approaches and the corresponding ground truth.
Figure 9: Qualitative comparison of normal estimation on synthetic images.

Figure 6: Ablation on joint-channel decomposition. Compared with 1-to-1 decomposition, joint decomposition produces cleaner, more coherent intrinsic maps and consistently achieves lower training loss, demonstrating the benefit of cross-channel interaction.

Figure 4: Dual cycle-consistent training. We couple decomposition and rendering through two reciprocal paths. The vanilla cycle constrains only endpoint reconstruction, whereas our dual cycle aligns corresponding predictions across the two paths, enforcing process-level reciprocity. Direct supervision is applied to available intrinsic channels for heterogeneous training data.
Figure 7: Ablation on cycle consistency. Compared with the vanilla cycle, our dual cycle better preserves the semantic roles of intrinsic channels while maintaining faithful RGB reconstruction.

Figure 17: Results of Inverse and forward rendering on real images. We evaluate our method on diverse real-world scenes, demonstrating its ability to jointly estimate clean and physically consistent intrinsic channels and rendering the input RGB images.

Figure 2: Joint intrinsic decomposition. Traditional approaches predict intrinsic channels independently, leading to physically inconsistent estimations such as appearance leaking between intrinsic channels. Our joint 1-to-N decomposition allows information to be exchanged across channels, encouraging mutually coherent intrinsic maps that better explain the observed RGB image.

papers.abstract: Procrustes-Wasserstein alignment jointly estimates a matching and rotation without supplied correspondences, but alternating minimization can stop at suboptimal solutions. Rubix solves the equally weighted planar problem globally under squared Euclidean loss. Each matching $σ$ of two centered $n$-point sets defines a complex correlation $z_σ=\sum_i\bar x_i y_{σ(i)}$. Their convex hull is the permutation polygon: supporting vertices give optimal matchings at fixed rotations, and the farthest vertex gives the global alignment. We prove the sharp bound of $n(n-1)$ vertices for $n\ge2$, answering Rote's rotation-assignment open problem. In exact arithmetic, assignment queries recover the polygon in $\mathcal O(n^5)$ operations. Assignment-based bounds extend the approach to three-dimensional rotations and partial matching at a supplied translation through branch-and-bound. On timed MPEG-7 shape pairs, Rubix attains every numerical reference value in 12 ms on average, 50 times faster than a rotation grid at the same accuracy. Its distances improve gravity-aligned matching of real 3D scans, shape retrieval and noisy crystal classification over alternating minimization.
bullets: Addresses suboptimal solutions from alternating minimization in Procrustes-Wasserstein alignment.
Represents each matching as a complex correlation; polygon supporting vertices encode optimal matchings for rotations, while the farthest vertex yields the global alignment.
Proves a sharp upper bound of n(n−1) polygon vertices and resolves Rote’s rotation-assignment open problem.
Recovers the polygon via assignment queries in O(n⁵) exact-arithmetic operations; extensions cover 3D rotations and partial matching with supplied translation.

On timed MPEG-7 pairs, reaches all numerical reference values in 12 ms on average—50× faster than an equally accurate rotation grid—and improves several downstream matching tasks over alternating minimization.
