papers.title: Rubix: Global Correspondence-Free Point Set Alignment through Assignment Geometry
papers.tldr: Rubix globally solves correspondence-free planar point-set alignment by converting matching-and-rotation search into geometry of a permutation polygon.

papers.abstract: Hybrid solid-state LiDAR sensors are making their way into production vehicles, yet the data they produce differs structurally from that of the established spinning mechanical sensors behind today's autonomous-driving datasets: it is ring-free, dense, cluttered, and concentrated in a frontal field of view. The classical geometric methods that autonomous vehicles rely on for drivable space computation and navigation assume the ordered ring-and-column structure of a 360-degree spinning LiDAR and degrade or fail on this data, while learned alternatives are computationally heavy, hard to certify, and trained almost exclusively on spinning-LiDAR data. We demonstrate that the same dense, per-curve geometry is instead an opportunity to close the divide between the industry's preferred sensors and autonomous-driving research. We present GHySSeg, a purely geometric method that segments ground and drivable road from a single hybrid solid-state LiDAR frame by tracing each scan curve and reading two geometric signatures, a step in height and a fold-back in range, with no training and no graphics processing unit. To evaluate it, we release HySoLiD-Drive, the first public benchmark dedicated to ground and road segmentation on an automotive hybrid solid-state LiDAR, comprising 100 manually labeled and 7000 unlabeled frames recorded by two vehicles in real driving. On this benchmark, GHySSeg surpasses both geometric and learned state-of-the-art baselines across ground and road segmentation, reaching an intersection-over-union of 0.907 for road and 0.896 for ground at over 0.96 precision, while running in real time at about 22 milliseconds per frame on a single core.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between ring-free, front-facing hybrid solid-state LiDAR and methods designed for spinning 360° LiDAR.
Traces each scan curve and detects two geometric cues: height steps and range fold-backs.
Introduces HySoLiD-Drive, a benchmark with 100 labeled and 7,000 unlabeled real-driving frames from two vehicles.
Reports 0.907 road IoU and 0.896 ground IoU, with over 0.96 precision and roughly 22 ms per frame on one CPU core.

papers.abstract: Human manipulation data are widely used to train robots for human-like dexterity. However, low-cost, large-scale collection in the wild remains challenging. Existing methods remain limited in geometrically grounded metric-scale reconstruction, real-world generalization and inference speed. We present WinDEX, integrating (1) geometric-temporal optimization for metric 3D hand annotation from in-the-wild egocentric stereo videos, combined with visual-inertial SLAM for world-frame reconstruction; (2) WinDEX-Net, an end-to-end, fisheye-native network combining calibrated stereo, local detail and temporal context, with a data-model flywheel of model-assisted annotation and retraining; (3) distilled models for offline reconstruction and causal streaming, supporting reinforcement learning and teleoperation; and (4) low-cost CyberCap stereo-inertial capture, forming the WinDEX-Hand dataset with 1,000 hours of training annotations and held-out human-annotated in-the-wild 2D and independent optical motion-capture evaluation sets. Offline reconstruction runs at 43.61 FPS and causal streaming at 171 FPS. On held-out data, offline reconstruction achieves state-of-the-art accuracy: 14.5 pixels in-the-wild reprojection error and, with visual-inertial odometry, 37.29 mm world-frame joint error. We achieve 7.6 and 3.6 times the task success rates of reinforcement learning policies trained with WiLoR and HaWoR motion references, respectively, and demonstrate real-time arm-hand teleoperation. Project website: https://fruitrabbit.github.io/WinDEX/.
authors: Hongyu Ma, Hairong Qu, Shiqi Zhao, Yongsong Yang, Kai Shi, Jiahao Ai, Xin You, Peng Yin
bullets: Addresses the challenge of collecting large-scale, geometrically grounded human manipulation data in unconstrained environments.
Combines geometric-temporal optimization and visual-inertial SLAM with WinDEX-Net, a fisheye-native stereo network using local detail and temporal context.
Provides distilled offline and causal-streaming models, plus a low-cost CyberCap capture system and the WinDEX-Hand dataset.
Achieves 43.61 FPS offline and 171 FPS streaming; reports 14.5-pixel reprojection error and 37.29 mm world-frame joint error on held-out evaluations.
Motion references improve reinforcement-learning task success by 7.6× over WiLoR and 3.6× over HaWoR, with demonstrated real-time arm-hand teleoperation.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 4D driving-scene reconstruction enables efficient modeling of dynamic autonomous-driving scenes, but current methods suffer from two complementary failure modes: semantic leakage of traffic participants into the static representation and geometric drift of Gaussian locations across viewpoints. We propose \textbf{IGRecon4D}, a feed-forward dynamic scene reconstruction framework that addresses these failures with training-time instance-prior distillation and LiDAR-anchored Gaussian positioning. Specifically, an instance-level semantic branch provides a potentially dynamic participant prior, which is distilled into dynamic-mask learning through the Instance-Dynamic Consistency Constraint to encourage high-recall localization of traffic-participant regions prone to dynamic-static leakage. In parallel, sparse LiDAR measurements guide dense depth estimation, and the resulting depths are back-projected to anchor Gaussian positions for improved multi-view geometric consistency. Experiments on the Waymo Open Dataset and zero-shot evaluation on nuScenes demonstrate improved full-image reconstruction on the main benchmark and stronger traffic-participant-region reconstruction under cross-dataset evaluation.
authors: Yifei Tong, Ziyang Huang, Yizhao Han, Xiaoxiao Long, Hao Zhu
bullets: Targets semantic leakage of traffic participants into static representations and viewpoint-dependent Gaussian drift.
Distills instance-level semantic priors into dynamic-mask learning using an Instance-Dynamic Consistency Constraint.
Uses sparse LiDAR to guide dense depth estimation and anchor Gaussian positions for better multi-view consistency.
Improves full-image reconstruction on Waymo Open Dataset and traffic-participant reconstruction in zero-shot nuScenes evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of IGRecon4D. Given multi-camera videos, camera parameters, and sparse LiDAR depth maps, IGRecon4D predicts Gaussian attributes, LiDAR-anchored Gaussian positions, dynamic masks, and instance-level semantic masks. The instance-level semantic branch supplies a potentially dynamic participant prior for dynamic-mask supervision, while the dynamic masks decompose the scene into static and dynamic Gaussians for rendering.

Figure 2: Dynamic-static Gaussian rendering. Dense depth maps are back-projected with camera parameters to obtain Gaussian positions. The predicted dynamic masks allocate traffic-participant regions with high potentially dynamic prior to per-frame Gaussians and the remaining regions to the global static Gaussian set, while sky Gaussians model low-opacity sky regions. All Gaussian components are jointly rendered with a differentiable rasterizer.

Figure 8: Qualitative comparison with additional methods on the Waymo Open Dataset. IGRecon4D better preserves traffic participants and static background details than feed-forward baselines, with fewer participant-region omissions and sharper object boundaries.

Figure 7: Instance-level semantic predictions. The instance-level semantic branch is evaluated as a source of a potentially dynamic participant prior for IDC rather than as a standalone segmentation model; the predicted masks provide usable instance-level supervision for dynamic-mask learning.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on the Waymo Open Dataset. IGRecon4D better preserves traffic participants and static background details than feed-forward baselines, with fewer participant-region omissions and sharper object boundaries.

Figure 4: Novel-view synthesis from interpolated camera poses. We render from interpolated viewpoints between Camera 0 and Camera 1, and between Camera 0 and Camera 2, and compare IGRecon4D with DGGT [19] under identical camera poses. cam0_1 and cam0_2 denote the interpolated viewpoints between Camera 0 and Camera 1, and between Camera 0 and Camera 2, respectively. IGRecon4D produces fewer geometric shifts and stronger multi-view consistency.

Figure 5: Qualitative ablation study. Replacing IDC-supervised dynamic-mask learning with a DGGT-initialized dynamic head reduces high-recall localization of traffic-participant regions, while replacing LiDAR-guided depth estimation with DPT-style depth prediction introduces geometric misalignment and degrades rendering quality.
Figure 9: Additional qualitative ablation results. The examples compare IGRecon4D with RGB-only input, removal of sky Gaussians, and direct use of SAM3 masks.
Figure 6: Qualitative zero-shot reconstruction on nuScenes. Without fine-tuning on nuScenes, IGRecon4D preserves traffic participants more reliably than feed-forward baselines.

Figure 10: Qualitative comparison of temporal interpolation results. Ground truth (GT), IGRecon4D, and DGGT are shown from left to right. Red boxes highlight regions where DGGT produces visible artifacts on traffic participants.
Figure 11: Qualitative evaluation of predicted dynamic masks. RGB images, SAM3-generated pseudo ground-truth masks, our predictions, and DGGT predictions are shown from left to right.
Figure 12: Failure case in a nighttime scene. Ground truth (GT) and our reconstruction are shown side by side. The red box highlights a visible reconstruction artifact.

papers.abstract: Recovering 3D pose and shape of birds from single images is bottlenecked by the long tail of avian diversity: out of ~10,000 species, only a few dozen have 3D-labeled training data, and in-the-wild test sets routinely contain species never seen at training. Generalizing across clades is therefore a central problem. The current state of the art, AniMer+, mitigates it with a family-level contrastive loss that conveys only a binary same-family indicator per pair and discards the continuous structure of the species tree. We propose a taxonomic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck prior on the shape code of the AVES parametric bird mesh model: a multivariate Gaussian whose covariance decays exponentially with Linnaean rank distance, with a learnable selection strength and noise scale. The prior generalizes family contrastive into a continuous, generative form, exposing the graded cross- and within-family similarity that a binary indicator cannot, and brings continuous comparative phylogenetics in as a biology-grounded inductive bias for the long tail. Our method improves over AniMer+ on both metrics of the unseen-species CowBird benchmark and on CtrlAVES3D, while remaining comparable on seen-species CUB. A permutation ablation isolates taxonomic structure from generic Gaussian smoothing, and a rank-granularity ablation identifies cross-order distinctions (the structure beyond a family-vs-not indicator) as the dominant source of the unseen-species gain.
authors: Yunchan Jeon, SooGon Kim, Seungwook Kim, CheolWon Lee, Jongmin Lee
bullets: Addresses poor cross-species generalization caused by limited 3D-labeled bird data and long-tail diversity.
Replaces AniMer+’s binary same-family contrastive signal with a continuous, generative prior based on Linnaean rank distances.
Applies the prior to the shape code of the AVES parametric bird mesh model, with learnable selection strength and noise scale.
Outperforms AniMer+ on both metrics for unseen-species CowBird and on CtrlAVES3D, while remaining comparable on seen-species CUB.
Ablations attribute the unseen-species gain mainly to taxonomic structure, especially distinctions across orders beyond family-level labels.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method at a glance. (a) The AniMer+ [1] encoder produces AVES [12] shape codes β from a single image. (b) Across species, β is regularized by an OU [10] prior parameterized by learnable (α, σ,µ) over a fixed Linnaean [2] rank distance matrix; the NLL of this Gaussian is LOU. (c) LOU replaces the family-level contrastive term of AniMer+ (wcon=0), so that on birds Ltotal = LAVES + λOULOU. Blue: the existing network and fixed taxonomy. Orange: what we add.

Figure 4: The prior tightens the shape codes without distorting phylogenetic signal. (a, b) What tightens: k-NN family purity rises and the spread of the per-species mean β falls with λOU on CtrlAVES3D [29] training codes; the 10−4 bars are a single constant-LR run. (c) What is preserved: the β distance between the mean shape codes of two species measures how different the model predicts their shapes to be. All 136 species pairs, sorted along the x-axis by this distance without the prior (gray), move closer at λOU=10−5 (orange, seed 0) but stay in nearly the same order.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison on two CUB [32] test images (top) and two CowBird [6] test instances (bottom). For each species, the first panel shows the input with the ground-truth keypoints (green dots) and a red circle on the baseline’s worst keypoint; the retrained AniMer+ baseline (red crosses) and the OU fine-tune (blue crosses) follow, and gray lines join each prediction to its ground-truth keypoint. The badge is the per-image PCK@0.1.

Figure 1: Beyond family labels. The 17 training species of CtrlAVES3D on the Linnaean tree [2], colored by order. The height at which two lineages join marks their lowest shared rank, from same family up to outgroup; each rank sets the distance dtax that our prior reads (Figure 2b). The familysupervised contrastive loss of AniMer+ [1] keeps a single bit of this tree: whether a pair joins below the dashed red line. Our Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) prior uses every rank, pulling the shape codes of two species together more strongly the more closely they are related, so the shape space carries graded structure rather than a same-family indicator.

Figure 3: Real vs. permuted taxonomy ablation. CowBird [6] AUC and PCK@0.1 under three configurations: (a) the AniMer+ [1] baseline, (b) the OU prior with a label-permuted distance matrix, and (c) the OU prior with the real Linnaean [2] distance matrix (both OU runs at λOU = 10−4, constant learning rate; Section 4.1).

Table 1: Comparison against AniMer+ [1] on the avian benchmarks. CUB [32] and the CtrlAVES3D [29] test split evaluate seen-species; CowBird [6] is the unseen-species out-ofdistribution (OOD) benchmark. For ours we report the mean ± sample standard deviation over five random seeds. AniMer-A [20] is the avian-only variant; AniMer+ and ours are unified bird+mammal models; AVES and HMR2.0 are the baselines reported by AniMer+.

Table 3: Procrustes-aligned 3D errors on the CtrlAVES3D test split (309 images, 17 species). pa-MPJPE denotes the mean per-joint position error; pa-MPVPE denotes mean per-vertex position error. Lower is better. Ours is a single run (seed 0). Values follow our canonical-frame scaling; see Appendix S6 for details.

Table 2: Rank-granularity ablation: progressively richer distance matrices on the same operating point as Figure 3. The family-only kernel uses values in {0, 1, 5} (same family vs. not), the order-only refinement uses {0, 1, 2, 5} (adds the same-order distinction), and the full Linnaean kernel uses {0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6} (cross-order ordinals as the default). All three kernels use 0 for the same species and 1 for the same family, and differ only above the family level; genus-level structure cannot be varied on this training set, because the 17 species contain no congeneric pair. We use 5 rather than 6 as the cross-order placeholder for the family-only and order-only kernels so that they share a single cross-order bin, isolating the rank-granularity axis from changes in cross-order distance scale.

papers.title: Beyond Family Labels: A Taxonomic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Prior for Avian 3D Shape Recovery
papers.tldr: A taxonomic Ornstein–Uhlenbeck prior improves single-image 3D bird shape recovery for species unseen during training by modeling graded phylogenetic similarity.

papers.abstract: Egocentric hand motion provides physical motion supervision for dexterous manipulation and vision-language-action pretraining. Reliable use of this supervision requires accurate and temporally coherent 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space. Existing methods typically lift framewise estimates produced under weak perspective into world coordinates. By ignoring joint-dependent depth variation at close range, this approximation couples errors in translation, orientation, and articulation that persist after world lifting and worsen under occlusion. We present MetricHand, a geometry-aware flow matching framework for 4D hand reconstruction in metric world space. MetricHand encodes depth priors from hand-object interaction regions into joint-associated representations that preserve local spatial structure and metric scale. Fused with visual features, this geometry guides coarse metric estimation and conditions every step of temporal generation. The model jointly recovers world-space translation, global orientation, MANO articulation, and shape, while structural priors and temporal context support estimation under partial occlusion. MetricHand reduces camera-space MPJPE by 49.3% and 52.9%, absolute world-space MPJPE by 28.7% and 21.7%, and wrist localization error by 48.5% and 37.9% relative to HaWoR, respectively. World-space acceleration error decreases by 44.2% and 64.3%, demonstrating improved temporal fidelity alongside more accurate absolute localization.
authors: Yibo Bai, Likui Zhang, Jinglei Zhang, Zhengbin Pang, Xingshen Song, Xiaoqing Yin, Jinsheng Deng
bullets: Addresses errors caused by lifting framewise, weak-perspective hand estimates into world coordinates, especially at close range and during occlusion.
Encodes depth priors from hand–object interaction regions into joint-associated representations that preserve local geometry and metric scale.
Fuses geometric and visual features for coarse metric estimation and conditions each step of temporal generation.
Jointly predicts world-space translation, global orientation, MANO articulation, and hand shape.
Reports substantial reductions in camera-space and world-space MPJPE, wrist error, and acceleration error relative to HaWoR.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of MetricHand. Depth priors supply metric placement cues and local hand– object surface geometry. RGB–D fusion supports coarse hand estimation, while topology-aware sampling associates multi-scale evidence with projected joint anchors. Observation quality and a spatiotemporal memory queue preserve reliable joint-associated context across windows. The resulting conditions are supplied to every flow-matching step to jointly recover world-space wrist translation, global orientation, articulation, and shape. Camera motion defines the metric world reference.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of world-space hand trajectories on HOT3D and ARCTIC. Input frames run from top to bottom within each row. Green meshes show ground truth; pink, purple, orange, and blue show WiLoR-SLAM, Dyn-HaMR, HaWoR, and MetricHand, respectively. Closer overlap with the green GT meshes indicates higher hand-pose accuracy along the displayed world-space trajectories.

Table 3: Component and geometry-conditioning ablations on HOT3D and ARCTIC. Position errors are in mm and world acceleration error in m/s2 (↓). Controls follow Sec. 4.3; Table 2 compares depth representations.
Table 2: Depth representation ablation on ARCTIC. The first four controls share a metric regression head. Position errors are in mm (↓).

papers.title: MetricHand: Geometry-Aware Flow Matching for 4D Hand Reconstruction in Metric World Space
papers.tldr: MetricHand uses geometry-aware flow matching to reconstruct temporally coherent 4D hand motion directly in metric world space, improving localization and motion fidelity under occlusion.

papers.abstract: Even in multi-camera setups, occlusions can leave individual body joints with only a single usable 2D observation. Such an observation defines a viewing ray but leaves the joint's depth undetermined. We introduce Body of Evidence (BoE), a multi-view 3D human pose estimator that predicts per-camera joint depths alongside 2D joint locations. To reduce monocular depth ambiguity, we propose geometry-conditioned depth prediction, which combines image features with previously reconstructed 3D body geometry as contextual depth cues. We further introduce learnable depth-aware triangulation (LDAT), which augments differentiable algebraic triangulation with predicted depth constraints, enabling reconstruction even from a single contributing camera while preserving the benefits of geometric triangulation when multiple views are available. The reconstructed 3D poses subsequently guide depth prediction in the next iteration, allowing depth estimates and 3D geometry to progressively refine each other. Experiments on CMU Panoptic demonstrate state-of-the-art in-domain performance and superior average performance across evaluated camera subsets and unseen camera arrangements. BoE is particularly effective under sparse camera coverage, outperforming the previous state of the art by 10.6 AP25 points in the challenging three-camera setting.
authors: Erik Brorsson, Kilian Freitag, Josef Bengtson, Kristofer Bengtsson, Lars Hammarstrand, Knut {\AA}kesson, Fredrik Kahl
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity of joints observed by only one camera, where 2D observations provide a viewing ray but not depth.
Predicts per-camera joint depths using image features and previously reconstructed 3D body geometry.
Uses learnable depth-aware triangulation to combine predicted depth constraints with geometric triangulation, including single-view reconstruction.
Iteratively refines depth estimates and 3D pose geometry using each to guide the other.
On CMU Panoptic, achieves state-of-the-art in-domain results and improves prior state of the art by 10.6 AP25 points with three cameras.

figures.caption: Figure 2. BoE decoder architecture and geometry-conditioned depth estimation. (a) Each decoder layer extracts image evidence through projective attention and predicts per-view 2D joint locations, confidences, depths, and depth gates. Learnable depth-aware triangulation (LDAT) fuses these measurements to update the 3D poses, while separate branches update appearance features and predict pose scores. (b) Target-depth masking (TDM) constructs a separate joint sequence for each target joint, excluding only its own reference-depth embedding while retaining its image feature. (c) Pose-context modeling (PCM) processes the masked sequences using a shared encoder and selects the contextualized feature of each target joint for depth prediction.

Figure 1. Overview of BoE. Starting from initial 3D pose queries, the decoder projects joints into calibrated camera views to extract image evidence. Each view provides 2D joint and geometryconditioned depth predictions, which are combined through LDAT to update the 3D poses. The updated poses serve as references for subsequent decoder layers, enabling iterative refinement.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of BoE and MVGFormer [19] on CMU3. RGB images with predicted 2D poses and projected ground-truth poses are shown on the left, and reconstructed 3D poses on the right. Ground truth is shown in red, while predictions are shown in other colors. BoE more accurately reconstructs heavily occluded joints, including the right hand and foot of the orange pose, the feet of the turquoise pose, and the left leg of the blue pose (colors refer to the top-row predictions).

Ground truth is shown in red, while predictions are shown in other colors. Both methods produce similar 3D reconstructions in this example.

The latter is obtained by removing the depth constraints from LDAT while keeping the predicted 2D observations fixed. Rows correspond to decoder layers, and columns group joints by the number of contributing cameras, defined by the views used for triangulation rather than ground-truth visibility.

papers.abstract: The blind perspective-$n$-point (PnP) problem is to estimate the pose of a calibrated camera from 2D and 3D point sets with unknown correspondences. We show that, for complete, noiseless observations, fourteen permutation-invariant image moments up to order four identify a fixed camera pose for almost every 3D point set containing at least twenty points. Our learning-free method, MomentPnP, matches these moments between the observed 2D points and the projected 3D points to initialize a camera pose without correspondences and refines the pose and correspondence weights using expectation--maximization. Across the test sets of three benchmarks, our method reduces median rotation error by $5$--$170\times$ relative to the best learned baseline, both with and without outliers. We recover accurate poses even with as many outliers as inliers. On dense ETH3D scans, pose accuracy improves as the point sets grow, even as individual correspondences become harder to resolve.
authors: Subhransu S. Bhattacharjee, Dylan Campbell, Rahul Shome
bullets: Addresses the blind PnP problem for calibrated cameras with unknown correspondences.
Fourteen image moments up to order four identify the pose for almost every noiseless 3D point set with at least 20 points.
Uses a learning-free moment-matching initialization, followed by joint pose and correspondence-weight refinement.
Across three benchmarks, reduces median rotation error by 5–170× versus the best learned baseline, with and without outliers.
Remains accurate with as many outliers as inliers; on dense ETH3D scans, accuracy improves with larger point sets.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of MomentPnP. (a) Cameras are searched over centers and orientations, and observed features averaged once. (b) Moment matching refines the best cameras, raising the cutoff from 4 to 20. (c) EM refines fits with soft correspondences. (d) The alignment check accepts poses whose observations lie much closer to their nearest projections than to the next, and the most likely accepted pose or alternative is returned. Orange: observations. Blue: model points and projections. Gray: unmatched points, unselected poses.

Figure 4. Qualitative results on real-world scenes. Columns are images, titled by scene and number of observations, and rows are methods. Orange points are observations, and blue crosses are projections under the recovered pose. Below each panel is its rotation error, in bold where lowest in the column, and a green border marks an error below 1◦. Model points come from the released structure-from-motion reconstructions of Cambridge Landmarks [40], Phototourism [37], 7-Scenes [62] and ETH3D [65], and from LiDAR for Data61 [56].

Figure 9. Independently selected inputs. (a) Facade 26, recovered from SIFT detections and a model built from other photographs. The camera is orange, with pink rays to matched model points. (b) Meadow, where only the pink diamonds belong to reconstruction tracks. (c) Facade laser scan, where pink diamonds lie within 3.4 pixels of blue projections.

Figure 5. Rotation-error distribution without outliers. Each curve gives the percentage of frames below each rotation error, averaged with equal weight over the MegaDepth, ModelNet40 and Data61 test sets. The vertical line marks 1◦.

papers.abstract: Image-to-3D foundation models have improved 3D reconstruction, but typically produce monolithic representations without explicit part-level structure. Part-aware generation and learning-based assembly methods often require part-level supervision, category-specific priors, or paired part-layout training data. We instead consider a practical but underexplored setting in which independently prepared or generated 3D parts have no predefined inter-part relationships, shared coordinate frames, or consistent scales, and must be assembled into a reference-consistent object from a single image. We present VA-Assembly, a training-free framework for 3D part assembly through part-level transformation estimation using view-aligned diffusion guidance. Given a reference image and fixed 3D part geometries, VA-Assembly optimizes each part's translation, rotation, and scale. We condition a frozen view-conditioned diffusion model on same-view renderings of a reference-derived monolithic 3D representation, producing score gradients geometrically aligned with the part configuration. This guidance provides multi-view structural cues under large initial misalignment. By repurposing pretrained visual-structural priors as transformation-level supervision, VA-Assembly requires no annotated part layouts, predefined part taxonomies, category-specific assembly training, or bounding-box-based layout initialization. Experiments compare VA-Assembly with geometric registration and compositional layout baselines using each baseline's supported transformation components, showing improved part-wise transformation estimation. Ablation studies show that view-aligned conditioning, rather than diffusion guidance alone, is critical for reliable transformation gradients. Updating only part transformations preserves explicit component separability and supports component-level editing, replacement, and reconfiguration.
authors: Yeon-Jae Kim, Sangwon Kang, Byung-Kwon Min
bullets: Addresses assembly when parts lack shared coordinate frames, consistent scales, and predefined inter-part relationships.
Optimizes each part’s translation, rotation, and scale using a frozen view-conditioned diffusion model.
Uses same-view renderings of a reference-derived monolithic representation to provide structurally aligned transformation gradients.
Requires no part-layout annotations, category-specific priors, assembly training, or bounding-box initialization.
Outperforms supported geometric-registration and compositional-layout baselines in part-wise transformation estimation; ablations identify view-aligned conditioning as critical.

papers.abstract: Trajectory rendering, which renders novel views of a reconstructed 3D scene along a camera path, is a core operation in digital twins and autonomous inspection. Structured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders a single view in real time by decoding sparse anchors into Gaussians on demand, but it renders a trajectory view by view: every view projects all anchors to select them, re-decodes anchors already requested by neighboring views, and runs all steps on the GPU while the CPU idles. We treat this as a spatial data management problem, where anchors are spatial objects, views are range queries, and decoded Gaussians are shared derived data, and propose GDM-GS, which removes redundancy at three levels. Within a view, an anchor index and an occluder index answer each view as a holed-frustum range query, so out-of-view and provably hidden anchors are never decoded. Across views, shared materialization decodes each requested anchor once per group of consecutive views while preserving each view's selection. Across processors, a hybrid pipeline balances selections between the CPU and the GPU before grouped decoding under bounded memory. Experiments on large-scale public scenes show that GDM-GS substantially reduces trajectory rendering latency while preserving image quality.
authors: Haolun Ma, Ziyi Liu, Zizhuo Xu, Chuhan Hu, Lei Li
bullets: Frames trajectory rendering as spatial data management: anchors are spatial objects, views are range queries, and decoded Gaussians are shared data.
Uses anchor and occluder indexes to query holed frustums, avoiding decoding anchors that are out of view or provably occluded.
Shares decoded Gaussians across consecutive views, decoding each requested anchor once per view group while preserving per-view selection.
Employs a hybrid CPU–GPU pipeline to balance selection and grouped decoding under bounded memory.
Experiments on large-scale public scenes report substantially lower trajectory-rendering latency with preserved image quality.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot monocular metric depth models are evaluated by averaging metric and scale-aligned scores across datasets. Averages cannot show how many images still have severely wrong metric depth, whether depth is under- or overestimated, or whether different models fail on the same images. We propose an evaluation built on per-image results: the failure rate (metric $\delta_1$ < 0.5); scale-aligned metrics for structure, and the bias, dispersion and absolute error of the alignment scale for scale; and a cross-model comparison that separates shared from model-specific failures. We apply it to 11 recent architectures with and without ground-truth intrinsics (18 model evaluations) on the 7 everyday-scene benchmarks (4,406 images) used by MoGe-2. Metric depth estimation is not solved in everyday scenes, and the remaining difficulty is mainly scale: the best of the 18 evaluations still has a failure rate of 7.7% (datasets weighted equally); pooled over all failures, 78.8% have intact structure, and after scale correction 98.3% no longer fail. Images failed by at least 6 architectures make up 7.3% of the data, concentrated on HAMMER and DIODE; even when selected only by architectures of other families, they hold 34% to 40% of the error of the top 6 models, against 14% to 18% for as many random images from the same datasets. Adding objects reduces the scale error of most models; ground-truth intrinsics and, in most families, larger models reduce the failures but do not remove them. We recommend reporting failure rates, structure and scale separately, and results stratified by how many models fail. We will release the code, the per-image results with shared-failure labels, and two diagnostic sets built from TUM RGB-D.
authors: Hualie Jiang, Yujie Luo, Ziyang Song, Ximeng Li, Zhiqiang Lou, Rui Xu
bullets: Average scores hide severe, directional, and shared failures across images and models.
The proposed evaluation separates failure rate, structural accuracy, and scale bias, dispersion, and error, while identifying shared versus model-specific failures.
Across 18 evaluations on 4,406 images, the best failure rate remains 7.7%; 78.8% of failures retain intact structure and 98.3% disappear after scale correction.
Failures shared by many architectures are concentrated on HAMMER and DIODE; objects, ground-truth intrinsics, and larger models often reduce—but do not eliminate—them.
The authors recommend reporting per-image failure rates, separate structure/scale metrics, and results stratified by the number of failing models.

papers.abstract: Vision-based 3D occupancy prediction provides a dense semantic representation of scenes for autonomous driving and embodied perception, yet remains vulnerable to occlusion, depth ambiguity, and projection errors that induce spatially varying reliability in voxel features. Existing methods typically map voxel representations to semantic predictions without explicitly modeling such observation-induced feature variations. To address this limitation, we propose VoxSAOR, a semantic-aware occupancy robustification framework that models aleatoric uncertainty through feature-space proxies. It first quantifies Local Semantic Consistency (LSC) to derive a voxel-wise structural stability prior and uses cross-view semantic consensus to filter unreliable semantic correspondences. Within each semantic category, spatially matched stable and ambiguous voxels form stable-to-ambiguous feature transitions, which are modeled by a class-conditional diagonal Gaussian distribution, capturing both feature displacement and dispersion. Guided by these proxy distributions, Aleatoric Regime Ensemble Learning (AREL) trains independently parameterized prediction heads using feature perturbations at progressively increasing scales, with perturbation strength modulated by structural reliability. At inference, proxy modeling and sampling are disabled, and all heads process the same observed features; their output probabilities are then averaged to produce a deterministic consensus prediction without requiring sampling. Experiments across multiple datasets and occupancy backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of VoxSAOR in improving semantic occupancy prediction, long-tail recognition, and predictive calibration. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/MengfeiD/VoxSAOR.
authors: Mengfei Duan, Yuheng Zhang, Guoqiang Zhao, Yuanfan Zheng, Kailun Yang, Zhiyong Li
bullets: Targets errors from occlusion, depth ambiguity, and projection that make voxel features spatially unreliable.
Uses Local Semantic Consistency and cross-view semantic consensus to estimate structural stability and filter unreliable correspondences.
Models stable-to-ambiguous feature transitions with class-conditional diagonal Gaussian proxies.
Trains independently parameterized heads with reliability-scaled perturbations, then averages their predictions at inference without sampling.
Experiments across multiple datasets and backbones report gains in semantic occupancy, long-tail recognition, and predictive calibration.

papers.abstract: Robot policy pretraining based on human videos is crucial for improving the policy's generalization ability. One main challenge for this task is the lack of explicit action-relevant representations in such unlabeled data. Recent works tend to estimate 3D hand motion trajectories from videos using 3D foundation models (3D FMs). However, they keep solely the sparse trajectories as supervision, ignoring the rich, fine-grained information produced during the trajectory extraction process. To address this issue, we propose LSA, a hierarchical robot policy pretraining framework that includes three phases: Lift, See, and Act. Specifically, the Lift phase elevates 2D video observations into dense 3D representations by adaptively aligning features in the policy's shallow layers with the intermediate representations extracted from multiple 3D FMs. Building upon these lifted representations, the See phase equips the policy with explicit geometric and interactive awareness through dual guidance. It introduces depth-map reconstruction to help the model comprehend 3D spatial layouts and utilizes hand region cues to explicitly supervise the encoder's attention toward task-relevant interaction hotspots. Empowered by the dense 3D representation learning and precise spatial guidance, our policy achieves robust and accurate robotic manipulation in the Act phase. Extensive experiments on diverse simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that LSA significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. The project page is available at: https://yiyuan00.github.io/Lift-See-Act.
authors: Yiyuan Ge, Changxing Ding, Ziyu Hao, Zijie Zheng, Xiangmin Xu
bullets: Addresses the lack of action-relevant supervision in unlabeled human videos for robot policy pretraining.
Lift aligns shallow policy features with intermediate representations from multiple 3D foundation models to create dense 3D representations.
See adds depth-map reconstruction and hand-region guidance for spatial understanding and task-relevant attention.
Act uses these representations for robotic manipulation across diverse simulated and real-world tasks.
The abstract reports significant gains over current state-of-the-art methods, without specifying quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides spatially resolved gene expression measurements, but most 3D ST datasets are acquired as independently processed 2D sections. Computational approaches span slice registration and integration, explicit or generative interpolation, and coordinate-field modeling. Within the last family, implicit neural representations (INRs) offer a continuous, coordinate-queryable parameterization, but standard isotropic coordinate encodings do not explicitly reflect that serial-section measurements are dense in-plane and sparse along the axial direction. We present HoloGene, an anisotropic conditional INR framework for estimating continuous 3D gene-expression fields from pre-registered ST sections. Its central contribution is an acquisition-aware factorization that couples dense in-plane synthesis with sparse axial evolution using established GAE, FiLM, pseudo-label supervision, and CORAL components. HoloGene compresses high-dimensional expression profiles into a graph-autoencoder latent manifold, uses pseudo-label-derived signature conditioning to provide coarse intra-section context, and applies depth-dependent FiLM modulation to model axial variation. A signature-stratified correlation-alignment regularizer encourages cross-slice covariance alignment in latent features. Using held-out measured sections as cross-sectional references, HoloGene improves reconstruction accuracy and biological preservation metrics compared with general-purpose INRs and adapted spatial-transcriptomics baselines. These results support anisotropic conditional modeling as a practical strategy for estimating 3D expression fields from discontinuous ST sections. Code is available at https://github.com/Szym29/HoloGene.
authors: Yumin Zheng, Qingtian Zhu, Ziyan Zhu, Kailu Song, Yinqiang Zheng, Jun Ding
bullets: Addresses the challenge that serial ST data are dense within sections but sparse along the axial direction.
Uses a conditional implicit neural representation with graph-autoencoder latent compression, pseudo-label signature conditioning, and depth-dependent FiLM modulation.
Applies correlation alignment to encourage consistent cross-slice covariance in latent features.
Evaluations on held-out measured sections show improved reconstruction accuracy and biological preservation versus general-purpose INRs and adapted ST baselines.
Scope: designed for pre-registered ST sections and estimates, rather than directly measuring, continuous 3D expression.

papers.abstract: We present a method for inferring the interior temperature distribution of a solid object from registered multi-view visible-spectrum and thermal images, even when the thermal views cover only part of its surface. We formulate steady-state heat conduction as a Laplace boundary value problem and solve it with a direct boundary integral equation discretized over a point cloud: a Gaussian reconstruction of the visible-spectrum images supplies the boundary geometry, and the thermal images supply the boundary data. We do not build surface or volume meshes at any stage in our method. Instead, we sample collocation points from rendered depth without the pixels at depth discontinuities, and use a density subtraction that keeps the interior evaluation accurate up to the surface. The whole chain is differentiable, and we use it to recover the pose and depth of heating pipes, insulation defects, and the shape of cracks from thermal images. We validate our method through experiments on boundary value problems with Dirichlet-only and mixed Dirichlet and Robin boundaries, using synthetic and real captured data on scenes with challenging topology. These experiments show that our method matches analytical solutions and has better accuracy than FEM solvers.
authors: Liu Zhenyuan, Bharath Seshadri, Bailey Miller, George Kopanas, Ionnais Gkioulekas, Bernd Bickel
bullets: Addresses inference of interior temperatures when thermal images cover only part of an object’s surface.

Experiments on synthetic and real data, including Dirichlet and mixed Dirichlet–Robin boundaries, match analytical solutions and outperform FEM solvers in accuracy.

papers.abstract: Geometric deep learning has made available a large variety of structurally equivariant neural network architectures, meaning a particular transformation of their input causes a predictable transformation of their output. But structural equivariance is a very strong inductive bias that can limit performance if chosen poorly. In contrast, choosing an architecture with low geometric bias necessitates data augmentation to obtain correct behavior; extending the training process. We propose a novel neural network architecture that is soft equivariant; we select a set of symmetry groups and during training the network will become equivariant only to those symmetry groups that are appropriate given the training data. After training we can inspect the network to obtain a symmetry fingerprint that will tell us exactly which symmetries ended up being relevant and to what degree. We show how our architecture and the fingerprinting process work in the case of an image classification task.
authors: Bart M. N. Smets, Gijs Bellaard, Pieter Wils
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between overly restrictive built-in equivariance and costly data augmentation.
Introduces an architecture that can become equivariant to selected symmetry groups based on the training data.
Provides a post-training fingerprint indicating which symmetries are relevant and to what degree.
Demonstrates the architecture and fingerprinting process on image classification.

papers.abstract: Lightweight 3D building models support urban spatial analysis, but their production often requires dense scene reconstruction, building extraction, and mesh simplification. Although 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is more efficient than conventional multi-view stereo, existing large-scale methods lack semantic selection and parallel instance-level training. We present SemLite-GS, a building-centric framework that reconstructs lightweight building meshes from large-scale UAV oblique imagery. First, an orthographic reference map establishes globally consistent building identities, which are propagated to oblique views to form camera-instance pairs and regions of interest. Second, semantic-selective parallel PGSR training jointly processes multiple pairs within relevant image regions while updating only target Gaussians; contextual Gaussians remain fixed to preserve visibility. Third, architectural planes extracted from rendered depth, opacity, and normal maps guide signed distance field optimization, producing meshes with adaptive polygon allocation and well-defined structural boundaries. Experiments on multiple large-scale UAV datasets demonstrate that our SemLite-GS substantially reduces building reconstruction time compared with representative full-scene 3DGS methods. With comparable polygon budgets, SemLite-GS achieves superior preservation of dominant planar structures and sharp architectural transitions compared with conventional dense reconstruction followed by mesh decimation. The source code is available at https://github.com/IRIS-LAB-whu/SemLite-GS.
authors: Tengfei Wang, Xin Wang, Zihan Li, Quanjian Ji, Yifei Yu, Dong Lin, Zongqian Zhan

Uses an orthographic reference map to establish building identities and create view-specific regions of interest.

Experiments on multiple large-scale UAV datasets show reduced reconstruction time and better preservation of planar structures and sharp transitions at comparable polygon budgets.

papers.abstract: Which depths in a new camera view are determined by finitely many source-depth measurements? Pointwise uncertainty bounds do not answer this question: unobserved geometry between samples can change which surface is encountered first. We study a bounded Lipschitz class of continuous source inverse-depth fields with interval observations and known camera pose. Building on classical Lipschitz envelopes, we characterize the exact set of attainable first-hit depths and construct a globally admissible scene for every value in that set. The set can be disconnected. We also give a necessary and sufficient test for several proposed depths to be first hits of one shared scene. An epipolar reduction uses scalar cone inequalities without enumerating surfaces. In a rectified model with source spacing $h$, interval half-width $\varepsilon$, baseline $b$, and slope bound $L$, we prove a sharp worst-case inverse-depth diameter of $\max\{Lh+2\varepsilon,2\varepsilon/(1-bL)\}$ when $bL<1$, subject to sufficient depth and domain range for attainment. Exact samples still give the sharp bound $Lh$ at $bL=1$, while above this threshold ambiguity need not vanish as sampling becomes arbitrarily dense. Any positive measurement uncertainty can destroy uniform stability at the critical threshold. We provide constructive examples, an exact rational validation oracle, and a frozen ten-scene evaluation using reference, stereo, and learned-depth observations. The experiments separate solver correctness under the scene assumptions from failure of those assumptions: fixed learned-depth bands often yield narrow but incorrect sets. The results identify what a specified scene class permits; they do not infer a continuum regularity or physical-scene guarantee from sampled predictions.
authors: Hamidreza Hasani Balyani, Mahtab Movahhedrad, Seyed Pouyan Mousavi Davoudi
bullets: Pointwise uncertainty bounds are insufficient because unsampled geometry can change the first surface encountered in a new view.
Using Lipschitz envelopes and an epipolar reduction, the authors characterize the complete attainable set of first-hit depths and construct a valid scene for every attainable value.
They provide a necessary-and-sufficient test for whether multiple proposed first hits can arise from one shared scene, even when the attainable set is disconnected.

In a rectified setting, the sharp worst-case inverse-depth diameter is max{Lh+2ε, 2ε/(1−bL)} for bL<1; ambiguity can persist above the critical threshold, and measurement noise can destroy stability at it.
A rational validation oracle and ten-scene evaluation distinguish solver correctness under the model from failures of the assumed scene class, including narrow but incorrect learned-depth bands.

papers.abstract: 3D object detection is critical for intelligent transportation systems. LiDAR has been widely adopted for accurate geometric measurements; however, purely geometric representations remain ambiguous under sparse observations and occlusions, while cross-sensor multimodal fusion suffers from calibration and synchronization errors. To overcome these challenges, we leverage an Ouster LiDAR to construct PALIN (Pixel-Aligned LiDAR-NIR), a large-scale intrinsically pixel-aligned multimodal dataset jointly capturing geometry and NIR intensity, comprising approximately 8,000 annotated frames from static urban intersections and diverse mobile suburban scenes. Building upon this dataset, we propose CMambaFusion, a novel fusion framework consisting of a four-directional Cross-Mamba module for bidirectional cross-modal interaction and a Gated Concat-Mamba module for joint feature refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PALIN enables effective multimodal learning, and CMambaFusion achieves superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs over both LiDAR-only and representative fusion baselines.

CMambaFusion uses a four-directional Cross-Mamba module for bidirectional cross-modal interaction.
A Gated Concat-Mamba module performs joint multimodal feature refinement.
Experiments show effective multimodal learning and a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off against LiDAR-only and representative fusion baselines.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D understanding aims to localize and segment arbitrary objects beyond predefined categories. However, existing approaches based on Gaussian Splatting often rely on expensive preprocessing and lengthy training, limiting their applicability when fast and lightweight solutions are desired. We propose a lightweight, training-free framework for query-driven 3D instance segmentation on Gaussian Splatting. Instead of conventional mask-wise CLIP embeddings, we use dense pixel-level CLIP features to preserve fine-grained semantic information and enable flexible text-driven localization without relying on predefined instance proposals. Given a text query, we identify a high-quality target region in a carefully selected pivot view and propagate it across views using a video segmentor, providing consistent and comprehensive coverage of the target instance. We then lift the resulting 2D tracklets to 3D Gaussians through a novel visibility voting strategy, yielding accurate 3D segmentation masks with clean object boundaries. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on LERF-OVS, ScanNet, and ScanNet++, competitive results on 3D-OVS, and significant speedups over existing open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods. These results highlight the effectiveness of our framework for efficient open-vocabulary 3D understanding without per-scene training.
authors: Nhat-Quynh Le-Pham, Khoi Nguyen, Binh-Son Hua
bullets: Uses dense pixel-level CLIP features instead of mask-wise embeddings for fine-grained, proposal-free localization.
Selects a target region in a pivot view and propagates it across views with a video segmentor.
Lifts 2D tracks into 3D Gaussians using visibility voting to produce consistent segmentation masks.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on LERF-OVS, ScanNet, and ScanNet++, competitive results on 3D-OVS, and significant speedups.
Supports efficient open-vocabulary 3D understanding without per-scene training.

The resulting masks are lifted to 3D Gaussians via visibility voting, forming an occlusion-aware 3D instance mask, which is rendered at novel views to obtain high-quality 2D instance segmentation.

papers.abstract: Considering the motion continuity and stability of 3D objects over short inter-frame intervals, introducing multi-frame settings in scene flow estimation can potentially address occlusion. In this paper, we propose a two-frame backbone, SimpleFlow3D, which integrates dense information from the image plane and sparse information from the depth dimension in a decoupling-followed-by-coupling manner by hierarchically constructing the 3D motion feature. SimpleFlow3D achieves SOTA results with minimal parameters. We also propose a weight-sharing multi-frame framework to splat the previous 3D motion feature to the current estimation process. The framework unifies the first and non-first frame inference by constructing pseudo inputs. After combining the proposed framework and backbone, the newly born multi-frame method SplatFlow3D further advances the state of the art. It achieves lower errors than the two-frame backbone, with fewer parameters than current methods. On both KITTI and Spring, SplatFlow3D ranked 1st over all published and submitted methods. Experiments show that SplatFlow3D improves occlusion handling, non-rigid motion estimation, and generalization to real-world scenes. Code is available at https://github.com/wwsource/SplatFlow3D.
authors: Bo Wang, Dekang Zhu, Jian Li, Zhipeng Meng, Bo Wang, Dewen Hu
bullets: SimpleFlow3D decouples image-plane and depth information before coupling them to construct hierarchical 3D motion features.
A weight-sharing multi-frame framework splats prior 3D motion features into the current estimation process using pseudo inputs.
The multi-frame design improves occlusion handling, non-rigid motion estimation, and real-world generalization.
SplatFlow3D reports the best performance on KITTI and Spring among published and submitted methods, while using fewer parameters than current methods.

papers.abstract: Robust 3D lane detection requires accurate metric road geometry recovery from visual inputs, yet conventional RGB-based approaches suffer from fragile lane evidence under adverse illumination, motion blur, and long-range perspective compression. Event cameras offer complementary high-temporal-resolution, high dynamic-range structural cues that are robust to these challenges, but their sparse, motion-dependent responses cannot be directly fused into consistent 3D geometry. In this paper, we present the first attempt to introduce event cameras into 3D lane detection. To enable systematic research, we first build two multimodal benchmarks with metric 3D lane annotations: DSEC-3DLD (real-world sequences) and Ev-OpenLane (large-scale simulated sequences). We further propose RETR, a structure preserving transformer that converts complementary RGB and event observations into coherent 3D lane geometry. RETR first aligns modality consistent evidence through Reciprocal Context Flow Fusion, then preserves thin and uncertain lane structures with Uncertainty Aware Structural Consolidation, and finally decodes ordered lane hypotheses using a Geometry State Decoder with proposal conditioned initialization, reference conditioned query evolution, and diversified geometric inquiry. Extensive experiments show that RETR achieves state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks, especially showing strong improvements in challenging lighting and complex road geometry scenarios. Code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/duskswell/RETR.
authors: Jingtao Dong, Hao Zhuang, Hao Yang, Liyuan Pan, Wei Liang
bullets: Introduces DSEC-3DLD and Ev-OpenLane, multimodal benchmarks with metric 3D lane annotations.
Fuses RGB and event evidence using Reciprocal Context Flow Fusion to align complementary cues.
Preserves thin and uncertain lane structures through Uncertainty Aware Structural Consolidation.
Decodes ordered 3D lane hypotheses with a geometry-focused state decoder.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks, with notable gains under challenging lighting and complex road geometry.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of RETR. RETR converts synchronized RGB and event observations into metric 3D lane geometry through a structure-preserving RGB-event pipeline. Modality-specific encoders first extract multi-scale RGB and event features {Fl r}Ll=1 and {Fl e}Ll=1. RCF aligns both modalities at each scale by using a co-activation response Ml to emphasize jointly supported lane evidence and bidirectional Cross Attention Blocks (CAB) to exchange complementary context, producing fused features {Zl}Ll=1. UASC aggregates the fused hierarchy into Fc while preserving thin and uncertain lane structures. It combines context and structural branches and gates detail refinement using high-frequency response A, learned detail cue D, and entropy-based uncertainty E. The query generator and geometry decoder finally predict ordered 3D lane hypotheses, including lane existence, 3D coordinates, and visibility.

papers.abstract: Aerial perception systems are increasingly expected to support diverse tasks, yet existing solutions remain fundamentally tied to task-specific outputs. Detection, segmentation, and other perception objectives are usually learned either by separate models or by sharing a backbone with multiple task heads, leaving the model itself unaware of the common structure underlying these tasks. We are interested in asking: can a single perception representation support different levels of understanding without being designed for any specific task? We notice that occupancy is a promising task-agnostic representation for drone perception. By modeling the spatial existence and semantics of the environment, it naturally bridges different perception granularities, from coarse scene understanding to fine-grained object localization. Therefore, we introduce AerialOcc, a unified occupancy-based perception model that enables multiple drone perception tasks from a single inference process, without maintaining task-specific prediction heads. To facilitate this direction, we construct AerialOcc-20K, a large-scale multi-class occupancy dataset for aerial environments. Extensive experiments show that AerialOcc achieves competitive performance across diverse perception tasks while preserving a unified architecture. Our findings demonstrate that occupancy can serve as a universal perception interface, offering a new perspective toward flexible and scalable visual intelligence for autonomous drones from a common 3D scene representation. Models and data are publicly available at https://github.com/guxiang2002/AerialOcc
authors: Fan Liu, Xiang Gu, Baoyu Lv, Chuanyi Zhang, Liang Yao, Yuye Ma, Yuhui Zheng
bullets: Addresses the fragmentation of drone perception systems built around separate models or task-specific heads.

Reports competitive performance across diverse perception tasks with one unified architecture.
Models and data are publicly available; specific quantitative results are not stated in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Occupancy estimation for automated vehicles is a crucial task that builds a 3D map using vehicle sensors. This map allows the vehicle to identify drivable areas and various obstacle classes. The task involves complex subtasks such as depth estimation, object classification, and segmentation to align semantic information with the 3D grid. Moreover, producing these estimations from multiple sensors demands significant computational power and memory, as high-dimensional data fusion requires complex feature extraction and processing. Consequently, most existing methods rely on large and computationally intensive architectures that are not suitable for real-time or real-world applications. We present a real-time, lightweight architecture that leverages camera and radar sensors through a residual multi-stage head. Unlike prior methods that rely on heavy camera-only blocks, our architecture employs camera-radar fusion and lightweight components. Additionally, we introduce a task-specific data augmentation strategy that enhances data diversity and improves generalisation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance, attaining 45.7 mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) on Occ3D and 41.9 Ray-level Intersection over Union (RayIoU) (41.9) on OpenOcc datasets, running at 17.2 frames per second (FPS) and using only 5.3 GB of memory, compared with 4.1 FPS and 7.7 GB for STCOcc.
authors: Ruan Bispo, Tim Brophy, Reenu Mohandas, Anthony Scanlan, Ciaran Eising
bullets: Targets the high cost and complexity of multi-sensor 3D occupancy estimation for automated vehicles.
Uses a residual multi-stage head with lightweight camera–radar fusion instead of heavy camera-only blocks.
Introduces task-specific data augmentation to improve data diversity and generalisation.
Reports 45.7 mIoU on Occ3D and 41.9 RayIoU on OpenOcc.
Runs at 17.2 FPS with 5.3 GB memory, compared with 4.1 FPS and 7.7 GB for STCOcc.

papers.abstract: A query-based multi-view 3D detector can transfer well to a new calibrated camera network and still produce badly fragmented tracks: on the AI City Challenge 2026 Track 1 validation set, the frozen Sparse4D detector behind the official challenge winner splits each Person identity into a median of eight fragments, and half of the gaps between fragments exceed the horizon of a causal tracker. We show that most of the remaining headroom of such a system lies after detection. Keeping the public detector frozen, we add (i) class-wise source selection between two input scales, which recovers small and distant people from a 0.75x pass while leaving large objects at the scale the detector was trained for; (ii) a geometry-to-appearance bridge that projects every 3D box into all calibrated views, matches it to 2D person detections, and aggregates robust track-level re-identification descriptors; and (iii) constraint-aware consolidation, which combines a causal short-gap stitch with offline centroid-linkage clustering under two hard constraints, temporal exclusion and metric 3D reachability, plus class-aware long-gap stitching for rigid objects. Every association stage changes object identities only. On the challenge evaluation server the system scores 62.3947 3D HOTA (DetA 57.4501, AssA 56.8131, LocA 80.1272), first on the general leaderboard snapshot of 30 October 2026 (second at the time of writing, after a competitor's detector update) and 5.63 points above our reproduction of the official winner; the constrained association stage alone contributes +3.73 HOTA through a +5.49 AssA gain at unchanged DetA. Controlled fixed-box validation studies, a constraint ablation, sensitivity curves, and a catalogue of negative results support the design.
authors: Abdullah Naeem, Anav Katwal, Ayon Day, Md Tamjidul Hoque
bullets: The detector transfers to new camera networks but produces heavily fragmented person tracks, leaving major performance headroom after detection.
Class-wise selection between 0.75× and native input scales recovers small or distant people while preserving the trained scale for larger objects.
Projected 3D boxes link detections across calibrated views to build robust track-level re-identification descriptors.
Causal short-gap stitching and offline constrained clustering enforce temporal exclusion and metric 3D reachability, with class-aware long-gap stitching for rigid objects.
The full system reaches 62.3947 3D HOTA; constrained association alone adds 3.73 HOTA via a 5.49 AssA gain without changing DetA.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have demonstrated its effectiveness for photorealistic novel view synthesis. However, extracting clean, watertight, explicit surface meshes from 3DGS remains a critical challenge. Previous methods approximate geometry via discrete Marching Tetrahedra, where each grid vertex is assigned a single scalar signed distance value. At complex geometric boundaries and thin structures, this suboptimal parameterization forces severe compromises across shared vertices, causing gradient collisions and geometric frustration. Furthermore, existing optimization objectives neglect element shape conditioning, producing degenerate triangles. We introduce TopSDF, a framework that models the signed distance state as a multivariate Gaussian random field. By learning latent topological covariances across tetrahedral vertices, our formulation expands local degrees of freedom for SDF estimates, allowing the candidate mesh vertices to be placed flexibly along the bipolar edges in the tetrahedra as driven by such topological correlation. Concurrently, we directly integrate variational meshing energies into the joint optimization, coupled with an energy-driven Gaussian densification strategy to improve triangle mesh quality. Our experiments across Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and ScanNet++ show that TopSDF achieves state-of-the-art mesh-based novel view rendering (+0.86 dB PSNR on Mip-NeRF 360) and triangle-mesh quality (from 0.37 to 0.49 aspect ratio).
authors: Khoi Do, Yu-kun Lai, Binh-Son Hua
bullets: Addresses geometric compromises at complex boundaries and thin structures caused by assigning one SDF value per grid vertex.
Represents SDFs as a multivariate Gaussian random field with learned topological covariances across tetrahedral vertices.
Jointly optimizes variational meshing energies and uses energy-driven Gaussian densification to reduce degenerate triangles.
Evaluated on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and ScanNet++; reports +0.86 dB PSNR on Mip-NeRF 360 and aspect-ratio improvement from 0.37 to 0.49.
Scope: focuses on extracting explicit triangle meshes from 3DGS while retaining high-quality novel-view rendering.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Framework overview and training loop (formalized in Algorithm 1). We revisit the suboptimality in triangle mesh extraction from 3DGS caused by the gradient frustration in a single SDF tetrahedral grid. We propose to assign learnable topological features based on Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space at each grid vertex, allowing us to expand the SDF degrees of freedom in localized space. During training, we dynamically adjust candidate vertices by obtaining per-edge relation feature 𝑓𝜙 (v)𝑇 𝑓𝜙 (v) , and then calculate the topological SDF ℎ∗ using Eq. (6) at each grid vertex. The training procedure is as follows: Starting with normal-oriented Gaussians, we sample a set of pivots, assign learnable normals u and SDF y, and obtain the topological SDF ℎ∗. We then perform Marching Tetrahedra on the Delaunay grid formed by pivots; the extracted mesh is regularized via normal-depth alignment loss, while the Tetrahedral grid is regularized by meshing energies, which is used for Gaussian densification.

papers.title: TopSDF: Topological Signed Distance Field for High-Quality Triangle Mesh Extraction from 3D Gaussian Splatting

papers.abstract: Repeated airborne LiDAR surveys are costly, while stored 3D geometry can become outdated between observations. Existing change-detection methods compare observed epochs. However, they do not quantify the validity of geometry that has not been revisited. We distinguish observation, existence and geometric validity using a probabilistic filter over five geometric transitions: persistence, modification, growth, removal and replacement. The framework learns class-specific continuous-time transition priors from interval-censored observations and combines shape residuals with LiDAR free-space evidence. Functional anchors enable prior sharing across sites with different survey frequencies. In controlled experiments with misspecified dynamics and 60% visibility, our method reduces combined error from 36.9% to 16.5% and expected calibration error (ECE) from 0.19-0.32 to 0.017. Cross-site sharing reduces ECE at two-survey sites from 0.156 to 0.029. On Urb3DCD-v2, the method achieves 9.8% combined error and 0.016 ECE, outperforming baselines at 12.6% and at least 0.070, respectively. Re-survey prioritisation improves only modestly over random selection with two observations. Code and an evaluation protocol are released at https://github.com/anwaarua/life4d.
bullets: Addresses the lack of validity estimates for geometry that has not been recently observed.
Models persistence, modification, growth, removal, and replacement using continuous-time, class-specific transition priors.
Combines shape residuals with LiDAR free-space evidence; functional anchors support prior sharing across sites with different survey frequencies.
Reduces combined error and calibration error in controlled experiments and achieves 9.8% combined error with 0.016 ECE on Urb3DCD-v2, outperforming reported baselines.
Re-survey prioritisation provides only modest gains over random selection with two observations; code and an evaluation protocol are released.

papers.abstract: Implicit and explicit representations of geometry are central in computer graphics applications and come with their pros and cons. With surface sampling being faster on explicit representations and spatial queries being faster on implicit representations, finding efficient conversions between them is a highly desirable property. We present TetraCoder, a single resolution hash-free adaptive tetrahedral encoding that links an explicit tetrahedral spatial encoder with an underlying implicit signed distance field (SDF). The resulting hybrid implicit-explicit space is continuous piecewise affine (CPWA) by design, allowing to obtain an exact correspondence between the implicit SDF and the explicit analytic mesh. TetraCoder's design comes with additional perks, in particular: (a) it scales better than multi-resolution encoding methods due to its single resolution optimizable grid, (b) unlike hash-based methods, it is not affected by collisions, (c) it enables fast tetrahedral ray-tracing, geometry and appearance editing, directly through its adaptive tetrahedral scaffold. We demonstrate the versatility of TetraCoder by showing an improvement over state-of-the-art methods on multiple tasks: 2D/3D fitting from images and point clouds, 3D novel view synthesis, 3D reconstruction, and geometry/appearance editing.
authors: Daniele Della Pietra, Antonella Rech, Nicola Conci, Nicola Garau
bullets: Uses a single-resolution adaptive tetrahedral grid to connect an explicit tetrahedral encoder with an implicit signed distance field.
Produces a continuous piecewise-affine representation with exact correspondence between the SDF and analytic mesh.
Avoids hash-grid collisions and is designed to scale better than multi-resolution encodings.
Enables fast tetrahedral ray tracing plus direct geometry and appearance editing.
Improves over prior methods across image and point-cloud fitting, novel view synthesis, reconstruction, and editing tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. We present TetraCoder, an adaptive tetrahedral encoding for neural fields. Multiresolution hash encoding (left) interpolates features on fixed spatial grids at multiple resolutions. Its trilinear interpolation does not produce a piecewise-affine encoding, making analytic mesh extraction impractical. To address that tetrahedral multiresolution hash encoding (center) subdivides these grids into fixed tetrahedra and uses barycentric interpolation to obtain a piecewise-affine encoding. TetraCoder (right) instead uses a single-level, hash-free encoding defined on an adaptive tetrahedral volumetric mesh. Combined with a piecewise-affine decoder, this representation enables fast analytic mesh retrieval. Unlike other encodings, TetraCoder supports novel view synthesis, scene reconstruction, 3D appearance and geometry editing within a unified framework.
Fig. 3. R3 – Analytic extraction and grid-based extractors on the same frozen Lego field. SSDF measures mesh–field agreement.

Shading highlights the visited cells, while green arrows indicate face normals. Dashed lines illustrate barycentric interpolation of vertex features within the target triangle (𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐). Gray markers denote additional samples along the ray.

papers.abstract: Affine correspondences (ACs) enable robust and efficient solvers for multiple-view geometry by constraining the local geometry of point correspondences (PCs). Despite their utility in minimal solvers, AC estimation remains understudied. We revisit AC estimation beyond local image patches, extending it to the image and image-pair levels. Rather than estimating the components of the affine transformation separately, we learn the full 4-DoF matrix jointly. Building on this formulation, we introduce ALoMa, an AC estimator using LoMa keypoint descriptions, demonstrating consistent improvements across a wide range of downstream tasks. Code at https://github.com/davnords/loma.
authors: David Nordstr\"om, Georg B\"okman, Viktor Larsson, Fredrik Kahl, Jonathan Ventura
bullets: Affine correspondences can yield efficient, robust minimal solvers but their estimation is relatively understudied.
The approach extends affine-correspondence estimation to image- and image-pair levels, beyond local patches.
It jointly predicts the full 4-DoF affine transformation matrix rather than estimating components separately.
ALoMa builds on LoMa keypoint descriptions and reports consistent improvements across a broad range of downstream tasks.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward multi-view transformers such as VGGT recover the cameras and geometry of a video in one pass, but the cost of their cross-frame attention grows quadratically with the frame count, and their accuracy drops on long videos. Most remedies approximate attention over all frames within a budget or select a few keys by their content. We hypothesize that the keys of a long video can be chosen without looking at its content, and our experiments on VGGT and $\pi^3$ support it: a few dozen evenly spread frames can serve as the keys of every frame. We present EcoVGGT, a training-free inference framework whose keys form a Pinned Key Set of 31 such frames. A pin pass stores their tokens in a Scene Cache, and the other frames read it in independent batches that reproduce joint inference with these keys exactly, at a constant cost per frame. An Online Stream updates the pinned frames during recording. Six middle global blocks align the frames and form a reusable VGGT module: the Alignment Score reads their attention to flag failures, and Alignment Refocusing reduces them by fine-tuning only these blocks (3.6 GPU hours). EcoVGGT ($\pi^3$) matches the success rate of $\pi^3$ on 1,000-frame ScanNet videos at 13.8 times its speed. With refocusing, EcoVGGT (VGGT) raises the success rate of VGGT from 70% to 82% at 8.5 times its speed on 500 frames. EcoVGGT reconstructs 4,000 frames on one GPU, and EcoVGGT ($\pi^3$) streams 1,000 frames at 18.6 frames per second with the lowest online absolute trajectory error.
authors: Hongsen Cao, Shanxin Yuan, Mona Jaber, Ahmed Sayed
bullets: Addresses quadratic cross-frame attention costs and accuracy degradation on long videos.
Uses a training-free Pinned Key Set of 31 frames, cached once and reused by independently processed frames.
Supports online streaming by updating pinned frames during recording.
An Alignment Score detects failures, while Alignment Refocusing fine-tunes six global blocks to improve robustness.
On long ScanNet videos, it matches or improves baseline success rates while achieving substantially higher speed and scaling to thousands of frames on one GPU.
