papers.abstract: Automated lidar feature detection from lidar point clouds can support archaeological surveys, but models trained in one landscape may transfer poorly to another because of differences in terrain, vegetation, acquisition characteristics, and feature morphology. We address this problem for cross-region detection of ancient terraces using transductive unsupervised domain adaptation that exploits an unlabelled target survey. We propose MELD (Multi-level Embedding-space Latent Diffusion), which trains separate diffusion denoisers on target-domain representations at four hierarchical PointNet++ feature levels. These target distribution priors are then used to refine source representations during supervised training and target representations during inference, allowing adaptation to act directly on the multi-scale features consumed by the segmentation decoder. We additionally investigate local geometric descriptors derived from K-nearest-neighbour neighbourhoods, including surface normals, slope, and aspect. MELD is evaluated bidirectionally between the Teyuna and Miraflores lidar surveys in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Colombia, against a source-only model and nine configurations of established domain adaptation approaches. MELD raises F1 over the source-only model from 0.397 to 0.459 for Teyuna-to-Miraflores transfer and from 0.557 to 0.594 in the reverse direction, achieving the highest F1 among the evaluated adaptation methods in both directions. Adding local geometry further raises F1 to 0.542 and 0.606, respectively. Multi-level ablation shows that refining all four PointNet++ levels provides the strongest performance in both directions. These results show that explicit modelling of target feature distributions in hierarchical point cloud feature space, complemented by local geometry, provides an effective route to cross-region archaeological mapping without target labels.
authors: Sina Mohammadi, Roderik Lindenbergh, Javier Ruiz-P\'erez, Marco Madella, Sebastian Fajardo
bullets: Addresses poor transfer caused by differences in terrain, vegetation, acquisition, and terrace morphology.
Uses transductive unsupervised adaptation with an unlabelled target survey and diffusion denoisers at four PointNet++ feature levels.
Refines source features during training and target features during inference, with optional local geometry descriptors such as normals, slope, and aspect.
Across bidirectional Teyuna–Miraflores transfer, F1 improves from 0.397 to 0.459 and from 0.557 to 0.594; local geometry raises these to 0.542 and 0.606.
All four hierarchical feature levels perform best in ablation, supporting multi-scale target-distribution modelling.

figures.caption: Figure 2: High-level overview of the MELD framework. During joint training, unlabeled target/test features train the level-specific diffusion denoisers, while labeled source features are refined by the target-trained denoisers and decoded under source ground-truth supervision. The diffusion loss updates the denoisers, whereas the segmentation loss updates PointNet++ through the straight-through refinement path. A held-out source-validation set ranks checkpoints by adapted validation F1. At inference, the top three paired PointNet++ denoiser checkpoints are applied independently to all target/test points using deterministic target-guided DDIM refinement; their terrace-class probabilities are averaged point-wise and thresholded at 0.5 to obtain the final binary prediction. No target labels are used for adaptation or checkpoint selection. Preprocessing and the PointNet++ backbone are detailed in Figure 3, target domain latent diffusion adaptation in Figure 4, and source-feature refinement with the straight-through estimator in Figure 5; adapted inference is described in Section 3.5.

Figure 3: PointNet++ segmentation backbone. Each 20m × 20m point cloud tile is converted by sampling or padding into a fixed 4096-point input patch, which is then normalized. The patch may contain either only xyz coordinates (C = 3) or xyz coordinates augmented with optional KNN-derived geometric features (C = 9), including normals, slope, and sine/cosine of aspect. The encoder comprises four set-abstraction (SA) layers that progressively reduce the number of points while increasing feature dimensionality, producing hierarchical latent features Z1, Z2, Z3, and Z4. The decoder then uses four feature-propagation (FP) stages with interpolation and skip connections to recover pointwise features at the original resolution. A per-point classification head, implemented with 1× 1 convolutions, batch normalization, ReLU, dropout, and log-softmax, produces per-point class log-probabilities; applying exp(·) yields the corresponding per-point class probabilities. The generic Zl notation used in this figure denotes the multi-level encoder features that serve as latent representations in the target-adaptation and source-refinement stages, where they are written explicitly as Zl tar and Zl src in Figures 4 and 5, respectively.

Figure 1: Reference terrace annotations for the two study regions. Left: Teyuna (Ciudad Perdida); right: Miraflores. Reference terrace annotations are shown over the labelled study extents. Mapped terraces cover approximately 6.5% of the labelled Teyuna extent and approximately 1.5% of the Miraflores extent.

Figure 5: Source refinement for supervised segmentation training. A labeled sourcedomain input patch Xsrc is passed through the shared PointNet++ encoder to obtain hierarchical latent features Zl src for l ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}. At each feature level, the encoder output is tokenized into U l 0,src, partially noised to a shared starting depth tl0, and then refined token-wise through a deterministic DDIM reverse process using the level-specific target-trained denoiser Dl. The refined token matrix Ũ l 0,src is unflattened to Z̃l src and supplied to the decoder through a straight-through estimator (STE), so that the decoder uses the refined features in the forward pass while segmentation gradients flow back to the original encoder features during backpropagation. The decoder output is supervised by the source ground-truth labels using the class-weighted NLL loss Lseg. The figure shows the principal configuration in which all four PointNet++ feature levels are refined. During training, source refinement is stochastic overall because the initial Gaussian perturbation is sampled randomly, whereas the subsequent DDIM reverse trajectory is deterministic conditional on the resulting partially noised token.

Figure 4: target domain latent diffusion adaptation. Unlabeled target domain input patches Xtar are passed through the shared PointNet++ encoder to obtain multi-level latent features Zl tar, l ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}. At each level, the target features are detached from the backbone and flattened into token matrices U l 0,tar, so the target domain diffusion objective does not propagate gradients into PointNet++. Each token is independently assigned a diffusion timestep tli and perturbed with Gaussian noise according to the forward diffusion process. A level-specific denoiser Dl(·, ·;ϕl), conditioned on the noisy token and its timestep embedding, predicts the added noise. Within each level, the same denoiser is shared across all tokens, while denoiser parameters are not shared between feature levels. The level-wise noise-prediction losses are computed as mean-squared error between the sampled and predicted noise and are combined into the total diffusion loss Ldiff . Consequently, target domain adaptation updates only the denoiser parameters ϕl, allowing the denoisers to learn the latent feature distribution of the unlabeled target domain for subsequent source-feature refinement and adapted inference. The figure shows the principal configuration in which all four PointNet++ feature levels are active; the level-ablation experiments use the corresponding subsets of these levels.15

Figure 6: Precision–recall curves for the three principal configurations, averaged over three random seeds. The left panel shows Teyuna → Miraflores and the right panel Miraflores → Teyuna. Solid lines show the mean across three random seeds, and shaded regions indicate one standard deviation across seeds. The compared configurations are sourceonly PointNet++, MELD, and MELD+geometry.

Table 1: Cross-region terrace detection (point level, all points): F1 as mean ± standard deviation over three random seeds. Single applies adaptation at the deepest level (l = 4); multi at all four levels (l ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}). Mean is the unweighted average of the two directions. Best result per column in bold. The target-only oracle (italic) is an in-domain supervised reference trained with five-fold cross-validation on the evaluation region of each direction; it is not a competing UDA method and is reported for context only.

Table 2: MELD level ablation: effect of activating diffusion adaptation at different PointNet++ feature levels (no KNN features; adaptation enabled). The first column lists the active level set. F1 as mean ± standard deviation over three random seeds. Best result per column in bold.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes MELD, a multi-level latent-diffusion adaptation method for cross-region point cloud segmentation, effectively combining 3D perception with foundation model techniques.
papers.title: Multi-level latent-diffusion adaptation for cross-region point cloud segmentation of ancient terraces
papers.tldr: MELD adapts lidar point-cloud terrace segmentation across archaeological regions by refining hierarchical features with target-domain latent diffusion, improving cross-region F1 without target labels.

papers.abstract: Arbitrary-scale light field spatial super-resolution reconstructs high-resolution views at any requested scale from low-resolution multi-view observations. Gaussian primitives enable continuous reconstruction, but generating separate primitive sets for each view redundantly encodes shared scene structure across views and causes the primitive count grow linearly with the number of views. To avoid such redundancy, we propose MacroGS, a feed-forward decoder that jointly predicts a single shared Gaussian set per macro pixel rather than generating separate sets for each view. Disparity-dependent replacement and angle-conditioned appearance allow each set to be reused across all output views, keeping the predicted primitive count independent of the number of views at each requested scale. The decoder iteratively predicts per-primitive disparities, retrieves the corresponding multi-view features, and updates the primitive states. Gaussian splatting and residual refinement then reconstruct the output light field. Despite being learned without geometric supervision, the predicted disparities strongly correlate with underlying scene geometry. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that MacroGS integrates effectively with diverse light field encoders, improving reconstruction quality at fixed scales while achieving leading performance across most evaluated arbitrary-scale settings. The decoder also achieves speedups of approximately $2$-$10\times$ over state-of-the-art implicit light field decoders and $10$-$18\times$ over the view-wise Gaussian baseline.
authors: Zeqiang Wei, Angulia Yang, Min Xu
bullets: Targets redundant, view-wise Gaussian representations whose primitive count grows with the number of output views.
Predicts one Gaussian set per macro pixel and reuses it across views through disparity-dependent replacement and angle-conditioned appearance.
Iteratively updates primitive states using predicted disparities and retrieved multi-view features, followed by Gaussian splatting and residual refinement.
Improves reconstruction quality at fixed scales and performs strongly across most arbitrary-scale evaluations on five benchmarks.
Reports roughly 2–10× speedups over implicit light-field decoders and 10–18× over a view-wise Gaussian baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The framework of MacroGS for arbitrary-scale LFSSR. From the encoder features F, MacroGS infers one set G of K Gaussian primitives per macro pixel, shared by all views, through (a) initialization from all views and (b) R rounds of iterative cross-view reading. (c) View-conditioned rendering splats the set into every view at scale s, and a view-wise convolutional branch R adds a residual correction.
Figure 3. Error maps of GSASR, SEIIF and MacroGS from ×2 to ×8, using (a) DistgSSR and (b) EPIT encoders.

Figure 1. Gaussian representations of a 2 × 2 light field at one requested scale; colours mark the K primitives. Only the primitives generated at the red pixel are drawn; every LR pixel generates its own set. (a) Applying an image Gaussian decoder [5, 24, 42] separately to each SAI gives UV Khw primitives (K per pixel in each view) with separately predicted geometric parameters. (b) MacroGS jointly predicts K primitives from the angular observations of each macro pixel and shares them across all SAIs, giving Khw primitives. Each primitive’s disparity controls its displacement across views.
Figure 5. Mean disparity maps from MacroGS with RASLF at ×4, on one scene per benchmark. Each map is normalized separately, and darker is closer.

papers.title: MacroGS: Macro-Pixel Shared Gaussian Primitives for Arbitrary-Scale Light Field Super-Resolutio

papers.abstract: Generating realistic 3D brain MRI volumes from sparse anatomical priors is a highly ill-posed yet clinically valuable problem, with important applications in data augmentation, simulation, and downstream neuroimaging analysis. In this work, we investigate the challenging task of synthesising full 3D brain MRI volumes conditioned solely on vascular label maps. While vascular structures provide strong anatomical and topological cues, they occupy only a small fraction of the brain volume and offer no direct information about surrounding tissue appearance. To address this challenge, we propose Vessel2Brain, an edge-aware multi-scale conditional flow matching framework that explicitly incorporates vascular structure information into the generative process. Our approach formulates vessel-guided brain image synthesis as a conditional continuous flow, enabling stable training and flexible generation while preserving structural correspondence. A multi-scale flow matching strategy is introduced to jointly model global anatomical coherence and fine-grained local details, with auxiliary velocity predictions providing additional supervision across spatial resolutions. Furthermore, we design an edge-aware objective that emphasises vascular boundaries during training, encouraging anatomically faithful tissue synthesis around vessel structures. We evaluate Vessel2Brain on two public 3D brain MRI datasets with paired vascular annotations. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art generative models in terms of reconstruction accuracy, structural consistency, and distributional realism.
authors: Zhi Chen, Tianyang Zhang, Theodoros N. Arvanitis, Le Zhang
bullets: Addresses the ill-posed task of synthesizing full brain MRI volumes from vascular label maps that provide limited tissue-appearance information.
Uses conditional continuous flow matching to preserve correspondence between generated anatomy and vessel structures.
Combines multi-scale modeling for global anatomical coherence and local detail with auxiliary velocity supervision.
Adds an edge-aware objective to improve tissue synthesis around vascular boundaries.
Evaluated on two public paired 3D brain MRI datasets, with reported gains in reconstruction accuracy, structural consistency, and distributional realism over existing generative models.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed Vessel2Brain framework. Given a 3D vascular label map and a time step t, a UNet-style FlowNet conditioned on timestep and label embeddings learns a velocity field for conditional flow matching. Velocity fields are predicted at multiple spatial resolutions through a main velocity head and an auxiliary velocity head. Edge-aware weighting derived from Sobel operators on the vascular volume emphasises vessel boundaries during training. The predicted velocity fields are integrated to generate the final 3D brain MRI volume, while auxiliary outputs provide additional multi-scale supervision.

Fig. 3. Qualitative comparison on the TopBrain Challenge dataset. The visualization setting and column order are the same as in Fig. 2. Vessel2Brain produces more anatomically coherent brain structures and clearer local details than competing methods under sparse vascular conditioning.

Fig. 2. Qualitative comparison on the CereVessMRA dataset. From left to right: vascular mask, ground-truth brain MRI, 3D Pix2Pix, LDM, 3D VAE, Med-DDPM, and the proposed Vessel2Brain. Results are visualized on representative sagittal, coronal, and axial slices. The highlighted regions and corresponding zoomed-in views illustrate finegrained anatomical details. Compared with baseline methods, Vessel2Brain generates more anatomically consistent brain structures while better preserving vascular-aligned tissue appearance under sparse vessel conditioning.

Table 1. Quantitative comparison on the CereVessMRA dataset. Results are reported as mean ± standard deviation. ↑/↓ denote that higher/lower values indicate better performance. Vessel2Brain consistently outperforms representative GAN-, VAE-, and diffusion-based baselines across all metrics, highlighting its effectiveness for vesselguided 3D brain MRI generation under sparse conditioning.

Table 2. Quantitative comparison on the TopBrain Challenge dataset. The evaluation protocol, metric definitions (↑/↓), and reporting format (mean ± std.) are the same as in Table 1. Vessel2Brain achieves the best performance across all metrics, indicating strong generalization under increased dataset heterogeneity.

papers.title: Vessel2Brain: Edge-Aware Multi-Scale Flow Matching for 3D Brain Image Generation from Vessel Masks
papers.tldr: Vessel2Brain generates realistic 3D brain MRI volumes from sparse vascular masks using edge-aware, multi-scale conditional flow matching.

papers.abstract: Recent open-vocabulary multi-view indoor 3D detection methods typically follow a point-cloud-driven pipeline, where pseudo 3D boxes are generated from reconstructed or estimated geometry and semantic labels are inferred from projected regions. However, such a design makes box generation dependent on the completeness of point clouds and restricts semantic learning to local appearance, causing inferior 3D object localization and open-vocabulary classification. In this paper, we present See and Detect, an image-driven framework that uses multi-view images as the primary evidence for 3D box and semantic label generation. For box generation, we first discover object candidates from individual images, enabling objects missing in point clouds to be recovered from visual evidence. However, single-view predictions are often noisy and redundant. To address this, we propose multi-view consensus box consolidation to fuse spatially consistent predictions across views, and box quality assessment to reduce the impact of boxes with partial object coverage. For semantic label generation, we introduce context-aware semantic learning, where semantic labels are queried from full image context, enabling more accurate semantic prediction. Extensive experiments on ScanNet and ARKitScenes demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art open-vocabulary multi-view 3D detection performance while running over 500$\times$ faster than the previous state-of-the-art method.
authors: Yating Xu, Na Zhao, Chenhan Jiang, Qingwen Zhang, Jiankang Deng, Jifei Song
bullets: Addresses point-cloud incompleteness and limited local appearance in existing open-vocabulary multi-view 3D detectors.
Generates 3D box candidates from individual images, then fuses consistent predictions across views with multi-view consensus box consolidation.
Uses box quality assessment to reduce errors from boxes that only partially cover objects.
Applies context-aware semantic learning by querying labels from full image context.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on ScanNet and ARKitScenes, with over 500× faster runtime than the previous best method.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Comparison of training pipelines for open-vocabulary multi-view 3D object detection. (a) Existing methods [7, 12] propose pointcloud-driven approach for 3D box and semantic label generation, which leads to (i) missing object discovery and (ii) incorrect semantic label generation. (b) See and Detect (Ours) proposes a multi-view image-driven approach: objects are discovered through cross-view visual evidence, and semantic labels are generated by considering image contexts.

Figure 2. Our framework. During training, it is optimized by two main objectives: (1) a Weighted Localization Loss Lwloc, where generated pseudo 3D boxes are weighted by the quality scores Q (Eqn. 3) based on their geometric consistency (details shown in Fig. 3); and (2) a Text-3D Contrastive Loss Ltext-3D, which aligns 3D features f3D with semantic labels inferred from MLLM by jointly considering local appearance and global context. We apply Semantic-aware Negative Class Selection to generate informative negative classes.
Figure 5. Qualitative results of open-vocabulary multi-view 3D object detection on ScanNet60.

Figure 3. Image-Driven Pseudo Box Generation. We perform single-view 3D object detection for each image using Cubify Anything. A scene-level undirected graph is constructed where edges represent spatial overlap (Eqn. 1). Multi-View Consensus Box Consolidation is applied to fuse consistent predictions and suppress spurious single-view detections. Finally, each box is assigned a quality score Q through Box Quality Assessment based on cross-view visibility I(vi) and SAM-based object coverage check S(vi), which weights the localization loss during training.

Figure 4. Box quality assessment. (a) shows a pseudo box with incomplete object coverage due to detection from local image views. (b) shows a pseudo box with complete object coverage. We project the boxes to the nearby view vi for box quality assessment. The quality score Q can correctly reflect box quality.

Table 3. 3D pseudo box evaluation on ScanNet200 and ARKitScenes dataset. We report recall (R) and precision (P) at IoU thresholds of 0.25 and 0.50. Best results are marked bold.

papers.tldr: See and Detect uses multi-view images rather than point clouds as the main evidence for open-vocabulary 3D detection, improving object recovery, localization, and semantic labeling while running over 500× faster than the prior state of the art.

papers.abstract: Multi-view 3D transformers such as VGGT reconstruct a scene from a set of unposed images in a single forward pass, predicting camera poses, depth and 3D points, but the cost of their global attention grows quadratically with the num- ber of images. Accelerators borrowed from large language models assume that each token attends to only a few oth- ers; on these models they lose accuracy or gain little speed. We study the global attention of three multi-view transform- ers on seven datasets and find that every layer plays one of three roles: it averages over the whole scene, matches points across many images, or anchors on the first image, whose coordinates the outputs use. Building on this anal- ysis, we propose Regime-AWare ATTention Approximation (RAWATTA), a training-free method that runs attention in 8- bit precision and keeps 16-bit precision only in the layers where a worst-case calibration check requires it. Its fast set- ting, RAWATTA-Fast, also approximates attention in a few averaging and anchoring layers, while matching layers and the first image keep all their keys. On a 12 GB GPU at 50 im- ages, RAWATTA runs VGGT faster than the released code, mostly through our CUDA engine, and loses at most about one point of pose accuracy (AUC@3) on any dataset; RAWATTA-Fast is slightly faster and less accurate. Both fit 200 images, where the released code runs out of memory at 100.
authors: Muhammed Izzet Sezer, Sevval Belkis Dikkaya
bullets: Global attention in multi-view 3D transformers is costly because its complexity grows quadratically with the number of images.
The study identifies three layer roles: scene-wide averaging, cross-image point matching, and anchoring to the first image.
RAWATTA uses 8-bit attention by default and retains 16-bit precision when a worst-case calibration check requires it.
RAWATTA-Fast additionally approximates attention in selected averaging and anchoring layers while preserving full keys for matching layers and the first image.
On VGGT, RAWATTA is faster than the released implementation, loses at most about one AUC@3 pose-accuracy point, and supports 200 images on a 12 GB GPU where the baseline runs out of memory at 100.

papers.abstract: Interactive 3D segmentation models such as nnInteractive turn a few spatial prompts (points, scribbles, boxes) into accurate volumetric masks, but a human still does the annotation work: finding each structure, placing prompts, checking the result and correcting it. General-purpose AI agents can now interpret images, call tools and write code. We show that such agents can take over this work without additional training: the user makes a request in plain language, and the agent works out what has to be segmented, locates the targets, prompts nnInteractive, inspects the 3D result, corrects it and responds to feedback. Asked for 'the muscles used for chewing', an agent identifies and segments the masseters and pterygoids; asked to count liver lesions, it writes its own code to find candidates and splits a merged lesion on request. Our open-source nninteractive-agent provides nnInteractive as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), together with a skill that encodes how experienced users prompt it. On a benchmark spanning CT, MRI, PET and micro-CT of humans, a mouse and an ant (14 images; 51 targets from organs and tumours to muscles, foot bones, vessel trees and an insect brain), Claude Code and Codex reach a mean Dice of 0.81 and 0.84 from the request alone; when told where each target is, both reach 0.85 and prompt nearly as effectively as an oracle that places prompts using the reference segmentation. A text-prompted 3D model (VoxTell) is more accurate on most standard radiological targets but less robust: it returns an empty mask for one of them and fails on the leg muscles, the foot bones, the mouse and the ant, where the agents remain accurate. Code: https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nninteractive-agent
bullets: Addresses the need to automate the human steps required by interactive 3D segmentation.
Uses nnInteractive through MCP tools plus a prompting skill, requiring no additional agent training.
Agents segment diverse targets across CT, MRI, PET, and micro-CT from plain-language requests.
Claude Code and Codex achieve mean Dice scores of 0.81 and 0.84 from requests alone, rising to 0.85 when target locations are provided.
Agents are less accurate than VoxTell on many standard radiological targets but more robust on challenging cases such as leg muscles, foot bones, mouse, and ant data.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing reference videos as editable dynamic 3D scenes is an important path toward controllable video generation for filmmaking: these scenes provide modifiable, renderable visual proxies that enable explicit control over scene layout, subject actions, and camera behavior. To evaluate agents' ability to reconstruct editable dynamic 3D scenes from dynamic reference videos, we introduce CineRecon, a benchmark comprising 50 reference videos and 360 annotated evaluation clips. The reference videos span film, real-world footage, and games. Given a complete video, an agent uses tools to construct, animate, render, and refine its reconstruction. We evaluate this task under three representation settings: Proxy, Simplified, and Detailed. These settings increase geometric and appearance requirements while retaining the same requirements for spatial relations, camera behavior, and subject dynamics. This design tests whether agents can reproduce the events in a video when detailed appearance is unnecessary, and how performance changes as representation requirements increase. For evaluation, we construct checklists that associate observable properties and events with specific entities and times. A vision-language judge compares timestamp-aligned reference and rendered frames across 11 categories, grouped into camera, static, and dynamic consistency dimensions. We evaluate 12 models using their corresponding agent harnesses and find failures across all three dimensions. Subject motions and interactions remain difficult to reproduce even under the Proxy setting.
bullets: Introduces a benchmark with 50 reference videos and 360 annotated evaluation clips spanning film, real-world footage, and games.
Tests three reconstruction settings—Proxy, Simplified, and Detailed—with progressively stricter geometry and appearance requirements.
Uses entity- and time-specific checklists plus a vision-language judge comparing aligned reference and rendered frames across 11 categories.
Evaluates 12 models through their agent harnesses and observes failures in camera, static-scene, and dynamic consistency.
Subject motions and interactions remain challenging even when only proxy representations are required.

papers.abstract: Conditional neural fields represent signals continuously, but their effectiveness depends on how the conditional latent representations are inferred from observed data. In meta-learning, this encoding occurs through gradient updates induced by the decoder, tying representation learning directly to decoder design. We formalize this connection by interpreting latent optimization as an optimization encoder, unifying the roles of second-order differentiation, latent parameterization, and task supervision. This concept enables second-order meta-learning for end-to-end training of the encoding procedure alongside the decoder, and clarifies which learning pathway first-order approximations discard. Guided by this view, we introduce Attentive Latent Fields (MetaLF), an equivariant transformer-based neural field that contextualizes a latent pointcloud through self-attention. These interactions shape both field predictions and the updates that construct their representation, allowing local observations to inform coherent non-local structure. Disentangling the inner encoding objective from outer task supervision unifies reconstruction, classification, and segmentation within an end-to-end meta-learning framework, using reconstruction-only latent adaptation at test time. Controlled experiments on polynomial fields link latent coordination to lower effective rank and stronger alignment with the underlying function space. Across image and 3D shape reconstruction, MetaLF improves fidelity within three to five gradient updates, while supporting semantic prediction across images, shapes, and volumes. Together, these findings position the optimization encoder perspective as a unified basis for designing neural fields around how representations are constructed, coordinated, and used.
bullets: Motivation: Neural-field performance depends on how latent representations are inferred, but this process is tightly coupled to decoder design and often simplified by first-order approximations.
Method: Formalizes latent optimization as an optimization encoder and trains the encoding procedure jointly with the decoder using second-order meta-learning.
Model: MetaLF uses an equivariant, self-attentive transformer to coordinate latent pointclouds, enabling local observations to shape coherent non-local structure.

Findings: Controlled polynomial-field experiments associate latent coordination with lower effective rank and better alignment with the underlying function space; image and 3D reconstruction improves within 3–5 updates.
Scope: The framework supports reconstruction, classification, and segmentation, with reconstruction-only latent adaptation at test time.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Second-order meta-learning trains an optimization encoder whose behaviour is shaped by decoder architecture. (a) A conventional encoder maps an observed signal to a latent representation zi, which the decoder evaluates at a query coordinate x. (b) In meta-learned neural fields, an explicit encoder is replaced by K gradient updates on z, forming an optimization encoder. Second-order differentiation propagates the outer objective Lout through these unrolled updates, jointly shaping the finite-step encoding behavior and the decoder fθ. (c) Because the decoder induces the latent updates, its architecture shapes the resulting adaptation trajectory. ENF represents a local fitting model, lacking direct exchange of context among localized latents. MetaLF instead coordinates these latents through attention. This shared context produces coherent updates that quickly capture non-local structure, as illustrated by fitting cardiac signed distance functions.

Figure 5: MetaLF is equivariant under a group action defined by its bi-invariant feature a. Rows show translationequivariant (Rn) and roto-translation-equivariant (SE(n)) MetaLF models on CelebA and ACDC myocardium. Columns show ground truth, reconstruction in the canonical frame, pose-only translation, joint translation of poses and queries, pose-only roto-translation, and the corresponding joint roto-translation. Acting on poses alone transforms the represented field; applying the same group element jointly to poses and queries preserves predicted values at corresponding coordinates when the model respects that symmetry. Accordingly, joint translations match the canonical reconstruction in every row, whereas joint roto-translation does so only for the SE(n) models.

Figure 3: MetaLF as an optimization encoder. (a) K gradient updates encode observations into a spatially grounded, globally contextualized latent representation through SE(n)-equivariant self-attention (SA) layers and cross-attention (CA) with a query coordinate. (b) During meta-training, task-specific outer objectives can shape the decoder through second-order gradients across the adaptation steps. Global contextualization of the latent point set therefore enables flexible meta-training: the same inner-loop encoder can learn representations tailored to diverse downstream objectives.

Figure 1: Example use case of MetaLF meta-learning latent cardiac shape representations [3]. The first three panels illustrate smooth shape recovery as a shared latent pointcloud z is refined over k = 1, . . . , 5 gradient steps. MetaLF learns contextualized latent representations that preserve detail while capturing the underlying function, an ill-posed task for local representation models such as ENF [4].

Figure 6: Training progress on CIFAR10 reconstruction for MAML (blue) and FOMAML (red). (a) MAML develops a higher latent effective rank, while the first-order controls remain at lower ranks. (b) MAML generally has smaller upper response factors, although these fluctuate during training. (c) MAML’s reconstruction error decreases substantially over training epochs, whereas the first-order controls plateau after an initial improvement. (d) Both methods perform best near the three-step training horizon, with reconstruction error gradually increasing under further adaptation.
Figure 10: Uncurated examples generated using latent rectified flow based on the reconstruction meta-learned MetaLF (MetaLF-Diffuser) representation models.

Figure 7: Optimization encoder-side coupling (top) and decoder-side attention routing (bottom) evaluated on the polynomial fields dataset, shown with increasing number of MetaLF self-attention layers (NSA) for N = 25 latent tokens. Additional layers allow information to propagate beyond local latent neighborhoods while retaining the spatial structure of the representation.

Figure 4: A receiving latent j attends to neighbouring source latents j′ using bi-invariant geometric attributes aj′→j . Keys and values combine this geometry with the source content cj′ , and their attention-weighted aggregation produces the updated feature h′ j .

Figure 8: Qualitative example for OMBRIA meta-segmentation, illustrating the 25th percentile, median, and 75th percentile MetaLF test-set performance sample in terms of IoU. In the median case, SpatialFuncta and ENF produce extensive false-positive flood predictions around cloudy regions, whereas MetaLF largely suppresses them. This pattern is consistent with non-local latent interactions using broader spatial context to resolve ambiguous local signals.
Figure 9: Reconstruction quality as a function of latent pointcloud size. The example uses MetaLF with NSA = 4 and per-latent content size of D = 64.

papers.title: Optimization Encoders: Rethinking Second-Order Meta-Learning for Neural Fields
papers.tldr: The paper reframes latent gradient adaptation as an optimization encoder and introduces MetaLF, a second-order meta-learned neural field that coordinates latent representations for efficient reconstruction and semantic prediction.

papers.abstract: Predictive video encoders provide dense visual representations, but adapting them to 3D reconstruction requires accurate depth, camera poses, and cross-view geometry. We study supervised RGB-only multi-view reconstruction using an architecture that combines video-pretrained features, camera estimation, scene aggregation, epipolar transport, and residual pointmaps. Experiments compare global and spatial camera regression with joint relative objectives on CO3D, alongside an independently trained TUM RGB-D model. On 168 CO3D five-view windows, the spatial-camera configuration achieves 29.3% lower absolute trajectory error than the global-camera configuration, but performs worse than identity poses in trajectory error and worse than the global configuration in depth error. The joint relative-objective configuration improves normalized intrinsics error and similarity-aligned Chamfer distance from 0.6447 to 0.5573, but increases raw Chamfer distance from 3.5535 to 4.4374. On 163 indoor windows, camera error is 0.3063 m versus 0.3694 m for identity poses, while depth error is 0.4279 versus 0.2516 for constant median depth. Refinement worsens indoor camera error, and additional experiments show competing depth and pose effects. Overall, the results distinguish representation adaptation, aligned shape, and raw reconstruction, highlighting the need for isolated component and encoder comparisons before attributing reconstruction gains to predictive video pretraining.
bullets: Evaluates supervised RGB-only reconstruction using video-pretrained features, camera estimation, scene aggregation, epipolar transport, and residual pointmaps.
On CO3D, spatial camera regression reduces trajectory error versus global regression, but identity poses achieve better trajectory error and global regression achieves better depth error.
Joint relative objectives improve normalized intrinsics and similarity-aligned Chamfer distance, while worsening raw Chamfer distance.
On indoor windows, estimated poses improve camera error over identity poses but have worse depth error than constant median depth; refinement further harms camera accuracy.
Results emphasize separating representation adaptation, camera estimation, aligned shape, and raw reconstruction when evaluating predictive video pretraining.

figures.caption: Figure 2: CO3D geometric trade-offs. The spatial-camera configuration has lower camera ATE than the global-camera configuration. The relative-objective configuration has lower intrinsics and aligned-surface errors than the spatial-camera configuration, but higher depth and raw-surface errors. Dashed controls are training-median depth, identity cameras and training-median intrinsics. The configurations differ jointly in architecture, supervision and selection criterion.

Figure 1: Our reconstruction architecture. Video-pretrained features are extracted separately from each image. Explicit camera estimation and epipolar transport provide multi-view geometry. Dashed arrows denote a training-only observedview distillation objective. Cross-view rendering supervision is omitted for clarity.

Figure 4: First test window for each setting: CO3D spatial camera and the independently trained TUM model. Each RGB row is followed by signed depth error, predicted minus reference. White pixels lack valid reference depth. Color ranges are [−3, 3] in CO3D coordinates and [−1.5, 1.5] m on TUM, with saturation beyond the limits. Blue indicates depth underestimation. These windows illustrate failure patterns rather than the distribution of all errors.

Figure 3: Indoor generalization and geometry. The model improves camera ATE over identity but has higher depth error than training-median depth. Reference fitting substantially changes surface F-score. Validation AbsRel improves during training while the selected model’s held-out-sequence error remains higher. The test line represents one selected model, not repeated test evaluation over training.

Figure 5: Five-view camera centers in the first test window of CO3D and TUM. Orthographic XY and XZ projections use the same reference frame for predictions and labels, with no fitted trajectory alignment. Lines connect the sampled views in temporal order. CO3D compares the three configurations on identical observations; TUM compares initial and refined predictions from its independently trained model. These local windows do not constitute a full-sequence trajectory.

Figure 7: Confidence reliability and target retrieval for the relative-objective CO3D model. Left: observed relative-depth success versus predicted confidence on valid test pixels. Right: validation target retrieval over training, with the selected model marked. Later retrieval improvements are not measurements of the model used for the primary reconstruction tables.

Figure 8: Depth and camera validation measurements over 20 epochs. Markers with black outlines identify the selected epochs: 14, 12 and 9 for global camera, spatial camera and relative objectives on CO3D, and 18 for the independently trained TUM model. Vertical dotted lines separate the frozen, partially adapted and alignment-focused stages. The two TUM camera curves use identical observations and alignment.

Figure 10: TUM multi-view depth predictions for the first test window. Rows show RGB, reference depth and the independently trained indoor model’s prediction. Depth uses one shared scale in meters across all views and both depth rows. Invalid reference depth and letterbox padding are excluded from the depth display.

Figure 6: XZ projections of reconstructed pointmaps for the first test window. Gray denotes the fixed reference surface; blue denotes predicted points after confidence 0.005 and support filtering. The right column uses a separate reference-fitted similarity transform per window. Axes are identical within each row, and points are subsampled only for display. The two CO3D configurations share their reference window; the indoor row uses TUM meters. Shape after reference fitting is distinct from unaligned accuracy in the first-view coordinate frame.

Figure 12: Depth and camera trade-offs in the two three-view component suites. Each metric is divided by its own suite’s baseline error, with lower values better. papers.abstract: Pore-space evolution and fluid displacement influence how rocks transmit and store fluids, affecting geological carbon storage, underground hydrogen storage and groundwater contaminant transport. A single time-resolved micro-CT experiment may produce tens to hundreds of three-dimensional images, and segmentation is required to quantify physical properties and run image-based simulations. Traditional methods such as thresholding perform poorly on noisy, low-contrast images and need manual adjustment per image; 3D deep learning networks segment each image without temporal information, so their errors vary between images and could be mistaken for physical change. Here we introduce a transformer-based 4D segmentation framework combining spatial and temporal information. It uses sequential images to resolve ambiguous phase assignments and separate physical change from segmentation error. The method is tested on images of mineral dissolution: it measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries more accurately than an equivalent 3D model that ignores temporal information. It also captures the increase in permeability verified against reference segmentations and flow simulations. The advantage transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining. On two other datasets of fluid displacement, it reduces spurious changes in predicted rock and porosity fluctuations and accurately identifies filling events. Spatiotemporal segmentation turns sequences of hundreds of three-dimensional images into more reliable quantitative measurements of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement without per-image parameter adjustment to support the analysis of time-resolved CT imaging.
authors: Zhuangzhuang Ma, Rukuan Chai, Qianqian Ma, Yanghua Wang, Branko Bijeljic, Martin J. Blunt
bullets: Addresses noisy, low-contrast CT images where conventional segmentation requires image-specific manual tuning and independent 3D models can confuse segmentation errors with physical change.
Combines spatial and temporal information in a 4D transformer framework to resolve ambiguous phase assignments across image sequences.
More accurately measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries than a comparable spatial-only 3D model in mineral-dissolution experiments.
Captures permeability increases consistent with reference segmentations and flow simulations, and transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining.
Reduces spurious rock and porosity fluctuations while identifying filling events in fluid-displacement datasets.

papers.abstract: We present Kosmo-GFM, a scene reconstruction system that integrates a geometry foundation model (GFM), a pose optimization engine (PoseEngine), and reconstruction-derived supervision from KosmoWorld. GFM predicts camera parameters, depth, cross-view correspondences, and dynamic 3D points from images and videos. PoseEngine combines these predictions with geometric optimization to recover scene-level camera poses and geometry for downstream 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting. KosmoWorld generates images and geometric supervision from reconstructed real-world scenes to improve GFM's geometric predictions. On the Sparse and Medium subsets of SpatialBench, GFM achieves the lowest absolute relative depth error and the highest relative-pose AUC at 5 degrees among the compared methods. It also achieves the lowest mean endpoint errors for dynamic points and scene flow across the five evaluated datasets. Across 34 scenes completed by all compared reconstruction systems, PoseEngine achieves the highest scene-averaged pose AUC at thresholds of 1, 3, and 5 degrees, with a cumulative runtime of 14.07 hours, approximately 20% of GLUEMAP's 69.67 hours. PoseEngine Flash provides a further accuracy-efficiency trade-off, with a measured mixed-precision runtime of 2.62 hours, approximately 4% of GLUEMAP's runtime. Separate scaling experiments show generally favorable trends with increased data, model computation, and training budgets. These results support the use of learned geometric priors within a scene-level reconstruction pipeline.

papers.abstract: LiDAR is a core sensor for autonomous driving, yet it is highly vulnerable to fog. Fog scattering produces strong backscatter near the sensor and attenuates reflections from objects behind it, so weak object returns are often discarded by the peak detection that converts received signals into point clouds. Full-waveform LiDAR (FWL), which records the received optical signal before peak detection, retains these weak returns, but the lack of suitable data has prevented research on recovering fog-hidden objects from FWL. We present Fog-FWL, a dataset foundation for this task that consists of a real-world benchmark, Fog-FWL-Real, and a large-scale synthetic training set, Fog-FWL-Sim. Fog-FWL-Real contains 7,527 real foggy FWL frames from 8 scenes and 58 sequences, which is 579x larger than the only existing real foggy FWL data, together with histogram-level Object/Fog/Noise labels, 10,719 3D bounding boxes, and three difficulty levels defined by the attenuation of object reflections. Fog-FWL-Sim contains 12,000 frames generated by our physics-based simulator, Fog-FWL-Simulator, which integrates spatially heterogeneous fog density fields, time-resolved light transport including multiple scattering, and a photon-counting SPAD receiver model. The two subsets share the same sensor format and annotation protocol, enabling a strict sim-to-real evaluation in which no real waveforms are used for training. Our analysis shows that, under the hardest condition, object returns are included in the three strongest peaks for only 34.9% of object rays, underscoring the need for waveform-level recovery. Fog-FWL-Real, Fog-FWL-Sim, and the Fog-FWL-Simulator will be publicly released to facilitate research on fog-robust LiDAR perception.

Fog-FWL-Sim provides 12,000 simulated frames generated with heterogeneous fog, multiple-scattering light transport, and a photon-counting receiver model.
Shared formats and annotations support strict sim-to-real evaluation without using real waveforms for training.

papers.abstract: Image-to-3D generative models now produce asset-quality textured meshes, but at minutes per asset they remain slow to iterate with and costly to deploy. Prior work has mostly accelerated the sampling of the networks, and where it also optimizes the mesh processing, it trains its own generators. We instead start from a publicly released pipeline and ask how much of its end-to-end time can be saved. Profiling the public Pixal3D pipeline shows that its latency is dominated by what happens after the networks: the four rectified flows take 14% of the wall-clock time and mesh post-processing takes 85%, most of it in CPU-based UV unwrapping. We therefore first rebuild the mesh post-processing on the GPU and take it off the critical path, then cut the per-evaluation overhead of the flows and distill them from 76 to 8 network evaluations. The resulting pipeline, Sprint3D, reduces the median time per asset from 133 s to 4.05 s on one H200 GPU at the same export settings (33$\times$). At the same time, on 2,653 held-out Toys4K objects it improves every input-view normal metric of the Pixal3D protocol, with a slightly lower mean silhouette IoU, lower point-cloud alignment scores and less fine texture detail. The rebuilt post-processing alone also speeds up TRELLIS.2, which uses the same export code, by 6.7$\times$ without a detectable change in the evaluated metrics.

It reduces rectified-flow evaluations from 76 to 8 and cuts per-evaluation overhead.
On one H200 GPU, median generation time drops 33× under the same export settings.
Quality improves on input-view normal metrics, but silhouette IoU, point-cloud alignment, and fine texture detail decline; the post-processing optimization also speeds TRELLIS.2 by 6.7×.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing optically thick media from photographs requires modeling multiple scattering and its response to changes in extinction. Frozen-source tomography discards this derivative; differentiable path tracing estimates it through expensive, noisy sampling. We instead predict the multiple-scattering field with a neural operator and differentiate through it during inverse rendering, while computing transmittance and single scattering directly. A further challenge arises during optimization: an operator that predicts the field accurately on held-out media can still produce poor derivatives at the density states visited by the optimizer. We address this by fine-tuning on states generated during inversions driven by the operator, using Monte Carlo scattering-field supervision. On held-out optically thick clouds, our method improves relighting over frozen-source tomography at equal time and outperforms differentiable path tracing given substantially more time. Training on inversion trajectories also improves derivative alignment at visited states and reduces optimization drift.
bullets: Frozen-source tomography ignores how multiple scattering changes with extinction, while differentiable path tracing is expensive and noisy.
The method predicts the multiple-scattering field with a neural operator and differentiates through it; transmittance and single scattering are computed directly.
Fine-tuning on optimizer-generated inversion states improves derivative alignment where optimization actually occurs.
On held-out optically thick clouds, the approach improves relighting over frozen-source tomography at equal time and outperforms differentiable path tracing with substantially more time.
Trajectory training reduces optimization drift.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Method overview – (a) The inversion renders the training views with exact transmittance and single scattering, and with the multiple-scattering source predicted by Gϕ. Differentiating through the operator supplies Jmulti,ϕ for the density update; an occasional Monte Carlo correction ∆ adjusts the values only. (b) The operator is pretrained on generic media, fine-tuned for the target regime, and further trained on density states visited during inversion.

Figure 6. What is reconstructed – Vertical density slices: a ramp without the light-side derivative, speckle for PRB, clumps for ours (number: relative density error over the grid, lowest in bold). Top: near the median margin among the 6 of 12 media where ours has the lowest density error of the methods shown (PRB after 30 min is lower on five Cloudy ones); below: the media of Fig. 5.

Figure 5. Two more held-out clouds – The media of the main evaluation at the 25th and 75th percentile of our gain over Frozen Source (procedural cumulus, maximum optical depth 45 and 60), shown as in Fig. 1 under their most back-lit new light (errors saturate at 20% of the exposure); without the light-side derivative large parts of the clouds are relit wrongly.

Figure 2. Why the missing derivative matters – In the forward pass both methods render all orders of scattering. In the backward pass, Frozen Source [27] holds the scattered light fixed (stop-gradient): the gradient reaches a local density change δσt only along its line of sight (camera side). Ours also differentiates through the neural operator Gϕ, whose learned nonlocal gradient (red) captures how δσt redistributes the scattered light far beyond that line (the exact direct-beam term is not drawn).

Figure 4. Accurate multiple-scattering derivatives at low cost – Response of the multiple-scattering source (angular mean; shared color scale, red: increase, blue: decrease) to a local density increase v (circle; vertical slice of the cloud of Fig. 1; arrow: input light). One Monte Carlo central difference (7.4 × 109 photons per evaluation) takes 23 min and reaches our error; ours takes 77 ms (each on one B200, offline training excluded): about 17,000 times faster for this directional derivative (not inversion gradients or PRB). Cosine and errors are σs-weighted against a reference of two independent estimates (45 min in total; the first is shown). Top right: error over time (Monte Carlo: noise; ours: bias).

Figure 7. Trajectory training reduces optimization drift – The medium of Fig. 1 after 16 min on all 32 views, final iterate without held-out selection: relit (top, PSNR) and density slice (bottom, density error). With the scope operator the iterate runs into density spikes; with the trajectory operator it stays far closer to the truth.

papers.abstract: Cameras and LiDARs (Light Detection and Ranging) provide complementary observations of the same scene: cameras capture rich appearance cues while LiDAR sensors provide accurate geometric measurements. In this work, we address the problem of fine image-to-point cloud registration from a single image and a roughly estimated camera pose. On robotic platforms, residual reprojection errors of several pixels are commonly observed even after calibration due to temporal desynchronization, mechanical vibrations, or inaccuracies in point cloud reconstruction. Such errors can lead to decimeter-level geometric discrepancies at moderate distances and significantly affect multiple downstream tasks, such as dense cross-modal supervision, texture mapping, and semantic label transfer. To address this challenge, we introduce ReFineR: an offline framework to finely register individual images to pre-reconstructed point clouds. ReFineR builds upon differentiable point splatting rasterization and a smooth Gradient Orientation Measure (GOM) to iteratively refine the camera pose through analysis-by-synthesis optimization. We evaluated the method on a curated dataset of manually calibrated images collected from heterogeneous data sources. Furthermore, we show that an automatic point cloud rescale factor can be estimated prior to optimization, enabling robust refinement across a wide range of scenarios using a single scale-invariant formulation. The project page can be found at https://refiner-project.github.io/
authors: Ugo Insalaco, Jean-Emmanuel Deschaud, Pierre Dellenbach
bullets: Addresses residual image–LiDAR misalignment caused by calibration, synchronization, vibration, and reconstruction errors.
Uses differentiable point-splatting rasterization and a smooth Gradient Orientation Measure for analysis-by-synthesis pose optimization.
Estimates an automatic point-cloud rescale factor before optimization for robust, scale-invariant refinement.
Evaluated on manually calibrated images gathered from heterogeneous data sources.
Targets improved dense cross-modal supervision, texture mapping, and semantic label transfer.

papers.abstract: Calibrated multi-view hand reconstruction has advanced rapidly, yet the effectiveness of existing methods depends strongly on real captured data, which is costly to acquire, limited in hand-geometry diversity, and often affected by imperfect annotations. Synthetic data offers a scalable alternative with accurate supervision, but a substantial synthetic-to-real appearance gap hinders its use. To address this, we introduce Hand in Silhouette (SilHand), a calibrated multi-view hand reconstruction framework that operates on binary hand masks, obtainable at low cost either automatically or manually, to reduce the synthetic-to-real observation gap. Rather than relying on RGB features for 3D lifting, SilHand projects metric 3D hypotheses into each view to query and fuse mask-ray evidence for hand reconstruction. This mask-centric formulation enables training on a large-scale synthetic dataset comprising 46.8k grasping poses and 60k free-hand samples, providing broad coverage of hand geometry while directly transferring to real captured hand geometry. Across five real-world benchmarks, SilHand improves relative reconstruction accuracy from 49.2% to 63.4% using masks rendered from reference hands. Moreover, reconstruction accuracy improves consistently as the synthetic training set grows, indicating that broader geometric coverage translates into better real-world performance. While achieving such diversity is difficult with real captured data, it becomes practical under our mask-centric formulation. Finally, SilHand remains robust under mask corruption, with reconstruction error increasing by at most 1.63 mm. Together, these results support binary masks as an effective interface for learning hand reconstruction from synthetic geometry.
authors: Leiyao Cui, Lecheng Ruan, Zihang Zhao
bullets: Targets the costly, limited, and imperfectly annotated real data required for calibrated multi-view hand reconstruction.
Projects metric 3D hand hypotheses into each camera and fuses mask-ray evidence for reconstruction.
Trains on synthetic data covering 46.8k grasping poses and 60k free-hand samples, enabling broad hand-geometry diversity.
Improves relative reconstruction accuracy from 49.2% to 63.4% across five real-world benchmarks using masks rendered from reference hands.
Performance improves with larger synthetic training sets and remains robust to mask corruption, with error increasing by at most 1.63 mm.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Framework of SilHand. Given calibrated multi-view binary masks, SilHand projects points from a shared metric 3D grid into each view to query mask and Plücker-ray features, which are fused by cross-view attention and a 3D CNN into a shared 3D representation. From this representation, SilHand first estimates the global hand pose, canonicalizes the 3D evidence, and then uses a token-query decoder to predict the hand pose and shape parameters.

papers.abstract: Dynamic reconstruction from casual video must preserve valid subject motion while suppressing transient occluders, shadows, and volumetric effects. Existing methods either suppress valid motion through static-scene assumptions or model all observations jointly, producing ghosting and unstable geometry. We introduce ReCan-GS, a 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that separates coherent scene content from inconsistent observations. It derives a Jacobian-based deformation-sensitivity score from the learned deformation field, using it as an empirical proxy for reconstruction ambiguity. The score guides separation into dynamic Core Gaussians and per-view Distractor Gaussians, or post-hoc pruning of sensitive Core Gaussians. The same criterion supports removal of spatial occluders, photometric artifacts, and evolving smoke or fog without masks, pretrained segmenters, or medium-specific supervision. Experiments on synthetic and real dynamic scenes and synthetic smoke/fog scenes demonstrate its usefulness across the evaluated distractor regimes.
authors: Joel Julin, Liuyue Xie, Ananya Bal, Mose Sakashita, Koichiro Niinuma, Laszlo A. Jeni
bullets: Addresses ghosting and unstable geometry caused by jointly modeling valid motion and inconsistent observations.
Uses a Jacobian-based deformation-sensitivity score as a proxy for reconstruction ambiguity.
Separates coherent dynamic content into Core Gaussians and inconsistent observations into per-view Distractor Gaussians, or prunes sensitive Core Gaussians post hoc.
Handles spatial occluders, photometric artifacts, smoke, and fog across synthetic and real evaluated scenes.
Scope is limited to the distractor regimes and experiments described in the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 2. An overview of our ReCan-GS pipeline. The scene is modeled with two components: dynamic Core Gaussians (G) and per-view Distractor Gaussians (Gdist). An MLP deforms the core Gaussians over time (t). A Jacobian-based uncertainty signal, derived from the deformation field, guides the optimization to penalize unstable motion in the core layer, effectively forcing transient effects into the distractor layer.

Figure 3. Qualitative results on dynamic scenes with distractors. Columns 2–3 are dynamic reconstruction methods that jointly model all motion, often producing ghosting from transient occluders. Columns 4–5 are standard distractor-removal methods that assume a static scene and therefore struggle with valid dynamic content. ReCan-GS explicitly decomposes inconsistent observations into a distractor layer and recovers a clean, stable core reconstruction.

Figure 4. Smoke removal results. ReCan-GS separates slow-moving volumetric distractors from the core scene by detecting deformationspace instability, enabling clean smoke-free reconstructions where appearance-based methods leave residual haze.

Figure 7. Hierarchical Sensitivity. Post-hoc pruning removes the top 0%, 5%, 7%, and 15% most uncertain Core Gaussians, ranked by accumulated deformation sensitivity. Without pruning, transient hands and moving cast shadows remain. Removing the top 5% primarily suppresses the hands, while pruning the top 7% and 15% additionally suppresses moving cast shadows.

Table 2. Quantitative results on dynamic scenes with distractors, grouped into static distractor-removal and dynamic reconstruction methods. Higher is better for PSNR/SSIM and lower for LPIPS; best results per scene are in bold. Real-scene holdout frames are distractor-free, so these metrics do not fully measure retained distractor geometry; see Table 3.

Table 3. Retained distractor geometry. Three human annotators and three VLM judges rate per frame how strongly the distractor is reproduced (1 = absent, 5 = fully reproduced); mean severity and (% of frames rated ≥ 3). VLMs score all distractor-present frames (Bottle: 534, Jeep: 345); the Human column averages three annotators over the same 50 frames per method, who agree closely (mean pairwise quadratic-weighted κ = 0.85, Spearman ρ = 0.87 over 900 paired ratings). On Jeep, no annotator rated any ReCanGS frame ≥ 3. Per-annotator scores are on the project website.
Table 1. Feature comparison. Our method uniquely supports distractor removal in fully dynamic scenes without pretraining.

Table 4. Fog/smoke removal on synthetic scenes with fog-free ground truth. Appearance-based methods misidentify volumetric fog as stable background; ReCan-GS removes it without any fog-specific design. Best results in bold.

papers.tldr: ReCan-GS reconstructs dynamic scenes from casual video while removing transient occluders and volumetric artifacts without masks or specialized supervision.

papers.abstract: Low-level clouds are one of the largest sources of uncertainty in climate predictions, partly because we lack detailed three-dimensional (3D) measurements of their internal structure. Here, we present HybridCT, a cloud tomographic reconstruction scheme accelerated by machine learning (ML) that recovers 3D cloud extinction directly from passive multi-angle observations. An ML emulator maps radiances from multiple viewing angles to cloud optical thickness (COT), producing path-integrated projections, and a Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART) explicitly inverts these projections to retrieve 3D extinction. Training observations are generated from synthetic 3D cloud fields using radiative transfer simulations for nine viewing angles between $\pm$70$^{\circ}$. HybridCT reconstructs extinction with RMSE 13.3 km$^{-1}$ in 3.5 s, compared to 22.7 km$^{-1}$ in approx. 30 min for the state-of-the-art physics-based tomography framework AT3D, a speedup exceeding 500$\times$. HybridCT thus provides a scalable route toward large-scale observations of 3D cloud structure relevant to radiative-budget interpretation and evaluation of high-resolution cloud simulations.
authors: Linda Forster, Nicholas J. LaHaye, Marcin J. Kurowski, Anna Jungbluth, Bernhard Mayer, Anthony B. Davis
bullets: Addresses uncertainty in climate predictions caused by limited measurements of low-level cloud internal structure.
An ML emulator converts radiances from nine viewing angles into cloud optical-thickness projections, which SART inverts into 3D extinction.
Trained using radiative-transfer simulations of synthetic 3D cloud fields.
Reaches 13.3 km⁻¹ RMSE in 3.5 seconds, versus 22.7 km⁻¹ in about 30 minutes for AT3D—over 500× faster.
Scope: the approach is demonstrated with synthetic training observations and aims to support scalable cloud-structure observations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of HybridCT. (1) Multi-angle passive radiances are first mapped to cloud optical thickness projections using a U-Net. (2) The resulting projections are then inverted with an explicit SART tomography solver to reconstruct the three-dimensional cloud extinction field.

papers.abstract: Cross-view pose estimation estimates a ground camera's geographic pose by matching onboard sensor data with geo-referenced overhead imagery. This is particularly relevant when GNSS is unreliable, for example under forest canopy or in urban canyons. Existing metric cross-view benchmarks, such as VIGOR and cross-view KITTI, are dominated by urban and road scenes with strong human-made structure without off-road terrain. We introduce GOOSELoc, a multimodal benchmark for ground-to-aerial localization in unstructured environments, including forests, fields, and rural tracks. GOOSELoc comprises 9,356 scenes recorded across all four seasons around Munich, Germany, pairing geo-referenced aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB imagery and 3D LiDAR point clouds. Paved/unpaved labels enable analyzing the impact of terrain structure, while the seasonal recordings allow studying the appearance gap to mostly summer-captured orthophotos. To assess the transferability of existing methods, we adapt and fine-tune four state-of-the-art cross-view localization baselines on GOOSELoc. Despite task-specific fine-tuning, the performance degrades substantially in off-road environments. We therefore propose a multimodal baseline combining surround-view imagery and LiDAR geometry, improving localization performance and providing a stronger reference for future work. Data and baselines are released at https://gooseloc.github.io.
authors: Fabian Deuser, Peter Mortimer, Robin-Nico Kampa, Anna B\"o{\ss}end\"orfer, Mirko M\"ahlisch, Martin Werner, Norbert Oswald
bullets: Targets ground-to-aerial localization when GNSS is unreliable, especially in forests, fields, and rural tracks.
Provides 9,356 georeferenced scenes near Munich across four seasons, pairing aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB and 3D LiDAR.
Includes paved/unpaved terrain labels and seasonal variation to study terrain structure and appearance gaps.
Fine-tuned state-of-the-art baselines degrade substantially off-road, while the proposed RGB–LiDAR baseline improves localization performance.
Data and baselines are publicly released for future research.

GOOSELoc is the only benchmark pairing surround-view imagery and LiDAR against official orthophotos, and the only one combining paved-to-off-road coverage with a controlled seasonal ground-aerial gap. McPed [40] is the closest multimodal relative: RGB + LiDAR from a single forward-facing 79◦ camera on a tracked robot, recorded in clear weather without a seasonal protocol, with SLAM-derived ground truth and per-sequence rather than geographic splits. papers.title: GOOSELoc: A Multimodal Benchmark for Ground-to-Aerial Localization in Unstructured Off-Road Terrain
papers.tldr: GOOSELoc introduces a multimodal benchmark showing that cross-view localization methods struggle in seasonal, unstructured off-road environments and benefit from combining RGB imagery with LiDAR.

papers.abstract: Latent 3D representations have significantly expanded the capabilities of modern shape modeling, enabling compact encoding of 3D scenes and supporting powerful 3D generative models. Despite this progress, current representations struggle to capture the fine details of complex objects, fundamentally limited by the capacity of their latents. However, scaling latent capacity at training time is computationally expensive and often infeasible under memory limits, and naively increasing the number of latents at inference fails to make effective use of the added capacity. In this paper, we address both challenges with \textit{split-and-scale}, a method that effectively expands latent capacity at inference while keeping training cost tractable. Our key observation is that by representing 3D scenes as continuous functions of 3D coordinates, a single pretrained tokenizer can be applied at inference to arbitrarily small sub-regions of a scene, allocating the same latent capacity to a smaller spatial extent and thus capturing far higher detail. We validate this insight by conducting extensive ablations to study the trade-offs between compute, memory, latent capacity, and reconstruction quality, demonstrating our inference-time scaling method achieves quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory limits. We further demonstrate that split-and-scale supports high-quality generative modeling, training an autoregressive 3D generator that performs competitively with state-of-the-art baselines.
authors: Dorian Chan, Muhammed Kocabas, Xiaoming Zhao, Oncel Tuzel, Jen-Hao Rick Chang
bullets: Addresses limited latent capacity for modeling fine details in complex 3D objects.
Uses continuous coordinate-based scene representations to tokenize arbitrarily small sub-regions at inference.
Explores trade-offs among compute, memory, latent capacity, and reconstruction quality through ablations.
Achieves quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory limits.
Also supports high-quality generative modeling with an autoregressive 3D generator.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic scenes and objects from monocular egocentric video is crucial for embodied AI, yet existing 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) approaches struggle with everyday interactions involving topological changes, such as cutting, assembly, opening, or closing. Since 4DGS methods rely on deforming a fixed representation, events that split, merge, or reveal surfaces cause severe visual artifacts. To address this challenge, we introduce TopoEgo, the first benchmark dedicated to topological changes in egocentric video (covering fission, fusion, open, and close), alongside Topo-4DGS, a topology-aware reconstruction method. Topo4DGS jointly models part-level motion and time-varying surface support by assigning independent rigid transformations to interacting parts and dynamically activating or deactivating Gaussians as surfaces appear, disappear, or separate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Topo-4DGS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 4DGS approaches across topological changes, especially on post-event frames. Code and data will be made publicly available.
authors: Leonardo Vanni, Stefano Gasperini, Federico Tombari, Chiara Plizzari
bullets: Addresses failures of existing 4DGS methods on splitting, merging, opening, and closing interactions.
Introduces TopoEgo, a benchmark covering fission, fusion, opening, and closing in egocentric video.
Assigns independent rigid motion to interacting parts and activates or deactivates Gaussians as surfaces change.
Outperforms existing 4DGS approaches across topological changes, particularly in post-event frames.
Code and data are planned for public release.

papers.abstract: Language moved from many task-specific models to one unified model: a single generative model with a single generative training task that handles all of them within the same backbone, and keeps improving with data, parameters and compute. We believe the bitter lesson applies just as much to computer vision, 3D and spatial understanding, in the end to visual intelligence: the effort should go into general architectures that solve all these tasks in a unified way, and into scaling them, rather than into task-specific designs. We test this on monocular geometry, a task that has belonged to specialised architectures for years. Iris-Z is a general image generator that produces appearance and geometry together. A single backbone denoises, reasons about and understands the image and its depth at the same time, and one set of weights generates images with their depth, estimates depth from photographs and paints images onto a given depth. At enough scale it surpasses state-of-the-art specialists on established depth benchmarks while keeping the generative abilities of the backbone it started from without specialized layers. We release two models for the community.
bullets: Targets task-specific monocular geometry architectures with a unified, scalable alternative.
Uses one backbone to jointly denoise, reason about, and understand images and depth.
Supports image-plus-depth generation, depth estimation from photographs, and image synthesis conditioned on depth.
At sufficient scale, surpasses specialist models on established depth benchmarks while retaining generative capabilities.
Releases two models for community use.

papers.abstract: Engineering design studies produce a few tens to a few hundred simulations of one problem, each on its own mesh, and their surrogates are retrained for every study. Tabular foundation models instead infer a new task from its examples in one forward pass, after pretraining on synthetic tasks. We demonstrate the feasibility of in-context learning for physical field prediction on unstructured meshes. A single model, PhysICL, pretrained solely on procedural tasks, predicts fields, with quantiles, directly on each query mesh from labeled simulations, without updating its weights. The same checkpoint accepts variable numbers of context examples, scalar inputs and input fields, and any number of output fields, while mesh size and connectivity can vary within a task. Its procedural prior draws generic laws and boundary-element physical models on morphed 2D and 3D template meshes, evaluated only at the points the model samples, fast enough that tasks generated on the fly by CPU workers keep the GPUs busy throughout pretraining. On five PLAID datasets never seen in pretraining, its field error decreases as the context grows and, from $K = 32$, is below that of the nearest context simulation on every dataset and context draw. It is on par with per-dataset reduced-order models on two of them, behind them where the fields are low-rank. On AhmedML surfaces with a median of 1.1 million nodes, twenty times the largest pretraining mesh, its fixed spatial budgets keep the peak GPU memory at $K = 64$ at 4.27 GiB, against 4.07 GiB on the 6,000-node meshes of 2D\_MSHE. Finally, on 2D\_MSHE, far from the prior, fine-tuning on procedural tasks that reproduce its geometry and loads, without any of its outputs, at a tenth of the pretraining cost, divides the stress error by 2.7.
bullets: Targets engineering studies with limited simulations, where conventional surrogates must be retrained for each problem.
Uses procedural priors over generic laws and boundary-element models on morphed 2D/3D meshes, with quantile field predictions from context examples.
Handles variable context sizes, scalar inputs, input/output fields, mesh sizes, and mesh connectivity in a single checkpoint.

On five unseen PLAID datasets, error improves with more context and beats the nearest context simulation from K=32; performance matches reduced-order models on two datasets but trails them for low-rank fields.
Maintains low peak memory on million-node AhmedML meshes; geometry/load-specific procedural fine-tuning reduces 2D_M​​SHE stress error by 2.7× without using target outputs.
