papers.abstract: Controllable real-world video generation models can condition on a rendered graybox proxy video, which fixes layout, motion and camera. Coding agents can build such videos by reconstructing a 4D scene in Blender, yet no benchmark checks both these videos and the long, multi-shot scenes behind them. We introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene reconstruction: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. Its 242 tasks span four input kinds, including scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos. Each delivery is scored along two evaluation dimensions. Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the code and compares the exported 4D scene with hidden ground truth facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether the facts that pass can be recognized in the proxy video. We analyze the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 frontier coding agents and identify three key observations. First, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. Second, all agents seem to already master basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. Third, agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Agents thus need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.
authors: Yuzhe Chen, Muxi Diao, Lele Yang, Wenbin Xu, Xuyang Liu, Qile Su, Changyi Liu, Jiankang Chen, Kaiyu Jiang, Haoyu Zhang, Hongyi Fu, Jianxiong Wang, Tianke Zhang, Haonan Fan, Yingxin Li, Bingyi Li, Xu Wang, Xuanyu Zheng, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Wentao Zhang, Jiale Cao

papers.abstract: Deep-learning-based magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction holds great promise for accelerating acquisitions, yet its clinical translation remains bottlenecked by poor generalizability across unseen scanners, populations, anatomies, and protocols. Gathering sufficiently diverse clinical datasets to overcome this bottleneck is hindered by high acquisition costs, privacy restrictions, and institutional biases. Here, we introduce Scalable Inverse Model (SIM), a framework that systematically co-designs physics-simulated training data, model architecture, and learning paradigms around scalability--leveraging compute scaling to overcome historical data bottlenecks and achieve robust zero-shot MRI reconstruction. Across 14 public and in-house datasets--spanning seven international centers, five vendors, field strengths of 0.3-7 T, over ten anatomical regions, more than ten acquisition protocols, downstream quantitative and molecular tasks, and a 150-scan blinded radiologist study--SIM demonstrates robust zero-shot generalizability, recovering fine anatomical details while suppressing aliasing artifacts where conventional deep-learning methods fail. Attention-map analyses confirm that SIM learns physically explainable, dynamically adaptive reconstruction primitives rather than anatomy-specific priors. SIM establishes a scalable, privacy-preserving, and democratized infrastructure for universal MRI reconstruction, providing a blueprint for generalizable AI across inverse problems in medical imaging.
authors: Hong Shang, Zijian Zhan, Sen Jia, Xiang Fan, Jintao Meng, Yang Zhou, Xiang Zhou, Tianyu He, Xinran Chen, Qiaoling Zeng, Keyan Yu, Jianhua Yao, Dong Liang
bullets: Addresses poor generalization of deep-learning MRI reconstruction caused by limited, biased, and costly clinical data.
Co-designs simulated training data, model architecture, and learning paradigms to replace historical data scaling with compute scaling.
Evaluated across 14 public and in-house datasets spanning multiple centers, vendors, field strengths, anatomies, protocols, and downstream tasks.
Reports recovery of fine anatomical detail and suppression of aliasing artifacts where conventional methods fail, including a blinded radiologist study.
Attention analyses suggest the model learns physically explainable, dynamically adaptive reconstruction primitives rather than anatomy-specific priors.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of SIM, a compute-scalable framework for zero-shot MRI reconstruction. a, The physics-simulated data engine transforms arbitrary images into paired training data comprising undersampled multi-coil k-space measurements (X) and ground-truth targets (Y ). This pipeline strictly obeys multi-coil MRI forward physics to align simulated and real measurement characteristics, effectively closing the simulation-to-real gap. Simultaneously, it expands image and acquisition diversity to overcome historical data bottlenecks, enabling models to learn fundamental inverse mappings. b, SIM adopts the multi-channel Vision Transformer (mcViT)—a high-capacity architecture with minimal MRI-specific inductive bias—to absorb diverse simulated data and learn robust reconstruction priors at scale, replacing hand-crafted architectures designed for data-scarce regimes. c, Pairing large-scale simulated data with high-capacity architecture reveals power-law scaling relationships with dataset size, model size, and patch count, mirroring scaling behaviors in natural language and vision. Crucially, these scaling gains transfer directly to real clinical data, confirming that the simulation engine effectively bridges the simulation-to-real gap. d, Comprehensive zero-shot evaluation across public and in-house datasets—spanning diverse scanner hardware, populations, anatomies, protocols, downstream quantitative and molecular imaging tasks, and a clinical reader study—demonstrates that SIM achieves vastly superior generalizability over traditional real-data learning paradigms.

Fig. 3 Scaling laws in reconstruction. a, In-distribution scaling for simulated data. Reconstruction performance improves smoothly as dataset and model size increase in tandem. Scaling model size yields sustained performance gains when not bottlenecked by data diversity, analogous to scaling laws observed in LLMs[48]. b, In-distribution scaling for real fastMRI. Scaling model size fails due to pronounced overfitting (Extended Data Fig. A1b) from inadequate data diversity; despite comparable dataset size to simulated data, real fastMRI exhibits high inter-dataset similarity. c, Transfer scaling comparing training data. Scaling behavior learned on simulated data transfers effectively to diverse real-world datasets, successfully bridging the sim-to-real gap. Real fastMRI alone shows no scaling benefit and transfers poorly to OOD test sets; combining fastMRI with simulated data restores OOD scaling, demonstrating that high-diversity simulated data are essential to unlock scaling laws in MRI reconstruction. d, Transfer scaling comparing model architectures. When trained on 1.1 million simulated samples, conventional architectures designed for small-data regimes with hard-coded domain priors (such as E2EVarNet) are outperformed on OOD test sets by mcViT—a generic Vision Transformer with minimal inductive bias—underscoring the need to co-design data and models for scaling regimes. Experiments in a–c utilize mcViT. Across a–d, retrospective equispaced undersampling is applied at a 3.2× effective acceleration factor. ID, in-distribution.

Fig. 4 Zero-shot reconstruction. a, Quantitative comparison. Both SIM and SIM-Zero (trained exclusively on simulated data) outperform all competing baselines across 8 out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks, with SIM exceeding the top baseline by 1.06–3.95 dB in PSNR and 0.008–0.045 in SSIM, and SIM-Zero performing only marginally below SIM. Error bars indicate mean ± s.d. Full comparisons against 9 state-of-the-art methods are in Extended Data Fig. A3. ID, in-distribution. b, Qualitative comparison. Representative reconstructions, error maps, and reference images. SIM recovers fine anatomical detail matching ground truth without perceptible aliasing artifacts (see Extended Data Fig. A4 for additional visual comparisons). XGY, Xingaoyi. c, Cross-protocol transfer. Models were trained on fastMRI Brain data partitioned by protocol (T1, contrast-enhanced T1 [CE], T2, FLAIR). E2EVarNet trained on real data exhibits a diagonal performance, degrading on unobserved protocols due to overfitting. Conversely, SIM displays uniform performance across protocols due to domain-agnostic simulated data. Across a–c, retrospective equispaced undersampling is applied at a 3.2× effective acceleration factor.

Fig. 2 Data simulation pipeline, feature representation, and ablation study. a, Data simulation pipeline. The workflow transforms arbitrary natural images into paired training data comprising undersampled multi-coil k-space measurements and ground-truth targets. The physical mapping between measurement and target strictly obeys multi-coil MRI forward physics. FT, Fourier transform; iFT, inverse Fourier transform; rss, root-sum-of-squares. b, Data visualization in a shared representation space. While real datasets show a clustered distribution with limited diversity, simulated data display diverse local contrast patterns relevant to clinical imaging at the patch level. Each dot represents a 14 × 14 image patch in the DINOv2 feature space[55] after dimension reduction using principal component analysis and linear discriminant analysis to two primary discriminant axes, color-coded by dataset source. LDA, linear discriminant analysis. c, Ablation study demonstrating the effectiveness of key simulated data design features in closing the simulation-to-real gap, as well as the impact of model architectural choices and learning objectives engineered to leverage simulated training data. Error bars represent mean ± s.d. Retrospective equispaced undersampling is applied at a 3.2× effective acceleration factor.

Fig. 8 Visualization of SIM attention maps. a, Attention maps of individual heads across layers, demonstrating that SIM intrinsically captures generic image structures and spatial relationships tied to undersampling physics via large-scale domain-agnostic training, thereby achieving physically explainable and broadly generalizable reconstruction. b, Attention maps aggregated across all layers and heads, showing that SIM dynamically adapts its attention to aliasing source regions as changes in acceleration alter the spatial aliasing distance. Two example query patches are shown under effective acceleration factors of 3.2× and 4.2×. For a and b, arrows and boxes on input images indicate query patches. AF, acceleration factor.

Fig. 5 Zero-shot quantitative MRI. a,b, Representative single-echo reconstructions, derived T ∗ 2 maps, and corresponding error maps evaluated on the public AHEAD dataset (MP2RAGEME sequence, Philips 7 T) (a) and an in-house cohort (MULTIPLEX sequence, UIH 3 T) (b). SIM’s zero-shot capability enables reliable downstream parametric mapping. Skull stripping is applied, and display windowing and leveling are adjusted per echo image and matched between reconstructions and reference images. Retrospective equispaced undersampling is applied at a 3.2× effective acceleration factor. c, Quantitative comparison of T ∗ 2 mapping across all slices evaluated by mean absolute error (MAE) at effective acceleration factors of 3.2×, 4.2×, and 5.1×. SIM consistently outperforms baselines across sequences and acceleration factors. Error bars represent mean ± s.d. AF, acceleration factor.

Fig. 7 Zero-shot clinical applications. a, Representative reconstructions of SIM and E2EVarNet at effective acceleration factors of 3.2×, 4.2×, and 5.1× for an in-house Alzheimer’s disease cohort with three contrasts: T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and T2-FLAIR. Red arrows indicate residual aliasing artifacts. b,c, Quantitative evaluation in terms of PSNR (b) and SSIM (c). Error bars represent mean ± s.d. d–f, Blinded reader study in which 1,050 MRI volumes were evaluated independently by two board-certified radiologists. d, Radiologist ratings of overall image quality evaluated on a 5-point Likert scale (5 = excellent, 1 = unacceptable); each dot represents an individual rating. e, Radiologist ratings of clinical usability evaluated on a 3-point categorical scale (diagnostic, screening-only, non-diagnostic). f, Inter-reader agreement for image quality and clinical usability ratings. Statistical significance was assessed using two-sided paired Student’s t-tests for quantitative metrics (b,c) and two-sided clustered Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for radiologist ratings (d,e); significance levels are denoted as ****P < 0.0001. Inter-reader agreement was quantified using quadratically weighted Cohen’s κ for image quality ratings and linearly weighted Cohen’s κ for clinical usability. For d and e, ratings from two radiologists are pooled for visualization. AF, acceleration factor; VN, E2EVarNet; x3, x4, and x5, effective acceleration factors of 3.2×, 4.2×, and 5.1×, respectively.

Fig. 6 Zero-shot molecular MRI. a, Representative SIM reconstructions of dynamic CEST images (shown at offset frequencies of 1.1 ppm and 3.6 ppm) and derived dynamic maps of PCr and tCr∗ (a weighted sum of PCr and Cr[71]), evaluated on an in-house dataset monitoring calf-muscle recovery using an in-scanner exercise protocol[71] (UIH 5 T). b, Dynamic recovery curves within the calfmuscle region of interest (ROI). SIM achieves image quality virtually identical to the reference across all dynamic timepoints, enabling faithful preservation of dynamic physiological responses. For b, data points represent mean values, and error bars indicate s.d. across all pixels within the calf-muscle ROI. For a and b, retrospective equispaced undersampling is applied at a 5.1× effective acceleration factor. PCr, phosphocreatine; Cr, creatine; τ , metabolic recovery time constant.

papers.abstract: In Gaussian-based semantic occupancy prediction, overlapping primitives can provide ambiguous class predictions, making their joint interpretation important for voxel classification. However, current methods using spatially weighted mixtures neglect explicit modeling of cross-primitive dependencies, limiting the readout's ability to utilize category-specific relational evidence. Hence, we introduce CGOcc, a supervised multi-camera framework that explicitly models Cross-Gaussian dependencies for 3D semantic Occupancy prediction. CGOcc integrates appearance and geometric observations to refine Gaussian states and encodes cross-Gaussian dependencies in a diagonal-plus-low-rank representation. To incorporate these dependencies into voxel classification, CGOcc uses a class-conditional projection to extract diagonal and signed cross-Gaussian statistics without constructing a dense dependency matrix. The readout then refines occupied-class probabilities using these statistics while preserving a learned reference's occupied mass and free probability. Extensive experiments on nuScenes demonstrate CGOcc achieves state-of-the-art performance, with larger gains at high Gaussian overlap and improved predictions near boundaries. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of covariance-aware prediction and support its synergy with geometric interaction.
authors: Zirui Huang, Jiongle He, Yunfan Zeng, Yuanzhi Lu, Guangye Li, Boyan Tang, Weite SU, Pedro V. Sander, Amy Hui Zhang
bullets: Addresses ambiguity from overlapping Gaussian primitives whose class predictions are difficult to interpret jointly.
Refines Gaussian states using both appearance and geometric observations in a supervised multi-camera framework.
Represents cross-Gaussian dependencies with a diagonal-plus-low-rank structure and extracts class-conditional statistics without a dense dependency matrix.
Refines occupied-class probabilities while preserving the learned reference’s occupied mass and free probability.
Experiments on nuScenes report state-of-the-art performance, with stronger gains under high overlap and near boundaries; ablations support covariance-aware prediction and geometric interaction.

papers.abstract: Thermal infrared imaging is vital for applications like search-and-rescue and autonomous navigation, yet trans- lating it into 3D scene representations remains a critical bottleneck. The low-texture nature and view-dependent emissivity of thermal images cause standard pose estima- tors to fail catastrophically, collapsing standard 3D Gaus- sian Splatting pipelines under sparse-view constraints. Fur- thermore, existing thermal reconstruction methods rely heavily on dense capture and computationally expensive per-scene optimization. Critically, many of these ap- proaches depend on aligned RGB-thermal datasets to ob- tain reliable camera poses and initial point clouds, ren- dering them unusable in purely thermal, unposed envi- ronments. To break this bottleneck, we present Thermal- Splat, the first generalizable, feed-forward Gaussian splat- ting framework that reconstructs 3D scenes directly from sparse thermal images without requiring known camera poses, RGB guidance, or per-scene training. We over- come thermal-specific challenges using a soft census loss for brightness-invariant structural matching and a bound- ary structure loss to explicitly supervise temperature discon- tinuities. Trained on an aggregated multi-source dataset, ThermalSplat synthesizes sharp reconstructions of unseen scenes in a single feed-forward pass. Extensive experi- ments demonstrate that ThermalSplat holds a strict advan- tage over scene-specific thermal splatting methods in the sparse regime. Furthermore, even compared against these baselines operating under their ideal dense capture set- tings, ThermalSplat achieves superior perceptual fidelity. By eliminating the need for computationally expensive per scene optimization, ThermalSplat offers an efficient and generalizable approach to thermal 3D reconstruction.
authors: Prasanna S, Gopi Raju Matta, Divya Madhuri Vemunuri, Kaushik Mitra
bullets: Addresses failures of standard pose estimation and 3D Gaussian Splatting caused by low texture and view-dependent thermal emissivity.
Uses soft census loss for brightness-invariant structural matching and boundary structure loss to preserve temperature discontinuities.
Trained on aggregated multi-source thermal data to reconstruct unseen scenes in a single feed-forward pass.
Reports superior sparse-regime performance over scene-specific thermal splatting methods, including stronger perceptual fidelity than dense-capture baselines.
Scope: designed for purely thermal, sparse-view, unposed reconstruction without aligned RGB data.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Qualitative comparison against scene-specific, optimization-based thermal reconstruction methods with dense input views. Despite generalizing from only two unposed views in a single feed-forward pass without RGB guidance, ThermalSplat (Ours) achieves visual fidelity and boundary sharpness that rivals or exceeds heavily optimized, dense multi-view baselines (Thermal3DGS, ThermalGaussian, and PhysIR).

Figure 2. Qualitative comparison of novel view synthesis. ThermalSplat (Ours) captures sharper temperature discontinuities and more faithful structural details compared to thermally fine-tuned baselines (MVSplat+, SPFSplat+, NAS3R+).

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison on the unseen SEAR dataset. PhysIR-Splat collapses on the Metallic-container scene, producing a uniform output, whereas ThermalSplat (Ours) preserves sharp thermal boundaries and scene structure across all scenes.

Table 1. Motivation for pose-free thermal reconstruction. We evaluate state-of-the-art Structure-from-Motion (SfM) methods on our thermal test scenes by measuring the number of successfully registered images for pose estimation and the resulting extracted 3D points. While dense inputs yield partial success, these methods fail to extract reliable 3D points in the sparse (2-view) setting, highlighting the fundamental necessity of our pose-free framework.

Table 3. Quantitative comparison of novel view synthesis performance across six held-out thermal scenes. In the absence of existing generalizable frameworks for sparse-view thermal reconstruction, we benchmark against state-of-the-art RGB models. We first evaluate these models using zero-shot inference and, for a fair comparison, also fine-tune them on our aggregated thermal dataset. The fine-tuned versions are denoted with a superscript plus (+).

Table 2. Quantitative comparison against scene-specific optimization methods. We evaluate baselines under their ideal Dense multi-view setting (top) and under the heavily constrained Sparse two-view setting (bottom). ThermalSplat (Ours) operates strictly from two unposed views, outperforming baselines in the sparse regime and rivaling them in the dense regime. Best results per setting are shown in bold.

Table 4. Two-view pose estimation performance measured by the Area Under the Curve (AUC, %) at error thresholds of 5◦, 10◦, and 20◦. We report rotation, translation, and overall errors. For each image pair, the overall error is simply the larger of its rotation or translation error.

Table 1. Composition of the aggregated thermal dataset constructed from five publicly available datasets. The number in parentheses next to each dataset name indicates the total number of scenes contributed by that dataset. The complete corpus contains 63 scenes, partitioned into 57 training (unmarked) and 6 test (bold) scenes.
Table 4. Cross-dataset generalization results on the SEAR dataset. Best results are highlighted in bold.

Table 6. Ablation study evaluating the contribution of each proposed loss component. Reference rows establish baselines using an RGB-pretrained backbone applied zero-shot (Naive transfer) and fine-tuned with thermal photometric supervision .

papers.selection_reason: Feed-forward thermal 3D Gaussian splatting from sparse unposed images; fits 3D vision.
papers.title: ThermalSplat: Generalizable Pose-Free Gaussian Splatting for Sparse-View Thermal 3D Reconstruction

papers.abstract: Scene graphs provide a compact, structured representation of environments by capturing objects and their spatial or semantic relationships in a form suitable for embodied agents. Existing 3D scene graph generation methods often rely on depth sensing at inference, either to associate object instances across views via point cloud overlap or to compute inter-object relations from geometric cues, limiting deployment to platforms with depth sensors. We propose IncR-3DSGG, which builds 3D scene graphs incrementally from posed\footnote{RGB images with camera extrinsics estimated by an off-the-shelf visual SLAM system.} RGB images, eliminating the use of depth sensors at inference. Our method leverages a Parametric Relation Predictor (PRP) that learns to estimate pairwise distances and relative angles between objects from 2D visual features and 2D geometric cues, using 3D geometric supervision available only during training. These learned pairwise measurements are fused across views through Pose Graph Optimization (PGO)~\cite{grisetti2010tutorial} to recover metrically grounded 3D object positions and build a globally consistent 3D scene graph incrementally. On the real-world 3RScan~\cite{wald2019rio} dataset, our method attains $52.2$ mean object recall and $30.8$ mean predicate recall under the 3DSSG~\cite{wald2020learning} evaluation protocol, against $27.0$ and $17.6$ for MonoSSG~\cite{wu2023incremental}, while using no depth or reconstructed geometry at inference. This shows that relations and metrically grounded 3D object representations can be predicted from posed RGB images alone.
authors: Mrunmai Phatak, Daniel Kienzle, Roman K\"uble, J\"org H\"ahner, Rainer Lienhart
bullets: Addresses the need for depth sensors in existing 3D scene graph generation systems.
A Parametric Relation Predictor estimates object distances and relative angles from 2D visual and geometric cues.
Pose Graph Optimization fuses these predictions across views to recover consistent 3D object positions and relations.
On 3RScan, it achieves 52.2 mean object recall and 30.8 mean predicate recall, compared with 27.0 and 17.6 for MonoSSG.
Scope: inference requires posed RGB images from visual SLAM, while depth or 3D geometry is used only during training.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our IncR-3DSGG framework. papers.abstract: 6-DOF pose estimation of large and heavy industrial objects, such as large piping systems in shipyards and structural components in petrochemical plants, remains relatively underexplored in robotic perception. Repeatedly repositioning large objects is physically and spatially demanding, making it difficult to acquire real training data with sufficient pose diversity. Synthetic data offer a scalable alternative, but faithfully reproducing real RGB-D observations, particularly the structured measurement errors of real depth sensors, remains difficult. We propose MiniPose, a practical pipeline for miniature-based real RGB-D data collection that addresses both the data-acquisition burden and the sim-to-real gap. We fabricate a scaled-down replica and capture RGB-D data of it in diverse poses using a real RGB-D camera. RGB images are used directly, while depth maps are converted to a geometrically consistent representation of the full-scale object via a simple inverse scaling transformation. This allows training to incorporate real appearance and sensor measurement characteristics that are difficult to reproduce using synthetic data alone. To examine whether the benefit depends on a particular network, we evaluate two RGB-D pose estimators with different formulations, PVN3D and RDPN6D. Mixing at most 1,000 miniature images per pipe type, less than 10\% of the training data, with 10,000 synthetic images improves the mean ADD-S AUC across pipe types over synthetic-only training for both estimators. A comparison with training on full-scale real data further suggests that miniature data can serve as a proxy where full-scale collection is difficult, reducing the data-collection burden for large industrial objects.
authors: Hyunjun Kim, Youngjin Seo, Sungwon Seo, Jiyou Shin, Kunwoo Kim, Chanyong Park, Hyungpil Moon
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of physically repositioning large objects to obtain diverse real training poses.
Captures miniature RGB-D observations with a real sensor, using RGB directly and inversely scaling depth to represent the full-scale object.
Combining up to 1,000 miniature images per pipe type with 10,000 synthetic images improves mean ADD-S AUC over synthetic-only training for both PVN3D and RDPN6D.
Results suggest miniature data can proxy full-scale real data while reducing collection effort.
Scope: evaluated on large industrial pipe types and two RGB-D pose estimators.

papers.tldr: MiniPose uses scaled-down replicas to cheaply collect realistic RGB-D training data for 6D pose estimation of large industrial pipe segments.

papers.abstract: Deep-learning-based 3D MRI reconstruction is limited in practice by the GPU memory and compute cost of full-volume training; 3D acquisitions are thus most often reconstructed by 2D models applied slice-by-slice and then stacked, which ignores through-plane (stacking-axis) structure. We reconstruct in full 3D and ask whether a model can be trained at low resolution (fast and memory-feasible) yet deployed at higher resolution. This coarse-to-fine strategy needs reliable cross-resolution performance, but standard networks are resolution-specific and degrade substantially when evaluated outside the training setting. We therefore use resolution-agnostic neural operators (NOs) and propose KIR-NO (k-space-to-Image Reconstruction Neural Operator), a discretization-agnostic framework for accelerated 3D MRI reconstruction. KIR-NO is trained with full backpropagation on low-resolution volumes and applied zero-shot to higher-resolution volumes at inference. Its core building block is a 3D neural operator based on discrete-continuous convolutions: convolutional filters are parameterized in a continuous basis and sampled at arbitrary voxel resolutions while preserving the local inductive bias of convolution. KIR-NO integrates these learned operators with physics-based consistency: a k-space neural-operator head first refines the undersampled Fourier measurements, and image-space neural-operator cascades then refine the reconstruction through interleaved data-consistency updates. Across 3D knee and brain MRI benchmarks, KIR-NO improves over classical and CNN baselines: it improves over a state-of-the-art 3D CNN by 2.2 dB PSNR at half resolution under 4x acceleration on SKM-TEA, with gains persisting at 8x and 16x. These results show that resolution-agnostic operators make coarse-to-fine 3D MRI reconstruction - cheap low-resolution training with high-resolution deployment - practical across anatomies.
authors: Jiayun Wang, Ram Daftari, Weijie Gan, Valentin Duruisseaux, Ruibo Wang, Armeet Singh Jatyani, Boris Bonev, Anima Anandkumar
bullets: Addresses the high GPU cost of full-volume 3D MRI reconstruction, which often leads to slice-wise 2D processing that misses through-plane structure.
Uses resolution-agnostic neural operators with continuous-basis 3D convolutions that can be sampled at arbitrary voxel resolutions.
Combines a k-space neural-operator head with image-space operator cascades and interleaved physics-based data consistency.
Trained on low-resolution volumes and deployed directly at higher resolution without retraining.
Outperforms classical and CNN baselines across knee and brain MRI benchmarks; gains over a 3D CNN reach 2.2 dB PSNR at half resolution under 4× acceleration on SKM-TEA, and persist at 8× and 16×.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a–c) Three deep learning architectures for 3D MRI reconstruction. (a) 2D CNN: GPUmemory limits force slice-wise 2D models that stack into a volume, losing inter-slice consistency. (b) 3D CNN: fixed discrete kernels are tied to the training grid, so cross-resolution transfer is unreliable. (c) 3D Neural Operator (KIR-NO, ours): discretization-agnostic — trained on memoryfriendly coarse volumes and deployed at higher resolutions without retraining. (d) Resolution robustness: PSNR at quarter/half/full resolution on SKM-TEA (quarter-trained); KIR-NO leads throughout. (e) Convergence (SKM-TEA, half-res, 4×): first epoch to reach each PSNR threshold; KIR-NO reaches 34 dB ∼6× faster than the 3D CNN. Figure 2: Our KIR-NO architecture. Undersampled multi-coil k-space measurements k̃ are first refined by a k-space neural-operator head NOk (Eq. 1), then mapped to image space (inverse Fourier transform F−1 and coil combination) and refined by an unrolled cascade of image-space neural operators NOi (Eq. 2, where ℓ indexes the cascade) interleaved with data-consistency updates, producing the final 3D reconstruction x̂. Operator layers learn continuous kernels built on discrete-continuous convolutions, in contrast to fixed-resolution conventional CNN kernels.

papers.title: Coarse-to-Fine 3D MRI Reconstruction via Resolution-Agnostic Neural Operators
papers.tldr: KIR-NO enables memory-efficient low-resolution training of full 3D MRI reconstruction models that transfer zero-shot to higher-resolution scans.

papers.abstract: Accurate lung tumor segmentation in computed tomography (CT) is essential for treatment planning, response assessment, and quantitative imaging analysis. However, 3D lung tumor segmentation remains challenging because tumors occupy only a small portion of the whole volume and exhibit heterogeneous appearances across anatomical locations. In patch-based training and sliding-window inference for 3D medical image segmentation, location-dependent heterogeneity is further amplified because cropped image patches provide limited global anatomical context, making it difficult for a model to adapt its feature processing according to the anatomical region from which each patch is extracted. To address this limitation, we propose an Anatomical Prior-guided Routing Module (APRM) for lung tumor segmentation. For each image patch, we obtain anatomical prior information of regional occupancy and deterministically select an anatomical routing gate. The selected gate then performs sparse feature routing over a shared expert adapter pool, enabling anatomy-specific feature adaptation while sharing expert capacity across regions. We evaluate APRM on two datasets with various backbone networks and demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline models. Furthermore, feature visualizations show that APRM produces different feature responses depending on patch location, indicating that the proposed routing mechanism effectively adapts feature processing according to anatomical context.
bullets: Lung tumors are small, heterogeneous, and difficult to segment when patch-based processing lacks global anatomical context.
The Anatomical Prior-guided Routing Module determines each patch’s regional occupancy and selects a corresponding routing gate.
Sparse routing over a shared expert adapter pool enables anatomy-specific feature adaptation while sharing capacity across regions.
Evaluations on two datasets and multiple backbones show consistent improvements over baseline models.
Feature visualizations indicate that the module produces location-dependent feature responses.

papers.abstract: In the era of large models, stereo matching is developing towards generalizable foundation models trained on million-scale synthetic images. However, how model performance scales up with synthetic data is still underexplored. In this work, we preliminarily investigate the in-domain and cross-domain data scaling laws in stereo matching. A realistic synthetic dataset, named XStereo, containing 200 thousand samples is first built to serve as a high-quality benchmark for data scaling research. In-domain training on five large-scale datasets demonstrate a two-regime scaling behavior with data, transitioning from the standard power law to saturation, where the critical transition point is approximately invariant under a fixed model. Cross-domain performance exhibits a substantially weaker and less predictable dependence on the source-domain data scale. The distribution and coverage diversity are more effective for diminishing domain gaps. More instructive suggestions are provided for high-efficiency data construction and training. The insightful findings are significant verification and extension of the existing scaling laws in both language and vision, paving the way to efficient and stronger stereo matching. The XStereo dataset is public at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Tong-Zhao/XStereo.
bullets: Introduces XStereo, a realistic synthetic benchmark with 200,000 samples for studying stereo data scaling.
Finds two in-domain scaling regimes: a power-law improvement followed by saturation.
Reports that the transition point is approximately stable for a fixed model.
Shows cross-domain performance depends weakly and unpredictably on source-domain data size.
Suggests prioritizing distribution diversity and coverage for efficient data construction and training.

papers.abstract: Robust depth estimation aims to maintain high-quality depths across diverse conditions. However, most existing methods estimate depth without taking into account the object-level information. As a result, the predicted depth may easily deviate within objects and become blurred under adverse conditions. To overcome this weakness, we propose RoSAMDepth, a novel framework that can assist robust self-supervised depth estimation in leveraging rich and diverse object-level priors from the Segment Anything Model (SAM). We focus on incorporating object-level information across three key aspects: a segment-guided representation contrasting method that injects object-level awareness into the feature representation space; an adaptive regional outlier masking strategy combined with a regional Gaussian likelihood loss that enforces regional depth smoothness; and an object-level reliability estimation strategy that mitigates the influence of unreliable supervision. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and diverse weather conditions demonstrate that our method produces sharper, more accurate depth predictions, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/xagao/RoSAMDepth.
bullets: Addresses blurred or inconsistent depth predictions within objects, especially under adverse conditions.
Uses SAM-derived object information for segment-guided contrastive representation learning.
Applies adaptive regional outlier masking and a regional Gaussian likelihood loss to encourage smooth regional depth.
Estimates object-level supervision reliability to reduce the impact of unreliable training signals.
Experiments across multiple datasets and weather conditions show sharper, more accurate predictions and consistent state-of-the-art performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Illustration of the proposed method. Given the SAM masks, we leverage object-level priors to improve depth estimation Ds in two complementary ways: 1) Object-aware representation learning: SRC injects segment priors into multi-scale features. 2) Depth learning with object-level priors, AROM generates an outlier-suppressed mask Mout, which is paired with Lrgl to enforce consistent depth within each region. Concurrently, ORE estimates object-level reliability to form a reliability-weighted map Wrel, combined with Mout to modulate the distillation loss Ld.

papers.abstract: Recent diffusion models have achieved impressive progress in single image to multi-view generation by synthesizing consistent novel views efficiently. Existing methods usually explicitly or implicitly couple geometry inference and texture synthesis, making generation vulnerable to inaccurate geometry prediction. Although several geometry-guided methods have explored decoupling, they usually treat predicted geometry as a fixed condition and do not explicitly model whether the geometry is reliable. We therefore propose Reliability-Guided Multi-View Generation (RGMV), which comprises a parameter-free Self-Consistency Geometry Gate (SCG) and a Reliability-aware Geometry Injection (RGI) module. Specifically, a geometry proposal generator produces multiple geometry predictions for the same reference image and target viewpoints under different stochastic sampling configurations. SCG measures their spatial agreement to derive a reliability map, which RGI uses to modulate the injection strength of geometry-conditioned residuals in the RGB synthesis model. Moreover, RGMV can adapt to different geometry proposal generators. As a result, RGMV preserves stronger geometric guidance in stable regions while attenuating unreliable geometry cues before they propagate into multi-view RGB generation. Extensive experiments show that reliability-aware geometry injection improves the geometric quality of multi-view generation. Code: https://github.com/WISLab-GDUT/RGMV.
bullets: Existing methods can suffer when inaccurate geometry is coupled with texture synthesis or treated as a fixed condition.
RGMV generates multiple geometry proposals and uses their spatial agreement to estimate a reliability map.
Its parameter-free Self-Consistency Geometry Gate guides the Reliability-aware Geometry Injection module in modulating geometry-conditioned residuals.
The approach preserves stable geometric guidance while attenuating unreliable cues before RGB synthesis.
Experiments show improved geometric quality in multi-view generation, and the framework can work with different geometry proposal generators.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of RGMV. Given a reference image and target camera poses, an off-the-shelf geometry proposal generator produces K stochastic sets of multi-view normal predictions. The first prediction set serves as the anchor normal condition to produce multi-level geometry residuals. In parallel, Self-Consistency Geometry Gate (SCG) in (a) groups normal predictions by target view, measures their per-pixel angular disagreement, and converts it into per-view spatial reliability maps. Reliability-aware Geometry Injection (RGI) module in (b) resizes and affinely calibrates the corresponding reliability map at each denoising level l to obtain R̃v,l, which selectively modulates the geometry residual before it is injected into the multi-view diffusion backbone.
Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison on rendered objects with ground-truth target views. Each row shows the multi-view results of one method under the same target viewpoints.

Fig. 4: Qualitative comparison on real captured images without ground-truth target views. The examples are organized by representative failure modes commonly observed in multi-view generation. Each pair compares a baseline result with its corresponding RGMV result under the same input and target viewpoints.

papers.abstract: Radar systems can recover scene geometry and recognize predefined categories, but these outputs do not provide a persistent spatial representation for open-ended language queries. Such queries require linking observations from different viewpoints to the same physical locations. We present TextRadar, a framework that constructs a scene-level 3D occupancy-language field from panoramic radar observations. The field combines occupancy with scale-dependent language features at surface locations, allowing the reconstructed scene to be queried with new descriptions. A single-frame radar distillation model predicts aligned ranges and language features from each radar observation. Using radar-estimated poses, we register these predictions to reconstruct the field from radar alone in a new scene. Experiments on approximately 20k synchronized observations across seven buildings demonstrate scene-level natural-language querying and prompt-free semantic visualization. Analysis of camera-to-radar concept transferability shows stronger agreement for structures, materials, and human poses than for colors and printed text.
bullets: Addresses the lack of spatially persistent, language-queryable representations in radar-based scene understanding.
Distills each radar observation into aligned geometry and language features, then registers them using radar-estimated poses.
Constructs a scene-level field combining occupancy with scale-dependent language features at surface locations.
Demonstrates natural-language querying and prompt-free semantic visualization across seven buildings and about 20k synchronized observations.
Concept transfer is stronger for structures, materials, and human poses than for colors and printed text.

figures.caption: Fig. 13 Overview of the TextRadar framework. A rotating mmWave radar provides high-resolution panoramic RF measurements, while a front-facing camera supplies multiscale language supervision during data collection. Building on these inputs, TextRadar jointly learns geometry and language-aligned embedding from RF measurements and builds a scene-level 3D occupancy-language field, which supports several tasks.

Fig. 3 Scene-level natural-language querying of small structures and objects. The field localizes architectural structures, including (a) “Stairs” and (b) “Windows,” as well as compact objects, including (c) “Trash bin” and (d) “Human.” The RGB images provide representative observations of the queried regions, with dashed boxes indicating the corresponding targets. For categories with multiple instances, such as stairs and windows, the system simultaneously highlights geometrically separated regions throughout the scene.

Fig. 2 Scene-level natural-language querying of large building structures. The reconstructed geometry is colored according to the cosine similarity between the scene-level feature at each surface point and the CLIP text embedding of the query. Warmer colors indicate higher semantic relevance. The queries (a) “Ceiling” and (b) “Floor” activate complementary upper and lower surfaces across multiple corridors and room regions. The spatially coherent responses over distant parts of the environment show how the persistent occupancy-language field associates related structures across a common 3D coordinate system.

Fig. 5 Natural-language querying of high-level concepts. The prompts describe human configuration, affordances, and functional regions: (a) “Standing” localizes a standing person, (b) “Going down” highlights a descending staircase, (c) “Things to sit” retrieves a bench and other seating, (d) “Taking a rest” identifies a shared seating area, (e) “Entrance to other places” highlights doorways and passages, and (f) “Working region” identifies the occupied workspace in a laboratory office. These examples show responses to contextual prompts beyond direct object and material names.

Fig. 9 Radar-camera feature disagreement. The top row highlights concepts dominated by visual content: (a) televisions and monitors, (b) information signs, and (c) exhibition boards. The bottom row highlights appearance-dependent concepts: (d) ribbed texture, (e) yellow color, and (f) roughness and grid patterns. Dashed boxes mark the relevant regions in the RGB observations. While the camera-derived features clearly distinguish these regions by displayed content, color, or fine surface appearance, the radar-predicted features often assign them similar embeddings and thus fail to distinguish them.

Fig. 1 TextRadar constructs a scene-level 3D occupancy-language field from radar observations. A robot collects panoramic mmWave measurements along a trajectory (left). Surface geometry and language features predicted from these measurements are integrated in shared 3D coordinates (center). The right panels illustrate natural-language querying, prompt-free semantic visualization, and camera-to-radar concept transferability. The query “Things to sit” highlights a bench, while the feature visualization reveals semantic organization without specifying a prompt. Comparisons of radarpredicted and camera-derived features show stronger agreement for structures, objects, materials, and human poses than for colors and printed text.

Fig. 8 Prompt-free semantic visualization of material-related regions. The examples show (a) wood doors, (b) a glass window, and (c) a metal cabinet. The highlighted material regions occupy distinct portions of the projected feature space and therefore appear with colors different from their surrounding walls and structures. The agreement between the radar-predicted and camera-derived PCA images indicates material-related information being retained beyond range geometry alone.

Fig. 6 Prompt-free semantic visualization of general indoor structures. For each example, the rows from top to bottom present the rendered panoramic RGB image, the predicted range image, the three-component PCA projection of the radar-predicted CLIP features, and the corresponding camera-derived reference projection. The predicted and reference features are projected using a shared PCA basis, and the three principal components are mapped to RGB channels. Similar colors therefore indicate nearby positions in the projected semantic feature space, rather than predefined semantic classes. Large structural regions, including ceilings, floors, walls, corridor openings, and wall-mounted structures, form spatially coherent groups in the radar-predicted visualization and broadly agree with the camera-derived reference.

Fig. 4 Geometry and natural-language queries. Each example shows, from top to bottom, the rendered panoramic RGB reference, the range image predicted from the radar measurement, the query-relevancy map obtained from the radarpredicted CLIP-aligned features, and the corresponding map obtained from the camera-derived reference features. Warmer colors indicate higher cosine similarity to the text query. The queries cover materials, including (a) “Glass,” (b) “Metal,” and (c) “Marble”; objects, including (d) “Trash bin,” (e) “Chairs,” and (f) “Human”; and structures, including (g) “Stairs,” (h) “Floor,” and (i) “Ceiling.” The radar-predicted maps localize both compact objects and extended structural regions, remain spatially consistent with the recovered geometry, and broadly agree with the camera-derived reference maps.

Fig. 7 Prompt-free semantic visualization of structures and objects. The examples examine (a) stairs, (b) humans, and (c) chairs, with two scenes shown for each concept. The dashed boxes in the rendered RGB image indicate the structures or objects of interest. A shared PCA projection is used for each prediction-reference comparison, allowing their color organization to be compared directly. Stairs, human silhouettes, and individual chairs emerge as coherent regions whose boundaries follow the corresponding geometry, despite some differences in their sizes, shapes, and spatial extents.

Fig. 11 Example scenarios in our dataset. The dataset spans common indoor environments, including hallways, lounges, offices, classrooms, and open floor areas. These examples are captured by the front-facing camera on the robot and illustrate the visual context used to generate language supervision.

Fig. 12 Radar-camera feature disagreement around glass. Each column presents one example, and the rows show the rendered panoramic RGB reference, the radar-predicted range image, and the pixelwise cosine similarity between radarpredicted and camera-derived CLIP features. papers.abstract: Embodied systems need geometric perception that exploits available observations beyond images alone. Recent feed-forward 3D models incorporate geometric priors, including camera poses, intrinsics, and depth. However, handling noisy poses, preserving accurate priors, and recovering physical scale require more than simply accepting these inputs. We introduce \emph{Vision-Prior Geometry Grounded Transformer} (VPGGT), a VGGT-based framework that extends OmniVGGT for prior-aware embodied perception. We formulate sensor-motivated pose corruptions from ground-truth trajectories for training and introduce a parameter-free \emph{prior residual connection} (PRC) to mitigate \emph{prior dilution}, where predictions are less accurate than their supplied pose priors. Our noise formulation targets camera poses; supplied intrinsics and depth receive no additional corruption. We further introduce \emph{Metric Global Attention}, which conditions a global scale token on available pose and depth scales and predicts a shared metric scaling factor for the geometric outputs. Experiments across four datasets show that \emph{PRC} improves translation-direction accuracy and joint pose AUC over a matched training baseline when camera priors are provided for all views, under both exact and corrupted poses. These results support explicit prior access during refinement as a useful addition to feature-level conditioning.
bullets: Addresses noisy camera poses, prior dilution, and missing physical scale in prior-aware geometric perception.
Introduces sensor-motivated camera-pose corruption for training while leaving supplied intrinsics and depth uncorrupted.
Adds a parameter-free Prior Residual Connection to retain and refine pose priors explicitly.
Uses Metric Global Attention to predict a shared scale factor from available pose and depth scales.
Across four datasets, PRC improves translation-direction accuracy and joint pose AUC with exact or corrupted pose priors.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of VPGGT. Images and optional camera or depth priors are encoded and processed by a shared alternating-attention backbone. PRC places available camera priors in the camera head’s refinement state after its initial prediction. A Scale Encoder conditions a global token on available metric-scale statistics, using learned placeholders when they are absent. The camera, depth, and pointmap heads predict geometry, and a scale head supplies a shared factor that converts translations, depths, and points to metric units.

All views receive camera priors; no depth is supplied. Colors distinguish methods and markers distinguish datasets. Dashed lines show input-prior scores. Reset is a state intervention, not a learned iteration.

papers.abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/
authors: Amani Kiruga, Zhiyi Li, Ruojin Cai, Hansen Lillemark, Xiaoshan Wu, Ayush Tewari, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses the split between feedforward geometry predictors and generative visual models for partial 4D scene observations.
Uses modality- and time-dependent noise levels to jointly model video and geometric representations.
Learns from heterogeneous datasets with varying subsets of visual and geometric annotations.
Supports inference-time search over plausible scene hypotheses, using RGB-derived geometric evidence without ground-truth geometry.
Outperforms non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including sparse-observation settings.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of camera-controlled generation. Given the first and last RGB frames and a target camera trajectory, we compare generated intermediate frames against ground truth and baseline video generation methods. UGG better preserves scene identity and dynamic content compared with the generic video completion baselines.

Figure 3: Conditional completion with noise as masking. We specify each task by the clean/noisy pattern over RGB, depth, camera-ray, and text tokens. Clean tokens provide observed context, while noisy tokens are denoised as missing targets, enabling generation and prediction with the same model architecture.

Figure 2: Generative-predictive transformer. We model RGB, depth, and camera pose as spatially aligned tokens, with camera pose represented as dense ray maps. Partial observations are zero-noise context tokens, while missing modalities are noisy tokens to be denoised. A unified transformer processes all tokens with modality-specific projections and feed-forward layers together with shared multimodal self-attention, enabling information exchange across modalities. The decoded RGB, depth, and ray maps form a complete 4D scene representation for cross-modal generation, geometric prediction, and inference-time consistency search.

Figure 1: A unified model for generation and prediction. We formulate visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion in a single joint model over RGB, depth, and camera pose. Given arbitrary partial observations, ranging from a text prompt to RGB sequences with geometric cues, our model jointly uses these modalities to infer a complete 4D scene representation, enabling both generation from sparse inputs and geometric prediction from observations.

Figure 6: Depth prediction qualitative comparison. The white box marks the region shown in the zoom-in columns, ordered as GT, Ours, ChronoDepth, and Geo4D from left to right. Our predictions preserve sharper local structures and object boundaries in the highlighted regions. Evaluation results. Table 2 reports camera pose estimation results. In the dense setting, UGG achieves lower ATE and RPEt than the external baselines across all five datasets. For example, ATE is reduced from 0.190 to 0.087 on ScanNet++ compared with Geo4D. Figure 5 visualizes representative trajectories. Our predictions better follow the ground-truth motion, while RayDiffusion and Geo4D produce collapsed paths in challenging examples. In the sparse setting, UGG obtains the lowest tAE and RPEr across all five datasets. These results suggest that the model can infer reasonable relative camera poses from only the first and last RGB frames, despite the ambiguity of sparse observations.

Figure 7: Test-time search with increasing sample budget. We sample up to 16 candidate completions and select one using the image-based depth or pose verifier. The dashed line shows the single-sample result, and the solid curve shows the selected result as L increases. Search improves several pose and depth settings, showing that the generative model produces useful candidate diversity.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison of estimated camera trajectories. The temporal evolution of each trajectory is encoded by a color gradient, from purple (start) to red (end). Ground-truth trajectory is shown in black. The leftmost column shows representative RGB frames from the input video. papers.tldr: UGG unifies 4D scene generation and geometric understanding by modeling RGB video, depth, and camera pose as conditional completion in one generative framework.

papers.abstract: Estimating 3D head expression from a single image requires mapping visual appearance to underlying facial geometry. We propose ViGA-FLAME, a two-stage framework that aligns semantic visual features with a structured geometric latent space. First, a Parametric-Geometric Variational Autoencoder (PG-VAE) learns a unified representation of canonical head surfaces and FLAME parameters, supporting both detailed surface reconstruction and interpretable parameter recovery. Supervision on geometry and parameters, together with consistency between the two decoding branches, connects surface detail with parametric structure. Second, a trainable Visual-Geometric Adapter (ViGA) maps features from a pretrained semantic visual encoder into this latent space. Asymmetric attention enables ViGA to align semantic image features from the visual encoder with the structured geometric information represented in the PG-VAE latent space, without altering the original visual stream. By grounding image evidence in this latent prior, ViGA-FLAME enables robust 3D head expression estimation across severe facial deformations and large viewing angles, efficiently improving robustness over competing feed-forward methods.
authors: Wen Hao He, Jiacheng Wu, Jie Chen
bullets: Uses a two-stage framework combining geometric representation learning with visual-to-geometric adaptation.
PG-VAE jointly represents canonical head surfaces and FLAME parameters through geometry, parameter, and cross-branch consistency supervision.
A Visual-Geometric Adapter uses asymmetric attention to align semantic image features with structured geometric latents without modifying the original visual stream.
Targets robustness under severe facial deformations and large viewing angles.
The abstract reports improved robustness over competing feed-forward methods, without providing quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D foundation models recover geometry at high fidelity, yet inference memory constraints keep them from processing long sequences natively. Current streaming systems work around this limit with sliding-window chunking, which introduces severe monocular scale ambiguity. Resolving this ambiguity requires Sim(3) registration that stays accurate and efficient under outlier contamination. We introduce Sim(3)-TurboReg, which reformulates the compatibility graph construction of TurboReg by replacing absolute distance constraints with a strict Tri-Scale Consistency (TSC) criterion. Our analysis shows that TSC suppresses both mismatching and coordinate-distortion outliers. We integrate the resulting solver into existing streaming systems and obtain high-fidelity, kilometer-scale reconstruction for feed-forward models. On controlled unknown-scale registration at 90% outliers, ours matches RANSAC accuracy with 92.5% lower median latency. In DA3-Streaming on KITTI, ours improves mean ATE RMSE by 22.2% and reduces mean end-to-end time by 16.6%. Code: https://github.com/ivan-zzj/Sim3-TurboReg
authors: Zijun Zhou, Shaocheng Yan, Zhenjun Zhao, Yutong Hu, Ke Yang, Yingdong Gu, Pengcheng Shi, Jiayuan Li
bullets: Addresses monocular scale ambiguity caused by sliding-window processing in long-sequence 3D reconstruction.
Replaces TurboReg’s absolute distance constraints with a Tri-Scale Consistency criterion to suppress mismatching and coordinate-distortion outliers.
Integrates the solver into streaming systems for high-fidelity, kilometer-scale reconstruction.
At 90% outliers, matches RANSAC accuracy with 92.5% lower median latency.
On KITTI DA3-Streaming, improves mean ATE RMSE by 22.2% and reduces mean end-to-end time by 16.6%.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Sim(3)-TurboReg overview. Left: core registration on Stanford Bunny and Dragon at 60% and 90% outliers. At 90% outliers, TEASER++ fails while our method matches RANSAC accuracy at lower latency. Right: streaming integration with DA3-Streaming on KITTI-00 and TUM Floor-01, comparing IRLS and our backend. Sequence ATE RMSE decreases from 11.21 to 7.67 m (31.6%) on KITTI-00 and from 7.47 to 6.58 cm (11.9%) on Floor-01.

Fig. 2. Pipeline of Sim(3)-TurboReg. Putative matches are converted to tri-scale cues: an edge scale sij and two endpoint local scales si, sj . The TSC graph retains edges whose three scales agree (∆ij ≤ τ ), and 2nd-order scoring weights edges by shared-neighbor support. TurboClique extracts triplets, followed by a degeneracy filter for near-collinear configurations. Umeyama hypotheses are ranked by full-set inlier voting to obtain the Sim(3) estimate.

Fig. 3. Both outlier types in real streaming correspondences and their synthetic geometric models. (a) Type 1 mismatching outliers: paired points link different scene regions despite high descriptor similarity. (b) Type 2 coordinate-distortion outliers: pairs select the same landmark but undergo coherent displacement. Node scales use bilateral kNN (k = 6), τ = 0.15 (illustrative settings; experiment defaults differ).

papers.abstract: Real-time robotic perception requires accurate LiDAR semantics under limited resources. Bird's-eye-view (BEV) aggregation is efficient but can mix differently labeled surfaces in columns. We present HiPFuse, a point-BEV fusion framework that exchanges point and height-partitioned BEV features across horizontal scales, combining point-wise detail with 2D spatial context from one LiDAR scan. Fixed height assignments preserve separate vertical aggregation groups, with auxiliary supervision of initial BEV features using targets from the same 3D cells. A dual-scale BEV context module adds broader context from a coarser grid. On SemanticKITTI and MCD, HiPFuse achieves 63.7% and 62.5% mIoU at 14.2 and 22.4 FPS on Jetson AGX Orin, respectively, exceeding the 10 Hz scan rate. Separate training and evaluation show indoor applicability. Replacing only the baseline semantic front end with HiPFuse in fixed robotic systems reduces odometry absolute trajectory error RMSE by 10.6% on average across two outdoor sequences and increases accepted-loop recall by 8.7 percentage points on SemanticKITTI. Qualitative semantic maps show more continuous road labeling. Our code is available at https://github.com/haiyang2022/HiPFuse.
authors: Haiyang Wu, George Vosselman, Ville Lehtola
bullets: Addresses BEV column mixing, which can merge surfaces with different semantic labels.
Exchanges point and multi-scale, height-partitioned BEV features from a single LiDAR scan.

Achieves 63.7%/62.5% mIoU at 14.2/22.4 FPS on Jetson AGX Orin for SemanticKITTI/MCD, exceeding 10 Hz.
Improves downstream robotic odometry and loop-closure recall when replacing the semantic front end.

papers.title: HiPFuse: Real-Time LiDAR Semantic Segmentation for Robotic Perception on Edge Devices

papers.abstract: Establishing dense correspondence between high-resolution 3D shapes remains challenging due to the spatial--spectral coupling at the core of many functional-map methods, which grows quadratically with mesh resolution. We observe that this coupling is equivalent to a scaled dot-product attention formulation, with learned descriptors serving as queries and keys and spectral basis functions as values. This connection makes efficient attention implementations directly applicable to shape matching and an effective mechanism for scaling spatial-spectral coupling. We show that optimized quadratic attention implementations can scale modern deep functional map pipelines to large mesh sizes, improving both runtime and memory consumption, while sub-quadratic methods introduce errors, particularly for non-isometric shape pairs, where an exact coupling proves most necessary. These insights motivate \textit{Geo-FlashAttention}, which restricts the exact softmax to geometry-selected surface patches and achieves near-linear empirical scaling while preserving correspondence accuracy of exact implementations. Across six standard benchmarks and three functional-map pipelines, rigorous analysis shows that efficient couplings preserve correspondence accuracy. At $60k$ vertices, these insights reduce peak training memory from 106.08 to 5.67\,GiB, with Geo-FlashAttention being $1.5\times$ faster per training step than FlashAttention. This enables end-to-end learning for correspondence problems on large meshes such as cortical surfaces, where high resolution is required to preserve disease-relevant intricacies of the surface geometry. Project page available https://spatial-spectral-attention.github.io/
authors: Bence Demeter, Kilian Ehrenreich, Amelie Kleber, Ioana Oprisiu, Philipp Spohn, Christian Wachinger, Fabian Bongratz, Lennart Bastian
bullets: Functional-map coupling scales quadratically with mesh resolution, limiting dense correspondence on large surfaces.
The paper identifies this coupling with scaled dot-product attention, enabling optimized attention implementations for shape matching.
Sub-quadratic approximations can introduce errors, especially for non-isometric shape pairs requiring exact coupling.
Geo-FlashAttention applies exact softmax attention only to geometry-selected surface patches.

Across six benchmarks and three pipelines, efficient couplings preserve accuracy; at 60k vertices, memory drops from 106.08 to 5.67 GiB, and Geo-FlashAttention is 1.5× faster per step than FlashAttention.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of Geo-FlashAttention. (1) Target N and source M are partitioned into geometrically derived patches A and B based on vertex positions. (4) The R best-scoring source patches per target patch form the support Sa,R, so every row keeps exactly R patches. (5) A fused block-sparse kernel evaluates the exact softmax without materialising Π̃ (R) NM .

Comparing shape vertex features requires O(nM · nN ) operations, which is infeasible with current strategies.

Figure 4. Comparing attention computations. (1) Dense softmax forms the full nN × nM correspondence matrix, while FlashAttention (2) tiles A through on-chip memory. (3) Linear attention replaces the softmax kernel by a feature map φ approximating the product. (4) Geo-FlashAttention evaluates exact softmax attention on the induced vertex support by S.

papers.selection_reason: Connects functional-map spatial-spectral coupling to attention and uses efficient attention to scale shape correspondence; relevant to 3D vision and efficient attention.
papers.title: Spatial-Spectral Coupling as Attention: Scaling Shape Correspondence to High-Resolution Surfaces

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models are pretrained on satellite and aerial imagery, but whether such an encoder beats a strong generic one for few-label land-use/land-cover mapping remains unclear, as prior comparisons rarely isolate the pretraining data. We study five matched pairs of Earth-observation (EO) and generic encoders sharing objective and architecture (DINO/SatDINO, DINOv3/DINOv3-SAT, MAE/SatMAE, MAE/Scale-MAE, CLIP/RemoteCLIP) within a benchmark of 14 frozen encoders on five RGB scene-classification datasets (0.06-30 m GSD). With native preprocessing, we evaluate k-NN, linear and attentive probes and image retrieval over six low-label splits, using paired per-image significance tests. EO pretraining is not uniformly helpful: on most datasets and metrics, it significantly improves three pairs (SatDINO, Scale-MAE, RemoteCLIP, the latter evaluated only on unseen datasets) and significantly hurts two (linear probe: DINOv3-SAT by up to 22.5 points, SatMAE by up to 8.8), with opposite outcomes even for two MAEs pretrained on the same fMoW-RGB imagery. These effects are robust to patch-token pooling and attentive probing, concentrate on small man-made objects, and are largest with 1-5% labels. Across encoders, the silhouette score of frozen embeddings predicts k-NN accuracy and retrieval mAP almost perfectly (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.96$ on four of five datasets). Pretraining on satellite imagery is thus not a reliable selection criterion; candidate checkpoints must be validated on target data.
authors: Sandarbh Agrawal, Rakshith Sathish, Ashwathi Nambiar
bullets: Compares five architecture- and objective-matched EO/generic encoder pairs among 14 frozen encoders across five RGB scene-classification datasets and six low-label splits.
Tests k-NN, linear and attentive probes, and image retrieval using native preprocessing and paired per-image significance tests.
EO pretraining significantly helps some pairs but hurts others—even for MAEs pretrained on the same fMoW-RGB imagery.
Effects are strongest with 1–5% labels, concentrate on small man-made objects, and persist across token pooling and attentive probing.
Frozen-embedding silhouette score strongly predicts k-NN accuracy and retrieval performance on four of five datasets.

papers.title: Satellite Pretraining Is Not One Thing: A Matched-Pair Study of Generic and Earth-Observation Foundation Models for Scene Classification

papers.abstract: Internet photos of a scene differ in exposure, illumination and transient objects such as passers-by, so one set of Gaussian colours cannot explain all photos (the in-the-wild setting). Recent in-the-wild Gaussian Splatting methods mostly report hours of per-scene optimization. We present FastWild-GS, which describes each photo by a 128-dimensional Photo Appearance Token and a per-channel transform, a scale and an offset applied to the rendered image (six parameters); a small MLP predicts the colour of each Gaussian from this token and a per-Gaussian feature, replacing the spherical-harmonics colour. The same transform is applied to the renders that score Gaussians for densification and pruning, so appearance differences between photos are not counted as reconstruction error. On PhotoTourism, FastWild-GS trains in 8.8 minutes per scene with the lowest LPIPS among the compared methods, 23x faster than AsymGS, the next best in LPIPS. On NeRF-OSR, it has the best average PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS among the compared methods in 9.7 minutes per scene.
authors: Donghun Ryu, Seokhyun Kim, Minhyeok Lee
bullets: Addresses exposure, illumination, and transient-object differences across internet photos.
Represents each image with a 128-dimensional Photo Appearance Token plus six channel-wise transform parameters.
Uses a small MLP to predict Gaussian colours from the photo token and per-Gaussian features.
Applies appearance adaptation during densification and pruning to avoid treating inter-photo differences as reconstruction error.
Trains in 8.8–9.7 minutes per scene and achieves the best reported perceptual or reconstruction metrics on PhotoTourism and NeRF-OSR among compared methods.

papers.abstract: Multimodal remote sensing pretraining commonly relies on exact instance-level correspondence across modalities, implicitly treating strictly paired observations as a prerequisite for learning transferable representations. In this work, we revisit this assumption by relaxing cross-modal correspondence from the instance level to the semantic level. We introduce Semantic Pairing (SemPair), a pairing-relaxed pretraining strategy that replaces exact instance pairs with class-consistent cross-instance pairs. To characterize the effect of correspondence relaxation, we formulate a latent-factor model that separates cross-modal dependence into shared semantic structure and instance-specific correlation, showing that SemPair preserves the former while marginalizing instance-specific cross-modal correlations in expectation. We further introduce Mixed Pairing (MixPair) as a controlled interpolation between semantic and exact pairing to study correspondence granularity along a continuous spectrum. Extensive experiments consistently show that SemPair achieves transfer performance comparable to exact pairing (ExaPair), while MixPair reveals a non-monotonic relationship between downstream transfer and the instance-pairing ratio. These results demonstrate that exact instance correspondence is not a prerequisite for effective multimodal remote sensing pretraining and establish cross-modal correspondence granularity as an important design dimension for transferable multimodal representation learning. More broadly, this finding suggests a practical route toward scaling multimodal pretraining with reduced dependence on costly instance-aligned data.
authors: Xianping Ma, Yu Zhang, Mingzhe Jiang, Wanxin Xie, Qing Zhu, Nan Xu, Xiaokang Zhang, Yuanxin Ye
bullets: Reframes cross-modal pairing from exact instance alignment to class-consistent semantic alignment.
Uses a latent-factor analysis to show semantic structure is preserved while instance-specific correlations are averaged out.
Introduces MixPair to continuously control the degree of exact versus semantic pairing.
Experiments find SemPair performs comparably to exact pairing, while transfer varies non-monotonically with the exact-pair ratio.
Suggests reducing reliance on costly instance-aligned multimodal data for scalable pretraining.

This motivates SemPair, which preserves semantic consistency while relaxing exact instance identity.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Semantic Pairing (SemPair) to relax cross-modal correspondence in remote sensing pretraining. This advances Multimodal Foundation Models (spatial understanding) and 3D Vision (scene understanding).
papers.title: Relaxing Cross-Modal Correspondence for Multimodal Remote Sensing Pretraining
papers.tldr: SemPair shows that multimodal remote sensing pretraining can learn transferable representations from semantically matched, non-identical cross-modal pairs rather than requiring exact instance correspondence.

papers.abstract: 3D reflection removal is crucial in applications demanding high-fidelity visualization, such as museum exhibitions. In this work, we propose Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting (RF3DGS), a novel method for superior reflection removal. RF3DGS exclusively leverages a widely-adopted photometric prior for reflection removal: that the minimum pixel intensity across multi-view images corresponding to the same 3D point strongly correlates with reflection-free information. However, generalizing this principle to a 3D Gaussian Splatting within a multi-view context is non-trivial. To address this, RF3DGS first optimizes a vanilla 3DGS model using a geometric prior to estimate a coarse, reflection-free depth map for each view. Leveraging these depth maps and photometric prior, a 3D warping process aggregates reflection-free information from auxiliary views to construct a clean transmission pseudo-label for a given reference view. This pseudo-label provides a robust self-supervised signal for optimization. We further introduce an Adaptive Twin Rendering (ATR) loss to synergistically utilize this pseudo-label while preserving high-frequency details from the original, reflection-degraded images. By adeptly fusing these internal 3D self-priors with the ATR loss, RF3DGS demonstrates state-of-the-art reflection removal performance across both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we establish the first 3D reflection removal benchmark, based on the Unity rendering engine, for rigorous quantitative evaluation.
authors: Qiang Wen (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology), Guotao Meng (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology), Junhong Ruan (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology), Hongyu Liu (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology), Chenyang Lei (Huawei Research), Qifeng Chen (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology)

papers.abstract: Monocular depth foundation models make it tempting to replace depth sensors on mobile robots with a single RGB camera. We show that, used off the shelf, this is unsafe: in a simulated indoor navigation benchmark, a standard Nav2 stack driven by Depth Anything V2 (metric) collides in 63\% of 120 episodes, because the model systematically over-estimates the distance to nearby obstacles. We propose a lightweight plug-in module that turns predicted depth into \emph{safe depth}. A 0.58\,M-parameter head on top of the \emph{frozen} depth model predicts, per pixel, a log-depth correction $\mu$ and an uncertainty $\sigma$, trained with a $\beta$-weighted Gaussian negative log-likelihood. The navigation stack consumes the one-sided bound $\hat d_{\text{safe}}=d\,e^{\mu-k\sigma}$, where $k$ is set by conformal calibration on a held-out world, and uncertainty also decides which pixels may be treated as floor. The correction halves the depth error (AbsRel $0.262\rightarrow0.134$) and reduces near-range over-estimation from 59.8\% to 12.0\%. In navigation, safe depth raises the success rate from 37\% to 70\% and lowers collisions from 63\% to 3\%, close to the 2\% of ground-truth depth. A constant safety margin calibrated to the same pixel coverage reaches only 30\% success because it freezes the robot; uncertainty-aware safety wins 52 of 56 discordant paired episodes against it. Gains hold on glass, texture-less walls and dark regions.
bullets: Off-the-shelf Depth Anything V2 depth caused collisions in 63% of 120 simulated navigation episodes, mainly by over-estimating nearby obstacle distances.
A lightweight 0.58M-parameter head predicts per-pixel log-depth corrections and uncertainty while keeping the depth model frozen.
Conformal calibration converts predictions into a one-sided safe-depth bound, with uncertainty also guiding floor-pixel selection.
Safe depth reduced AbsRel from 0.262 to 0.134 and collisions from 63% to 3%, while raising navigation success from 37% to 70%.
The approach outperformed a constant safety margin and retained gains on glass, texture-less walls, and dark regions.
