papers.abstract: Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as an efficient representation for novel view synthesis, offering fast differentiable rendering and high visual fidelity, and has increasingly been extended to surface reconstruction. However, the relationship between depth information and reconstruction error remains insufficiently explored, limiting the principled design of geometric optimization strategies. To fill the above gap, we propose DepthGS, a depth-guided Gaussian splatting framework. We derive theoretical relations between depth discrepancies and reconstruction error under single-view and multi-view settings, and rigorously establish corresponding upper bounds on reconstruction error. The above analysis informs the design of adaptive regularization strategies in both single-view and multi-view optimization. More specifically, for single-view optimization, we propose a depth-difference-guided adaptive normal regularization strategy that modulates the normal constraint strength using a geometric reliability weight computed from local depth differences. For multi-view optimization, we introduce a cross-view depth consistency regularization strategy that promotes consistency between neighboring-view depth maps and the corresponding depth predictions obtained by transforming the current view's depth predictions into those neighboring views. Extensive experiments on DTU, Mip-NeRF360, and Tanks and Temples demonstrate that DepthGS achieves competitive performance in both surface reconstruction and novel view synthesis.
authors: Xiao Ren, Yu Liu, Ning An, Jian Cheng, Xin Qiao, You-Fu Li, He Kong
bullets: Addresses the underexplored link between depth discrepancies and reconstruction error in 3DGS.
Derives reconstruction-error upper bounds for both single-view and multi-view settings.
Uses depth-difference-guided adaptive normal regularization for single-view optimization.
Enforces cross-view depth consistency during multi-view optimization.
Experiments on DTU, Mip-NeRF360, and Tanks and Temples show competitive reconstruction and novel-view-synthesis performance.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed framework. The Gaussian representation is initialized from a sparse point cloud and used to render the distance and normal maps. Unbiased depth maps are then derived from these rendered quantities. The discrepancy between the unbiased depth and rendered distance is used to compute the depth-difference-based weight W∆D , which modulates the single-view normal constraint Lsvgeo. In the multi-view branch, coordinate transformations establish depth correspondences between neighboring views to construct the cross-view depth consistency constraint Lmv D . The proposed constraints are jointly optimized with the baseline objectives to improve surface reconstruction and multi-view geometric consistency.

papers.abstract: Photorealistic and metrically consistent world representations are a primary requirement for LiDAR--inertial--visual SLAM systems that serve robots over continuous operation. 3D Gaussian splatting makes such representations attainable by supplying an explicit, renderable, and queryable scene model. We present GEMOR-GS (Global Extrinsic-calibration-refined Mapping and Online Relocalization for 3D Gaussian-Splatting SLAM) to make the Gaussian map geometrically accurate, globally refined, and re-enterable, providing a better appearance for robot perception and decision-making. To improve the 3DGS map, the LiDAR--camera extrinsic is first estimated offline by direct-method alignment over dedicated calibration segments and reused by all following online and offline processes. Under the calibrated geometry, keyframe poses and Gaussian parameters are refined alternately under a gated differentiable-rendering and LiDAR--projection objective. The final global reconstruction is then rebuilt from the refined keyframe schema with all online constraints lifted. For the robot SLAM lifecycle, the method recovers the pose from the 3DGS map after tracking loss through an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP coarse localization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement. Experiments on one self-collected and five public sequences quantify each element: the offline reconstruction wins all paired keyframes against the online map by 14.3--19.9 dB, improves PSNR by approximately 9 dB over Gaussian-LIC2, and achieves 86--100% held-out relocalization success tied to extrinsic quality. The results show that GEMOR-GS improves the geometric accuracy, appearance fidelity, and re-enterability of the 3DGS map, serving as a dependable robot world model for SLAM and downstream tasks.
authors: Yuchen Yang, Ming Ding, Xinyu Wu, Hesheng Wang
bullets: Targets photorealistic, metrically consistent world models for continuous LiDAR–inertial–visual SLAM.
Calibrates LiDAR–camera extrinsics offline, then jointly refines keyframe poses and Gaussian parameters using rendering and LiDAR projection objectives.
Reconstructs a globally optimized map from refined keyframes without online constraints.
Relocalizes through an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP initialization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement.
Across one self-collected and five public sequences, reports 14.3–19.9 dB gains over the online map, about 9 dB higher PSNR than Gaussian-LIC2, and 86–100% held-out relocalization success.

figures.caption: Figure 1: System overview. The online track 1O runs an IESKF over LiDAR, inertial, and visual measurements against a compact Gaussian tracking reference, and keyframes accumulate under the five-channel contract into the shared keyframe schema. The offline track 2O consumes the keyframe schema: joint optimization refines keyframe poses and map, after which global reconstruction reinitializes the Gaussians into the final 3DGS model. The calibration refinement 3O is an independent process: the extrinsic is estimated once per sensor rig by direct-method calibration and reused by both tracks. The bypass relocalization path 4O matches descriptors against the relocalization database upon tracking loss and hands the refined pose back to the front end.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction (3R) from unconstrained multi-view images has recently emerged as a prominent research direction in 3D computer vision. Various foundational reconstruction models have been proposed with different architectures and reconstruction paradigms. Despite being trained on large-scale perspective datasets with substantial computational resources, these models generally struggle to generalize to non-perspective images. This limitation hinders their deployment in applications involving arbitrary, unknown, and potentially heterogeneous camera models. To build on the capabilities of existing reconstruction models with minimal retraining, we propose Camera3R, a low-rank adaptation framework that efficiently extends perspective-pretrained 3R networks to any other camera models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, with only 0.5% additional parameters and less than a day of training, Camera3R adapts a foundational 3D reconstruction model to non-perspective cameras while fully preserving its original performance on perspective inputs. Code is available at https://github.com/android-xr/camera3r.
authors: Ruxiao Duan, Yunwen Zhou, Erin Hong, Dongxu Zhao, Eric Turner, Federico Tombari, Alex Wong
bullets: Existing 3D reconstruction models often fail to generalize beyond perspective images.
Camera3R uses low-rank adaptation to extend pretrained reconstruction networks with minimal retraining.
The framework adds only 0.5% parameters and trains in less than a day, according to the abstract.
Experiments show adaptation to non-perspective cameras while preserving performance on perspective inputs.

figures.caption: Figure 1: 3D reconstruction from heterogeneous cameras. Given an image sequence of arbitrary, unknown, and mixed camera models, our method reconstructs the scene in a single forward pass.

Figure 2: Camera-agnostic feed-forward reconstruction. Given an input sequence from arbitrary, unknown, and mixed camera models, we adapt a perspective-pretrained reconstruction network by camera-specific LoRA experts. Each frame is passed to a camera router, which selects the corresponding LoRA expert to adapt the model to the frame’s camera geometry, enabling pose and dense geometry (depth, ray directions, etc.) prediction from non-perspective cameras. Perspective frames bypass the adaptation, preserving the original behavior of the pretrained backbone.

Figure 3: Cross-camera data augmentation for model adaptation. Multi-view 3D reconstruction data from fisheye and panoramic sequences are augmented by synthesizing diverse camera projections. For fisheye sequences, we randomly preserve the original views, create additional fisheye distortions, and undistort the image to obtain perspective views. For panoramic sequences, we randomly preserve the original views, apply rotations, and render fisheye or perspective images by sampling from the panoramic sphere. Dense ground truth quantities such as depth and ray maps are transformed together with the image, providing geometrically aligned supervision across various camera models.

papers.abstract: Accurate localization of abnormalities in three-dimensional (3D) CT scans is essential for linking automated predictions with clinically relevant pathological findings. We propose Uni-Loc, a vision-language framework that unifies pathology classification and 3D localization using scan-level supervision. Uni-Loc derives both predictions and localization maps from spatial similarities between pathology-conditioned queries and image features. A token-to-voxel upsampling module enables high-resolution localization, while gradient-guided thresholding identifies pathology regions without additional learned parameters. Evaluated on five localization tasks comprising 355 annotated CT scans, Uni-Loc achieves macro-averaged voxel-level AUROC/AUPR of 96.1\%/34.5\%, outperforming relevance propagation (80.7%/13.9%) and gradient saliency (88.7%/8.1%). Uni-Loc also achieves classification AUROC of 88.39% on CT-RATE and 78.03% on RAD-ChestCT, improving over a matched baseline. These results demonstrate effective 3D pathology localization without requiring pathology-specific voxel-level supervision.
authors: Hao-Chih Lee, Zahi A. Fayad, Xueyan Mei
bullets: Addresses the challenge of clinically meaningful 3D pathology localization from weak, scan-level supervision.
Generates pathology predictions and localization maps from pathology-conditioned query–image feature similarities.

Across five tasks and 355 annotated CT scans, achieves 96.1% voxel-level AUROC and 34.5% AUPR, outperforming the compared saliency methods.
Reports classification AUROCs of 88.39% on CT-RATE and 78.03% on RAD-ChestCT, improving over a matched baseline.

papers.abstract: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipelines struggle with severely underexposed images, producing unstable colors, floating artifacts, and incomplete reconstructions in dark regions. To better account for noise in these low-light observations, RAW images offer a natural basis for noise-aware reconstruction by preserving linear sensor measurements and providing access to noise metadata. We present RetinexGS, a RAW-domain 3DGS framework that combines Retinex-inspired appearance modeling with sensor-informed optimization for low-light novel-view synthesis. We factorize each Gaussian's color into a view-independent base color and a shared, position- and view-dependent modulation field, regularizing the two components separately to constrain appearance learning from noisy observations. We use DNG noise metadata to weight the reconstruction loss for signal-dependent noise, while distortion-aware rendering avoids spatially resampling RAW targets. To address sparse geometry in dark regions, we introduce depth-guided initialization. We evaluate RetinexGS on three public RawNeRF scenes and two custom-captured low-light RAW scenes. With all methods trained on the same RAW inputs for each scene, RetinexGS outperforms LE3D and RawNeRF in mean sRGB PSNR by 2.18 dB and 2.71 dB respectively, across the five scenes, while supporting real-time novel-view rendering.
authors: Yulang Fei, Huaiyuan Weng, Chul Min Yeum
bullets: Targets unstable colors, floating artifacts, incomplete geometry, and noise in severely underexposed 3DGS reconstructions.
Factorizes Gaussian color into view-independent base color and shared position/view-dependent modulation, with separate regularization.
Uses DNG noise metadata for signal-dependent loss weighting and distortion-aware rendering without spatially resampling RAW targets.
Evaluated on three public RawNeRF scenes and two custom low-light RAW scenes, outperforming LE3D and RawNeRF in mean sRGB PSNR by 2.18 dB and 2.71 dB, respectively.
Supports real-time novel-view rendering; evaluation is limited to five low-light RAW scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: RetinexGS overview. Given noisy low-light RAW images and their DNG metadata, RetinexGS optimizes a Gaussian scene representation through three components. (1) A per-Gaussian base color Ri and a shared, position- and view-conditioned modulation Li(µi,di) define the primitive color Ci = Ri ⊙ Li(µi,di). Separate regularization constrains the two factors. (2) Distortion-aware rasterization renders these colors directly onto the packed RAW grid, where training combines DNG-informed noise weighting, a log-domain reconstruction loss, and appearance regularization. (3) A frozen monocular depth prior supplies additional initialization points through dark-region sampling and distortion-aware unprojection. The DNG ISP branch is used only for visualization and evaluation.

Our method produces fewer floating artifacts, more accurate color, and better details in dark regions.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing high-fidelity LiDAR simulation scenes from real-world driving logs is essential for cost-effective safety validation of autonomous driving systems. While simulators based on Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve realistic scene reconstruction, their large-scale adoption is limited by slow rendering speeds. Recent 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) approaches have improved rendering efficiency through explicit primitive representation and differentiable rasterization. However, existing 3DGS-based methods remain largely restricted to rigid vehicles and produce redundant primitives through unconstrained densification. To address these limitations, we propose URL-Sim, a unified and regulated dynamic LiDAR simulation framework. URL-Sim constructs a dynamic Gaussian scene graph that decouples the modeling of traffic participants, including vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists, enabling accurate reconstruction of heterogeneous dynamic objects within a single framework. It further introduces a regulated Gaussian densification strategy that ranks primitives with multi-dimensional importance scores and allocates Gaussians to the most critical regions while keeping the total primitive count bounded. Experiments on the Waymo and KITTI-360 datasets demonstrate that URL-Sim achieves higher quantitative accuracy and visual quality than existing baselines under comparable primitive budgets, and accurately recovers the geometry and poses of diverse dynamic traffic participants.
authors: Kefei Qian, Xipeng Feng, Jie Li, Long Cao, Yuhan Chen, Xiangfei Huang, Guofa Li
bullets: Targets slow NeRF-based rendering and limitations of existing 3D Gaussian splatting methods for dynamic objects.
Builds a dynamic Gaussian scene graph that separately models vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists within one framework.
Uses multi-dimensional importance scores to regulate Gaussian densification and prioritize critical regions under a fixed primitive budget.
Experiments on Waymo and KITTI-360 show higher accuracy and visual quality than baselines at comparable primitive counts.
Recovers the geometry and poses of heterogeneous dynamic traffic participants.

papers.abstract: We present DynaMesh, a dynamic texture generation method for 3D meshes. Given a textureless shape and a text prompt describing an effect, our method produces an appearance that evolves while the object's geometry remains unchanged. Previous works on dynamic 3D content generation have focused on motion, where an object's geometry and position change while keeping its appearance the same. Methods on texture generation sit on the other side of the problem, painting appearance onto a shape as a fixed surface property and not as an evolving process. Neither addresses a visual effect that propagates on a 3D object. A natural route consists of two generators: a video model that shows the effect from a single view, and an image-to-3D generator that lifts each frame to 3D. However, the latter has no notion of time, so running it per video frame produces a sequence that flickers, loses effect details, and yields a different mesh at every video frame. Our method addresses these failures by conditioning a video model on a render of the mesh and the prompt to obtain a reference video, then running a frozen image-to-3D generator on the video with two changes. The conditioning of each frame is blended over a temporal window, and low-rank adapters are fit per shape to restore the lost details. The mesh is encoded once for the whole sequence, so geometry is constant by construction, and the output is a single mesh with a texture per frame. Applied to various objects and effects, DynaMesh substantially improves over recent video-to-4D and texturing methods, and can generalize its temporal effect to different shapes never seen during training. Our project page is at https://threedle.github.io/dynamesh/.
bullets: Addresses the gap between dynamic 3D motion and static texture generation by modeling effects that propagate over an object’s surface.
Uses a mesh- and prompt-conditioned video model to create a reference effect sequence.
Applies a frozen image-to-3D generator with temporally blended conditioning and shape-specific low-rank adapters to preserve consistency and details.
Encodes geometry once, producing one unchanged mesh with a texture for each video frame.
Improves over recent video-to-4D and texturing methods across varied objects and effects, and transfers effects to unseen shapes.

figures.caption: Figure 3. System overview. A render of the input mesh, together with a text prompt describing the effect, is passed to a video generation model, which returns the reference video for our pipeline. The 3D generator then produces the textured object at every frame. Our temporal cross-attention (the new module) conditions each frame’s generation on a window of neighboring video frames. Low-rank adapters on the attention modules are fit per scene to recover detail. Geometry is shared across frames, so the output is one mesh whose texture evolves with the video.

Figure 4. Method overview. The token maps of an eleven-frame window are blended by a temporal attention layer. The blend conditions the generator’s spatial cross-attention, which writes the frame’s appearance onto the voxel tokens of the input mesh, and the 3D self-attention then propagates that appearance across the surface. Every weight except the rank-4 adapters on those two attentions is frozen.

Figure 2. Gallery of results. Four objects driven by four different effects. Each panel shows the driving video as a film strip and, below it, our output rendered from two novel viewpoints. The texture remains coherent even at viewpoints unseen in training.

Figure 5. Generalization. Per-scene adapters fit on a reference video are applied, without any retraining, to meshes never seen during fitting. Both effects clearly propagate on the new shapes according to the video. The adapters change only how appearance is generated, and each object keeps its own geometry, so the same spreading blots or lava cracks work even on different shapes.

Figure 8. Qualitative comparison. We compare our method against the baselines on one reference video (top strip), with each method shown at four timesteps from a single unseen view. The baselines either flicker or degrade the geometry at that view. Only our method tracks the effect consistently and preserves the shape’s geometry.

Figure 6. Temporal coherence. A chair with moss spreading over its surface is shown at four time frames. The insets magnify the same patch of the backrest. Frozen TRELLIS.2 changes the texture abruptly from one moment to the next (flickers), while our method keeps the moss growing smoothly, as in the video.
Figure 7. Making an existing static texture dynamic. Our method can operate on objects with a given texture and make it change over time, as shown for the moving spots over the duck.
Figure 10. Additional gallery. DynaMesh generates a different temporal effect for each object, and the effect holds at an unseen viewpoint despite being fit to a single camera.

Figure 12. Comparison at the second novel view. All methods are shown from a camera behind the object, which none of them was supervised on, at the same four frames as Fig. 11. The baselines that construct their own geometry or operate in video space lose the effect. In contrast, our method presents the same texture it shows at the supervised view, since the effect is written onto the input mesh rather than onto a camera.

Figure 14. Continuing an effect across clips. A second reference video, generated from the last frame of the first, continues the same effect, so a progression that does not fit in one clip can be carried across several.
Figure 11. Qualitative comparison. Given the same reference video, the baselines either lose the effect or distort the geometry at the unseen viewpoint, whereas DynaMesh preserves both.

Figure 9. Failure case. DynaMesh relies on effects where the property of the pattern is local. Here, it replicates the local patterns (flowers, dots, etc.), but it does not recover them from unseen views, since the flowers and lines follow a global arrangement that a single view does not capture.

Figure 13. Flicker over the clip. We plot flicker at each time step for frozen TRELLIS.2 and for DynaMesh, over the 42 objects of Tab. 1. The gap holds across the whole clip and is largest at the start, before the frozen texture settles.

Figure 15. MeshNCA conditioning. Conditioned on a single frame, MeshNCA reproduces it and does not advance through time, so its result reflects the conditioning image rather than the progression of the effect.

Table 3. LLM as a judge. We ask a vision-language model three questions about each rendered clip, at the supervised view and at the three unseen views, over all 42 objects with three repeats per clip. Effect fidelity is the percentage of five yes/no questions passed, while temporal coherence and geometry are rated from 1 (worst) to 5 (best). Our method scores best at the unseen views on all three questions, and the gap to the video-based baselines widens as the camera moves away from the supervised one.
Figure 16. Temporal window width. Widening the conditioning window reduces flicker, but fidelity peaks at a width of five and declines beyond it, so we select eleven to balance the two.

Table 1. Quantitative comparison over 42 objects and effects and all 150 frames. Flicker and acceleration are per-step temporal errors, and PSNR/SSIM, fidelity metrics to the ground truth video, are computed in the supervised view against the video. We achieve better results than state-of-the-art methods. †SV4D 2.0 and DG4D are grayed out as their outputs have fewer frames and cannot be measured on the same frame grid, discussed more below.
Table 5. Judge protocol. We ask three questions about every rendered clip, each scored against the reference its claim needs.

Table 4. LLM as a Judge for Generalization. Flicker, acceleration, and judge scores (Q1 effect fidelity, Q2 temporal coherence) for each adapter on the shape it was fit on and averaged over eleven unseen shapes. Effect fidelity is the percentage of five shape-neutral questions passed per effect, generated from the reference video, so the same questions score every shape. The transferred effects keep the temporal quality and the fidelity of the source result.

Table 7. Implementation details. We list the generator, the blending window, the adapter, the loss, and the hardware used to produce every result in the paper. All objects are fit with these same values.

Table 6. Temporal operator ablation. We compare two learned temporal operators against the parameter-free blend, at the same eleven-frame window with everything else held fixed. Metrics in the table are computed on the texture rather than on the renders, so they differ from Tab. 2. The blend has lower flicker and acceleration on all 42 objects, at a cost of 0.07 dB in PSNR and 0.002 in SSIM.

papers.abstract: Despite impressive progress, existing feed-forward large 3D reconstruction models produce a single, irrevocable prediction. When these models fail, there is no mechanism to correct their mistakes. To address this limitation, we introduce Click3R, a framework for interactive geometric correction of feed-forward models using sparse human correspondence clicks. Given an image pair and a small set of cross-view point correspondences provided by a user, Click3R injects geometric constraints into the 3D reconstruction networks through a lightweight point correspondence adapter, enabling the model to resolve ambiguities in challenging scenarios such as repetitive textures, symmetric structures, large viewpoint changes, or textureless regions. To evaluate interactive reconstruction, we curate a challenging benchmark specifically designed to expose failure modes of existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction methods. Experiments show that Click3R reduces reconstruction error with as few as a single correspondence click, improving performance on both standard and our curated benchmarks. Our results highlight that sparse human interaction provides an effective and practical mechanism for correcting geometric reconstruction errors.
bullets: Addresses the irreversibility of feed-forward 3D reconstruction predictions.
Injects sparse geometric constraints through a lightweight point correspondence adapter.
Targets ambiguities from repetitive textures, symmetry, viewpoint changes, and textureless regions.
Introduces a challenging benchmark focused on failure modes of existing methods.
Reduces reconstruction error with as few as one correspondence click on standard and curated benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: CLICK3R architecture. A shared ViT encoder processes the two input images. Correspondence prompts are tokenized using our correspondence tokenizer (Section 3.2). A symmetric point correspondence adapter, implemented as a lightweight transformer with self-attention and cross-attention (Section 3.3), updates the decoder-input features for each view. The asymmetric decoder then interprets the updated embeddings and passes them to the original DUSt3R [44] heads to predict 3D pointmaps and confidence.

Figure 1: Overview. Given (a) an image pair and sparse correspondences (colored dot clicks), CLICK3R conditions DUSt3R [44] to produce accurate 3D reconstruction. (b) DUSt3R fails on a scene with limited overlaps. (c) With as few as two clicks, CLICK3R recovers correct geometry.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison. Each example features challenging geometry, such as large baselines, limited co-visibility, or substantial viewpoint changes. The input image pair with user-provided correspondence prompts (colored dots) is shown on the left, followed by each model’s reconstruction. CLICK3R produces more accurate and consistent 3D reconstructions, with prompted correspondences aligning more closely in 3D. Additional qualitative results are provided in Appendix Figure 13.

Figure 6: Prompt count ablation on Hard3DBench. Pose accuracy of CLICK3R as a function of K (red), with baselines shown as horizontal lines. Top: in-distribution (404 pairs); bottom: out-of-distribution (300 pairs). All methods use 224×224 resolution.

Figure 3: Hard3DBench. Statistics shown for the 2-view stereo subset of Hard3DBench. (a) Hard3DBench produces substantially larger pretrained DUSt3R rotation errors than the regular benchmark. (b) Failure category distribution. (c) Example image pairs in Hard3DBench.

Figure 10: What the adapter changes. Per-token relative feature change induced by the adapter, with K=8 prompt locations shown as cyan dots. Bright regions indicate tokens whose features were modified most (each view uses its own color scale). The adapter updates every token, most strongly near the prompt correspondences.
Figure 12: A screenshot of the labeling tool we build to harness human labeled correspondences.

Figure 14: Failure cases of CLICK3R. Each panel: input pair (left), ground truth (middle), CLICK3R with clicks (right). (a) Near-zero overlap showcasing fundamental limitation of click-based supervision. (b) Extreme rotations cause geometric distortion that clicks cannot resolve. (c) In large-scale scenes, regions far from clicked correspondences still deform. (d) Clicks on featureless surfaces are inherently ambiguous and provide insufficient geometric signal.

Figure 11: How prompts reshape decoder cross-attention. Each row shows a query patch in view 1 (green cross) and its decoder cross-attention map over view 2. Without prompts (middle), attention is diffuse. With K=8 prompts (right, cyan dots), attention concentrates on the correct corresponding region.

Figure 7: Robustness to photometric augmentations. We perturb view 2 with brightness scaling or Gaussian noise and report RRA@15° on 100 hard OOD pairs. Prompts consistently improve accuracy, with the largest margin under heavy noise (σ=0.3): 55% vs. 6%.

Figure 13: Additional qualitative comparisons. On challenging pairs, different baselines fail in different ways: DUSt3R may produce a distorted reconstruction on a pair where Pi3 succeeds, or vice versa. CLICK3R with sparse correspondence clicks consistently recovers accurate geometry.

Figure 9: Pose error distribution (aggregated over the three datasets of Table 1 at 224×224, max(Rerr, Terr) in degrees). CLICK3R with prompts produces the sharpest peak near 0◦ and the shortest tail. The fraction of pairs exceeding 15◦ error drops from 9.4% (DUSt3R) to 2.8% (CLICK3R with prompts), a 3.4× reduction in pose failures.

Table 1: Standard benchmark results on held-out splits of CO3D, ScanNet++, and ARKitScenes. All methods use 224×224 inputs; gray rows are VGGT and Pi3X at both 518 (native) and 224 resolutions, shown only as reference and not included in the bold/underline ranking. DUSt3R (retrained) is our re-trained DUSt3R baseline using the same training data as CLICK3R for fair comparison; ±x.x denotes the mAA@30 difference from this baseline. Table 2: Hard3DBench results on the 2-view (left) and 5-view (right) subsets. In-distribution samples come from held-out splits of datasets used to train DUSt3R and CLICK3R; out-of-distribution samples come from datasets absent from training. CLICK3R K denotes K GT correspondences as prompts (per pairwise forward in the 5-view setting). For 5-view evaluation, all DUSt3R-family methods (including CLICK3R) follow DUSt3R’s global alignment protocol over the C(5,2) pairwise predictions. Comparison methods use 224×224 resolution except MASt3R (512); gray rows are VGGT and Pi3 at both 518 (native) and 224 resolutions, shown only as reference and not included in the bold/underline ranking. Methods below the dashed line share identical training data; +x.x denotes mAA improvement over DUSt3R (retrained). Pointmap Error is the median across pairs/tuples. Best in bold, second best underlined.

Table 8: Ablation of training strategies on all evaluation sets (mAA@30°, %). All variants train the correspondence adapter. Same random GT clicks for every model. H3B: Hard3DBench 2-view. Best in bold.

Table 3: Human-labeled correspondence evaluation. 100 out-of-distribution pairs with humanannotated correspondences. CLICK3R (human) uses sparse clicks from a human annotator; CLICK3R (random GT) uses K=4 randomly sampled ground-truth correspondences as an oracle upper bound. +x.x denotes improvement over DUSt3R (retrained). Best in bold, second best underlined.

Table 9: Pose accuracy at stricter thresholds on the standard benchmark. mAA at 5°, 15° and 30° for every row of Table 1, on the same pairs; the mAA@30° columns equal Table 1. Gray rows are reference only and not ranked. ±x.x denotes the difference from DUSt3R (retrained). Best in bold, second best underlined.
Table 4: Runtime and model complexity. GPU compute time measured on a single A100 (224×224, bf16). CLICK3R without prompts has identical cost to DUSt3R; K=8 prompts add 5% overhead.

papers.abstract: Modern digital phenotyping pipelines require the precise measurement of a range of 3D morphological plant traits. The accurate, high throughput acquisition of these traits helps breeders and researchers accelerate the development of new varieties, techniques and products. Recent advances in 3D technologies have enabled a rapid transition from 2D to 3D pipelines, but high throughput acquisition of digital 3D twins of plants remains a significant challenge due to complex morphology, thin structures and occlusions. In this paper we present Plant Orbiter, a new approach to generating 3D plants that leverages recent advances in video diffusion to produce high quality 3D Gaussian Splats of plants from a single image. We show that our method more accurately recreates plant morphology than other state-of-the-art methods, achieving the highest 3D F-score against all baselines, while being more practical for high throughput pipelines due to easier alignment and reduced cost of camera placement. Combined with a 2D diffusion model, we show that our method also achieves state-of-the-art results in the generation of 3D plant models from a text prompt.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of high-throughput 3D plant acquisition under complex morphology, thin structures, and occlusions.
Uses video diffusion to generate orbit-camera views and reconstruct plants as 3D Gaussian Splats.
Produces more accurate plant morphology than prior methods, attaining the highest 3D F-score against reported baselines.
Offers easier camera alignment and lower camera-placement costs for high-throughput pipelines.
Combined with a 2D diffusion model, achieves state-of-the-art text-to-3D plant generation.

papers.abstract: In production systems, 3D geometry is represented by primitives such as points, lines, and triangles, as rendering hardware is optimized to generate images from them very efficiently. Learning such primitives from images by volume rendering is challenging, as they are Dirac masses defined at infinitesimal locations in space. EWA splatting, Poisson reconstruction, and 3D Gaussian Splatting overcome this by convolving Dirac masses with a low-frequency kernel, a recipe that generalizes along two axes: the kernel and the primitive. As points and triangles have already received significant attention, we investigate this recipe for curvilinear primitives, and introduce Spaghetti Splatting. We approximate curves by polylines whose convolution converges to that of the continuous curve, and volume render each segment so that connected segments composite without overcounting at their joints. For fast training and inference, we linearize the camera projection per segment, which also accommodates kernels beyond Gaussians, such as Beta kernels. As a point is a curve of zero length, our representation is a strict superset of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It remains competitive with the state-of-the-art on general scenes, outperforms methods specialized to line-like geometry, natively supports anti-aliasing, and produces long connected strands that are directly amenable to physics simulation.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of learning infinitesimal curve-like Dirac masses from images.
Approximates continuous curves with polylines whose convolved representation converges to the curve.
Composites rendered segments at joints without overcounting and linearizes camera projection for efficiency.
Supports kernels beyond Gaussians, including Beta kernels, and strictly generalizes 3D Gaussian Splatting.
Remains competitive on general scenes, surpasses line-specialized methods, supports anti-aliasing, and produces physics-ready connected strands.

figures.caption: Figure 7. Comparison on Mip-NeRF 360, Shelly, and Fuzzy – (a, b) Unlike point-based primitives [8, 14, 29], our method can reconstruct thin elongated geometry effectively. (c) We can also model wide texture-less areas, like the dark shadow on the figure, with wide kernels, unlike Line Primitives [34]. We mark the three best values in each column with gold, silver, and bronze medals.

Figure 4. Overview – (Left) Our representation is a set of learnable polyline primitives convolved with Gaussian or Beta kernels. (Middle) Without loss of generality, we render each segment individually: we first project it onto the image plane, and then evaluate the integral of the convolution along the ray in screen space using the closed-form integrals of Section 3.3, which yields a per-segment screen-space rendering. The segments are then composited along each ray to obtain the accumulated color. (Right) We compute the L1 loss between the rendered image and the ground-truth image, and backpropagate its gradient to the parameters of the primitives.

Figure 3. Inside our spaghetti – We visualize the Dirac measure of Kheradmand et al. [14] (left), and of our Spaghetti Splatting (right) for the Bonsai scene from Mip-NeRF 360 [2]. (middle) We show one RGB render, not repeated, as it is visually identical for both representations. While 3DGS models thin strokes with scattered points (e.g. the bicycle spokes), our segments form continuous strokes that follow edges.

Figure 8. Comparison with Gaussian Haircut [43] – averaged over two datasets: GeomHair [15] (selected 8 hairstyles) and the curly hair model of Yuksel [42]. Top: strands of the curly hair model in a held-out view, one random color per strand. Our strands closely match the ground-truth strands, whereas those of Gaussian Haircut are poorly structured.

Figure 2. Kernel ⊛ dirac – Since Dirac masses and convolution kernels are independent degrees of freedom, we can modify either one to obtain a different differentiable primitive. The first column shows that convolving a point mass with a Gaussian or a Beta kernel yields the primitives of 3DGS [13] and DBS [16], respectively. Replacing the point mass with a line segment, while retaining either kernel, yields the primitives in the middle. Finally, we connect these segments into a polyline, which yields our curvilinear primitive. In the bottom row, we convolve the same Dirac masses with an anisotropic Beta kernel. For visualization, we shade the primitives with the normals of their convolution surfaces [4].
Figure 5. Convergence – A curve rendered as a polyline of 4, 8, 16, and 32 Beta segments rasterized independently converges to the smooth curve without knots at the joints.

Figure 6. Densification – We take inspiration from the densification strategy of 3DGS MCMC [14], but adapt it to our primitives. When the opacity of a segment falls below a threshold, MCMC relocation moves it, potentially breaking up the polyline it was in. The relocation target is then sampled in two ways. Long segments are split into two, short segments are cloned.

Table 1. Ablations – Averaged over Fuzzy, Shelly, and MipNeRF 360; each row removes one component (✗). The size of a connected component is its number of segments; a segment without a joint has size 1.

papers.selection_reason: Novel curvilinear primitive representation for 3D scene rendering, extending 3D Gaussian Splatting.
papers.title: Spaghetti Splatting: Differentiating Curvilinear Dirac Masses via Convolution
papers.tldr: Spaghetti Splatting enables efficient differentiable rendering and learning of curvilinear 3D primitives by convolving curves with kernels and volume-rendering their polyline approximations.

papers.abstract: To address unreliable cross-view association in long-sequence feed-forward dense SLAM, this letter presents V3DSAM, an open-vocabulary semantic dense SLAM system that establishes physical correspondences at both the scene and object levels. The system combines feed-forward geometric estimates from VGGT-SLAM 2.0 with open-vocabulary semantic observations from SAM3. We introduce semantic-geometric dual-scale loop verification, which identifies false loop closures using pixel-level bidirectional reprojection and object-level 3D spatial correspondences, without accessing backbone-internal features. We further propose geometry-anchored persistent instance mapping, which defines physical instances through class-constrained 3D connectivity in an optimized global coordinate system and assigns global IDs without inter-frame identity propagation. The proposed verifier rejects all four false loop candidates in our TUM RGB-D evaluation, while long-sequence ScanNet experiments show improved instance identity consistency. Thus, V3DSAM reduces dependence on internal backbone features and temporal ID propagation for robust long-term cross-view association.
bullets: Targets unreliable cross-view association in long-sequence dense SLAM.
Combines VGGT-SLAM 2.0 geometric estimates with SAM3 open-vocabulary semantic observations.
Uses pixel-level bidirectional reprojection and object-level 3D correspondences to reject false loop closures.

papers.abstract: Raw radar spectra are widely viewed as too cluttered and noisy for direct representation learning, motivating handcrafted reductions, sparse point clouds, or compact Doppler descriptors in radar perception. We challenge this assumption and argue that the main limitation lies not in the raw representation itself, but in the absence of a learning objective that separates structured signal from noise. Handcrafted reductions partially address this problem but impose rigid assumptions about what constitutes signal, discarding weak yet informative structure while retaining artifacts that fit the reduction model. Once removed, such information cannot be recovered by supervised learning. We propose an alternative: structure is the component of a radar spectrum that remains reconstructable under localized corruption, while noise is the component that does not. This perspective motivates self-supervised masked modeling for dense radar spectra without predefined signal-noise separation. We instantiate it with Leakage-aware Spectral MAE, a masked autoencoder for raw radar cubes using a corruption strategy inspired by cross-bin energy spreading caused by spectral leakage. We also demonstrate the importance of Doppler organization: treating Doppler as a primary spatial dimension in an x-y-D representation, with height encoded as features, substantially outperforms naive channel stacking and enables effective learning from dense 4D spectra. Without handcrafted reductions, our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art radar-based detectors and point-cloud-based self-supervised learning (SSL) counterparts. These results establish raw radar spectra as an effective representation for 3D perception when paired with an appropriate pretraining objective.
bullets: Handcrafted reductions and sparse representations may discard weak but informative structure and preserve reduction-specific artifacts.
The paper defines structure as spectrum content recoverable after localized corruption, distinguishing it from unreconstructable noise.

The approach consistently outperforms radar detectors and point-cloud SSL counterparts without handcrafted reductions.

papers.abstract: Foundation models increasingly combine geometry, semantics, and spatial context for three-dimensional scene understanding, but their suitability for forensic crime scene reconstruction remains unclear. This study presents a structured forensic evaluation framework for egocentric foundation models and demonstrates it using the Egocentric Foundation Model for 3D (EFM3D). Four simulated indoor crime scenes were recorded with Meta Project Aria Gen~1 at Robert Gordon University's East Lodge House forensic training facility. The framework evaluates room-scale reconstruction, semantic scene understanding, computational performance, and forensic suitability. Across the four scenes, EFM3D generated meshes averaging $12{,}668\pm2{,}430$ vertices and $24{,}838\pm4{,}903$ faces, with 39,529 recorded semantic predictions spanning 21--24 categories at a mean confidence of 0.40. Because reference meshes and expert-labelled 3D ground truth were unavailable, these statistics are treated as descriptive outputs rather than measures of geometric or detection accuracy. Final inference runs processed $1{,}388\pm203$ snippets per scene at $0.69\pm0.01$ samples/s and required $50.77\pm6.12$ minutes per recording. A seven-criterion capability profile indicated stronger support for room geometry, furniture localisation, scene context, and spatial relationships than for fine-scale forensic evidence. The results position EFM3D as a complementary tool for contextual documentation and scene review rather than a replacement for high-fidelity forensic capture. The framework provides a reproducible basis for evaluating future egocentric foundation models in specialised forensic settings.
bullets: Addresses the unclear suitability of egocentric foundation models for crime scene reconstruction.
Evaluates room-scale geometry, semantic understanding, computational performance, and forensic suitability across four simulated indoor scenes.
EFM3D produced descriptive meshes and semantic predictions, but unavailable reference meshes and expert 3D labels prevented accuracy measurement.
The model showed stronger support for room geometry, furniture localisation, scene context, and spatial relationships than for fine forensic evidence.
Inference required substantial processing time, supporting use as a complementary review tool rather than a replacement for high-fidelity forensic capture.

papers.abstract: This paper presents DPGS-SLAM (Diffusion-Prior and Provenance-Aware Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM) for dense mapping in environments containing dynamic objects. Objects in dynamic motion remain a significant challenge for dense visual SLAM since dynamic observations can contaminate camera tracking and scene reconstruction. Although 3DGS (3D Gaussian splatting) enables efficient dense mapping, existing 3DGS-SLAM systems may exhibit instability when dynamic objects violate their underlying static-scene assumption. Excluding dynamic observations can reduce their influence on tracking and mapping, but may leave occluded static backgrounds missing or weakly constrained. Our proposed DPGS-SLAM is a monocular RGB SLAM framework that supports provisional representations of insufficiently observed static backgrounds through asynchronous diffusion-based background completion and provenance-aware Gaussian mapping. Dynamic regions are identified through optical-flow-based motion discovery and temporally consistent mask propagation by SAM2. For selected keyframes, a fine-tuned diffusion inpainting model generates plausible background appearance in occluded regions, while metric depth predicted from completed images initializes provisional Gaussian primitives. Provenance labels distinguish generated primitives from observation-supported primitives, excluding generated content from camera-pose estimation and observed-map optimization. When previously occluded backgrounds become visible, eligible generated primitives are removed, and observation-supported primitives are independently initialized from real RGB observations and predicted depth. Experimental results demonstrated competitive camera tracking, with average ATE RMSE values of 1.2 cm on TUM RGB-D and 2.7 cm on BONN RGB-D datasets. On StaDy4D, DPGS-SLAM improved average PSNR by 4.60 dB over WildGS-SLAM using only monocular RGB input.
bullets: Addresses tracking and reconstruction errors caused by dynamic objects violating static-scene assumptions.
Uses optical-flow motion discovery and SAM2 mask propagation to identify dynamic regions.
Completes occluded backgrounds with diffusion inpainting and initializes provisional Gaussians from predicted metric depth.
Provenance labels prevent generated content from influencing camera-pose estimation and observed-map optimization; generated primitives are removed when real observations appear.
Reports competitive tracking on TUM RGB-D and BONN RGB-D, and a 4.60 dB average PSNR improvement over WildGS-SLAM on StaDy4D using monocular RGB.

papers.abstract: Single-view 3D hair reconstruction has progressed rapidly, but many methods optimize for visual plausibility rather than producing strand assets that can be directly used in grooming, editing, or simulation pipelines. We propose SAFE-Hair, a framework that reconstructs explicit strand grooms from a single portrait by decoding hair from persistent follicles in a canonical scalp-UV domain. Given a fitted template head, SAFE-Hair projects self-supervised image features onto the scalp, uses a conditional Rectified Flow model to generate latent scalp fields, and decodes occupancy, segment directions, length allocation, and total length at a fixed set of scalp follicles. This representation enforces scalp-rooted strand identities by construction and enables direct export with follicle IDs and guide-family metadata. We further introduce attachment, collision, and bending priors to improve geometric validity without per-subject test-time optimization. To evaluate both reconstruction fidelity and asset usability, we introduce HairBench-3D, a benchmark built from public 3D hair assets with standardized alignment, rendering, resampling, and metrics for geometry, direction consistency, invisible-region completion, silhouette agreement, and collision. SAFE-Hair improves Chamfer distance from 3.74 mm to 3.28 mm, F-score from 77.9 to 81.7, invisible-region F-score from 66.1 to 69.8, and penetration ratio from 4.8% to 3.9% over the strongest baseline.
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually plausible single-view hair reconstruction and strand assets usable for grooming, editing, and simulation.
Projects self-supervised image features into a canonical scalp-UV domain and generates latent scalp fields with conditional Rectified Flow.
Decodes strand occupancy, directions, length allocation, and total length at fixed follicles, preserving strand identities and export metadata.
Introduces attachment, collision, and bending priors without per-subject test-time optimization.
Presents HairBench-3D and reports improved Chamfer distance, F-score, invisible-region completion, and penetration ratio over the strongest baseline.

A conditional Rectified Flow model transforms Gaussian noise into a latent scalp field Z. A shared follicle decoder queries Z at persistent canonical follicles {ur}Rr=1 and predicts occupancy, segment directions, length allocation, total length, and export descriptors. The final strand curves are obtained by forward integration from fixed scalp roots, yielding explicit scalp-rooted strands with stable follicle identities and groom metadata for downstream export.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models have demonstrated strong generalization under large-scale pre-training, yet they struggle in long-tail scenarios such as low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction, and test-time adaptation. We observe relational attention structure collapse, manifested as the failure of cross-view correspondences, as a primary cause of these limitations. While adaptation offers a practical way to bridge this gap, existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) approaches mainly perform channel-wise feature adjustment and lack mechanisms to explicitly adapt relational structures, leaving correspondence failures unresolved. In this work, we formulate adaptation of 3D reconstruction models as a problem of correspondence recovery under domain shift and propose 3R-Adapter, a PEFT paradigm for long-tail 3D reconstruction scenarios. Our method consists of three components: Deformable Retrieval for task-adaptive relation candidate retrieval, Relational Rewiring for reconstructing cross-view relational structures, and Consistency Refinement for injecting the rewired relations into stable predictions. Extensive experiments on low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction, and test-time adaptation demonstrate that our approach significantly improves robustness over existing PEFT methods while maintaining efficient lightweight adaptation. Our code is released at https://github.com/PKU-OV3-LAB/3R-Adapter.
bullets: Targets long-tail settings including low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction, and test-time adaptation.
Attributes failures to collapsed relational attention and disrupted cross-view correspondences.
Introduces three components: Deformable Retrieval, Relational Rewiring, and Consistency Refinement.
Experiments report improved robustness over existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods while preserving lightweight adaptation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The data scaling bottleneck in 3D pre-training and our relational adaptation paradigm. (a) While foundation models thrive on massive data, they struggle to generalize to long-tail 3D domains due to the high cost of dense 3D ground truth. (b) Conventional PEFT methods (e.g., LoRA, Adapter) rely on implicit, channel-wise feature adjustment, which struggle to model the correspondence relationship in data-scarce scenarios. In contrast, our 3R-Adapter shifts the paradigm to explicit relational adaptation via Deformable Retrieval, Relational Rewiring, and Consistency Refinement, effectively establishing robust cross-view correspondences without destroying pretrained priors.

Figure 3: The overall pipeline of the proposed 3R-Adapter. To enable efficient adaptation for complex long-tail scenes, our 3R-Adapter modulates the network via three cohesive modules: Deformable Retrieval extracts view-specific anchors and estimates spatial offsets alongside routing weights; Relational Rewiring establishes explicit geometric correspondences across views through deformable spatial sampling; and Consistency Refinement integrates the relational features back into the main stream via a learned gating mechanism, effectively enforcing cross-view consistency.

Figure 2: Relational attention structure collapse in long-tail scenarios. (a) In data-rich daytime scenes, the pre-trained 3D reconstruction model produces concentrated cross-view attention, allowing a selected query token to attend to consistent physical counterparts across reference views. (b) For selected low-light queries, the attention distribution becomes diffuse and fragmented, indicating degraded relational routing and unreliable correspondence modeling. This observation suggests that long-tail adaptation requires explicitly restoring cross-view relational structures, motivating the design of 3R-Adapter.
Figure 4: Qualitative results on joint human-scene reconstruction. 3R-Adapter produces more consistent human mesh recovery and cleaner scene geometry under complex human-scene interactions.

papers.abstract: We present UltraVoxelGS, a 3D ultrasound reconstruction method that achieves both fast reconstruction and physically faithful rendering for the first time, bringing live spatial feedback during 2D ultrasound scanning within reach. This is made possible by a feed-forward design that predicts a complete Gaussian scene representation from posed ultrasound images directly, entirely bypassing the per-scene optimization bottleneck that has confined prior methods to offline use. Realising such feed-forward prediction in this setting is non-trivial: unlike natural images, ultrasound slices share at most one-dimensional intersections and exhibit view-dependent appearance due to acoustic propagation and attenuation, violating the dense overlap and photometric consistency assumed by existing feed-forward Gaussian methods. Hence, to achieve fast reconstruction, we introduce a feed-forward voxel-to-Gaussian pass that decouples representation size from input count by lifting all posed slices into a fixed-size voxel support and predicting Gaussian parameters directly. For faithful rendering, we propose ultrasound-aware appearance rendering strategy factorize reflection from cumulative attenuation during training and exploit appearance continuity among spatially adjacent slices for efficient Render-time Appearance Adaptation. On both real-world and simulated datasets, UltraVoxelGS achieves best PSNR/SSIM compared with per-scene optimization baselines while reducing inference from 10-20 minutes to approximately 10 seconds (over 35 times faster) and scales to sequences exceeding 1,000 frames. Code is available at https://github.com/YuebyYue/UltraVoxelGS-camera-ready.
bullets: Addresses the slow, offline nature of existing 3D ultrasound reconstruction methods and the sparse overlap and view-dependent appearance of ultrasound images.
Uses a feed-forward voxel-to-Gaussian pipeline that lifts all posed slices into a fixed-size voxel support, decoupling representation size from input count.
Models ultrasound appearance by separating reflection from cumulative attenuation and adapting rendering using continuity across neighboring slices.
Achieves the best reported PSNR/SSIM against per-scene optimization baselines on real and simulated datasets.
Reduces inference time from 10–20 minutes to approximately 10 seconds and supports sequences longer than 1,000 frames.

(b) Ultrasound-aware appearance rendering uses Decoupled Reflection and Attenuation Rendering (DRA) to render each target slice as cumulative attenuation A modulating anisotropic reflection R̂ for image-level supervision. papers.abstract: The wide field of view of fisheye cameras and the simplicity of a monocular setup make monocular fisheye visual odometry (VO) attractive for robotic localization and mapping. Nevertheless, scale drift remains a major challenge over long trajectories. Unsupervised depth learning can help to mitigate this issue, but the pronounced distortion of fisheye images poses challenges for accurate depth estimation. This article presents S$^2$D-FVO, a monocular fisheye VO framework integrating spherical bundle adjustment (SBA)-guided unsupervised depth learning to improve scale consistency and depth estimation accuracy. Given that pixel reprojection residuals do not uniformly reflect angular deviations between viewing rays and that the first-order linearization of a scalar angular reprojection residual is insensitive to perturbations along one tangent direction, SBA employs tangent-space angular reprojection residuals derived from the spherical logarithmic map. These residuals retain sensitivity along both tangent directions, with their norms equal to the corresponding scalar angular residuals. A median depth-based scale regularization term is further integrated into SBA to constrain the reconstruction scale. Building on these formulations, SBA replaces the pose estimation network during unsupervised depth learning, providing more reliable relative poses for view synthesis. In turn, depth estimates from the well-trained depth estimation network provide scale references for SBA, improving scale consistency while allowing individual 3-D landmark positions to be refined. Extensive experiments conducted on multiple public datasets, as well as two newly collected large-scale datasets, demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms representative existing approaches in both depth and trajectory estimation accuracy and is applicable to different camera models.
bullets: Addresses long-trajectory scale drift and fisheye distortion challenges in monocular VO.
Uses tangent-space angular reprojection residuals from the spherical logarithmic map to preserve sensitivity in both viewing-ray tangent directions.
Adds median-depth-based scale regularization to constrain reconstruction scale.
Replaces the pose estimation network during unsupervised learning, while learned depth provides scale references for bundle adjustment.
Experiments on public and newly collected datasets show improved depth and trajectory estimation and applicability across camera models.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation has advanced through large-scale pretraining and strong visual backbones, yet metric depth remains sensitive to scene-level scale. Indoor rooms and outdoor driving scenes occupy very different depth ranges, but most depth decoders infer this global structure implicitly from visual features. We ask whether scene-level semantic structure can instead act as an upstream prior that shapes the metric output space before dense prediction. We present LangDepth (SemanticBins), a monocular depth architecture that couples strong visual features with a scene-conditioned output space. A frozen CLIP encoder and a learnable bank of scene- and geometry-oriented concept keys convert image features into a compact scene descriptor, without requiring per-image text or an external captioner. A Scene Prior Module (SPM) maps this descriptor to a scene-conditioned metric depth interval, providing a global range anchor before dense decoding. In parallel, a DINOv2-L backbone with a lightweight FPN extracts dense visual features, and a Per-Pixel Assignment Network (PPAN) assigns pixels to the scene-prescribed bin structure. A confidence gate fuses the dense visual estimate with the SPM prior. We train LangDepth jointly on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI under a modest supervised depth budget, without web-scale depth supervision or pseudo-labelled depth data. A single model achieves delta_1 = 0.960 on NYU, 0.960 on KITTI, 0.887 on DIODE indoor, 0.946 on iBims-1, and 0.861 on SUN RGB-D. Beyond aggregate accuracy, the SPM predicts compact indoor ranges and much wider outdoor KITTI ranges, the gate becomes SPM-dominant on outdoor scenes, and perturbing the routed scene context causes large drops on KITTI and iBims-1. These results support scene-conditioned output spaces as a practical and interpretable mechanism for cross-domain monocular depth estimation.
bullets: Addresses scene-scale variation between indoor and outdoor environments, which can make metric depth estimation sensitive to global range.
Uses a frozen CLIP encoder and learned scene/geometry concept keys to form a compact scene descriptor without per-image text or captioning.
A Scene Prior Module predicts a scene-conditioned depth interval, while DINOv2-L, an FPN, and PPAN perform dense depth decoding with confidence-gated fusion.
Trained jointly on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI with modest supervised depth data, the single model reports strong results across NYU, KITTI, DIODE, iBims-1, and SUN RGB-D.
Scene priors adapt to compact indoor versus wider outdoor ranges; disrupting routed scene context substantially harms performance on KITTI and iBims-1.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: LangDepth (SemanticBins) pipeline. The input image is encoded by a frozen CLIP ViT-B/32, whose image features are routed through learnable scene and geometry concept keys to produce a compact scene descriptor z. The Scene Prior Module (SPM) uses only z to predict a scene-conditioned range (dmin, dmax), ordered bin centres {ck}Kk=1, and a global prior over those centres. In parallel, DINOv2-L with a lightweight FPN extracts dense visual features. PPAN conditions these features on z and predicts per-pixel bin weights {Wk}Kk=1 and a gate map g. Depth fusion forms the visual estimate dvis = ∑ k Wkck and the SPM prior dSPM = ∑ k πkck, then outputs d̂ = g ⊙ dvis + (1− g)⊙ dSPM.

Table 3: SPM range statistics. The SPM predicts compact indoor ranges and a much wider outdoor range for KITTI. The learned prior over bin centres is highly concentrated across datasets, indicating that the SPM primarily acts as a sceneconditioned range predictor and global scale anchor.
Table 4: Confidence gate statistics. KITTI is strongly SPM-dominant, while indoor datasets are more balanced or slightly vision-dominant.

Table 2: Component ablation study. papers.abstract: Creating high-quality 3D content has traditionally required specialist expertise and experience with complex tools. The growing ecosystem of AI-assisted creativity demands accessible and intuitive 3D generation systems. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising directions, yet extending their generative capabilities to 3D remains fundamentally challenging because existing 3D representations are not naturally compatible with language-based reasoning. Current approaches either depend on expensive fine-tuning or impose restrictive structural priors that sacrifice expressiveness and exclude organic shapes. We argue that the mismatch between LLM-native reasoning and conventional 3D parameterizations is a core bottleneck of LLM-driven 3D generation. To address this, we introduce the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS), a representation designed around semantically meaningful, interpretable part-level abstractions that are naturally understood by both humans and LLMs, enabling expressive, editable, and open-domain 3D generation without imposing restrictive geometric priors or expensive fine-tuning. Building upon HPS, we introduce SurfScaff3D, an interactive framework for text and image-to-3D generation. HPS inherits the flexibility of B-spline patches, while exposing an interface that leverages open-world capabilities of foundation models to reliably generate 3D. Its hierarchical part-level semantic labels enable targeted, natural-language edits at any level of granularity without re-running generation. Further, HPS offers explicit per-patch control over surface detail, enabling more expressive geometry capable of representing arbitrary objects. Extensive experiments against state-of-the-art LLM-based 3D generation methods demonstrate strong geometric fidelity, semantic alignment, and flexible editing across diverse object categories.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between LLM reasoning and conventional 3D parameterizations.
Introduces Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS), built from flexible B-spline patches with interpretable, part-level semantics.
Supports interactive text-to-3D and image-to-3D generation without expensive fine-tuning or restrictive geometric priors.
Enables targeted natural-language edits at multiple granularities and explicit per-patch surface-detail control.
Experiments report strong geometric fidelity, semantic alignment, and flexible editing across diverse object categories.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of SurfScaff3D. SurfScaff3D iteratively constructs an HPS representation by programmatically generating surface geometry and verifying its local geometry through rendered views. HPS organizes geometry as a hierarchical semantic tree of B-spline surface patches with explicit patch-level control over surface variation, enabling both structured mechanical objects and organic shapes. The examples illustrate how frequency and amplitude help in modelling diverse objects. A critic evaluates rendered outputs and provides targeted feedback, forming a closed-loop refinement process that progressively improves prompt alignment and geometric fidelity. The critic loop executes for a fixed number of N iterations unless an early stopping criterion is met.

papers.abstract: Monocular 3D detection (Mono3D) hinges on recovering depth from a single image, for which the geometric formulation $z \approx f \cdot H / h_{2D}$ is widely adopted due to its simplicity and direct grounding in projective geometry. We show that this formulation harbors a systematic, projection-induced bias: substituting the 2D bounding-box height $h_{2D}$ recovers the depth of an object's visible front surface rather than its center, causing size-dependent underestimation that persists even under ground-truth inputs. We address this front-surface bias with MonoPCA, a unified framework built on a projection-consistent reformulation. At its core, PCDepth retains the measurable $h_{2D}$ and closes the gap to center depth through an orientation- and size-aware correction derived from perspective geometry, eliminating the bias without introducing ill-posed regression targets. Because PCDepth couples depth to predicted object size and orientation, attribute perception becomes essential. We therefore introduce GeoAlign, a teacher-student framework that transfers geometric representations from Vision Foundation Models into a lightweight student, strengthening attribute perception at no inference cost. Across four challenging benchmarks, MonoPCA achieves SoTA performance, including a +1.44% AP$_{3D}$ gain on the KITTI leaderboard and +2.80% on Omni3D$_{OUT}$. Code is available at https://github.com/alanzhangcs/MonoPCA.
bullets: The common depth estimate based on 2D box height systematically underestimates object-center depth, even with ground-truth inputs.
PCDepth retains measurable 2D height and applies an orientation- and size-aware perspective correction without ill-posed regression targets.
GeoAlign transfers geometric representations from vision foundation models to a lightweight student at no inference cost.
MonoPCA reports state-of-the-art results across four challenging benchmarks, with gains of 1.44 AP3D on KITTI and 2.80 on Omni3D_OUT.
The approach depends on accurately perceiving object size and orientation because these attributes are coupled to depth estimation.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of MonoPCA. The conventional geometric depth z = f ·H/h2D recovers the visible front surface rather than the object center, causing a systematic projection bias. PCDepth corrects this bias analytically by adding an orientation- and size-aware offset, making depth an explicit function of the predicted 3D size and yaw. This shifts the bottleneck onto attribute accuracy, which GeoAlign strengthens by distilling representations from a Mixture-of-Backbone (MoB) teacher into a ResNet student via Hierarchical Feature Alignment (HFA).

Figure 2: Geometric basis of PCDepth. (a) Source of the front-surface bias. Under perspective projection, the 3D bottom center (red) is self-occluded by a nearer surface point (green) that projects higher on the image plane, while the visible bottom of the box corresponds to a still-closer point (yellow), giving h′ 2D < h2D. The conventional estimate z = f ·H/h2D therefore recovers the frontsurface depth rather than the center depth. (b) h′ 2D is depth-dependent. As the center depth changes from z1 to z2, the surface point defining h′ 2D shifts (green to purple), so h′ 2D is not directly observable and its regression is ill-posed. (c) Recovering center depth via an optical-axis correction. zgeo recovers the front-surface depth, displaced from the object center by an offset ∆ along the optical axis: ∆ ≈ W/2 at γ = 0◦ (Left), ∆ ≈ L/2 at γ = 90◦ (Middle), and ∆ ≈ L 2 | sin γ| + W 2 | cos γ| for arbitrary yaw (Right), giving z = zgeo +∆.

Figure 1: (a) Depth error under ideal inputs. We evaluate the GeoDepth formulation [69] using ground-truth f , H , and h2D. Even with these oracle inputs, GeoDepth incurs a non-trivial error that grows with object scale, revealing a structural rather than statistical bias. Our PCDepth substantially mitigates this bias across all categories. (b) Geometric origin of the bias. Under perspective projection, the 3D bottom center (red) is self-occluded by a nearer surface point (green) that projects higher on the image plane, while the visible bottom in the image corresponds to a still-closer surface point (yellow). The commonly adopted formulation z = f ·H/h2D therefore recovers the depth of the visible front surface rather than that of the object center, systematically underestimating depth.

Figure 7: PCDepth generalizes across detectors. Replacing only the depth head with PCDepth yields consistent gains, indicating that the improvement stems from correcting the projection bias rather than architectural interactions.
Figure 5: Details of Mixture-of-Backbone. MoB adaptively fuses a convolutional pyramid with a single-scale VFM branch at every scale.

Figure 4: GeoAlign reduces depth error through the attributes PCDepth depends on. Per-distance errors on KITTI Val for 3D size (Left), orientation (Middle), and depth (Right). GeoAlign consistently lowers size and orientation errors across all ranges, and since PCDepth computes depth analytically from these two attributes, the improvements propagate directly to depth.

papers.abstract: Controlled acquisition setups are widely used for high-accuracy multi-view 3D surface reconstruction, as they allow sensor configuration, image resolution, viewpoint distribution, and illumination to be specified. Yet benchmarking remains difficult, since reconstruction accuracy depends jointly on the reconstruction paradigm, object properties, and acquisition regime. Existing benchmarks often restrict viewpoint coverage, resolution, or illumination, which can bias comparisons towards methods suited to the chosen setting. Others lack accurate 3D ground truth or quantified image-to-geometry alignment, limiting their use for metric surface evaluation. We introduce Martine, a benchmark for controlled 3D object surface reconstruction. Martine comprises 28 objects, including transparent materials and fine structures, captured at 9568 x 6376 pixels from 84 views over a spherical cap under both single-light and multi-light regimes. It provides object-independent camera calibration, accurate 3D ground-truth scans, calibration and image-to-geometry accuracy quantified on test images, and 3D property masks for analysing errors by material properties, visibility, curvature and fine structures. Experiments across photogrammetry, classical multi-view stereo, neural implicit surfaces, Gaussian-splatting-based reconstruction, and multi-view photometric stereo show that Martine enables regime-aware evaluation with explicit control over reference-data accuracy. The benchmark resolves sub-millimetric reconstruction differences, with a best observed Chamfer distance of 0.058 mm over the evaluated visible surface.
bullets: Includes 28 objects, including transparent materials and fine structures, captured at high resolution from 84 spherical-cap views under single- and multi-light settings.
Provides accurate 3D ground-truth scans, object-independent camera calibration, quantified image-to-geometry alignment, and property-based 3D masks.
Supports regime-aware comparisons across photogrammetry, classical multi-view stereo, neural implicit surfaces, Gaussian-splatting methods, and multi-view photometric stereo.
Enables analysis by material, visibility, curvature, and fine structures while resolving sub-millimetric reconstruction differences.
The best observed Chamfer distance was 0.058 mm on the evaluated visible surface.

papers.abstract: 3D visual grounding (3DVG) localizes language-referred objects in 3D scenes, with broad applicability in both indoor and outdoor environments. However, existing 3DVG research focuses on static indoor objects, limiting its use in dynamic outdoor autonomous driving. Motion descriptions, which capture the temporal dynamics of moving objects, offer a promising way to address this challenge. We therefore introduce MoT3DVG, a large-scale dataset for dynamic-aware outdoor 3DVG with temporally evolving motion descriptions. It contains 850 scenarios with 31,128 frames from nuScenes dataset, and provides 144,568 language prompts with motion-aware descriptions for dynamic objects across time. We further propose DynaVG, a novel framework that effectively leverages temporal cues for outdoor 3DVG. In addition to the standard modality-specific encoders, DynaVG introduces a Short-Long Integrated Dynamic Encoding (SLIDE) module before the language-point cloud alignment. SLIDE models both local motion cues and global temporal context via short-term window encoding and long-term window shifting. Extensive experiments demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG, validating the effectiveness of motion-aware encoding. Our work reveals open challenges and promising directions for future research in outdoor 3DVG.
bullets: Targets the gap between static indoor 3D visual grounding and dynamic outdoor autonomous-driving scenarios.
Provides 850 nuScenes scenarios, 31,128 frames, and 144,568 temporally evolving motion-aware prompts.
DynaVG uses the SLIDE module to capture both short-term local motion and long-term temporal context before language–point cloud alignment.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG and support the value of motion-aware encoding.
The benchmark also highlights open challenges for future outdoor 3D visual grounding research.

papers.abstract: Streaming 3D foundation models (3DFMs) estimate camera poses and dense geometry online, but they fall short of SLAM: their predictions are fixed once emitted, so loop closures cannot correct accumulated drift. With such models already providing strong geometric capability, a central question for SLAM becomes how to schedule their inference and how to keep its results as revisable state. We present Map2SLAM, which keeps LingBot-Map frozen, trains only a lightweight retrieval head, and builds SLAM on the model's inference interface, turning its predictions into observations of an external persistent SLAM state. The front-end tracks every incoming frame with the model's causal streaming inference and decides which frames are written to the persistent state as keyframes. The back-end asynchronously decides when and which past frames to re-observe, re-running the model's joint inference over them with fresh context; verified loop observations correct the trajectory online, and segment observations refine dense geometry after the sequence. All invocations share a single frame encoder pass per image, whose cached features also drive loop retrieval, so frequent re-invocation incurs no additional encoding cost. Map2SLAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on KITTI, VBR, and Oxford Spires, reducing mean ATE by over 40% compared with the best uncalibrated baselines, while maintaining real-time tracking at over 28 FPS at a resolution of $518\times154$ on an NVIDIA RTX 5090D GPU. Please visit our project page at https://robbyant-research.github.io/Map2SLAM/.
bullets: Addresses drift accumulation because streaming model predictions are fixed after emission and cannot be corrected by loop closures.
Uses causal streaming inference for frame tracking, while selecting keyframes to write into persistent SLAM state.
An asynchronous back end re-observes past frames with fresh context to verify loops, correct trajectories, and refine dense geometry.
Shares one frame-encoder pass across invocations; cached features also support loop retrieval without extra encoding cost.
Reports state-of-the-art results on KITTI, VBR, and Oxford Spires, with over 40% lower mean ATE than the best uncalibrated baselines and tracking above 28 FPS at 518×154 on an NVIDIA RTX 5090D.
