papers.abstract: Medical Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) leverages the semantic richness of radiology reports to learn 3D representations, yet current architectures remain fundamentally anatomy-agnostic. While clinical diagnostics rely on organ-specific context, standard encoders apply a uniform, dense parameterization to all volumetric patches, and existing Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers gate on isolated local features without explicit access to the organ composition of the scan or crop. We propose Anatomy-Activated Mixture-of-Experts (A$^{2}$MoE), a framework that incorporates anatomical inductive biases within the model's computational path. A$^{2}$MoE introduces two key components: (1) a Histogram Representation Router (HRR) that conditions expert selection on global visual context and a predicted anatomical composition histogram, encouraging anatomy-dependent expert weighting; and (2) an Organ-Query Multi-Scale Projector (OQMSP) that utilizes learnable queries to extract organ-level embeddings for fine-grained alignment without requiring manual annotations at inference. By routing at the patch level rather than the token level, A$^{2}$MoE reduces routing complexity by orders of magnitude while satisfying load balancing by construction. Pre-trained on over 60,000 multi-phase CT scans, A$^{2}$MoE achieves state-of-the-art performance across segmentation, classification, and detection benchmarks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our anatomically grounded inductive biases support robust generalization to MRI and ultrasound, establishing a scalable foundation for medical representation learning. The code is available at https://github.com/gmum/A2MoE.
bullets: Addresses anatomy-agnostic encoders and local-only MoE routing in 3D medical VLP.
Uses a Histogram Representation Router to select experts based on global context and predicted anatomical composition.
Introduces an Organ-Query Multi-Scale Projector for fine-grained organ-level alignment without manual inference-time annotations.
Patch-level routing lowers routing complexity and enforces load balancing by construction.
Pre-trained on over 60,000 multi-phase CT scans, it reports state-of-the-art results across segmentation, classification, and detection, with generalization to MRI and ultrasound.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the A2MoE architecture. Given a 3D CT input XI n, the Histogram Representation Router (HRR) combines visual context and anatomical composition to predict stagespecific expert weights shared across spatial positions. These weights combine the outputs of all experts {E(s) k }Ks k=1. OQMSP uses shared organ queries Q to aggregate multi-scale encoder features Xs into organ-level visual embeddings Zvis. These are aligned with corresponding text embeddings ztxt, obtained through a frozen text encoder and a trainable linear projection, using Lalign. A parallel decoder combines encoder features with spatial skip connections and is supervised by Lseg. At inference, anatomical composition is predicted from image features.
Figure 4: Qualitative segmentation results. Comparison of A2MoE against the top four baseline methods. Key differences are highlighted in red bounding boxes (see Appendix F for more samples).

Figure 15: Critical difference (CD) diagrams comparing ten segmentation methods across six benchmark datasets for DSC (top; higher is better) and HD95 (bottom; lower is better). Average ranks are computed independently per dataset and then averaged across all six benchmarks; rank 1 denotes the best-performing method. Horizontal brackets connect groups of methods for which no statistically significant difference was detected (Friedman test followed by Nemenyi post-hoc test, α=0.05). Our proposed method A2MoE is evaluated in two configurations: #2 +A2MoE applied on top of SegMamba, and #3 +OQMSP, which further extends it with organ-query-guided semisupervised pre-training; #1 SegMamba serves as the baseline. The full model (#3 +OQMSP) achieves the best average rank on both metrics (DSC: 1.00, HD95: 2.25) and is statistically distinguishable from the majority of competing methods (p = 4.51 · 10−8 and p = 1.88 · 10−6, respectively).
Figure 3: An overview of OQMSP. Learnable organ queries {qc}C−1

Figure 1: Comparison of MoE routing strategies. (a) MoE routing: The input feature map x is pooled to form a global visual context, which is passed through an MLP router to produce logits over K experts. Softmax-normalized weights are then used to compute a convex combination of expert outputs Ek(x). Routing depends solely on visual features. (b) In addition to visual context, a foreground-normalized organ-composition histogram h̃ is embedded and fused with visual features to jointly condition the router. Each foreground entry represents the corresponding organ’s share of the total foreground voxel mass in the input crop. A learnable class-to-expert affinity matrix A(s) introduces a structural prior via a log-probability term log(h̃Ã(s) + ϵ), biasing expert selection toward anatomically consistent assignments. The resulting logits are softmax-normalized to obtain routing weights, and the final output is computed as a weighted sum of expert responses.

These high-fidelity masks serve as a structured anatomical prior, providing localized supervision for image-text alignment and ensuring that the joint embedding space preserves the underlying biological topology.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in vision foundation models (VFMs) has made automated open-vocabulary 3D bounding box annotation increasingly feasible by jointly leveraging LiDAR point clouds and images. However, partial observations remain a major challenge in sparse driving scenes, where visible LiDAR points often cover only a small fraction of the object's surface and provide insufficient cues for estimating its full spatial extent. As a result, existing methods often produce mislocalized boxes or leave objects unlabeled. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{\Ours{}}, an automated annotation framework that leverages image-generated 3D assets as amodal geometric priors for partially observed objects. By establishing correspondences between input images and rendered views of 3D assets, \Ours{} robustly aligns canonical amodal geometry with partially observed world-space LiDAR point clouds. To improve temporal consistency and reduce computational cost, \Ours{} generates a single asset per instance, estimates its metric scale once at a single frame and propagates it across frames for dynamic instances, and aggregates multi-frame observations for static instances. 3D object detectors trained on annotations from \Ours{} improve performance over strong baselines by 14.1 mAP on the nuScenes dataset and by 12.45 AP at IoU 0.5 for the vehicle class on the Waymo Open Dataset (WOD). Our project page is available at: \href{https://oliver0922.github.io/AmodalBox/}{https://oliver0922.github.io/AmodalBox/}
bullets: Addresses box mislocalization and missed objects caused by sparse, partial LiDAR observations in driving scenes.
Aligns canonical amodal 3D asset geometry with partially observed world-space LiDAR using image-to-rendered-view correspondences.
Improves consistency and efficiency by estimating each instance’s scale once, propagating it across dynamic-object frames, and aggregating observations for static objects.
Detectors trained on AmodalBox annotations improve by 14.1 mAP on nuScenes and 12.45 AP at IoU 0.5 for vehicles on Waymo Open Dataset.

papers.abstract: Few-shot depth completion aims to recover dense metric depth from sparse measurements using only a small number of target-domain annotations, offering a favorable balance between annotation cost and model adaptation. We propose LIFT, a framework that harnesses both depth and feature priors from a frozen pretrained monocular depth estimation (MDE) foundation model for few-shot depth completion. Specifically, LIFT first estimates local scale and shift parameters on a coarse grid and interpolates them into smooth, dense parameter fields, providing a spatially adaptive metric depth initialization. It then progressively refines this initialization through multi-scale depth propagation guided by foundation features. Finally, a lightweight residual decoder combines multi-level foundation features with propagation correction to refine the metric depth. Extensive experiments on NYUv2 and KITTI-DC demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art few-shot performance. The source code will soon be released.
bullets: Addresses dense metric depth recovery when only a small number of target-domain annotations are available.
Estimates spatially varying local scale and shift fields on a coarse grid, then interpolates them for metric depth initialization.
Progressively propagates and refines depth at multiple scales using features from the frozen foundation model.
Uses a lightweight residual decoder to combine foundation features with propagation corrections.
Reports state-of-the-art few-shot performance on NYUv2 and KITTI-DC; code is planned for release.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed LIFT framework. Given an RGB image and sparse depth, the frozen MDE foundation model provides relative depth and multi-level features. The final metric depth is obtained by combining the coarse metric depth, propagated depth, and predicted residual.

papers.abstract: Generating high-fidelity voxels while keeping their lightweight nature remains an open problem in computer vision. Current generators are either high-fidelity but computationally heavy, or lightweight but of lower fidelity. Hierarchical methods keep the lightweight nature of voxels. However, their coarse levels, which decide where all finer cells can appear, are generated with the least information about the shape and are never revisited, so they are often plausible but wrong. Our key insight is to let finer cells take part in deciding coarse cells. To this end, we propose JoVox, a discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint distribution of all levels of the voxel hierarchy, instead of a separate distribution for each level, so that coarse cells can be predicted with finer cells already generated nearby. Within this framework, we further introduce a two-level prediction, which outputs the cells two levels finer at once instead of one level finer, halving the number of levels that the network processes and yielding voxels of higher fidelity. We also introduce an unmasking strategy that revisits early decisions once finer cells are generated and corrects inconsistencies in masked diffusion models. Our framework outperforms the baselines on both unconditional and image-conditioned voxel generation. Compared with the current state-of-the-art TRELLIS.2, we achieve 8x higher training throughput, 1/15 of the FLOPs in a forward pass, train on 4 vs. 32 GPUs, and obtain higher quality with an 11% lower Chamfer distance.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between voxel fidelity and computational efficiency.
Uses discrete flow matching to learn the joint distribution across all voxel hierarchy levels.
Introduces two-level prediction to process half as many hierarchy levels.
Adds unmasking to revise coarse decisions when finer cells reveal inconsistencies.
Outperforms baselines and reports higher quality than TRELLIS.2 with substantially lower compute and training cost.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis, but deployment budgets vary across devices and network conditions. Most compact methods target one operating point, so another budget requires a separate representation. SHIN is a scalable 3DGS hierarchy with a reusable Base and additive enhancement layers, so each higher-quality operating point extends rather than replaces the decoded representation. Constructing this hierarchy requires deciding which Gaussians each stage adds and how much spherical-harmonic (SH) appearance each retains, because these choices remain fixed in later prefixes. SHIN derives one shared Gaussian order from multi-scale position-scale sensitivity and divides each stage budget between adding Gaussians and retaining SH bands using calibrated gradient-based scores per byte. Lightweight opacity updates adjust compositing while transmitted geometry and SH coefficients remain unchanged. Across three benchmarks, SHIN progressively improves one cumulative representation and achieves the best PSNR-size efficiency in every overlapping comparison with the multi-rate and progressive baselines.
bullets: Addresses the need for different 3DGS operating points across devices and network conditions.
Uses a reusable Base plus additive enhancement layers, forming cumulative quality prefixes.
Ranks Gaussian additions using multi-scale position-scale sensitivity and allocates each stage’s byte budget between Gaussians and spherical-harmonic appearance bands.
Applies lightweight opacity updates while keeping transmitted geometry and SH coefficients unchanged.
Across three benchmarks, reports the best PSNR-size efficiency in every overlapping comparison with multi-rate and progressive baselines.

papers.abstract: AI agents can generate as-built Building Information Models (BIMs) from reality-capture data, but the evidence required for accurate reconstruction remains unclear. This paper presents Agent2BIM, an agent-based Scan-to-BIM framework, and evaluates seven capture configurations in a research laboratory and a mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) scene. Inputs include 360° panoramas, smartphone video, smartphone LiDAR, terrestrial laser scanning (TLS), TLS with posed panoramas, and imagery supplemented by prior IFC models. Outputs are compared against TLS-verified reference models for component detection, geometric accuracy, and MEP connectivity. In the laboratory, component recall ranged from 84% to 100%, but only 9% of components reconstructed from panoramas were within 20 cm of their reference positions, compared with 86% using smartphone LiDAR. In the MEP scene, scale-free inputs recovered 11 - 43% of components, versus 75 - 93% for metric inputs. Prior IFC models improved MEP reconstruction but could propagate inaccuracies. The results highlight the complementary roles of visual and metric evidence in agent-based Scan-to-BIM.
bullets: Evaluates seven reality-capture configurations in laboratory and MEP scenes against TLS-verified reference models.
Assesses component detection, geometric accuracy, and MEP connectivity.
Panorama-based reconstructions detected many components but achieved limited positional accuracy; smartphone LiDAR substantially improved it.
In the MEP scene, metric inputs recovered more components than scale-free imagery.
Prior IFC models improved MEP reconstruction but could propagate existing inaccuracies.

papers.abstract: Recent large human reconstruction models create remarkable animatable 3D avatars from a single image, but their appearance remains entangled with the illumination and cannot be relighted. In contrast, existing 3D relightable-avatar reconstruction methods typically require person-specific optimization. We present ZARA, a zero-shot feed-forward framework that reconstructs an animatable 3D Gaussian avatar together with its intrinsic attributes from a single image. ZARA couples a pretrained large-scale human reconstruction model with a Material Transformer to inherit geometry priors while learning material-aware Gaussian representations. To preserve localized details, we introduce Gaussian-aligned material feature fusion strategy, which injects multi-scale material features onto individual Gaussians and combines them with geometry tokens. As most human-avatar datasets lack ground-truth material maps, we use pseudo-material labels as conditioning inputs and supervision targets during training. We further introduce MatFace regularization to preserve facial structure and color in albedo prediction under unreliable facial pseudo-material supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ZARA reconstructs animatable and relightable humans within tens of seconds without person-specific optimization or post-processing, outperforming existing baselines in both relighting quality and materials generalization ability. As the ability of recovering the physically-based-rendering attributes of the human, ZARA also enables direct material editing of the avatar's appearance.
bullets: Addresses appearance–illumination entanglement in single-image human reconstruction and avoids person-specific optimization.
Combines a pretrained human reconstruction model with a Material Transformer to predict material-aware Gaussian representations.
Uses Gaussian-aligned multi-scale material feature fusion to preserve localized details and combine material information with geometry.
Trains with pseudo-material labels and introduces MatFace regularization to improve facial albedo structure and color.
Experiments show reconstruction in tens of seconds, improved relighting and material generalization over baselines, and support for direct material editing.

papers.abstract: We present a hypernetwork that generates the parameters of an implicit neural representation (INR) for a given signal in a single forward pass, without test-time optimization. Existing hypernetworks for this problem either ignore the chain-rule structure of the test-time optimization that produces an INR or, when they preserve it, instantiate the structure with MLPs whose parameter count grows quartically in target-network width. Our central contribution is to show that this parameter-count cost is structural to the MLP instantiation, not to the optimization-oriented principle of preserving chain-rule structure, and to resolve it by replacing the MLP body with attention. The resulting hypernetwork combines three design choices: an output-neuron-centric tokenization that aligns the token axis with each layer's output-neuron axis; an information-flow consistency rule that fixes the role of every cross-attention module from the representation its output should occupy; and a token-space iterative rollout that realizes the five quantities one optimization step on the target INR computes as five cross-attention modules with parameter count independent of target-network width. Across five 2D and 3D INR generation benchmarks, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art single-pass and optimization-oriented baselines; scales to target-network widths at which the MLP-based optimization-oriented paradigm exhausts GPU memory; and produces the highest result on NeRF generation without ground-truth INR weights supervision.
bullets: Existing optimization-oriented hypernetworks preserve test-time optimization structure but can require parameter counts that grow quartically with target-network width.
The method replaces the costly MLP body with attention while retaining the chain-rule structure of an optimization step.
It uses output-neuron-centric tokenization, information-flow-consistent cross-attention, and token-space iterative rollout.
Across five 2D and 3D INR benchmarks, it outperforms reported single-pass and optimization-oriented baselines.
It scales to target widths that exhaust GPU memory for MLP-based approaches and achieves the highest reported NeRF-generation result without ground-truth INR-weight supervision.

papers.abstract: Transparent-interface reconstruction must recover glass surfaces even when most observed color comes from the scene behind them. We present ClearForm, a shared-planar-Gaussian method for jointly reconstructing transparent interfaces and the appearance seen through them. We identify and analyze the Geometry-Appearance Compositing Dilemma (GACD): when the same transparency-dependent alpha controls both color and geometry, revealing the background can weaken a transparent surface's contribution to geometric reconstruction. We derive its effect on plane-based depth estimation, identify a mechanism that can weaken geometric learning, and quantify the loss of interface support through controlled comparisons. To address this conflict, we develop geometry-preserving dual-opacity surface reconstruction. Shared planar Gaussians retain interface contributions in geometry compositing while modeling transmission and sparse reflection in RGB, supported by transparency-aware geometric constraints. To manage the different primitive-visibility requirements of these compositors, we introduce Dual-Evidence Lifecycle (DEL), which retains Gaussians supported by multi-view geometry or RGB reconstruction evidence. On 3D-FRONT-T, ClearForm achieves 27.05 mm Chamfer distance (CD) and 0.928 F1, compared with 59.18 mm CD for our PGSR reproduction and the reported 34 mm CD and 0.836 F1 for GLINT. On TransLab, it achieves 1.65 mm CD, 0.963 F1, and 40.14 dB PSNR. In matched ablations, dual-opacity compositing reduces CD from 59.25 to 27.09 mm, while DEL improves PSNR by 2.06 dB. Our project page is available at https://hajeongx.github.io/clearform/.
bullets: Identifies the Geometry-Appearance Compositing Dilemma, where transparency can reveal backgrounds but weaken geometric learning of glass surfaces.
Uses shared planar Gaussians with dual-opacity compositing: interface support is preserved for geometry, while transmission and sparse reflection are modeled in RGB.
Introduces transparency-aware geometric constraints and Dual-Evidence Lifecycle (DEL) to retain primitives supported by either multi-view geometry or RGB evidence.
Achieves 27.05 mm Chamfer distance and 0.928 F1 on 3D-FRONT-T, and 1.65 mm CD, 0.963 F1, and 40.14 dB PSNR on TransLab.
Matched ablations show dual-opacity greatly reduces CD, while DEL improves PSNR; the method targets transparent-interface reconstruction with shared planar structure.

papers.abstract: Domain adaptive point cloud completion (DA PCC) aims to bridge the geometric discrepancy between labeled source domains and unlabeled target domains for accurate 3D shape completion. Existing methods based on CNNs, Transformers, and Mamba-like sequence models still face challenges from limited receptive fields, high computational complexity, insufficient geometric bias, and serialization sensitivity. Recently, Receptance Weighted Key Value (RWKV) provides a linear-complexity alternative for long-range sequence modeling. However, adapting RWKV to DA PCC remains challenging due to the lack of explicit geometric priors, the mismatch between recurrent modeling and coarse-to-fine generation, and unstable target-domain adaptation. To address these challenges, we propose DAPointRWKV, a novel RWKV-based framework for DA PCC. DAPointRWKV consists of three components: Geometry-Aware RWKV (GA-RWKV) Backbone, RWKV-Oriented Progressive Decoder (RWKV-PD), and Dual Structural Regularization (DSR). Specifically, GA-RWKV introduces geometry-aware recurrent representation learning, RWKV-PD bridges RWKV token representations with coarse-to-fine reconstruction through local token-guided refinement, and DSR stabilizes target-domain transfer through visible-structure anchoring and complete-shape hypothesis stabilization. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that DAPointRWKV consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
bullets: Targets the geometric gap between labeled source and unlabeled target domains in 3D shape completion.
Introduces a Geometry-Aware RWKV backbone for recurrent geometric representation learning.
Uses an RWKV-Oriented Progressive Decoder to support coarse-to-fine reconstruction with local token-guided refinement.
Applies Dual Structural Regularization to anchor visible structures and stabilize complete-shape hypotheses during target adaptation.
Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show consistent improvements over existing methods.

(b) The RWKV-Oriented Progressive Decoder is proposed to convert RWKV features into progressively refined point sets through coarse-to-fine reconstruction with local token-guided refinement. (c) Dual Structural Regularization is presented to regularize target-domain completion by enforcing observation anchoring and hypothesis stabilization.

papers.abstract: Pose awareness characterizes the extent to which a learned feature space aligns with the underlying object-pose manifold, such that observations with similar poses exhibit greater feature similarity than those with increasingly different poses. While such structure is desirable for pose-sensitive 3D vision tasks, visual foundation models pre-trained on individual 2D images typically lack explicit 3D or pose supervision. This raises a fundamental question: Do 2D visual foundation models exhibit pose awareness after large-scale pretraining? To answer this question, we introduce PoseBench, a systematic benchmark to probe pose awareness in pretrained visual features. Our evaluation follows a progressive design: held-out rendered views probe intrinsic pose-aware structure under controlled conditions, while real-image queries evaluate how robustly this structure remains accessible under real-world variations. We further introduce pose-graph-based refinement as a complementary probe of compatibility between feature neighborhoods and the underlying pose manifold. Across 31 publicly available checkpoints from 10 pretraining families, PoseBench reveals that pose awareness is an implicit but non-uniform property of 2D visual foundation models, and consistent gains from pose-graph refinement suggest that feature spaces retain structure compatible with the underlying pose manifold. PoseBench therefore provides a systematic basis for understanding and selecting pretrained features for pose-sensitive 3D vision tasks.
bullets: Benchmarks pose awareness through progressively harder probes, from controlled rendered views to real-image queries.
Introduces pose-graph refinement to test compatibility between feature neighborhoods and the underlying pose manifold.
Evaluates 31 publicly available checkpoints spanning 10 pretraining families.
Finds pose awareness is present but varies across models, while refinement consistently reveals additional pose-compatible structure.
Supports understanding and selecting pretrained features for pose-sensitive 3D tasks.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction turns an uncalibrated monocular stream into a dense point cloud in a single inference pass, orders of magnitude faster than classical structure-from-motion (e.g., COLMAP), and reliable on the weakly textured, repetitive surfaces where keypoint matching fails outright. However, raw point clouds lack the object identity, physical properties, and watertight volume required for robot learning. This gap widens under robot-native capture. A camera mounted on a robot constrained to a few degrees of freedom sees each object only partially, and the repetitive, weakly textured structure of an office makes distinct workstations nearly indistinguishable, leaving redundant and partial observations that downstream reconstruction cannot resolve. Existing image-to-3D generation methods struggle with these conditions, hallucinating geometry under incomplete views and confusing repeated instances. We present OfficeTwin, a robot-native framework that converts these incomplete observations into simulation-ready digital twins. OfficeTwin first imposes metric and structural constraints, then exploits the office's structural redundancy by registering repeated cubicles into a shared canonical frame, where complementary observations recover geometry occluded in any single view without hallucination. On a real office scan, OfficeTwin recovers every cubicle as an individually watertight, metric solid, outperforming feed-forward reconstruction and generative baselines that fail to produce simulation-ready assets.
bullets: Addresses incomplete, weakly textured, and redundant office observations from cameras with limited robot motion.
Imposes metric and structural constraints before reconstruction.
Registers repeated cubicles into a shared canonical frame to recover occluded geometry without hallucination.
Produces individually watertight, simulation-ready cubicle models on a real office scan.
Outperforms feed-forward and generative reconstruction baselines that fail to create simulation-ready assets.

papers.abstract: Geometric foundation models estimate dense geometry and camera parameters from monocular images, but reliable SLAM also requires consistent scale and accurate data association across successive reconstructions. We present DASH-SLAM, a monocular SLAM system that integrates metric depth predictions from pretrained Depth Anything 3 into a shared-keyframe pose graph without task-specific fine-tuning. DASH-SLAM derives scale corrections from depth ratios at shared anchor images and accumulates them across reconstructions, with a damping factor controlling their influence. These corrections rescale odometry translations, loop constraints, and map geometry. Experiments on TUM, Replica, and 7-Scenes show that DASH-SLAM outperforms state-of-the-art methods. We evaluate performance using both rigid and similarity alignment to distinguish metric-scale fidelity from accuracy up to scale. We further evaluate DASH-SLAM on four challenging sequences in perceptually-degraded environments from the Unified Autonomy Stack field dataset, covering tunnels, fog, and a frozen lake. On these sequences, DASH-SLAM outperforms the foundation-model SLAM state-of-the-art and maintains tracking where classical SLAM methods fail.
bullets: Addresses inconsistent scale and data association across monocular reconstructions.
Uses metric depth from pretrained Depth Anything 3 without task-specific fine-tuning.
Estimates scale corrections from depth ratios at shared anchor images and accumulates them with damping.
Rescales odometry translations, loop constraints, and map geometry.
Outperforms state-of-the-art methods on standard benchmarks and challenging tunnel, fog, and frozen-lake sequences, maintaining tracking where classical SLAM fails.

The back end propagates metric scale across consecutive submaps through their shared anchor frames. The loop-closure thread detects revisited places and passes loop constraints to the back end, which optimises the global pose graph.

papers.abstract: Interactive VR/MR applications demand photorealistic 3D representations that support real-time rendering and object-level manipulation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves high rendering quality, it represents scenes as unstructured, monolithic primitives. Existing object-aware 3DGS methods jointly optimize geometry and semantic states but suffer from two key failure modes: noisy foundation-model masks on complex geometry, and label-geometry coupling, in which co-optimized identity gradients mislabel boundary Gaussians. We introduce RigidGS, an end-to-end pipeline that decouples geometric learning from object identity. We propose a depth- and temporally-aware mask refinement module that addresses two complementary SAM2 failures: over-inclusion on thin structures and under-inclusion on multimodal-depth objects. We then determine object identities entirely upstream via COLMAP projection voting and freeze them during training, directing mask supervision solely toward geometric optimization. Refined masks alone substantially improve competing methods, yet a residual gap in label-geometry coupling persists that our fixed-identity design eliminates. RigidGS outperforms prior object-aware 3DGS methods on LLFF/NVOS, Mip-NeRF~360, and iNeRF360, improving segmentation and boundary IoU by 7.7 and 14.5 points on LLFF/NVOS. Finally, RigidGS enables real-time rigid-body manipulation on Meta Quest~2 without mesh extraction. Our code and project page are available at https://gyreyirisansah.github.io/rigidgs.
bullets: Addresses noisy foundation-model masks and identity–geometry coupling in object-aware 3DGS.
Uses depth- and temporally-aware mask refinement to correct thin-structure over-inclusion and multimodal-depth under-inclusion.
Assigns object identities upstream through COLMAP projection voting and freezes them during training.
Improves segmentation and boundary IoU by 7.7 and 14.5 points on LLFF/NVOS, respectively, over prior methods.
Supports real-time rigid-body manipulation on Meta Quest 2 without mesh extraction.

papers.abstract: The development of deep learning-based medical AI depends on high-quality annotated data. Yet, dataset creation remains constrained by the need for expert radiologist annotations, limiting curated datasets to relatively small cohorts. To overcome this limitation, recent efforts increasingly aggregate disparate public datasets into large-scale dataset collections. However, combining datasets at scale often obscures data provenance, introducing substantial risks of reuse propagation, unintended leakage, bias amplification and distorted data distributions. In this work, we study these problems on a massive collection of 565k 3D radiological images across 1034 public datasets and provide practical resources to address them. Firstly, we formalize dataset collections as a distinct paradigm in medical image analysis and characterize their structural challenges, including reuse propagation, duplication, and provenance fragmentation. Secondly, we perform a large-scale empirical study of duplication on this collection and demonstrate extensive exact and near-duplicate reuse across public datasets via perceptual hashing and manual tracing, identifying a lower bound of 118k duplicate pairs. We make the perceptual hashes publicly accessible for comparison through our website, providing researchers with a standardized reference for identifying potential overlaps and shared provenance. Thirdly, since hashing alone cannot detect all duplicates, we introduce MAP (Metadata for Aggregation and Provenance), a lightweight, portable metadata profile for documenting provenance, known overlaps, and deduplication decisions in dataset collections. Our contributions help dataset collections shift from coarse aggregations to reliable and provenance-aware data scaling mechanisms in medical image analysis. A web tool supporting our work is available at https://mic-dct.dkfz.de/.
bullets: Analyzes 565k 3D radiological images from 1,034 public datasets.
Identifies challenges including reuse propagation, duplication, provenance fragmentation, leakage, bias amplification, and distorted distributions.
Finds at least 118k duplicate pairs through perceptual hashing and manual tracing.
Publishes perceptual hashes and a web tool to help researchers identify overlaps and shared provenance.
Introduces MAP, a portable metadata profile for recording provenance, overlaps, and deduplication decisions.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Cross-dataset overlap network revealed by exact and near-duplicate 3D medical images. Node size indicates the number of images in a dataset, edge size indicates the number of duplicate links associated with a dataset, and shaded regions denote connected components in the overlap graph. The largest component contains 107 datasets, including widely reused datasets and collections such as AMOS, KiTS, and AbdomenAtlas, illustrating that public dataset collections are not independent flat unions but part of a densely connected reuse ecosystem. Because perceptual hashing detects visual identity rather than causal lineage, edges should be interpreted as evidence of image-level overlap rather than complete provenance relationships.

papers.abstract: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and dynamic range for uncooperative spacecraft pose estimation, but models trained on synthetic event streams must generalize to the noise, background activity, and contrast variation of physical sensors. We present a comparative systems study of two independently developed approaches to synthetic-to-real, event-based 6-DoF spacecraft pose estimation. The first is a modular pipeline that combines learned keypoint detection and unlabeled target-domain adaptation with geometry-based pose recovery and temporal smoothing. The second directly regresses translation and rotation from global and cropped event representations using an apparent-scale cue, physics-motivated synthetic corruptions, and feature-consistency regularization. We evaluate both systems under the same SPARK 2026 hidden-test protocol on the real-event split of SPADES, with predictions for all test frames. The results reveal a component-wise reversal concealed by the aggregate challenge score: direct regression reduces orientation error by 22.7% (1.1767 to 0.9101 rad) and obtains a 13.4% lower composite score, whereas the modular pipeline reduces relative translation error by 78.7% (0.1335 to 0.0285). Archived configurations and a qualitative failure case identify plausible explanations for these complementary error profiles, without isolating their causes. These findings motivate a testable hybrid design that combines direct orientation estimation with geometry-constrained translation recovery.
authors: Pruthvi Nandan Janga, Kashyap Hegde Kota, Bharatesh Chakravarthi
bullets: Addresses synthetic-to-real 6-DoF pose estimation from noisy, variable real event-camera data.
Compares a keypoint-plus-domain-adaptation pipeline with geometry-based recovery against direct pose regression.
Direct regression uses global/cropped event representations, apparent scale, synthetic corruptions, and feature consistency.
On the SPADES real-event split, direct regression lowers orientation error by 22.7% and composite score by 13.4%; the modular system lowers relative translation error by 78.7%.
The study identifies complementary error profiles but does not isolate their causes; a hybrid approach is proposed for future testing.

papers.abstract: We present PoseRieFlow, a compact flow-matching framework for text-conditioned generation of whole-body 3D human poses. Prior text-to-pose methods either neglect articulated hands or model rotations in Euclidean space despite their non-Euclidean geometry. PoseRieFlow instead formulates generation directly on the product manifold of SMPL-H joint rotations, learning a text-conditioned vector field that transports samples from an isotropic $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ Gaussian prior to the data distribution along Riemannian geodesics. A part-tokenized Diffusion Transformer aggregates the 52 joints into eight body-part tokens, allocating a dedicated token and nonlinear projector to each hand, and restores per-joint resolution through part-specific decoders, shortening the sequence while improving kinematic fidelity over per-joint tokenization. With only 21.6M trainable parameters, PoseRieFlow supports expressive SMPL-H generation with detailed hand articulation at a fraction of the scale of recent LLM-based generators. On PoseScript, it attains the lowest whole-body kinematic error among all hand-producing methods, with consistent kinematic gains from the Riemannian formulation over its Euclidean counterpart at every practical inference budget, while distributional and retrieval metrics remain comparable between them.
authors: Jan Spindler, Bardia Ardakanian, Patrick Stotko, Reinhard Klein
bullets: Addresses missing hand articulation and the mismatch between rotations’ non-Euclidean geometry and Euclidean pose modeling.
Learns a text-conditioned vector field on the product manifold of SMPL-H joint rotations, transporting an isotropic SO(3) Gaussian prior to the pose distribution along Riemannian geodesics.
Uses eight body-part tokens, dedicated hand tokens, and part-specific decoders to shorten sequences while preserving per-joint detail.
With 21.6M trainable parameters, it achieves the lowest whole-body kinematic error among hand-producing methods on PoseScript.
Riemannian modeling consistently improves kinematic metrics over its Euclidean counterpart, while distributional and retrieval metrics remain comparable.

figures.caption: Figure 2. PoseRieFlow architecture. Part-specific input projectors (linear for body parts, MLPs for the hands) map the noisy pose Rt (52 joints, 6D-encoded) to eight anatomical part tokens with part-type embeddings. Each DiT block applies self-attention over the part tokens, cross-attention to frozen Flan-T5-Base text features, and a SwiGLU FFN, modulated by AdaLN conditioned on the timestep with zero-initialised gates. Mirrored decoders map each token back to its joints, yielding the per-joint tangent velocity v̂θ (Sec. 3.3).

Figure 3. Qualitative whole-body generation. “The right hand is reaching up, the right elbow is in l-shape and the left arm is beneath the right arm and the left elbow is bent a bit. The right knee is located in front of the left knee, rather bent and the torso is upright with the left hand located behind the right hand.” PoseRieFlow and the PoseScript VAE produce articulated SMPL-H hands. The body-only LLM baselines emit flat, fingerless hands. Headings aligned as in Sec. 4.1.

At xt the network regresses the tangent velocity (Eq. 4), and integration stays on M.

papers.abstract: In this paper, a 3D backbone network (SpconvTransformer) based on the fusion of convolutional architecture branch and Transformer architecture branch is proposed. The convolution branch uses 3D sparse convolution and submanifold convolution to learn local voxel features and semantic information, and the Transformer branch uses the self-attention mechanism to model the remote relationship between voxels, uses the broad receptive field to capture rich context information, and complementing the advantages of the two architectures by fusing the local features extracted from the two branches and the global features solves the problem of limited receptive fields of 3D convolutional neural networks. The experimental results show that the average accuracy of SpconvTransformer in 3D object detection and bird's-eye view detection tasks reaches 81.45% and 88.09%, respectively, and the average directional similarity reaches 91.10%, which is significantly better than other existing algorithms.
authors: Muyun Li, Weizheng Jin, Yuan Sun
bullets: Addresses the limited receptive field of conventional 3D convolutional detectors.
The convolution branch extracts local voxel features and semantics using sparse and submanifold convolutions.
The Transformer branch captures long-range voxel relationships and broader contextual information through self-attention.
Feature fusion combines complementary local and global representations for 3D object and bird’s-eye-view detection.
Reported average accuracies are 81.45% for 3D detection and 88.09% for bird’s-eye-view detection, with 91.10% average directional similarity.

papers.abstract: Online 3D street-scene asset construction turns multi-view video into a continually updated scene of independently editable objects. The central challenge is to accumulate partial, intermittent observations under motion and occlusion without fragmenting identities or mixing evidence across objects. To address this challenge, we propose Video2Asset, an online framework for constructing persistent 3D assets from multi-view video. Using occupancy as an intermediate representation, we construct identity-aware observations with Historical Carrier Guidance for instance decoding and an identity encoder fusing instance-aligned 3D features with multi-view appearance. Accumulated-Evidence Association compares current observations with identity, geometric, and appearance evidence accumulated within asset records to determine identity inheritance and update world-coordinate states. We instantiate meshes from an asset library using these states and combine them with an occupancy-derived static background to support scene visualization, mesh replacement, object deletion, and trajectory editing. Experiments on several datasets demonstrate improvements in temporal identity consistency and asset quality across multiple occupancy models, including a 15.4% reduction in asset fragmentation on nuScenes with SGE.
authors: Zihan Zheng, Chunlei Cai, Zhenlong Wu, Linjun Li, Yichen Gong, Xiaoyun Zhang, Qiang Hu
bullets: Addresses identity fragmentation and evidence mixing during continual scene reconstruction.
Uses occupancy-based identity-aware observations, Historical Carrier Guidance, and an identity encoder combining 3D and multi-view appearance features.
Associates observations with asset records using accumulated identity, geometric, and appearance evidence in world coordinates.
Instantiates editable meshes from an asset library and reconstructs a static background for visualization and object-level editing.
Improves temporal identity consistency and asset quality across occupancy models, including a 15.4% reduction in asset fragmentation on nuScenes with SGE.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Video2Asset. (a) Multi-view video is converted into identity-aware observations through occupancy modeling. The observations are associated with persistent asset records to update world-coordinate states and construct an editable 3D scene. (b) Historical Carrier Guidance (HCG) aligns previous instance masks to guide query-conditioned aggregation of current occupancy features. papers.abstract: Sparse query-based 3D detectors commonly encode heterogeneous semantic, geometric, and motion information into unified latent queries, including when explicit 3D anchors are used. We introduce ExQuery, an explicit structured query framework for temporal 3D object detection. Each decoded query is organized into a shared semantic context slice and physical-state-specific slices for center, dimensions, orientation, and velocity. This structure is preserved from prior encoding to branch-specific regression and is reused to reconstruct temporal queries: predicted physical states are transformed by ego motion, classification scores form soft semantic priors, and the reconstructed query is fused with the stored latent instance feature through gated affine modulation. Experiments on the nuScenes benchmark show that our method achieves competitive detection performance, and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of our proposed modules.
authors: Honglin Sun, Yifei Zhang, Junyang Zhang, Kenji Hashimoto
bullets: Addresses the mixing of semantic, geometric, and motion information in unified latent queries.
Organizes each query into shared semantic context plus separate slices for center, dimensions, orientation, and velocity.
Reconstructs temporal queries using ego-motion-transformed states, soft classification priors, and gated fusion with latent instance features.
Experiments on nuScenes report competitive detection performance, with ablations supporting the proposed modules.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed framework. Multi-view images are encoded into image features, while learnable 3D anchor priors, consisting of explicit physical states and class embeddings, are encoded into input queries. The Transformer decoder takes both newly encoded queries and propagated queries to predict 3D bounding boxes. At each time step, the top-K predictions together with their corresponding instance features are stored in a memory queue and propagated to the next frame, enabling structured query-state propagation with explicit physical states and semantic-context priors.

Figure 4: Structured query physical-slice intervention. We zero out each physical slice before the prediction heads and report the signed metric difference. The dashed line separates detection metrics from box-quality error metrics. This intervention probes functional attribute alignment of the physical slices.

Figure 1: Comparison of different query formulations. (a) Learned queries represent object states as opaque latent vectors. (b) Prior-encoded queries introduce explicit physical priors but still decode them into a single mixed representation. (c) Our structured query state preserves shared semantic-context and physical-state-specific slices for attribute-aware prediction.

Figure 3: Mutual gated affine fusion for temporal query propagation. The score-derived semantic prior and predicted physical state form the explicit structured query qexp, while the stored decoder feature forms the implicit branch qimp.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces ExQuery, a structured query framework for temporal 3D object detection that explicitly encodes physical states and semantic context.
papers.title: ExQuery: Explicit Structured Query Priors for Temporal 3D Object Detection
papers.tldr: ExQuery improves temporal 3D object detection by explicitly separating semantic and physical-state information within structured queries and reconstructing them across time.

papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar offers a privacy-preserving and illumination-robust alternative for human mesh reconstruction (HMR). However, high-fidelity radar HMR remains challenging. Sparse point cloud-based methods suffer from information loss and missed detections, while raw radar tensor methods like RT-Mesh lack fine-grained semantics and explicit local body modeling. In this paper, we propose RadarDINO, a radar HMR framework that distills visual semantics from a DINOv3 teacher into 3D radar representations and introduces explicit geometric supervision. DINOv3 descriptors are transferred to radar voxels via calibrated RGB-radar geometry, providing voxel- and body-part-level supervision for part-aware radar representations. We further incorporate vertex- and joint-losses to directly constrain reconstructed geometry. On the M4Human dataset, our method outperforms the SOTA baseline across all three evaluation splits.
authors: Furkan Mert Algan, Zhifan Ni, Eckehard Steinbach
bullets: Addresses information loss in sparse radar point clouds and weak semantics in raw radar tensor methods.
Distills DINOv3 visual descriptors into 3D radar voxels using calibrated RGB–radar geometry.
Provides voxel- and body-part-level supervision for part-aware radar representations.
Uses vertex and joint losses to directly constrain reconstructed human geometry.
Outperforms the prior state-of-the-art baseline on all three M4Human evaluation splits.

Fig. 3. Visualization of RT HMR under non-in-place actions.
Fig. 2. Visualization of distilled radar DINO features.

Table 1. Comparison of radar-based HMR methods on M4Human [14] under the ALL protocol. We report MVE, MJE, MRE, and TE under three data splits, together with model parameters and computational cost. Lower is better for all metrics.
Table 2. Ablation study on radar encoder initialization and fine-tuning strategies under the most challenging S3 split.

papers.selection_reason: Distills a visual foundation model (DINOv3) into mmWave radar representations for human mesh reconstruction, combining multimodal distillation and 3D reconstruction.
papers.title: RadarDINO: Distilling a Visual Foundation Model into mmWave Radar for Human Mesh Reconstruction
papers.tldr: RadarDINO improves privacy-preserving human mesh reconstruction from mmWave radar by transferring visual semantics and applying explicit geometric supervision.

papers.abstract: Non-contact fruit sizing from RGB-D imagery reaches sub-centimetre accuracy on workstation hardware, but in-field grading requires the same pipeline to run on a low-power single-board computer, and the cost of that transition is rarely reported. We deploy a curvature-aware cucumber length-measurement pipeline (YOLO26n detection, prompt-based segmentation and a medial arc spline estimator) on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and a Raspberry Pi 4, and characterize both against an RTX 3050 Ti workstation by replaying 50 identical greenhouse captures of 7 specimens, with specimen-level cluster-bootstrap statistics. Accuracy is preserved: mean absolute error (MAE) is 0.58 cm (95% CI 0.46-0.69) on both the workstation and the Jetson at matched precision, with a paired difference of zero. TensorRT FP16 compilation cuts Jetson detection latency 2.57x, giving two operating points on one board: 72 ms per fruit at 0.84 cm, or 2.74 s at 0.64 cm. Four ablations map the design space. For prompted segmentation backends, measurement accuracy is fixed by the backend and reproduces across platforms to within 0.01 cm, while its cost is fixed by the platform and varies 214x, so the two choices are separable. Whole-graph INT8 quantization of the NMS-free detection head fails structurally, returning no detections, because one output tensor carries both pixel coordinates and confidences; we show that no calibration strategy can avoid this. Excluding the head restores function at 1.37x. Energy per fruit is 42.2 J on the Jetson, and its 7 W mode consumes 73% more than its 15 W mode. The Raspberry Pi with MobileSAM costs 2.5x more per fruit than the Jetson with SAM despite drawing 47% less power, and it runs without thermal throttling under sustained load. The results define an accuracy-throughput-energy envelope with three non-dominated configurations and give rules for selecting among them.
authors: Manveen Kaur, Rajmeet Singh, Saeed Mozaffari, Majid Ahmadi, Shahpour Alirezaee
bullets: The pipeline combines YOLO26n detection, prompted segmentation, and medial arc spline estimation, evaluated on identical greenhouse captures across a workstation, Jetson Orin Nano, and Raspberry Pi 4.
Jetson accuracy matches the workstation at 0.58 cm MAE; TensorRT FP16 enables either 72 ms-per-fruit processing at 0.84 cm MAE or 2.74 s at 0.64 cm MAE.

Segmentation accuracy is largely backend-dependent, while segmentation cost is platform-dependent; whole-graph INT8 quantization fails for the coupled detection output, but excluding that head restores operation at 1.37× speedup.
Jetson energy use is 42.2 J per fruit; its 7 W mode consumes more energy per fruit than its 15 W mode, while the Raspberry Pi runs without thermal throttling but costs more energy per fruit.
The study identifies three non-dominated accuracy–throughput–energy configurations and provides selection rules for edge deployment.

papers.selection_reason: Characterizes the accuracy, throughput, and energy of an RGB-D cucumber sizing pipeline deployed on edge devices, relevant to efficient AI and 3D vision applications.
papers.title: CucumberVision at the Edge: Accuracy, Throughput, and Energy of RGB-D Cucumber Sizing on Jetson Orin Nano and Raspberry Pi 4
papers.tldr: A curvature-aware RGB-D cucumber-sizing pipeline preserves sub-centimetre accuracy on the Jetson Orin Nano while revealing clear accuracy, throughput, and energy trade-offs across edge hardware and configurations.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art stereo matching models predominantly predict the disparity of only the left (reference) view. However, applications such as per-eye AR/VR rendering, novel view synthesis, or two-view depth fusion require disparity for both views, and need those two maps to agree. The usual workaround of running the network a second time on the horizontally flipped and swapped pair gives two independent predictions that can be inconsistent, especially on transparent surfaces, in textureless regions, and at occlusion boundaries. We introduce cross-injection (CI), a lightweight extension for iterative (refinement-based) models that can be added to any pretrained left-only iterative matcher. It couples the two passes by injecting the explicit, signed left-right inconsistency as an additional input cue at every step of the refinement stage. We empirically show that CI substantially reduces left-right disagreement on every benchmark (more than halving it on Booster for FoundationStereo), while largely preserving sharp object boundaries. Furthermore, using two state-of-the-art stereo matching models, we show that CI also reduces the single-view disparity error, making it a worthwhile extension even if only left disparity is needed.
authors: Manuel Knott, Diogo Luvizon, Daniel Scharstein, Elias Vansteenkiste
bullets: Addresses inconsistent disparities from independently processing original and flipped/swapped stereo pairs.
Injects the explicit signed left-right disparity disagreement into both refinement passes at every iteration.
Can be added as a lightweight extension to pretrained left-only iterative stereo models.
Substantially reduces disagreement across all evaluated benchmarks, including more than halving it on Booster for FoundationStereo.
Also lowers single-view disparity error, while largely preserving sharp object boundaries.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the proposed cross-injection architecture. Two refinement passes (the left pass and the flipped-swapped right pass), whose feature encoders and GRU share weights, each iteratively update their own disparity. At every step, each pass receives its own masked left-right inconsistency with respect to the other view (Fig. 3, Eq. 2) as an additional input cue, injected through a zero-initialized encoder. Because the encoder emits zero at initialization, augmenting an already-trained refiner with cross-injection reproduces its original (uncoupled) behavior exactly, and the cross-view correction is learned by fine-tuning.

Figure 4. FoundationStereo zero-shot predictions on selected ETH3D [42] samples with and without our cross-injection method. Even though we are not addressing the ambiguity for transparent objects directly, left/right predictions are more consistent in which visible layer to predict (a). The CI model also successfully corrects major (b) and minor (c) disagreements between the views. Background shrubs in (b) lose some degree of detail.

Figure 5. FoundationStereo zero-shot predictions on selected Booster [39] (half resolution) samples with and without our cross-injection method. CI corrects errors caused by reflections (a), transparency (b+c) and other random failure modes (d).

Figure 6. FoundationStereo zero-shot predictions on selected KITTI-15 [35] samples with and without our cross-injection method. (a) shows occasional “smearing” effects on thin vertical structures such as traffic signs or street lamps in front of the sky. Interestingly, this failure mode was already present in FoundationStereo, but our method seems to amplify it. (b) shows an example where both models predict equally sharp edges on road signs and high frequency details (vegetation).

Figure 3. Illustration of the proposed cross-injection mechanism. The detached partner prediction is horizontally flipped and warped into the frame of the own prediction, using the own disparity as the shift field (Eq. 2), and subtracted from the own prediction. The resulting signed inconsistency (“consistency vector”) is passed explicitly to the refiner’s GRU block. We do this with a tensor of shape (B, 2, H,W ): the two channels are (i) the signed inconsistency with zeros at non-co-visible pixels, and (ii) the binary co-visibility mask derived from warping. This way, the model can distinguish non-visibility from perfect consistency.

Figure 1. Sample predictions with and without our proposed cross-injection (CI) extension. CI can be added to any iterative stereo matcher (here FoundationStereo [57]) and substantially improves left-right consistency between two otherwise independent inference passes (left example); it also reduces per-view failure modes (right example). Here, we show two examples from the Booster dataset [39] where inconsistent predictions arise mainly on reflective and transparent surfaces. Additional visualizations are shown in Figs. 4, 5 and 6.

Table 2. Cross-injection improvements generalize to different base models. For each base model we report three rows: the public checkpoint, a matched fine-tune under the identical recipe but without cross-injection (“+ FT (no CI)”), and our cross-injection fine-tune. The middle row is the control: it isolates what CI contributes from what simply training longer on our data mixture contributes. Findings: against the matched control, CI improves left-right consistency on every benchmark for all three base models, with the largest relative effect on Booster, which is built around transparent and specular surfaces (for S2M2-XL, KITTI-12 is marginally larger). Disparity error (both views where GT is available) also improves against the control on all but one of the fifteen accuracy cells (S2M2-L Booster-H). Bold: best per base model.

Table 1. Ablation experiment for component validation. All runs are fine-tuning runs based on FoundationStereo. Checkmarks indicate which components each run uses: LR-consistency loss (LR), cross-injection (CI) refiner, and bidirectional stop-gradient routing (SG). All metrics are reported as mean±std of six checkpoints created during the last 10k steps of training. Findings: LR consistency improves with the loss alone (b), only slightly with CI alone (c), and substantially when both are combined (d). However, CI with a symmetric consistency loss leads to (slight) oversmoothing on edges and degradation of occluded predictions. SG largely recovers this regression at the cost of

papers.selection_reason: Introduces 'Cross-Injection' for iterative stereo matching to ensure left-right consistency. This is a direct contribution to 3D reconstruction and geometry.
papers.title: Left-Right-Consistent Iterative Stereo Matching via Cross-Injection
papers.tldr: Cross-injection turns left-only iterative stereo matchers into coupled two-view predictors that substantially improve left-right consistency while preserving accuracy and boundaries.

papers.abstract: Real-time 3D human mesh recovery from a single image on mobile devices is a challenging problem with many applications, including robotics, biomechanics, AR/VR, and exergames. Current state-of-the-art models are either too slow to run efficiently on mobile devices or sacrifice accuracy for speed. We present InstantHMR, a family of open-source single-image regressors suited for mobile inference, based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) parametric model and trained exclusively on publicly available annotations from the SAM 3D Body dataset. Our approach achieves remarkable performance on a Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU, recovering a 6,890-vertex body mesh in 5.5 ms per person, and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU. This speed surpasses all existing methods we evaluated. On mobile, it is 12x faster than the single mobile-compatible method that slightly outperforms ours in accuracy, while achieving competitive accuracy with 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB and 41.7 mm on RICH. To ensure fair comparisons, we re-evaluate 11 state-of-the-art methods under a unified protocol aligned with the closest MHR-based competitors, including Meta's official MHR-to-SMPL conversion, and report their reproduction results. Additionally, we measure latency across eight different targets, ranging from desktop TensorRT to two phone NPUs. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Naturalpad-studio/InstantHMR.
authors: Mohamed Adjel (LAAS-GEPETTO), Kahina Chalabi (LAAS-GEPETTO), Vincent Bonnet (LAAS-GEPETTO)
bullets: Targets real-time human mesh recovery for mobile applications such as AR/VR, robotics, biomechanics, and exergames.
Uses lightweight single-image regressors based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) model, trained only on public SAM 3D Body annotations.
Reports competitive accuracy: 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB, and 41.7 mm on RICH.
Runs at 5.5 ms per person on a Galaxy S23 NPU and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU.
Provides open-source code and models, plus unified latency and reproduction evaluations across multiple methods and hardware targets.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of the methods that run on a phone NPU. For each image, left: the predicted mesh projected into the image; right: the same mesh seen from the side. On the EMDB-1 [15] images (columns 1–3), the side view also shows the ground-truth mesh in green; the prediction is placed on its hips and scaled to its size, but not rotated. The COCO [24] images (columns 4–5) are in the wild and have no 3D ground truth. Under each method: its latency per person on the Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU.

Figure 1. Accuracy against latency on a phone. EMDB-1 PAMPJPE (24 joints, lower is better, up) against model latency per person on the NPU of a Samsung Galaxy S23 (log scale, faster is left), for every method under the protocol of Sec. 4. InstantHMR’s

Figure 2. InstantHMR. A 288 px crop around the person goes through a convolutional HGNetV2 encoder (shown: the first principal component of its second-stage features, 36× 36, contrast-stretched) down to 9× 9 image tokens. A 4-layer transformer decoder refines 71 learned queries (one for the body, one per keypoint) by attention among themselves and to the image tokens; the box’s position in the full frame (two viewing angles and the size over the focal length) is embedded and added to every query. The body query feeds the MHR and camera heads, from which the rig’s forward kinematics (FK) gives the posed mesh; each keypoint query feeds a SimCC head that classifies its x and y over 96 bins (shown over the crop: for each keypoint, the product of its two distributions). Every visual is the real output of InstantHMR-M on a 3DPW test frame [40]. InstantHMR-M has 32.2 M parameters: 13.6 M in the backbone, 16.8 M in the decoder, and 1.8 M in the projections, queries and heads.

Table 1. Latency on eight targets. Model latency per person crop in ms, batch 1, up to a 6,890-vertex posed mesh. EMDB-1 PA-MPJPE (mm, 24 joints, Tab. 2) is shown for context. Methods are grouped by whether they run on a phone NPU at all; within a group, fastest first.

Table 2. Accuracy under one protocol. Every method is scored on the same frames with the same ground truth (Sec. 4): ground-truth person boxes, the calibrated focal length, and, for MHR methods, Meta’s official MHR-to-SMPL conversion. Errors in mm on every 10th frame of EMDB-1 and 3DPW, and on the 21,287 test crops of RICH listed by CameraHMR, scored on the 24 joints regressed from the mesh. Groups and order as in Tab. 1. Blue: ours. Bold: best in the column; underlined: best among the methods that run on a phone NPU.

Table 3. The InstantHMR family. Nano, tiny, small and medium use HGNetV2-B0, B1, B2 and B4 backbones; M-C is the medium architecture trained only on commercially usable images (Harmony4D and COCO). Protocol of Tab. 2. Latency per person: RTX 4070 with TensorRT fp16, Samsung Galaxy S23

Table 4. Design ablation. PA-MPJPE (mm) as in Tab. 2; each row is a full training run. Crop framing: the share of standard crops, the rest zoomed out, zoomed in or shifted. The input-size pair uses an earlier recipe (hence 49.8, not 48.8 mm); other backbones in the supplementary material.

papers.title: InstantHMR : Real-Time Human Mesh Recovery on Your Phone

papers.abstract: 3D part decomposition is a central capability for editable asset creation, yet existing workflows typically segment a completed mesh as a post-processing step, making the result sensitive to geometric artifacts, texture ambiguity, and limited part-level annotations. We present OmniLatent, a unified latent modeling framework for 3D part decomposition. Instead of predicting part labels in isolation, OmniLatent learns a shared latent space that jointly encodes geometry, deformation, appearance, and binary part IDs, allowing data-rich geometric and visual priors to support data-scarce part learning. Given a single input image, the base model generates geometry, deformation, texture, and surface part IDs in one pass, producing a part-aware 3D asset without a separate segmentation stage. We further tune the pretrained model for two extensions: a point-prompt adapter that maps arbitrary 3D point prompts with binary part IDs into latent tokens for full segmentation, refinement, and part subdivision, and an amodal part completion model that completes partial surface masks into a coherent full-object decomposition through dynamic per-part token allocation, cross-attention to the given geometry latent, and alternating part-local and global attention. Extensive experiments show that OmniLatent produces semantically meaningful part segmentations with precise boundaries, supports interactive part editing, and completes partial part observations while preserving global object consistency.
authors: Yunhan Yang, Yunfei Zhao, Zeqiang Lai, Jiachen Xu, Minxiu Wang, Xintong Han, Xiangyu Yue, Xihui Liu, Chunchao Guo
bullets: Addresses fragile post-hoc mesh segmentation affected by geometric artifacts, texture ambiguity, and scarce part annotations.
Uses a unified latent space for geometry, deformation, appearance, and binary part IDs, leveraging richer visual and geometric priors.
Generates geometry, texture, deformation, and surface part IDs in one pass without a separate segmentation stage.
Adds point-prompt editing and subdivision, plus amodal completion of partial part masks using dynamic part tokens and local/global attention.
Experiments report meaningful segmentations, precise boundaries, interactive editing, and globally consistent completion.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Unified part segmentation and refinement using images, 2D masks, and point prompts. We adopt an MM-DiT architecture that integrates multiple control signals: interactive regions and geometric conditions are injected via channel concatenation with the noisy latent, while other conditions are incorporated through sequence concatenation.

Fig. 2. Unified Latent Modeling and Pretraining. OmniLatent performs 3D part decomposition through unified latent modeling. Geometry, deformation, appearance, and binary part IDs are encoded into a shared OmniLatent space, then generated by an MM-DiT backbone from an input image with optional 2D mask conditions. The aligned latent space allows geometric and visual priors to support surface part segmentation, and the pretrained model can further be adapted for point-prompted control and amodal part completion. The left branch shows the cascaded VAE decoder: SDF reconstruction defines the surface, whose vertices subsequently query deformation, appearance, and Part IDs from the same latent tokens.

Fig. 7. Point-prompted part control. OmniLatent supports three prompt-driven editing modes: (a) Full segmentation from sparse point prompts, (b) Part refine for correcting an initialized segmentation, and (c) Part subdivision for splitting a coarse part into finer components.

Fig. 6. Qualitative comparison of surface part segmentation on PartObjaverse-Tiny-wt. OmniLatent produces semantically coherent regions and cleaner boundaries by decoding part IDs from a latent space aligned with geometry and appearance.

Fig. 5. Surface part segmentation and amodal completion results. For each example, OmniLatent produces complete surface part segmentation and further completes partial surface masks into complete object-level parts, preserving global structure while recovering missing components.

Fig. 9. Visual comparison of geometry generation. Despite its unified design, our method still produces high-quality generations, providing strong geometric understanding that benefits part decomposition.

Fig. 8. Qualitative comparison on amodal part completion. Given full geometry and partial surface masks, OmniLatent preserves visible part evidence and completes coherent full-object parts, producing cleaner part geometry and more consistent object structure than X-Part, HoloPart, PartPacker, and OmniPart.

Fig. 10. Unified generation and mask-guided surface part segmentation. OmniLatent jointly generates geometry, deformation, appearance, and surface part IDs from a single image, and can use 2D segmentation masks as controllable guidance for part granularity.

Fig. 4. Amodal part completion. Given full geometry and partial surface masks for all parts, OmniLatent allocates tokens dynamically according to visible part size. RoPE-anchored tokens preserve observed surface evidence, while no-RoPE completion tokens represent unobserved regions. A geometry latent enters through cross-attention, and alternating part-local and global attention layers complete all parts into a consistent full-object part layout.

Fig. 12. Ablation study on Condition-Aware 3D Rotary Position Embedding.

papers.selection_reason: Unified latent model for 3D part decomposition and generation, fitting 3D foundation models.
papers.title: OmniLatent: Unified Latent for 3D Part Modeling
papers.tldr: OmniLatent jointly generates 3D geometry and part decomposition from a single image in a shared latent space, enabling editable, complete, and interactive part-aware assets.

papers.abstract: Recognizing geometric texture patterns on 3D models is critical for applications such as heritage protection, model editing, and 3D printing. Existing 3D model segmentation methods predominantly focus on identifying high-level semantic parts, thereby failing to capture middle-level textures. While recent Vision-Language Models can perform image segmentation with appropriate text prompts, they still struggle to recognize 3D geometric textures. In this work, we present a method that segments 3D mesh models based on middle-level geometric textures. We further introduce a new geometric texture segmentation benchmark and fine-tune SAM3 accordingly. The segmented texture regions are then clustered based on DINO feature similarity and lifted from 2D to 3D. Additionally, we develop an interactive tool to enable both 3D model editing based on our segmentation results and model retrieval from the dataset based on geometric and texture similarity. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing methods in segmenting geometric textures and can facilitate various applications.
authors: Weidan Xiong, Kaijie Qu, Shihao Feng, Shunqi Fan, Rongyu Xiong, Hui Huang
bullets: Addresses the gap between semantic-part segmentation and recognition of geometric textures on 3D models.
Introduces a geometric texture segmentation benchmark and fine-tunes SAM3 for the task.
Clusters segmented regions using DINO feature similarity, then lifts the results from 2D images to 3D meshes.
Provides an interactive tool for texture-aware 3D editing and model retrieval.
Experiments report significant improvements over existing methods, though the abstract gives no quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Understanding building facades is central to urban digital twins, heritage modelling, and sustainable city analysis, yet existing LiDAR benchmarks stop at geometry and semantic segmentation and offer little support for reasoning about the functional role of each architectural element. We introduce HFX3D, a large-scale urban facade benchmark of approximately 492 million LiDAR points from 26 buildings in Halifax, Canada, captured across four seasons, day and night, and varied weather. Each facade is annotated at three tiers, semantic, instance, and per-instance functional attributes, making it, to our knowledge, the first facade dataset to pair geometry and semantics with functional labels. Annotations are produced by a semi-automatic pipeline that combines geometry-guided heuristics with expert validation. We benchmark representative point-based, graph-based, convolutional, and transformer architectures and find that semantic segmentation is already challenging under severe class imbalance, while instance separation of repetitive structures and functional reasoning from geometry are substantially harder. The benchmark establishes a new foundation for function-aware 3D urban understanding. Project page: https://jijup.github.io/hfx3d-benchmark/ ; code: https://github.com/jijup/hfx3d-benchmark

papers.abstract: We propose, HaNDF, object-conditional neural distance fields as data-driven priors for modeling the plausible hand-object configurations, in the product manifold of hand articulations. While recent unconditional generative priors showed success in modeling human pose, hands are versatile articulated bodies often found in interaction with other objects. This makes it crucial to develop a generative prior which can model the plausible hand poses conditioned on the object under interaction. To this end, our HaNDF proposes a geometry-aware, object-conditioned neural distance field, representing the plausible articulations in the zero-level set of a conditional field. We leverage tools from Riemannian geometry to (i) represent plausible hands in the zero level-set of an object-induced neural field, and (ii) project a given pose onto this field. Using HaNDF, we can also optimize for a plausible condition, determining the object under interaction. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that our HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand-object interaction, suitable for applications such as pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.
authors: Zuhao Liu, Melih Darcan, Zhengdi Yu, Riza Alp Guler, Tolga Birdal
bullets: Addresses the need for hand-pose priors that account for the interacted object, beyond unconditional pose models.

Evaluations show utility for pose refinement, occluded-hand reconstruction, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.

papers.abstract: We introduce SM4RT, a multi-task cascade feed-forward model for dynamic scene reconstruction from RGB videos. While existing feed-forward approaches typically address geometry reconstruction and motion estimation separately--and often predict motions in a single coordinate frame that must account for camera movement--SM4RT solves these tasks sequentially by first reconstructing 3D geometry and then bootstrapping motion estimation from the predicted structure. By expressing each pixel's 3D motion in its corresponding camera frame, SM4RT reduces ambiguity arising from camera motion. To address the sparsity of real-world motion labels, SM4RT further incorporates a weakly supervised loss that regularizes unlabeled point motions using labeled point positions at the other time step. We evaluate motion estimation on three dynamic-scene datasets--Kubric, Waymo, and Point Odyssey--and SM4RT achieves the best performance on most metrics compared with prior baselines. We additionally benchmark geometry reconstruction on five dynamic scene datasets and show that SM4RT achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. Overall, our unified framework demonstrates that combining geometry reconstruction and motion estimation in a cascade not only avoids performance trade-offs but also enhances motion estimation through improved geometric reasoning.
bullets: Targets joint geometry reconstruction and motion estimation for dynamic scenes.
Sequentially reconstructs 3D structure first, then bootstraps motion estimation from it.
Represents per-pixel 3D motion in the corresponding camera frame to reduce camera-motion ambiguity.
Uses a weakly supervised loss to regularize unlabeled point motions from labeled positions at another time step.
Shows best motion-estimation performance on most metrics across Kubric, Waymo, and Point Odyssey, with competitive geometry results on five datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the framework. SM4RT is a multi-task cascade feed-forward model for dynamic scene reconstruction. It first performs geometry reconstruction using a DUSt3R backbone (blue modules), then feeds the predicted 3D geometry into a transformer-based decoder followed by a DPT head to estimate motion (red modules). SM4RT trains the network with a fully-supervised regression loss Lconf based on ground-truth dynamic point maps and object flow; at the same time, it incorporates a weakly-supervised Chamfer loss LCD that regularizes unlabeled point motion based on labeled point positions from the other time step, to handle the sparsity of motion labels.
