In contrast, SM4RT is the best among all models for dynamic scene reconstruction.

By voxelizing the 3D Euclidean space, we compute the Chamfer loss within each voxel, approximating nearest-neighbor search while filtering invalid matches. papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint. This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely execute manipulation from the exact same base pose used during demonstration collection due to navigation uncertainty, localization drift, and environmental constraints. Recent approaches use novel-view synthesis (NVS) to augment demonstrations with unseen viewpoints, but they assume static scenes and therefore fail to re-render the manipulated object during the post-contact interaction phase, leaving the most critical parts of the demonstration unaugmented. We present MOMASPLAT, a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions. Our key insight is that standard MoMa data collection naturally provides the multiview observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. MOMASPLAT combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematics-based action retargeting to separately reconstruct the scene and manipulated object, render them from novel viewpoints, and generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. MOMASPLAT substantially improves robustness to unseen base poses, more than doubling the average success rate of the strongest baseline and maintaining non-trivial success at large base displacements where all baselines fail, while reducing the need for largescale real-world data collection.
bullets: Addresses the sensitivity of imitation-learned visuomotor policies to camera and robot-base viewpoint changes in mobile manipulation.
Separately reconstructs static scenes and manipulated objects using 3D Gaussian Splatting and feed-forward 3D foundation models.
Uses kinematics-based action retargeting to render novel viewpoints and pair them with geometrically consistent transformed actions.
Evaluated on five real-world tasks with rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, plus simulation-based fidelity validation.
More than doubles average success over the strongest baseline and retains non-trivial success at large base displacements where baselines fail.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of MOMASPLAT. 3D Reconstruction: We build 3D models of the environment from the navigation and manipulation data. We estimate camera poses via structure-from-motion and fit a 3D Gaussian Splatting model of the static scene, Gscene. For the dynamic objects, we segment each manipulated object and estimate its per-frame pose trajectory with a feed-forward 3D foundation model; since the scene and object poses lie in separate reference frames, we align them with a Sim(3) transformation and fit a separate object model Gobj. Synthesizing Demonstrations from Unseen Base Poses: Given a robot base pose, T̃ , sampled around the original demonstration poses (left), we render the scene and object from the new viewpoint, transform the source end-effector trajectory into the new base frame to render the robot from a simulator, and composite the three streams into a photorealistic novel observation. Paired with the transformed actions ã1:Lj , this forms a synthetic demonstration; repeating across sampled poses yields the generated dataset. Imitation Learning: the policy is trained on the union of source and generated demonstrations.

Fig. 4: Policy success across base poses. For each task, we evaluate 12 unseen base locations distributed across categorical distance bins that vary per task, with 3 trials per pose, and report success rate by distance to the nearest demonstration pose. The shaded gray region denotes the original base poses; locations 5–50 cm away are unseen deployment poses. MOMASPLAT maintains substantially higher success as the base pose shifts away from the source demonstrations (where Source Only is labeled “Original data only”).

Fig. 1: MOMASPLAT. Starting from mobile-manipulation data collected at the original base pose (white and red robot), MOMASPLAT synthesizes demonstrations from sampled novel base poses (yellow-outlined gray robot). The top-right sequence shows the source manipulation demonstration, while the bottom-right shows the corresponding synthesized trajectory, including the dynamic object as it is moved by the robot. Augmenting the source manipulation dataset with these demonstrations enables execution from unseen deployment-time base poses (blue-outlined gray robot).

Fig. 5: Spatial distribution of policy evaluation poses. Top-down view of each task showing the table and target-object locations, the original demonstration base poses, and the test base poses used for policy evaluation. Original demonstration poses are marked with circles, while evaluation poses are marked with squares; arrows indicate the robot heading at each pose. Evaluation poses are colored by MOMASPLAT policy success rate, providing spatial context for the distance-based results in Fig. 4.

Fig. 3: Tasks and scenes used in our experiments. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world manipulation tasks across three scenes (top: scenes; bottom: per-task close-ups), covering manipulation of both rigid and articulated objects. The simulated scene and its task, SIM PICK-PLACE BOTTLE (right of the dashed lines), are used to measure the fidelity of MOMASPLAT’s generated demonstrations against ground truth.

papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave radar resolves the micrometer displacements of a moving body as micro-Doppler, enabling gait, gesture, activity, pose and vital-sign sensing. Each task relies on a downstream model trained on real data, yet radar datasets lag orders of magnitude behind vision and language. Brute-force collection will not close that gap, and existing synthesis methods (forward-only simulators, learned generators and static-scene inverse renderers) cannot fit a real capture of a moving body, leaving a sim2real gap. We present 4D Point Splatting (4DPS), a physics-based differentiable renderer that fits an explicit moving scene to a real capture. Using the synchronized camera to initialize the room and body, we represent the scene as oriented points carrying material, normal and velocity, and splat each point into range and Doppler bins. Our output is the raw complex return a real radar records, so we apply the same signal processing on the rendered data to obtain any representation for training any SOTA downstream model. We fit 235 sequences on HuPR and 100 on RT-Pose, two datasets with different radars. Our reconstructions set the state of the art, with median correlations of 0.940 and 0.830 on range-azimuth, 0.829 and 0.695 on range-Doppler, and 0.988 and 0.966 on micro-Doppler. Our renders also set the state of the art in downstream sim2real gap. On RT-Pose, a pose model trained on them reaches 21.9 cm MPJPE on real data, against 16.7 cm for real training and 127.6 cm for the RF-Genesis baseline, where both the rendered- and real-trained models learn nearly the same features. Our custom CUDA kernels fit a sequence in 5.7 minutes on HuPR and 12.9 on RT-Pose on one H100, making dataset-scale inverse rendering of mmWave radar possible for the first time. This work can enable synthetic data generation for any human-centered downstream task and model, and scene editing for data augmentation.
bullets: Addresses the shortage of mmWave radar datasets and the sim2real gap for moving-body sensing.
Represents scenes with oriented points carrying material, surface normal, and velocity, then splats them into range–Doppler bins.
Renders raw complex radar returns, allowing standard signal processing and training for diverse downstream models.
Achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction correlations on HuPR and RT-Pose across range-azimuth, range-Doppler, and micro-Doppler representations.
Enables dataset-scale inverse rendering, fitting sequences in minutes on a single H100 and improving real-data pose performance over a prior rendering baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Differentiable 4D point-splatting renderer for mmWave radar; transferable to 3D scene representation and synthetic data generation.
papers.title: 4D Point Splatting for mmWave Radar Micro-Doppler Differentiable Rendering
papers.tldr: 4D Point Splatting is a physics-based differentiable renderer that fits moving human scenes to real mmWave radar captures, enabling realistic synthetic data generation and improved sim2real performance.

papers.abstract: Hand avatar reconstruction typically relies on multi-view capture or per-subject optimization, limiting its scalability. We introduce InstantHand, a feed-forward framework that constructs an animatable 3D Gaussian hand avatar from a single image using off-the-shelf MANO, camera, and mask estimates, without test-time optimization. Image-averaged losses provide insufficient supervision for alpha leakage, which thickens thin finger contours. To address this issue, we propose a Soft Alpha Band regularizer that concentrates supervision on silhouette boundaries. Furthermore, colors regressed from image features can drift toward a learned prior even in observed regions. Our Reliability-gated Appearance Transfer preserves observed appearance by transferring source colors according to each Gaussian's rendering contribution, while completing unobserved regions using the learned prior conditioned on global source identity. InstantHand constructs an avatar in 2.84 seconds and renders at 161 FPS, matching per-subject-optimized baselines on InterHand2.6M and remaining competitive in zero-shot evaluation on HanCo.
bullets: Addresses the scalability limits of multi-view capture and per-subject optimization.
Uses feed-forward reconstruction with off-the-shelf MANO, camera, and mask estimates.
Introduces Soft Alpha Band regularization to sharpen thin finger boundaries and reduce alpha leakage.
Uses Reliability-gated Appearance Transfer to preserve visible colors and complete unseen regions with a learned prior.
Builds avatars in 2.84 seconds and renders at 161 FPS, matching optimized baselines on InterHand2.6M and remaining competitive zero-shot on HanCo.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Avatars reconstructed from fully estimated inputs (SAM 3 mask, WiLoR MANO and camera) for original and edited source images. Top: an unseen InterHand2.6M test subject, with hand-drawn tattoos composited onto the source image. Bottom: an in-the-wild image released with OHTA [23], with its skin tone darkened by an image generation model. Edited rows reuse the mask, MANO, and camera of the original row, and each column shows the same pose and view.

Figure 2: Overview of InstantHand. A frozen DINOv3 encoder provides image features Fs that serve as keys and values for a conditional transformer, whose query tokens are point-embedded MANO-surface anchors obtained from the MANO layer (β,θmean). The resulting geometry and appearance tokens are decoded by scale, offset, and color heads into a canonical Gaussian hand Gcan with fixed rotation r0 and opacity α0. Reliability-gated Appearance Transfer then composes local source evidence and a global source identity under the source mask Ms to update only the Gaussian colors (c0i →c∗i ), and the avatar is animated by MANO-driven deformation W and rendered by R.

Figure 3: Reliability-gated Appearance Transfer. The Stage-1 appearance prior is refined with Gaussian footprint-aligned local evidence (Prior Refinement) and conditioned on the global source identity, which also generates a source-conditioned prior bank (Identity Conditioning). The composed representation is decoded into an observed color, an appearance gate, and a source-level shift (Appearance Prediction), and Appearance Composition blends these with the base colors under the reliability γi to produce the final Gaussian colors c∗i . Dashed arrows denote conditioning. Three further inputs of Eq. 11 are omitted for clarity. The source identity also enters Prior Refinement, and the local evidence and base colors also enter Identity Conditioning.

papers.title: InstantHand: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting for Animatable Hand Avatar Reconstruction from a Single Image
papers.tldr: InstantHand rapidly reconstructs an animatable 3D Gaussian hand avatar from one image without test-time optimization, while preserving silhouettes and observed appearance.

papers.abstract: Online 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructs a scene during capture: each keyframe spawns primitives once and refines them for only a few dozen iterations, leaving little chance to fix poor initialization or missing detail. Gaussians are also inherently soft, needing many overlaps for solid surfaces. We present Hierarchical Incremental Beta Splatting (HIBS), which brings beta kernels to incremental reconstruction. Their shape parameter interpolates between a soft, Gaussian-like profile and a flat-topped, near-opaque surfel, acting as a confidence dial for geometry. Our confidence-aware spawning uses geometric observability and multi-view depth agreement to initialize both opacity and shape, producing solid primitives where geometry is verifiable and soft, correctable primitives where it is not. As online densification, error-driven relocation recycles stale primitives into photometric-error hotspots. Bounded beta kernel support enables exact tile culling and faster rasterization, and a closed-form, shape-preserving merging formulation provides a level-of-detail (LOD) hierarchy for fast optimization and real-time rendering. On Mip-NeRF 360 in the on-the-fly protocol, HIBS improves PSNR by up to 0.8 dB while reducing optimization time by up to 40%. Project page: https://linus-franke.com/hibs/
bullets: Addresses poor primitive initialization, missing detail, and the softness of Gaussians in short online optimization windows.
Uses geometric observability and multi-view depth agreement to set primitive opacity and kernel shape according to geometric confidence.
Relocates stale primitives to photometric-error hotspots during online densification.
Exploits bounded beta-kernel support for exact tile culling and faster rasterization, plus closed-form merging for LOD optimization and rendering.
On Mip-NeRF 360 under the on-the-fly protocol, reports up to 0.8 dB higher PSNR and 40% lower optimization time.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our pipeline. An RGB stream is registered with camera parameters estimated online [42]. Each keyframe spawns beta primitives using geometric observability and depth agreement, keeping uncertain primitives soft. Near-dead primitives are relocated to high-error regions, followed by a short 30-iteration optimization burst with our fused rasterizer. Periodically, small-footprint primitives are merged hierarchically using closed-form moment matching that preserves their solidity.

Figure 7. Quality during reconstruction. Top: mean PSNR over test views registered so far versus reconstruction progress, for our method and i3DGS. Bottom: PSNR immediately after each view’s registration versus just before the next test view arrives. Points above the diagonal show improvement after registration.
Figure 6. Qualitative comparison against baselines on the 3DGS benchmark: TRUCK, and FLOWERS scenes.
Figure 13. Qualitative comparison against online reconstruction methods on GARDEN, FOREST1, UNIVERSITY2, FR1/DESK, and SMALLCITY (top to bottom).
Figure 14. Additional qualitative comparisons against online reconstruction methods: BONSAI, COUNTER, FOREST2, FR2/XYZ, and FR3/OFFICE (top to bottom).

Figure 10. Spawn-confidence signals on UNIVERSITY2. Primitive locations are colored by geometric observability cz , MVS–monocular agreement cmvs, and their product c. The two signals fail in different regions: distant trees have low observability, while dense foliage has poor depth agreement despite sufficient baseline. Their product therefore assigns solid, opaque initialization to well-constrained surfaces and soft initialization to ambiguous regions.

Figure 4. Online confidence field. After the first orbit (left), many background primitives remain uncertain, and the table reconstruction is fuzzy. After the second orbit (middle), accumulated multiview evidence solidifies most primitives. In the final reconstruction (right, novel view rendering), these areas are largely solidified, while uncertainty remains around the reflective table center.

Figure 5. Merging beta primitives. KL-style merging of beta primitives (middle) similar to merging of Gaussians (left) leads to oversized and solid primitives. Instead, we use moment merging (right), keeping the footprint.

Figure 12. Memory and capacity over reconstruction. GPU memory remains bounded while active capacity saturates on GARDEN. Relocation redistributes this capacity over time, whereas hierarchy offloading allows the model to grow on SMALLCITY without increasing the GPU footprint.

Figure 8. Half-maximum scale compensation. Without compensation, lowering β broadens the kernel; with the proposed compensation, all profiles share the same half-maximum radius, isolating shape changes from footprint changes.

Figure 9. Online confidence field on a walking capture (UNIVERSITY2), analogous to Fig. 4: renders over their perprimitive shape field (β, warm = soft). As the walk advances, accumulated multi-view evidence solidifies the traversed corridor of the scene behind the camera, while freshly entered and peripheral regions remain soft probes — the field marks the reconstruction frontier of an unbounded capture live, at no quality cost.
Figure 15. Additional qualitative comparisons against offline baselines: BICYCLE, KITCHEN, ROOM, TREEHILL, and GARDEN (top to bottom).

Figure 11. Error-driven relocation on GARDEN. Left: incoming keyframe and per-pixel error at 22.6 dB. Middle: dead primitives relocated to high-error contributors, with render-preserving opacity and scale correction. Right: the subsequent 30-iteration burst increases quality to 24.5 dB.
Figure 16. Additional qualitative comparisons against offline baselines: BONSAI, COUNTER, DR. JOHNSON, TRAIN, STUMP, and PLAYROOM (top to bottom).

Table 16. Results on the full 3DGS benchmark. Nine MipNeRF360, two Tanks&Temples, and two Deep Blending scenes. papers.abstract: We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic of the reconstructed geometry, while the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers can still vary substantially across scene scales and camera configurations. This mismatch induces systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale targets, leading to ambiguous supervision. To address this, we propose SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which canonicalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to provide a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. To rigorously assess our method, we further establish a systematic benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and challenging extrapolated viewpoints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SplatAnything achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains under substantial variations in scene scale and viewpoint. Project page: https://zju3dv.github.io/SplatAnything
bullets: Existing methods normalize global radial distance but leave neighboring Gaussian spacing inconsistent across scene scales and camera setups.
This mismatch shifts Gaussian-scale targets and creates ambiguous supervision.
The proposed GSNorm canonicalizes a robust scene-level Gaussian-spacing statistic as a consistent spatial reference.
A benchmark evaluates diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and extrapolated viewpoints.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance, with especially strong gains under large scale and viewpoint variations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Architecture of SplatAnything. Given N input images and optional camera parameters, a frozen geometry foundation model first estimates multi-view geometry. We convert the geometry from its native radial-distance-normalized space to the proposed Gaussian-spacing-normalized space and predict per-pixel Gaussian attribute through a Gaussian backbone and a lightweight GShead.

Figure 2: Normalization space. (a) Radial Distance Normalization canonicalizes a global radial statistic but leaves Gaussian spacing varying across scenes and camera configurations, resulting in inconsistent supervision targets. (b) Gaussian Spacing Normalization canonicalizes a representative statistic of Gaussian spacing, providing a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction.

papers.abstract: Medical 3D scans and reports are inherently hierarchical, with diagnostic cues concentrated in specific anatomical regions across multiple levels of organization. Yet, most medical vision-language models ignore this structure and fail to focus on clinically relevant anatomy. We introduce MedHiVE, which combines hierarchical vision-language Soft Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) with contrastive learning to jointly model fine-grained anatomy and global scan context. To our knowledge, MedHiVE is the first framework to route both vision and text tokens through a two-level SMoE hierarchy organized by anatomical scale, coupling this with report-derived anatomy-level contrastive alignment for 3D medical imaging. This replaces the direct region-text alignment of statically pooled features and vision-only hierarchical routing of prior work with dynamic, slot-based cross-modal information flow across anatomical scales. MedHiVE operates via a two-level, learnable token-routing mechanism, where local image and text features are first routed through a local SMoE and then fused by a global SMoE into unified multimodal representations. Contrastive learning aligns both anatomy-level and global vision-language representations in a unified space. Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision, MedHiVE consistently surpasses 11 state-of-the-art methods across 6 datasets on 3 tasks: segmentation, classification, and detection, demonstrating the importance of hierarchical modeling. The code for MedHiVE is at github.com/szczurek-lab/MedHiVE.
bullets: Addresses the failure of existing models to capture clinically relevant anatomy across hierarchical scales in 3D scans and reports.
Routes both image and text tokens through local and global anatomy-organized Soft Mixture-of-Experts layers.
Uses anatomy-level and global contrastive alignment to learn unified vision-language representations.
Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision and evaluated on segmentation, classification, and detection across 6 datasets.
Reports consistent improvements over 11 state-of-the-art methods; the approach is scoped to 3D medical imaging and the evaluated tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of the MedHiVE framework. A hierarchical encoder processes a 3D CT scan and anatomy masks alongside a full report representation zTi and anatomy-specific snippet representations zTi,a, extracted through a frozen text encoder. The global vision representation zIi is contrasted with zTi , while local vision representations zIi,a are aligned with zTi,a for each anatomical structure a. This yields anatomy-aware vision-language representations that enhance downstream segmentation, classification, and detection.

Figure 4. An overview of the 2D projections of anatomical segmentation masks from the Merlin dataset [6]. We consider 14 abdominal anatomical groups to facilitate analysis and model training (see Table 3). These projections illustrate the spatial distribution of the anatomies across representative slices.

Figure 2. Overview of the HiVEL layer. Global and anatomylevel vision tokens and text tokens are routed to E global experts FFNG and F local experts FFNL via first-level routers. The resulting slots are concatenated and processed by a second-level router. Global vision and text tokens are fused with H shared experts FFNS outputs via residual connection, yielding enhanced vision tokens x̂ and text tokens t̂. Vision tokens are used at all stages s ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}, while text tokens are enabled at s ∈ {3, 4}.
Figure 6. Text preprocessing pipeline.

Figure 10. Qualitative evaluation of tooth segmentation on the GEPAR3D test set. We benchmark MedHiVE against ground truth labels and four state-of-the-art baselines. MedHiVE exhibits superior spatial and semantic consistency, leveraging its ability to capture long-range dependencies for large-scale dental arches while preserving high-fidelity boundaries in smaller, individual tooth structures. While competing methods frequently suffer from topological discontinuities (e.g., fragmented roots) or oversegmentation in high-density regions, our approach maintains global structural integrity and local connectivity. The zoomed-in regions (red boxes) highlight MedHiVE’s robustness in resolving ambiguous inter-proximal boundaries where baseline models typically fail to maintain clear separation.

Figure 9. Qualitative multi-class segmentation results on the KiTS 2023 internal test set. We evaluate the proposed MedHiVE against ground truth annotations and four state-of-the-art baselines for the joint segmentation of the kidney parenchyma, cysts, and tumor masses. MedHiVE demonstrates superior spatial and semantic consistency by effectively modeling the hierarchical dependencies between nested structures; it captures the global morphology of the kidney while maintaining high-fidelity boundaries for small, low-contrast cysts and heterogeneous tumor regions. Unlike competing methods, which frequently exhibit topological fragmentation or semantic leakage (e.g., misclassifying tumor voxels as healthy tissue), our approach preserves structural integrity across varying object scales. The zoomed-in insets highlight MedHiVE’s ability to resolve ambiguous boundaries in complex cases of multi-focal cystic disease, where baseline models suffer from oversegmentation and loss of connectivity.

Figure 8. Qualitative multi-organ segmentation performance on the AMOS-CT validation set. We compare the proposed MedHiVE against ground truth labels and four state-of-the-art baselines across 15 abdominal organs. MedHiVE demonstrates superior spatial and semantic consistency, leveraging long-range dependency modeling to maintain the global anatomical context of large-scale organs (e.g., liver, stomach) while ensuring high-fidelity boundary localization for small, low-contrast structures (e.g., adrenal glands, gallbladder). While competing methods frequently suffer from inter-class leakage and topological discontinuities in anatomically crowded regions, our approach preserves structural integrity and inter-organ spatial relationships. The highlighted regions (red boxes) illustrate MedHiVE’s robustness against oversegmentation at organ interfaces, where baseline models often fail to resolve clear semantic boundaries due to similar intensity profiles in non-contrast CT.

Figure 7. Qualitative segmentation results on the PANORAMA test sets. We compare the proposed MedHiVE against the ground truth and four state-of-the-art baselines. MedHiVE demonstrates superior spatial and semantic consistency, accurately capturing long-range dependencies in large-scale structures (e.g., the pancreas parenchyma) while maintaining high-fidelity boundaries for fine-grained objects like PDAC lesions and pancreatic ducts. Unlike competing methods that suffer from topological discontinuities or oversegmentation, our approach consistently preserves structural integrity across varying object scales.

Figure 3. Qualitative segmentation results on four datasets, from top to bottom: PANORAMA, AMOS, KiTS and GEPAR3D. Comparison of MedHiVE with the top five baselines. Red boxes highlight significant artifacts or missing components in baseline predictions. MedHiVE shows superior consistency with the ground truth in these challenging regions.

Figure 11. Qualitative comparison of visual grounding performance on external in-house abdominal CT scans with kidney lesions. Each row displays a representative abdominal CT slice paired with its corresponding part of radiology report describing kidney tumors or cysts; in the absence of voxel-wise annotations, the report serves as the reference. Grounding predictions are shown for MedHiVE (left), Merlin (center), and fVLM (right). All models are fine-tuned on KiTS 2023. MedHiVE segments lesions consistent with the radiology reports, whereas Merlin and fVLM overshoot the lesion extent or place predictions in a kidney the report leaves unremarkable (red boxes).

Figure 5. Visualization of the 3D projections of anatomical segmentation masks from the Merlin dataset [6], shown from the front, left, right, and back views. These projections highlight the global structural consistency and anatomical coherence of the segmented structures. Consistent with the 2D setting, we consider 14 abdominal anatomical groups for clarity and downstream processing (see Table 3). The multi-view renderings provide a qualitative assessment of segmentation quality across the full 3D volume.

Table 4. Quantitative segmentation and detection performance on the PANORAMA test sets (NIH, MSD, and In-house). Evaluation metrics include mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm), while PDAC detection efficacy is measured via Sensitivity and Specificity (%). The best results are highlighted in bold. MedHiVE demonstrates state-of-the-art performance, particularly in the challenging task of PDAC segmentation, where it significantly outperforms existing Transformer and Mamba-based architectures. Notably, our method achieves a substantial boost in mDSC for the In-house PDAC dataset (65.8%) and the Overall PDAC average (54.2%), representing a major improvement over the second-best performing models. Additionally, MedHiVE exhibits the lowest mHD95 and the highest sensitivity for patient-level detection, underscoring its clinical utility in identifying low-contrast ductal adenocarcinomas across diverse multi-center cohorts.

Table 5. Quantitative segmentation results on the KiTS dataset. Performance is evaluated across three distinct labels: Kidneys, Tumor, and Cyst. Results are reported in DSC (%) for individual classes, with mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm) representing the overall average performance. MedHiVE achieves the highest performance in mDSC and mHD95, consistently outperforming both CNN-based and advanced sequence-modeling baselines. Specifically, the model shows a marked improvement in the segmentation of small, irregular structures compared to pure Mamba or Transformer architectures. The achievement of the lowest mHD95 further validates our method’s precision in boundary localization, demonstrating its robustness in handling the high anatomical variability and complex pathologies inherent in kidney tumor imaging. The best results are bolded.

Table 6. Quantitative multi-organ segmentation performance on the AMOS-CT dataset. The evaluation encompasses 15 distinct anatomical structures across a wide range of scales and morphologies. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results per category indicated in bold. MedHiVE achieves superior overall performance, demonstrating a high degree of robustness across both large, high-contrast organs (e.g., Liver, Spleen) and smaller, more complex structures (e.g., Adrenal Glands, Duodenum). Notably, our method establishes a new state-of-the-art for the Pancreas and Duodenum, which are traditionally challenging due to their low-contrast boundaries and proximity to the gastrointestinal tract. Furthermore, the significant reduction in mHD95 compared to both Transformer-based and pure Mamba-based baselines indicates a superior ability to preserve global topological consistency while maintaining fine-grained local details. MedHiVE exhibits competitive or superior Dice scores across the majority of classes, underscoring the generalizability of our proposed architecture.

Table 7. Detailed quantitative evaluation of tooth segmentation on the GEPAR3D test set. Results are categorized by individual teeth following the FDI World Dental Federation notation across all four quadrants. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results per category indicated in bold. MedHiVE achieves the highest overall segmentation accuracy and the lowest mHD95 among all compared methods. The performance is notably consistent across different tooth types, effectively bridging the gap between large molars and smaller incisors. In particular, our model demonstrates superior precision in the upper and lower left quadrants, where it maintains high fidelity for complex occlusal surfaces and inter-proximal spaces. The significant reduction in the average Hausdorff distance suggests that MedHiVE is less prone to the isolated voxel noise and topological errors that often degrade the clinical utility of baseline segmentation outputs.

Table 1. Comprehensive performance comparison across segmentation, classification, and detection tasks. Segmentation performance is reported in mDSC (%), while PDAC classification and detection are reported via Sensitivity (%), Specificity (%), and mAP (%). VRAM is measured in gigabytes (GB) (↓), and speed in million voxels per second (MV/s) (↑). The best results are bolded.

Table 8. Quantitative segmentation performance on the ToothFairy2 dataset subset. Evaluation follows the FDI World Dental Federation notation across the upper and lower dental arches. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results highlighted in bold. MedHiVE demonstrates a clear state-of-the-art advantage, particularly in maintaining structural continuity across the most challenging anatomical sites. Our method significantly outperforms all baselines in the posterior extremities, specifically the third molars (FDI 18, 28, 38, 48), where standard models typically struggle with severe under-segmentation or total loss of connectivity. Furthermore, MedHiVE attains the second-best mHD95 among all methods. These results validate the robustness of our approach in handling the high morphological variability and lower image quality characteristic of the ToothFairy2 benchmarks, ensuring precise tooth-by-tooth delineation across the entire oral cavity.

Table 12. Ablation study on the AMOS-CT validation set across 15 organ classes. We evaluate the impact of the Text (T) supervision and Contrastive Loss (CL) components on segmentation accuracy (mDSC) and boundary precision (mHD95). The results demonstrate that incorporating textual representations (Config #2) consistently improves performance for anatomically complex organs, while the full MedHiVE framework (Config #3) achieves the highest overall accuracy and a significant reduction in Hausdorff Distance (mHD95 from 5.0 to 3.6 mm). This suggests that the joint contrastive objective effectively regularizes the latent space, particularly benefiting small-scale structures such as the adrenal glands and duodenum. B, T, and CL indicate baseline, text-conditioned representations, and contrastive loss, respectively. The best results are bolded.

Table 10. Ablation study on the PANORAMA and in-house datasets demonstrating the impact of multi-modal supervision. We evaluate our proposed method across three diverse test sets: NIH (public), MSD (public), and a multi-institutional In-house dataset. Segmentation quality is measured through mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm). Additionally, we report patient-level PDAC detection performance using Sensitivity/Specificity (%). The results indicate that while text guidance (T) significantly improves tumor localization, the addition of contrastive learning (CL) is crucial for refining boundary transitions, as evidenced by the reduction in mHD95. The best results are bolded.

Table 11. Ablation study on the KiTS dataset demonstrating the impact of multi-modal supervision. We evaluate the incremental contribution of text-based prompts (T) and contrastive learning (CL) over the baseline (B) architecture. Segmentation performance is reported via class-specific DSC (%) for Kidneys, Tumors, and Cysts, alongside aggregate mDSC (%) and mHD95 (mm) metrics. The results indicate that text guidance (T) primarily benefits cyst segmentation, while the addition of contrastive learning (CL) yields the largest gain for tumors and further reduces mHD95. The best results are bolded.

Table 14. Ablation study on the GEPAR3D dataset, including ToothFairy2 subset across 32 individual tooth classes (FDI notation). We evaluate the contribution of Text (T) conditioning and Contrastive Loss (CL) on fine-grained dental segmentation. While the baseline (Config #1) performs adequately on centralized teeth, the integration of textual representations (Config #2) provides a significant performance boost in boundary precision, reducing mHD95 from 6.5 to 2.0 mm. Notably, the full MedHiVE framework (Config #3) demonstrates superior robustness in segmenting distal molars (e.g., FDI 18, 28, 38), which are typically prone to severe imaging artifacts and morphological variation. This confirms that the contrastive objective effectively regularizes the feature space for anatomically rare or obscured structures. This indicates that the benefit of the anatomy-level contrastive objective can depend on overlap between the pre-training anatomy inventory and the target structures. B, T, and CL denote baseline, text-conditioned representations, and contrastive loss, respectively. The best results are bolded.

Table 13. Ablation study on the GEPAR3D test set, excluding ToothFairy2 subset across 32 dental classes (FDI notation). We quantify the influence of Textual Supervision (T) and Contrastive Loss (CL) on fine-grained segmentation. The inclusion of text-conditioned representations (Config #2) yields substantial gains in semantic recognition across the dental arch. Crucially, the full MedHiVE framework (Config #3) achieves the highest boundary fidelity, reaching sub-millimeter precision (mHD95: 0.5 mm). This indicates that the contrastive objective mitigates surface errors effectively in anatomically complex regions, such as the lingual surfaces of incisors (FDI 11, 21) and the occlusal pits of molars (FDI 36, 46), where baselines exhibit higher spatial variance. As this dataset covers dental anatomy absent from our pre-training inventory, the anatomy-level contrastive objective is expected to contribute less here. B, T, and CL denote baseline, text-conditioned representations, and contrastive loss, respectively. The best results are bolded.
Table 3. List of selected anatomies.

Table 9. Comparative quantitative analysis of tooth segmentation on the full dataset, including GEPAR3D [42] and ToothFairy2 [8, 9, 31] subsets. Evaluation is conducted for individual teeth using FDI World Dental Federation notation across all four quadrants. mDSC is reported in (%) and mHD95 in (mm), with the best results bolded. MedHiVE achieves the highest overall mDSC, particularly in the segmentation of molars and premolars. MedHiVE achieves the second-best mHD95, indicating precise boundary localization. Notably, the performance gap is most pronounced in the posterior regions, where complex root morphologies and proximity to distal anatomical landmarks typically challenge standard segmentation models. These results underscore the effectiveness of our architectural design in maintaining local precision while capturing the global context of the complete dental arch.

papers.abstract: Generating compositional 3D scenes from a single image requires recovering detailed object geometry and coherent spatial arrangements. Existing object-to-scene methods, including SAM3D and MIDI, extend object generation through image-context reasoning or inter-instance modeling. Coordinating objects remains challenging with limited scene-level supervision. Directly extending object-centric generators to entire scenes can degrade geometry and fail to preserve instance scale, orientation, and pose. We propose Bri3D, a framework bridging scene-level structural reasoning and object-level generative priors through instance-aware voxel scene anchors. Bri3D predicts a color-coded scene scaffold encoding coarse object geometry and spatial arrangements. Each instance is extracted as a scene anchor and refined into a pose-preserving, prior-compatible voxel support, enabling a frozen object generator to synthesize detailed textured geometry in the anchor-defined spatial reference. This coarse-to-fine design separates scene organization from object-scale detail synthesis, focusing scene-level training on spatial organization and anchor refinement while reusing pretrained object priors. Experiments demonstrate improvements in scene layout, object geometry, visual quality, and generalization. Bri3D predicts scene layouts efficiently; full scene generation is faster than SceneGen and SAM3D.
bullets: Addresses poor coordination between object geometry and scene-level spatial organization in single-image 3D generation.
Predicts a color-coded voxel scene scaffold encoding coarse object geometry and spatial arrangements.
Extracts each instance into a pose-preserving, prior-compatible scene anchor for refinement.
Reuses pretrained object-level generative priors while training scene components mainly for organization and anchor refinement.
Reports improved layout, geometry, visual quality, and generalization, with faster full-scene generation than SceneGen and SAM3D.

figures.caption: Figure 4 Generalization to diverse room scenes. The upper three rows compare reconstructions of a living room, a garage, and a classroom, with the input image followed by the results of DepR, PartCrafter, MIDI, SceneGen, SAM3D, and Bri3D. These examples cover different object categories, scales, and degrees of occlusion. The lower row shows a multi-room overview and reconstructions of its bathroom, bedroom, living room, and kitchen, each generated from a separate room-level input. Together, the examples illustrate object reconstruction across varied scene configurations and room types.

Figure 2 Overview of Bri3D. The Scene Scaffold Generator and Anchored Voxel Refiner replace the voxel-generation stage of a two-stage object generator, while its detail-synthesis stage remains frozen. SC-VAE denotes the StructureColor VAE, and snowflakes indicate frozen modules. The scaffold is generated in latent space and decoded at 1283; each object is refined to a 643 voxel support. The anchor initialization follows Eq. 5, including object-wise latent normalization.

Figure 3 Qualitative results on the 3D-FRONT [12] test set. Our method generates more plausible layouts and higher-fidelity geometry, consistent with the quantitative improvements. Red boxes indicate inferior baseline results.

Figure 5 Comparison of 3D scene layouts and failure cases. (a) Columns show the RGB input, ground-truth layout, and predictions from MIDI [18], SceneGen [28], SAM3D [3], and Bri3D. Red wireframe boxes mark the groundtruth object extents, making displacement, missing instances, and shape deviations visible. Bri3D better follows the reference arrangements in these examples. (b) Red rectangles highlight our failures: nearby objects may merge in the cluttered seating area (Case 1), and some instances may be omitted in the densely populated classroom (Case 2).

Figure 6 Color-coded scene scaffold vs. connected component analysis. From left to right: RGB input, instance label map, geometry-only CCA result, and the predicted color-coded voxel grid. In the upper example, CCA groups the refrigerator, microwave, and table into one connected region; in the lower example, it merges the touching bed components and teddy bear. The predicted instance colors provide additional separation cues at these contacts, allowing joint position–color clustering to recover distinct object anchors. Colors indicate instance identity rather than surface texture.

Figure 7 Preliminary attempt on structural elements. From left to right: RGB input, label map including structural regions, predicted color-coded voxel grid, and reconstructed scene mesh. The dining-area and bedroom examples include room surfaces together with foreground furniture, illustrating how structural labels can extend the scaffold beyond object instances. This extension depends on reliable labels for those regions and remains preliminary; floors, walls, and ceilings are excluded from the main Bri3D experiments and quantitative results.

Figure 8 Additional qualitative comparisons and robustness to imperfect segmentation. (a) Geometry and layout comparisons with MIDI and SAM3D on indoor and outdoor scenes; MIDI is shown with normal shading. Bri3D produces coherent layouts and faithful object geometry, while MIDI suffers from distorted shapes and implausible arrangements. (b) With an erroneous instance label map (Wrong Seg), Bri3D exhibits only local cracks, whereas SAM3D produces incorrect object partitions and collisions, including interpenetration between the teddy bear and the bed.

Figure 9 Robustness to instance segmentation granularity, label colors, and implausible partitions. From left to right: input image, input instance segmentation, predicted semantic voxel grid, and reconstructed textured meshes with bounding boxes. The first two rows show the same tabletop scene containing a bottle, a mug, a large box, a ball, and two small stacks of blocks. The segmentation changes only the grouping of these small stacks: each stack receives one label in the first row, while its individual blocks receive separate labels in the second row. The last two rows show deliberately implausible partitions of a chair, together with changes in instance label colors. Despite these inconsistent instance boundaries, Bri3D preserves the overall object geometry and spatial arrangement.

Table 4 Ablation studies of Bri3D. Rows (b)–(f) progressively introduce the components of the Scene Scaffold Generator. Rows (g)/(h) compare interpolation and latent refinement from (f); (i)/(j) apply detail synthesis after (h). All retain the anchor boxes and BBox IoU of (f). We evaluate scene- and object-level geometry, layout accuracy, and visual similarity on 300 scenes paired with rendered images and ground-truth 3D scenes. The best results are in bold; the second-best results (SAM3D in all reported columns) are underlined.

BBox IoU is in [0, 1]; collision rate is the percentage of overlapping object pairs. ∗Ours reports scaffold-stage anchor BBox IoU and collisions after separately voxelizing extracted instances. Times outside parentheses are for scaffold prediction; parentheses and baseline times report full generation.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting have enabled efficient and photorealistic head avatar reconstruction, yet monocular video-based or image-based methods still suffer from under-constrained geometry and texture, leading to artifacts such as blurring, stretching, and temporal instability. We present EDGAR (Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement), a conditional diffusion framework designed to enhance the quality of Gaussian avatars by correcting artifacts while preserving identity fidelity. To train EDGAR, we construct EDGAR-SET, a hybrid triplet dataset composed of real-captured and synthetic-rendered samples, which simulates realistic Gaussian avatar failure cases by pairing degraded renderings with ground-truth and reference images. EDGAR refines degraded frames through a fusion block that injects identity features extracted by the self-supervised Sapiens model into a one-step diffusion backbone, enabling effective artifact removal without sacrificing efficiency. Our EDGAR model incorporates a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to address diverse degradation types and severity levels. The refined multi-view renderings are subsequently used as pseudo-targets to optimize a single underlying Gaussian avatar, so that the final avatar can be rendered without applying EDGAR to every output frame. Experiments on three different Gaussian avatar reconstruction methods, each evaluated under three different settings, show improvements in both perceptual and reconstruction measures over the raw outputs and an SDEdit-style refinement baseline. In addition, cross-view evaluation demonstrates improved calibrated consistency, while tests under large yaw and open-mouth expressions verify robustness under extreme settings. These results collectively indicate a useful operating regime for recoverable appearance artifacts. The code is available at https://kwanyun.github.io/edgar/
bullets: Addresses blur, stretching, geometric and texture errors, and temporal instability in monocular or image-based Gaussian avatars.
Trains on EDGAR-SET, combining real and synthetic degraded/ground-truth/reference triplets to simulate recoverable failures.
Uses identity features from Sapiens, a one-step conditional diffusion backbone, and a Mixture-of-Experts design for varied degradation types and severities.
Refined multi-view renderings supervise optimization of one Gaussian avatar, avoiding diffusion refinement at every output frame.
Across three reconstruction methods and three settings, improves perceptual, reconstruction, and cross-view consistency measures, including challenging yaw and open-mouth cases.

papers.abstract: Accurate 4D reconstruction remains challenging: jointly estimating camera motion, scene geometry, and non-rigid deformation entails highly nonconvex optimization, making global optimality difficult to guarantee. We present XM4D, a framework for accurate and efficient 4D reconstruction built upon certifiably globally optimal geometric optimization. By separating the estimation of camera motion from non-rigid deformation, we formulate both stages as structured quadratically constrained quadratic programs (QCQP) that admit semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations and verifiable global optimality certificates. For camera motion estimation, we lift static point tracks into 3D using foundational depth prediction models and formulate a scaled bundle adjustment problem that jointly estimates camera poses, depth scales, and static landmarks. By analytically eliminating translations and landmarks, we reduce the problem to a QCQP over scaled rotations. For non-rigid reconstruction, we represent dynamic motion using an embedded deformation graph (EDG) and show that its tracking, rigidity, and temporal regularization objectives similarly reduce to a rotation-only QCQP. Both problems admit SDP relaxations that we solve efficiently with a GPU-accelerated Burer-Monteiro solver based on Riemannian optimization. The recovered geometry further initializes dynamic Gaussian splatting for photometric refinement. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate accurate camera motion estimation on both static and dynamic scenes, efficient optimization that scales to thousands of frames, and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering quality.
bullets: Addresses the nonconvex challenge of jointly estimating camera motion, scene geometry, and dynamic deformation.
Separates camera motion estimation from non-rigid reconstruction, formulating both as rotation-focused QCQPs with SDP relaxations and global-optimality certificates.
Uses depth prediction for scaled bundle adjustment and an embedded deformation graph for dynamic motion.
Solves the relaxations with a GPU-accelerated Burer–Monteiro/Riemannian optimizer, then refines geometry with dynamic Gaussian splatting.
Experiments on seven benchmarks show accurate motion estimation, scalability to thousands of frames, and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering quality.

papers.abstract: Knowledge of the hidden interior structure of an object, including the presence and location of cavities, is essential for predictive simulation, robotic manipulation, and nondestructive inspection. However, such cavities leave no direct signature on the static visible surface, making collision-induced deformation one of the few cues used to infer their presence. Structure from Collision (SfC) addresses this problem by recovering the hidden interior structure of an object from multiview observations of a collision event. SfC is challenging for two reasons: hidden cavities are only indirectly observable through surface motion, and voids correspond to the absence of material, making direct optimization using standard density representations difficult. The density-based SfC baseline inherits both difficulties. Surface-matching gradients do not directly indicate the cavity location, while density gradients can be weak or uninformative inside or near void regions. Therefore, we reformulate SfC as hypothesis-space reasoning, representing hidden cavities as explicit structural hypotheses whose variables encode available structural assumptions rather than relying on implicit density updates. A global stage performs gradient-free optimization over this hypothesis space using forward-only material point method (MPM) simulation. A local stage then refines the selected hypothesis as a Lagrangian particle system through gradient-based optimization using differentiable MPM simulation. On the SfC benchmark, our method improves hidden-structure reconstruction and future prediction over the density-based SfC baseline. Interior-topology stress tests and robustness analyses characterize its scope and limitations. The project page is available at https://www.kecl.ntt.co.jp/people/kaneko.takuhiro/projects/sfc-hypothesis/.
bullets: Infers otherwise invisible interior cavities from multiview observations of an object collision.
Replaces difficult density optimization with explicit hypotheses encoding structural assumptions.
Uses global gradient-free search with forward-only MPM simulation, followed by local gradient-based refinement with differentiable MPM.
Improves hidden-structure reconstruction and future prediction over a density-based SfC baseline on the SfC benchmark.
Stress tests and robustness analyses define the method’s scope and limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of hypothesis-space reasoning for SfC. (0) Dense particle initialization is reconstructed from multiview observations following GIC [3]. The initial rollout shows the dynamics before hypothesis optimization. (I) Global hypothesis optimization consists of (1) instantiating cavity hypotheses and (2) scoring them with forward-only MPM simulation using a collision-adjacent loss. (II) Lagrangian particle refinement: (3) the selected hypothesis is refined using differentiable MPM simulation with physical and geometric constraints. This two-stage framework separates coarse structural reasoning from fine geometric refinement.

papers.abstract: Recent innovations in medical imaging have markedly improved brain tumor identification, surpassing conventional diagnostic approaches that suffer from low resolution, radiation exposure, and limited contrast. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is pivotal in precise and accurate tumor characterization owing to its high-resolution, non-invasive nature. This study investigates the synergy among multiple feature representation schemes such as local Binary Patterns (LBP), Gabor filters, Discrete Wavelet Transform, Fast Fourier Transform, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Gray-Level Run Length Matrix alongside five learning algorithms namely: k-nearest Neighbor, Random Forest, Support Vector Classifier (SVC), and probabilistic neural network (PNN), and CNN. Empirical findings indicate that LBP in conjunction with SVC and CNN obtained high specificity and accuracy, rendering it a promising method for MRI-based tumor diagnosis. Further to investigate the contribution of LBP, Statistical analysis chi-square and p-value tests are used to confirm the significant impact of LBP feature space for identification of brain Tumor. In addition, The SHAP analysis was used to identify the most important features in classification. In a small dataset, CNN obtained 97.8% accuracy while SVC yielded 98.06% accuracy. In subsequent analysis, a large benchmark dataset is also utilized to evaluate the performance of learning algorithms in order to investigate the generalization power of the proposed model. CNN achieves the highest accuracy of 98.9%, followed by SVC at 96.7%. These results highlight CNN's effectiveness in automated, high-precision tumor diagnosis. Code: https://github.com/asifrahman557/BrainTumorDetection
bullets: Evaluates LBP, Gabor filters, wavelets, FFT, CNN features, and gray-level run-length features with several classifiers.
LBP combined with SVC and CNN showed high specificity and accuracy; statistical tests supported LBP’s relevance.
SHAP was used to identify the most influential features for classification.
On the reported small dataset, SVC reached 98.06% accuracy and CNN 97.8%; on a larger benchmark, CNN reached 98.9% and SVC 96.7%.
The study focuses on automated MRI diagnosis and evaluates performance across datasets, but the abstract does not detail clinical deployment or broader validation.

papers.abstract: Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) cardiac MRI enables non-invasive assessment of left atrial (LA) scar, an imaging marker associated with atrial fibrillation ablation outcome. However, automatic scar segmentation is hindered by low contrast, the thin atrial wall, scarce labels, and extreme class imbalance. Conditional diffusion offers iterative mask generation, but its suitability for sparse 3D LA scar segmentation remains unclear. To address this gap, we propose Conditional Mask Diffusion (CMDiff), which predicts clean masks using a dynamic-encoder-conditioned 3D sinusoidal UNet. We compared CMDiff with a deterministic baseline on identical cases in five-fold cross-validation of 60 scar-labelled public LASCARQS subjects, with 48 training and 12 held-out cases per fold. CMDiff achieved a scar DSC of 0.47 $\pm$ 0.08, HD95 of 12.89 $\pm$ 6.39 mm, and ASD of 1.91 $\pm$ 0.96 mm, compared with deterministic baseline values of 0.51 $\pm$ 0.08, 10.86 $\pm$ 5.39 mm, and 1.58 $\pm$ 1.03 mm, respectively. Under the same implementation, clean-mask prediction performed substantially better than the noise-prediction configuration evaluated in this study. Thus, CMDiff was technically feasible but did not improve segmentation performance: DSC was lower, and both HD95 and ASD were higher. Direct mask diffusion therefore provides an analytical alternative, but not a competitive performance advance for this task. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/jizhang02/CMDiff.
bullets: Addresses low contrast, thin atrial walls, scarce labels, and severe class imbalance in LGE MRI scar segmentation.
Uses a dynamic-encoder-conditioned 3D sinusoidal UNet for iterative clean-mask generation.

papers.abstract: Point clouds represent 3D object geometry as sets of spatial coordinates. A fundamental task in their analysis is keypoint detection, i.e., identifying a sparse subset of points that captures the most salient features. While supervised methods rely on manual annotations, unsupervised approaches leverage intrinsic geometric properties to localize keypoints without human input. We introduce GEKey, a self-supervised framework that uses the geodesic eccentricity transform, an SE(3)-invariant geometric measure, to identify instance-specific salient points. These points serve as pseudo-labels to train a model that aligns its predictions with the object's intrinsic structure. GEKey is simple, efficient, and robust, preserving intra-class variation by balancing instance-specific and category-level structure. Extensive experiments on ShapeNetCoreV2, KeypointNet, CAPE, ITOP, and DeformingThings4D show state-of-the-art performance in both keypoint detection and alignment, with strong resilience to noise, downsampling, deformations, and real-world conditions. The code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/Pierreoo/GEKey.
bullets: Targets sparse 3D keypoint detection while preserving salient geometric structure and intra-class variation.
Uses an SE(3)-invariant geodesic eccentricity transform to generate pseudo-labels.
Trains a model to align predicted keypoints with each object’s intrinsic geometry.
Reports state-of-the-art keypoint detection and alignment across five datasets.
Robust to noise, downsampling, deformations, and real-world conditions.

papers.abstract: Articulated 3D assets are essential for robotic simulation and training, yet their generation from casual images poses a key challenge: recovering part geometry and kinematics that remain mutually consistent. We present ArtCrafter, a novel feed-forward generative model for controllable generation of articulated 3D objects from a pair of images, one depicting the object in the rest state and the other in the open state. At the core of ArtCrafter is a DiT-based generative model that jointly produces part-level meshes for both articulation states in a single forward pass. Inspired by Slot Attention, its denoising process operates on a $1+2N$ slot layout comprising one shared base slot and $N$ paired rest/open slots, encouraging each pair to bind to the same kinematic part. To ensure geometrically consistent and disjoint part generation, we introduce Triplet Attention to enforce cross-state geometric consistency between paired rest/open slots anchored through the shared base slot, and a repulsion loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rep}}$ on decoded part point clouds to prevent inter-part penetration throughout denoising. Given the resulting paired meshes, URDF joint parameters---type, axis, origin, and range---are derived analytically from the rigid transformation between each rest/open pair, providing an interpretable alternative to learned joint-parameter regression. Extensive experiments on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets demonstrate that ArtCrafter outperforms existing method under the same dual-state setting in geometry quality and articulation precision, while remaining competitive with methods operating under different input settings and paradigms.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of jointly recovering part geometry and motion from casual images.
Uses a DiT-based model with shared and paired rest/open slots to generate all part meshes in one pass.
Introduces Triplet Attention for cross-state consistency and a repulsion loss to avoid inter-part penetration.
Derives joint type, axis, origin, and range analytically from paired rest/open mesh transformations.
Experiments on in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets show improved geometry quality and articulation precision under the same dual-state setting.

figures.caption: Figure 1: ArtCrafter pipeline. Two input images (Irest, Iopen) are encoded into state features conditioning 2N + 1 noisy latent slots — base B, rest slots R1. . .RN , open slots O1. . .ON — each augmented with learnable part and state embeddings. Each 3D DiT block refines slots through: Local Attn (intra-slot), Triplet Attn (Ri ↔ Oi anchored through B), State Cross Attn (rest→ frest, open→ fopen, base→both), and Global Attn (all 2N+1 slots). The frozen VAE decoder produces part meshes from denoised slots. (a) Analytic joint derivation: joint parameters are derived deterministically from Ti = Topen,i ·T−1 rest,i with no learned head. (b) Geometric regularization: the frozen point decoder decodes ẑ0|t to per-slot point clouds; Lrep penalizes inter-part overlap.

Figure 3: Qualitative results on URDF-Anything+ [35] and OOD test sets. Each row shows rest and open-state renders for the input image(s) on the left, and colors denote part identity. ArtCrafter produces clean part boundaries and geometry quality aligned with the inputs. DIPO predicts plausible kinematic behavior for certain examples (two doors of oven) but its retrieved meshes are limited on unseen objects. PhysX-Anything (single image) can produce aligned geometries but struggle with fine-grained details (e.g. pedal bin, oven) and could hallucinate on rare objects (mirror).

Figure 2: Per-slot decoded geometry across denoising timesteps. Rows compare ArtCrafter (Ours), FM-I (independent per-state), and FM-II (unstructured joint generation) on the same object; columns progress from pure noise (t = 1) to clean output (t = 0). Each cell shows a split render of rest (left) and open (right) states overlaid on the object silhouette (gray); colors encode part identity: base (cyan), part 1 (orange), part 2 (pink). ArtCrafter achieves consistent cross-state binding by t = 0; FM-I produces inconsistent binding and incompatible part scale across the two independent runs; FM-II shows no clean part separation in either state. Bottom: decoded meshes per slot at t = 0, from which joint parameters are derived analytically.

papers.abstract: Event cameras are neuromorphic vision sensors with pixels that independently and asynchronously respond to brightness changes at microsecond resolution, supporting state estimation under rapid motion, motion blur, and high dynamic range (HDR) illumination. This also enables capture of high-frequency blinking patterns from light-emitting diodes (LEDs). Based on this, we propose a real-time event-based framework for LED tracking and six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) relative pose estimation using pulse-width modulation (PWM)-encoded LED markers. Multiple LEDs share a common blinking frequency and encode identities through distinct PWM duty cycles, reducing frequency-resource requirements and computational cost. Our dual-rate asynchronous tracking framework combines low-rate LED detection with high-rate raw-event updates, maintaining robust LED identity association and accurate pixel-level tracking under rapid motion. LED identities and positions establish reliable 2D-3D correspondences for real-time metric 6-DoF relative pose estimation. Extensive evaluations on a self-collected dataset demonstrate robustness under large motion flow and transient image-plane LED overlap. Furthermore, we develop a coordinated robotic platform comprising a quadrotor and a Mecanum-wheeled mobile robot, demonstrating the proposed framework's potential for closed-loop drone guidance through hovering and target-following experiments under time-varying HDR illumination, with onboard deployment on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. The dataset and implementation will be released to facilitate further research.
bullets: LEDs share one blinking frequency while distinct PWM duty cycles encode marker identities, reducing frequency and computation demands.
A dual-rate asynchronous tracker combines low-rate LED detection with high-rate event updates for pixel-level tracking and identity association.
Known LED identities and positions provide 2D–3D correspondences for metric relative pose estimation.
Evaluations on a self-collected dataset show robustness to large motion and temporary image-plane LED overlap.
A quadrotor–mobile-robot platform demonstrates onboard closed-loop hovering and target following under time-varying HDR illumination.

papers.abstract: Georeferenced 3D reconstruction from ground images requires recovering not only the local scene geometry, but also localizing every camera center and 3D point in a geographic coordinate frame. Existing cross-view geo-localization methods are able to estimate the GPS coordinate of a single ground camera, but do not reconstruct dense 3D geometry, while recent feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction models predict point maps and camera poses only in a local coordinate frame. We introduce X-VGGT, a feed-forward cross-view geometry transformer that unifies these tasks by jointly processing a set of ground-level images and a georeferenced satellite image to predict ground-view camera poses, dense 3D point maps, and a scene-level transform parameterized by gravity, scale, yaw and translation. This transform projects the local reconstruction into the satellite plane, resulting in the geo-registration of all ground images with the georeferenced satellite image. We further propose an evaluation protocol for this joint task and show that, across multiple cross-view datasets, X-VGGT produces accurate georeferenced reconstructions and outperforms prior cross-view geo-localization and multi-view 3D reconstruction models.
bullets: Addresses the gap between cross-view GPS localization and local-frame multi-view 3D reconstruction.
Processes multiple ground images with a georeferenced satellite image in a feed-forward geometry transformer.
Predicts camera poses, dense 3D point maps, and a scene transform covering gravity, scale, yaw, and translation.
Introduces an evaluation protocol for jointly assessing georeferenced reconstruction.
Shows accurate reconstructions across multiple cross-view datasets and outperforms prior localization and reconstruction models.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of X-VGGT. The model jointly processes N ground-level images and a georeferenced satellite image with an Alternating Attention (AA) Transformer. Ground-view patch tokens are decoded by the camera and DPT heads to predict camera poses Ĉi and dense point maps X̂i, while the satellite token is decoded by the Satellite Alignment Head (SAH) to estimate the transformation Gϕ from the local 3D reconstruction to the satellite coordinate frame. Gϕ is parameterized by a gravity vector g for ground-plane projection, a scalar α for metric conversion, and a planar rotation ψ and translation t that align the projected points with the satellite image.

Figure 3: Qualitative results. We show two sample predictions from the Metropolis (top) and KITTI (bottom) datasets using X-VGGT. From left to right: input ground views, predicted 3D reconstruction, pixel-level geo-registration, and camera geo-localization. Our method jointly reconstructs the groundview scene while projecting both image pixels and camera centers into the satellite coordinate frame.

Figure 1: Georeferenced cross-view 3D reconstruction. Given a set of ground-level images and a georeferenced satellite view, X-VGGT predicts camera poses, 3D point-maps, and a georeferencing transform Gϕ(·). By projecting the 3D reconstruction into the satellite plane, our model can georegister every pixel in the ground images, localize their cameras, and generate metric depth maps.

Figure 5: Example from the Sat-MegaDepth split. The ground images at both sides are taken from the original MegaDepth [23] dataset. We obtain high-resolution orthorectified satellite images covering the location of all ground views from Google Maps.

Ground-truth and predicted depth maps share the same colormap and range across all examples; error maps use a separate shared scale. All values are in meters. Missing ground-truth depth is shown in black, and errors are computed only where ground-truth depth is available.
Figure 4: Effect of the number of ground frames on Metropolis. Additional ground views reduce both camera localization and orientation errors.

Figure 8: Qualitative comparison with baselines. We compare X-VGGT against the baselines on camera geo-localization across the four evaluation datasets. From top to bottom: KITTI, Mapillary Metropolis, WRIVA, and ACC-NVS1.

papers.abstract: Physically based inverse rendering is an ambiguous problem, allowing independently optimized material variables to absorb appearance variations caused by illumination. Learned material predictions provide useful cues about which surface points have similar materials. Existing approaches often incorporate these cues through auxiliary regularization losses. Instead, we propose a novel prior-guided reparameterization of the material optimization space. We fuse multi-view material predictions onto a mesh and construct a permutohedral lattice in the resulting prior feature space. Surface points with similar predictions share lattice variables, restricting the material field to a prior-defined subspace that is optimized jointly with geometry and illumination using a purely photometric objective. Experiments on three synthetic benchmarks demonstrate improved material decomposition and relighting, with results on par with the strongest baseline on Stanford-ORB. As a complete system, our method improves relighting PSNR by 1.4-1.5\,dB over the strongest evaluated mesh-based baseline on Synthetic4Relight and TensoIR-Synthetic. Analysis of the optimization shows that shared variables pool per-vertex photometric gradients into updates that are more consistent across sampled views. In a controlled comparison within the same pipeline, the restricted subspace, despite its reduced degrees of freedom, yields more accurate material decomposition than both unrestricted per-vertex optimization and a regularization loss built from the same prior.
bullets: Addresses ambiguity where material variables can absorb illumination effects.
Fuses multi-view material predictions into a mesh and builds a permutohedral lattice over the resulting prior feature space.
Shares lattice variables among surfaces with similar predicted materials, jointly optimizing materials, geometry, and illumination using only photometric supervision.
Improves relighting PSNR by 1.4–1.5 dB over the strongest mesh-based baseline on two synthetic benchmarks and matches the strongest baseline on Stanford-ORB.
The restricted subspace outperforms unrestricted per-vertex optimization and an equivalent prior-based regularizer in controlled material-decomposition comparisons.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline overview and prior-space material updates. Multi-view images supervise surface reconstruction and provide material predictions. Input RGB refines predicted albedo before fusion onto the initial mesh. The fused prior defines a fixed permutohedral lattice over albedo RGB, roughness and metallic. Per-vertex photometric gradients are splatted onto the lattice, and the resulting updates are sliced back onto the mesh vertices. For visualization, the lattice is drawn as a regular 3-D grid. In the 5-D permutohedral lattice, each vertex uses the six corners of its enclosing simplex.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison. Novel views and relighting on Synthetic4Relight Chair and Stanford-ORB Gnome, and relighting on DTC-Synthetic Teapot. Boxes mark enlarged regions. Numbers are full-image PSNR (PSNR-H on Stanford-ORB).

Figure 5. Effect of prior quality. Mean albedo and relighting PSNR on Synthetic4Relight of ours and the prior-loss control with increasing prior quality, and of the no-prior variant. The two lowest levels apply material confusion to the predicted prior. Thumbnails show the fused prior albedo on Hotdog used for that quality level.

Figure 4. Update consistency across sampled views. Materiallogit update energy at step 100 for the three controlled variants of Sec. 6.1. Their energy is split into noise ( ) and a consistent component attributed to the photometric loss ( ) and the prior loss ( ). Mean over 15 scenes.
