papers.tldr: A prior-guided reparameterization constrains material optimization to improve physically based inverse rendering and relighting without auxiliary regularization losses.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning has given rise to vision foundation models that learn general-purpose image representations transferable across downstream tasks, yet representation learning for 3D scenes has not achieved comparable success. Motivated by this, we identify key limitations of current 3D representation learning approaches and revisit their core design choices. We first replace the commonly used hierarchical PTv3 backbone with the Volume Transformer, a ViT-like architecture for 3D scenes. We then redesign two core objectives of modern approaches built around student-teacher networks: matching representations across views and predicting masked content from visible context. For the first objective, we separate the roles of teacher and student: the teacher provides clean, consistent targets while the student learns invariance to stronger perturbations. For the second objective, we prevent the student from accessing the masked geometry and instead require it to infer missing representations from visible context only. Finally, we redesign 2D-to-3D knowledge distillation, replacing direct regression of view-dependent image features with view-consistent supervision. Together, these changes form VINO, a framework that learns semantic representations of 3D scenes without labels. VINO substantially improves dense linear probing across indoor and outdoor benchmarks and transfers strongly to out-of-domain settings.
bullets: Targets the gap between successful 2D vision foundation models and less effective 3D scene representation learning.
Replaces the hierarchical PTv3 backbone with a ViT-like Volume Transformer for 3D scenes.
Separates teacher and student roles for view matching, using clean teacher targets and stronger student perturbations.
Enforces masked-content prediction from visible geometry only and introduces view-consistent 2D-to-3D distillation.
Achieves substantial gains in dense linear probing across indoor and outdoor benchmarks, with strong out-of-domain transfer.

figures.caption: Figure 3: VINO Overview. Overlapping global and local views are sampled from a 3D scene. The EMA teacher encodes clean global views and softly assigns their tokens to learned prototypes, producing balanced targets. The prototypes are optimized independently by encouraging balanced and consistent assignments across global views. The student encodes strongly augmented local views and masked global views. Local-view embeddings, through a projection head, predict the targets of corresponding global-view tokens. Masked view embeddings provide context to a cross-attention-only predictor that predicts the targets at masked locations.

Figure 1: Self-supervised 3D Representations. We propose VINO, a framework for learning semantic representations of 3D scenes with no labels. Trained on 3D data only, VINO captures semantic similarity better than Sonata (Wu et al., 2025), as shown in PCA projections (top) and cosine-similarity maps (bottom). Sonata yields qualitatively similar representations across backbones, whereas VINO better distinguishes semantically different but geometrically similar regions, for example, chair and table legs, and captures semantic similarity across geometrically different instances, as illustrated by one plant strongly activating the other.

Figure 8: Qualitative results on Replica. VINO features of a large indoor scene from Replica (Straub et al., 2019). We visualize PCA on the bottom left and cosine similarity maps between tokens marked with a red cross and the other 3D tokens.

Figure 9: Qualitative results on SemanticKITTI. VINO features of an outdoor scene from SemanticKITTI (Geiger et al., 2012; Behley et al., 2019). We visualize PCA (top) and cosine similarity maps between the token marked with a red cross and all other 3D tokens (middle and bottom).

Figure 2: Comparison of Training Views. Sonata (Wu et al., 2025) geometrically corrupts all views and retains masked tokens in the student encoder. In contrast, VINO keeps the teacher’s global views clean, removes masked tokens from the student encoder, and applies geometric corruptions only to local views.

Figure 4: Representation Artifacts. We observe high-norm token artifacts in the representations (left). Register tokens largely eliminate these artifacts, but early in training, the learned representations still strongly reflect local voxel occupancy. papers.abstract: Multi-perspective-camera systems are widely adopted since they provide broad visual coverage for autonomous driving, motivating the synthesis of a unified wide view from spatially separated observations. In this work, we formulate wide view synthesis (WVS), which aims to synthesize a geometrically consistent wide view at a specified virtual viewpoint from multiple perspective cameras. Unlike conventional image stitching, WVS requires reasoning about 3D geometry and visibility to handle depth-dependent parallax and occlusions arising from spatially separated camera centers. While vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-fidelity view synthesis, its reliance on per-scene optimization limits its applicability to driving scenes. Furthermore, WVS introduces additional challenges, *e.g.*, peripheral stretching under perspective projection and photometric inconsistencies across cameras. To address these challenges, we propose **Wide-View Gaussian Splatting (WV-GS)**, a feed-forward Gaussian-splatting framework that synthesizes wide views without per-scene optimization. Specifically, we introduce Piecewise Perspective Rendering (PPR) to mitigate peripheral stretching through local perspective projections sharing a common camera center, and Spatial Affine Photometric Modeling (SAPM) to account for camera-dependent photometric variations during training. We further introduce **WideDrive**, a synthetic benchmark providing dense ground-truth wide views and adapt a LiDAR-projected sparse-reference protocol to real-world datasets. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of WV-GS for WVS. Dataset and code will be publicly released.
bullets: Wide-view synthesis must handle depth-dependent parallax, occlusions, peripheral stretching, and cross-camera photometric differences.
WV-GS uses Piecewise Perspective Rendering to reduce peripheral distortion with local projections sharing one camera center.
Spatial Affine Photometric Modeling addresses camera-dependent appearance inconsistencies during training.
The authors introduce WideDrive, a synthetic benchmark with dense ground-truth wide views, and a LiDAR-projected sparse-reference protocol for real data.
Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of WV-GS; code and data are planned for release.

papers.abstract: Hybrid Mesh-Gaussian rendering combines compact textured surfaces with flexible 3D Gaussian primitives, offering an efficient alternative to purely Gaussian scene representations for structured environments. Existing scene-reconstruction hybrids commonly follow an additive formulation, where Gaussian residuals compensate for errors left by the mesh. However, not every Mesh-Gaussian conflict is caused by missing content: residual geometry errors, occlusion mismatch, texture-projection artifacts, and view-dependent appearance can make the same mesh content consistent in one view but inconsistent in another. We therefore formulate hybrid rendering as a multi-view inconsistency problem and present Gaussolve, a subtract-and-refill framework that selectively dissolves inconsistent mesh content before residual Gaussians refill the revealed regions. We introduce a lightweight Neural Dissolve Field, parameterized by scalar spherical-harmonic Gaussians, to learn where and from which viewing directions mesh content should be dissolved. A continuous transmittance fusion rule progressively exposes residual Gaussians behind the dissolved mesh, preserving their reconstruction gradients and avoiding hard visibility discontinuities. Experiments on structured and semi-structured scenes demonstrate higher visual fidelity with fewer Gaussian primitives and faster rendering. Project page: https://ooosn.github.io/gaussians-can-subtract/
bullets: Frames hybrid rendering as a multi-view inconsistency problem rather than purely additive mesh-error correction.
Uses a Neural Dissolve Field to predict which mesh regions should be dissolved and from which viewing directions.
Applies continuous transmittance fusion to reveal residual Gaussians smoothly while preserving reconstruction gradients.
Experiments on structured and semi-structured scenes report higher visual fidelity, fewer Gaussian primitives, and faster rendering.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Gaussolve. Figure 1. Gaussians Can Subtract. Existing hybrids primarily compensate for mesh errors by adding Gaussian residuals. Gaussolve instead introduces a subtractive Neural Dissolve Field that selectively dissolves inconsistent mesh content and lets residual Gaussians refill the revealed regions. This explicit subtract-and-refill decomposition improves visual quality while retaining a compact hybrid representation. Compared with existing methods, Gaussolve achieves a more favorable quality–compactness trade-off by allowing meshes and Gaussians to cooperate rather than compete.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art feedforward reconstruction models perform poorly on in-the-wild object-centric photo collections. They are trained largely on single-session object captures whose images vary in viewpoint while the object and its environment remain nearly fixed. Public photo archives contain a different form of multi-view data. They hold found photos of the same object or design: photos taken independently by many people across years, environments, cameras, and sometimes physical units. In this work, we introduce Trainspotting, a dataset of 12,068 objects and 311,886 photos from Wikimedia Commons. We reconstruct each object to recover camera poses, multi-view stereo depth, and object masks. We categorize the objects into three regimes: objects fixed at one site, objects that move between sites, and designs shared by many physical units. Evaluating recent feedforward reconstruction models on Trainspotting shows that they fail most severely in the last two regimes. Fine-tuning VGGT-$\Omega$ on Trainspotting significantly improves camera pose, depth, and 3D geometry on held-out objects. We observe similar improvements on the independent NAVI in-the-wild benchmark, which contains photos of each object in different environments. Performance on conventional benchmarks remains largely unchanged.
bullets: The dataset contains 12,068 objects and 311,886 Wikimedia Commons photos collected across people, years, environments, cameras, and physical instances.
It reconstructs camera poses, multi-view stereo depth, and object masks, while categorizing objects by whether they stay at one site, move between sites, or represent shared designs.
Recent feedforward models struggle most with objects that move or have multiple physical units.
Fine-tuning VGGT-$\Omega$ on Trainspotting improves pose, depth, and 3D geometry on held-out objects and also improves performance on the NAVI benchmark.
Conventional benchmark performance remains largely unchanged after fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting enables efficient generalizable novel view synthesis, but existing pixel-aligned methods often generate highly redundant Gaussian primitives, causing the final representation size and rendering cost to grow rapidly with image resolution and the number of input views. We propose BudgetSplat, a budget-controllable feed-forward framework that adapts the final Gaussian representation to a user-specified preservation ratio. Rather than treating compaction as simple importance ranking, we formulate it as a joint problem of importance estimation, spatial coverage, and cross-view redundancy. A single trained model supports varying numbers of context views and multiple test-time budgets without per-budget retraining or per-scene compression. To realize this formulation, Intra-Cross Mask Supervision provides structure-, coverage-, and redundancy-aware guidance for learning Gaussian importance, while budget-conditioned feature modulation adapts Gaussian opacity and attributes to the requested preservation ratio. Coverage-Aware Budget Selection further combines patch-wise pre-selection, view-wise opacity ranking, and 3D redundancy suppression to construct compact yet spatially distributed Gaussian representations. Experiments on indoor reconstruction and cross-dataset generalization demonstrate consistent quality--size trade-offs across different input view counts and preservation ratios, substantially reducing final representation storage and rendering cost while preserving rendering quality.
authors: Yuxi Hu, Jun Zhang, Wei Mao, Yuchen Rao, Friedrich Fraundorfer
bullets: Addresses redundant Gaussian primitives that make representation size and rendering cost grow with image resolution and input views.
Jointly models Gaussian importance, spatial coverage, and cross-view redundancy rather than relying on simple importance ranking.
Uses Intra-Cross Mask Supervision and budget-conditioned feature modulation to adapt Gaussian attributes to different preservation ratios.
Coverage-Aware Budget Selection combines patch pre-selection, view-wise opacity ranking, and 3D redundancy suppression.
Experiments show consistent quality–size trade-offs across varying input views and budgets, without per-budget retraining or per-scene compression.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of BudgetSplat. (A) Given 𝑁 posed context images, a pixel-aligned reconstruction backbone estimates dense geometry and base Gaussian features. (B) During training, Intra-Cross Mask Supervision constructs pseudo importance targets that preserve high-frequency structures, maintain sparse coverage in low-frequency regions, and down-weight redundant cross-view observations. (C) Budget-Conditioned Feature Modulation injects the user-specified preservation ratio 𝜌 into the base Gaussian features before parameter prediction, allowing the predicted opacity and Gaussian attributes to adapt to the requested budget. (D) Coverage-Aware Budget Selection combines patch-wise pre-selection, view-wise global opacity ranking, and 3D redundancy suppression to retain a compact and spatially distributed Gaussian representation. A single trained model supports arbitrary test-time preservation ratios 𝜌 ∈ (0, 1] without retraining.

papers.abstract: Radiologists interpret computed tomography (CT) scans by jointly determining what a finding represents and where it lies in three-dimensional (3D) anatomy. However, CT models have treated CT interpretation and 3D segmentation as separate tasks, leaving textual findings spatially unverifiable and overlooking potential synergy between clinical understanding and spatial perception. Here we present HoloCT, a generalist 3D foundation model unifying CT interpretation and voxel-level segmentation by jointly modelling whole-volume context and fine-grained anatomical detail, providing 3D masks as evidence. We curated HoloDATA, comprising 195,921 CT scans from 73 public datasets and six clinical cohorts, with 6.2 million instruction dialogues and 2.8 million CT-mask pairs. Across 346 tasks spanning segmentation, lesion screening, visual question answering, and report generation on 61 internal and 12 external datasets, HoloCT outperformed specialist and foundation models. In multicentre validation across 11,455 clinical CT scans from five hospitals, HoloCT outperformed competing models in lesion segmentation and report generation by 18.2 and 15.3 points. It also achieved 85.1% mean accuracy in screening thyroid tumours and colon lesions, exceeding all four participating radiologists in a retrospective reader study. Further analyses revealed bidirectional semantic-spatial synergy: language-guided segmentation delineated unseen anatomical structures and lesions as well as diffuse free-text findings, outperforming the leading approach by 22.1 points, whereas prompting the model to generate corresponding 3D masks alongside its textual outputs significantly improved interpretation performance. HoloCT shows that clinical understanding and spatial perception can be learned together within a single foundation model and offers a path towards more accurate and reliable CT analysis.
authors: Yulu Xie, Zilong Li, Shen Xu, Yifan Bai, Liuhong Shi, Jiao Chen, Xianglei Kong, Wenchao Zhu, Na Shen, Xianghua Ye, Yang Yan, Jiaju Zheng, Yunsong Peng, Yanzhou Su, Chaohui Yu, Hao Luo, Fan Wang

Uses whole-volume context and fine-grained anatomical detail, trained with large-scale CT scans, instruction dialogues, and CT-mask pairs.

Reported strong gains in multicentre validation, including 18.2-point improvement in lesion segmentation and 15.3-point improvement in report generation.
Shows bidirectional semantic–spatial synergy: language improves segmentation, while generated masks improve interpretation.

papers.tldr: HoloCT unifies 3D CT interpretation with voxel-level segmentation, using spatial masks to make findings verifiable and improving performance across diverse clinical tasks.

papers.abstract: Loop closure detection conventionally cascades separate models for global retrieval, geometric verification, and relative pose estimation, leading to redundant computation and disconnected visual representations. We propose UniLoop, a unified framework that reuses the hierarchical representations of the pretrained geometric foundation model throughout this pipeline. A shared image encoder produces features for compact global descriptors; the same features are passed to the cross-view decoder for pairwise verification; and the original geometric predictions provide relative camera constraints for pose-graph optimization. Experiments on place recognition, loop verification, and relative pose estimation show that UniLoop improves loop-closure robustness and accuracy while reducing redundant backbone computation relative to modular pipelines. UniLoop achieves the best Recall@10 on MSLS (96.6) and Pitts30k (99.3) among the compared methods, while its verification branch reaches 95.63 AP and 96.29 ROC-AUC, surpassing the existing geometric verification baselines.
authors: Jingwen Yu, Pengyu Wang, Jin Wu, Weinan Chen, Ping Tan, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency and disconnected representations of cascaded loop-closure pipelines.
Uses a shared image encoder for global descriptors, cross-view verification, and geometric pose constraints.
Supports pose-graph optimization through relative camera predictions from the geometric model.
Reports Recall@10 of 96.6 on MSLS and 99.3 on Pitts30k.
Verification achieves 95.63 AP and 96.29 ROC-AUC, outperforming the cited geometric verification baselines.

The SALAD head aggregates the resulting single-view tokens into normalized global descriptors gi and gj for candidate retrieval. For each shortlisted pair, the same tokens are passed to the cross-view decoder to obtain pair-conditioned features. A lightweight verification head predicts the loop probability ploopij , while the retained MASt3R’s camera and pointmap heads recover the geometry used to construct relative-pose constraints for pose-graph optimization. Blue and green denote the two input views and their corresponding feature streams.

papers.title: UniLoop: Unified Loop Closure Detection from Retrieval to Geometric Verification and Relative Pose Estimation
papers.tldr: UniLoop unifies retrieval, geometric verification, and relative pose estimation by reusing representations from a pretrained geometric foundation model, improving accuracy while reducing redundant computation.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward geometric foundation models enable dense monocular reconstruction without requiring camera calibration, but independently reconstructed submaps can accumulate scale drift, and even a valid revisit can yield an inconsistent cross-submap measurement. We extend VGGT-SLAM 2.0 with fixed-root scale anchoring and short-sequence-assisted direct loop connections. SALAD selects an image pair between the initial submap and each eligible new submap; joint VGGT inference then uses learned implicit semantic-geometric cues to supply a scale-only anchor while preserving the original overlap chain. For loop closure, neighboring image pairs support a consistency check and translation-scale alignment. Each accepted candidate contributes one robust Sim(3) factor between existing center-frame nodes, without an auxiliary loop submap. A 17-sequence comparison lowers mean Sim(3) ATE on nine TUM sequences from 0.1018 to 0.0451 m relative to the VGGT-SLAM 2.0 baseline. Anchoring improves all seven no-loop module ablations. On three Clio scenes, a fixed-loop comparison favors the direct connection pipeline over the tested auxiliary-submap pipeline. A separate candidate audit exposes additional rejections of visually overlapping pairs by the short-sequence check. These comparisons distinguish the gains from long-range scale anchoring and loop connection choices from the limitations of candidate verification.
authors: Ziyi Jin, Kangjin Yu, Beichen Wang, Can Jiang, Zhongpu Xia, Jie Xu
bullets: Addresses scale drift across independently reconstructed submaps and inconsistent measurements during revisits.
Uses fixed-root scale anchoring: selected cross-submap image pairs provide a scale-only constraint through joint VGGT inference while preserving overlap chains.
Uses neighboring image pairs to verify loop consistency and align translation scale, adding robust Sim(3) factors without an auxiliary loop submap.
On nine TUM sequences, mean Sim(3) ATE decreases from 0.1018 m to 0.0451 m versus VGGT-SLAM 2.0; anchoring helps all seven no-loop ablations.
Candidate verification can reject visually overlapping pairs, indicating a scope or limitation of the short-sequence consistency check.

papers.title: Scale Anchoring via Implicit Semantics and Sequence-Consistent Loop Closure for VGGT-Based SLAM

papers.abstract: Monocular 3D object detection offers a low-cost route to 3D perception, but it remains fundamentally ill-posed, since depth must be inferred from a single view. Recent transformer-based detectors learn geometry purely from image features and 3D box annotations, lacking the high-level semantic priors that vision-language models (VLMs) acquire from large-scale pretraining. VLMs offer such priors, but deploying one directly as a detector is impractical due to its heavy inference cost. We propose MonoLaDN, a language-guided denoising framework that transfers the geometric reasoning of a VLM into a monocular 3D detector while keeping the deployed model purely vision-based. During training, a frozen VLM produces structured reasoning about each object's occlusion, depth, dimension, and angle from the image and its ground-truth boxes. We encode this reasoning into queries, perturb them with noise, and train the detector to reconstruct the clean reasoning. Reconstructing the corrupted reasoning forces the detector's depth-guided features to internalize the VLM's geometric priors, so this knowledge remains available even after the reasoning path is discarded at inference, adding no latency or parameters to the deployed model. Experiments on KITTI 3D and nuScenes show that MonoLaDN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art detectors and generalizes well to new domains.
authors: Kiet Dang Vu, Cao Le Minh Khoa, Nguyen Viet Tri Pham, An Nguyen Gia, Tam Le Thuc Ho, Duc Dung Nguyen
bullets: Addresses the ill-posed depth estimation problem in monocular 3D detection.
Uses a frozen VLM during training to reason about object occlusion, depth, dimensions, and angles.
Encodes and noise-perturbs this reasoning, training the detector to reconstruct the clean version and absorb geometric priors.
Discards the reasoning pathway at inference, so the deployed detector remains purely vision-based with no added latency or parameters.
Experiments on KITTI 3D and nuScenes report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art detectors and strong cross-domain generalization.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of MonoLaDN. During training, a 3D Reasoning Generation stage queries a frozen VLM with the image and ground-truth 3D boxes to produce structured reasoning about each object’s occlusion, depth, dimension, and angle. A text encoder and noise injector turn this reasoning into perturbed queries, decoded jointly with the N learnable object queries under a Language-Guided Mask and trained to reconstruct the clean attributes, alongside the detection loss. At inference, the reasoning path is discarded, leaving a purely vision-based detector with no added cost.

Fig. 1: Comparison of paradigms for monocular 3D detection. (a) VLM-based methods carry rich semantic and geometric priors but are too costly for real-time inference. (b) Traditional vision-only detectors are efficient yet lack such priors, learning geometry only from image features and box annotations. (c) Our MonoLaDN injects VLM-derived 3D reasoning into a depth-guided detector during training, so it gains these priors while keeping a vision-only, efficient model at inference.

Fig. 5: Qualitative results on KITTI val set. (a) MonoDETR [45]. (b) MonoDGP [26]. (c) MonoLaDN (Ours). For each image set, the top row presents the camera-view visualization, while the bottom row offers the corresponding bird’s-eye view. Ground-truth bounding boxes are rendered in green, and predictions are shown in order: red, yellow, blue. We also circle some objects to highlight the difference between other state-of-the-art methods and our method.

Fig. 5: Additional qualitative results on KITTI val set. (a) MonoDETR [45]. (b) MonoDGP [26]. (c) MonoLaDN (Ours). For each image set, the top row presents the camera-view visualization, while the bottom row offers the corresponding bird’s-eye view. Ground-truth bounding boxes are rendered in green, and predictions are shown in order: red, yellow, blue. We also circle some objects to highlight the difference between other state-of-the-art methods and our method.

Fig. 4: Object reconstruction heads. Each attribute output Êa is decoded into the box component it reasons about. The occlusion output Êocc has no box target of its own and is broadcast as shared visibility context (dashed) to the dimension, depth, and angle heads. When a head takes more than one embedding, the inputs are averaged before the head; the 2D center head uses the mean of all four outputs. The reconstructed components are supervised by the same 2D and 3D objectives as the detection loss.

Fig. 3: 3D Reasoning Generation. The object-centric visual input and a geometryto-language mapping are fed to a frozen VLM. The mapping discretizes each attribute into an ordinal label: depth by distance binning, angle by viewpoint sectoring, dimension by shape-archetype matching, and occlusion by combining truncation and occlusion flags. The VLM then produces structured reasoning per attribute.

Fig. 2: Decoder self-attention under the Language-Guided Mask on the KITTI val set. Each row is one scene. The left column shows the image with all projected ground-truth 3D boxes (the target object in orange, others in green) and the generated reasoning for its four attributes. The right column shows the decoder self-attention matrix over the W = 4M + N queries, ordered as the 4M reasoning queries followed by the N = 50 learnable queries; the red lines separate the two groups and the thin gray lines delimit the four-attribute block of each object.

Fig. 1: Deformable cross-attention of the reasoning queries on the KITTI val set. Each row is one object, and the four columns show the occlusion, depth, dimension, and angle reasoning queries. For each query, we accumulate its deformable sampling locations at the final decoder layer, weighted by the corresponding attention weights, into a Gaussian heatmap overlaid on the image (red high, blue low). The target object is marked in green, and the generated reasoning for each attribute is shown beneath its column.

Fig. 3: Designs of the language-guided attention mask. Black entries are blocked and white entries are permitted. The leakage-prevention mask Alp stops the learnable queries from attending to any reasoning query. The separated-reasoning mask Asr lets each reasoning query attend to all reasoning queries of the same object and to those of the same attribute across objects. The attribute-isolated mask Aai is a stricter variant that additionally blocks different attributes of the same object from attending to each other.

Fig. 4: Strategies for forming the perturbed queries. All three start from the ground-truth 3D boxes and end with perturbed queries, but inject noise at different stages. BBox perturbation perturbs the boxes before the VLM, so the reasoning is generated from corrupted geometry. Reasoning perturbation generates clean reasoning and then applies text augmentation to the reasoning text before encoding. Embedding perturbation (ours) encodes the clean reasoning and injects learned noise in the embedding space.

Table 2: Comparison on the KITTI test set for the pedestrian and cyclist categories at IoU = 0.5, reporting AP3D|R40. Best in bold.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) becomes increasingly difficult to scale to long multi-view sequences. Anchor-based compression methods such as ZPressor alleviate representation growth by decoding Gaussians only from a compact set of anchor feature maps, but keeping these anchors fixed forces each one to aggregate an increasing number of support views. We identify this representation--fusion mismatch and introduce \textbf{CrossPressor}, a training-free method for scalable anchor-based fusion. CrossPressor preserves all decoder-facing anchor queries while constraining the view-growing support sequence through coverage-cycled evidence routing, distributing retained spatial evidence across support views and fusion layers while keeping all support views represented. Routing before K/V projection, together with joint context packing, further reduces support-side fusion cost without retraining. CrossPressor maintains reconstruction quality close to dense fusion while achieving up to $26.12\times$ faster cross-view fusion and $1.43\times$ end-to-end acceleration on long input sequences. Our project page is at: https://yuhsihu.github.io/CrossPressor.
authors: Yuxi Hu, Wenhao Dong, Jun Zhang, Friedrich Fraundorfer
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between fixed anchor representations and growing multi-view support sequences.
Routes spatial evidence across support views and fusion layers using coverage-cycled evidence routing.
Retains all decoder-facing anchor queries while reducing support-side fusion cost through pre-projection routing and joint context packing.
Achieves up to 26.12× faster cross-view fusion and 1.43× end-to-end acceleration without retraining.
Maintains reconstruction quality close to dense fusion on long input sequences.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of CrossPressor. We keep the original ZPressor [25] pipeline unchanged, including anchor selection, anchor–support grouping, the anchor-query pathway, and the downstream prediction modules. One representative anchor–support group is expanded to compare the fusion stage. The original dense fusion (top) uses all support features as K/V evidence for cross-attention, whereas CrossPressor (bottom) preserves the full anchor-query pathway and routes only the support-side features before K/V projection. For cluster stride sc, the sc × sc grid enumerates the s2c possible spatial sampling offsets. We index the offset assigned to support view v at fusion layer ℓ by pℓc,v = (rc(v) + κℓ) mod s2c , where rc(v) is the support-view rank and κ is the layer-wise increment. Moving across support views advances the sampling pattern by one offset, while moving across fusion layers advances it by κ, distributing the retained spatial evidence across both dimensions. The selected support features are gathered and packed into a compact sequence before the original K/V projection and cross-attention, producing the same updated-anchor interface for the unchanged downstream prediction pipeline.

Figure 1. Representation–fusion mismatch and CrossPressor. ZPressor [25] bounds the decoder-facing representation by decoding Gaussians only from a compact set of anchor feature maps. As more context views are assigned to these anchors, the dense support features used to construct each anchor continue to grow. CrossPressor keeps the anchor representation unchanged while routing a bounded support sequence across cameras and spatial locations, with spatial sampling offsets varied across fusion layers. Gray tokens denote dense support evidence, while green tokens indicate routed evidence from different support views.

Figure 3. Runtime scaling on MVSplat–ZPressor. As the number of context views increases, dense cross-view fusion becomes progressively more expensive, whereas CrossPressor remains nearly flat. The resulting end-to-end speedup reaches 1.43× at 256 views.

As the number of context views increases, dense fusion memory grows steadily, whereas the fusion-only incremental peak of CrossPressor remains nearly flat. papers.selection_reason: Introduces CrossPressor, a training-free method for scalable cross-view fusion in 3D Gaussian Splatting, addressing representation growth and fusion speed.
papers.title: CrossPressor: Scalable Cross-View Fusion for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting

papers.abstract: We present the Rohbau3D-Semantics dataset, which adds dense semantic and instance-level labels to laser scans of the previously released Rohbau3D domain data from shell construction sites. The dataset comprises 504 point cloud scenes from 14 survey sites, each captured with a terrestrial laser scanner and stored in a scanner-centered local coordinate system. Unlike point clouds sampled from reconstructed meshes or synthetic building models, the data preserve the characteristic properties of real laser scanning, including non-uniform sampling, measurement artifacts, reflections, and fine geometric detail. Combined with manual labels, expert oversight during pointwise annotation, and full-scene review, this yields a high-quality benchmark for semantic scene understanding in complex built environments. The dataset includes 17 class labels of building components and one background class, along with instance annotations for object-level analysis. In addition to the 3D point clouds, the release also provides scripts for deriving geometrically aligned panoramic and cube-map representations of color, LiDAR reflection intensity, depth, surface normals, semantic labels, and instance labels from the 3D arrays. We describe the acquisition pipeline, annotation protocol, quality-control process, and panorama-generation procedure, and provide benchmark splits and baseline experiments for semantic segmentation. By combining precise terrestrial laser scans, dense annotations, and a wide variety of shell-construction scenes, Rohbau3D-Semantics bridges the gap among synthetic indoor datasets, mesh-derived benchmarks, and smaller construction-specific resources. The dataset is intended to support research on 3D scene understanding, construction-site analytics, and multimodal scene analysis in the built environment. Access and download the full dataset via https://github.com/RauchLukas/rohbau3d

Includes scripts for aligned panoramic and cube-map views of color, intensity, depth, normals, semantic labels, and instance labels.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity 3D geometry generation requires maintaining global structural coherence alongside fine-grained surface details. While recent coarse-to-fine frameworks leverage Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) to condition local queries, we reveal a critical training-inference resolution discrepancy: coordinate guidance and geometric supervision are aligned during training, whereas inference decodes high-resolution geometry from coarse spatial coordinates. This mismatch introduces a severe distribution shift that degrades fine details. To overcome this, we propose Resolution-Decoupled Training (RDT), which anchors RoPE guidance at 512 resolution while supervising geometry at 1536, enabling robust detail extrapolation. Additionally, to eliminate high-resolution data bottlenecks, we present Dual3D-300K, a large-scale paired dataset comprising 300K watertight 3D point clouds explicitly aligned across 512 and 1536 resolutions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RDT substantially improves sharp geometric regions, while Dual3D-300K offers a scalable benchmark for high-resolution 3D generation.
authors: Jiale Zhang, Yang Liu, Chengyang Li, Jin Yuan, Qianxi Jia, Taicheng Huang
bullets: Identifies a training–inference resolution discrepancy that causes distribution shift and loss of fine surface details.
Uses Resolution-Decoupled Training (RDT): RoPE guidance at 512 resolution with geometry supervision at 1536 resolution.
Introduces Dual3D-300K, a paired dataset of 300K watertight point clouds aligned across 512 and 1536 resolutions.
Experiments show improved generation of sharp geometric regions and provide a scalable benchmark for high-resolution 3D generation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed RDT-3D framework. Training (Left): RDT-3D decouples spatial guidance from geometric supervision. Coarse point clouds (5123) provide spatial query locations injected into the DiT via ROPE, while fine point clouds (15363) are encoded into high-resolution GT shape latents for diffusion training. Inference (Right): Spatial queries sampled from a coarse mesh guide the trained DiT to generate fine shape latents, which are subsequently decoded into a high-fidelity 3D mesh via Marching Cubes.
Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison with state-of-the-art methods. Compared to existing approaches, our method captures significantly finer geometric details and produces sharper surface reconstructions.
Fig. 4: Qualitative comparison for ablation study. RDT recovers sharper edges and thinner structures.

papers.title: RDT-3D: Resolution-Decoupled Training for High-Fidelity 3D Geometry Generation
papers.tldr: RDT-3D addresses resolution mismatch in coarse-to-fine 3D generation by training coarse spatial guidance with high-resolution geometric supervision.

papers.abstract: While single-image 3D texture generation has advanced significantly, conditioning texture synthesis on multi-view reference images remains largely under-explored, despite its necessity for resolving surface ambiguity in unobserved regions. In this paper, we propose RouTex, a novel multi-reference 3D texture generation framework based on in-context Diffusion Transformers (DiT). Our key insight is that native 3D Rotary Position Encoding (RoPE) inherently possesses spatial addressing capabilities. We introduce Positional Routing (PR) to reprogram 3D RoPE along spatial and semantic dimensions, establishing explicit reference-to-view correspondence without introducing additional parameters. To execute this routing efficiently, Dual-Granularity Attention (DGA) combines per-view local attention for fine texture fidelity with global joint attention over deduplicated references for cross-view consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RouTex achieves new state-of-the-art performance in multi-reference 3D texture generation.
authors: Chengyang Li, Yang Liu, Jiale Zhang, Qiang Rao, Wei Zhang, Taicheng Huang
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in unseen surfaces that single-image texture generation cannot resolve.
Introduces Positional Routing to reprogram native 3D RoPE without adding parameters.
Uses Dual-Granularity Attention: local per-view attention for texture detail and global attention for cross-view consistency.
Experiments show state-of-the-art performance in multi-reference 3D texture generation.

papers.abstract: A 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction inherits arbitrary units from structure-from-motion, so it cannot be measured or used to place AR content until someone supplies a scale. Both standard recipes are fragile on real captures: on five indoor scenes with tape-measured ceilings, a quantile floor-to-ceiling heuristic errs by 27% and metric-depth alignment by 35-71% across three networks. We present METRIC-GS, a selective scale estimator for real indoor photographs: it reads the scale off the reconstruction's own semantic content and, just as importantly, refuses when the evidence is thin. A frozen 2D teacher labels Gaussians by visibility-aware voting; instance-level size priors for architectural and furniture classes (doors, tables, the floor-to-ceiling gap) are fused by a robust maximum-likelihood step; and an inlier-mass test turns thin evidence into an explicit abstention that doubles as a router to a heavyweight metric model. On 47 ScanNet++ scenes with laser ground truth, with a configuration frozen before public evaluation, the estimator alone cuts the heuristic's mean error from 21.1% to 16.6% (9.3% on the 28 scenes it acts on) at ~11 s per scene. MASt3R remains the more accurate standalone estimator (9.9%), but routing only our refusals to it matches running it everywhere with 60% fewer invocations; this selective hybrid is the configuration we advocate. Visibility-aware voting raises the scenes the estimator can act on from 16 to 28 at unchanged deployed accuracy. Applied unchanged to 13 phone and drone captures of our own, on which MASt3R fails its own registration gate 12 times, the system improves all five captures it acts on and degrades none. We also report that a current feed-forward metric model scores 2.3% on a benchmark inside its training mixture and 28-35% on captures it has never seen: a published metric-scale number is a best case, not a deployment estimate.
bullets: Addresses the arbitrary scale of structure-from-motion reconstructions, which limits measurement and AR placement.
Uses visibility-aware semantic voting, architectural and furniture size priors, robust maximum-likelihood fusion, and an inlier-mass abstention test.
On 47 ScanNet++ scenes, reduces mean heuristic scale error from 21.1% to 16.6% overall and 9.3% on scenes where it acts, at about 11 seconds per scene.
Routing only abstentions to MASt3R matches running MASt3R everywhere while invoking it 60% less often.
Visibility-aware voting increases actionable scenes from 16 to 28; results also show strong variation in metric-model performance across seen and unseen captures.

papers.selection_reason: Metric-scale estimation for 3D Gaussian splatting is a 3D vision method for recovering real-world geometry from reconstructed scenes.
papers.title: METRIC-GS: Selective Metric-Scale Estimation for 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: METRIC-GS estimates metric scale directly from semantic content in 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructions and abstains when evidence is insufficient, enabling efficient routing to a stronger metric model.

papers.abstract: Humans can easily recognize the same objects across different viewpoints of a 3D scene, whereas teaching models such multi-view-consistent perception typically requires videos or calibrated multi-view captures, which are considerably more expensive and less diverse than large-scale monocular data.~In this paper, we introduce Feature Puzzles, a novel framework for learning multi-view-consistent segmentation using only single-image semantic segmentation supervision. Specifically, we propose a simple yet effective pipeline that constructs multi-view-consistent segmentation pseudo-labels through image cropping and geometric transformations. We further introduce a lightweight, plug-and-play network that leverages the multi-view-consistent image features learned by existing pretrained 3D foundation models and the generated pseudo-labels to perform multi-view-consistent segmentation. Importantly, our flexible framework supports various types of prompts provided from one or multiple views and can be readily extended to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation. Under this single-image supervision, our feed-forward model achieves the best mIoU on NVOS, remains competitive on SPIn-NeRF and ScanNet++ against baselines using per-scene optimization or in-domain multi-view training, and demonstrates zero-shot transfer to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation. Visual comparisons are available on our project page: https://featurepuzzles.github.io/
authors: Jiahao Ma, Qiang Zhang, Miaomiao Liu, David Ahmedt-Aristizabal, Chuong Nguyen
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited diversity of video or calibrated multi-view supervision.
Builds multi-view-consistent segmentation pseudo-labels through image cropping and geometric transformations.
Adds a lightweight, plug-and-play feed-forward network using pretrained 3D foundation-model features.
Supports prompts from one or multiple views and can extend to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation.
Achieves the best mIoU on NVOS, remains competitive on SPIn-NeRF and ScanNet++, and transfers zero-shot to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation.

papers.selection_reason: Single-image-supervised multi-view 3D-aware segmentation built on pretrained 3D features, with strong spatial-intelligence and 3D vision relevance.
papers.title: Feature Puzzles: Single-Image Supervision for Multi-View 3D-Aware Segmentation
papers.tldr: Feature Puzzles learns multi-view-consistent and open-vocabulary 3D segmentation from only single-image semantic labels by generating geometric pseudo-labels and exploiting pretrained 3D features.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting is prone to overfitting because limited observations leave many Gaussian primitives weakly constrained, yet their contributions are still accumulated through alpha blending. Without uncertainty estimation, the renderer cannot distinguish unreliable primitives from well-constrained ones, allowing their erroneous contributions to corrupt novel-view synthesis. We introduce UGOD, an uncertainty-guided framework that estimates a view-dependent uncertainty score for each Gaussian and uses it to regulate its rendering contribution. A lightweight uncertainty head conditioned on Gaussian attributes and viewing direction predicts this score, which then drives a differentiable opacity-modulation mechanism that attenuates high-uncertainty primitives before compositing. During training, a detached soft-dropout branch applies an uncertainty-controlled continuous keep mask to discourage the model from relying on poorly constrained Gaussians and thereby reduce overfitting. Crucially, detaching the uncertainty score prevents gradients from this stochastic regulariser from biasing or collapsing the uncertainty prediction. Experiments on Mip-NeRF~360 and LLFF show that UGOD improves sparse-view novel-view synthesis while producing more compact Gaussian representations than the compared methods. These results demonstrate that Gaussian uncertainty provides an effective rendering-time control for sparse-view reconstruction.
bullets: Sparse observations leave many Gaussian primitives weakly constrained, causing erroneous contributions during alpha blending.
A lightweight uncertainty head predicts uncertainty from Gaussian attributes and viewing direction.
Differentiable opacity modulation attenuates high-uncertainty Gaussians before compositing.
Detached uncertainty-controlled soft dropout regularizes training without biasing or collapsing uncertainty estimates.
Experiments on Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF report improved sparse-view novel-view synthesis and more compact representations than compared methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of UGOD. Sparse input views are reconstructed by SfM and initialise 3D Gaussian primitives (left). For each visible Gaussian, the uncertainty head combines the viewing direction, HashGrid position encoding, geometric attributes, and compressed SH appearance to predict a view-dependent uncertainty ui (lower left). This score drives two gradient-decoupled mechanisms (centre): normalised uncertainty differentiably gates opacity before compositing, whereas its detached copy determines the training-only Concrete soft-dropout probability. The resulting Gaussians are jointly optimised using supervised depth, pseudo-view depth, and photometric losses (right). At inference, soft dropout and relative-uncertainty gating are disabled, and deterministic raw-uncertainty opacity modulation is used.
Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison on MiP-NeRF 360 (24/8 views) and LLFF (3 views). Each non-GT panel reports the displayed-view PSNR and final Gaussian count.
Fig. 5: Photometric residuals for 3DGS*, DropGS, and FSGS, and UGOD’s predicted uncertainty. Rows show MiP-NeRF 360 bonsai (24 views) and LLFF horns and fern (3 views).
Fig. 1: Average PSNR and final-Gaussian reduction versus 3DGS* across MiPNeRF 360 (24/8 views) and LLFF (3 views). Higher is better on every axis; UGOD leads all six.

papers.selection_reason: Sparse-view 3D Gaussian splatting with uncertainty-guided opacity/dropout; fits 3D scene generation interest.
papers.title: UGOD: Uncertainty-Guided Opacity and Dropout for Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: UGOD estimates per-Gaussian, view-dependent uncertainty to suppress unreliable primitives and reduce overfitting in sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting.

papers.abstract: Super-resolution and quality enhancement of 1.5\,T brain MRI are normally validated with image-fidelity metrics, although their purpose is to improve downstream analysis. We study whether enhancement improves tissue segmentation, and for which segmenters. We propose an unpaired, physics-guided training pipeline for a lightweight ($\le$2.5\,M parameter) recurrent convolutional enhancer: a six-module stochastic 1.5\,T degradation operator, a residual adversarial network that adds scanner-specific texture without moving anatomy, and a cycle-consistent objective with an anti-identity penalty that rules out the copy solution. We then train U-Net, Swin-UNet and wavelet token-mixing segmenters \citep{jeevan2023wavemix} from scratch on either raw or enhanced 1.5\,T images of the same subjects, using identical labels and subject-level splits, for three enhancer variants and two datasets. On ABIDE (41 held-out subjects, FreeSurfer labels) enhancement significantly improves the wavelet segmenter (mean Dice $+0.014$, Wilcoxon $p=3.5\times10^{-5}$; CSF $+0.018$, grey matter $+0.013$), significantly degrades the U-Net ($-0.008$, $p=5.1\times10^{-4}$) and leaves Swin-UNet unchanged. On IXI, whose labels come from FSL-FAST, enhancement lowers Dice for all nine pairings, almost entirely through CSF; we trace this to spatially implausible CSF voxels in the labels that penalise smoother predictions. Enhancement of low-field MRI should therefore be validated per downstream model and against reliable labels.
bullets: The study evaluates enhancement by downstream segmentation rather than image-fidelity metrics alone.
It uses an unpaired, physics-guided pipeline with a lightweight recurrent convolutional enhancer, stochastic degradation, scanner-texture modeling, and cycle-consistent training.
On ABIDE, enhancement improved WaveMix segmentation, degraded U-Net, and did not change Swin-UNet performance.
On IXI, enhancement reduced Dice for all tested segmenter–enhancer pairings, mainly because of implausible CSF labels.
Results support validating MRI enhancement per downstream model and against reliable annotations.

The output has the same resolution as the input (scale = 1: quality enhancement, not spatial upscaling). Dashed orange: cycle-A re-degradation consistency. Bottom: a frozen 3T-trained segmentation backbone provides the downstream Dice evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a physics-guided training pipeline for MRI super-resolution and evaluates its impact on downstream task-aware segmentation.
papers.title: MRI Super-Resolution with RCDM/WaveMix and Task-Aware Segmentation
papers.tldr: Enhancing 1.5T brain MRI can help, hurt, or have no effect on tissue segmentation depending on the segmenter and label quality.

papers.abstract: The release of SAM 3D Body is a recent development in human mesh recovery, demonstrating improved performance in producing clean, topologically coherent meshes from single images. By leveraging the Momentum Human Rig (MHR), it achieves robustness to occlusion and diverse poses. However, our evaluation reveals a specific and consistent limitation: the model struggles to reconstruct detailed anthropometric deviations, particularly in populations exhibiting distinctive morphological alterations such as geriatric muscle atrophy, scoliosis, or pregnancy, even when these features are prominent in the input image. In this paper, we investigate this phenomenon not as a failure of the model's capacity, but as a byproduct of the "perception-distortion trade-off". We posit that the architectural reliance on the low-dimensional parametric MHR representation, combined with semantic-invariant conditioning (DINOv3) and annotation-based alignment, creates a pervasive "regression to the mean" effect. We analyze these mechanisms to understand why individual biological details are smoothed out. Furthermore, we state our contributions by proposing specific, constructive pathways for future work, such as implicit-explicit hybrid representations and Medical-in-the-Loop alignment, to extend the baseline performance of SAM 3D Body into the high-precision medical domain.
authors: Aizierjiang Aiersilan, Ruting Cheng, James Hahn
bullets: Identifies consistent under-reconstruction of features such as geriatric muscle atrophy, scoliosis, and pregnancy-related morphology.
Attributes this to a perception–distortion trade-off and regression toward average body shapes.
Links the effect to the low-dimensional MHR representation, semantic-invariant DINOv3 conditioning, and annotation-based alignment.
Proposes implicit–explicit hybrid representations and Medical-in-the-Loop alignment as directions toward medical-grade fidelity.

The missing biological signature of each target population is highlighted by a red dashed bounding box, underscoring the systemic “regression to the mean.”

papers.selection_reason: Investigates limitations of a 3D human mesh recovery foundation model and proposes pathways for improving anthropometric fidelity.
papers.title: Investigating Anthropometric Fidelity in SAM 3D Body
papers.tldr: SAM 3D Body produces coherent human meshes but tends to smooth distinctive anthropometric features, limiting high-precision medical reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Accurately assessing the risk of cesarean section (CS) delivery is critical, especially in settings with limited medical resources, where access to healthcare is often restricted. Early and reliable risk prediction allows better-informed prenatal care decisions and can improve maternal and neonatal outcomes. However, most existing predictive models are tailored for in-hospital use during labor and rely on parameters that are often unavailable in resource-limited or home-based settings. In this study, we conduct a pilot investigation to examine the feasibility of using 3D body shape for CS risk assessment for future applications with more affordable general devices. We propose a novel multi-view-based Transformer network, MvBody, which predicts CS risk using only self-reported medical data and 3D optical body scans obtained between the 31st and 38th weeks of gestation. To enhance training efficiency and model generalizability in data-scarce environments, we incorporate a metric learning loss into the network. Compared to widely used machine learning models and the latest advanced 3D analysis methods, our method demonstrates superior performance, achieving an accuracy of 84.62% and an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.724 on the independent test set. To improve transparency and trust in the model's predictions, we apply the Integrated Gradients algorithm to provide theoretically grounded explanations of the model's decision-making process. Our results indicate that pre-pregnancy weight, maternal age, obstetric history, previous CS history, and body shape, particularly around the head and shoulders, are key contributors to CS risk prediction.
authors: Ruting Cheng, Boyuan Feng, Yijiang Zheng, Chuhui Qiu, Aizierjiang Aiersilan, Joaquin A. Calderon, Wentao Zhao, Qing Pan, James K. Hahn
bullets: Addresses the lack of accessible CS-risk models that work outside hospitals and during labor.
Introduces a multi-view Transformer combining medical data with 3D optical body scans from weeks 31–38 of gestation.
Uses metric-learning loss to improve training efficiency and generalizability in data-scarce settings.
Reports 84.62% accuracy and 0.724 AUC-ROC on an independent test set, outperforming compared methods.
Integrated Gradients highlights pre-pregnancy weight, maternal age, obstetric history, previous CS, and head/shoulder body shape as influential factors.

papers.selection_reason: Multi-view transformer on 3D body scans for medical prediction; relevant to 3D perception and geometry, though not a 3D foundation model.
papers.title: MvBody: Multi-View-Based Hybrid Transformer Using Optical 3D Body Scan for Explainable Cesarean Section Prediction

papers.abstract: Reliable evaluation of visual 3D reconstruction and depth estimation in vegetation-rich outdoor environments is limited by the scarcity of geometric ground-truth data and the cost of complete scanner surveys. We present a LiDARbased reference-generation pipeline for evaluating the zero-shot performance of feed-forward visual-geometry models alongside conventional structure-from-motion (SfM) methods. The pipeline reuses camera images, LiDAR scans, and reference poses from existing multi-sensor localization datasets to generate per-view depth maps and visible reference point clouds. To address visibility errors in accumulated LiDAR scans, we introduce the LargeDepth-Gap Visibility Score (LDGVS) for point-wise visibility filtering and automatic scale selection in Hidden Point Removal(HPR). Experiments on TartanAirV2 and TartanGround show that, compared with Poisson surface reconstruction, which is an approach suited to completed scan surveys, the combined HPR and LDGVS filtering retains approximately three times the point density at comparable absolute relative error. We also apply the pipeline to the BotanicGarden dataset to systematically compare depth estimation and 3D reconstruction methods. Feedforward methods produce dense depth predictions efficiently, but their 3D reconstructions can contain duplicated structures. Conventional SfM generally produces more coherent geometry, but its reconstructions remain sparse and more prone to failure in challenging vegetated scenes. The benchmark toolkit and datasets will be released.
authors: Zhipeng Zhong, Matthew Coombes, Cunjia Liu
bullets: Addresses the lack of geometric ground truth and high cost of complete scanner surveys in outdoor vegetation environments.
Combines camera images, LiDAR scans, and reference poses from existing multi-sensor datasets to produce depth maps and visible reference point clouds.
Introduces the LargeDepth-Gap Visibility Score (LDGVS) for filtering visibility errors and selecting Hidden Point Removal scales automatically.
On TartanAirV2 and TartanGround, HPR with LDGVS retains about three times the point density of Poisson reconstruction at comparable absolute relative error.
Finds feed-forward methods produce dense but sometimes duplicated geometry, while SfM yields more coherent yet sparse and failure-prone reconstructions.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Visualization of the reference data generated by the proposed pipeline in BotanicGarden. Top: the accumulated scene-level reference point cloud and the camera trajectory shown in red. The colored boxes indicate the two individual-view examples below. Bottom: for each example, the upper row shows the corresponding visibility-filtered point cloud in the camera frame, and the lower row shows the projected sparse reference depth image.

papers.abstract: Accurate vegetation-encroachment assessment and risk mitigation require electric utilities to accurately locate and characterize distribution-network assets, including poles and power lines, and distinguish among medium-voltage, low-voltage, neutral, and telecommunication lines. Mobile and aerial Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) point clouds provide detailed 3D representations of these assets and their surroundings. However, power-line detection and reconstruction remain challenging because conductor returns are often sparse, incomplete, noisy, or occluded by vegetation. These challenges are especially significant in distribution networks, where lower pole heights and complex line configurations place conductors close to trees. In addition, mobile and aerial LiDAR datasets differ substantially in point density, viewing geometry, spatial coverage, and occlusion patterns. We propose a robust and automated reconstruction method combining scaled density-based clustering, robust polynomial fitting, and iterative fragment merging to recover individual conductors under severe data incompleteness and occlusion. Following semantic classification, the same reconstruction pipeline processes both mobile and aerial LiDAR data without modality-specific code or parameter tuning. The method is evaluated through degradation experiments, benchmarking, parameter sensitivity analysis, and large-scale validation. On the aerial dataset, it achieves 96.87% precision, 96.66% recall, a 96.76% F$_1$-score, and a geometric RMSE of 0.127 m. On the mobile dataset, where conductor-level reference annotations were unavailable, it achieves a point-to-model RMSE of 0.045 m and a reconstruction coverage of 95.27%. Source code, documentation, and evaluation data are publicly available at https://github.com/varen-project.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity photovoltaic (PV) module mapping requires complete instance recovery and accurate delineation. Vision foundation models offer zero-shot segmentation, but converting incomplete and inconsistent predictions across views into a complete, geometrically accurate map of individual modules remains challenging. We propose the Multi-View PV Module Mapper (MV-PVMapper), a training-free framework coupling vision foundation models with unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) photogrammetry. First, Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) generates candidates from original images using text prompts. Their contours are then transferred into object space through per-module slope correction to limit distortion from surface-model noise, and verified against representative module dimensions to guide cross-view instance selection. Finally, accepted instances return to all covering images as box prompts for SAM~3, supplementing text prompts with spatial cues for iterative segmentation, verification and fusion. On five-direction surveys of three operational rooftop PV plants at approximately 1 cm nadir ground sampling distance, two feedback iterations recover 7,710 of 7,711 reference modules with no false positives at an intersection-over-union (IoU) matching threshold of 0.5. Macro-averaged area precision and recall reach 99.00 % and 98.52 %, respectively. Averaged across sites, the aggregated Jaccard index reaches 97.55 %, compared with 60.73 % and 41.24 % for orthomosaic segmentation and multi-view pixel-voting baselines, respectively; average precision at the stricter IoU threshold of 0.95 reaches 95.67 %. Ablation studies show that module-size constraints are critical for instance separation, while slope correction and feedback to all covering views improve boundary accuracy. These results are achieved without task-specific image annotation or segmentation-model weight updates.

papers.abstract: Vertical forest structure influences fire behavior by regulating understory-to-canopy fuel connectivity, yet operational fuel-type models represent this complexity through discrete classes that only indirectly capture vertical continuity. High-density point clouds offer an opportunity to characterize vertical fuel connectivity in a more explicit and continuous manner, but specific methodological approaches are still required. We applied Gaussian decomposition to vertical height profiles derived from terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) point clouds across 25 permanent forest plots to characterize geometric vertical fuel continuity. A multiscale analysis spanning from the plot scale to ~0.5 $m^2$ units was used to evaluate geometric, probabilistic, and overlap metrics for characterizing fuel strata. The method reproduced the vertical transition between shrub and tree strata, with median Pearson correlations ranging from 0.83 to 0.96 across analysis levels. Probability density overlap metrics and separability indicators, such as the Jeffries-Matusita distance, provided complementary descriptors of vertical continuity. Intermediate spatial scales (3-6 m cells) provided a useful compromise between spatial detail and the consistent representation of shrub-canopy interaction patterns. Finer scales increased variability due to point density reduction and profile irregularity, and low mean squared error values were found insufficient as sole performance indicators. Gaussian decomposition applied to TLS point clouds enables explicit quantification of vertical fuel continuity, a limitation of current discrete classification systems. Continuous vertical connectivity metrics derived from this approach offer a pathway for improving ladder fuel characterization and strengthening decision-making support in wildfire risk assessment.
authors: Jes\'us Torralba, Luis \'A. Ruiz, Pablo Crespo-Peremarch, Marina Sim\'o-Mart\'i, Juan Pedro Carbonell-Rivera

papers.abstract: We introduce iMED, the first synchronized multi-endoscope dataset for robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS), designed to address a fundamental limitation in surgical vision benchmarking: the absence of independent held-out viewpoints. Existing surgical datasets capture single-trajectory sequences from a single endoscope, making it impossible to distinguish geometric generalization from photometric interpolation along a narrow forward-facing path. iMED provides 340 sequences ~170K synchronized timepoints with 4 views per timepoint) recorded simultaneously from two independent stereo endoscopes across ex vivo, postmortem, and live surgical settings, spanning 14 specimens with diverse anatomical regions and motion regimes. The dataset includes calibrated camera intrinsics, ArUco-based frame-wise pose estimates with uncertainty quantification, instrument segmentation masks, and rich clinical metadata. Using a train-on-one-endoscope, test-on-another evaluation protocol, we benchmark 23 state-of-the-art methods across rigid and deformable novel view synthesis, pose estimation, feature matching, and monocular depth estimation. Our experiments show that methods relying primarily on photometric supervision degrade substantially under this held-out-endoscope setting, while methods with explicit geometric regularization are more robust across views in our benchmark. Notably, large-scale foundation models transfer surprisingly well to surgical imagery, often outperforming domain-specific models, suggesting pitfalls in current fine-tuning protocols. iMED establishes a new evaluation protocol for geometric generalization in surgical vision.

papers.abstract: Spatiotemporal scene reconstruction with Dynamic Gaussian Splatting (DGS) fundamentally depends on perfect temporal synchronization across all cameras, an assumption rarely achievable in practice. Industry-standard synchronization requires expensive specialized hardware and complex setup, while data-driven alternatives including audio-based alignment, geometry matching, and pose tracking remain limited by restrictive environmental or scene-specific assumptions. To overcome these limitations, we propose Phase-DGS, a framework that replaces conventional timestamps with a semantic phase representing each frame's inherent state within the underlying motion cycle. Frames capturing the same motion state share the same phase regardless of which camera records them or when, naturally establishing spatiotemporal correspondence across unsynchronized cameras. We validate Phase-DGS under temporal offsets, frame drops, and camera freezes, achieving up to +8.5 dB PSNR improvement over baselines while enabling seamless integration with existing DGS backbones including RealTime-4DGS and FreeTimeGS.
authors: Hosung Jeon, Jun Young Jeong, Sangwoon Kwak, Joonsoo Kim, Sangmin Kim, Jaesik Park, Won-Sik Cheong, Hyon-Gon Choo
bullets: Addresses the need for precise camera synchronization in Dynamic Gaussian Splatting.
Represents each frame by its state within an underlying motion cycle, enabling cross-camera correspondence despite timing differences.
Designed to handle temporal offsets, dropped frames, and camera freezes.
Integrates with existing DGS backbones, including RealTime-4DGS and FreeTimeGS.
Reports up to 8.5 dB PSNR improvement over baselines in the evaluated settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Training pipeline of Phase-DGS. Multi-view data provides camera parameters (view matrix, focal length, resolution) and an RGB image. The phase projector module predicts a phase value from the RGB image, replacing the timestamp input of the 4DGS backbone. The feature bank serves as a learnable reference repository that enforces cross-camera phase coherence, so that identical motion states share the same phase across all views. Training is guided by three losses: a Rendering loss between the rendered and input images, a monotonic loss, and a phase consistency loss.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison with enlarged views under the Synced condition. While baseline models exhibit ghosting and geometric distortion, Phase-DGS consistently reduces artifacts in rendered images. →: visual artifact.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison under the synchronized condition (Synced) and the unsynchronized condition (Shifted and Dropped) on Nvidia Dynamic Scene dataset and SelfCap datasets. Phase-DGS consistently produces cleaner renderings while baselines exhibit ghosting and geometric distortion.

Figure 1: Conceptual diagram of Phase-DGS. (a) In an unsynchronized multi-view dataset, images sharing the frame index are actually captured at different time instants. The proposed phase extraction module estimates an inherent semantic phase from each input image, which is then used to train 4DGS. (b) The graph shows the estimated phases across cameras. When a sequence is offset, the phase shifts along the x-axis direction; when frozen, the phase is predicted parallel to the x-axis; and when dropped, the phase is predicted parallel to the y-axis.

papers.abstract: We introduce BhopalMLS, a large-scale Mobile Laser Scanning (MLS) dataset from a dense, heterogeneous urban environment in Bhopal, India, with mixed traffic, informal structures, and narrow unplanned streets. It spans approximately 10 km of road corridors with over 1.2 billion points and 19,518 annotated instances across 62 fine-grained static categories, grouped into 12-class and 21-class benchmark taxonomies; 6 optional moving-class subclasses support dynamic-object analysis. Existing 3D datasets, collected in well-planned cities, are structurally more uniform than such unplanned settings, and lack their subtype diversity. On semantic and instance segmentation at both granularities, fine-tuned foundation models surpass supervised baselines: Utonia(L) reaches 71.28% mIoU (vs. PTv3's 68.04% from scratch) and 44.07% mAP50 on the 12-class benchmark. Cross-region experiments against four established datasets (Ke-MLS, Toronto-3D, Paris-Lille-3D, SemanticKITTI) reveal a consistent asymmetric transferability: models trained on BhopalMLS transfer better than the reverse on every pair, for both Utonia(L) and Concerto(L) (mean 21.5, up to 36 mIoU points), holding even when the target is denser. Factor-controlled retraining at a fixed label budget, repeated on both models, attributes this to the coverage of BhopalMLS's subtype inventory rather than to dataset size or corridor geometry: collapsing each class to a single subtype costs 13.0 and 13.3 mIoU points for Utonia(L) and Concerto(L). BhopalMLS therefore offers a testbed for 3D perception beyond well-planned cities. Data and an interactive viewer are at https://geoai4cities.github.io/bhopalmls.

Cross-region models trained on BhopalMLS transfer better than models trained on four established datasets, with gains attributed to subtype coverage.
Collapsing each class to one subtype reduces performance by 13.0–13.3 mIoU points, supporting the importance of fine-grained diversity.

papers.abstract: Coarse-to-fine image-to-point-cloud (I2P) registration risks discarding correct but ambiguous patch pairs, while retaining more candidates repeats fine matching over overlapping patches. SparseGraph-I2P aims to improve registration recall by increasing the inlier ratio at the pose solver, using sensor or monocular depth. A Coarse Hypothesis Graph combines appearance with depth-derived first- and second-order compatibility to select a fixed budget of patch pairs. Sparse Fine Matching decodes each queried pixel once and skips pixel--point comparisons covered by an ancestor patch paired with the same point-cloud region. With sensor depth, depth-aware filtering ranks correspondences by SC2 spectral support for a single EPnP solve. With monocular depth, depth or inverse depth is calibrated from correspondence geometry before filtering. SparseGraph-I2P achieves the highest registration recall and lowest latency among the compared methods on RGB-D Scenes V2 and 7-Scenes with sensor depth. With predicted depth, it retains the highest recall on RGB-D Scenes V2 at an additional calibration cost. Code will be released.

papers.abstract: 3D semantic scene completion plays a critical role in enabling various downstream tasks within autonomous systems by estimating both missing geometric structures and semantic information in scene data. In this work, we introduce a unique neural framework that integrates state space modeling with diffusion-based generative approaches to enhance 3D point cloud semantic scene completion. We propose \textit{MPath Mamba} diffusion network, leveraging a skip-triple Mamba structure, dimensional decomposition residuals, and multi-directional dilations within multi-path data to efficiently process long-sequence data for feature extraction. The proposed method operates in the conditioned latent space of a variational autoencoder, enhanced by a state-space mechanism to improve 3D point cloud representation and reconstruction. Extensive experiments conducted on the SemanticKITTI benchmark demonstrate that our approach achieves highly competitive performance for 3D point cloud semantic scene completion.
authors: Li Liang, Naveed Akhtar, Jordan Vice, Anwaar Ulhaq, Ajmal Saeed Mian
bullets: Targets 3D semantic scene completion for autonomous-system applications.
Uses a skip-triple Mamba structure, dimensional-decomposition residuals, and multi-directional dilations in a multi-path architecture.
Operates in a VAE-conditioned latent space to improve point-cloud representation and reconstruction.
Experiments on SemanticKITTI show highly competitive completion performance.
The abstract does not specify quantitative results or limitations.

The scene completion network operates within the latent space of a Variational Autoencoder (VAE), incorporating two conditioning sub-networks, Multi-Scale Fusion Blocks (MSFusion), and MPath Mamba diffusion denoising network. A modular segmentation network performs 3D semantic segmentation.
Fig. 2: MPath Mamba flow. Data is divided into multiple paths based on dilation rates, with each path providing three directional components as input to MPath Mamba.

papers.abstract: Online 3D Gaussian mapping enables fast and high-fidelity novel view synthesis, with broad applications in augmented reality, robotics, and autonomous systems. However, many current methods assume static scenes or filter out dynamics as outliers. In this paper, we study in-view scene changes where objects are manipulated in front of the camera within a single online sequence, unlike prior works that detect changes outside the camera view or between separate captures. This setting entangles transient and persistent dynamics, as objects can be distractors while moving and persistent once they settle. While recent studies start to address distractors by removing them for clean static background, in-view scene changes remain underexplored. To resolve this, we present SettleSplat, a monocular mapping system that maintains up-to-date 3D Gaussian maps under such changes. Specifically, we lift coarse per-pixel uncertainty into Gaussian dynamicity field, then prune transient ones. For persistent changes, we derive geometric contradictions weighted by parameter-free rendered depth uncertainty to separate true changes from under-optimized regions. On Bonn and Co-Fusion, SettleSplat achieves consistent 3D Gaussian maps, outperforming current baselines on both full images and change regions while maintaining comparable speed.
authors: Anh Thuan Tran, Xiyun Song, Yubin Zhou, Heather Yu, Jana Kosecka, Liang Peng
bullets: Addresses in-view scene changes, where moving objects may be transient distractors or persistent changes.
Uses per-pixel uncertainty to construct a Gaussian dynamicity field and prune transient geometry.
Identifies persistent changes through geometric contradictions weighted by rendered depth uncertainty.
On Bonn and Co-Fusion, outperforms baselines on full images and changed regions while maintaining comparable speed.

figures.caption: Figure 2. System overview. Given monocular RGB frames (a), SettleSplat estimates depth, then tracks and maps with the DROID-W backbone (b) while learning per-Gaussian dynamicity field δ that prunes transient distractors. During refinement (c), geometry contradiction score g, derived from the rendered map and estimated depth and weighted by the rendered depth uncertainty, is integrated with the tracking uncertainty into reliability map r. Frames before the settlement frame K are weighted by W = r2, while later frames supervise the settled scene without masking.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison on Bonn (rows 1–3) and Co-Fusion (rows 4–6), covering moving, adding, and removing objects. Red boxes show the change regions. At old object locations, baselines leave ghosting artifacts, while SettleSplat reconstructs the updated scene cleanly. For added and moved objects, SettleSplat preserves appearance and detail, whereas the baselines blur or miss them. For removed objects, SettleSplat is competitive with other baselines while reducing ghosting.
