papers.abstract: Dynamic driving scene reconstruction has made remarkable strides in recent years by leveraging generative priors, particularly in the quality of novel trajectory rendering. Nevertheless, a significant gap remains between the generated data and real-world sensor observations, severely hindering further improvements in reconstruction fidelity. In this paper, we present ReconDreamer#, a self-evolving framework that synergizes reconstruction and generation for dynamic driving scenes, which substantially bridges the gap between synthesized novel trajectory data and recorded real-world observations. Within this self-evolving closed-loop framework, the generative and reconstruction models mutually reinforce each other through iterative refinement, ultimately yielding a significant enhancement in the 3D representation capability of the reconstruction model. Additionally, we introduce a geometry-prior-based adaptive ground model to further enhance the rendering quality of the reconstruction model. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we conduct comprehensive evaluations on Waymo, nuScenes, PandaSet, and EUVS benchmarks. Specifically on Waymo, at a 6-m lateral shift, ReconDreamer# improves NTA-IoU and NTL-IoU by 8.8% and 3.0%, respectively, and reduces FID by 15.1% relative to ReconDreamer++.

Evaluated on Waymo, nuScenes, PandaSet, and EUVS benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Large 3D repositories make it easy to collect assets, but difficult to determine whether they can be reused reliably across scene assembly, editing, rendering, game production, and training-data construction. An asset can look plausible in RGB while hiding disconnected geometry, problematic UV organization, or materials that fail to resolve correctly after import. We introduce Diagnostic Rendered Evidence (DRE): aligned beauty, wireframe, and UV-seam-plus-wireframe views scored by pass-specific frozen ViT classifiers and combined through late fusion. On 1,234 human labeled TexVerse assets, nested grouped evaluation achieves 86.36% balanced accuracy and 88.32% bad-asset recall. On a separate, balanced 764 external reference test, DRE achieved 88.9% balanced reference-label accuracy. Our method requires only an imported asset and renderer-derived evidence, without repository identity, creator, popularity, text, or source metadata at inference. Our results support cross-corpus portability and show that purpose built diagnostic views expose defects that just the beauty views can miss. Webpage: https://rbz-99.github.io/is-this-3d-asset-usable/

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery builds on accurate observations interpreted through domain knowledge and reasoning. For scientific 3D data, this requires understanding structures and spatial relationships, from protein contacts to anatomical organization. Existing multimodal benchmarks largely evaluate text and 2D images, while scientific 3D evaluations vary in representations and protocols across disciplines, limiting cross-disciplinary comparison. To assess these foundational capabilities, we introduce ScienceVision, a cross-domain benchmark for scientific 3D understanding and reasoning through expert-level visual question answering (VQA). We construct 250 questions, with 50 each from Biology, Chemistry, Medical Imaging, Mechanical CAD, and Architecture, through a pipeline combining synthetic question generation with domain-expert review and annotation. Each task pairs a native 3D artifact with a scientific question, a specified response format, and a task-specific reference answer, requiring domain knowledge to be applied to geometric or topological evidence. We evaluate 12 models on the same questions in three settings: visual question answering with native 3D artifacts accessed through an agent harness's file and code-execution tools; the same workflow augmented with expert-inspired viewer inspection and measurement tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP); and visual question answering from prescribed rendered 2D images using an agent harness. All settings use the same task-specific deterministic final-answer scoring. The inspection environment supports view changes, target isolation, and slice inspection. In this main comparison, the best mean answer score is 0.53 out of 1. Mean scores in the native-artifact workflow without additional MCP tools exceed those in the rendered-image workflow for every model, by 17.2 percentage points on average.
authors: Tianyi Ma, Jing Gu, Haozhe Zhao, Liang Chen, Yunfan Zhang, Haijun Su, Jialong Wu, Le Xue, Arnav Das, Dustin Tran, Yinfei Yang, Andrew Dai, Kuan Li
bullets: Introduces 250 expert-reviewed 3D VQA questions spanning Biology, Chemistry, Medical Imaging, Mechanical CAD, and Architecture.
Pairs each native 3D artifact with a scientific question, required response format, and task-specific reference answer.
Evaluates 12 models using native 3D artifacts, optional inspection tools, and prescribed rendered 2D images under a shared scoring protocol.
The best mean score is 0.53/1; native-artifact workflows outperform rendered-image workflows by 17.2 percentage points on average.
Tasks require interpreting geometric and topological evidence with domain knowledge.

papers.abstract: Intracardiac flow is driven by complex, and time-varying cardiac motion and interaction with the heart valves, producing complex flow features that may provide valuable information for disease diagnosis and treatment planning. 4D Flow MRI enables non-invasive, time-resolved measurement of three-dimensional cardiovascular velocity fields. However, substantial noise and limited spatial and temporal resolution limit its ability to accurately resolve flow features. We propose 4D-MRAR (4D Magnetic Resonance Augmented Reconstruction), a deep learning (DL) method to super-resolve and denoise 4D Flow MRI data. Unlike prior DL methods that train and infer on static vascular regions, our method predicts intracardiac flow within hearts undergoing large deformation. Moreover, it uniquely allows for simultaneous super-resolution in 3D space and time. The method combines a residual convolutional neural network, a recurrent neural network, and an implicit neural field to predict high-resolution velocity and pressure fields while efficiently enforcing the governing equations of fluid flow during training. Trained on a synthetic dataset obtained from computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of left ventricle (LV) flow, our method generalizes to synthetic whole-heart 4D flow MRI data, and demonstrated promising performance on real 4D Flow MRI. The produced super-resolved flow fields exhibit significantly improved accuracy and greater consistency with the governing equations of blood flow compared with prior methods.
authors: Yusuf A. Ozturk, Jie Zheng, Fanwei Kong
bullets: Addresses noise and limited spatial-temporal resolution that obscure clinically relevant intracardiac flow features.
Combines residual and recurrent neural networks with an implicit neural field to predict high-resolution velocity and pressure.
Efficiently incorporates blood-flow governing equations during training and handles large cardiac deformation.
Trained on CFD-generated left-ventricle flow, it generalizes to synthetic whole-heart data and shows promising results on real 4D Flow MRI.
Produces more accurate, physically consistent flow fields than prior methods, though training relies on synthetic CFD data.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art bronchoscopy guidance systems and computer-aided diagnosis methods have emerged as important tools for early lung cancer detection. Effective use of these tools depends on being able to accurately link a patient's bronchoscopic airway exam video to their pre-operative 3D chest CT scan. Unfortunately, the derivation of such links, which include bronchoscope depth and camera motion, from the exam video remains an open problem. Building on recently proposed 3D-vision foundation models, we propose DUNEDepth, a hybrid architecture that combines a shared DUNE ViT encoder, a twin MASt3R cross-attention decoder structure, and a prediction head that includes elements of the MASt3R and Reloc3r models. To fine-tune the architecture to our application, we utilize an integrated hybrid synthetic-supervised/self-supervised training strategy that draws on both bronchoscopic video and CT-derived virtual bronchoscopic views. Experiments drawing on bronchoscopic video sequences demonstrate that DUNEDepth more accurately derives depth information and camera motion trajectories than previously proposed self-supervised methods.
authors: Qi Chang, Austin Kao, Ange Lou, William E. Higgins
bullets: Addresses the open problem of recovering bronchoscope depth and pose from examination video.
Combines a shared DUNE ViT encoder, twin MASt3R cross-attention decoders, and a MASt3R/Reloc3r-inspired prediction head.
Uses hybrid training with bronchoscopic video and CT-derived virtual bronchoscopic views, combining synthetic-supervised and self-supervised signals.
Experiments on bronchoscopic video sequences show improved depth and camera-trajectory estimation over prior self-supervised methods.

papers.abstract: A substantial line of work builds rotation invariance directly into point cloud architectures. We benchmark 10 architectures (PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN, RIConv, RIConv++, RISurConv, PointMLP, PointTransformer, and the equivariant VN-PointNet and VN-DGCNN) across 5 domains under pose, noise, and occlusion, and analyze the results with confirmatory hypothesis tests rather than point estimates. The three rotation-invariant (RI) architectures achieve the best pose robustness but rank among the lowest on noise robustness in 4 of 5 domains. We ask whether this cost is intrinsic to invariance or specific to how invariance is obtained. We retrain all 10 architectures unchanged, with a simple invariance loss on the embedding and three training seeds each, and evaluate all models on the independently designed ModelNet40-C. Invariance training transfers narrowly but reliably. It improves exactly the corruption families its perturbations target wherever the baseline has headroom (mean occlusion +10.5, lidar +13.4 percentage points of accuracy). At matched training budget the best standard backbone and the best RI architecture end on par on unseen corruptions (within 2.5 percentage points in every seed), and invariance-trained RIConv++ is the most seed-stable top model. Once rotation augmentation is widened, standard backbones concede only a flat, angle-independent accuracy offset under full-sphere rotation. We release the benchmark along with a package for analyzing point cloud robustness and reproducing our results.
authors: Abdulla Nasir Chowdhury, Gulpi Qorik Oktagalu Pratamasunu, Kazuhiro Fukui
bullets: Benchmarks 10 point-cloud classifiers across 5 domains under pose, noise, and occlusion using confirmatory hypothesis tests.
Rotation-invariant models provide the strongest pose robustness but rank near the bottom for noise robustness in 4 of 5 domains.
A simple embedding-level invariance loss transfers narrowly, improving targeted corruption families when baseline headroom exists.
On independently designed corruptions, the best standard and rotation-invariant models perform similarly; invariance-trained RIConv++ is the most seed-stable top model.
Wider rotation augmentation leaves standard backbones with a consistent, angle-independent accuracy gap under full-sphere rotations; the benchmark and analysis tools are released.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a statistical benchmark for rotation-invariant point cloud architectures, relevant to robust 3D perception for robotic navigation and manipulation.
papers.title: Do We Still Need Rotation-Invariant Architectures? A Statistical Robustness Benchmark for Point Cloud Classification
papers.tldr: Rotation-invariant architectures excel under pose changes but sacrifice noise robustness; targeted invariance training can narrow this gap without a clear overall winner.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles require robust perception systems to operate safely under diverse environmental conditions. While cameras provide high-resolution visual data, their performance significantly degrades in low-light and adverse weather. High Definition (HD) radar offers superior reliability and angular resolution under such conditions but lacks rich visual feature recognition. LiDAR, though expensive, delivers highly precise distance measurements and dense point clouds. Each sensor exhibits unique trade-offs, necessitating the development of advanced sensor fusion algorithms to harness complementary strengths while minimizing computational complexity and maintaining accuracy. In this study, the proposed fusion architecture performs early fusion by combining camera images with perspective-view point cloud data from HD radar and LiDAR sensors. The proposed model is trained to detect vehicles and segment free drivable space simultaneously. Experiments are performed on the RADIal dataset where we demonstrate that fusing point cloud data with camera images in front-view surpasses the performances of the most recent standalone and fusion models.
bullets: Addresses camera degradation in low-light and adverse weather by combining complementary camera, radar, and LiDAR sensing.
Uses perspective-view point-cloud projection for early fusion with camera images.
Trains a multi-task model for simultaneous vehicle detection and free-space segmentation.
Evaluated on the RADIal dataset.
Reports performance exceeding recent standalone and fusion models, without quantitative results in the abstract.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Architecture Overview: Camera-Radar-LiDAR early fusion by concatenation performing vehicle detection and free space segmentation simultaneously. The predicted free drivable space is in green and the detected vehicles in blue.

Fig. 2: Deep Seeing Through Sensors: Early fusion is performed using inputs from (a) the camera, (b) a sparse radar point cloud, and (c) a dense LiDAR point cloud. The encoder comprises a pre-encoder followed by four ResNet-50-style blocks, whose output feature maps are denoted as x0, x1, x2, and x3. A thick purple arrow indicates the connection from the encoder to the decoder, through which the encoded features are upsampled to higher spatial resolutions. The dashed lines indicate skip connections that preserve spatial information. The final outputs are produced by a Detection Head and a Segmentation Head, and the corresponding prediction results are illustrated in Fig. 1 and Fig. 3.

Fig. 3: Qualitative evaluation on the test set: (a) ground truth, (b) camera-only predictions, and (c) camera–radar–LiDAR fusion results. The green regions denote free-space segmentation, while the blue regions indicate detected vehicles.

papers.abstract: Automatic rigging is a fundamental task for both static 3D and dynamic 4D mesh animation, yet existing methods do not provide a unified feedforward solution for these two settings. While static 3D riggers achieve strong quality, they often provide limited control over bone count and become temporally unstable when applied frame by frame to dynamic meshes. Existing 4D methods, in contrast, typically rely on expensive per-sequence optimization. We propose MoTWorld, a template-free, data-efficient framework for unified 3D and 4D skeleton generation. Built on flow matching, MoTWorld generates temporally aligned skeletons for an entire sequence in a single feedforward pass, while naturally handling single-mesh 3D rigging. The model further supports explicit skeleton-count control, uncertainty estimation for candidate selection, and masking-based interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting. To address limited paired 4D rigging data, we adopt a curriculum that initializes from large-scale 3D rigging data and adapts to mid-scale 4D mesh-skeleton data. Experiments show that MoTWorld achieves strong static 3D rigging performance with controllable bone complexity, as well as high-quality and temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction results.
authors: Fengzhi Guo, Nate Morrill, Shiqi Li, Cheng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of a unified approach for 3D rigging and temporally stable 4D skeleton generation.
Generates an entire 4D sequence jointly in a single feedforward pass, while also supporting single-mesh 3D rigging.
Provides explicit control over skeleton count, uncertainty-based candidate selection, and masking-based interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting.
Uses a curriculum from large-scale 3D rigging data to mid-scale 4D mesh–skeleton data to reduce dependence on paired 4D training data.
Reports strong 3D rigging quality and high-quality, temporally consistent 4D reconstruction and prediction.

figures.caption: Figure 1: FLOWRIG unifies rigging for both 3D and 4D meshes. Compared with prior methods such as Puppeteer (Song et al., 2025a) and UniRig (Zhang et al., 2025a), our model delivers accurate 3D rigging, preserves 4D temporal consistency, supports controllable bone count, achieves faster inference, and enables 4D skeleton prediction, including interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting.

Figure 2: FLOWRIG overview. We encode meshes into conditioning tokens, and initialize noisy skeleton slots, which are processed by a flow matching transformer to predict temporally aligned skeleton representations. The predicted features are decoded by the skeleton, graph, and uncertainty heads to recover 3D/4D rigging outputs, with uncertainty used for sample selection. n denotes the skeleton count, and ϕ denotes the unconditional token.

Figure 4: Static Reconstruction. Numbers from top to bottom are J2J, J2B, and B2B for each instance. Compared with baselines, our model preserves finer geometric details and achieves more accurate mesh alignment.

Figure 3: Data-efficient curriculum training. We first train on static 3D rigging, then adapt to 4D reconstruction, and finally enable prediction through masked conditioning. During the final stage, we use diverse masking patterns, including interpolation, forecasting, backcasting, and random masking, to expose the model to different temporal prediction settings. This schedule transfers large-scale 3D supervision to the data-scarce 4D setting.

Figure 5: Dynamic reconstruction and prediction. Blue indicates reconstruction with mesh guidance, while yellow indicates predictions without mesh guidance. In (b), from top to bottom, it shows interpolation, forecasting, and backcasting, respectively. Refer to the demo video for a clearer comparison.

Figure 6: Analysis of bone count control. Our model can freely control the number of bones to adjust skeletal detail, while existing baselines do not provide this level of controllable output granularity.

Table 1: Static skeleton reconstruction comparison. Our methods achieves strong reconstruction fidelity across diverse out-of-domain static datasets. Ours* utilizes uncertainty as selection score to select the best candidate from the 5 samples and outperforms all baselines on Articulation-XL 2.0 and Diverse-Pose. On ModelsResource, its zero-shot performance approaches that of RigAnything trained directly on the same dataset. See the "Baselines" paragraph for citations of these models.

Table 2: Dynamic quantitative comparisons on TexVerse dynamic dataset. N is time window length. PuppeteerD* means we finetuned Puppeteer-diverse model (Song et al., 2025a) on TexVerse training dataset. Ours* utilizes uncertainty as selection score to select the best candidate from the 5 samples.
Table 3: Ablation studies on data sources. Metrics are evaluated on the TexVerse test set with T = 24.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a unified framework for 3D/4D skeleton generation using flow matching, bridging 3D vision, video generation, and robotic rigging/kinematics.
papers.title: FlowRig: Unified Skeleton Generation for 3D and 4D Meshes via Flow Matching
papers.tldr: MoTWorld uses flow matching to generate controllable, temporally consistent skeletons for both static 3D and dynamic 4D meshes in one feedforward framework.

papers.abstract: Feedforward 3D reconstruction has largely followed an {appearance-driven paradigm}: multi-view images are encoded into visual representations, cross-view correspondence is implicitly inferred from learned features, and 3D primitives are subsequently predicted from these representations. However, calibrated cameras and sparse metric measurements already provide explicit constraints on where the same physical point should appear across views. We propose a novel paradigm, \textbf{Geometry-Conditioned Feedforward Reconstruction}, in which metric geometry establishes cross-view correspondence before the 3D representation is formed, while learned visual features refine rather than discover this correspondence. Based on this paradigm, we introduce \textbf{GeoForward}. Sparse LiDAR points are unprojected into 3D and analytically projected across calibrated cameras to provide metric correspondence anchors. A bounded continuous local search then refines these anchors using visual features, and the resulting geometry-conditioned representation is fused with global multi-view context from VGGT. The shared representation drives separate metric-depth and Gaussian-attribute prediction, establishing a direct path from explicit geometry to both Gaussian centers and spatial attributes. A sparse 3D refinement module subsequently improves local attribute compatibility while preserving the geometrically determined centers. For temporal reconstruction, endpoint Gaussians are composed using vehicle masks and motion priors. On nuScenes, GeoForward achieves the lowest cross-camera depth-consistency error and Chamfer distance among the compared methods while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality. These results demonstrate that explicitly conditioning correspondence formation on metric geometry provides an effective alternative to purely appearance-driven feedforward 3D reconstruction.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of appearance-driven correspondence inference in sparse-view feedforward 3D reconstruction.
Analytically projects sparse LiDAR points across calibrated views, then refines correspondences with a bounded visual-feature search.
Fuses geometry-conditioned features with global multi-view context to predict metric depth, Gaussian centers, and spatial attributes.
Uses sparse 3D refinement for local attribute compatibility and supports temporal reconstruction with masks and motion priors.
On nuScenes, reports the lowest cross-camera depth-consistency error and Chamfer distance among compared methods, with competitive reconstruction quality.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of GeoForward. Given calibrated multi-view images and sparse LiDAR, GeoForward first establishes metric cross-camera correspondences through geometric projection and continuous local refinement. The aligned features are fused with global multi-view context and jointly condition metric depth and Gaussian-attribute prediction. A sparse 3D refinement module further improves local attribute consistency, while vehicle masks and motion annotations enable temporal Gaussian composition at arbitrary query times.
Figure 4: Qualitative reconstruction results. For each method, the upper row shows visual-view RGB renderings, and the lower row shows the corresponding depth maps. GT denotes ground truth.

Figure 6: Qualitative ablation results on nuScenes. For each of two scenes, the upper row shows RGB renderings and the lower row shows depth maps. We compare variants without LiDAR-guided alignment, the Gaussian head, or motion compensation with the full GeoForward model and ground truth (GT).
Figure 5: LiDAR retention ablation on nuScenes. Performance largely saturates after retaining 25% of the LiDAR points, with only minor changes at higher sampling densities.

Figure 3: Metric-guided cross-view alignment. Sparse LiDAR provides a metric correspondence anchor by projecting a 3D point from the reference view into a context view using calibrated geometry. A bounded continuous offset then locally refines the projected location using visual features, after which the context feature is re-sampled at the refined coordinate.

Figure 7: Qualitative comparison with baselines. Three driving scenes are shown, each with RGB renderings above the corresponding depth maps. Columns compare Envision4D, StreetForward, STORM, PVG, DeformableGS, GeoForward, and ground truth (GT).

Figure 8: Six-camera qualitative results on nuScenes. Each row shows one scene. From left to right, the columns correspond to CAM BACK, CAM BACK LEFT, CAM BACK RIGHT, CAM FRONT, CAM FRONT LEFT, and CAM FRONT RIGHT. Each camera view shows the rendered RGB image above its colorized predicted depth map.

papers.title: GeoForward: Geometry-Guided Cross-View Alignment for Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: GeoForward uses calibrated-camera geometry and sparse LiDAR to establish cross-view correspondences before predicting 3D Gaussians, improving geometric consistency in feedforward reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Robust 3D point-cloud recognition is critical for robotics, mapping, and urban sensing, yet point-cloud classifiers often suffer performance drops under domain shifts caused by sensor changes, environmental variation, and acquisition artifacts. Many existing adaptation methods are difficult to deploy in practice because they require access to source data or the internal parameters of the source model, which may be restricted by privacy, licensing, or security constraints. We present 3D-BBDA, a backpropagation-free black-box domain adaptation framework that adapts a source-trained predictor to unlabeled target data using only black-box outputs. Our method performs pseudo-label guided prototype-based alignment and employs a weighted prediction module to fuse source logits with alignment logits, reducing sensitivity to noisy pseudo-labels. To stabilize prototype memory when pseudo-label coverage is incomplete, we construct a Gaussian-perturbed prototype prior from unlabeled target predictions and use it as a fallback for missing or unreliable class prototypes during alignment. Experiments on four corrupted 3D benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines. On ModelNet-40C, 3D-BBDA achieves mean errors of 32.08% (PointNet) and 29.62% (GDANet), outperforming Source-only (35.88% / 34.03%) and BFTT3D (33.78% / 32.36%). 3D-BBDA requires only a single forward pass with no gradient updates making it suitable for real-time, privacy-preserving deployment in transferable 3D recognition pipelines. Project page is available at https://visdomlab.github.io/3D_BBDA
bullets: Addresses domain-shift degradation from sensor changes, environmental variation, and acquisition artifacts.
Uses pseudo-label-guided prototype alignment and weighted fusion of source and alignment logits.
Builds a Gaussian-perturbed prototype prior to handle missing or unreliable class prototypes.
Experiments on four corrupted 3D benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines.
Requires a single forward pass, supporting real-time and privacy-preserving deployment.

papers.abstract: We introduce CoLa3D, a simple and effective model for composable 3D scene decomposition that, given a single whole-scene latent from either a single image or an existing scene mesh as input, directly outputs a set of object meshes with consistent spatial layout that can be assembled back into a coherent scene. CoLa3D introduces a novel paradigm for 3D scene decomposition within a shared whole-scene latent, unlike alternatives that perform per-object generation in canonical spaces and then glue the objects back together with fragile pose and scale estimation. The network is a lightweight, flexible, and scalable query-based transformer that accepts various types of queries, including 2D masks, 3D points, and learnable queries, and learns to decompose the scene into objects in a compact latent space. On both synthetic and real-world datasets, CoLa3D achieves state-of-the-art performance on composable 3D scene decomposition, substantially improving global scene-level consistency and object-level quality while running 2 times faster and using less than 1% of SAM 3D's training data. Visible depth on par with MoGe2 further confirms that latent decomposition preserves accurate visible scene geometry while producing physically complete, decomposable object meshes.
bullets: Takes a single-image or existing-mesh whole-scene latent as input and outputs object meshes that reassemble into a coherent scene.
Uses a lightweight, scalable query-based transformer with 2D-mask, 3D-point, or learnable queries.
Performs decomposition directly in a shared latent space, preserving global layout and object-level quality.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on synthetic and real-world datasets, runs 2× faster, and uses less than 1% of SAM 3D’s training data.
Produces physically complete meshes with visible depth comparable to MoGe2.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of CoLa3D. Starting from an RGB image or a holistic scene mesh, CoLa3D first obtains a structured scene latent zs geo with TRELLIS.2 [76] and augments it with 3D semantic features zs sem from Utonia [87]. A lightweight decomposition transformer then uses mask, learnable, or point queries to decompose zs = zs geo + zs sem through L blocks of self-attention, cross-attention to frozen DINOv3 [52] features f img, and alternating Latent-to-Query/Query-to-Latent cross-attention. Finally, a multi-hot assignment extracts per-instance latents {zo k}, which are decoded in parallel by the shared decoder D into aligned object meshes and can be recomposed in the global 3D space.
Figure 4: Qualitative results on real-world scenes. CoLa3D produces coherent decompositions on Replica and ScanNet++ images, demonstrating robust generalization from synthetic training data.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparisons on synthetic data. Compared with baselines, CoLa3D produces spatially coherent object meshes with correct relative positions and scales.
Figure 5: Architecture details of the attention block used in the Query-Based 3D Latent Decomposition Transformer.
Figure 6: Decomposition from holistic scene meshes. CoLa3D produces coherent object-level meshes across generated and existing holistic scene meshes.
Figure 7: Additional qualitative comparisons on synthetic scenes. We show more results on the 3D-FRONT InstPIFU split and MetaScenes following the same layout as fig. 3.
Figure 8: Additional qualitative comparisons on real-world scenes. We show more zero-shot results on Replica and ScanNet++ following the same layout as fig. 4.
Table 5: Detailed per-dataset inference time. We report the average per-scene inference time in seconds.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces CoLa3D, a query-based transformer for decomposing 3D scenes into composable object meshes from single-image or mesh inputs, directly addressing 3D scene understanding and generation.
papers.title: CoLa3D: Composable Latent 3D Decomposition
papers.tldr: CoLa3D decomposes a whole-scene latent into spatially consistent, composable object meshes while avoiding separate canonical-space generation and fragile pose alignment.

papers.abstract: Class-incremental learning (CIL) for outdoor 3D object detection remains largely underexplored. Existing outdoor studies are limited to single-benchmark evaluations, with SDCoT++ considering KITTI and CL2OD considering nuScenes under different incremental settings. This makes it difficult to assess whether observed continual-learning behavior generalizes across autonomous-driving benchmarks. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first unified cross-benchmark analysis of outdoor class-incremental 3D object detection across multiple autonomous-driving benchmarks, covering both two-task and multi-stage settings. We investigate: (1) how severely existing 3D detectors forget previously learned classes, (2) how incremental training exposes the stability-plasticity dilemma between knowledge retention and new-class acquisition, and (3) which forms of supervision are most effective for balancing these objectives. We introduce CL3DOD, a class-incremental 3D detection framework that restores missing supervision for previous classes using predictions from the previous-stage detector, preserves old-class responses through query-wise knowledge distillation, and employs EMA-based temporal consistency regularization. Experiments on KITTI and nuScenes reveal a consistent stability-plasticity dilemma across both benchmarks. CL3DOD generally achieves a more favorable stability-plasticity balance than controlled incremental baselines and improves upon published prior methods in the reported benchmark comparisons. This advantage persists across multiple incremental stages, demonstrating strong retention of previously learned knowledge while maintaining effective new-class acquisition. Our code, evaluation setup, and incremental task splits will be publicly released.
bullets: Provides the first unified cross-benchmark study covering two-task and multi-stage incremental settings.
Finds consistent forgetting and a stability–plasticity trade-off across both autonomous-driving benchmarks.
Restores previous-class supervision using prior-detector predictions, query-wise knowledge distillation, and EMA temporal consistency.
Reports a more favorable stability–plasticity balance than controlled baselines and improvements over published methods in the evaluated comparisons.
Scope is limited to the KITTI and nuScenes benchmarks and the incremental settings studied.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of CL3DOD at incremental task Tt. A frozen previous-stage teacher provides Old-Class Supervision and Query-Wise Knowledge Distillation through shared queries, while an EMA teacher provides Temporal Consistency Regularization.

Ground-truth boxes are color-coded by class: Car (blue), Pedestrian (yellow), Cyclist (magenta), Van (cyan), and Truck (green), while predicted boxes are shown in red. Fine-tuning exhibits severe forgetting of previously learned classes, whereas Freeze-and-Add retains some previous-task detections but shows limited adaptation across the incremental sequence. CL3DOD produces a more complete set of detections, illustrating a more favorable balance between retention and acquisition after the three-task sequence.

papers.title: CL3DOD: Understanding the Stability-Plasticity Dilemma in Outdoor Class-Incremental 3D Object Detection
papers.tldr: CL3DOD analyzes and mitigates the stability–plasticity dilemma in outdoor class-incremental 3D object detection across KITTI and nuScenes.

papers.abstract: Most image-based 3D reconstructors primarily recover visible surfaces, producing partial point clouds with large holes and leaving unobserved geometry unresolved. To address this limitation, we introduce AnchorComplete, a framework that reconstructs complete scene meshes from partial point clouds while preserving observed geometry and supporting scenes of varying scales. Building on TRELLIS.2, our method combines partial-point conditioning, which integrates global scene tokens with local spatial evidence to anchor generation to the input, and metric-scale coarse-to-fine generation, which progressively refines scene geometry within fixed-size windows while maintaining global structural consistency. Experiments on Replica and SCRREAM demonstrate that AnchorComplete consistently outperforms strong baselines in complete-scene reconstruction, particularly under sparse-view settings.
bullets: Addresses holes and unresolved geometry in image-based 3D reconstruction, which typically recovers only visible surfaces.
Combines partial-point conditioning with global scene tokens and local spatial evidence to preserve input geometry.
Uses metric-scale coarse-to-fine generation in fixed-size windows while maintaining global structural consistency.
Outperforms strong baselines on Replica and SCRREAM, especially in sparse-view settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ANCHORCOMPLETE. From a partial, colored point cloud, Stage 1 generates a metric-scale octree coarse to fine, one window at a time, and Stage 2 generates shape latents on the finest level, which are decoded, merged and meshed once. Each window is conditioned on its parent occupancy and visible points through the local path (warm start) and on its points through anchor tokens read by cross-attention (global path).

Figure 4: Qualitative reconstruction results on Replica (Straub et al., 2019) and SCRREAM (Jung et al., 2024). Given the same DA3 point cloud as input, our method achieves better scene completion performance.

papers.selection_reason: Complete scene mesh reconstruction from partial point clouds built on TRELLIS.2, a generalist 3D foundation model.
papers.title: AnchorComplete: Recovering Complete Scene Meshes from Partial Point Clouds
papers.tldr: AnchorComplete reconstructs complete, globally consistent scene meshes from partial point clouds by anchoring generation to observed geometry and refining at metric scale.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a vital tool in novel view synthesis. 3D Gaussian functions with attributes like color, opacity, and scale are stacked together to explicitly model a radiance field. However, discrete 3D Gaussians usually produce poor depth with few geometry details but lots of floaters, which hinders the effective modeling of smooth radiance fields. To address this issue, we propose to learn a radiance field within a continuous view-dependent color field parameterized by neural networks. With continuous constraints in color, the bias on low-frequency signals of neural networks can highly encourage the geometry modeling to contribute to high-frequency color variations on images, getting rid of solely relying on the color attribute itself. Moreover, we impose a constraint to improve the Lipschitz continuity of the neural color field, making large changes of each Gaussian's color also match with large changes of its position in terms of a ratio. To this end, we additionally introduce novel self-learning strategies to improve the learning of the neural view-dependent color field without any external knowledge or priors, aiming for better generalization on unseen scenes. Our numerical and visual comparisons on widely used benchmarks justify our idea and show better ability of high fidelity geometry recovery in 3DGS. Project page: https://github.com/yangyixi21/Neural-Color-Fields-3DGS.
bullets: Addresses poor depth, limited geometric detail, and floaters caused by discrete 3D Gaussians.
Represents view-dependent color with neural networks to encourage geometry to explain high-frequency image variations.
Adds a Lipschitz-continuity constraint linking large color changes to proportionally large positional changes.
Uses self-learning strategies to improve neural color-field learning and generalization to unseen scenes.
Experiments on widely used benchmarks show improved high-fidelity geometry recovery in 3DGS.

papers.abstract: Among visual localization strategies, scene coordinate regression (SCR) has emerged as an attractive approach for its compactness, accuracy, and speed. Despite these advantages, SCR models generalize poorly across substantially different camera models, such as omnidirectional or strongly rectified imagery. This limitation arises because, changes in field of view, lens distortion, or rectification-induced resampling can make the same scene content appear differently depending on its pixel position, degrading localization accuracy. To cope with this limitation, we introduce Ray-SCR, a lightweight extension to existing SCR architectures that conditions local visual features on their calibrated viewing rays and refines neighboring ray-conditioned features with a shallow local Transformer. We further formulate supervision directly in ray space and use sparse SfM points as metric anchors that link observations across views and camera models. Taken together, these components enable a single scene representation built from a panoramic mapping sequence to accurately localize query images captured with very different cameras, including pinhole, fisheye, and omnidirectional cameras. We evaluate Ray-SCR across multiple SCR architectures and on datasets with pinhole, fisheye, and omnidirectional cameras. The proposed ray conditioning substantially improves generalization across cameras and leads to state-of-the-art localization performance in these challenging cross-camera settings. The project page is available at https://jaeminch0.github.io/ray-scr-generalizing-scene-coordinate-regression-across-camera-models/.
bullets: Addresses poor SCR generalization caused by changes in field of view, lens distortion, and rectification.
Adds ray-conditioned local features and a shallow local Transformer to refine neighboring features.
Uses ray-space supervision and sparse SfM points as metric anchors across views and cameras.
A single panoramic scene representation supports localization from pinhole, fisheye, and omnidirectional queries.
Evaluations across multiple SCR architectures and camera datasets show improved cross-camera generalization and state-of-the-art localization performance.

The Ray Adapter then injects camera-geometry information by encoding the associated viewing rays into the features and locally processing groups of neighboring features with a lightweight Transformer. The adapted features are subsequently passed through the standard SCR pipeline. Here, ACE-G is shown as an example, using a DINO encoder together with trainable scene-specific map codes.

papers.abstract: Classical structure-from-motion reconstruction proceeds iteratively, refining camera poses and scene geometry from a current estimate. This allows maps to easily expand without recomputing already computed views, or geometry estimates to improve as more observations are provided. Most geometric foundation models, however, predict entire geometry in a single forward pass or update a recurrent state as frames arrive sequentially, making this expansion and refinement non-trivial. We introduce Solv3R, a looped transformer that learns to continue solving multi-view geometry from its current state. Importantly, its update operator is independent of the iteration count, allowing previously refined and newly introduced views to be jointly updated regardless of how ``solved'' they are. We train the operator to preserve accurate reconstructions under continued iteration and correct inaccurate states, enabling refinement of fixed image collections and integration of new observations. Representations of solved views can also be cached once and reused as geometric context across iterations, enabling compact and efficient key-value caching. We analyze the solver dynamics and compare it with the state-of-the-art, demonstrating that a single learned solver supports offline reconstruction, incremental reconstruction, relocalization, and streaming without task-specific training or modules. The code and models will be made publicly available at https://ubc-vision.github.io/solv3r/.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of refining or adding views in geometric foundation models that rely on one-shot or sequential-state prediction.
Uses an iteration-independent update operator that jointly updates previously solved and newly added views.
Trains the solver to preserve accurate reconstructions while correcting inaccurate intermediate states.
Caches solved-view representations as reusable geometric context for more compact and efficient iterations.
Demonstrates broad reconstruction capabilities without task-specific training or separate modules.

papers.abstract: Urban photogrammetric point clouds are commonly processed as local 3D patches, limiting the context available for distinguishing geometrically similar categories. Orthographic projection of the same data yields a co-registered digital orthophoto map (DOM)/RGB-D representation that supports efficient large-context modeling but compresses vertical geometry. Existing projection--point methods mainly fuse these two representations at the feature level while retaining a classifier shared across all samples. We present the Aerial Content-Aware Sample-Adaptive Classifier (ACASAC), which complements feature fusion with decision-level adaptation. A point-aligned aerial region bridges the full aerial crop and local 3D patch. ACASAC models scene-to-local variation within the projection and the representation discrepancy between aligned 2D and 3D supports, then transfers both relations to refine the local point class representation. The refined representation, scene-level aerial context, and fixed fused-head prior jointly form a classifier for the current sample. ACASAC improves the fixed dual-representation head by 2.1 and 2.7 mIoU points on SensatUrban and UrbanBIS, respectively, and by 2.1--2.3 points across four tested encoder combinations.
bullets: Local 3D patches lack sufficient context for distinguishing geometrically similar urban categories.
The method combines orthographic DOM/RGB-D large-context information with local 3D point features.
A point-aligned aerial region links the full aerial crop and local 3D patch.
It models scene-to-local variation and 2D–3D representation discrepancies to refine per-sample class representations.
It improves the fixed dual-representation head by 2.1 mIoU points on SensatUrban and 2.7 on UrbanBIS, with gains of 2.1–2.3 points across four encoder combinations.

papers.abstract: Range-image-based point cloud super-resolution provides an effective way to reconstruct sparse outdoor point clouds by projecting low-resolution LiDAR scans into a regular 2D representation. However, current methods still face three challenges. First, range images exhibit pronounced vertical nonuniformity, with sparse observations in distant regions and denser observations in nearby regions. Some cross-scale fusion mechanisms do not account for the varying reliability of features at different vertical positions, allowing invalid values and noise from distant sparse regions to propagate into the decoder. Second, a single convolutional or sequence-modeling architecture often struggles to preserve both local high-frequency geometric details and global long-range dependencies, resulting in over-smoothed reconstructions. Third, smooth transition depths near foreground-background boundaries can produce spike artifacts when the 2D range image is back-projected into 3D. To address these issues, we propose a point cloud super-resolution method based on multi-scale spatial priors and joint local-global modeling. The design comprises a spatially gated fusion module, a multi-granularity local-global cooperative perception module, and 2D median-residual denoising. Experiments on KITTI-360 and nuScenes demonstrate effective reconstruction, with IoU scores of 0.4703 and 0.3593, respectively, supporting the feasibility of the proposed method for range-image super-resolution.
bullets: Addresses vertical nonuniformity in range images, loss of fine geometric detail, and spike artifacts at foreground-background boundaries.
Uses a spatially gated fusion module to limit the propagation of unreliable features from sparse distant regions.
Employs multi-granularity cooperative local-global perception to capture both high-frequency local structure and long-range dependencies.
Applies 2D median-residual denoising to reduce artifacts before back-projecting the range image into 3D.
Experiments on KITTI-360 and nuScenes report IoU scores of 0.4703 and 0.3593, respectively.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic novel- view synthesis with real-time rendering, yet fine-grained di- agnosis of its rendering artifacts remains challenging. These artifacts are typically spatially localized and exhibit diverse degradation patterns, making them difficult to character- ize using global quality metrics and image-level assessment benchmarks, which provide no explicit indication of where they occur or what types of artifacts they represent. To ad- dress this limitation, we introduce GaussFlaw-80K, the first large-scale dataset for fine-grained perceptual diagnosis in 3DGS. Constructed through a model-assisted human-in-the- loop pipeline, GaussFlaw-80K contains 80,049 artifact re- gions across 14,289 rendered images, each annotated with a pixel-level mask and one of eight flaw labels spanning ge- ometric, blending, and photometric degradations. These an- notations turn 3DGS artifact diagnosis into an explicit and measurable task. Building on this dataset, we propose Ge- oCritic, a geometry-guided multi-task model that integrates RGB appearance with depth-derived cues to jointly localize artifacts and classify their flaw types. Beyond evaluation, we further demonstrate the downstream benefits of fine-grained diagnosis through three complementary targeted operations: Gaussian densification, attribute correction, and outlier prun- ing. Experiments show that GeoCritic achieves an AUC-J of 0.9507 and an Acc@1 of 80.08%, while diagnosis-guided re- finement improves all reported global and crop-level metrics across diverse datasets and 3DGS backbones.
bullets: 3DGS artifacts are spatially localized and varied, which global quality metrics and image-level benchmarks cannot adequately diagnose.
GaussFlaw-80K contains 80,049 artifact regions from 14,289 rendered images, with pixel-level masks and one of eight flaw labels.
GeoCritic combines RGB appearance and depth-derived cues to jointly localize artifacts and classify their types.
The model achieves an AUC-J of 0.9507 and Acc@1 of 80.08%.
Diagnosis-guided densification, attribute correction, and outlier pruning improve reported global and crop-level metrics across datasets and 3DGS backbones.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has shown considerable potential for novel view synthesis (NVS) and 3D reconstruction. Feed-forward methods avoid costly per-scene optimization, but fixed image or spatial resolutions limit their ability to allocate primitives according to local complexity. We present OctreeSplat, a hierarchical octree-guided feed-forward Gaussian splatting. OctreeSplat extracts multi-view features and geometric priors from a frozen visual foundation model (VFM), constructs a hierarchical octree, and predicts densification scores. The resulting representation allocates Gaussian primitives at spatially varying densities according to local complexity. Stochastic solids volume rendering improves depth rendering, strengthens geometric supervision, and supports surface reconstruction. When camera parameters are available, an optional test-time optimization (TTO) module improves agreement between predicted and ground-truth parameters. Training updates only 76 million additional parameters and requires 35 GPU-hours. Experiments on Replica, TUM, Tanks and Temples, and DTU demonstrate competitive RGB view synthesis, depth synthesis, and surface reconstruction. OctreeSplat reduces the number of Gaussian primitives while maintaining high reconstruction quality.
bullets: Addresses fixed-resolution limitations in feed-forward Gaussian splatting by adapting representation density to local scene complexity.
Extracts multi-view features and geometric priors from a frozen visual foundation model to build an octree and predict densification scores.
Uses stochastic solids volume rendering to improve depth rendering, geometric supervision, and surface reconstruction.
An optional test-time optimization module improves camera-parameter agreement when camera information is available.
Experiments across Replica, TUM, Tanks and Temples, and DTU show competitive RGB/depth synthesis and surface reconstruction with fewer Gaussian primitives.

DPT and SPUNet construct multi-resolution voxel features and predict Gaussian parameters and densification scores, which guide adaptive octree subdivision to construct an octree-aligned Gaussian representation that adapts to local scene complexity. Stochastic-solid volume rendering provides RGB and geometric supervision.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing detailed geometry and realistic appearance from a single RGB image is essential yet fundamentally challenging due to inherent ambiguities such as occlusion, lighting variations, and texture-geometry entanglement. While recent diffusion-based generative models have significantly improved novel view synthesis, existing approaches suffer from two critical limitations: lack of cross-view geometric consistency and insufficient cross-domain semantic alignment. To address these issues, we introduce UniCross3D, a unified cross-view and cross-domain diffusion framework designed explicitly for consistent and physically coherent 3D generation. UniCross3D features two novel contributions: (1) a cross-view latent regularization that enforces cross-view geometric consistency across synthesized viewpoints by penalizing latent variance, and (2) a cross-domain mutual information objective grounded in the physics of image formation, explicitly aligning synthesized color and normal maps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniCross3D achieves significantly improved view consistency and semantic alignment over state-of-the-art methods and yields higher-fidelity reconstructions, particularly under challenging textures and ambiguous viewpoints.
bullets: Addresses ambiguities from occlusion, lighting, and texture–geometry entanglement in single-RGB-image 3D generation.
Uses cross-view latent regularization to reduce geometric inconsistencies across synthesized viewpoints.
Introduces a physics-grounded mutual information objective to align synthesized color and normal maps.
Experiments report better view consistency, semantic alignment, and reconstruction fidelity, especially for challenging textures and ambiguous viewpoints.

papers.abstract: 3D generation, editing, and completion are typically treated as regenerating the complete 3D asset under task-specific constraints, even when only a local region needs modification. This leads to task isolation, inconsistency in content that should remain unchanged, and dependence on task-specific paired data. We address these issues with a key observation: the three tasks all synthesize a designated region while keeping the rest intact---the full region for generation, the target region for editing, and the missing region for completion. We term this paradigm Selective Modeling and build SeMo3D upon it; it naturally unifies the three tasks, preserves unchanged content by construction, and enables training without paired editing or completion data, since any 3D asset can be partitioned into a selected region and its context. For training, we propose region-selective denoising, which randomly selects regions of varying sizes on standard 3D assets and applies noise and loss only to them, jointly learning all three tasks. For architecture, we propose Omni3DiT, a multi-condition 3D diffusion transformer that distinguishes regions to create from those to retain and fuses image, text, and point guidance for fine-grained control. Experiments across three benchmarks show SeMo3D surpasses state-of-the-art methods on all tasks, delivering multimodal controllability in generation and strong consistency and accuracy in editing and completion. SeMo3D further serves as a unified modeling tool for agents, enabling efficient 3D creation through natural-language interaction. Project page: https://xiaokunsun.github.io/SeMo3D.github.io/.
bullets: Reframes all three tasks as synthesizing a selected region while retaining contextual content.
Uses region-selective denoising to train jointly on standard 3D assets without paired editing or completion data.
Introduces Omni3DiT, a multi-condition 3D diffusion transformer supporting image, text, and point guidance.
Experiments across three benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance across generation, editing, and completion, with controllability and consistency.
Supports natural-language-driven 3D creation for agents.

papers.abstract: Engineering drawings specify mechanical parts through orthographic projections. Recognizing which part a drawing depicts underlies part search, design reuse, and digitization, yet no public benchmark measures whether vision models can do it. We introduce Blueprint2CAD, a benchmark for drawing-to-render correspondence: given an orthographic line drawing and a shaded render, usually from another viewpoint, decide whether they show the same part. Its data layer, BlueCAD-30K, applies an open drafting pipeline to 29,925 Zero-to-CAD models, adding view-aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings from six viewpoints, and surface-type metadata. Frozen encoders retrieve the matching part from a 10,000-model gallery with up to 65% Recall@1 when viewpoints are known but 43% when they are not, and the four encoders we test lie within six points of each other: viewpoint, not backbone, is the bottleneck. Six zero-shot vision-language models reach only 0.52-0.67 verification accuracy, with model-specific Yes/No biases that chain-of-thought shifts but does not remove; a quick LoRA fine-tuning on in-domain pairs improves verification accuracy by a few points but sharpens these biases and leaves the viewpoint failure intact.
bullets: Introduces drawing-to-render correspondence: deciding whether an orthographic drawing and shaded render depict the same part.
Builds BlueCAD-30K from 29,925 CAD models with aligned renders, clean and dimensioned drawings across six viewpoints, and surface metadata.
Frozen encoders achieve up to 65% Recall@1 with known viewpoints, falling to 43% when viewpoints are unknown.
Zero-shot vision-language models reach 0.52–0.67 verification accuracy and exhibit model-specific Yes/No biases.
LoRA fine-tuning slightly improves accuracy but does not solve viewpoint failures and intensifies bias.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation aims to predict depth maps from single RGB images (forgoing the need for stereo camera pairs) and has seen impressive leaps in performance in recent work due to the introduction of affine-invariant losses and the use of foundation model features. These monocular depth models predict affine-invariant depth, which describes the relative positions of objects in the scene instead of absolute depth. While these models demonstrate strong performance on single image benchmarks and qualitatively consistent predictions in video, their effectiveness at preserving consistent spatial structure has been less thoroughly explored. Many potential real-world applications, such as handling video streams as input, rely on coherent three dimensional consistency in scenes. Further, anchoring relative depth predictions to a metric reference for a given scene is a key challenge for applying monocular depth models to real-world situations. We develop a novel evaluation protocol for monocular depth models using video sequences with moving camera positions to test the consistency of prediction across variation in viewpoint. We demonstrate this methodology over diverse, real-world video sequences where we are able to anchor depth model output to metric depth values using structure from motion. Our work demonstrates open challenges in the development of broadly applicable monocular depth foundation models, particularly with their ability to provide temporal consistency over long time frames. We also identify challenges in the straightforward adoption of structure-from-motion as a metric grounding tool for monocular depth estimation models.
bullets: Motivation: Strong single-image benchmark performance does not guarantee coherent 3D structure over video or viewpoint changes.
Method: Evaluate predictions on real-world video sequences with moving cameras and use structure from motion to anchor affine-invariant depth to metric values.
Findings: The evaluation exposes challenges in achieving temporal consistency over long time periods.
Scope: It also reveals limitations in directly using structure from motion for metric grounding of monocular depth.
Contribution: A viewpoint-sequence benchmark methodology for assessing consistency and metric applicability of monocular depth models.

papers.abstract: Language and vision models became data-efficient by pretraining on plentiful unlabelled data; physical field models have such data, over ten million 3D shapes, but geometry pretraining designs its targets rather than deriving them from the physics. Euler-Lagrange geometry pretraining derives them: for attached flow, a shape enters the flow's Euler-Lagrange equation only through coefficients that distance and normal line (the normal up to sign) fix to first order. Their reconstruction error therefore bounds what a representation loses about any field, and fine-tuning on costly simulations need only assemble the global field. We realise it in AREALS, a masked surface autoencoder whose areal tokens carry position, normal and area, pretrained self-supervised and sign-free on 61,822 raw meshes. Because the operating condition enters only through the far field, sensors can supply it: AREALS completes a hidden field in one forward pass without condition labels. It matches the accuracy of the same architecture trained from scratch with half the simulations on DrivAerML and DrivAerNet++ and about a quarter on WindsorML. On DoubleDelta wings, 20 sensors give $3.9\times$ and $4.0\times$ lower field and force error than GABI, a Bayesian inversion method with a learned prior, and beyond the training angles pretraining halves the error.
bullets: Motivated by the abundance of unlabeled 3D shapes and the cost of physics simulations, the work derives geometry-pretraining targets from the Euler-Lagrange equation for attached flow.
AREALS is a sign-free masked surface autoencoder using tokens that encode position, normal, and area, pretrained self-supervised on 61,822 raw meshes.
Sensors provide operating conditions, allowing one-pass completion of hidden fields without condition labels.
AREALS matches a scratch-trained model using half the simulations on DrivAerML and DrivAerNet++, and about one quarter on WindsorML.
With 20 sensors on DoubleDelta wings, it achieves 3.9× lower field error and 4.0× lower force error than GABI; pretraining also halves error beyond training angles.

figures.caption: Figure B.1. The Euler–Lagrange construction and its guarantees. Assuming only locality, the shift symmetry, rotations and Galilean boosts fixes the flow’s Lagrangian density as the pressure, with the gas’s equation of state the only free function; making its integral stationary gives the Euler–Lagrange equation, the law the flow obeys. Each guarantee on the right follows from this construction, and its last line says what AREALS builds in or learns from it.

(B) The level sets and steepest lines of the distance are those coordinates; the value, Hessian and third derivative of ηS = 1 2 d2S give the wall, its normal lines and their spreading W (Lemma 1). papers.abstract: Monocular semantic SLAM aims to reconstruct scene geometry and build semantic maps from RGB observations. Existing Gaussian-based methods often attach semantic labels or features to evolving Gaussian primitives, making semantic fusion difficult to maintain and increasing reconstruction overhead. Hybrid Gaussian--voxel representations provide more stable semantic support, but often rely on RGB-D input or known poses and do not revise historical semantic evidence after geometry updates. We present UniGS-SLAM, an RGB-only framework that decouples open-vocabulary semantics from Gaussian reconstruction while preserving bidirectional interaction. Foundation priors enhance monocular depth and pose estimation, while semantic observations are fused into an independent sparse voxel map with observation provenance, enabling historical contributions to be revised as reconstruction evolves. The fused semantics further guide Gaussian filtering and local surface refinement. Experiments on Replica, ScanNet, and KITTI-360 show leading tracking, rendering, and geometric reconstruction performance among representative RGB-only methods, together with strong open-set semantic mapping on Replica and ScanNet. We also achieve a 2.37-fold reconstruction speedup over the fastest compared semantic SLAM baseline. Project page: https://3dagentworld.github.io/UniGS-SLAM/.
bullets: Addresses unstable semantic fusion and costly reconstruction in Gaussian-based monocular semantic SLAM.
Uses foundation priors to improve monocular depth and pose estimation while decoupling semantics from Gaussian reconstruction.
Stores semantics in a provenance-aware sparse voxel map, allowing historical evidence to be revised after geometry updates.
Uses fused semantics to guide Gaussian filtering and local surface refinement.
Reports leading performance among representative RGB-only methods on Replica, ScanNet, and KITTI-360, with a 2.37× reconstruction speedup over the fastest compared semantic SLAM baseline.

papers.abstract: The efficiency and fidelity of 3D Gaussian Splatting critically depend on adaptive density control, which grows and suppresses Gaussian primitives throughout optimization. However, the standard pipeline still relies on heuristic view-space gradients, scale thresholds, and global opacity resets, rather than explicitly assessing the loss-reducing effect of each split, clone, or opacity update. This mismatch can allocate primitives to already-sufficient regions, miss under-reconstructed structures, and destabilize training through blanket opacity changes. In this work, we recast adaptive density control as a collection of local loss-reduction decisions. We derive efficient Taylor-based per-Gaussian surrogates that predict the objective change caused by three primitive-level operations: splitting, cloning, and opacity decay. This yields a unified loss-aware framework with three components. First, we extend second-order splitting to a normalized joint position-scale space, enabling children to adapt not only their locations but also their anisotropic extents. Second, we formulate duplicate cloning as a surrogate minimization problem, selecting only Gaussians whose duplicated contribution is predicted to improve reconstruction and assigning each child a principled opacity. Third, we replace global opacity reset with selective soft opacity decay that weakens harmful primitives while preserving useful ones. Across standard 3DGS benchmarks, our method produces more targeted primitive allocation and achieves improved rendering quality with comparable or smaller Gaussian budgets compared to baselines.
bullets: Replaces heuristic gradients, scale thresholds, and global opacity resets with per-Gaussian loss-reduction decisions.
Uses efficient Taylor-based surrogates to estimate the objective change from primitive-level operations.
Extends second-order splitting to joint position-scale space for adaptive child locations and anisotropic extents.
Selects beneficial clones with principled opacity and applies selective soft decay to harmful primitives.
Improves rendering quality with comparable or smaller Gaussian budgets across standard 3DGS benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our framework. (a) During training, we accumulate per-Gaussian surrogate statistics, including the joint splitting matrix and surrogate terms for cloning and opacity decay. At each densification interval, these surrogates determine whether each Gaussian is split, cloned, or assigned opacity decay. (b) For each Gaussian, we sequentially evaluate splitting, cloning, and opacity decay using accumulated loss-aware surrogate statistics. Joint splitting computes a loss-reducing direction in the joint position-scale space and initializes two children with corresponding position and log-scale perturbations. Cloning minimizes a local Taylor-based surrogate with respect to the duplicate opacity and appends a duplicate child when it is predicted to decrease the loss. Opacity decay similarly estimates a loss-reducing opacity decay strength and selectively decreases the opacity of Gaussians whose current contributions are predicted to be harmful.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on standard 3DGS benchmarks. Red boxes highlight zoom-in regions where our method better preserves fine details and object boundaries.

Figure 1: Intuition of our loss-aware adaptive density control (ADC). We visualize the effect of each density-control operation from the same intermediate state at the 3,000th training iteration. (a) Splitting: we compare the position-only split of [32] with our position-scale split, visualizing splitting Gaussians as ellipsoids. While the position-only split produces misplaced offspring around the thin bicycle handle, our position-scale split places offspring more appropriately and forms the handle structure more faithfully. (b) Cloning: we compare standard 3DGS and ours by individually cloning candidate Gaussians and measuring the resulting loss change; green/red indicate candidates whose duplication decreases/increases the loss. Our cloning selects mostly loss-reducing candidates and recovers missed structures, whereas heuristic cloning introduces loss-increasing candidates. (c) Opacity decay: we compare the opacity reset of standard 3DGS with our selective opacity decay. Opacity reset makes all Gaussian primitives nearly transparent, leading to unstable training. In contrast, our method weakens only Gaussians predicted to hinder optimization. (d) Component comparison: standard 3DGS relies on heuristics. SteepGS improves splitting with a position-only loss-aware rule but keeps cloning and opacity update heuristic. Our method applies loss-aware decisions to position-scale splitting, cloning, and opacity decay.

papers.abstract: Learning semantic representations for 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently emerged as a promising direction for 3D scene understanding. However, existing 2D-to-3D semantic lifting approaches rely primarily on 2D segmentation supervision and lack object-level priors, causing the learned representation to be driven by local mask evidence rather than holistic object structure. In this paper, we present VLSplat, a vision-language guided approach for object-centric semantic lifting in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our method augments mask-based lifting with object-level semantic priors derived from vision-language models and refines Gaussian representations using an object-group scene graph. The refinement is performed through two language-guided modules: intra-group refinement suppresses semantic noise within object groups, while inter-group acquisition expands object support regions by incorporating structurally relevant candidates from neighboring groups. Extensive experiments on indoor scene datasets demonstrate that VLSplat improves the semantic consistency and structural completeness of object-level categories. Our code and models are available at https://vlsplat.github.io/.
bullets: Targets semantic lifting methods that rely on local 2D mask evidence and lack holistic object-level structure.
Uses vision-language models to provide object-level semantic priors alongside mask-based lifting.
Builds an object-group scene graph with intra-group refinement to reduce semantic noise.
Uses inter-group acquisition to expand object support with structurally relevant neighboring candidates.
Experiments on indoor scene datasets show improved semantic consistency and structural completeness of object categories.

Throughout 3D Gaussian optimization, the semantic representation and scene graph are iteratively updated, allowing object-centric reasoning over Gaussian groups. The scene graph further guides language-based intra-group refinement and inter-group acquisition, improving semantic consistency and structural completeness.

papers.abstract: We introduce Spade-SLAM, a self-supervised dense visual SLAM framework that substantially narrows the long-standing performance gap to supervised methods in a zero-shot setting. By demonstrating that high-fidelity tracking can be achieved without explicit ground-truth pose and depth labels, our approach offers a highly effective and label-efficient alternative to fully supervised pretraining. Our core contribution is a complementary sparse-to-dense training regime: While a warping-based photometric loss provides a dense training signal, we stabilize the optimization and suppress drift in ambiguous regions using a sparse correspondence loss derived from image feature matches. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Spade-SLAM significantly improves robustness and accuracy compared to existing self-supervised baselines, closely rivaling SLAM systems trained with explicit pose and depth supervision. The code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/JulianPSchmitt/Spade-SLAM.
bullets: Addresses the performance gap between self-supervised and supervised dense visual SLAM.
Combines dense warping-based photometric loss with sparse correspondence loss from image feature matches.
Uses sparse matches to stabilize training and reduce drift in ambiguous regions.
Experiments show improved robustness and accuracy over self-supervised baselines, approaching supervised systems.
Code is planned for public release.

papers.abstract: In autonomous driving, 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation is expected to adapt to evolving environments and recognize previously unseen categories, making generalized category discovery under test-time adaptation (GCD-TTA) an important problem. However, existing works treat GCD and TTA separately, while the limited semantic information in 3D point clouds makes GCD-TTA under domain shift more prone to feature collapse when combining GCD with TTA. To address this issue, we propose a two-stage framework for GCD-TTA in 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation. Specifically, in the first stage, we adaptively aggregate local 3D features according to geometric density variations and obtain reliable pseudo labels under a global class-wise prototype consistency constraint. In the second stage, we cast category discovery as an optimal transport assignment process for globally consistent grouping of novel categories. Meanwhile, semantic features from 2D vision foundation models are fused with 3D point cloud features to enrich 3D semantic information and promote a more separable feature space. Extensive experiments on Synth4D to SemanticKITTI, SynLiDAR to SemanticKITTI, and Synth4D to nuScenes demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework. Under a unified evaluation protocol, our method achieves the best overall mIoU on 9 out of 10 benchmark splits and improves the overall mIoU by up to 12.21 points over the strongest re-implemented baseline.
bullets: Addresses feature collapse when jointly performing category discovery and test-time adaptation under domain shift.
Aggregates local 3D features using geometric density variations and enforces global class-wise prototype consistency for reliable pseudo-labels.
Models novel-category discovery as an optimal-transport assignment problem for globally consistent grouping.
Fuses semantic features from 2D vision foundation models with 3D features to create a more separable representation.
On three cross-domain benchmarks, achieves the best overall mIoU on 9 of 10 splits and improves mIoU by up to 12.21 points over the strongest re-implemented baseline.

papers.abstract: Understanding and reasoning over 3D scenes from point clouds is essential for a broad range of AI applications. Recent 3D large language models have shown promising results, yet they still face two fundamental limitations: (i) insufficient capability for grounded multi-step reasoning in complex 3D scenes, and (ii) a text-centric inference paradigm that lacks effective interaction between textual reasoning and visual evidence. As a result, these models often fail to verify intermediate inferences, disambiguate similar object instances, and avoid hallucinations. To address these limitations, we propose MMCoT$^3$, the first 3D-Text Interleaved Chain-of-Thought (CoT) framework for 3D scene understanding. The core idea is to explicitly interleave textual reasoning with task-relevant 3D evidence, enabling the model to consult scene observations throughout the reasoning process. In addition, since a textual mention in 3D scenes may correspond to multiple candidate objects, naive object-mention alignment can inject incorrect evidence and mislead subsequent reasoning. To mitigate this multi-instance ambiguity, we design an ambiguity-aware evidence aggregation mechanism that uses query-guided cross-attention to fuse candidate object tokens and inject both evidence and ambiguity cues into the reasoning process. To better equip the model with multi-step reasoning capability, we further develop PointCoT, a large-scale 3D-specific CoT instruction tuning dataset with approximately 176.2K instances spanning captioning, question answering, dialogue, and planning tasks. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks show that our method consistently improves performance and achieves state-of-the-art results, validating the effectiveness of our proposed ambiguity-aware 3D-text interleaved reasoning for 3D scene understanding.
bullets: Addresses weak grounded multi-step reasoning and text-centric inference in 3D large language models.
Interleaves task-relevant 3D scene evidence with textual chain-of-thought reasoning.
Uses query-guided cross-attention to aggregate candidate objects while preserving ambiguity cues.
Introduces PointCoT, a 176.2K-instance 3D chain-of-thought instruction-tuning dataset covering captioning, QA, dialogue, and planning.
Experiments on six benchmarks report consistent improvements and state-of-the-art performance.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Construction of the 3D-text interleaved multi-modal CoT. Starting from a scene point cloud and a textual CoT, the framework first matches object-related mentions with candidate 3D objects, then performs query-based token fusion and ambiguity modeling to obtain evidence and ambiguity cues. These tokens are injected into the reasoning chain to form the final 3D-text interleaved multi-modal CoT.
