papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation requires accurate metric depth, yet commodity RGB-D cameras often fail on non-Lambertian objects such as transparent, reflective, and translucent materials, producing holes, structured noise, and biased depth. Most restoration methods produce only a single depth map, treating noisy and reliable regions uniformly for downstream tasks while ignoring regional uncertainty. We present UA-Depth, an uncertainty-aware depth restoration framework that iteratively co-refines depth and pixel-wise uncertainty, and uses uncertainty-gated features to suppress unreliable cues for stable updates. To strengthen zero-shot behavior, UA-Depth leverages a frozen depth foundation model as a prior to initialize missing or unreliable depth, and applies two-stage MAD-weighted log-depth scale normalization to reduce outlier bias in relative-to-metric alignment. We introduce an eight-dataset zero-shot benchmark across diverse scenes, materials, and sensors. Across these benchmarks, UA-Depth achieves the best mean rank among representative baselines, with particularly strong gains on datasets dominated by transparent and reflective objects. Beyond depth metrics, we demonstrate downstream improvements in category-level 6D pose estimation and 6D grasp synthesis by exploiting the predicted uncertainty. \emph{Code, models, and data for training and evaluation will be released upon publication.}
bullets: Targets holes, structured noise, and bias in RGB-D data from transparent, reflective, and translucent objects.
Iteratively co-refines depth with pixel-wise uncertainty and gates features to suppress unreliable cues.
Uses a frozen depth foundation model for initialization and MAD-weighted log-depth normalization for relative-to-metric alignment.
Evaluated zero-shot across eight datasets spanning diverse scenes, materials, and sensors.
Achieves the best mean rank among representative baselines and improves category-level 6D pose estimation and grasp synthesis.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Detailed overview of Depth-Uncertainty Co-Refinement with Uncertainty-aware Context Feature Calibration (UCFC). We run T ConvGRU refinement steps: at step t, the ConvGRU updates the hidden state Ht and predicts residual updates that refine depth Dt and uncertainty Ut. UCFC is applied at each iteration to calibrate both RGB and depth context features using the predicted uncertainty, gating unreliable regions before they are fused into the ConvGRU update.

Fig. 7. Qualitative zero-shot comparison on in-the-wild RGB-D scenes captured with a RealSense D435. Pixels are ranked by predicted uncertainty and retained from low to high uncertainty; we plot mean REL (risk) versus retained fraction (coverage). Lower AURC indicates better uncertainty ranking.

Fig. 2. Overview of UA-Depth. Given an RGB observation and a sensor depth map, we first extract RGB features with relative depth using a frozen DAV2 backbone [31]. We then derive two feature streams for refinement: an RGB context feature obtained by projecting DAV2 features through a lightweight feature transfer MLP, and a sensor-depth context feature produced by a context network (Sec. III-B). In parallel, the proposed ADF module (Sec. III-C) initializes metric depth and uncertainty by aligning the relative depth to valid sensor measurements and filling missing regions. Starting from this initialization, the Depth-Uncertainty Co-Refinement module (Sec. III-D) jointly updates depth and uncertainty over several iterations, and finally upsamples the predictions to the input resolution via convex sampling [32]. We discuss uncertainty modeling in Sec. III-E. For the mixed-dataset model, Robust-SN (Sec. III-F) replaces the scale–shift alignment in ADF with robust log-depth alignment and normalization, and is applied during both training and inference.

papers.abstract: Understanding holistic 3D human motion and the surrounding environment from egocentric video is fundamental for applications in AR/VR and robotics. Although these tasks are inherently coupled, existing methods treat them separately. In particular, egocentric motion reconstruction methods typically assume access to metric, gravity-aligned camera trajectories from specialized inertial sensors. Recovering such trajectories from monocular egocentric video remains a significant challenge due to rapid head movements and motion blur. We present EgoMo3R, a joint optimization framework that simultaneously reconstructs 3D human motion and scene geometry from casual egocentric video. It leverages the robustness of low-level visuo-geometric primitives, including monocular depth, optical flow, and point tracks, integrated with a diffusion-based human motion prior via first-order optimization. We propose an alternating optimization scheme that establishes a synergistic feedback loop: scene reconstruction provides physical grounding and trajectory conditioning for the motion prior, while the motion prior regularizes the camera trajectory and anchors the scene in a metric, gravity-aligned world frame. We evaluate EgoMo3R on the highly dynamic sequences of the EgoExo4D and Nymeria datasets and show that it outperforms specialized baselines in both 3D scene reconstruction and egocentric motion estimation.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of estimating metric, gravity-aligned camera trajectories under rapid head motion and blur.
Combines monocular depth, optical flow, and point tracks with a diffusion-based human motion prior.
Uses alternating optimization so scene geometry guides motion and trajectory estimation, while motion regularizes and anchors the scene.
Evaluated on dynamic EgoExo4D and Nymeria sequences.
Outperforms specialized baselines in both 3D scene reconstruction and egocentric motion estimation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Given an input video I , we leverage a monocular depth estimator to obtain relative depth Dr as a geometric base, optimizing only the per-frame scales S to derive metric depth D. Our framework jointly optimizes for camera poses C, which transform metric depth into a global worldframe pointmaps PW , and 3D human motion M . We employ an alternating optimization strategy: (1) Scene Refinement updates C and S using optical flow, point tracks, and a scene-alignment loss to anchor the reconstruction in a canonical frame provided by motion; (2) Motion Alignment refines M by leveraging a diffusion motion prior conditioned on C. This synergistic loop prevents optimization collapse and ensures physically grounded joint 3D scene and motion reconstruction.

Figure 5: Point-tracking Failure: Inaccurate long-range correspondences from the point-tracking model cause EgoMo3R to predict stationary camera trajectory (green) and stationary motion (blue), whereas the groundtruth camera and motion trajectories (grey) move in a straight line.

Figure 1: Given an egocentric video, EgoMo3R optimizes for camera poses, 3D pointmaps, and human motion in a common gravity-aligned metric reference frame. We also show two additional views of our scene and motion reconstruction on the side.

Figure 3: 3D Reconstruction: We visualize the predicted pointmaps and camera trajectories (green) against the groundtruth trajectories (grey). The inset shows our reconstructed scene overlaid with sparse groundtruth points (grey), demonstrating the metric accuracy and alignment of EgoMo3R. Please refer to our supplementary video for a better qualitative comparison.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of 3D human motion reconstruction. EgoMo3R effectively reconstructs physically grounded human motion that globally aligns well with the groundtruth. In contrast, errors in EgoEgo’s head trajectory estimation lead to significant global pose errors. While UniEgoMotion captures plausible local body poses, it similarly lacks the precise head tracking required for global accuracy. Please refer to our suppl. video for a better qualitative comparison.

Table 3: Human Motion Reconstruction: Lower values (↓) indicate better performance. Our method significantly outperforms baselines on head tracking and global motion metrics, while baselines retain local pose accuracy at the cost of significantly worse alignment between the motion and the scene.
Table 1: 3D Reconstruction: Comparison across metric and scale-invariant 3D reconstruction. Lower values (↓) indicate better performance. Our method outperforms all baselines by a significant margin.
Table 2: Camera Pose Estimation: Comparison across metric and scale-invariant camera pose estimation. Lower values (↓) indicate better performance.

Compared to direct optimization, alternation prevents the motion M from collapsing to a suboptimal solution while also improving camera pose and scene reconstruction. We report results after two rounds throughout the paper (gray rows). A third round further improves pose, accuracy, and MPJPE.

Rows 5–6 add the motion prior, optimized directly or in an alternating manner (ours, gray). Row 7 replaces the motion prior with a camera-smoothness prior.

Table 6: 3D Reconstruction: Comparison across metric and scale-invariant 3D reconstruction on three subsets (random, locomotion-heavy, rotation-heavy) of each dataset. Lower values (↓) indicate better performance.

Table 7: Camera Pose Estimation: Comparison across metric and scale-invariant camera pose estimation on three subsets (random, locomotion-heavy, rotation-heavy) of each dataset. Lower values (↓) indicate better performance.

Table 8: Per-Frame Depth Accuracy: Depth predicted by multi-view feedforward geometry models (top) and monocular depth models (bottom) on all frames of the EgoExo4D locomotion subset, using the full rectified frames (512× 512) and their central 384× 384 crop. Monocular depth models are more accurate than feedforward geometry models on every metric in both settings, which motivates their use as our geometry basis.

Table 10: Long Sequences: Results on 24 s EgoExo4D locomotion sequences, 3× the length of the main evaluation clips, with metric scale alignment. Lower values (↓) indicate better performance. Our motion prior, trained on 8 s windows, is applied over overlapping windows with MultiDiffusion [2]; the rest of the optimization is unchanged. VGGT runs out of memory on a 48 GB NVIDIA L40S GPU. Even without explicit loop closure, EgoMo3R remains best on all reconstruction metrics and on ATE, which we attribute to the long-range tracks from offline CoTracker3 [26].

Table 9: Sensitivity to Off-the-Shelf Priors: We replace the point tracker or the depth model in the scene-only setting (row 3 of Tab. 4). Lower values (↓) indicate better performance. Weaker priors degrade the results gradually, without catastrophic failure. The weaker tracker has the larger effect, mainly on ATE and RPE Trans, since less reliable long-range correspondences lead to more drift.

papers.abstract: Motivated by a problem in Generative Specification-Producing AIs (SPAIs), we focus on a problem of deep clustering of three-dimensional shapes specified by point clouds. After reviewing clustering and deep clustering, we study the fully unsupervised pipeline in which a FoldingNet autoencoder is first trained for reconstruction and then K-means++ is then applied to the resulting codewords. We report clustering accuracy (ACC), normalized mutual information (NMI) and adjusted Rand index (ARI) on ModelNet10 and ModelNet40 datasets, as a function of the number of clusters K. We also provide t-SNE visualizations of the codewords, and discuss the choice of K.
bullets: Targets deep clustering of three-dimensional shapes represented as point clouds.
Trains a FoldingNet autoencoder for point-cloud reconstruction, then clusters its codewords with K-means++.
Evaluates clustering using ACC, NMI, and ARI on ModelNet10 and ModelNet40 across different numbers of clusters.
Uses t-SNE visualizations to inspect latent codewords and discusses how to choose K.

papers.abstract: Advances in monocular depth estimation (MDE) now let an attacker generate depth from publicly available RGB images and submit forged RGB-D queries. Such attacks break a core assumption of RGB-D place authentication: that depth comes from a sensor. We study a presentation attack detection (PAD) classifier that uses geometric consistency between the enrollment and query views, as a software-layer defense. A three-stage evaluation shows how far this classifier detects software-injected depth, depending on how accurately the attacker knows the camera intrinsics. In the first stage, the attacker has only an estimate of the intrinsics, and the PAD classifier separates forgeries generated by all three MDE models with a validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.997-0.999. In the second stage, the attacker obtains the exact intrinsics, and the original PAD classifier falls to near chance (AUC 0.54-0.61); a retrained PAD classifier, however, still has the registration residual between enrollment and query as a cue. In the third stage, an oracle evaluation, in which the evaluator fits warps using the ground-truth 3D geometry, shows that detection falls to near chance only in its strongest case, where every valid query keypoint is given its ground-truth 3D coordinate. Of the detection cues, the reprojection error captures the attacker's misestimate of the intrinsics, whereas the registration residual remains even when the attacker knows the exact intrinsics.
bullets: Generated depth from public RGB images violates the assumption that RGB-D authentication depth comes from a sensor.
With only estimated camera intrinsics, the classifier detects forgeries from all three evaluated MDE models with validation AUC of 0.997–0.999.
Knowing the exact intrinsics reduces the original detector to near-chance performance (AUC 0.54–0.61), while retraining preserves detection using registration residuals.
Reprojection error reflects intrinsic-parameter mismatch; registration residual remains informative even when intrinsics are known.
Under an oracle using ground-truth 3D geometry, detection becomes near chance only in the strongest attack case, where all valid query keypoints receive ground-truth 3D coordinates.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates attacks on depth estimation for place authentication, relevant to 3D geometry and security in embodied systems.
papers.title: Detecting Generated-Depth Injection Attacks on RGB-D Place Authentication
papers.tldr: Geometric-consistency PAD can detect generated-depth injection attacks, but its effectiveness depends strongly on the attacker’s knowledge of camera intrinsics and 3D geometry.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting sorts every splat by depth in every frame. Viewers that draw splats with the hardware rasterizer and sort them on the CPU, as most web and mobile viewers do, spend most of the frame time in this sort. We present AbacusGS, which stores the blending order of a 3DGS scene in the scene layout. AbacusGS groups the splats into octree boxes of at most 128 splats and stores each box in order along an axis chosen at write time. In each frame, AbacusGS sorts only the visible boxes, and one dot product per box decides whether the box is read forward or backward. A short order-aware fine-tuning converts an existing 3DGS model, and the over operator of 3DGS stays unchanged. On 13 standard scenes, AbacusGS loses 0.13 dB PSNR on average against an equally fine-tuned 3DGS model. In an OpenGL viewer that orders splats on the CPU, AbacusGS renders frames 4.5 times faster than per-splat sorting. We also present a compact format of 17 bytes per splat and a CUDA tile renderer that use the same order. The code will be released.
bullets: Targets CPU-based per-splat sorting, a major bottleneck in web and mobile viewers.
Groups splats into octree boxes of up to 128 and sorts only visible boxes; one dot product selects each box’s traversal direction.
Uses short order-aware fine-tuning while keeping 3DGS’s blending operator unchanged.
Across 13 standard scenes, loses 0.13 dB PSNR on average versus equally fine-tuned 3DGS and renders 4.5× faster in an OpenGL CPU-sorting viewer.
Also provides a 17-byte-per-splat format and a CUDA tile renderer using the same ordering scheme.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces AbacusGS, an efficient rendering method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that avoids per-splat sorting, improving the efficiency of 3D foundation models.
papers.title: AbacusGS: Gaussian Splatting without Per-Splat Sorting
papers.tldr: AbacusGS accelerates Gaussian Splatting by storing approximate blending order in the scene, avoiding expensive per-splat depth sorting with only a small image-quality loss.

papers.abstract: Localized false-merge correction in connectomics requires converting an identified error into an executable native 3D partition. Still, neither intermediate correction predictions nor seeded graph solvers alone determine which native source-sink constraints should define that partition. We formulate this problem as a 3D-native partition-aware contact selection problem: selecting candidate contacts based on the complete partitions they induce. Our solution comprises two components: ContactCut (CC)-Auto, which uses learned single-contact selection, and ContactCut (CC)-Search, which enables bounded paired-contact search, generates compact alternatives, and applies learned panel ranking. On historical two-way false-merge corrections from MICrONS and FlyWire, CC-Auto improves failure-aware 3D partition (FA-3D Part.) mIoU by 5.9 and 3.4 points over the strongest graph-based controls and by 12.5 and 10.0 points over the best learned baselines. A MICrONS-trained ranker transfers to FlyWire with negligible degradation. CC-Search expands oracle reachability and prioritizes near-oracle alternatives. The code is available at https://github.com/bentake/ContactCut.
bullets: Targets the gap between detecting a false merge and defining executable source–sink constraints for a native 3D partition.
CC-Auto learns to select individual contacts; CC-Search performs bounded paired-contact search and ranks compact alternatives.
On MICrONS and FlyWire corrections, CC-Auto improves FA-3D Part. mIoU over graph-based controls and learned baselines.
A ranker trained on MICrONS transfers to FlyWire with negligible degradation.
CC-Search increases oracle reachability and prioritizes alternatives close to oracle solutions.

(b) Candidate contacts have centroids within 500 nm of the localized error cue x0 (red). Shown candidate centroids are green. The crossed marker denotes an excluded contact.
Fig. 2. Qualitative 3D-native correction results. Predictions are shown against the historical reference.

Fig. 3. Effect of contact selection. The red marker in (a) is the localized cue x0. This example shows how nearby contacts induce different partitions under the same graph-cut setup. e2 is selected by CC-Auto.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces ContactCut, a learned framework for 3D false-merge correction in connectomics. It uses learned selection and ranking for 3D partitioning, fitting 3D Foundation Models.
papers.title: ContactCut: A Partition-Aware Contact Selection Framework for False-Merge Correction in Connectomics
papers.tldr: ContactCut selects native 3D contacts for correcting false merges in connectomics, improving partition quality and supporting transferable, near-oracle alternatives.

papers.abstract: Streaming 3D reconstruction models keep past video frames in a recurrent state, fast weights from test-time training, or a key-value (KV) cache. Each written frame shifts the coordinate frame of later cameras or occupies GPU memory. Training-free rules decide what to write from a signal of the current frame. How much they write accounts for their mean accuracy: spending the update budget of a gate at uniformly spaced frames, with no signal, matches nine published gates, and the budget bounds the drift of the state wherever the writes fall. We propose SceneBound, a training-free rule that writes a frame only when its predicted camera pose lies at least a fixed radius from every stored keyframe. Its keyframe count stays within a constant factor of the covering number of the visited poses, the fewest views that keep a keyframe near every camera, so the count grows with the places visited and stays flat when the camera returns. In large scenes, SceneBound closes a submap once decoding its first frame again reveals drift. SceneBound uses one radius across four released models and three memory types. In the recurrent state of CUT3R and the KV cache of StreamVGGT, it achieves the lowest mean trajectory error among the published training-free rules we evaluate, in one pass and over nine passes of a scene, where its keyframes grow by 3% to 6%.
bullets: Uniformly spacing updates can match published signal-based gates, suggesting update budget largely determines mean accuracy and bounds state drift.
SceneBound stores a frame only when its predicted camera pose is outside a fixed-radius neighborhood of existing keyframes.
Its keyframe count tracks the covering number of visited poses: it grows with exploration but remains stable when the camera revisits locations.
For large scenes, it closes submaps when decoding the first frame reveals renewed drift.
Across four models and three memory types, it achieved the lowest mean trajectory error among evaluated training-free rules for CUT3R and StreamVGGT, with only 3%–6% keyframe growth over nine passes.

papers.abstract: Laser doppler vibrometer (LDV) scans can be used to detect defects and cracks in manufactured parts before they are deployed. This work presents a method for reconstructing the steady-state surface wavefield of a three-dimensional part by combining automated robotic manipulation with neural rendering. A six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) robotic manipulator (UFactory xArm6) with an embedded piezoelectric transducer presented an acoustically excited test article to a stationary LDV at a sequence of known orientations, yielding a set of complex-valued 2D scans with poses derived analytically from the arm kinematics rather than from image-based pose estimation. These scans were used to train a novel complex-nerfacto model, a modified Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) pipeline that replaces the standard three-channel RGB output head with a two-channel output. Complex-nerfacto represents the real and imaginary velocity components of a wavefield, preserving the complex measurement without quantization. Reconstructions of a welded aluminum cylinder and a welded T-bracket were evaluated against measured scans using Z-normalized cross-correlation (ZNCC). The complex-valued pipeline achieved a mean ZNCC of 0.60 at held-out viewing angles, compared with 0.28 for a baseline RGB nerfacto model trained on rendered images of the same data. The resulting surface wavefield reconstructions supported defect detection and characterization on complex components. We identify geometry reconstruction from sparse LDV scans as the remaining obstacle to practical deployment.
bullets: Automated 6-DOF manipulation presents parts at known poses to a stationary LDV, producing complex-valued scans.
A modified NeRF, complex-nerfacto, predicts real and imaginary wavefield velocity components without quantization.
Evaluated on a welded aluminum cylinder and welded T-bracket using Z-normalized cross-correlation.
The complex pipeline achieved mean ZNCC 0.60 versus 0.28 for the RGB nerfacto baseline at held-out viewing angles.
Practical deployment remains limited by geometry reconstruction from sparse LDV scans.

papers.abstract: Many vision benchmarks align a prediction to the ground truth before scoring it. If the alignment minimises the error, an input-free template scores the truth's distance from everything the alignment can reach, so the ground truth alone fixes how well a template can score, before any model runs. Camera pose is our central case. The absolute trajectory error (ATE), the standard camera-motion measure, aligns camera positions by a similarity transform. On the common Sintel protocol, an image-free constant-velocity line has a lower mean ATE than 10 of 11 recent models and 85 of 110 published methods, and on Lightspeed than 5 of 9 models and 10 of 11 published methods. The straightness of the true paths separates these two from TUM, ScanNet, DyCheck and ADT, where every model beats the line. A residual signal-to-noise criterion with the alignment's first-order refit predicts when straightening a prediction lowers ATE in all but one of 4010 model-clip evaluations, including all 504 on three benchmarks registered in advance. The alignment also ignores where cameras look: rotating a trajectory by 30 degrees against its orientations leaves ATE unchanged yet worsens the static-point reprojection of every model on Sintel, TUM and ScanNet. Fitting the alignment's rotation to the predicted orientations gives pose-anchored ATE (PA-ATE), a one-function change at about ATE's cost (37 vs. 34 microseconds per clip). It is never below ATE, ranks every image-free reference below every model on Sintel, tracks the reprojection error under controlled rotation and straightening, largely preserves the models' order, and exposes Lightspeed ground-truth orientations that the images contradict. Beyond poses, templates beat some published methods on KITTI video depth, SSP-3D body shape and NoW faces, and in video depth this distance sets KITTI apart from Sintel and Bonn.
bullets: ATE aligns camera positions by similarity transform, allowing a constant-velocity straight line to beat many published methods on Sintel and Lightspeed.
Whether this happens depends strongly on ground-truth path straightness; on TUM, ScanNet, DyCheck and ADT, all models outperform the line.
A residual signal-to-noise criterion predicts when straightening lowers ATE in 4009 of 4010 model-clip evaluations.
ATE ignores camera viewing direction: rotating a trajectory without changing positions leaves the score unchanged despite worse reprojection.
Pose-anchored ATE (PA-ATE) fits alignment rotation to predicted orientations, better reflecting orientation and reprojection errors while mostly preserving model rankings.

papers.tldr: Standard alignment-based pose metrics can make simple, image-free trajectories outperform learned models, so benchmarks should account for trajectory shape and camera orientation.

papers.abstract: Computational brain imaging is constrained by a mismatch between increasingly diverse tasks and scarce, heterogeneous clinical data. Although existing brain foundation models transfer pretrained representations, their knowledge remains entangled within model-specific features and fixed architectures. This paper proposes BrainGFM, a generative foundation model that extends knowledge transfer beyond representation reuse through a reusable and reconfigurable brain-imaging prior. By pretraining on a corpus of about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices, BrainGFM supported task-aligned data synthesis for low-data predictive learning and task-adapted post-training for image reconstruction. Across 48 downstream tasks, BrainGFM improved segmentation and classification under limited supervision and achieved high-fidelity image enhancement across heterogeneous imaging conditions. Multicenter clinical validation involving 4,796 stroke patients across two internal and four external centers demonstrated its applicability to three clinically relevant tasks around stroke cohorts. Blinded reader assessments showed that BrainGFM-generated FLAIR images approached acquired FLAIR in overall diagnostic quality. In a human-AI collaboration study, BrainGFM assistance yielded a 14% relative improvement in mean radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy. These findings support generative priors as a reusable foundation for heterogeneous computational brain-imaging applications.
authors: Multi-Center Cooperative Clinical Study Group for "Lesion-Phenotype Brain Mapping in Acute Stroke"
bullets: Addresses scarce, heterogeneous clinical data and the limitations of fixed, representation-based brain foundation models.
Pretrains a reusable, reconfigurable prior on about 1.3 million MRI and CT slices.
Supports task-aligned synthesis for low-data prediction and post-training for image reconstruction.
Improved segmentation and classification across 48 downstream tasks and enabled high-fidelity enhancement across imaging conditions.
Multicenter stroke validation showed clinical applicability; radiologist stroke-subtyping accuracy improved by 14% with AI assistance.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of BrainGFM for Computational brain imaging. a. Heterogeneity in brain diseases, patient populations, clinical status, acquisition protocols, and clinical centers produces heterogeneous brain imaging distributions and limits the generalization of DL models. b. Our BrainGFM-1.3M comprises about 1.3 million axial slices spanning major MRI sequences and CT, providing a large-scale dataset for brain generative pretraining. c. Our BrainGFM learns a reusable brain-imaging prior from generative pretraining on our BrainGFM-1.3M dataset. d. Task-specific conditioning controls the pretrained generator where class labels are used for class-conditioned synthesis, segmentation masks for spatially conditioned synthesis, and source images for brain image reconstruction. These conditions are combined with task-specific adaptation as detailed in Fig. 6b,c. e. Evaluation spans 48 downstream tasks, comprising 20 segmentation, 8 classification, and 20 imageenhancement tasks. f. Clinical validation in a multicenter stroke cohort assesses BrainGFM for TOAST stroke subtyping, lesion segmentation, and MRI sequence transformation, as well as its clinical utility in reader studies and radiologist-AI collaboration.

Fig. 6 BrainGFM architecture, generative pretraining and downstream adaptation. a. BrainGFM pretraining consists of brain-domain adaptation of a multi-scale visual tokenizer and next-scale autoregressive generative pretraining. A shared encoder (E) and vector quantizer (Q) map brain images and segmentation masks into multi-scale discrete tokens using a shared visual codebook. The autoregressive Transformer learns the distribution of tokens through coarse-to-fine next-scale prediction under categorical modality and sequence conditions. The pretrained decoder (D) reconstructs brain images or segmentation masks from generated tokens. b. Task-aligned data synthesis adapts BrainGFM with limited supervision using LoRA. For classification, task-specific class conditioning enables the synthesis of class-labelled images for training ResNet50. For segmentation, BrainGFM generates task-specific masks and synthesizes corresponding images, producing image-mask pairs for training UNet. c. Task-adapted post-training adapts BrainGFM for image enhancement using paired source-target images. Source-image tokens condition autoregressive prediction of target-image tokens, while LoRA is optimized using token-level prediction and image-level reconstruction losses.

Fig. 7 Data flow and study design of BrainGFM. a. Eleven public brain-imaging resources comprising 64,754 3D volumes and 1,295,080 axial slices were collected and partitioned into pretraining and held-out subsets. The pretraining subset was used for two-stage generative pretraining, including visual tokenizer training and autoregressive modeling.Heldout samples from nine shared datasets, together with 15 additional public datasets, supported downstream evaluation across 48 tasks, including segmentation (20 tasks), classification (8 tasks), and image enhancement (20 tasks). Task-specific training data were constructed through labeled image–mask pair generation, class-conditioned image synthesis, and source– target image pairing. b. Six clinical stroke cohorts comprising 4,796 patients and 4,829 cases from two internal centers (JLH and NFH) and four external centers (NJH, WXPH, NJPH, and CZSPH) were collected. Task-eligible cases were selected according to task-specific imaging and annotation criteria for lesion segmentation, TOAST subtyping, and DWI-to-FLAIR transformation. Internal-center data were used for task-specific training, including low-data settings, while separate internal and external test sets were used for clinical validation.

papers.abstract: Road infrastructure perception is a fundamental component of autonomous driving, as it recovers the structured road elements that define roadway geometry, delimit operational space, and encode traffic regulations. Although individual tasks such as lane detection, drivable-space estimation, traffic-sign recognition, and online map construction have been extensively studied, the field remains fragmented across task definitions, sensing assumptions, output representations, datasets, and evaluation protocols. This survey provides a function-oriented synthesis of road infrastructure perception. We first clarify its scope and organize existing studies into three complementary categories: geometric-structural, functional-spatial, and regulatory-semantic infrastructure. Based on this taxonomy, we review sensing modalities, scene representations, representative methods, benchmarks, and evaluation protocols, emphasizing the field's evolution from image-space recognition toward metric, vectorized, topology-aware, occupancy-based, and rule-grounded scene modeling. We further examine how representation choices affect evaluation and downstream usability, revealing limitations of current benchmarks in relation reasoning, temporal consistency, robustness, and planning-oriented assessment. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future directions toward unified infrastructure representation, open-environment generalization, relation- and rule-aware reasoning, and downstream-oriented evaluation. By connecting tasks, representations, and evaluation under a common functional framework, this survey aims to establish road infrastructure perception as a coherent foundation for map-compatible and behavior-relevant autonomous-driving scene understanding.
bullets: Organizes infrastructure into geometric-structural, functional-spatial, and regulatory-semantic categories.
Reviews sensing modalities, scene representations, methods, benchmarks, and evaluation protocols.
Traces a shift from image-space recognition toward metric, vectorized, topology-aware, occupancy-based, and rule-grounded modeling.
Identifies benchmark gaps in relation reasoning, temporal consistency, robustness, and planning-oriented evaluation.
Highlights future directions including unified representations, open-environment generalization, rule-aware reasoning, and downstream-focused assessment.

papers.abstract: Representing 3D shapes using a set of primitives - known as shape abstraction - is an actively studied problem in computer graphics with wide applications in shape understanding, analysis, and simulation due to the compactness and computational efficiency of the primitive-based representation. Prior work has primarily focused on geometry-aware shape abstraction, where the objective is to approximate the input shape with a minimal set of primitives while preserving geometric fidelity. However, these methods often overlook semantic consistency, inevitably leading to primitives that span across multiple semantic parts. Such inconsistency can cause undesirable artifacts in downstream tasks such as part-level shape editing or manipulation. In this paper, we introduce a new task - semantic-aware shape abstraction, where the goal is to produce abstractions that are both geometrically faithful and semantically consistent, ensuring that each primitive adheres strictly to a single semantic part without crossing semantic boundaries. We propose SemEllipsoid, a novel method to address this problem using ellipsoidal primitives. The core idea is to inject semantic constraints into the primitive optimization process leveraging the availability of semantic cues from large-scale foundation models. We design a fully differentiable projection-blending-evaluation scheme to measure semantic divergence against input semantic masks, and formulate an alternating optimization strategy to iteratively solve for optimal semantic assignment and primitive configurations. Our method is non-learning-based, requiring no data collection or network training, and generalizes well to shapes from arbitrary categories. It also supports different levels of abstraction according to user demand. Extensive experiments and evaluations validate the effectiveness of our approach across several 3D shape collections.
authors: Kuankuan Cheng, Haocheng Yuan, Changjian Li
bullets: Introduces semantic-aware shape abstraction to avoid primitives crossing semantic boundaries.
Uses ellipsoidal primitives with semantic cues from large-scale foundation models.
Employs a differentiable projection–blending–evaluation scheme to measure semantic divergence from input masks.
Alternates between semantic assignment and primitive optimization; the method is non-learning-based and needs no network training.
Supports user-controlled abstraction levels and generalizes across arbitrary shape categories, with experiments validating its effectiveness on several 3D shape collections.

papers.abstract: Dense 3D tracking from monocular video requires establishing point correspondences over time, estimating their depth, and inferring their trajectories during occlusion. Existing methods typically learn these tasks jointly, a demanding objective given the scarcity of 4D supervision. We show that strong pretrained 2D trackers and 3D geometry models provide an effective foundation: lifted trajectories, with occluded segments simply interpolated, already rival dedicated 3D trackers using the same geometry. However, lifted trajectories inherit correspondence and depth errors, and under occlusion, their depth comes from the occluder rather than the tracked point. We introduce ReLift, an efficient feed-forward framework that recasts dense 3D tracking as geometric trajectory repair and completion. At its core, a trajectory corrector alternates attention along and across trajectories to preserve reliable observations, repair corrupted positions, and complete missing motion. Using only geometric inputs allows us to train directly on 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors, decoupling training from images and from any specific tracker or geometry model. Concentrating 4D supervision on trajectory refinement yields a reusable model that consistently improves lifted trajectories across trackers and geometry providers without retraining, so it benefits directly from future advances in either component. On WorldTrack, ReLift achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy, improving on the strongest baselines by 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 on dynamic points, with faster configurations remaining competitive with leading 3D trackers while running faster than 4RC. Visit our supplementry page for more examples and code.

Achieves state-of-the-art WorldTrack accuracy, with gains of 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 APD on dynamic points; faster variants remain competitive.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning relies on asymmetry between what a model observes and what it must explain. Recent methods learn 3D geometry from unposed images by predicting cameras and scene structure, then rendering held-out views. To avoid trivial solutions, they impose this asymmetry in the input space, restricting how views interact through separate branches or masked attention. We revisit this design with geometric accuracy, rather than rendering quality, as the main objective. When a held-out view lies between context views, the context already constrains the geometry it observes. We therefore impose the asymmetry in the 3D representation space, excluding held-out views only from the reconstructed scene while a shared backbone uses all views for correspondence. This improves depth and pose estimation over input-space designs. We further exploit view density: sparse and dense observations depict the same scene but provide different amounts of correspondence. Aligning sparse-context features with dense-context features supplies a geometric training signal alongside rendering, without a pretrained geometric teacher. We additionally align features with a frozen vision foundation model, which brings further gains. None of these signals requires geometric annotation, and the resulting model improves geometry estimation over prior self-supervised methods. Controlled experiments isolate the contribution of each component, and self-supervised pretraining also improves subsequent supervised training.

papers.abstract: Camera localization methods are mostly multi-stage pipelines relying on dedicated and complex maps that are costly to construct, store, and maintain over time. Alternatively, well-structured maps that organize scenes with compact yet expressive primitives are often readily available, providing rich structural and semantic cues that humans can interpret. However, their potential for direct camera localization remains largely unexplored due to the significant modality gap between map primitives and visual observations. This motivates a new concept for localization, which estimates camera poses by grounding query observations to map primitives. In this paper, we instantiate the concept in the context of planar primitives with PGGT, the Primitive-Grounded Geometry Transformer network. Given a single query image and a set of planar map primitives, the network is trained to predict multiple localization targets for feed-forward 6-DoF camera localization that generalizes to unseen environments. With this straightforward and scalable architecture, our method pushes the state-of-the-art localization performance on both dense surface maps and minimal layout models. The code and models are available at https://github.com/3dv-casia/PGGT-Loc

papers.abstract: RGB-D SLAM requires accurate online tracking, high-quality rendering, and geometrically consistent reconstruction. Existing Gaussian SLAM methods mainly optimize Gaussian primitives with photometric, depth, or local frame-to-model constraints, which are often insufficient in indoor scenes with weak textures, large planar structures, noisy depth, and long trajectories. The resulting maps may suffer from pose drift, surface thickness artifacts, noisy normals, and blurred structural boundaries. We propose DrawSplat, an Atlanta World-guided implicit Gaussian SLAM framework for indoor reconstruction. DrawSplat follows a drawing-like process: explicit point-line geometry first sketches the structural layout, and implicit neural Gaussians then fill in high-fidelity appearance and continuous geometric details. It estimates camera poses, sparse geometry, and gravity direction through point-line joint tracking, infers structural planes from tracked lines using the shared-gravity component of the Atlanta World prior, and converts them into differentiable regularization terms on Gaussian centers and normals. To improve compactness and efficiency, DrawSplat further combines an anchor-based implicit neural Gaussian representation with adaptive structural sampling, which allocates Gaussian capacity to structurally informative regions. Experiments on multiple datasets show that DrawSplat achieves robust tracking, high-fidelity rendering, and strong geometric reconstruction among Gaussian-based SLAM systems, while maintaining a practical balance among quality, efficiency, and model size.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of DrawSplat. DrawSplat follows a hybrid Gaussian SLAM paradigm [36]: explicit point-line geometry provides stable tracking and structural cues, while the implicit Gaussian map is incrementally updated online for compact, photorealistic, and geometryconsistent reconstruction. Given an online RGB-D stream, the tracking front-end jointly estimates camera poses, selects keyframes, and builds a sparse 3D geometry map from point and line features. The mapping back-end converts tracked 3D points into a sparse feature grid and decodes implicit Gaussian primitives through lightweight MLPs. Structural 3D lines further induce structural planes constrained by the shared-gravity Atlanta World prior, which regularize Gaussian centers and normals during joint map optimization. The final system produces compact, photorealistic, and structurally consistent indoor reconstructions.

papers.abstract: High-resolution 3D indoor scene generation is crucial for immersive applications such as virtual reality, spatial computing, and robotics simulation. We introduce VoxLution, a coarse-to-fine transformer-based approach that generates high-fidelity indoor scenes with rich details, overcoming the overly smooth geometry typical of existing generative models. First, we generate a low-resolution spatial layout; then, based on this structural information, we progressively refine the scene geometry locally in chunks. Key to our approach is formulating 3D super-resolution as a sequence modeling problem over multi-resolution sparse voxel grids. To achieve this, we introduce a training-free, resolution-invariant tokenization scheme that compactly encodes the geometric information of eight octants into a single decimal number. We formulate the transformer sequence to include multiple resolutions, allowing the coarse layout to guide the generation of fine local details. To ensure coherence across local chunks, we incorporate adjacent chunk boundary information directly into the transformer sequencing. VoxLution achieves scene generation at a finer voxel resolution than existing baselines, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks with 59.6% lower FPD and 51.1% lower FID on 3D-FRONT, and 70.5% lower FPD and 73.8% lower FID on Scannet++.
authors: Daoyi Gao, Xinyi Zhang, Alexey Bokhovkin, Lei Li, Angela Dai
bullets: Targets overly smooth geometry in existing 3D scene generators for immersive applications.

Models 3D super-resolution as sequence generation over multi-resolution sparse voxel grids.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of VoxLution. We synthesize high-fidelity 3D indoor scenes as a multi-resolution autoregressive cascade, using a sparse resolution-invariant coding (ROC) for tokenization and chunked multi-resolution sequencing with cross-level and boundary neighbor conditioning. Left: Φ(0) generates the initial coarse scene structure as a single-level ROC sequence conditioned on the input scene-type label. Middle: each cascade transformer Φ(k) (k ≥ 1) consumes a sparse multi-resolution sequence with coarser-level and neighboring context, refining chunks to finer voxel resolution. Right: a sparse VAE Φm decodes the final voxel grid into dual-contouring attributes that produce the final triangle mesh.

papers.abstract: Coarse-to-fine 3D-native generation relies heavily on the first-stage sparse structure, which determines the global orientation and overall geometry for subsequent refinement. However, existing coarse generators suffer from two key limitations: their orientation is difficult to control due to ambiguous semantic canonicalization, and their structures are often inconsistent with input images due to weak 2D-3D grounding. We propose Coarse3D, a sparse-structure generation model that produces orientation-controllable and structurally faithful voxel geometry from arbitrary unposed images. Coarse3D introduces three designs: a first-frame anchored canonical space that aligns generation with the first input view while preserving object-centric normalization; a dual-tower DiT that couples generation with auxiliary feed-forward reconstruction to learn spatially grounded features; and spatial-prior guided attention that regularizes cross-attention with pixel-to-voxel correspondence. Coarse3D can directly replace the coarse stage of existing pipelines. Experiments show that it substantially improves sparse structure quality and consistently enhances final 3D generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Gaige Wang, Bowen Pan, Hao Ren, Jiangjing Lyu, Chengfei Lyu
bullets: Addresses poor orientation control and weak image-to-3D structural alignment in coarse 3D generation.
Uses a first-frame-anchored canonical space to align orientation with the input view while retaining object-centric normalization.
Combines a dual-tower DiT with auxiliary reconstruction to learn spatially grounded features.
Applies spatial-prior-guided attention using pixel-to-voxel correspondences.
Can replace existing coarse stages and consistently improves final 3D generation, with state-of-the-art performance reported.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of Coarse3D. (A) First-frame Anchoring rotates the canonical geometry to zero the first view’s azimuth, turning orientation prediction into a well-defined, first-frameconditioned task. (B) Dual-tower DiT couples an Image-Tower, supervised by auxiliary tasks (Lrecon) to encode cross-view geometry, with a Geometry-Tower predicting the velocity field (Lgeo) via layer-wise cross-attention, trained end-to-end. (C) Spatial-prior-guided Attention regularizes cross-attention with a rasterized voxel-to-pixel prior (Lattn), strengthening 2D-3D correspondence.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison across three baselines (TRELLIS, TRELLIS2, and ReconViaGen). For each baseline, we show the original result (Baseline) and the result after replacing its first stage with our Coarse3D (+ Ours). Anchored by the first frame of the multi-view input (leftmost), our method yields (i) more controllable orientations, (ii) higher structural fidelity, and (iii) seamless plug-and-play integration without modifying subsequent stages.

Figure 5: Effect of spatial-prior guided attention. For a representative voxel query, we visualize the attention map over pixel tokens of four input views. Top: spatial prior Asp derived from geometric projection. Middle: base model attention Adense, which spreads diffusely across the object. Bottom: our guided model concentrates on the pixels the query voxel actually projects to.

Figure 2: Comparison of three coordinate definitions: canonical space uses a fixed semantic orientation that is ambiguous; pixel-aligned camera space is aligned with the input view but not objectcentric; ours is aligned with the first input view and object-centric.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation is a fundamental capability for 3D spatial perception in robotic and intelligent systems. While data-driven discriminative methods have achieved compelling performance for monocular depth estimation, generative approaches can reconstruct fine structural details with stronger generalization. However, most existing generative diffusion models suffer from low inference efficiency caused by multi-step sampling, whereas single-step diffusion models struggle to recover high-fidelity depth maps. To mitigate these drawbacks, this paper presents FlowMoDE, a coarse-to-fine flow-matching-based framework for efficient, structure-aware monocular depth estimation supporting sim-to-real and cross-scene generalization. The core architecture first conducts coarse-level decoding conditioned on diffused features extracted from a pre-trained semantic encoder, and subsequently restores fine-grained structural patterns via expanded decoding layers. Trained exclusively on a single synthetic indoor dataset, our proposed method outperforms prior methods across five real-world indoor and outdoor datasets, yielding an average 14.1% reduction in relative error against state-of-the-art works as well as 9.9\% reduction in chamfer distance for point cloud reconstruction. We further validate the generalization capability of FlowMoDE on realistic robotic scenes, with qualitative comparisons against state-of-the-art methods. The project page is https://flowmode-shao.netlify.app/
authors: Liangjing Shao, Wanhao Liu, Jinsong Lin, Zhiwei Fang, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of multi-step generative depth models and the fidelity limitations of single-step alternatives.

Trained only on one synthetic indoor dataset while targeting sim-to-real and cross-scene generalization.
Outperforms prior methods across five real-world indoor and outdoor datasets, reducing relative error by 14.1% on average and point-cloud Chamfer distance by 9.9%.
Generalization is additionally assessed qualitatively on realistic robotic scenes.

papers.abstract: Single-exposure high dynamic range (HDR) novel view synthesis (NVS) recovers HDR scenes from low dynamic range (LDR) views captured at a single exposure and estimates camera response function (CRF) for LDR re-exposure. Without HDR ground-truth, using single-exposure LDR views as the sole source of direct supervision underconstrains HDR reconstruction and cannot ensure its faithful recovery, motivating the need for learned LDR-to-HDR reconstruction priors. Moreover, single-exposure LDR views supervise CRF only over a limited range, necessitating a learnable prior for reliable re-exposure beyond it. We propose PriorGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that addresses both challenges by (1) guiding HDR recovery with pseudo-HDR supervision from 2D single-exposure HDR reconstruction methods while anchoring it to input LDR views through a closed reconstruction loop; and (2) regularizing CRF modeling with a learnable prior that guarantees monotonicity and promotes plausible responses. Yet cross-view inconsistencies in independently generated pseudo-HDR targets impair scene reconstruction when HDR is encoded directly as Gaussian's color attribute. We therefore introduce a 3D base-gain HDR representation that factors HDR radiance into an LDR base and an overlaid 3D gain field, promoting robustness to such inconsistencies and enabling 3D HDR appearance editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate PriorGS's substantial superiority over baselines.
authors: Armin Shafiee Sarvestani, Sheyang Tang, Jialu Xu, Zhou Wang
bullets: Addresses underconstrained HDR recovery and limited camera response function supervision from single-exposure LDR views.
Uses pseudo-HDR reconstructions as guidance while enforcing consistency with input LDR images through a closed reconstruction loop.
Learns a monotonic CRF prior to support plausible LDR re-exposure beyond the observed intensity range.
Factors HDR radiance into an LDR base and 3D gain field, reducing the impact of inconsistent pseudo-HDR targets and enabling HDR appearance editing.
Reports substantial superiority over baselines in extensive experiments.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of PriorGS. Given single-exposure multi-view LDR captures of a scene, we reconstruct the 3D HDR scene as an LDR base extended by a 3D gain field. Input views supervise the LDR base, while pseudo-HDR targets generated by a 2D single-exposure HDR reconstruction model impose LDR-to-HDR prior on HDR recovery. We then re-expose the HDR view by a priorconstrained learnable CRF to match the same input view, which closes the reconstruction loop.

Figure 1: Given the same single-exposure inputs, methods lacking learned LDR-to-HDR priors reconstruct the LDR novel view faithfully but fail at HDR radiance recovery. We leverage this prior to recover radiance much closer to the GT. HDR results are tone-mapped identically for visualization.

Figure 12: Changes in an HDR view’s log-luminance histogram by varying ρ from 0.5 to 1.5 when ρ scales (a) 3D HDR radiance and (b) the 3D gain field. Increasing ρ for 3D HDR radiance scaling only shifts the histogram (equivalent to an exposure shift) and leaves the dynamic range (DR) unchanged. For 3D gain-field scaling, it instead changes the histogram and substantially expands the DR.

Beyond this range, MLP-based CRF curve exhibits RGB divergence, early saturation, and nonmonotonic behavior, resulting in poor rendering at test exposure that involves mapping to CRF’s unsupervised range. Our prior-constrained CRF maintains a plausible, monotonic response in this range, producing more faithful test-exposure renderings.

Figure 13: Further example of 3D HDR appearance editing via gain field scaling with ρ. We sweep ρ and show an HDR view at a low-exposure (top row) and after a fixed tone-mapping (bottom row). papers.abstract: Recent diffusion-based methods have substantially advanced image editing, yet parametric 3D control at the part level remains challenging. Existing approaches either operate on whole objects with manual rigging, or revert to 2D handles at the part level. They also struggle to model appearance and texture under large transformations, leading to unrealistic outputs in geometry-intensive edits. To address these limitations, we introduce RADI3N, a framework for semantically-grounded part-aware object manipulation with parametric 3D control. Our CS-ARAP deformation module suppresses rotation-field discontinuities at part boundaries via neighborhood covariance smoothing, producing structurally consistent deformations under complex part-level edits. We further introduce an inversion-free selective texture transfer mechanism that suppresses high-frequency positional biases and scales up low-frequency semantic cues within cross-image attention. This eliminates strict spatial bias and supports semantic matching, allowing source appearance to follow the edited part onto its new geometry. Experiments demonstrate that RADI3N achieves state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity, viewpoint consistency, and controllability.
authors: Abdul Wasi, Akhil Gorugantu, Mahesh Bhosale, Anjan Dutta, Junsong Yuan, Sauradip Nag, David Doermann
bullets: Addresses limitations of whole-object rigging and 2D part-level handles in geometry-intensive image editing.
Uses CS-ARAP deformation with neighborhood covariance smoothing to reduce rotation discontinuities at part boundaries.
Introduces inversion-free selective texture transfer to move source appearance onto edited geometry through semantic matching.
Experiments report state-of-the-art geometric fidelity, viewpoint consistency, and controllability.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the geometric editing pipeline. Intermediate renderings and source views condition the diffusion model via IP-Adapter for identity preservation. Stage 2 (Global 3D Refinement): The Stage 1 Jacobian field is refined using Lrefine, combining handle constraints with SDS gradients from the diffusion model, producing a semantically plausible mesh for final rendering.

papers.abstract: Egocentric videos offer an abundant source of hand-scene interactions for embodied learning, which requires recovering hands, camera, and scene consistently in a shared 3D world. Existing methods focus on either camera-frame hands or world-space hand trajectories, without jointly recovering the scene pointmaps or interaction information. Building a complete reconstruction from such specialized predictions therefore typically requires per-sequence optimization. We propose EgoHSI3R, a unified feed-forward framework for online 4D hand-scene interaction reconstruction from egocentric monocular video. To jointly recover these components, it maintains a recurrent scene representation that accumulates geometric evidence over time and provides a shared world space and scale. We introduce hand-centric prompts that fuse pretrained hand priors and local scene context, while MANO vertex queries attend to scene features to predict dense per-vertex contact. These designs enable a single network to jointly estimate camera motion, dense scene geometry, world-space bilateral MANO hands, and per-vertex hand contact. Despite operating causally, EgoHSI3R achieves the lowest world-space hand joint error on ARCTIC among the evaluated methods, while offering faster inference than existing world-space hand reconstruction pipelines and competitive camera and scene reconstruction accuracy.
authors: Mingzhi Pei, Zhangchen Ye, Ruoqu Chen, Liu Cao, Mengdi Xu
bullets: Addresses the lack of unified hand, camera, scene, and interaction reconstruction in existing methods.
Maintains a recurrent scene representation to accumulate geometry and establish shared world space and scale.
Uses hand-centric prompts combining pretrained hand priors with local scene context.
Predicts dense per-vertex contact through MANO vertex queries attending to scene features.
Reports the lowest evaluated world-space hand joint error on ARCTIC, with faster inference and competitive camera/scene accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of camera-space hand reconstruction. The predicted hand meshes are overlaid on the input egocentric frames. Our method produces accurate articulated hand poses and consistent alignment with the observed images.

Figure 3: Overview of EgoHSI3R. Each incoming egocentric frame is encoded by the scene encoder Es into image tokens, and each detected hand is processed by the pretrained hand encoder Eh. The Hand Prompt Builder fuses the hand prior with local scene context obtained via RoIAlign, producing scene-conditioned hand prompts. The decoder jointly processes scene tokens and hand prompts while reading from and updating a persistent scene state. The Scene Head predicts camera pose and world-space pointmaps, and the MANO Head reconstructs bilateral MANO parameters. The interaction-aware Contact Builder combines decoded hand tokens with local scene features, which are then used by the Contact Head to predict per-vertex contact and refine hand reconstruction. All outputs are produced online in a shared world space without test-time optimization.

Figure 2: Comparison of egocentric hand reconstruction paradigms. (a) Camera-centric methods recover articulated hands in the camera frame, without camera motion and reliable 3D placement. (b) World-space methods additionally estimate camera motion to recover hand trajectories in world space, but do not reconstruct the scene. (c) EgoHSI3R jointly recovers bilateral hands, camera pose, scene geometry, and dense hand contact in a shared world frame within a single online, feed-forward model.

papers.abstract: Chest computed tomography (CT) reports generated by large language models (LLMs) can describe positive findings that lack localized evidence in the scan. We propose EviGround-CT to verify these findings after report generation. A deterministic extractor identifies positive finding sentences, and a 3D grounding model predicts an evidence mask for each sentence. Using the full sentence retains anatomical location, laterality, and descriptive modifiers in the grounding query. We evaluate report generation on CT-RATE, and grounding and verification on a held-out 100-case ReXGroundingCT subset. Using the available annotations, sentence-grounded verification raises evidence-supported precision (ESP) from 0.263 to 0.365 across 137 extracted in-scope positives, compared with category conditioning. The corresponding unsupported positive finding rate falls from 0.737 to 0.635. The paired case-level bootstrap ESP difference is +0.102 (95% confidence interval: [0.028, 0.181]). The predicted masks associate individual report statements with spatial evidence that can be inspected alongside the CT.
bullets: Targets positive report findings that may lack localized support in the CT scan.
Extracts positive finding sentences deterministically and uses each full sentence as the grounding query.
A 3D grounding model predicts an inspectable evidence mask for every statement.
On annotated cases, evidence-supported precision increased from 0.263 to 0.365, while unsupported positives decreased from 0.737 to 0.635.
Evaluated on CT-RATE and a held-out 100-case ReXGroundingCT subset; scope is limited to available annotations and in-scope positives.

papers.abstract: Latent generative models make 3D medical image synthesis computationally practical by generating in a compressed space. However, we show that the common flat Euclidean assumption induced by $\ell_2$ objectives is imprecise: latent-space geometry is so strongly anisotropic that equal-magnitude errors can produce drastically different decoded distortions. We further find that this anisotropy has a clear feature: sensitive variation concentrates in a low-rank subspace. The dominant low-rank components capture the overall structure, encoding long-range, spatially coordinated variation while remaining resistant to local noise. Its orthogonal residual, in contrast, mainly captures local and image-specific variation. Motivated by this asymmetry, we introduce Latent Structure Flow (LSF). At each block, LSF decomposes the latent state into structure and residual, models structural changes with global context, and predicts residual variation locally while preserving a direct path for the input structure. LSF changes only the generator, leaving the frozen codec and pointwise training objective unchanged. Across cross-modality synthesis and tumor inpainting tasks, LSF outperforms all compared baselines on both global and tumor-specific metrics, demonstrating the benefit of explicitly modeling latent-space structure for 3D medical image synthesis.
bullets: The common flat Euclidean assumption for latent spaces can misrepresent decoded image distortions because sensitivity is direction-dependent.
Sensitive variation concentrates in a low-rank subspace capturing coordinated, long-range structure; the orthogonal residual captures local, image-specific details.
Latent Structure Flow (LSF) decomposes latent states into structure and residual, modeling them with global and local context respectively.
LSF modifies only the generator while keeping the codec frozen and the pointwise training objective unchanged.
Across cross-modality synthesis and tumor inpainting, LSF outperforms the compared baselines on global and tumor-specific metrics.

papers.abstract: Large-scale point cloud representations of complex geome tries incur prohibitive computational and memory costs, necessitating compressed implicit representations. To ad dress this, we propose a unified framework comprising im plicit geometric field representation, hierarchical frequency domain compression, and conditional high-frequency predic tion. Specifically, an unordered point cloud is mapped to an implicit field defined within its physical bounding box. A smooth Fourier pyramid is then constructed, where com pact low-frequency components capture the global geometry. Inter-scale high-frequency residuals are encoded to preserve the spatial information required for reconstructing fine geo metric details. To restore the high-frequency information lost during compression, we develop a hierarchical 3D neural net work. The reconstructed implicit field is converted back into a point cloud through isosurface extraction. Experiments on a complex-boundary point cloud with more than eight mil lion points demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a higher compression ratio than existing point cloud compres sion methods while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality.
bullets: Maps unordered point clouds to implicit fields within their physical bounding boxes.
Uses a smooth Fourier pyramid to retain global geometry in low frequencies and encode fine details as inter-scale high-frequency residuals.
Employs a hierarchical 3D neural network to predict missing high-frequency information after compression.
Reconstructs point clouds from the recovered implicit field through isosurface extraction.
On a point cloud exceeding eight million points, achieves a higher compression ratio than existing methods with comparable reconstruction quality.

papers.abstract: Reconstruct where the images provide evidence, and generate where they do not: recent success of spatial world models such as Atlas (World Labs Team, 2026) highlights the value of unifying reconstruction and generation in one model. Yet the two have long lived in separate paradigms with distinctive failure modes: feed-forward reconstruction averages ambiguity into blur, while conditional generation invents plausible but scene-inconsistent detail. In this work, we present a unified flow-based formulation for reconstruction and generation, where a shared clean-target predictor performs direct reconstruction at its single-step endpoint and unfolds conditional generation through multi-step flow. A controlled toy study reveals the mechanism: with a single step, the predictor collapses to the conditional mean just like feed-forward methods, favoring consistency over diversity. With multi-step inference, the fidelity of generated details grows with context richness: closer observations reduce ambiguity and yield better-matched details. We further instantiate the formulation in appearance and geometry 3D tasks. JiT-LVSM improves perceptual and distributional quality in novel view synthesis, while JUSt3R retains competitive single-step geometry prediction with additional multi-step inference capabilities that reduces veil and flying-pixel artifacts, producing cleaner surface structure with greater test-time compute. Together, they show that reconstruction and generation can share both a formulation and a backbone, with their behavior governed by denoising configuration---making unification surprisingly simple.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between blurry feed-forward reconstruction and scene-inconsistent conditional generation.
Uses a shared clean-target predictor: direct reconstruction at one step, conditional generation through multi-step flow.
A toy study shows single-step inference approaches the conditional mean, while richer context improves multi-step detail fidelity.
Applied to 3D appearance and geometry tasks, the approach improves novel-view quality and reduces veil and flying-pixel artifacts.
The formulation shares both backbone and behavior across tasks, with the denoising configuration controlling the reconstruction–generation trade-off.

papers.title: From Feed-Forward to Flow: Unifying Reconstruction and Generation Is Easier Than You Think

papers.abstract: We study domain generalization for LIDAR semantic segmentation. Deep neural networks achieve strong performance on 3D point clouds, yet real-world LIDAR exhibits sensor-specific sampling patterns that hinder transfer across datasets. In many applications, performance on completely unseen sensors is crucial. A model should preferably work on a new setup without prior access to its data or labels. To this end, we introduce a source-only training scheme that adds an occupancy prediction auxiliary objective. We aggregate source-domain scans into a simple world model and use it as the supervision signal, replacing single-scan standard segmentation training. A key property of our approach is that it does not alter the input scan. During training and testing the network consumes the same single-frame LIDAR input, only the supervision signal is enriched via the occupancy objective. At deployment, there is no runtime overhead as the auxiliary head can be dropped for pure segmentation, or kept to obtain scene completion alongside semantic segmentation. In an experimental evaluation across distinct LIDAR datasets, we demonstrate that a model's generalization to new domains can be significantly affected by how it is supervised. In certain setups, performance on unseen domains improves without any explicit domain adaptation (no target scans, no target labels, no sensor priors) and without prediction refinement. At the same time, our method maintains competitive source-domain segmentation performance and incurs no additional inference cost.
bullets: Targets sensor-specific sampling differences that hinder cross-dataset LiDAR segmentation.
Aggregates source scans into a world model and uses occupancy prediction as an auxiliary training objective.
The network still processes a single-frame scan; only the supervision is enriched.
Unseen-domain performance improves in some settings without domain adaptation, target scans, labels, sensor priors, or prediction refinement.
Source-domain performance remains competitive, with no runtime overhead; the auxiliary head can optionally provide scene completion.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Proposed method: We add an occupancy prediction task based on accumulated LiDAR points while training on the source domain to improve model generalization (orange blocks). papers.abstract: Reconstructing editable and compositional 3D scenes from a real image requires jointly reasoning about geometry, object structure, and spatial relationships. We introduce SceneEvolve, a framework that represents 3D scenes as executable code and improves reconstruction by evolving the harness around a small open-source agent. SceneEvolve combines SceneAct, a compositional semantic action interface built on parameterized primitives, hierarchical composition, and semantic spatial relations, with SceneHarness-RSI, which leverages a stronger teacher agent to iteratively evolve the harness using feedback from development-set reconstructions. Throughout harness evolution, the model parameters, action semantics, and execution backend remain fixed. The resulting harness provides a reusable reconstruction procedure that enables the small open-source model to reconstruct unseen scenes without parameter updates or teacher assistance. Across two in-domain datasets and one out-of-domain dataset, SceneEvolve with the comparatively compact Qwen3.8-27B model improves all four evaluated reconstruction metrics while reducing mean inference time by 47.0% relative to the base model. More notably, despite relying on a substantially smaller model, SceneEvolve achieves 32.3% higher reconstruction quality than the large proprietary GPT-5.6-Sol model, while reducing mean equivalent deployment cost by 59.8%. Furthermore, the harness evolved using Qwen3.8-27B also generalizes to Kimi-K3, achieving comparable reconstruction performance to GPT-6-Astra. The project page is https://haoyu-agent.github.io/SceneEvolve.
bullets: Represents scenes as executable code and uses compositional actions, parameterized primitives, hierarchical structure, and semantic spatial relations.
A stronger teacher iteratively evolves the reconstruction harness from development-set feedback while keeping model parameters, action semantics, and execution fixed.
The resulting procedure enables small models to reconstruct unseen scenes without further parameter updates or teacher assistance.
Across three datasets, the approach improved all four evaluated metrics and reduced mean inference time by 47.0% versus the base model.
It reportedly outperformed larger proprietary models in reconstruction quality and deployment cost, and transferred effectively to another model family.

papers.abstract: Uneven rotation and dropped frames make equal-angle assumptions unreliable for turntable reconstruction. We present OC-GS, an object-centric Gaussian splatting that refines each image's angle while maintaining a shared camera, rotation axis, and pivot. This orbit-consistent refinement jointly optimizes image-derived geometry and angles to reconstruct objects from sparse, irregular captures. On rendered objects with 12, 8, and 6 irregularly spaced views, OC-GS achieves mean foreground PSNR scores of 21.26, 19.36, and 15.83dB, respectively, exceeding all four evaluated pose-free Gaussian splatting baselines in each condition. Under a shared trainer, refining image-estimated angles improves mean foreground PSNR by 7.88dB over keeping those estimates fixed. An ablation study shows that both image-derived angle initialization and the shared motion model contribute to the improvement. On real captures, OC-GS's refinement increases mean foreground PSNR by 0.70dB. Results show that refining uncertain angles within a shared motion model improves reconstruction from sparse, irregular turntable captures.
bullets: Addresses uneven rotation and dropped frames that invalidate equal-angle assumptions.
Jointly optimizes image-derived angles and object geometry while sharing the camera, rotation axis, and pivot.
On rendered 12-, 8-, and 6-view captures, it achieves mean foreground PSNRs of 21.26, 19.36, and 15.83 dB, outperforming four evaluated pose-free baselines.
Angle refinement improves mean foreground PSNR by 7.88 dB over fixed image-estimated angles in a shared trainer; real captures improve by 0.70 dB.
Scope: evaluated on sparse, irregular turntable captures, with ablations confirming the value of angle initialization and the shared motion model.

papers.abstract: We present ClearGS for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) from handheld videos with uneven viewpoint coverage and mixed frame quality. Rather than selecting frames with binary decisions, ClearGS uses Reliability-aware View Allocation (RVA) to assign graded raw-supervision weights based on appearance reliability, degradation risk, and geometric utility, while weakly reactivating useful suppressed frames to maintain trajectory coverage. Since weighting cannot restore details lost to blur or distortion, ClearGS further introduces Render-Guided In-Video Restoration (RIVR). The current 3DGS render provides a pose-aligned structural candidate, a frozen no-reference restoration expert restores the corresponding raw video observation without any clean reference image, and no-reference perceptual scores select among the render, restored observation, and high-frequency fused candidate. ClearGS then applies Full-Trajectory Repair Consolidation to revisit accepted repairs and preserve details introduced early. On GS2E and GSOTM, ClearGS achieves state-of-the-art overall performance, with consistent CLIP-IQA and MUSIQ gains and LPIPS reductions in most degradation settings, without paired sharp supervision or matched clean references.
bullets: Addresses mixed frame quality, uneven viewpoint coverage, blur, and distortion in handheld-video 3DGS.
Uses Reliability-aware View Allocation to assign graded supervision weights and weakly reactivate useful suppressed frames.
Introduces Render-Guided In-Video Restoration, selecting among rendered, restored, and fused candidates with no-reference perceptual scores.
Applies Full-Trajectory Repair Consolidation to revisit repairs and preserve details added early.
Reports state-of-the-art overall performance on GS2E and GSOTM, with consistent gains in CLIP-IQA and MUSIQ and lower LPIPS in most degradation settings.

RIVR selects among the current render, restored raw observation, and detail-fused candidate using no-reference quality scores, then distills accepted pseudo observations with real observations.
